Yaron Zelekha slams Netanyahu's economic policy, vows to cut cost of living
Unknown

Prof. Yaron Zelekha, chairman of the Reservists-Economic Party, promised to rapidly reduce Israel's cost of living while criticizing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Thursday at a press conference in Modi'in, where he presented his party's economic plan.
“The reason Bibi attacks me is that he knows that once I become finance minister, the public will realize that life here could have been cheaper over the past twenty years,” Zelekha said.
He added, “Bibi sold the economy to monopolies and extortionists, and I will take it back. The choice isn't 'Bibi or not Bibi'; it is between the alliance of capital and power and your children."
Zelekha also challenged Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and former prime minister Naftali Bennett to a debate on economic policy, arguing that "politicians beholden to tycoons who finance their election campaigns would be unable to tackle the cost of living."
Zelekha plans for economic reforms as finance minister
In an interview with The Jerusalem Post on Tuesday, Zelekha warned that he would be willing to take down any government that prevented him from implementing his economic reforms.
“If anyone gets in my way, I will bring down their government,” he told the Post, adding that he would demand control of the Finance Ministry and the Competition Authority during coalition negotiations.
Zelekha said he would insist on having the authority to implement his economic program regardless of whether Netanyahu, Bennett, or Gadi Eisenkot becomes prime minister, and would be prepared to bring down the government if his efforts were obstructed.
“Within three months from the day I take my seat, you will not recognize the country,” Zelekha said, outlining a five-point plan aimed at reducing living costs by increasing competition and removing barriers to imports.
His proposed measures include abolishing all tariffs, eliminating import quotas, and preventing domestic manufacturers that hold monopolistic positions from also serving as importers.
He also promised to prohibit exclusive import agreements and prevent importers representing one major international manufacturer from securing control over imports from another manufacturer that would otherwise compete with it.
Zelekha further told the Post he would transfer the Competition Authority to the Finance Ministry, placing it under his supervision so that he could oversee enforcement of competition law.

Cuba expands renewable energy use amid U.S. fuel blockade: FM
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:11:32 CST
08:11:32 KST

HAVANA, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez said Thursday that renewable energy now accounts for more than one-fifth of the country's electricity generation as it seeks to reduce the impact of U.S. fuel restrictions.
In a post on X, Rodriguez said the Cuban government and Communist Party were responding to the U.S. energy blockade, which "aims to punish all Cubans," with "greater sovereignty and measures" to ease the impact of U.S. sanctions.
Cuba now has 144 solar parks with a combined installed capacity of 1,418 megawatts, while renewable sources account for 21.4 percent of national electricity generation, he said.
The country also has 44 solar-powered electric vehicle charging stations and 64 public charging stations, he said, adding that all polyclinics, nursing homes, maternity homes and funeral homes have been equipped with renewable energy facilities.
In January, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order imposing sanctions and tariffs on countries and entities supplying fuel to Cuba, a move Havana has condemned as an "energy blockade."
Over the past nine months, Cuba has received only one shipment of crude oil from Russia, totaling about 100,000 tonnes, only enough to meet the country's demand for two weeks.
Cuba is scheduled to submit a resolution to the UN General Assembly on Oct. 29 for the 34th time, calling for an end to the U.S. economic, commercial and financial blockade imposed on the island for more than six decades.
According to Cuban government figures, the blockade has caused nearly 179 billion U.S. dollars in economic losses. ■

Order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
23:11:10 UTC
08:11:10 KST

Order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House, sources say
NEW YORK/WASHINGTON, Oct 15 - The order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter.
The officials said leaders at the Defense Department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed.
The officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, did not specify who in the White House made the decision or who was responsible for implementing the order. The Pentagon is the biggest customer of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service.
Ukrainian officials said this week that military-grade Starlink receptors stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance systems over Ukrainian territory.
A person in Ukraine's Defence Ministry said on Thursday that the receptors were now working when in motion, but only at speeds of up to 100 miles per hour (160 kph).
US PRESSURES UKRAINE OVER REFINERY ATTACKS
The move to temporarily restrict the vital communications system came as President Donald Trump has pressured Kyiv to stop its attacks on Russian refineries, which he has blamed for the soaring energy prices that are denting his Republican Party's prospects in the November midterm elections.
But experts say that surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the US-Israeli war with Iran, which brought Iranian attacks on energy facilities and has largely shut the vital Strait of Hormuz.
In response to a request for comment about the order to limit Starshield, a senior US official said: "No such request was ever made by the president."
The White House did not respond to questions about whether other administration officials might have made the request.
Starshield was developed by SpaceX specifically for government and national-security customers, particularly the US Department of Defense. Starshield uses the Starlink constellation as its backbone.
Ukrainian officials said the restrictions complicated strike missions against Russian forces and logistics in occupied territory and slowed interceptor drones used to shoot down incoming Russian Shahed drones.
Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, said on X on Wednesday that because Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government, any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military or the president.
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.
The Department of Defense and the Ukrainian embassy in Washington also did not respond to requests for comment.
DECLINE IN RELATIONS
Relations between Kyiv and Washington have deteriorated in recent days following a meeting in Miami on October 9 that convened representatives from both countries as well as Europe and the World Bank.
Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, the Trump administration’s Middle East envoy, struck a tough tone with Ukraine in the meeting, according to a separate person familiar with the matter. They told Ukrainian officials that the US was frustrated with Kyiv's continued strikes on Russian refineries despite repeated requests from Washington to stop.
The US delegation also explained Washington's decision to strike a diesel deal with Russia, saying the White House hoped it would soften Moscow's stance on peace talks.
That deal, under which Russia will supply more than 2.25 million barrels of diesel to US and global markets, has triggered a backlash from some US lawmakers, who say it will give Moscow cash to pursue its war without forcing Russian President Vladimir Putin to make concessions to end the conflict.
In the days that followed, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and Trump criticized each other, with Zelenskiy calling the US decision on the Russian diesel deal "weak." Trump called for elections in Ukraine and Zelenskiy's ouster.
Behind the scenes, American officials threatened to stop providing intelligence to Kyiv about Russian missile launches that Ukraine uses to thwart attacks, as Reuters previously reported. Trump said on Tuesday Washington was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
Following the move to restrict Ukraine's access to Starshield, the Ukrainians made calls on Tuesday and Wednesday to find answers from senior officials at the White House, State Department and Pentagon, a senior Ukrainian official said, adding that Kyiv was told it was a White House decision.
The Pentagon has spent billions of dollars on the Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024. REUTERS

Roundup: 5 killed in presidential palace attack in Yemen's Aden as Houthis claim Saudi officers killed
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:11:09 CST
08:11:09 KST

RIYADH/ADEN, Yemen, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Five people were killed and 16 others wounded in an attack launched by the Houthi group on the presidential palace compound in the southern Yemeni port city of Aden, Yemen's government said Thursday, as Houthis claimed Saudi military officers were killed or wounded in the attack.
Minister of Public Health and Population Qassem Buhaibeh said in a statement that those killed and wounded included security guards and civilian employees working at the Al-Ma'ashiq Presidential Palace compound, the temporary seat of the internationally recognized Yemeni government.
Earlier on Thursday, a local security official told Xinhua that five missiles struck the presidential palace compound, while another attack targeted the headquarters of the Saudi-led coalition forces in Aden's Al Buraiqa district.
Loud explosions rocked Aden during the strikes, with smoke rising from the vicinity of the presidential palace, according to a Xinhua reporter on the ground.
Local sources told Xinhua that "high-level meetings" had recently been held at the compound to prepare Saudi-backed government forces for fighting the Houthis.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said the group targeted the "Saudi military operations headquarters" in Aden, without specifying its exact location.
Houthi-run al-Masirah TV, citing a Houthi military leader, later said Saudi military officers were killed or wounded in an attack targeting a "military operations headquarters run by Saudi officers" inside the presidential palace compound in Aden.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia or the Saudi-led coalition on the claim.
The attack marked a further escalation in the confrontation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, with the two sides trading intensified strikes in recent days.
The Saudi-led coalition said Thursday that Houthi attacks on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh have killed 17 people and injured more than 330 others since Oct. 1, with the airport coming under 20 attacks during the two-week period.
Meanwhile, the Houthis said Saudi warplanes conducted 65 air and missile strikes on Houthi-held areas in Yemen during the past 24 hours.
The UN Security Council on Thursday strongly condemned escalating Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, including attacks affecting civilian aviation and energy infrastructure.
Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly told reporters Thursday that the Houthis rejected Riyadh's call for a meeting in Oman "to resolve outstanding differences" at the beginning of this escalation in July, media reports said.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, forcing the government out of the capital. ■

U.S. stocks recover as sliding Treasury yields offset hot inflation data
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:10:38 CST
08:10:38 KST

NEW YORK, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- U.S. stocks recovered on Thursday as falling Treasury yields provided relief to equity markets, helping technology and semiconductor shares stabilize amid debt-financing worries.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 556.21 points, or 1.08 percent, to 52,177.69. The S&P 500 added 25.12 points, or 0.33 percent, to 7,744.06. The Nasdaq Composite Index increased by 20.16 points, or 0.08 percent, to 26,713.03.
Eight of the 11 primary S&P 500 sectors ended in the green, with health and materials leading the gainers by going up 1.84 percent and 1.71 percent, respectively. Meanwhile, energy and technology led the laggards by losing 1.55 percent and 0.54 percent, respectively.
Market sentiment found footing as benchmark borrowing costs retreated, allowing heavily pressured tech equities to pare steep losses.
In the AI infrastructure sector, cloud compute provider CoreWeave gained nearly 6 percent, reversing a portion of Wednesday's more than 15 percent drop triggered by concerns over excessive debt accumulation to finance its hardware expansion. Memory manufacturer Micron Technology also recovered most of its intraday decline, closing 1.87 percent higher.
Concerns across the AI ecosystem were compounded by a CNBC report that Anthropic's quarterly revenue reached 16.8 billion U.S. dollars in the third quarter. While representing massive growth, the pace raised questions among some market participants about whether revenue expansion remains swift enough to sustain lofty valuations across underlying chipmakers.
Despite the broader equity recovery, inflation pressures remained pronounced. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Thursday that the producer price index (PPI) for final demand jumped 1.3 percent in September, lifting the annualized wholesale rate to 6.3 percent, its fastest pace since 2022.
The sharp acceleration followed Wednesday's hotter-than-expected consumer price index (CPI) reading, further complicating the Federal Reserve's policy trajectory as officials weigh persistent price spikes ahead of their upcoming interest rate decision.
"Today's PPI report, after Wednesday's CPI, confirms inflation is getting worse as energy prices stay high," said David Russell, global head of market strategy at TradeStation. "Election or no election, prices are rising and the Fed might be forced to act."
According to CME FedWatch, traders now see a 29 percent likelihood the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its meeting in two weeks, and an 88 percent likelihood the central bank will lift rates at least a quarter-percentage point at its December meeting.
Broader market gains were underpinned by defensive and consumer-oriented sectors outside of technology. Walmart advanced 1.47 percent, after Deutsche Bank upgraded the stock to "buy" from "hold," citing a positive outlook for 2027. The bank expects incremental margins to improve and noted current inflation levels could help the company attract consumers.
Nike jumped more than 5 percent, leading consumer discretionary gainers. Apple, which on Wednesday joined Nvidia as the only companies ever to close with a market capitalization above 5 trillion dollars, ended 0.28 percent lower. ■

Zelensky rallies European allies as US support for Ukraine wanes
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky sought European backing Thursday after vowing to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries despite US President Donald Trump’s demands, as tensions with Washington escalated over sanctions, energy infrastructure attacks and restrictions on satellite communications.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky sought Thursday to rally European allies after saying Kyiv would no longer abide by US President Donald Trump's demands not to strike Russian oil refineries.
Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since last week, when Trump eased sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow releasing large amounts of diesel onto global markets.
Anger in Ukraine has been further heightened by outages to a critical US-provided satellite system that has hampered its military's ability to counter Russia's intense bombardments.
Against the backdrop of his latest falling-out with Trump, Zelensky met NATO chief Mark Rutte in Brussels and held a string of bilateral meetings with European leaders before he was set to join an EU summit on Friday.
"All of us in Europe want this war to end. And for that to happen, strong signals are needed – more real pressure on Russia and more defence support for Ukraine," Zelensky wrote online.
"It is especially important now to act together to protect lives."
Read moreWill Trump really pull the plug? Starlink restored but Ukraine's fate still uncertain
European leaders have broadly thrown their support behind Zelensky, as they look to weather the latest storm in Trump's volatile relations with Kyiv.
French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday said it was "crucial" that Ukraine receive "all the means necessary to protect itself" after meeting Zelensky.
"I can reassure you, dear Ukrainian friends and President Zelensky: YOU ARE NOT ALONE," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk posted online.
'Maximum destruction'
Zelensky has had to endure a rollercoaster relationship with Trump since the mercurial US leader returned to office last year.
In a move that risked infuriating Trump further, Zelensky told the Financial Times that Ukraine would no longer hold off targeting Russian refineries as Moscow was not abiding by a ceasefire on hitting energy infrastructure announced by the US leader.
As he met with Macron in Brussels, Zelensky said that the Kremlin had "launched yet another vile drone strike on Ukrainian energy infrastructure" in the city of Lutsk, causing blackouts.
"Russia has demonstratively disregarded the American president's proposal for an energy ceasefire. And now it is taking advantage of problems with Starlink operations to cause maximum destruction to everything that sustains everyday life," he wrote online.

The Kremlin meanwhile accused Ukraine of derailing US peace efforts by resuming its strikes on refineries, with Russian authorities reporting a drone attack on an oil refinery south of Moscow that caused a fire.
Kyiv "continues to launch strikes against these facilities," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
"It is coming into serious conflict with the peace efforts of the United States and American negotiators, who are making vigorous efforts to initiate the peace process," he added.

"Let them live here for two to three days. All these nighttime attacks, what people here are going through – blackouts, no electricity. And then maybe he'll see all this differently," 30-year-old Alyona Nikitina said.

Satellite row
Much of the outrage in Ukraine this week has been over restrictions to the Starshield satellite communications system that its military relies upon to detect incoming Russian attacks and to coordinate its frontline response.
Defence officials confirmed that the United States had threatened to withdraw intelligence-sharing if Ukraine continued long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries.
But tech billionaire Elon Musk, who has also called for Zelensky to be replaced as leader, said his SpaceX company was not behind any disruption to the Starshield system.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," he said.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he added, referring to Trump.

Meta unveils new ‘open’ AI model to rival Chinese competition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

Meta unveils new ‘open’ AI model to rival Chinese competition
- Meta launched Muse Spark Open, an open-weight AI model it says rivals leading Chinese systems and is its most capable US open-weight model to date.
- The model is built for coding and agentic work, with strong safeguards, and it can run on Apple’s M5 Ultra chips, showing a rare Meta-Apple link.
- The launch follows Meta’s new closed models Wonder and Wonder Full, as Zuckerberg shifts the firm to compete more directly with OpenAI and Anthropic.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – Meta on Oct 15 launched a new open-weight AI model which it claims rivals, and in some cases outperforms, similar products from leading Chinese developers.
Muse Spark Open “is the most capable US open-weight model to date”, Meta’s chief of AI Alexandr Wang wrote on X.
Unlike with so-called closed models – such as Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s ChatGPT – developers can download the parameters, or weights, of an open-weight model and then customise it.
Chinese developers have emerged as dominant players in the open-weight market for AI models over the past couple of years.
Alibaba’s Qwen, Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and Z.ai’s GLM models have been considered open-weight frontrunners globally, but Meta claims its new open model now competes on a similar level.
“Built for coding and agentic work”, Muse Spark Open “excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning”, Meta said in a blogpost, adding that “strong safeguards” have been integrated into the new model.
Muse Spark Open is also “optimised” to run on Apple’s advanced M5 Ultra chips, Meta said, signalling an unusual partnership between the two tech giants.
Meta boss Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X that the new model “runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work” with Apple and its new chief executive John Ternus.
Ternus, who took over as Apple’s chief from Tim Cook in September, responded that it is “amazing to run a model of Muse Spark Open’s calibre and scale this efficiently, right from your desk. Mac Studio keeps pushing the boundaries of on-device AI!”
Muse Spark Open still requires significant computing power, though.
Users can run the model on two Mac Studios with M5 Ultra chips to create a “supercomputer” on their own desktop, Meta said.
The launch comes just days after Meta announced its newest closed model.
On Oct 12, the company unveiled two new “frontier” models called Wonder and Wonder Full, which the company claimed rival the most advanced versions of ChatGPT and Claude.
Meta’s AI efforts were initially focused on open models, but more recently Zuckerberg has pushed the company to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic.
Meta launched its Spark model in April, marking a departure from its open-source model known as Llama, which lagged behind the rest of the industry. AFP

‘Our situation resembles the Holocaust’: Haredi candidate on draft-related travel bans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
22:56:05 UTC
07:56:05 KST

Elikim Stark, a new candidate for Israel's ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism party, drew condemnation Thursday after comparing travel restrictions imposed on Haredi men who have failed to report for military service to the situation of Jews during the Holocaust.
Speaking at an election rally in Beit Shemesh, Stark, who represents the Belz Hasidic community, said ultra-Orthodox men barred from leaving Israel because of outstanding military draft orders were struggling to arrange marriages with women from families living abroad. He said the restrictions forced prospective brides' families to travel to Israel instead.
"When people want to arrange a marriage with someone abroad, they have to come here because we cannot leave," Stark said. "I had committed myself not to talk about Holocaust stories in my early years, but I have no other way to describe it. Our situation is close to what it was during the Holocaust. It reminds me of the stories our grandparents told us."
Stark also sharply criticized Deputy Supreme Court President Noam Sohlberg, accusing him of encouraging hostility toward the ultra-Orthodox community.
"A new phenomenon has emerged, Sohlbergism, which says, 'Hit the Haredim and you'll be more of a man,'" Stark said. "In Israel, it's better to be a terrorist and kill entire families than to be Haredi."
Deputy Minister Yisrael Eichler, who attended the gathering, made another sweeping claim about the political rights of ultra-Orthodox Israelis. "I believe this is the last time they will allow Haredim to vote in elections," he said.
Stark, 34, is the new representative of the Belz Hasidic movement on the United Torah Judaism election slate, replacing Eichler, a veteran lawmaker. Although well known in political circles and among senior ultra-Orthodox religious leaders, Stark has spent much of his career operating behind the scenes, largely avoiding publicity, interviews and even photographs of his meetings.
Born in Belgium, he was raised and educated in Belz institutions in both Belgium and Israel. After marrying, he was appointed to lead a group of students who had arrived from the United States to study at the Mir Yeshiva in Jerusalem, where he taught and mentored students.
Several years ago, he was recruited into public affairs by the Belz rebbe, the movement's spiritual leader, and his son, Rabbi Aharon Mordechai Rokeach. Working alongside veteran community figures, Stark helped establish a committee responsible for advancing Belz's political and public interests.
He subsequently worked closely with Eichler, whom he is replacing on the party list, and was repeatedly entrusted with political and communal assignments on behalf of the rebbe's household.
Stark's remarks drew sharp criticism from political rivals ahead of Israel's October 27 election.
Yisrael Beytenu party leader Avigdor Lieberman denounced the comments, saying: "Appalling! A representative of United Torah Judaism, without whom Bibi has no government, explains that in Israel 'it's better to be a terrorist'! And if that weren't enough, he compared the situation of draft dodgers to that of Jews during the Holocaust. On October 27, we decide: It's either us or the draft dodgers!"
Ofer Winter, chairman of the Amcha Yisrael party, also condemned the remarks.
"The shocking statement by prospective Knesset member Elikim Stark is a disgrace to every Israeli and every Jew, all the more so for someone who may soon find himself serving in Israel's parliament," Winter said.
He argued that the comments did not emerge in isolation, accusing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and senior government officials of remaining silent in the face of anti-military rhetoric at demonstrations organized by the Jerusalem Faction, a hard-line ultra-Orthodox movement opposed to military conscription.
"This is further proof that Goldknopf must not become the 61st vote in the next coalition," Winter said, referring to United Torah Judaism politician Yitzhak Goldknopf and the minimum parliamentary majority needed to form a government.
"We call on the Haredi public, whom we cherish and respect, to reject these statements. We call on the prime minister and his ministers to condemn them immediately and unequivocally. Enough with the silence!"

At least 4, including 3 children, killed in US elementary school shooting
Authorities have indicated that the shooter was killed by gunfire, though details remain scant about the attack.
At least four people have been killed, including three children, in a shooting at an elementary school in Oregon, part of the northwestern United States, according to statements from law enforcement to CBS and CNN.
The shooting on Thursday took place at Silver Rail Elementary school in the city of Bend, about 160km (100 miles) southeast of Portland.
Authorities have said the shooter is dead, though it is unclear whether he is among the four people included in the initial death toll.
“We’re in the process at this time of going room by room and evacuating each of the people who are in that school,” said Sheila Miller, the communications manager for the Bend Police Department on Thursday. “This is the kind of thing we never want to see happen in Bend. It’s devastating.”
Miller said authorities received a call about a shot fired into a car outside the school at 12:59pm local time (19:59 GMT) and arrived on scene within minutes.
The suspect was shot and killed shortly after, though Miller said she did not know whether police or a bystander had subdued the alleged assailant.
The number and condition of those injured were not immediately known.
Kash Patel, the director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), said in a post on social media that the agency was on the scene assisting local law enforcement in the investigation.
“We will make every resource they need available,” he wrote.
Oregon Governor Tina Kotek also said she was closely monitoring the situation.
Jeff Merkley, who represents Oregon in the US Senate, was among the political leaders to offer condolences in the wake of the shooting.
“My heart is with the Bend community and all of the students and families affected. No one should have to fear violence at school,” he wrote in a post on the social media platform X.

Rotting meat smell sparks protest at Mexico's screwworm sterile-fly plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
22:41:09 UTC
07:41:09 KST

Rotting meat smell sparks protest at Mexico's screwworm sterile-fly plant
METAPA DE DOMINGUEZ, Mexico, Oct 15 - A rotten smell hanging over a town in Mexico's southern Chiapas state drove residents into the streets on Thursday to demand the removal of a sterile-fly plant at the center of the US-Mexican fight against the flesh-eating New World screwworm parasite.
Residents in Metapa de Dominguez compared the odor to rotting meat and spoiled food, describing it as “pungent in your nose and mouth” and causing nausea. The smell, once concentrated around the plant, could now be detected farther away, particularly when winds carried it across the town, protesters said. The odor had reached schools near the plant and disrupted classes.
"We don't care about the investment they made. What we want is for this plant to leave here, because the smell coming over the town is too much," said truck driver Mercedes Becerra de la Cruz.
The complaints come less than four months after Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and US Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins inaugurated the facility on June 27. The US Department of Agriculture invested $21 million toward the $51 million facility, part of a broader effort to halt a screwworm outbreak that disrupted the cross-border cattle trade.
Sterile flies are the main defense against screwworm, a parasite whose larvae burrow into the living flesh of cattle and other warm-blooded animals and can kill them if untreated.
Eradicated from the US decades ago, the pest has surged north from Central America through Mexico, prompting Washington to impose a more than year-long ban on Mexican cattle imports. The Metapa plant is expected eventually to produce 100 million sterile flies a week.
Mexico has recorded nearly 48,000 cases of screwworm in the current outbreak and the United States 53.
Inside the Metapa plant, millions of flies are bred each week, their larvae fed a carefully formulated mixture of egg, milk and powdered hemoglobin that mimics the nutrient-rich conditions of a wound. The flies are sterilized before being released by the millions to mate with wild females without producing offspring, gradually suppressing the population.
Outside its walls, residents said daily life has increasingly been shaped by an overpowering odor that drifts into surrounding neighborhoods and schools.
"We need the federal government to respond and have the plant relocated. It is far too close, right in the middle of the town," said 49-year-old homemaker Rosalba Merida Herrera. "For the sake of our children and our elderly, we are asking them to look at the situation, as this issue is now affecting the entire town."
A spokesperson for Mexico's Agriculture Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. REUTERS

Army Building Up New Space Operations Branch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
22:37:27 UTC
07:37:27 KST

The Army has long been dependent on space capabilities to navigate terrain, communicate in hard-to-reach areas, and identify and strike targets. Now, the service wants to deepen its space operations expertise and is making plans to expand its own cadre of operators in the coming years.
In June, the service established its a Space Operations Branch, consolidating space-related career paths and created to train Soldiers to operate and deploy space systems.
This week, during the annual Association of the U.S. Army Annual Meeting in Washington, after transverring 600 enlisted Soldiers into the branch Oct. 1, Army officials predicted the Space Operations Branch will eventually include thousands of officers and troops.
The 600 transfers were reclassified as 40D Tactical Space Operations Specialists, the Army’s Military Occupational Specialty code for space troops—uniting them with 40A Space Operations Officers. The enlisted Soldiers had previously been temporarily reassigned to space-related units from Air Defense Artillery, Signal, and Military Intelligence fields.
Speaking with reporters Oct. 14 during the conference, Col. Joseph Mroszczyk, director of the Army’s Transformation Integration Directorate for Space Superiority and High Altitude, said the service’s space operations cadre has almost doubled since 2012, and he expects that to continue within the new Space Operations Branch.
“When we talk about the branch and the targets, having a couple thousand dedicated folks within the branch, between the enlisted and the officer side, is a significant contribution across the service,” Mroszczyk said when asked if the Army has a target level of growth for the branch. He didn’t offer more specifics on how long it might take the service to get there.
After the Space Force was created in 2019, space operators and units transferred from the Air Force, Navy, and Army, with the bulk of Space Force operators coming from the Air Force. Army officials have continued to make the case that they need to have their own space-focused Soldiers. While critics charge that this risks duplicating effort and blurring roles and missions, the Army says the difference is that while the Space Force is focused on maintaining space superiority in orbit, its role is integrating space capability and effects into tactical multidomain operations from the ground.
Lt. Gen. John Rafferty, commander of the Army’s Space and Missile Defense Command, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an Oct. 13 interview that as demand for these capabilities grows, the Army needs to provide the same professional pathways and training for space operators that it does for other specializations, like artillery, infantry, and aviation.
“Training, education, experience, and talent management is how you create great leaders, and that’s how you build great units with great leaders,” Rafferty said. “It became apparent to the Army that in order to capitalize on the momentum, the gains that we’ve made in Army space-delivered capabilities, we need to professionalize the branch and do it fast.”
Rafferty highlighted a few areas where the Army expects to need more space personnel and effects in the coming years.
The service on Oct. 8 activated its a new Multi-Domain Task Force at Fort Carson, Colo., one of four elements stationed around the world and designed to integrate air, land, sea, space, and cyber operations in theater. A fifth is slated for activation in 2028. Each task force incorporates space effects, and Rafferty said that as the service adds more MDTFs, it will naturally need more space personnel and systems.
He also pointed to the creation of a new Theater Strike Effects Group at U.S. Army Pacific, which will require space support. The service also wants to expand the focus of its 1st Space Brigade—headquartered at Fort Carson, but distributed across six countries—beyond GPS, theater missile warning, and satellite communications into new capability areas. He did not provide details.
As for space systems, the Army hasn’t revealed plans to field its own satellites, but Rafferty and others said the service has an interest in building out an architecture of stratospheric platforms in the “near-space” region—between 60,000 and 100,000 feet in altitude.
“That’s a—no pun intended—space that is just ripe with potential, and the opportunities for various payloads to be on those is remarkable right now,” Rafferty said. “It’s affordable and scalable, and we’ve just got to really pursue that as part of the space branch growth.”
Mroszczyk described the region as a sort of transition point between the air and space domains where platforms could host a variety of payloads supporting missions like sensing and communications, and even serve as platforms for “launched effects”—the Army’s term for small, air- or ground-launched autonomous systems.
As an example, Mroszczyk said high-altitude platforms could form a “complementary” layer for some of the Space Force’s data transport efforts, like the Space Development Agency’s Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture or the Space Data Network. Systems in that layer could help distribute data during a conflict and provide resiliency should space systems be targeted.
He told reporters the Army is looking at a range of systems—from smaller platforms to larger balloons—and is planning multiple experiments in the coming year.
“That operational space allows some persistence and broad coverage in an area where you can deliver space-like capabilities in terms of payloads, but then also take advantage of the deep access that you get from a stratospheric balloon,” he said.

Unknown

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Hurricane Trudy strengthened to a Category 1 storm Thursday off Mexico’s Pacific coast, prompting warnings of intense rainfall, strong winds and hazardous sea conditions in the southern states of Guerrero and Oaxaca.
At 3 am local time, the storm’s center was located 480 kilometers (298 miles) southwest of Acapulco, a coastal city in Guerrero, and 735 kilometers (457 miles) southeast of Manzanillo, a port city in the neighboring state of Colima, according to Mexico’s National Water Commission (Conagua).
Trudy had maximum sustained winds of 120 kilometers (75 miles) per hour, with gusts reaching 150 kilometers (93 miles) per hour. It was moving northwest at 15 kilometers (9 miles) per hour, Conagua said in a post on the US social media platform X.
Intense rainfall is forecast for northeastern and southwestern parts of Oaxaca, while very heavy rain is expected in western, southern and eastern areas of Guerrero.
Wind gusts of 50-70 kilometers (31-43 miles) per hour and waves reaching 2-3 meters (6.5-9.8 feet) are also expected along the coasts of the two states, according to the agency.
Mexico’s National Civil Protection Coordination (CNPC), part of the Security and Citizen Protection Ministry, urged residents and visitors to avoid beaches and areas affected by strong waves.
The agency also advised people not to cross flooded streets, rivers or streams, warning against attempting to pass through areas where water levels could pose a danger.
The warnings come as Trudy moves northwest over the Pacific Ocean, with authorities monitoring its intensity and potential effects on coastal communities.
Residents in potentially affected areas are advised to follow official announcements as forecasts evolve and to take precautions against heavy rainfall, strong winds and dangerous sea conditions.
Conagua and civil protection authorities are providing updates to inform the public about the storm’s development and expected impacts.

UN warns of food shortages if Hormuz fertiliser crisis continues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
22:22:23 UTC
07:22:23 KST

Breadcrumb
UN warns of food shortages if Hormuz fertiliser crisis continues
A failure by the United States and Iran to agree within weeks on a UN-backed plan for moving fertiliser through the Strait of Hormuz could cause a food security crisis in parts of Asia and Africa, an official overseeing the proposed scheme said on Wednesday.
The United Nations set up a taskforce in March to facilitate passage of fertilisers through the strait. It is yet to implement the mechanism it drew up, but United Nations Under-Secretary-General Jorge Moreira da Silva said this could be activated within 7-10 days of an agreement between Washington and Tehran.
"It's absolutely crucial to get the deal in the next few weeks. Otherwise, we will miss the planting season," he said in an interview in Bangkok, on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings.
In response to questions from Reuters, a US State Department spokesman said the US military has assisted thousands of commercial vessels with transiting the strait.
"The United States will continue to take decisive action against Iran's attempts to disrupt freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and hold the global economy hostage," he said.
The White House and Iran's Embassy in Bangkok did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
Iran has sought to tighten its grip on the Strait of Hormuz since US and Israeli strikes on 28 February, using the chokepoint to pressure Washington, which has been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Before the war, the waterway handled roughly a third of globally traded urea - the world's most widely used fertiliser - and nearly half of seaborne sulphur, a key input. It is also a major conduit for global oil supplies.
Fertiliser shipments out of the Gulf region remained largely halted more than six months after the start of the conflict, the Washington-based International Food Policy Research Institute said in a note last month. Fertiliser products accounted for a "very negligible" share of the resumption of some shipping during a ceasefire between mid-June and mid-July, it said.
Five vessels a day
If the Hormuz disruption continues, commodity prices could rise by up to 81% for cereals, 66% for oil crops and 30% for animal products, according to an August report by the International Chamber of Commerce.
"If we miss that planting season, the productivity of agriculture would significantly drop and the impact on prices will significantly increase," said Moreira da Silva, who is also the executive director of the United Nations Office for Project Services.
The proposed operation would use a coordination centre in Oman to register vessels and coordinate safe passage, with UN monitors working alongside local authorities at Gulf ports to verify cargo loading.
The passage of only five vessels per day through Hormuz could keep fertiliser supplies flowing to countries in critical need, Moreira da Silva said.
Ships would be tracked during transit, and additional inspections could be carried out if countries raised concerns about a vessel or its cargo, he added.
Multiple shipping chokepoints
Iran and the United States have exchanged proposals through intermediaries since a June interim ceasefire collapsed, but efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have stalled over Tehran's conditions and Washington's insistence on addressing Iran's nuclear programme from the outset.
The proposed UN mechanism could operate alongside negotiations on a comprehensive deal aimed at securing lasting peace and freedom of navigation, Moreira da Silva said.
"What we are telling them is, while you continue your discussions towards a comprehensive deal, let us work, let us do our job," he said, declining to specify the exact bottlenecks to a deal as discussions continue with both sides.
Beyond the Hormuz crisis, a deteriorating situation in the Black Sea region, where cargo vessels have come under attack, and an offensive by Iran-backed Houthi militants along a key Red Sea shipping route are compounding the threat to global food security.
"What we are witnessing now is a concentration of factors," Moreira da Silva said. "Climate crisis, simultaneous disruption of maritime chokepoints on the Black Sea, on the Red Sea and on Hormuz."
(Reuters)

UN report warns global biodiversity action off track, urges implementation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:18:48 CST
07:18:48 KST

YEREVAN, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Thursday launched the first global assessment report on the implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, warning that global efforts remain off track to meet the 2030 targets despite widespread national commitments.
The State of Biodiversity Action report, released in the Armenian capital of Yerevan ahead of the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties (COP17) to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), evaluates collective progress under the landmark framework adopted in December 2022, which sets out 23 targets to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030 and four long-term goals for 2050.
According to the report, nearly 90 percent of the CBD's 196 Parties have established national biodiversity targets, close to 60 percent have developed national biodiversity strategies and action plans, and over 70 percent have submitted national reports. Indigenous peoples and local communities, subnational governments, businesses and civil society organizations have also registered around 5,000 commitments.
However, such widespread engagement has not yet translated into sufficient progress. None of the 23 global targets presents a fully positive picture, and fewer than half of the national targets assessed by Parties are currently on track, the report found.
While national targets address an average of 22 of the 23 global targets, many fail to cover their full scope. For instance, far fewer countries have committed to reducing harmful subsidies under Target 18 than promoting positive incentives, and current national pledges under Target 3 fall well short of the goal to conserve 30 percent of land and sea by 2030.
The report identified gaps in financing and other means of implementation, whole-of-government and whole-of-society action, as well as data and knowledge needed to track progress. Targets requiring action beyond environment ministries -- including business action, sustainable consumption, harmful incentives and finance -- are among those lagging furthest behind.
"The report shows that many of the critical elements of progress, including finance, capacity, cooperation and data, are still missing in action," Guterres said. "Nature won't thrive on good intentions."
The UN chief called for greater financial and technical support, particularly for developing countries, the reform of harmful subsidies, nature-positive investment, and stronger integration of biodiversity across public policies and budgets.
"The very biodiversity we depend on needs tangible progress, not more promises," Inger Andersen, executive director of the UN Environment Programme, said in the report's foreword, urging immediate action to overcome implementation challenges.
The report will inform the first global review of collective progress under the framework at COP17, scheduled for Oct. 19 through 30 in Yerevan. ■

UN report urges social inclusion amid rapid global transformation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:18:42 CST
07:18:42 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- A UN report released on Thursday called for greater social inclusion as rapid economic, digital and energy transformations risk leaving billions of people behind.
The World Social Report 2026, launched by the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs, warned that billions of people still lack access to the jobs, skills, services and protections needed to benefit from these changes.
Despite progress in income, education, health and access to services, significant gaps persist. In 2025, 58 percent of workers worldwide were informally employed, 27 percent of young women aged 15 to 24 were neither employed nor in education or training, and 26 percent of the global population lacked internet access.
Income inequality also rose in more than 50 countries between 2000 and 2024, including 23 high-income countries, according to the report.
The report warned that these disparities undermine productivity and resilience, while unequal access to digital technologies and artificial intelligence skills could further widen gaps in education, income and economic opportunity.
It estimated that delaying investment in social protection by 10 years could cost countries 12 percent of their economic output compared with those that invest early.
To ensure that the benefits of transformation are widely shared, the report outlined four priorities: building people's capacity to adapt, connecting everyone to the new economy, making labor markets work for people, and promoting shared prosperity.
In a video message marking the report's launch, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said social inclusion was not only a moral imperative but also an economic necessity, stressing that inclusive societies are more productive, resilient and prosperous.
"Transformations are inevitable. Inequality and exclusion are not," he said. "Let's work together to ensure that the profound transformations reshaping our world help build societies rooted in justice, dignity and opportunity for all." ■

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his British counterpart Wes Streeting discussed NATO burden-sharing, defense spending and military cooperation at the Pentagon on Thursday, according to the Pentagon.
The meeting marked Streeting's first visit to Washington since taking office in July and came as the Trump administration pushed European allies to assume greater responsibility for their conventional defense.
Hegseth emphasized that the longstanding relationship between Washington and London must continue to evolve to address emerging threats rather than rely solely on historical ties.
"(Rather,) they're about an ongoing partnership that needs to be active in a dangerous world (and) a dynamic world, and we welcome that," Hegseth told Streeting, according to the Pentagon.
Hegseth also outlined the concept of "NATO 3.0," a vision for shifting more responsibility for Europe's conventional defense to European members of the alliance.
The approach could allow the US to reduce its troop presence on the continent and redirect resources toward other regions, including the Pacific.
"It's been very encouraging under President (Donald) Trump's leadership to watch NATO step up," Hegseth said.
He also praised the UK for its plans to increase defense contributions.
Streeting backed the push for greater European responsibility, saying Britain was prepared to take a more active role in defending the continent and its interests.
"The UK is stepping up; we're stepping up willingly," Streeting said.
He also thanked Trump for encouraging European countries to take their defense responsibilities more seriously.
Streeting said the UK was undertaking its largest sustained increase in defense spending since the end of the Cold War to strengthen its military capabilities.
He argued that higher spending alone would not be sufficient, emphasizing the need to direct investments toward effective capabilities and accelerate the development of new military technologies.
"But to your point, it's not just about investing more; it's about investing in the right things and making sure that we're pushing the frontier of defense innovation and translating that innovation into capability a lot more quickly," Streeting told Hegseth, according to the Pentagon.
He also highlighted the need to reinforce Britain's defense industrial base and improve the speed at which technological advances are converted into operational military systems.
Hegseth similarly stressed the importance of expanding defense production in the US while working with allies to strengthen manufacturing capacity and supply chains.
"We talk about an arsenal of freedom here in the States, (about) building that and ensuring that our domestic manufacturing, our industry, our production lines, (are) made in America (at) speed, scale, (and) made with partners," he said.

UN chief frontrunner Rebeca Grynspan says UN has 'become too risk-averse'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
22:11:11 UTC
07:11:11 KST

UN chief frontrunner Rebeca Grynspan says UN has 'become too risk-averse'
UNITED NATIONS, Oct 15 - The United Nations has become too risk-averse and its next leader must be prepared to bear the cost of diplomatic failure and try again, Rebeca Grynspan, the frontrunner to be the next UN chief, told Reuters on Thursday.
She spoke ahead of another Security Council poll on Friday to gauge support for a new secretary-general to succeed Antonio Guterres, whose second five-year term ends on December 31.
Grynspan said the UN must also cut jobs, curb bureaucracy and stop agencies duplicating work, arguing that cost-cutting alone would not revive an institution struggling with shrinking resources and declining political clout.
“I think that the UN has become too risk-averse,” Grynspan said. “You are the one that has to take the cost of rejection, the cost of failure, and try again. That's the job of the UN.”
SHE URGES A MORE PROACTIVE UN
Grynspan, 70, a former Costa Rican vice president, called for a more proactive UN after the 193-member body was largely sidelined in wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and as it faces pressure from US President Donald Trump's administration to cut costs.
"Cost cutting is not enough. Yes, you can cut costs and make everything worse. If you don't reform, you will do everything worse than before. That's why I talk about refocusing," Grynspan, an economist, told Reuters.
Pointing to her tenure as head of the UN Conference on Trade and Development, Grynspan said she cut 20% of posts while sharpening its focus.
US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz has criticized what he called bureaucratic "bloat" and duplication at the UN and called for a clearer focus on peacekeeping.
Grynspan said she shared Waltz's concerns: "Some consolidation and rethinking of how to carry a mandate is necessary in many of the fields that have been expanding in the UN." She said she would appoint a person inside her office to "impose the discipline that is necessary for mandate implementation."
Grynspan pointed to her role in negotiations over the 2022 Black Sea Grain Initiative as a model for handling conflicts involving a permanent Security Council member. Russia withdrew from the agreement in 2023 and complained that key parts of the deal were never implemented.
“We didn't go to the press ... It was quiet diplomacy that worked,” she said. “This is not about being able to have total harmony in the international affairs ... it's about doing good.”
Grynspan said the UN already had the expertise, information and presence on the ground needed to play a larger diplomatic role but needed leadership capable of bringing those resources together.
“Peacemaking has to be at the center of the efforts of the UN,” she said, citing a rise in deadly interstate conflicts and calling for greater emphasis on mediation as well as prevention.
Grynspan also called for greater flexibility in peacekeeping, saying the secretary-general should work closely with the Security Council's five permanent members to find alternative models when traditional peacekeeping is not viable.
Pointing to the multinational support mission in Haiti, she said: “Why should we be so defensive? Why should it be only a UN peacekeeping force? ... Let's try to make Haiti work and learn from the experience.”
'GAME NOT OVER'
Grynspan, who will become the first female secretary-general in the UN's history if she wins, has come out ahead in four out of five informal straw polls, obtaining nine votes in favor last week, according to diplomats close to the process.
Securing the recommendation requires at least nine positive votes out of the 15 countries, and no "discourage" votes from the five permanent members: the US, China, Russia, France, and Britain. Friday's poll will for the first time use color-coded ballots revealing whether a veto power opposes a candidate.
Grynspan said she was the only candidate who has consistently reached nine votes in her favor, but she "wouldn't be surprised" if she got a discouraging vote from a veto power. She said such opposition has been overcome in past races.
Diplomats at the UN say several senior figures, including former and current foreign ministers and country leaders, are seriously considering entering the race.
Grynspan said she expected new names could enter the race after the Friday vote and added: "The game is not over -- we will have to continue working." REUTERS

G7 countries pledge 260 million euros for Chornobyl safety infrastructure repairs damaged in Russian attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
22:06:57 UTC
07:06:57 KST

G7 countries pledge 260 million euros to repair Chornobyl safety infrastructure damaged in Russian attack
Group of Seven (G7) nations will provide 260 million euros ($292 million) to help repair safety infrastructure at the Chornobyl Nuclear Plant damaged in a Russian attack, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) announced on Oct. 15.
"The G7 (Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States) expressed grave concern over the nuclear safety risks caused by the strike and pledged to mobilize funding to repair the New Safe Confinement," the EBRD said in a statement.
The New Safe Confinement is a massive, arching steel structure that was erected in 2016 to cover the remains of the reactor unit that exploded during the 1986 Chornobyl nuclear disaster. The structure encloses the original sarcophagus that was built shortly after the disaster to prevent the release of nuclear contamination.
The confinement structure, located about 130 kilometers (80 miles) north of Kyiv, was severely damaged in February 2025 after being struck by a Russian drone.
"This is a terrorist threat to the entire world," President Volodymyr Zelensky said at the time. "The only country in the world that attacks such sites, occupies nuclear power plants, and wages war without any regard for the consequences is today's Russia."
The attack breached the structure’s inner and outer protective structures, damaged critical systems, and "severely compromised its two primary functions: containing radioactive material and enabling the safe dismantling of the unstable original sarcophagus over Reactor Four," according to the EBRD.
The EBRD estimates that 500 million euros ($561 million) is needed to repair the structure, and the work must be completed by 2030 to limit the risk of corrosion and safeguard the structure’s 100-year design life.
Previously, the site was briefly occupied by Russian forces in the early days of the full-scale invasion. Russian troops held the station's staff hostage, creating significant risks to nuclear safety. On Mar. 31, 2022, Russian troops withdrew from the station. Turkish foreign minister says Türkiye-Azerbaijan ties built on 'unshakable' friendship, brotherhood

2026-10-15

Ruslan Rehimov and Seyit Kurt

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Thursday that the "two states, one nation" principle between Türkiye and Azerbaijan manifests itself across all areas, stressing that ties between the two countries have been tested during difficult times, including wars and crises.
Speaking to reporters in Azerbaijan’s capital Baku, where he is attending the 7th Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA), Fidan assessed Türkiye-Azerbaijan relations as well as developments concerning the Russia-Ukraine war and security in the Black Sea.
He said relations between Türkiye and Azerbaijan have gone through various historical tests and are built on solid strategic foundations.
"The principle of 'two states, one nation' manifests itself in all areas. There is an unshakable bond of friendship and brotherhood between our leaders. This is a bond that has been tested in very difficult times, in times of war and crisis," he said.
Fidan warns against exploiting differences between Türkiye, Azerbaijan
Noting that the two countries may occasionally have different approaches on certain issues, Fidan stressed that such differences should not be exploited to undermine the strategic relationship between Türkiye and Azerbaijan.
Pointing to the importance of the unshakable bonds and brotherly relations between the two countries, he said: "Today, the strategic solidarity demonstrated by the two countries is also being closely followed by the international community."
He said relations between Türkiye and Azerbaijan would continue to play a determining role in the future, as they have in the past, adding that attitudes that could erode those ties should be avoided.
Fidan said the Turkish and Azerbaijani publics have increasingly become integrated, with the spread of social media and communication channels allowing the two societies to influence one another.
He noted that there is intense interaction between the two countries in cultural, political, social and financial fields.
Fidan stressed that the leaderships of both countries are sensitive to the issue, adding that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan had conveyed instructions and directives to him ahead of his visit to Baku.
Acknowledging that there may be different approaches and perspectives on certain issues, Fidan said these could be discussed between the two countries in a manner consistent with their ties of brotherhood.
"We are an ancient nation. We sit down and discuss our own problems in a civilized manner, in a way befitting our ancient past and ourselves," he said.
Fidan stressed that there was no need to turn differences of opinion into instruments of propaganda through social media.
He said he also discussed these issues during his meeting with Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev, adding the Turkish side listened to Aliyev's views and perspective.
Fidan said the unshakable bond between the two countries' leaders would continue to exist in the strongest possible manner.
He added that efforts were being made on both sides to prevent the issue from being exploited and to ensure that no new obstacles emerge in the way of the brotherhood between Türkiye and Azerbaijan, urging all parties to exercise sensitivity in this regard.
Türkiye working to keep Black Sea outside Russia-Ukraine war
Turning to the Russia-Ukraine war, Fidan said Türkiye's position is in favor of ending the conflict.
He said Ankara has been making intensive efforts toward this goal and since the war has not been brought to a complete end is at least working to keep the Black Sea outside the conflict.
Fidan said he had also discussed the issue with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and listened to the Russian side's views, noting that Türkiye had previously held contacts on the matter as well.
He said Türkiye had presented a proposal it prepared to both Ukraine and Russia, listened to the positions of both sides regarding the proposal and was working on how the issue could be resolved in a more constructive manner.
Fidan stressed that navigational safety in the Black Sea is extremely important, pointing out that developments in the region closely affect global food markets.
He warned that wheat trade, particularly to African countries, was at risk and drew attention to rising food and energy prices.
Fidan said restrictions on trade in the Black Sea have serious negative consequences, noting that these problems are placing further pressure on the global economy, particularly developing countries, at a time when the Strait of Hormuz is closed and restrictions are occasionally being experienced in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Türkiye is doing everything it can to help resolve the issue, he said, adding that Ankara's efforts to ensure navigational safety in the Black Sea are continuing.

USAFA Board Calls for Opening Part of Long-Closed Chapel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
22:02:49 UTC
07:02:49 KST

The U.S. Air Force Academy’s Board of Visitors wants the service academy to partially reopen its iconic chapel ahead of schedule next year when it sheds the “big white box” that has enclosed it through years of renovations.
The idea is one of more than a dozen recommendations the board made in its semiannual report released Oct. 15, ahead of a planned Oct. 16 meeting.
The Cadet Chapel, designed by architect Walter Netsch Jr. and opened in 1962, is a National Historic Landmark, renowned for its use of tetrahedrons and its 17 spires. But it has been closed since 2019 for repairs due to leaks and water damage. Originally expected to cost $158 million and to be completed by 2023, renovation costs more than doubled to $335 million due to asbestos removal, among other problems, and the job won’t be finished until 2028.
The chapel has been enclosed in the “the box,” as cadets call it, for seven years. Locals and alums describe the scene as an “eyesore” and President Donald Trump has decried the troubled project, saying last October, “this mess should be investigated.”
At one point, officials feared the renovations wouldn’t be complete until spring 2029. But this summer, the Air Force Civil Engineer Center announced the box would start coming down in August 2027 and be fully deconstructed by January 2028. Chaplains will be allowed back in around April 2028, and the building will fully reopen to the public in August 2028. The news was hailed by local media.
USAFA’s Board of Visitors—a congressionally mandated oversight committee—called the new timeline “highly commendable,” but the board argues more can be done.
The board is “deeply concerned that the spiritual and character development of an entire generation of future officers is being compromised by the extended renovation timeline of the Cadet Chapel,” the report states. Members want to reopen the lower level of the chapel by December 2027, even as work continues on the upper level.
A white paper attached to the report makes the case that removing “the box”is a “strategic opportunity” to give cadets at least some access to the building, reorienting the eyesore to its spiritual purpose. To make that happen, the paper argues for:
- Accelerating the removal of the box by one month
- Prioritizing repairs and renovations for the lower level
- Creating “safe and isolated” access points for cadets to enter and exit the lower level
- Updating any legal and administrative frameworks to support the effort
The lower level of the building hosts Catholic and Jewish chapels, while the upper level has a Protestant chapel. The white paper argues that the lower chapels “can be dynamically time-shared” while the upper chapel is finished to “provide an immediate, centralized home for worship for all faith groups across the cadet wing.”
Assignments and Accreditation
Other Board of Visitors’ recommendations touch on USAFA’s role as an academic institution. One recommendation calls for the Air Force to “elevate the value” of an officer assignment to USAFA as a “career-enhancing duty” for Air Force and Space Force officers.
“While the Board fundamentally considers instructing and working at USAFA to be a premier developmental assignment, Career Field Managers are often reluctant to promote this duty,” the board report states. “Most positions at USAFA are not career-field-specific and therefore CFMs must ‘release’ officers to perform these duties. Career field management teams frequently view these releases as a ‘tax’ and perceive them negatively, as the individual is temporarily leaving their primary specialty.”
The issue is common to special duties such as recruiting, which also takes Airmen and Guardians out of their career field. To overcome the problem, the board wants the academy and Air Force Personnel Center to incentivize Academy duty by rewarding personnel who take USAFA assignments. They also recommend the Air Force examine promotion rates for officers who served as instructors to see whether the assignments improve or hurt career advancement.
More than 2,000 Airmen and Guardians work at USAFA, in jobs ranging from faculty to administration and support roles. In recent times, the number of uniformed faculty has grown as more military instructors have arrived in the wake of a rash of departures by civilian staff spurred by cuts to the federal workforce.
The exodus of civilian staff last year led one alumnus to file a complaint with the Higher Learning Commission, the academy’s accrediting institution. The complaint was settled without affecting the school’s accreditation. Meanwhile, the board report is calling for USAFA to sever its relationship with the HLC and instead join the other service academies and the Air Force’s other degree-granting institutions—including the Air Force Institute of Technology and Air University—to band together under a single accreditor.
A board working group favor joining the new Commission for Public Higher Education, founded by six states’ public university systems whose political leaders argue the new commission is needed to combat liberal bias and burdensome bureaucracy among current accreditors. The working group says CPHE “guarantees an apolitical baseline and alignment with requirements specific to the military education system.”
Previous Recommendations
The Board of Visitors is chaired Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas), a former by former F-22 pilot and academy alumnus. The boarfd’s previous report, released in February, called for the academy to grow its cadet wing by 10 percent and build a new “tri-complex” of buildings to house a new “Air, Space, and Cyber Education Center,” including a new “home” base for the U.S. Space Force.
The bulk of the recommendations in that February report remain open, awaiting action from Congress. Decisions could come in the 2027 National Defense Authorization bill, but the measure remains stalled and will not be resolved until after the midterm elections.

Family genetics study questions the role of genetic nurture in ADHD
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
22:00:31 UTC
07:00:31 KST

A large study of families suggests that a child’s overall attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder traits are primarily driven by their own genetics by mid-childhood, rather than by the indirect environmental influence of their parents’ genes. Researchers found a lack of evidence for parental genetic nurture effects at both age five and age eight, though they note that statistical limitations might obscure more subtle influences. The research was published in Behavior Genetics.
Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD, is a neurodevelopmental condition involving patterns of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. Decades of twin studies indicate that ADHD is highly heritable. This means a child’s own DNA plays a major role in whether they develop these behavioral traits.
However, genetic and environmental factors do not operate in isolation. In recent years, scientists have focused on how an individual’s traits might be shaped by the genes of the people around them. Because biological parents provide both their children’s DNA and their rearing environment, it is notoriously difficult to separate nature from nurture.
When parents’ genes influence their child’s environment, this process is known as an indirect genetic effect, or genetic nurture. For instance, a parent’s genetic makeup might influence their patience, parenting style, or the general household environment they create. This environment then affects the child’s development, meaning the parent’s genes have shaped the child’s traits from the outside in.
When indirect genetic effects are not accounted for, researchers risk overestimating the direct impact of a child’s own DNA. To better understand the origins of ADHD traits, researchers set out to untangle these direct and indirect genetic influences. Daniel L. Wechsler, a researcher at King’s College London, led a team to investigate whether parents’ genetic profiles exert indirect effects on a child’s ADHD traits over and above the child’s own direct genetic risks.
The researchers also wanted to see how these influences might shift as children grow. Previous research has explored these dynamics for specific traits like hyperactivity at single time points. The current project instead focused on overall ADHD scores across two distinct developmental stages, early and mid-childhood.
Wechsler and his colleagues utilized data from the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study, a population-based registry. They analyzed genetic data from mother, father, and child trios alongside survey data. The questionnaires asked parents to rate the frequency of specific behaviors, such as difficulty paying attention to tasks or acting without thinking.
A method called trio genome-wide complex trait analysis was used to examine around a million genetic variations across all three family members. These genetic variations, known as single-nucleotide polymorphisms, are tiny changes in the genetic code that can influence various physical and behavioral traits. Humans share the vast majority of their DNA, but these small variations make each person unique.
Unlike some genetic approaches that only look at specific genes tied to a known condition, this method captures the cumulative influence of all measured genetic variations. By modeling the genetic data from the whole family at once, the researchers could estimate the child’s direct genetic effects alongside the cumulative indirect environmental effects of both parents’ genes.
The first analysis focused on a large study sample of 12,374 family trios when the children were five years old. The initial statistical models at this age suggested that maternal indirect genetic effects accounted for nearly five percent of the variation in children’s ADHD traits. At the same time, the child’s direct genetic effects appeared to account for less than two percent.
However, when the researchers tested these findings against more stringent statistical models, the results failed to hold up. The model comparisons ultimately favored a scenario in which neither direct nor indirect genetic effects were present at age five. Large margins of error in the data prevented the team from confirming specific genetic effects at this age.
This lack of measurable direct genetic influence at early childhood was unexpected. ADHD is widely recognized as highly heritable, even in young children. The researchers suggested that ADHD traits might not fully manifest in a measurable way for many children by age five.
Alternatively, it is possible that children’s individual genetic propensities simply account for more variation in their behavior as they grow older. This pattern has been observed in other developmental traits, where the influence of a child’s own genetics becomes more apparent over time. In previous research utilizing an even larger sample of the same cohort, scientists found evidence for direct genetic effects on specific traits like hyperactivity and inattention as early as age three.
Next, the team conducted a similar analysis on an overlapping large study sample of 12,714 family trios when the children were eight years old. The preliminary models for this mid-childhood stage showed increased genetic influence overall. These early estimates pointed to roughly equal contributions, with the child’s own genes and the mother’s indirect genetic effects each accounting for about eight percent of the variation.
Once again, the researchers applied rigorous model comparisons to see which scenario best fit the data. At age eight, the most accurate model indicated that the child’s direct genetics played a role in their ADHD traits. This model, however, showed no evidence of indirect genetic effects from either parent.
Across both age groups, the team found no robust evidence that a mother or father’s genetic profile indirectly influences a child’s overall ADHD traits through the environment. The results at age eight suggest that a child’s own DNA is the primary biological driver of their overall ADHD traits by mid-childhood.
While the results appear to rule out genetic nurture for total ADHD traits, the researchers caution against drawing absolute conclusions. The statistical models were hampered by large margins of error, meaning the results were not statistically significant enough to firmly distinguish direct from indirect effects in the more complicated models. The study might simply have lacked the mathematical power to detect subtle indirect influences.
The decision to analyze total ADHD scores rather than breaking them down into specific categories might have also obscured important details. Past studies have successfully detected indirect genetic effects on specific behaviors like hyperactivity and inattention. This suggests that genetic nurture might operate on certain specific behaviors rather than the overarching condition.
Another limitation is that the survey data relied solely on the mothers’ assessments of their children. Mothers’ ratings could be influenced by their own perceptions or biases based on their specific interactions with the children. Utilizing teacher reports or formal clinical diagnoses could provide a more rounded perspective in future investigations.
Additionally, the genetic data came exclusively from families of European ancestry. This demographic focus limits how well the findings might apply to more diverse populations worldwide. Future research could benefit from even more massive study samples across diverse demographics to better separate these intertwined genetic signals.
The study, “Direct and Indirect Genetic Effects on Child ADHD Traits in Early and Mid-Childhood: Trio Genome-Wide Complex Trait Analyses in a Large Norwegian Birth Registry Cohort,” was authored by Daniel L. Wechsler, Espen M. Eilertsen, Yasmin I. Ahmadzadeh, Rosa Cheesman, Nicoletta Adamo, Laurie J. Hannigan, Eivind Ystrom, and Tom A. McAdams. Their work adds new context to the ongoing scientific effort to untangle the developmental roots of behavioral traits.

The China decoupling paradox: why the world still needs its manufacturing machine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15

07:00:15 KST

In FocusThe China decoupling paradox: why the world still needs its manufacturing machine
Chinese parts, machinery and know-how remain deeply embedded in countries seeking to build manufacturing industries of their own
Talk of global decoupling from China has persisted for years, as has speculation that emerging economies such as India and Vietnam could soon replace it as the “world’s factory”.
But for Indian hardware engineer Neeraj Arora, the growth of India’s electronics manufacturing industry has not eliminated the need to source components from China. Instead, it has changed the nature of those imports.
A decade ago, Arora imported finished phone chargers from the world’s second-largest economy. Today, more of these products can be made in India, even as manufacturers there still rely on Chinese parts for assembly.
“They don’t have a single industry; they have created an ecosystem,” said Arora, who has travelled repeatedly to Shenzhen, Dongguan and Guangzhou – southern China’s manufacturing hubs that offer a wide range of competitively priced parts, from power-switching transistors to charging chips.
