Israel halts commercial goods from entering Gaza; Hamas denies tax claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:57:58 UTC
06:57:58 KST

Israel halts commercial goods from entering Gaza; Hamas denies tax claims
The halt to commercial shipments, including fruit and winter clothing, cuts off a key source of critical supplies.
Israeli authorities say no commercial goods have entered Gaza for two days, citing what they claim is a tax dispute between local merchants and Hamas.
COGAT, or the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories, the Israeli military body that “oversees humanitarian affairs” in Gaza, announced the halt on Wednesday.
COGAT claimed that local merchants “made the decision in response to a 10,000 shekel ($3,220) fee imposed by Hamas on each truck entering Gaza” as well as a demand for 30 percent of all sales in Gaza to be carried out in cash.
This decision is expected to impact a crucial source of food and goods for the 2.1 million people in the Strip, who are completely reliant on Israel’s border crossings in a territory that is still suffering from famine.
Gaza’s government media office refuted the claims on Thursday and condemned the “blatant disinformation campaign and false statement”.
The media office instead said it was an attempt “to hold the government apparatus in Gaza responsible for the disruption of truck entry” and that the fee was a voluntary payment to a fund providing aid for those in need, such as widows and orphans.
It also said that cash payments were encouraged due to what it described as an acute cash shortage in the war-torn territory, but were never a mandatory requirement.
An already dire humanitarian crisis
The halt to commercial shipments, including fruit and winter clothing, cuts off a key source of food and other critical supplies as fears mount ahead of the encroaching winter.
Aid groups generally bring in staples such as flour, while merchants import more perishable foods like fruits and meat, according to data released earlier this year by COGAT.
The suspension is raising fears about affordability, with humanitarian workers saying a combination of aid and a robust commercial market is needed to keep prices under control.
“The humanitarian sector on its own cannot meet the needs of all the people,” said Shaina Low, a spokesperson for the Norwegian Refugee Council. “The markets need to be functioning.”
Local merchants step in
The head of Gaza’s private truckers union, Nahed Sheheiber, denied the Israeli narrative, saying: “The Israeli coordinator is claiming that Gaza’s merchants are responsible, but the truth is that the Israelis are the ones who imposed the restrictions.”
Following COGAT’s announcement, Sheheiber’s union met with Gaza’s Ministry of Economy to express concern and say Israel was citing fees levied by the ministry as a pretext to cut off commercial goods.
A global hunger monitor in July warned that more than two-thirds of people in Gaza could face acute hunger by the year-end.
Israel is obliged under a US-mediated agreement to allow a minimum of 600 trucks carrying humanitarian aid to enter Gaza each day.
Diplomats say that far fewer than 600 trucks normally enter Gaza each day. Sheheiber said the figure was closer to 300, with two-thirds carrying commercial goods.

NEW DELHI: The high-level committee studying causes and impact of "unnatural" demographic shifts in parts of the country has sought individual citizens' inputs on major demographic changes they have observed or studied over the past 15 years in the geographical areas they are familiar with.These geographical areas may be villages, towns, cities, districts, states/UTs, regions across India.In a questionnaire uploaded by the high-level committee on its dedicated portal, individual responders can provide causes of demographic changes, as perceived by them, besides detailing their likely effect on employment, education, healthcare, housing, infrastructure services, environment, social harmony and local economy. Individuals can also submit five recommendations to address these challenges.Wherever feasible, the committee requests, individuals must substantiate their responses with supporting material such as research reports, survey findings, case studies, photographs, audio-visual documentation, maps, official records, court records, media reports, publications or other relevant evidence.
Respondents can attach documents with their responses.The portal - inaugurated Wednesday by committee chairperson Justice Prakash Prabhakar Naolekar (Retd) - also puts out different sets of questionnaires for different stakeholders, including those in central ministries and departments, state govts, UT administration, NGOs, civil society, international organisations, think tanks, public servants and students.
The stakeholders can, through the portal, give inputs/data/information on any abnormal settlement pattern cause that may have altered the demographic character of a region. "These inputs will help the committee to analyse and identify causes of demographic changes and to recommend a well-organised and permanent operational system for the legal, fair and time-bound identification, detention, and deportation of illegal immigrants residing in the country," the committee said Wednesday.

Israeli rights groups report 22 accounts of prisoners being shot by guards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:49:08 UTC
06:49:08 KST

Abderaouf Arnaout and Ikram Kouachi
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Two Israeli human rights groups said Thursday that they had received at least 22 testimonies from prisoners and detainees, most of them Palestinians, who reported being shot and seriously wounded by Israeli prison guards.
The findings were included in a joint report by Physicians for Human Rights–Israel and the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel.
The organizations said they received the testimonies, most of them over the past year, from individuals who reported that prison guards had fired projectiles they described as rubber, plastic or sponge bullets.
They said 21 testimonies were given by Palestinian prisoners and one by a Jewish prisoner.
The accounts included incidents in which guards fired at prisoners from close range and inside cells, where prisoners had no room to move away from the source of the gunfire or take shelter.
The organizations documented cases at several prisons and detention facilities including Ofer, Ganot, Ketziot, Gilboa, Megiddo, Nitzan and Eshel.
The report revealed that a 45-year-old Palestinian prisoner was transferred to Soroka Medical Center in June after being shot with rubber bullets.
According to medical records, the prisoner sustained injuries to several parts of his body, including his testicles. He required surgery to remove his right testicle after it was completely ruptured.
In another case, a prisoner suffered a fracture to his left leg after being shot at close range.
Medical records confirmed that he was transferred to Soroka Medical Center, where he underwent surgery to stabilize the fracture.
The report also cited other injuries to the legs, abdomen, pelvis and hands.
Prisoners said they had been shot during raids carried out by guards or inside prison wings and cells. Some reported that they had not received medical examinations after being injured or had been denied appropriate treatment.
In one testimony, a prisoner at Ofer Prison said he had refused to return to his cell in protest against being denied treatment for scabies for months. He added that guards responded by shooting at him and using an electric stun device on his head.
After documenting the cases, the two organizations contacted the Israeli government's legal adviser and senior officials at the Israel Prison Service, calling for an end to the “uncontrolled use of gunfire against prisoners.”
They also called for disclosure of the types of weapons and ammunition used and the instructions governing their use.
In its response, the Israel Prison Service acknowledged using “less-lethal means” against prisoners.
It also rejected the demand for a comprehensive halt to their use.
Muhannad Abu Ghosh, head of the prisoners and detainees department at Physicians for Human Rights–Israel, said shooting at prisoners was not a new phenomenon but added that the recent period had witnessed an “unprecedented escalation” in its use.
He warned that the growing use of these means threatened prisoners' lives and could cause permanent harm.
Meanwhile, attorney Merav Ben Ze'ev, head of the legal department at the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel, criticized the Israel Prison Service's response.
Ben Ze'ev said the committee was considering taking further action against the practice, saying it “endangered prisoners' lives and constituted another means of torture.”
Around 9,350 Palestinians, including 350 children and 90 women, are being held in Israeli prisons, where human rights groups have reported widespread torture, starvation and medical neglect, contributing to dozens of deaths in custody.

Interests of homebuyers and sellers collide in fight for transparency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:49:06 UTC
06:49:06 KST

Victorian laws force house price transparency in national fight against underquoting
In short:
Victoria has introduced new laws to target real estate agents underquoting house prices to try to bring more transparency to the market.
Parts of the industry are supportive of the move but say the laws are confusing and inconsistent.
Industry figures say the laws do not take into account changing market and auction dynamics, which can significantly move the reserve price.
New laws will let prospective homebuyers know the price a seller is willing to say "yes" to.
The Victorian laws that took effect at the start of the month are being watched closely nationwide and bring radical transparency before and after sales.
They will force agents to:
- Make the reserve price public at least a week before an auction.
- Publish the sale price for at least 18 months after the sale.
The laws aim to reduce underquoting, when agents market a property for a price for well below what it is expected to sell for to artificially generate interest in a property.
"Victorians are sick of wasting their weekends chasing homes they were never going to get," said state Minister for Consumer Affairs Paul Edbrooke.
But Real Estate Institute of Victoria (REIV) chief executive Toby Balazs, who represents agents, opposes the details of the new laws.
"If you look at the problem that was trying to be solved, egregious underquoting, and the results — people wasting their time and money on getting things like building reports — that's a good thing," he said.
"We just don't think this is the way to do it."
The institute thinks potential buyers should have guidance on the likely range a property will sell, but not the precise figure.
Because most sales campaigns run for a month and the reserve price must be published 7 days before the auction, Mr Balazs argues there is little time to get feedback from potential buyers.
"What you're probably going to get is overquoting … because if I [quote] over, it's easier to come down."
He argues the seller (otherwise known as the vendor) "has a right to manage what is the sale of, most likely, their biggest asset".
Laws with good intent but poor design, expert argues
Independent property economist Cameron Kusher is all for crushing the scourge of underquoting, which is generally illegal in Australia.
But he does not think these laws will do it.
"Declaring [the reserve] on the morning of, or before the auction commences, is a much better solution than having to declare a week out," he said, because agents and the seller were still understanding who the bidders were likely to be and what they were willing to pay.
Cate Bakos, a buyer's advocate in Victoria, agreed and added that, while underquoting was a big problem, the new laws could make things more difficult for both vendors and buyers.
"It's been a problem for a long time. I've been in the industry for 23 years and it's been a problem for every single year,"
she said.
"Seven days is a long runway for vendors; I don't think it's enough, and it will make it really stressful for them."
She said that, ultimately, real estate agents would still find a way around the rules.
Confusion over new rules
Ray White Group managing director Dan White said the new laws were inconsistent and confusing for buyers, vendors and agents.
He said the government gave the company conflicting advice on whether the reserve could be changed after it was set. The government did not respond to ABC requests for clarification.
"The minister said you can change it, and the cabinet said you can't," Mr White said.
But, he said, the reserve was only one piece of information and buyers should do their own research.
While the new laws mean the property price statement now includes a swathe of facts about the property, Ms Bakos says this could make buyers feel more informed than they really are.
"I'm concerned that buyers will have a false sense of security."
It will now include new information such as the internal floor area and number of car spaces, but she says it misses key facts about the zoning and land quality.
"What's the point of counting bedrooms and car spots if it's in a flood zone?"
But a typical consumer might not understand these implications, which could significantly affect the property's value, she said.
Unclear if other states will follow
New South Wales has been cracking down on underquoting, but it is not using the same laws as Victoria.
In February, NSW Fair Trading introduced a Name and Shame register that publicly lists fines and breaches from real estate agents and strata managers, including underquoting.
The government conducted 131 inspections across July to September and 31 penalty notices were issued, totalling more than $68,000.
While underquoting is generally illegal across Australia, no other state has said it plans to introduce similar laws to Victoria.
Will this lower prices?
Victoria's property prices have been falling, or rising more slowly than other jurisdictions, in recent years.
Expanded supply and a swathe of new rules and taxes that have made property investment less attractive have seen the median property price fall to the lowest of all the capital cities bar Hobart and Darwin in recent data.
These changes are unlikely to alter that picture.
Property Council of Australia Victorian deputy executive director Andrew Lowcock said greater transparency alone will not solve housing affordability.
"The biggest drivers of prices remain supply and demand," he said.
"If Victoria wants more affordable housing, it needs to focus on getting more homes built."
Real Estate Institute of Victoria's Toby Balazs agrees.
"It won't affect prices at all," he said.
Ms Bakos said it was unlikely to affect prices over the longer term, but that adding the laws during a downward market was "terrible" timing.
"If you're in a hot market, you can set the reserve price as whatever you want."

No reservation for OBC, Dalits who convert: Supreme Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:46:00 UTC
06:46:00 KST

SC said backwardness suffered by the person in Hindu religion cannot be carried forward to the new religion embraced by him or her.
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Thursday ruled a Scheduled Castes/OBC person who converts from a Hindu social order to a non-Hindu social order will not be entitled to the benefits of reservation. The court held that reservation is attached to a constitutionally identified class and not to an individual as a personal entitlement, which can be transferred if a person converts.SC said backwardness suffered by the person in Hindu religion cannot be carried forward to the new religion embraced by him or her.The order came on a petition filed by then DMK-led Tamil Nadu govt challenging a Madras HC order quashing state govt's order to allow reservations for Dalit and OBC converts to Islam.As reservation is provided to some communities of other religions, which are recognised as backward classes in different states, a bench of Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and Shree Chandrashekhar held that conversion of OBCs/Dalits to a non-Hindu social order does not, by itself, confer membership of any particular notified backward class community of the adopted religion.
The apex court's verdict comes against the backdrop of growing demand for extending reservation to those OBCs/Dalits who converted to other religions.
"A person who converts from a Hindu social order to a non-Hindu social order cannot claim affirmative action under Article 16(4) of Constitution merely on the basis of the social backwardness associated with his pre-conversion status; the backwardness suffered in the antecedent social order cannot, by itself, be carried forward so as to confer upon him the status of a backward class in the religion to which he has converted," Supreme Courtsaid while quashing the Tamil Nadu order.

Trump administration sues California over noncitizens on voter rolls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:44:59 UTC
06:44:59 KST

Trump administration sues California over noncitizens on voter rolls
Lawsuit comes weeks before midterm elections and follows debunked claims of noncitizens voting in various states.
The administration of United States President Donald Trump has sued the state of California after the state missed a deadline to review a list of registered noncitizen voters sent to officials.
In the lawsuit, filed on Thursday in a US District Court in California, Department of Justice (DOJ) officials asked the court to prevent the state from counting mail-in ballots from voters on a list shared with the state that it said contained 20,000 noncitizens. The agency said it had attempted to “work collaboratively” with California to identify noncitizens registered to vote in the state, but “California made no serious effort to do so”.
The move follows a 48-hour deadline the DOJ gave California in letters sent to officials in several counties in the state on Tuesday, threatening further action if they did not review lists of allegedly ineligible voters the agency said it had shared.
California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, the top state official tasked with administering elections, responded to the letters, saying in a three-page letter that she wanted to “set the record straight” on events that transpired since July. The senior California official maintains that the administration is demanding “unprecedented measures that threaten thousands of Californians’ right to vote, based on unverifiable information or methodology that you still fail to explain or provide”.
Weber said she was informed that the lists provided to local officials include the names of roughly 20,000 individuals. Weber said no list was ever sent to her office. The department previously said it suspected “thousands” of registered voters of being noncitizens, and a lawsuit filed earlier Thursday by the Justice Department put the number at “tens of thousands”.
“Despite failing to send the list of alleged non-citizens to my office, you demand that we request transmittal of the list, review and confirm the citizenship status of each of the approximately 20,000 individuals on the list on the eve of an election and within a mere 48 hours,” she wrote. “This is an emergency of the DOJ’s creation.”
In a statement on Wednesday, election officials in Los Angeles County, one of the county offices that received the ultimatum from the DOJ, pointed out the threat was issued just 21 days before midterm elections. The county statement said it had received a thumb drive with the letter and a handwritten note with what appeared to be a password, but it would not attempt to access the drive because “we do not consider the device a secure medium”.
The county office said maintaining accurate voter lists was “a fundamental responsibility for our office” and that state laws clearly require that removing individuals be “based on verifiable information”.
Trump has repeatedly levelled the false claim that large numbers of noncitizens, who are legally not eligible to vote in federal elections, are casting ballots in Democratic-led states, including in California. State officials, including in California, have said the number of such voters is negligible and that the scale of the problem does not warrant intervention just weeks before elections, scheduled for November 3.
California Governor Gavin Newsom has sharply rebuked the DOJ lawsuit against his state, calling it a “sad, desperate attempt by” Trump to “suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day”.
“Courts have made clear the federal government has no role in running state elections,” Newsom said in a statement. “We will defend free and fair elections in the Golden State and call out every authoritarian attempt to undermine our democracy.”
Trump has long falsely claimed that noncitizen voting cost him the 2020 election, blaming it on Democrats, despite the issue being a very rare occurrence.
Courts have pushed back on Trump
Earlier this month, a federal judge in Florida ruled that a federal law criminalising voting by noncitizens was unconstitutional, delivering a major setback for Trump administration efforts to pursue such cases against individuals.
The court ruled that, under the US Constitution, only individual states have the authority to set voter qualifications, and that each one had already criminalised such voting by anyone who was not a citizen. Thus, it was up to the state to prosecute such individuals. The DOJ has at least 45 such cases pending nationwide, where the accused could now raise the same objection brought up in the Florida ruling.
Another federal judge ruled this month that the DOJ unlawfully sought state voter rolls for cross-checking them against a controversial federal immigration database to identify ineligible voters. The Trump administration has often touted the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) database, but numerous reports have found it inaccurate and capable of flagging citizens as noncitizens. Forcing states to use such a database would be unconstitutional, the judge said.
In September, the US Supreme Court rejected a Trump administration effort to restrict mail-in ballots for the November 3 elections, which Trump argued were especially susceptible to misuse by noncitizens because states were failing to verify who was sending them.
Two dozen states, led by Democrats, filed lawsuits against the Trump administration over attempts to limit mail-in voting, including an executive order directing federal agencies such as the US Postal Service not to handle mail-in ballots without verifying the eligibility of those casting them.
According to the Election Assistance Commission, a bipartisan government agency, around 30 percent of all ballots cast in the 2024 elections were sent by mail. Mail-in ballots are even more widely used in many western states such as California.

US considering easing sanctions on shadow fleet – Reuters
A US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Reuters, as reported by Ukrinform.
The discussions began several days after President Donald Trump temporarily suspended sanctions on Russian diesel fuel.
The current talks concern the possibility of allowing “legal oil” to be transported on vessels that were previously sanctioned, the US official said. This refers to oil and petroleum products not subject to US sanctions, rather than Russian or Iranian oil, which remains under US sanctions.
According to the official, the goal is to increase the volumes of oil and petroleum products shipped out of the Gulf.
According to the research firm Energy Aspects, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a video address to participants of the World Petroleum Congress, which is taking place in Riyadh this week, that the administration is discussing the possibility of easing sanctions on “shadow fleet” vessels. He said this would help reduce high freight rates, which have led to lower demand for U.S. oil.
Companies wishing to use sanctioned vessels would have to submit a request to the US Treasury Department, the official said.
The US Department of Energy said that any potential easing of sanctions on the shadow fleet would not help Russia transport oil or petroleum products.
High oil and fuel prices pose a political risk for Trump ahead of the U.S. midterm elections scheduled for November 3. Republicans hope to retain control of both chambers of Congress.
At the same time, easing the restrictions is unlikely to quickly increase available shipping capacity in the mainstream tanker fleet. Most vessels sanctioned because of their links to Russia or Venezuela are relatively old and generally in poor technical condition.
In addition, lifting the sanctions is unlikely to significantly lower freight rates, as vessel insurers would still be required to comply with regulatory requirements in the EU and the United Kingdom, maritime industry representatives said.
As reported by Ukrinform, US President Donald Trump said that preparations were underway in Greenland to launch large-scale exploration for oil, gas and other mineral resources.

The United States allowed Lukoil to continue operating abroad despite sanctions

The United States allowed Lukoil to continue operating abroad despite sanctions
Kyiv • UNN
The U.S. Treasury Department allowed transactions involving Lukoil’s assets abroad until April 24, 2027. Sanctions against the company remain in effect.
The U.S. Department of the Treasury has extended until April 24, 2027, the authorization to conduct transactions involving the foreign assets of the Russian oil company "Lukoil." The decision concerns a network of gas stations and enterprises in Bulgaria that came under U.S. sanctions. This is evidenced by documents from the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), reports UNN.
Details
The new general licenses authorize transactions involving foreign gas stations associated with Lukoil International GmbH, as well as a number of Bulgarian subsidiaries of the Russian oil giant.
In particular, the authorization applies to Lukoil Neftohim Burgas, Lukoil Bulgaria, Lukoil Aviation Bulgaria, and Lukoil Bulgaria Bunker. At the same time, the decision does not mean a complete lifting of sanctions against "Lukoil."
Why the U.S. extended the authorizations for the Russian company
The previous license for transactions involving foreign gas stations was valid until October 29, 2026. The U.S. Treasury has now extended its term by nearly six months.
The U.S. imposed sanctions on "Lukoil" on October 22, 2025. After that, the Russian company announced its intention to sell its foreign business.
To carry out such a deal, OFAC issued a separate license, the validity of which U.S. authorities have already extended repeatedly. The previous authorization to sell the assets was valid until October 22, 2026.
Thus, Washington is maintaining sanctions against the Russian company while at the same time permitting certain transactions involving its foreign assets.

futurewave’s arc silver bracelet politely tells you to put your phone down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:31:23 UTC
06:31:23 KST

futurewave’s arc silver bracelet politely tells you to put your phone down
no screen, no notifications, and no data to obsess over: the belgian studio imagines a connected object that knows when to leave us alone.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
FUTUREWAVE’S BRACELET USES HAPTIC FEEDBACK TO REDUCE SCREEN TIME
Belgian design studio Futurewave has unveiled Arc, a silver bracelet conceived to remind its wearer when it might be time to look away from their phone. Rather than adding another screen to an already crowded collection of connected devices, the concept takes the form of a sculptural piece of jewelry that delivers a discreet vibration when phone use exceeds a previously established limit. Made from Argentium silver and designed to be worn like a traditional open torc, Arc explores an unusual proposition for wearable technology: doing less, rather than more.
The idea is deliberately straightforward. Through a portal accessed from the phone, users select a group of applications and establish a threshold, such as 30 minutes of uninterrupted screen attention. Once that limit is reached, the bracelet sends a gentle pulse through its structure and into the wrist. If the wearer continues using the phone, a second identical pulse follows before the device falls silent and begins a new interval. There are no notifications to dismiss, applications to block or statistics to review. According to Futurewave, the system keeps no usage history and requires neither an account nor a subscription.
ARC BRACELET COMBINES ORGANIC FORMS WITH ARGENTIUM SILVER
Beyond its digital function, Arc has been conceived as a piece of jewelry in its own right. Its silhouette draws from the ancient torc, an open metal collar or bracelet associated with European Iron Age cultures, while its rounded, interconnected volumes evoke anatomical and natural structures. References explored during development include rib cages, wishbones, hydroids and chains of seed pods. The result is a continuous, sculptural form that wraps around the wrist without a clasp, hinge or visible fastening mechanism. Its design is intentionally gender-neutral, placing the emphasis on material and form rather than conventional jewelry categories.
The bracelet is designed to be shell-cast in Argentium silver, an alloy chosen for the finished object’s premium character. Its development involved a series of 3D-printed form studies, evolving from simple circular bands to more elaborate beaded and lobed surfaces. Stainless steel and titanium prototypes were also produced as part of the exploration. Developed by Hugo Simon, Pierre Heuson, Joachim Froment and Futurewave, the selected design conceals its technological components within the flowing metal structure. The ambition is for Arc to remain visually and physically compelling even without its digital function.
HAPTIC TECHNOLOGY HIDES INSIDE FUTUREWAVE’S SCREEN-FREE JEWELRY
Inside the proposed architecture, a piezoelectric element generates the brief tactile signals, selected for its ability to produce a clearly defined pulse. An ONiO zero low-power microcontroller manages the connection with the phone through Bluetooth Low Energy, while a flexible circuit board follows the curvature of the bracelet. The design also incorporates a 25 mAh curved battery, charging circuitry and piezoelectric energy harvesting. None of these components are intended to be visible from the outside. With no display, sound or illuminated indicators, the bracelet communicates exclusively through touch, leaving the surrounding world to provide the visual entertainment.
The project also raises a question about the relationship between luxury objects and technological obsolescence. ‘Jewellery first, one gesture inside it, and nothing kept,’ explains Cédric de Bellefroid, co-founder and CEO of Futurewave. The studio imagines a product whose value does not entirely depend on the lifespan of its electronics: once the technology stops working, the silver bracelet can simply remain a bracelet. Revealed in September 2026, Arc is currently a concept that has undergone 3D printing and prototyping, with no announced production or launch date. For now, it offers a rather elegant contradiction: another connected object designed to help us disconnect.
project info:
name: Arc
designer: Hugo Simon, Pierre Heuson, Joachim Froment, Futurewave | @futurewave_design
location: Brussels, Belgium

Late discord delays Franco-German deal on Made in Europe, car emissions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:22:12 UTC
06:22:12 KST

Late discord delays Franco-German deal on Made in Europe, car emissions
The draft pact supports tighter eligibility rules for non-EU countries to participate in public procurement and public support, and softens the 2035 combustion engine ban.
France's President Emmanuel Macron at the international Paris Motor Show at the Porte de Versailles in Paris on Oct. 12, 2026. | Thibault Camus/Pool/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — France and Germany on Thursday failed to agree a common position on the scope of the bloc’s future “Made in Europe” rules, as well as on greater flexibility for CO2 emissions cuts and the 2035 combustion engine ban.
The draft quid-pro-quo deal, which was first reported by POLITICO in July, marks a major convergence between the two countries and had been expected to be signed imminently. On Thursday evening, however, the agreement stalled amid opposition from Germany’s Social Democratic Party, the center-left junior partner in the ruling coalition, over concerns it dropped key environmental targets.
“A final agreement has yet to be reached,” a German government spokesperson said.
Advertisement
Earlier this week, French President Emmanuel Macron had suggested the ball was in the German court. “There are political constraints on the other side of the Rhine, and I completely respect coalition discussions,” Macron said Monday on the sidelines of the Paris car show.
Under the terms of the proposed deal, Germany would accept stricter Made in Europe criteria for the automotive sector in the Industrial Accelerator Act, which France has pushed for, in exchange for weakening the combustion engine ban, one of Berlin’s long-term demands.
"In light of the significant technological, economic and geopolitical changes since the existing regulatory framework was established, the Automotive Package should strike a better balance between climate objectives, industrial competitiveness, technological development and the strengthening of European value creation," the two countries wrote in a draft agreement obtained by POLITICO.
"Based on the Franco-German Ministerial Councils in 2025 and 2026, Germany and France therefore propose a balanced negotiating package combining ambitious CO₂ reduction targets with additional flexibility and targeted incentives for European value creation," the agreement adds.
Currently, the EU's target is for companies to reduce combustion engine emissions by 100% from 2021 levels by 2035, with the possibility to 'earn' 10% of emissions leeway through initiatives like offsets and investments.
Under the proposed deal, France and Germany want to soften the 2035 target to 90%, and to offer a further 10% leeway in exchange for investments in alternative fuels (for a combined 80%).
Advertisement
Crucially for steel manufacturers and Germany’s leftist SPD, the French-German agreement would axe the green steel investment requirement, removing a key incentive.
“This destroys the lead market for the steel industry,” an industry lobbyist told POLITICO on condition of anonymity to discuss the sensitive topic. In failing to put pressure on automakers to source green steel, the draft deal makes it a “nice-to-have” extra, they explained.
In a concession to Berlin, the draft agreement stresses that the so-called utility factor — which calculates plug-in hybrid emissions based on how often a vehicle’s electric motor is used vs. its combustion engine — should be calculated on lab-based results rather than real-world data, as required by the Commission. The change will help automakers sell more plug-in hybrids while still reaching the broader emissions targets.
In exchange for these emissions concessions, Germany endorsed France’s demand that the scope of the Made in Europe rules under the bloc’s Industrial Accelerator Act be restricted when it comes to the automotive sector.
The text only covers the EU’s 27 member countries and will be extended to the U.K. under certain conditions.
EU industry chief Stéphane Séjourné told POLITICO on Tuesday that he supported the deal as a way of breaking the impasse, and said the U.K. currently qualifies for Made in Europe.
Advertisement
The agreement could resolve a stalemate over both the CO2 regulation and the IAA, in which France and Germany have been on opposite sides. “The elements of this combined package should be adopted as soon as possible and at the same time,” the two countries wrote.
The British government welcomed the potential inclusion of the U.K. in the Made in Europe rules for cars.
“This is a Franco-German proposal and there is still a European process to run, but if confirmed, we welcome the objective to have the U.K. included in the Industrial Accelerator Act, and this would be good news for the British automotive industry and the jobs and investment it supports across the U.K.,” a No. 10 official said in a statement.
If approved, the comprehensive Franco-German deal will still have to be approved by other EU countries and by the European Parliament, which are currently discussing the Industrial Accelerator Act and the automotive package, including emissions targets for automakers.
Carlo Martuscelli, Francesca Micheletti and Graham Lanktree contributed to this report.

F-35 Drops 8 Bombs in Quick Succession During ‘Ripple’ Test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:17:47 UTC
06:17:47 KST

The Marine Corps recently conducted its first-ever “ripple” release of eight Small Diameter Bomb IIs from an F-35B, a key early step in proving out the capability for all F-35 variants.
A “ripple release” refers to munitions all being released in one pass instead of multiple go-arounds. Marine aviators from the Marine Operational Test and Evaluation Squadron 1 at Yuma Proving Ground, Ariz., conducted the test Sept. 15, retired Air Force Maj. Gen. Jon Norman, Raytheon’s vice president for air and space systems, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
SDB II, also called “StormBreaker,” is a 250-pound, low-yield, precision-guided munition that can hit moving targets in all weather conditions at ranges of at least 46 miles. It is a joint effort between the Air Force and Department of the Navy and is built by RTX’s Raytheon.
While software and other issues have delayed fielding StormBreaker on the F-35, the “ripple” capability could be critical to the Lockheed Martin-made stealthy fighter down the line, Norman argued.
“From a pilot perspective, it’s nice because you’re not sitting there exposing yourself when you have eight targets to address,” he said.
It also eliminates the need to do hands-on weaponeering for each bomb.
“You address the entire target set, so it’s less workload in the cockpit, and you’re able to achieve an effect that I think the pilots are really going to appreciate,” Norman said.
The networked missiles can also be confined to a defined kill box to ensure they strike only a specific area on the battlefield.
“We’re able to set boundaries,” Norman said. “So, you give it a kill box, and it’ll exclude everything outside of that and only hit within that kill box.”
That’s a key upgrade for the StormBreaker compared to what the bomb is replacing—cluster munitions. SDB II was developed to give pilots an option to replace legacy-era cluster munitions following the 2008 DOD policy directive, which set a 2019 deadline to stop using the area-saturation weapons that had high failure rates and could produce swaths of unexploded ordnance on battlefields.
So, a pilot could spot a boat swarm, quickly set the parameters, and then launch eight 250-pound missiles to destroy the mini-fleet in one pass, Norman said.
“Through automated target recognition software that’s built into it, we can hit prioritized threats,” Norman said. “So, if one fails or one gets shot down, then they just reorder the prioritization.”
F-35 Tests
Low-rate initial production on the StormBreaker started in 2015, and the Air Force cleared the bomb to go on its “objective” aircraft, the F-15E, in 2020. But the service hopes to integrate the munition onto many more platforms, including the F-35A. The Navy, meanwhile, cleared the SDB II to go on its F/A-18E/F this February, though its objective aircraft remains the F-35B and C.
But while the F-15 and F/A-18 carry the StormBreaker externally, the F-35 uses its internal weapons bays to maintain stealthiness, offering a new wrinkle to the ripple release process. The F-35B has the smallest internal capacity of the variants, to accommodate the fan that enables vertical landings.
The next ripple release test is planned for this quarter over a small range in Texas, Norman said.
“We’ll take those results then to the Air Force and to the Navy and the Marines and say, “we’ve demonstrated this capability, is this something you’re interested in?’” Norman told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
Future tests could include striking moving targets at sea with multiple munitions, Norman said—a particularly relevant capability, given reports of swarming boat attacks by the Iranian military in the Strait of Hormuz.
As Raytheon works on refining the “ripple eight” capability for operational use, the F-35 fleet is awaiting rolling software patches to fully incorporate the StormBreaker into its arsenal.
A July report from the Government Accountability Office noted that “SDB II initial capability on the F-35 is delayed 2 years, and program officials said that it might be delayed 2 more years due to F-35 software development issues.”
The F-35 fleet has undergone its third technology refresh, or TR-3, which upgraded the L3Harris core processor, replaced the aircraft’s memory storage unit, and installed multicore processors. But while a “truncated” version of TR-3 was completed in 2025, the fleet is still getting software patches to continue upgrades.
“Development on TR-3 was completed in 2025,” Lockheed Martin spokesperson Mireya Villarreal told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email. “We continue to build on this baseline through the Block 4 modernization program, which implements upgrades including additional weapons, electronic warfare capabilities and improved sensor technology to ensure the warfighter can defeat any threat.”
StormBreaker’s Future
in addition to the ripple release test, Norman said Raytheon is working to extend the StormBreaker’s 46-mile range by exploring engine efficiencies and design work on the bomb’s body.
“We don’t want to constrain pilots,” Norman said. “We want to give them their full operating envelope to be able to release this.”
At the program’s inception, the Pentagon planned to acquire 21,160 StormBreakers, but that figure has now risen to 31,800, according to the GAO report
“Last year we produced and delivered 1,500 StormBreakers. This year we’re increasing that,” Norman said. He could not provide specific numbers for this year’s deliveries.
“But it’s a significant increase, and we have capacity in the factory to increase more,” he said.

Fenerbahce defeated Serbia's Partizan 74-65 at home Thursday in the sixth round of the EuroLeague basketball competition, securing their second victory of the week.
Partizan made a fast start, opening the game with a 6-0 run behind three-pointers from Ethan Thompson and Lamar Stevens.
Fenerbahce responded but trailed 19-12 at the end of the first quarter.
The hosts gradually closed the gap in the second period, with Shane Larkin hitting Fenerbahce's first three-pointer of the game.
Fenerbahce went into halftime trailing 28-25.

Will Clyburn added a three-pointer as Fenerbahce continued to pull away, entering the final quarter with a 59-44 advantage.
Partizan reduced the deficit early in the fourth quarter, but Fenerbahce maintained their lead to secure a 74-65 victory.
The result gave Fenerbahce their fifth EuroLeague win of the season and their eighth victory over Partizan.
Fenerbahce also set a EuroLeague single-game record with 14 blocks against Partizan.
The Turkish side completed their double-header week with two wins, while Partizan suffered their third defeat of the competition.

Congo Ebola outbreak spreads to new province bordering Central African Republic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Congo Ebola outbreak spreads to new province bordering Central African Republic
DAKAR, Senegal - The ongoing Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo has spread to a new province bordering Central African Republic, two health officials said on Oct 15, posing a fresh challenge for authorities struggling to contain it.
North Ubangi becomes the eighth province to be affected by the outbreak of the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which was announced in mid-May and has become the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record, with more than 9,000 cases and more than 4,000 deaths confirmed.
Two cases have been confirmed in North Ubangi, the officials said. They have not been officially announced by Congolese authorities.
Ituri province remains the epicentre of the outbreak though cases have increased recently in North Kivu province. Cases have also been confirmed in South Kivu, Tshopo, Haut-Uele, Bas-Uele and South Ubangi provinces.
A health official in North Ubangi told Reuters on Oct 15 there had been a series of suspect deaths recently in a mining area in Wapinda health zone, close to the border with Bas-Uele, prompting samples to be analysed at a provincial laboratory and in Kinshasa.
In addition to spreading within Congo, the outbreak has also resulted in cases in Uganda, which was declared Ebola-free in August, and in Kenya, which announced its first Ebola infection earlier in October and announced a second case - a close family member of the first one - on Oct 14. REUTERS

A dangerous virus that has already claimed 130 lives is rapidly spreading across Europe
Kyiv • UNN
The EU has recorded 1,715 cases of West Nile virus, and 130 people have died. The infection is spreading to northern Europe through mosquito bites.
A record spread of West Nile virus, transmitted primarily through mosquito bites, has been recorded in European Union countries. This year, 1,715 people fell ill, 130 of whom died. Politico reports this, citing the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), writes UNN.
Details
Greece, Italy, and France were the hardest hit by the infection. However, medical professionals are drawing attention to a new trend—the virus is gradually spreading to northern Europe, where it had previously been detected much less frequently.
In particular, 59 cases of infection were registered in the Netherlands this year, and 15 in Belgium. ECDC experts warn that the spread of the infection to the north may continue in the coming years.
Why West Nile virus is dangerous and how to protect yourself
According to medical professionals, approximately 80% of those infected have no symptoms at all. In other cases, the disease may be accompanied by a fever and a general deterioration in well-being.
In severe cases, the virus can affect the nervous system, cause serious neurological complications, and lead to death.
The main route of infection is through the bites of infected mosquitoes. Therefore, European medical professionals recommend using repellents, wearing loose-fitting clothing that covers the body in the evening and at night, and installing mosquito screens on windows.
The ECDC emphasizes that everyone living in or traveling to regions where the virus has already been detected should follow these measures.

US Justice Department sues California for voter rolls, citing alleged noncitizens
Unknown

2026-10-15

06:14:36 KST

Diyar Guldogan
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
The US Justice Department, working with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), filed a complaint Thursday against California for its voter-registration lists, alleging that more than 20,000 people who are likely noncitizens are registered to vote in the state.
The federal government said its preliminary analysis identified individuals who may be ineligible to vote in federal elections after comparing publicly available California voter-registration records with federal immigration data. The review remains ongoing, according to DHS.
Federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections. The Justice Department alleges that California has allowed individuals believed to be ineligible to remain on its voter rolls and claims the state failed to take action after federal officials raised concerns.
“State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement.
Blanche said that if the allegations are established in court, California would have undermined confidence in the electoral system and violated laws protecting the country's representative system of government.
The Justice Department said it would continue investigating suspected voter fraud and pursuing legal action to enforce federal election laws.
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said federal officials reviewed publicly available California voter-registration files and compared relevant records with federal immigration data to identify people believed to be noncitizens.
“This preliminary analysis has identified a significant number of individuals in California who are likely noncitizens and appear to be registered to vote; the analysis and review remain ongoing,” he said.
The lawsuit is the latest move by President Donald Trump’s administration to expand federal oversight of elections ahead of the midterms on Nov. 3, as Republicans face a competitive fight to maintain control of both chambers of Congress.

15 major US media organizations move to unseal search warrant records for Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:12:43 UTC
06:12:43 KST

Yasin Gungor
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Fifteen prominent news organizations asked a federal court Thursday to unseal search warrant documents and supporting affidavits federal agents used during a raid on the Washington, DC home of US Rep. Ilhan Omar earlier this week.
News organizations told the court that Americans possess a fundamental constitutional entitlement to review why law enforcement entered an elected official's private residence, asserting that investigative materials become presumptively public after being executed and formally returned.
Fourteen media organizations, including Reuters, The Associated Press, The Washington Post, and CNN, filed a motion with the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. The New York Times is pursuing a separate legal challenge seeking disclosure.
The motions seek public disclosure of judicial records, including the search warrant and all attachments; the underlying warrant application; probable cause affidavits submitted by federal investigators; motions to seal; court sealing orders; the property inventory return from the Oct. 12 operation; and any related docket entries. The New York Times also requested any transcripts of court proceedings regarding the warrant.
The outlets argued that prior public acknowledgments by administration officials substantially undermine the government's justification for secrecy.
Organizations contended that targeted redactions can address legitimate operational sensitivities or individual privacy protections rather than blanket withholding of judicial records.
Citing the "experience and logic" legal doctrine, the group stressed that open access curbs potential investigative abuse, ensures judicial fairness and maintains confidence in legal procedures during a high-profile inquiry conducted weeks before an election.
The US will hold midterm elections on Nov. 3.
Federal agents executed a court-approved search warrant at Omar's residence at 6 am local time (1000GMT) Monday. The Justice Department confirmed that Homeland Security Investigations carried out the judicially authorized warrant as part of an active federal inquiry into immigration documents completed during her childhood, according to Fox News.
Omar criticized the search, describing the operation as an effort by the Trump administration to intimidate political opponents.
Tensions have escalated between Omar and US President Donald Trump about regional law enforcement, including an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) initiative in her home state of Minnesota. Trump has repeatedly linked the measures to fraud accusations involving the state's Somali community while targeting Omar's background and citizenship. Omar was born in Somalia.
Omar’s family came to the US in 1995, when she was a teen, after securing asylum.

Bus hits train stopped on French side of Channel Tunnel, with 19 injured
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15

Bus hits train stopped on French side of Channel Tunnel, with 19 injured
- Published
A bus has hit a stationary freight train near the French entrance to the Channel Tunnel, injuring the driver and 18 passengers, French authorities say.
The bus, which was carrying lorry drivers due to take a shuttle rail service, struck the train at the loading platform of the tunnel in Coquelles, near Calais, at 19:27 (18:27 BST) on Thursday.
The bus driver and one passenger were severely injured and evacuated by helicopter. None of the injuries were life threatening, a local official said.
Local sub-prefect Agathe Cury said freight and Eurostar passenger traffic through the tunnel had not been disrupted after a brief stoppage to evacuate injured people. An investigation has begun.
"Two trains were on either side of the platform. One was being loaded by heavy goods vehicles ahead of a cross-Channel journey, and another train that had previously been loaded was departing," Cury said.
"For a reason that currently remains unknown, the minibus collided with the departing train.
"The bus did not overturn, it is still upright – but the shock and the collision caused injuries to the people involved."
The incident involved a minibus transporting workers who were about to board Le Shuttle. All were men of different nationalities, she added.
It is not clear whether any British nationals are among the injured.
Cury said it was "the first time an incident of this type has occurred" on an Eurotunnel loading platform.
The BBC's Evan Davis, who was travelling through the Eurotunnel to Calais at the time of the incident, witnessed blue light vehicles "concentrated on one of the platforms" as he entered France.
"There were plenty of cars queueing up at check-in when I drove past just now, and I saw some cars going through check-in, so despite the collision they weren't being held," he said from the scene.
Photos published by local French newspaper La Voix du Nord, external showed a small bus with damage to its front and side standing alongside a train, among a crowd of emergency workers.
Eurostar has released an update saying: "An incident occurred several kilometers away from the Channel Tunnel.
"This incident does not involved or impact Eurostar trains running from and to London. All of Eurostar trains will run as expected."
The Eurotunnel runs under the sea between England and France, from Folkestone in Kent to Coquelles on the French side.
Three different rail services operate through the tunnel - the Eurostar, a passenger train that begins in London and goes to several European destinations, freight trains which transport goods and Le Shuttle, which transports vehicles.

At least five people were killed and 16 wounded Thursday when Yemen's Houthi forces struck the presidential palace complex in the southern city of Aden, as the group also claimed to have hit a Saudi fighter jet amid escalating hostilities with the Saudi-led coalition.
The missile and drone attack targeted Al-Maashiq palace, the headquarters of Yemen's internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government, marking the first such strike on the complex in the latest round of fighting.
Yemeni Health Minister Qasim Buhaibeh said the casualties included security guards and civilian employees, while Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani confirmed that the prime minister and Cabinet members were unharmed.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed responsibility for the attack, saying the group had targeted what it described as a Saudi military operations headquarters in Aden.
The Houthi-run SABA news agency alleged that Saudi officers operated the facility and that it housed weapons depots, claims that could not be independently verified.
Meanwhile, the Houthis released footage purportedly showing a missile striking a Royal Saudi Air Force Eurofighter Typhoon over Yemen's northern Saada province late Wednesday.
Saree claimed the fighter jet, which reportedly departed from Saudi Arabia's Taif Air Base, had been directly hit and was at risk of crashing.
However, the infrared footage appeared to show a missile detonating near the aircraft rather than striking it directly, with the pilot apparently maneuvering away from the explosion.
A visible trail from the aircraft's left wing raised speculation about possible damage from missile fragments, although neither the extent of any damage nor the authenticity of the footage could be independently confirmed.
Saudi authorities have not confirmed the incident, and there have been no verified reports of a fighter jet being shot down.
The missile involved was believed by some observers to be a Barq surface-to-air missile, a weapon associated with Houthi air defense systems and reportedly linked to Iranian missile technology.
The alleged engagement came as Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of intensifying missile and drone attacks against airports, ports and energy infrastructure across the kingdom.
Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki said Thursday that Houthi forces had launched 20 attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh this month, killing 17 people and injuring 333 others.
Separate attacks on Abha airport in southwestern Saudi Arabia killed three people and wounded 28, according to the coalition.
Maliki accused the Houthis of acquiring advanced weapons, including ballistic missiles, drones and explosive-laden boats, with assistance from regional actors.
He also said coalition forces had destroyed 127 weapons storage facilities and launch platforms in Yemen.
The coalition separately announced that it had intercepted and destroyed drones over Khamis Mushait and another area in southern Saudi Arabia.
Following the developments, the Houthis warned airlines that Saudi airspace and airports were unsafe, excluding the airspace above the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
The renewed violence follows the collapse of a prolonged lull in Yemen's civil war, which began in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention the following year.
Fighting resumed last month amid a broader regional conflict that erupted following U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
Yemeni government forces have since launched operations to recapture Houthi-held territory, including areas near the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a vital route for international shipping.
Humanitarian organizations have warned that the renewed fighting risks worsening Yemen's already severe humanitarian crisis.

====================================================================================================

ICE tactics spark debate before pivotal US midterm elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:02:31 UTC
06:02:31 KST

ICE tactics spark debate before pivotal US midterm elections
Polls have found that Trump’s hardline immigration enforcement effort has divided voters before the 2026 midterm race.
United States President Donald Trump’s mandate for aggressive immigration enforcement has fractured public support in advance of next month’s critical midterm elections.
In the lead-up to the November 3 vote, Fox News released a poll that found 53 percent of registered voters felt the immigration crackdown had “gone too far”.
That rate was even higher among demographics that may be key to the Republican Party’s prospects in November.
The poll, conducted in September, found that 60 percent of independent voters agreed with the idea that Trump’s immigration efforts have overreached. Two-thirds of Hispanic participants also agreed with the campaign having “gone too far”.
Experts say the political debate about immigration in the US has shifted since the last major election in 2024. At the time, the focus was largely on border security. But increasingly, attention has fallen on how enforcement operations are being conducted.
Cynthia Penaloza is among those questioning the Trump administration’s tactics.
In August, her sister, 23-year-old Joceline Penaloza Magana, was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in Houston, Texas, during a traffic stop. Joceline remains in custody to this day.
“We’re always afraid. We’re uncertain of what’s going to happen, if she’s going to be sent back to Mexico, if we’re ever going to be together again or how this is going to change our lives forever,” Cynthia told Al Jazeera correspondent Phil Lavelle.
She rejects Trump’s assertion that his administration’s immigration enforcement operations have targeted “the worst of the worst”.
Joceline, according to the Penaloza family, was an honour roll student who does not have a criminal record. She was brought to the US as a young child, about five years old.
“She’s always been a good girl,” Cynthia told Lavelle.
A focus on ‘criminals’
Still, the Trump administration has tied its campaign of mass deportation to efforts to control crime.
In a statement earlier this year, the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees immigration enforcement, credited Trump’s policies with having “unleashed ICE to target the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens, including pedophiles, murderers, gang members, terrorists, and rapists”.
Immigration arrests have been on the rise under Trump. In September, ICE announced it had tallied two consecutive months with more than 50,000 immigration arrests, beating a record set in June, when 43,900 people were detained.
Homeland Security has argued that approximately 70 percent of its immigration detainees are criminals, if pending charges are factored in.
But critics have questioned that statistic, given that the legal system in the US gives suspects the presumption of innocence until they are proven guilty in a court of law.
In other words, many of the accused could be acquitted or see their charges dropped. A large portion of those with criminal charges may also be accused of non-violent crimes.
Analysts have found that a majority of people currently in immigration custody are not considered criminals under the law. According to the Deportation Data Project, which analyses government data sets, some 70 percent of those held in ICE detention have no criminal record.
The Trump administration has nevertheless pushed to increase detentions.
“We need more. We need more arrests, and we need more deportations,” Tom Homan, the White House “border czar”, said in an interview in July.
Pushback on the campaign trail
The aggressive arrest tactics may have repercussions on the Republican campaign for the midterms, though.
Republicans are hoping to defend their majorities in both chambers of Congress, as well as in key state and local elections.
Trump made significant gains in the 2024 elections with Hispanic voters. During his re-election bid, he received nearly 48 percent support among Latinos, according to an exit poll from the Pew Research Center — up 12 percentage points from the 2020 election.
But Pew found that his gains may be eroding. Among the Hispanic voters who supported him in 2024, his approval rating has steadily declined, from a high of 93 percent at the start of 2025 to a low of 57 percent as of last week.
Some Republicans running in the midterm election, including Congress member Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida, have even openly criticised the president’s hardline immigration policies.
“Mr President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” Salazar said in an advertisement campaign launched in September. She cited the large number of immigrants who were arrested without a criminal record.
Other Republicans, however, blame previous presidencies for creating the conflict over immigration enforcement.
“A mess was created, and now cleaning it up is dirty business,” Jeremy Price, a Republican in Texas, told Al Jazeera. “You’re having to find people, arrest them against their will and remove them from the country because they don’t want to leave.”
Democrats, meanwhile, hope to convert that outrage over immigration enforcement tactics into votes, come November.
“I would hope they’d abolish ICE,” Richard Gonzales, the chair of the Hidalgo County Democratic Party in Texas, said in an interview with Al Jazeera’s Lavelle.
“I mean, in my perspective, I think that they’ve, the agency has just lost its identity, and there’s no way to rehabilitate that.”

"I think the US will find in the years and the decades to come that Ukraine will contribute a hell of a lot to American strength, both in terms of military power, but also its defense industrial base too," he said.
Streeting noted that while the United States is far removed geographically, "if aggression is rewarded, if borders can be redrawn by force, if the sovereignty of nations becomes negotiable, the consequences will not remain confined to Ukraine."
Fractures in US-Ukraine ties
Relations between Washington and Kiev have been increasingly tense in recent days, with President Donald Trump calling for Volodymyr Zelenskyy to be replaced after the Ukrainian leader slammed a US deal allowing more Russian diesel into global markets.
Trump also accused Zelenskyy of ignoring instructions to not strike Russian refineries, while Kiev and its European allies warned against easing pressure on Moscow.
Zelenskyy said on Thursday that Kiev would no longer abide by US President Trump's demands not to strike Russian oil refineries.
Zelensky met NATO chief Mark Rutte in Brussels and held a string of bilateral meetings with European leaders before he was set to join an EU summit on Friday.
"All of us in Europe want this war to end. And for that to happen, strong signals are needed — more real pressure on Russia and more defence support for Ukraine," Zelenskyy wrote online.
"It is especially important now to act together to protect lives."
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham also reiterated his "complete solidarity" with Zelenskyy over the weekend. Downing Street said the premier also pledged that Britain would "strengthen its sanctions on Russia."

AI Hacks Leave a Mess That AI Companies Aren’t Paying For
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:00:28 UTC
06:00:28 KST

When Philadelphia police criticized Anthropic last week for submitting a false tip about an unsolved murder, I thought it might become one of the first cases where an AI company faced legal consequences for misconduct by their agents.
The incident occurred on July 18, when Anthropic said it was testing its Claude Haiku 4.5 model’s ability to perform “example tasks on randomly selected webpages.” The model was instructed not to “submit anything destructive,” and yet, Claude filed a tip to police looking for information about an ongoing murder investigation. “I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area … during that time period,” Claude wrote. The submission, which didn’t include a name or contact information, landed in a spam folder, and officers didn’t review it until Anthropic discovered the gaffe on September 28 and notified the department October 7.
Knowingly providing fictitious information about a crime to police is a misdemeanor in Pennsylvania, but so far, authorities have not pressed charges against Anthropic, and it's unclear if they ever will. Solomon Leach, a spokesperson for the Philadelphia district attorney, says the office “does not comment on whether something is being actively investigated.”
Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Despite all the attention paid to OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face and many other examples of AI agent misbehavior that have come to light in recent months, only one major known lawsuit has been filed seeking to hold model makers liable. That case was brought by an advocacy group, rather than a direct hacking victim.
AI agents have interfered with hobbyist forums, government websites, and various software tools. The victims have shouldered some costs, including for extra strain on their servers and the time they have expended plugging latent security vulnerabilities.
Government regulators, including the European Union, the US Federal Trade Commission, and some US states, are reportedly still investigating OpenAI and Anthropic over the incidents. But a deference across continents toward promoting innovation could enable companies to escape any immediate penalties.
When Rick Elrod, a software engineer living in Germany, noticed a URL shortener he helps maintain behaving oddly recently, he called up two security researchers he was friendly with to see if they could diagnose the issue. The researchers found agents from Anthropic and other providers using the service, known as da.gd, to get around rules the AI labs put in place to control their behavior, Elrod says. (For instance, Anthropic says it limits the length of website addresses Claude can visit to prevent it from taking malicious actions by stuffing data onto the end of the URLs.)
Da.gd’s investigation and ongoing efforts to prevent further abuse of its tool have taken “a fair bit of time,” says Joe Needleman, one of the security researchers providing pro bono assistance. But he and the others supporting da.gd view the situation as a valuable learning opportunity.
“This was eye-opening,” Needleman says, adding that da.gd has “no means and no plans” to seek compensation from Anthropic for the cleanup, since “we saw many agents doing similar activities, not all was attributable to autonomous agents,” and “not all of it was Anthropic alone.”
Sellers of cybersecurity tools are eager to pass the buck to the victims. At an event this week hosted by the bug-hunting software developer Snyk, panelists from the startup, one of its investors, OpenAI, and Google all encouraged organizations to use AI agents to shore up their defenses against, well, other AI agents. “We've got to reinvent everything to match machine scale with machine scale,” said Ed Sim, a general partner at Boldstart Ventures. He and others expressed little interest in regulating AI labs.
Manoj Nair, chief technology and innovation officer at Snyk, said large businesses patch an average of one bug for every eight they find because of limited human resources. But he said it was imperative for people to hand over some of the bug hunting, fixing, and monitoring to AI agents. “You got to get to a point where you can fix everything, because in the age of agentic hacking, “those 10 things are gonna become 100 things before you know it.” He later added that AI “is not an adversity if you flip it to a strength.”
Some companies are responding to the call to arm up. Bank of America announced this week it had hired 1,000 contractors to remediate bugs discovered by AI. Nair said just last week he heard from major corporations who were willing to temporarily shut down their systems to prioritize plugging security holes.
Anthropic and OpenAI have said they expect to continue reporting concerning incidents from their own testing. But the companies’ revenues continue to surge, whether it be from attackers or defenders, as consequences prove elusive.

The Bend-La Pine School District said in a statement on social media that the Silver Rail Elementary School was under lockdown.

World's most heavily armed society
The United States, where firearms are readily available, is a frequent scene of gun violence, with thousands of people killed every year.
It has the highest rate of gun-related deaths among all developed nations.
The deadliest school shooting in US history took place at Virginia Tech on April 16, 2007, when South Korean student Seung-Hui Cho killed 32 people and wounded 17 others before taking his own life.

Persistent mass shootings in the US have repeatedly heightened public calls for stricter federal gun control measures.
Despite repeated calls over the years, the US Congress has yet to enact such restrictions.
The United States holds the highest rate of civilian firearm ownership globally, making it the world's most heavily armed society.

Zelensky rallies European allies as Trump ties slump
BRUSSELS - Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky sought to rally European allies on Oct 15 after saying Kyiv would no longer abide by US President Donald Trump’s demands not to strike Russian oil refineries.
Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since last week, when Trump eased sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow releasing large amounts of diesel onto global markets.
Anger in Ukraine has been further heightened by outages to a critical US-provided satellite system that has hampered its military’s ability to counter Russia’s intense bombardments.
Against the backdrop of his latest falling-out with Trump, Zelensky met NATO chief Mark Rutte in Brussels and held a string of bilateral meetings with European leaders before he was set to join an EU summit on Oct 16.
“All of us in Europe want this war to end. And for that to happen, strong signals are needed – more real pressure on Russia and more defence support for Ukraine,” Zelensky wrote online.
“It is especially important now to act together to protect lives.”
European leaders have broadly thrown their support behind Zelensky, as they look to weather the latest storm in Trump’s volatile relations with Kyiv.
French President Emmanuel Macron on Oct 15 said it was “crucial” that Ukraine receive “all the means necessary to protect itself” after meeting Zelensky.
“I can reassure you, dear Ukrainian friends and President Zelensky: YOU ARE NOT ALONE,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk posted online.
‘Maximum destruction’
Zelensky has had to endure a rollercoaster relationship with Trump since the mercurial US leader returned to office in 2025.
In a move that risked infuriating Trump further, Zelensky told the Financial Times that Ukraine will no longer hold off targeting Russian refineries as Moscow was not abiding by a ceasefire on hitting energy infrastructure announced by the US leader.
As he met with Macron in Brussels, Zelensky said that the Kremlin had “launched yet another vile drone strike on Ukrainian energy infrastructure” in the city of Lutsk causing blackouts.
“Russia has demonstratively disregarded the American president’s proposal for an energy ceasefire. And now it is taking advantage of problems with Starlink operations to cause maximum destruction to everything that sustains everyday life,” he wrote online.
The Kremlin meanwhile accused Ukraine of derailing US peace efforts by resuming its strikes on refineries, with Russian authorities reporting a drone attack on an oil refinery south of Moscow that caused a fire.
Kyiv “continues to launch strikes against these facilities,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
“It is coming into serious conflict with the peace efforts of the United States and American negotiators, who are making vigorous efforts to initiate the peace process,” he added.
In Kyiv, residents told AFP they sensed a change in Washington’s attitude towards Ukraine.
“Let them live here for two to three days. All these nighttime attacks, what people here are going through – blackouts, no electricity. And then maybe he’ll see all this differently,” 30-year-old Alyona Nikitina said.
Russia has intensified its bombardment of Ukraine and its capital in recent months, leading to mounting civilian casualties and disrupting daily life for citizens.
Satellite row
Much of the outrage in Ukraine this week has been over restrictions to the Starshield satellite communications system that its military relies upon to detect incoming Russian attacks and to coordinate its frontline response.
Defence officials confirmed that the United States had threatened to withdraw intelligence-sharing if Ukraine continued long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries.
But tech billionaire Elon Musk, who has also called for Zelensky to be replaced as leader, said his SpaceX company was not behind any disruption to the Starshield system.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” he said.
“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he added, referring to Trump.
Ukraine uses the Starshield system from Musk’s SpaceX for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territory and interceptor drones.
It is separate from the parallel Starlink civilian satellite system, which Ukraine also uses but not for offensive operations.
Speeds were slower on Wednesday, affecting connectivity, officials said. AFP

Defence writes off millions owed since the seventies
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:51:53 BST
05:51:53 KST

A write-off of almost £3.7m recorded in the Ministry of Defence’s accounts relates to money owed to the department by a foreign nation between 1971 and 2006, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked why the International Military Services outstanding claim write-off appeared in the annual report and accounts for 2024 to 2025, published on 4 November last year.
Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “The write off was due to a historical debt balance relating to monies owed to MOD between 1971 and 2006 by a foreign nation.”
International Military Services was the Ministry of Defence’s own arms sales company, set up to handle government-to-government defence exports and wound down from the mid-1980s. It has been in members’ voluntary liquidation for decades and exists now mainly to deal with the legal and financial tail of contracts signed half a century ago. Balances dating back to 1971 are therefore still passing through departmental accounts in 2026.
The best known of those tails is the long dispute with Iran over tanks ordered by the Shah before the 1979 revolution and never delivered. That case ran through the English courts and international arbitration for more than forty years and ended with a settlement, reported at around £400 million, paid in 2022 at the same time as the release of Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe and Anoosheh Ashoori. The write-off described here is a separate and far smaller item, and the department has not identified the country involved.
Losses and special payments of this kind are reported each year in a department’s accounts under Treasury rules, with any individual item above a threshold disclosed and explained. A debt that has sat on the books for decades is eventually written off when there is no realistic prospect of recovery, which is an accounting decision and not a forgiveness of the obligation.
