Saudi Arabia accuses Iran of encouraging Houthis in latest escalation
Saudi Arabia on Thursday accused Iran of encouraging Yemen's Houthis in the dramatic escalation of their fight with the kingdom, adding that the Islamic republic continued to arm and train the group.
In a virtual briefing with reporters including AFP journalists, Saudi Arabia's deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry said Riyadh was still in touch with Iran, but that Tehran did not appear ready to make concessions.
Saudi Arabia, the world's top crude oil exporter, has come under sustained attack by the Houthis in recent days, shifting the focus of the Middle East war that erupted with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
It has launched retaliatory strikes on Houthi strongholds in Yemen - one of the world's poorest countries - but the Iran-backed group remains undeterred.
"Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of UN security council resolutions," said Dr. Rayed Krimly, the deputy minister.
"We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," he added.
The official said the kingdom continued "to have direct communications with Iran", but added: "Overall, it doesn't seem yet that the Iranians are able to provide the necessary concessions for a solution."
In 2023, regional rivals Iran and Saudi Arabia reached a deal mediated by China to thaw a longstanding freeze in ties, but the latest violence might threaten to upend the entente.
The Saudi official went on to accuse the Houthis of refusing to meet in Oman in recent weeks as fighting ramped up between the two sides.
"At the beginning of this escalation, we asked them to meet in Muscat, Oman and they refused," he added.
"This was the last communication which happened a few weeks ago."
Airport strikes
On Saturday, a strike hit Riyadh's international airport, killing 13 people and wounding around 300 others, in the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in a decade.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis on Thursday said the group had attacked Riyadh's airport 20 times in October.
During a presentation in Riyadh covering the strikes, coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki said "the Houthis must immediately cease all terrorist operations targeting civilians and civilian facilities, including airports, ports, oil facilities, and infrastructure".
"The terrorist Houthi militias have worked to obtain advanced technologies with the help of regional actors," he said, adding that the group now had "ballistic missiles, attack and suicide drones, and fast explosive-laden boats".
Yemen's civil war reignited in July after a years-long UN-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle East war that has rocked the region and roiled energy supplies and markets.
The situation took a sharp turn for the worse in September, when the Houthis launched a lightning offensive that saw them capture swathes of new territory in Yemen, including along the Red Sea coast where a waterway crucial to global energy flows is located.
On Thursday, the Houthis fired missiles at the presidential palace in Aden, which also serves as the headquarters of the internationally recognised government, security sources told AFP, while a journalist saw smoke rising from the site.
"Houthi missiles targeted the Al-Maashiq presidential palace in Aden," the government's interim capital, three local police sources said on condition of anonymity, after residents of the southern city reported hearing explosions.
Since their offensive began, the Houthis have also repeatedly targeted Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognised government whose forces they are battling on the ground.
The attacks on Saudi Arabia have tested the country's infrastructure and resilience, the energy minister acknowledged earlier this week.
Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events this time of year, including its flagship investment conference drawing foreign leaders and business titans.
In Yemen, the conflict has caused what the United Nations calls one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, leaving most of the nation's population dependent on aid.

A mother’s touch helps premature babies grow strong in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:43:01 UTC
02:43:01 KST

A mother’s touch helps premature babies grow strong in Gaza
At Nasser Hospital, a kangaroo mother care pilot programme helps vulnerable newborns as Gaza’s healthcare system struggles with shortages.
Khan Younis, Gaza Strip – For 11 days after giving birth last month, Rania Fadel could not hold her newborn son.
The 24-year-old gave birth to twin boys, Ilyas and Yahya, on September 25.
While Yahya was born healthy, Ilyas was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit at Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, in southern Gaza, where he remained for nearly two weeks.
Born prematurely, Ilyas weighed just 1.4 kilogrammes (3 pounds) at birth, according to his mother. He had medical issues affecting his blood and lungs, she said, and needed specialised care in an incubator.
Rania herself was recovering from a Caesarean section when her son was taken into intensive care. For days, she could not hold him.
“When they called me to hold him, I rushed over,” she recalled. “I was in a hurry to get to him. It was such a feeling.”
As Ilyas’s condition improved and he moved from intensive care to the hospital’s neonatal care unit, Rania was able to hold him against her bare chest, introducing her to a form of care for low-birthweight newborns known as kangaroo mother care, part of a newly-launched programme at the hospital.
It involves prolonged skin-to-skin contact between a caregiver – ideally the mother – and baby, with exclusive breast milk feeding, and has been shown to have important health benefits for premature and low-birthweight babies.
“I was so happy. It was such a beautiful feeling,” Rania said.
During the session, a nurse helped Rania position Ilyas against her chest, with his skin touching hers. Rania said he remained there for about 90 minutes.
“He started breastfeeding from me, and he stayed a little longer,” she said. “I felt he was improving.”
For Rania, the contact also brought a sense of closeness after days of separation.
“The baby feels that his mother is there,” she said. “He feels safe. Honestly, it makes me very happy.”
Skin-to-skin
Kangaroo mother care involves placing a baby against a parent’s bare chest for skin-to-skin contact, alongside breastfeeding and appropriate medical care.
For premature and low-birthweight babies, it can help regulate body temperature, support breastfeeding and improve health outcomes.
World Health Organization (WHO) guidance says that kangaroo mother care has been shown to reduce neonatal mortality by 32 percent, and mortality by six months of age by 25 percent, compared with conventional care.
At Nasser Medical Complex, Khawla al-Madhoun, director of nursing at the hospital’s maternity and neonatal departments, described it as an integrated approach to newborn care that supports growth and strengthens the bond between mother and baby.
“When we place a baby on the mother’s chest, it helps the baby grow,” she said.
“We have seen babies who were unwell or underweight begin to grow faster with kangaroo care. This can help them leave the hospital sooner.”
The hospital has begun introducing kangaroo care through a pilot programme supported by WHO, the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), and the UN Population Fund (UNFPA). The agencies announced the initiative at Nasser Hospital in September, but the practice is being introduced gradually in its external neonatal care unit, where babies stay with their mothers, and in maternity wards after delivery.
Al-Madhoun said the team was also preparing a dedicated room and seeking equipment to make the sessions more comfortable.
The team aims for longer periods of skin-to-skin contact – WHO recommends at least eight hours per day – although its immediate target is at least two hours, depending on each family’s circumstances.
At Nasser, the team is currently prioritising babies who are medically stable and do not require oxygen support. Nurses monitor their vital signs and assess them throughout the process.
Al-Madhoun stressed that the technique cannot replace an incubator or other treatment when a baby needs intensive care.
“It can help babies grow, gain weight and leave the hospital earlier, but some babies need other interventions, such as respiratory support,” she said. “Those babies still need the incubator and the care it provides.”
Shortage of neonatal equipment
The need for specialised newborn care comes as Gaza’s health system continues to struggle with damaged facilities, shortages of equipment and overcrowded neonatal units.
Before Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023, Gaza had eight neonatal intensive care units with a total of 178 incubators, according to UNICEF.
By November 2024, three of those units had been destroyed by Israel, and the number of available incubators had fallen to about 54, a reduction of 70 percent. The shortage of equipment, compounded by limited supplies of fuel and electricity as a result of Israeli restrictions, put premature newborns at serious risk.
Israeli strikes have continued since an October 2025 “ceasefire”. Despite this supposed truce, and despite the delivery of some new equipment, the shortage of incubators and other equipment has persisted.
In May, UNICEF said it and its partners had supplied incubators and ventilators to hospitals in Gaza, while warning that neonatal units were still managing large numbers of fragile infants with limited equipment, space and power.
The war in Gaza has worsened living conditions for pregnant women with economic hardship, food shortages, poor nutrition and the harsh realities of displacement, including cooking over open fires and carrying water.
“These conditions have contributed to the rise in premature births and babies born with low birth weight who need specialised neonatal care,” al-Madhoun said.
Meanwhile, repeated displacement and overcrowding have placed further pressure on hospitals, including Nasser Medical Complex, which is already struggling with limited space and shortages of incubators and other essential neonatal equipment.
Newborn in a tent
Linda Abu Nasira’s baby girl is only three days old.
The infant initially developed a fever, which has since subsided, according to 23-year-old Linda.
As her daughter was being treated and breastfed, Linda was learning how to hold her against her chest under the guidance of the medical team.
The sessions were brief. Linda said she held her daughter against her chest for about 30 minutes at a time, repeating the process roughly every two hours, according to the instructions she had received.
“She is a little better than yesterday,” Linda said. “Little by little.”
Away from the hospital, Linda lives in a tent in al-Mawasi, in Khan Younis, where she is raising her two older children – aged three and two – while caring for her newborn.
She described the conditions as difficult, particularly when it comes to securing food and drinking water.
“We try to manage,” she said. “But it is not like before, or like the conditions you would expect when giving birth.”
She does not know how long the baby will need to remain under observation in the hospital’s external neonatal care unit.
“As a mother, it means a lot to me to feel that I am helping my daughter recover,” Linda said. “I hope she will recover and be discharged as soon as possible.”

No one's owning up to crippling Ukraine's military Starlink
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:42:50 UTC
02:42:50 KST

Nearly 48 hours after Ukraine's Starshield terminals started mysteriously malfunctioning, nobody in Washington, nor at SpaceX, has taken responsibility for the apparent decision to hobble Ukrainian military communications.
Starshield terminals — the militarized version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet system — began losing connectivity as they approached a certain speed, causing havoc among Ukrainian drone units.
The unexpected restriction disrupted active military operations, including the use of mid-range strike drones, as well as the interceptor drones Ukraine uses to help protect cities from Russia's ongoing aerial bombardment.
"The fact that nobody in Washington wants to own up to helping Russia kill Ukrainians shows how politically toxic this decision was," American journalist and commentator Michael Weiss told the Kyiv Independent.
The restrictions came as Ukraine continues to come under significant and sustained pressure from the Trump administration to cease attacks on Russian oil refineries, something Kyiv views as an essential part of its defense against Russia's invasion.
read also
Ukraine has repeatedly offered to observe an "energy ceasefire" which would see both sides cease attacks on energy infrastructure such as power plants, oil refineries, and oil terminals, something Russia has repeatedly refused to accept.
Ukrainian activist Serhii Sternenko, a former adviser to ex-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, was one of the first to raise the alarm about the restrictions on Oct. 14, saying that a "number of critical missions were disrupted."
"The restriction came without any warning," Junior Sergeant Dimko Zhluktenko of the 413th Unmanned Systems Regiment, told the Kyiv Independent. "In my estimate, that has already cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses."
As the scale of the problem became clearer over the course of the day, the question of who had actually ordered the restrictions grew louder, but there is still no definitive answer.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk shifted responsibility to the Pentagon and the Trump administration for the slowdown, saying on Oct. 14 that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government."
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS," he said in a reply to Fedorov on social media.
Axios, citing "U.S. officials," reported the restrictions were the result of a "technical malfunction in the system," though no further evidence of this has emerged.
According to Axios, the White House denied any role in imposing the restrictions and said it planned to contact SpaceX to determine what had happened. The Pentagon has not publicly explained the restrictions.
The move has sparked bipartisan anger in Washington, as a historically unpopular President Trump approaches midterm elections that the Republican Party is predicted to badly lose.
"I’m not holding my breath for Defense Secretary Hegseth to offer transparency, so we’ll be asking the DOD Inspector General to initiate an investigation and report back to Congress and the American People," Republican Senator Thom Tillis said on social media.
"At best, this was an unacceptable error or lapse, and at worst a conscious decision to clear the field for a Russian attack," Tillis said.
"Reports of Starlink failing in Ukraine are deeply alarming — potentially crippling air defense against Russia’s murderous missiles & drones. Trump & Musk must be held accountable," Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, who co-sponsored the Lindsey Graham Sanctions Act with the late senator from South Carolina, said on social media.
By the following day, Starshield was operating more reliably in Ukraine, but the new 160 km/h speed cap remained in place.
"We have now confirmed that Starshield works at 160 km/h, so those glitches have been fixed. But the cap itself is the problem. 160 km/h is not enough, and it limits how we can defend ourselves against the Russians," Zhluktenko told the Kyiv Independent.
"As of now, Starshield's operation has resumed and continues, as we have confirmed through reports from units," a source in the defense ministry told the Kyiv Independent.
"The Ministry of Defense is also continuing communication to clarify all the reasons and circumstances of yesterday's restriction," they added.
Other Ukrainian military units were still apparently experiencing intermittent problems, another Ukrainian military source said, speaking to the Kyiv Independent on condition of anonymity. “In some cases, it works perfectly, in some places it does not," they said.
Neither SpaceX nor the Pentagon responded to requests for comment from the Kyiv Independent.

In 100th lawsuit against Trump, California challenges immigration arrests near courthouses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:41:13 UTC
02:41:13 KST

In 100th lawsuit against Trump, California challenges immigration arrests near courthouses
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- California is challenging the practice of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arresting people for alleged civil immigration violations at or near state courthouses.
- State Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta said such arrests have long been barred because they are unconstitutional and deeply disruptive to the rule of law and the rights of victims, witnesses, defendants and other parties to court proceedings.
- Bonta said his office having to take the Trump administration to court 100 times in less than two years, often alongside other Democrat-led states, was a ‘sobering milestone.’
California sued the Trump administration for the 100th time in under two years Thursday, challenging the practice of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arresting people for alleged civil immigration violations at or near state courthouses.
California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta said such arrests have long been barred because they are unconstitutional and deeply disruptive to the rule of law and the rights of victims, witnesses, defendants and other parties to court proceedings.
“We’ve seen serious criminal charges dropped and entire cases jeopardized because victims and witnesses are too scared to come to the courthouse to testify,” Bonta said. “Our justice system cannot function this way.”
Bonta said his office having to take the Trump administration to court 100 times in less than two years, often alongside other Democrat-led states, was a “sobering milestone” and a reflection not of political interference on California’s part — as the president and his supporters have cast it — but of Trump’s nearly unbridled lawlessness.
“It’s very troubling when the most powerful person on the planet and the president of our country is the one trampling over the Constitution, breaking the law so blatantly and brazenly, so consistently, so frequently,” Bonta said.
Independent legal experts said several factors have driven the wave of lawsuits.
Federal officials have given California election officials 48 hours to prove the citizenship of voters flagged as potential noncitizens, or withhold their ballots.
Presidents from both parties have increasingly flexed their executive power, and state attorneys general have increasingly sued in response. During Trump’s first term in office, California — under the leadership of then-Atty. Gen. Xavier Becerra, a current gubernatorial candidate — sued the Trump administration more than 120 times over four years. Texas Atty. Gen. Ken Paxton — now a Republican candidate for Senate — sued the Biden administration just over 100 times in four years.
Trump in this term quickly began implementing an array of policies left over from his first term or outlined in the Project 2025 policy blueprint, many of which Bonta and other Democratic attorneys general were prepared to sue over, experts said.
Trump was also able to appoint a host of loyalists with the help of the Republican-controlled Congress, who helped advance policies that less loyal agency heads would have balked at, and which were sure to draw additional legal challenges, experts said.
Daniel Farber, a professor at UC Berkeley Law School and author of “Contested Ground: How to Understand the Limits of Presidential Power,” said California’s raft of lawsuits is a result of the current Trump administration “doing more aggressive things right off the starting block” — but also repeatedly targeting California specifically.
Bonta claimed in August that his lawsuits had saved California more than $200 billion, namely by reversing Trump cuts to federal funding meant for the state.
The White House has consistently derided Bonta’s litigation against the administration as baseless and misguided. White House spokesperson Lauren Bis on Thursday said Bonta should stop bragging about “filing frivolous lawsuits” and “focus on addressing problems in his own state.”
“The reality is, with well over 25 Supreme Court victories, the administration’s policies have been consistently upheld as lawful, despite some lower courts issuing an unprecedented number of lawless injunctions,” Bis said.
ICE, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment, has defended its arrests near courthouses as a “common sense” approach to apprehending offenders at times and locations where authorities know they will be.
The 100th case
Bonta’s lawsuit argues that such arrests are arbitrary and capricious given the chilling effect they have on justice in the state. They violate the Immigration and Nationality Act as intended by Congress, and interfere with California’s rights under the 10th Amendment to execute its “core sovereign judicial and police functions,” Bonta’s office said.
His arguments echo those made by other state officials in the past. During Trump’s first term, for example, then-California Supreme Court Chief Justice Tani G. Cantil-Sakauye called the arrests “disruptive, shortsighted and counterproductive.”
Arrests at or near courthouses began to rise again after Trump took office in January 2025. An ICE memo, issued in May 2025, said agents could conduct “civil immigration enforcement actions in or near courthouses when they have credible information that leads them to believe the targeted alien(s) is or will be present at a specific location.”
Incidents quickly began cropping up. In June 2025, ICE agents arrested two women outside a Los Angeles County courthouse after a hearing in a local criminal case. The same unfolded across the state.
Alejandro Barraza, a criminal defense and immigration attorney, said he has witnessed the effect firsthand.
In October 2025, a client was arrested driving home from a hearing at the Riverside County Hall of Justice. In December, another client was arrested leaving the Rancho Cucamonga courthouse. And a third client chose to plead guilty in his criminal case rather than go to jury trial, despite Barraza’s advice that the case was worth fighting, for fear of being arrested by ICE.
“The victims are losing,” Barraza said. “Our clients are losing their rights to due process. Everyone is losing.”
In June, U.S. District Judge P. Casey Pitts in San Francisco struck down ICE’s expanded courthouse arrest policies nationwide. Although the lawsuit focused on immigration courthouses, the ruling also covered state criminal courthouses, restoring earlier restrictions that barred civil immigration arrests in or near courthouses except in limited circumstances. The Trump administration is appealing the ruling.
Since then, California court officials have tracked arrests by federal agents and reported them to the Judicial Council of California. Thirty people were taken into custody in June, 29 in July, 19 in August and 14 in September.
Three lawsuits filed Friday challenge the Trump administration’s rollback of vehicle mileage rules as illegal, including one led by California.
State legislators have tried to push back. Last month, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a law strengthening California’s protections against civil arrests for people traveling to, attending or leaving courthouses for lawful purposes. The measure extends those protections to public ways within 1,000 feet of court facilities, while preserving an exception for arrests made under a valid judicial warrant.
Bonta said his lawsuit is necessary despite the new California law, in part because the Trump administration thinks that “no state law applies to them,” and courts have in some cases agreed — including the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, which this week blocked a state law that would have required federal immigration agents to display identification while working in the state.
The wider legal battle
Bonta’s office has had substantial success in halting some of the Trump administration’s biggest policy moves — including its plans to end birthright citizenship for the U.S.-born children of immigrants, its worldwide tariffs, its deployment of National Guard troops in Los Angeles and other U.S. cities, and its withholding of billions of dollars in federal funding allocated to the state by Congress.
Michael McConnell, director of the Constitutional Law Center at Stanford Law School, said many of California’s lawsuits have been “legally meritorious,” as there is a “whole lot of legal error” coming out of the Trump administration — with a “lot of the overreach” having been “facilitated by the lack of internal checks” from loyal Trump agency heads.
However, he also said that as a California taxpayer, he doesn’t “appreciate having government using my tax dollars for what essentially are in many cases ideological lawsuits, even if meritorious,” because private litigants can and often do bring lawsuits of their own. He said he felt the same way about many of the lawsuits brought against the Biden administration by Republican states.
Bonta said he is proud of his team for challenging the Trump administration every time they believed it had broken the law and harmed California, despite Trump’s intentional effort to make that difficult.
“It was a shock and awe,” he said. “It was flood the zone. It was trying to overwhelm with speed and volume, and we kept pace every time.”
What happens next, he said, will depend on Trump. If he keeps breaking the law in ways that hurt the state or its residents, Bonta said he’ll keep getting sued by California.

Speaker of Hungarian parliament meets with her Ukrainian counterpart and confirms support for Ukraine's path to EU

Speaker of Hungarian parliament meets with her Ukrainian counterpart and confirms support for Ukraine's path to EU
Ruslan Stefanchuk, Speaker of the Verkhovna Rada (Ukrainian parliament), has met with Speaker of the Hungarian Parliament Ágnes Forsthoffer, stating that Ukraine and Hungary have opened a new chapter in inter-parliamentary relations.
Source: European Pravda, citing Stefanchuk on Facebook
Details: Stefanchuk said the head of the Hungarian parliament expressed support for the Ukrainian people and confirmed Hungary's readiness to continue helping Ukraine and Ukrainians. She also reaffirmed support for Ukraine's movement towards the European Union.
Quote from Stefanchuk: "We also spoke about shared pages of history, including tragic ones. Ukrainians survived the Holodomor, and Hungarians survived Soviet repressions and forced labour, known as 'malenki robot'. Our nations know very well what the violence that came from Moscow means."
Details: The speakers of both parliaments discussed steps to step up inter-parliamentary cooperation.
Background:
- In September, Hungarian Parliament Speaker Ágnes Forsthoffer, along with other officials, refused to meet with her Ukrainian counterpart in Budapest.
- Relations between Ukraine and Hungary have now temporarily improved: Prime Minister Péter Magyar confirmed he would meet with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on the sidelines of the EU summit on 15-16 October.
- On 12 October, the Ukrainian parliament approved amendments to the law on education. The changes are necessary for Hungary to agree to the opening of negotiating clusters 2 and 3 in Ukraine's EU accession talks.

It’s not the old two-party politics – but Labour and the Tories now know they can shun their populist challengers | Gaby Hinsliff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:40:36 UTC
02:40:36 KST

Ask a straight question, get a straight answer. It’s how politics is supposed to work but almost never does, which is why on the rare occasions it happens the result can be faintly chaotic. What did Andy Burnham mean when he said – in response to a question from the Tory MP Harriett Baldwin – that Labour couldn’t partner with the Green party while it remains wedded to the “Zionism is racism” motion its members have just endorsed? Were Green MPs now barred from a future coalition government? If so, what about councils where they are currently sharing power with Labour?
Though Burnham was only confirming what ministers have been arguing privately for days, at first nobody seemed to know: tellingly, it took almost 24 hours for the Labour party chair, Bridget Phillipson, to confirm that unless local Green groups disowned that idea sharpish, “Labour will bring any such local arrangement to an end”. So much for cuddly cross-party Andy, who always seemed so relaxed about rainbow coalitions. Now elected Greens in places such as Sheffield or Lewes must choose between power and members’ wrath, a useful rehearsal for what a hung parliament might feel like.
Westminster is increasingly realising that while nobody knows quite what’s in Burnham’s head except Burnham, unlike most prime ministers he is surprisingly liable just to tell you. He did it earlier this week on a podcast, pointing out that Russia tried to interfere in the Brexit vote (which is true, albeit the sort of truth that for complicated reasons prime ministers don’t generally dwell on). Now the safety catch is off again.
What did he mean with his comments about Labour and the Greens? Most likely just what he said: that the Greens crossed a line and it cannot be overlooked, especially by a party still recovering from its own battle with antisemitism. Green members did not just vote to adopt a policy that would condemn every Jew who believes in the right to a Jewish homeland, including those who simultaneously support the creation of a Palestinian state. The motion they backed advocates turning all of historic Palestine into a Palestinian state, a one-state solution wiping Israel off the map. Much as Kemi Badenoch did recently by insisting that her English-born children have every right to be considered English, no matter what the ethno-nationalists of Reform and Restore say, Burnham was simply showing that he has limits: this far, and no further.
Something has shaken loose over the party conference season. What we are seeing isn’t the return of two-party politics – things are still too volatile for that – but the return of leaders confident enough to set boundaries on what had become an almost abusive relationship with the public. They are no longer quite so terrified of naming extremism when they see it. More surprisingly, neither is behaving like a party needing to beg for coalition partners, whatever the electoral maths says.
After a period shadow boxing a prime minister who never seemed to know what he thought, Badenoch now faces one who does. That has brought drama back to the middle of politics and not just the radical edges, with genuine differences emerging between Labour and the Tories ahead of the budget over tax and spend, national security v social security, public v private ownership and the respective claims of younger and older people.
Her new strategy is not a million miles from the one outlined this week by the thinktank Bright Blue, in a paper on how the traditional European right can combat far-right populism: adopt draconian immigration policies but make the economy the actual focus of your campaign, and hold the line that citizenship can be earned rather than being determined by ethnicity (the chilling line peddled by some of those in Reform and Restore who argue openly that you have to be white to be properly English).
Though the polls still suggest the Tories can’t win without some kind of deal with Reform, the broad message of a conference speech in which Badenoch painted her rivals as aggressive weirdos who “threaten journalists, call veterans traitors and debate whether my mixed-race children are English” was that it would be a cold day in hell before that happened. That decision looks smarter with every passing journalistic exposé involving the kind of Reform councillor who thinks King Charles should be decapitated for supposedly being a secret Muslim.
Burnham didn’t go quite so studs-up on the Greens, but then he doesn’t need to. The party is already openly agonising about that anti-Zionism motion, opposed by four out of five of its elected MPs. The prospect of being politically ostracised for it may now strengthen the hand of Greens who think this freakishly hot summer might have been better spent campaigning on the climate crisis, not swerving questions about Israel’s right to exist. Yet there are risks for Burnham here, all the same.
Research by the pollster More in Common suggests that “progressive activists”, the group most commonly torn between voting Green or Labour, are significantly more likely than the average British voter to think worse of someone identifying as a Zionist. When Burnham called the Green motion antisemitic and wrong, he was confronting people whose support he may need in some Labour seats.
Sanctioning West Bank settlements, as this government has now done, isn’t enough for some of them: they want Burnham explicitly to call the Gaza war a genocide and stop proscribing Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation. (Polanski was notably quick to leap to the defence of the Irish novelist Sally Rooney, after it emerged her books are being withdrawn from sale in Britain because of her promise to donate royalties to Palestine Action: knowing where the money could be going leaves her publishers open to potential prosecution under anti-terrorism law, just for handing over her earnings.)
It’s technically possible that like some desiccated calculating machine, Burnham has crunched the numbers on all this and concluded that distancing himself from a row that has reportedly made one in three British voters less likely to vote Green (according to Opinium) is mathematically preferable.
But it’s more likely he was just doing the thing that got him here in the first place, and following his gut. If he can’t say what he thinks even now, in what passes for a honeymoon period, he never will. If basic norms are not enforced, they very quickly cease being norms. And if the Labour party can only win by sidling uncomfortably close to the kind of people it was until recently expelling for antisemitism – well, it’s not much of a Labour party. The chaos, in that sense, is probably just beginning.
- Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

The State Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) said it has charged Russian serviceman Leonid Ryzhikov, who is suspected of shooting five unarmed Ukrainian soldiers and a 60-year-old civilian man in Kharkiv region.
According to a Telegram post by the SBU on Thursday, 36-year-old Russian citizen Leonid Ryzhikov, with the call sign "Yula," was detained on October 14 in Kharkiv. According to the investigation, he was drafted into the Russian army in late July after serving an eight-year prison sentence for causing grievous bodily harm and theft. He served in the 2nd Battalion of the 1009th Motorized Rifle Regiment of the 68th Motorized Rifle Division of Russia's sixth Combined Arms Army and fought in Kharkiv region.
SBU said that in early October, Ryzhikov fled from positions near the village of Starytsia in Chuhuiv district following shelling by Ukrainian forces and headed toward Kharkiv, hiding in forest belts. During his escape, according to the investigation, he stole civilian clothing from an abandoned private home.
"As the SBU has established, on October 5-6, while at the positions of the Russian occupation forces near the village of Starytsia in Chuhuiv district, Ryzhikov came under fire from the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Armed with an AK-74 assault rifle, he fled the area and began walking toward the city of Kharkiv, hiding in the woods," the agency said.
The investigation established that on October 13, near the village of Mykhailivka in Kharkiv district, Ryzhikov shot and killed a 60-year-old local resident who was fishing at a pond, after which he threw the body into the water. On the same day, in the village of Momotove, he broke into a private residence where five unarmed Ukrainian servicemen in civilian clothing, who were not participating in combat operations, were temporarily staying, and shot them, including those who were asleep.
After the killings, the suspect hid an AK-74 assault rifle on a nearby property, but law enforcement officers later located and seized the weapon.
Based on the evidence gathered, the suspect was notified of charges under Part 2 of Article 438 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (war crimes resulting in loss of life). The penalty for this offense is life imprisonment.
As previously reported, on October 13 in Kharkiv region, an unknown assailant shot and killed five Ukrainian servicemen with an automatic weapon.

Demonstrators clashed with police overnight in Porto, after officers moved in to remove tents. Protest organisers say at least 35 people were injured.
Housing rights protesters have denounced what they describe as a violent police operation early Thursday morning, when officers attempted to remove people camping in Praca D. Joao I, a square in central Porto, Portugal.
The most tense moments reportedly occurred at around 3 am, after police arrived to disperse the demonstrators. The Housing Movement condemned the police intervention, describing it as "disproportionate and unjustified".
"The movement strongly denounces the use of extreme, disproportionate and unjustified force during the police operation at the camp, which remained peaceful from the outset and never incited violence," it said in a statement, adding that 37 people were injured during the operation, including two who suffered fractures.
'A more forceful intervention was necessary'
Speaking to CNN Portugal on Thursday morning, Leonor Figueiredo, a representative of the movement, insisted that protesters had been at the site "peacefully" and said there was therefore no justification for the police intervention.
"Pedro Duarte said he was going to be ruthless and now we have seen it, we have understood the message," Figueiredo said, referring to remarks made on Wednesday by Porto's mayor, who had pledged not to allow any form of camping in the city.
A source at the Porto Metropolitan Command of the Public Security Police (PSP) confirmed to Euronews that "a more forceful intervention was necessary" at the site, but said it was too early to provide further details, including the number of people injured, and promised more information later.
Police also confirmed that the protest had been fully dispersed and that "nothing further remains" at the scene.
Several demonstrators had been staying in the square since Saturday, many of them sleeping outdoors after the tents set up during the initial protest were removed by the city council.
Human chain 'brutally harassed'
On Wednesday, following a public assembly, they decided to continue protesting over the housing crisis and to pitch tents again overnight.
Speaking to CNN Portugal, Pedro Manuel, a spokesperson for the movement, said the first attempt to remove the protesters took place at around 2 am, with cleaning vehicles used to try to disperse those present. He maintained that there had been no confrontation with the authorities.
"We formed a peaceful human chain to prevent them from taking away our tents. They waited until the media had left and then drove away in their vehicles," the spokesperson said.
"At around 3 am, they came back, and we formed a human chain again, peacefully, to defend our right to protest and keep the tents," the demonstrator said.
According to Pedro Manuel, it was at that point that police began "harassing protesters with brutality", in an operation he described as "criminal".
Speaking to the Lusa news agency on Thursday, the spokesperson insisted that the protest was "authorised until the 20th".
Porto City Council vows to be 'absolutely ruthless'
Before the police operation, Porto City Council had already warned that it would prevent any form of camping in the city.
"It is obvious that Praça D. João I is not a campsite and will not be turned into one. We will be absolutely ruthless with any attempt to erect tents in that area," Porto's mayor said on the sidelines of the Fábrica 2030 conference, as quoted by Lusa.
Pedro Duarte said that the "right to demonstrate is not in question", but that it "cannot clash with the freedom of everyone else in the city".
"Portuguese law is very clear and states that demonstrations cannot continue beyond a certain time, generally 12.30 am," he added.

Ukraine transfers samples from national seed collection to Global Seed Vault on Spitsbergen
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
20:39:52 EEST
02:39:52 KST

Ukraine has transferred seed samples from its national collection to the Global Seed Vault on the Svalbard Archipelago in Norway – an international reserve for the conservation of plant genetic resources, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine.
"A total of 773 seed samples from 10 agricultural crops (triticale, barley, buckwheat, millet, peas, white lupine, vetch, Sarepta mustard, alfalfa, and clover). This is the second transfer of Ukrainian genetic material to Svalbard and the first since the start of the full-scale invasion," the ministry said on the Telegram channel.
It is noted that this is an important step toward preserving the national plant gene pool and agrobiodiversity amid the war.
"Preserving the national plant gene pool is a matter of our national security and ensuring food stability for future generations. Amid the war unleashed by Russia, Ukrainian agricultural science and strategic resources have come under direct threat. Transferring the duplicate collection to the Global Seed Vault in Svalbard ensures that the unique achievements of Ukrainian plant breeders will be reliably protected from any security risks. "We are grateful to our international partners for their support in protecting our agricultural heritage, which is Ukraine's significant contribution to global food security," Minister of Agrarian Policy and Food of Ukraine Taras Vysotsky said.
In total, material representing approximately 10% of Ukraine's entire national seed collection (which comprises over 154,300 samples) has already been transferred.
The preservation of the collection was made possible thanks to a FAO initiative with financial support from the EU and in collaboration with the National Academy of Agrarian Sciences of Ukraine (NAAS), the Crop Trust, and NordGen, as well as with technical support from the International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture. As part of the project, 51,000 samples were transported to western Ukraine, and a permanent backup center was opened at the end of 2025.
Ukraine acceded to the International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture in August 2026.

Two ships sink near Hormuz after being hit by projectiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:38:56 UTC
02:38:56 KST

Breadcrumb
Two ships sink near Hormuz after being hit by projectiles
A container ship and a dry bulk carrier sunk near the Strait of Hormuz inside 24 hours on Wednesday after being hit by projectiles in separate incidents, maritime officials said on Wednesday.
Attacks around the waterway have surged over the past 10 days, with Iran saying it is stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions introduced last month.
The Singapore-flagged GFS Pride, a small container vessel with a capacity of 2,824 20-foot equivalent units (TEU), sank while sailing through the strait, according to maritime security sources.
"GFS PRIDE sustained damage and a fire on board, and has since sunk. All 21 crew members were safely evacuated. No injuries have been reported," the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) said in a statement on Wednesday, adding that the vessel had been sailing through the strait on Tuesday.
In a separate incident, the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao sank close to the strait, weeks after being struck by a projectile on September 23, data from UN shipping agency the International Maritime Organisation showed on Wednesday.
One crew member was killed, the rest of the crew evacuated straight after the strike, maritime sources said.
Its UAE-based manager Peonies Shipmanagement FZE could not be immediately reached for comment.
The GFS Pride and Cape Dao are the second and third vessels to have sunk since the US-Iran war began on February 28, according to an analysis of IMO casualty data.
"MPA is deeply concerned about the continued attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz," the Singapore authority said.
"Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable, and a breach of international law."
GFS Pride's United Arab Emirates-based manager, GFS Ship Management FZE, could not be immediately reached for comment.
"The latest incidents reinforce the continuing threat to commercial shipping transiting the Strait of Hormuz," maritime risk management company MARISKS said on Wednesday.
"The threat is not confined to tankers, with container vessels and bulk carriers also sustaining serious damage."
A sharp escalation in threats to commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade passed before the war, has heightened concerns about security in the waterway.
Tehran has sought to tighten its grip on the waterway since US and Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February, restricting transit in an effort to gain leverage over Washington.
Iran is increasingly deploying new tactics against vessels transiting the strait as it seeks to keep oil prices elevated and influence US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters.
While Iran and the US have focused their attacks on tankers, cargo and container vessels have also been attacked, immobilised or sunk.
The Maltese-flagged container ship Safeen Prestige was hit by a projectile in March and later sank north of the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards attacked and seized the container ship MSC Francesca in April.
(Reuters)

Britain is providing Ukraine with a new batch of long-range Storm Shadow missiles — media
Kyiv • UNN
London is providing Kyiv with additional Storm Shadows to counter Russian strikes on civilian infrastructure. The number of missiles has not been disclosed.
The United Kingdom is providing Ukraine with an additional batch of long-range Storm Shadow missiles to help it disrupt Russian military operations targeting civilian infrastructure ahead of winter. People familiar with the situation said, reports UNN, citing Bloomberg.
According to sources who agreed to provide the information on condition of anonymity, the supply of these British-made cruise missiles was discussed during a meeting between Prime Minister Andy Burnham and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in London on Wednesday. The weapons shipment had not previously been announced publicly.
The United Kingdom and other allies of Ukraine are stepping up support for the war-torn country. This is happening as U.S. President Donald Trump announced last week that he had reached an agreement with President Vladimir Putin on placing Russian diesel fuel on the global market. On Wednesday, in an interview on the program "Piers Morgan Uncensored," Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he felt betrayed by events in recent days — in particular, the diesel-fuel agreement, Trump’s announcement of an "energy ceasefire," as well as problems with Ukrainian troops’ access to SpaceX satellite technology.
The publication notes that the United Kingdom has been supplying Ukraine with Storm Shadow missiles since 2023, although their use was initially restricted to the combat zone within Ukrainian territory. At the end of 2024, Ukrainian forces expanded the geography of their use, striking military facilities on Russian territory with British cruise missiles for the first time.
According to the sources, the United Kingdom considers Ukraine’s use of long-range weapons against Russian facilities involved in attacks on civilians and infrastructure to be defensive actions. In recent weeks, Russia has increased production of jet-powered drones and missiles to intensify attacks on Ukraine, so it is important for Kyiv to have the ability to counter these actions, the sources said.
The Trump administration urged Kyiv to stop drone attacks on Russian oil refineries, but the strikes resumed on Thursday — in response to ongoing Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy facilities. As evidence of differences between the positions of the British and U.S. governments, the sources said that, in London’s view, Ukraine should not stop striking Russia until Moscow itself abandons such actions.
The media outlet notes that the British government declined to comment. It does not disclose exactly how many Storm Shadow missiles have been supplied to Ukraine during the war and does not report on each individual delivery. Storm Shadow missiles, produced by MBDA, have proven highly effective at penetrating Russia’s air-defense system and striking military and industrial facilities. These highly precise air-launched missiles have a range of more than 250 kilometers (155 miles); they are difficult to defend against because they fly at high speed while following the contours of the terrain.
In August, Burnham announced that the United Kingdom would provide Kyiv with technical documentation for long-range missiles so that Ukraine could establish their production on its own territory, although implementing the project will likely take some time.
In addition, Britain is developing low-cost long-range strike systems for Ukraine that will not depend on the supply of components or data from the United States.

Ukraine launches TOP-50 ranking of distributed generation solutions and energy storage systems

The Interfax-Ukraine news agency, together with the public organization League of Energy Development of Ukraine, announces the launch of the Energy Resilience Ukraine 2026 project — the TOP-50 ranking "Distributed Generation and Energy Storage Solutions", aimed at identifying and systematizing the most effective solutions in the field of Ukraine's energy resilience.
The project is intended to bring together, within a single information and analytical space, manufacturers and suppliers of energy equipment, installers and engineering companies, businesses, communities, state-owned enterprises, associations of co-owners of apartment buildings (OSBBs), and critical infrastructure facilities implementing distributed generation, energy storage systems, cogeneration and solutions to ensure energy autonomy.
Installers and engineering companies can apply to participate in the ranking by completing the form: https://forms.gle/6acdhW2tXtpjE6k29
Businesses and state-owned enterprises that have already implemented distributed generation and autonomous power supply projects: https://forms.gle/t5EZDtJt2HhS3qPt5
"Over recent years, energy resilience has evolved from a purely sector-specific issue into one of the key factors of the country's economic security. Today, businesses, communities and consumers need not just information about available equipment, but a clear point of reference: which technologies are already actually working in Ukraine, who is implementing them and what practical results they deliver. Energy Resilience Ukraine 2026 is intended to become precisely such a reference point. The task of Interfax-Ukraine in this project is to ensure maximum information openness, publicity and accessibility of its results," said Maksym Urakin, Deputy Director of the Interfax-Ukraine news agency.
The ranking will include projects and companies associated with solar and wind energy, cogeneration, hybrid energy systems and Energy Storage. Solutions implemented for autonomous, backup or partially autonomous power supply to enterprises, communities, OSBBs, households and critical infrastructure facilities will be evaluated separately.
The structure of Energy Resilience Ukraine 2026 includes four main blocks: installation companies and equipment suppliers, enterprises, regions, and the most effective implemented projects.
In addition to the overall TOP-50, the organizers plan to establish 12 thematic clusters. In particular, installers, solar energy solutions for businesses, residential solar power plants and solar installations for OSBBs, developers of cogeneration projects and wind power plants, energy equipment suppliers and Energy Storage providers will be evaluated separately.
Separate categories will be dedicated to businesses and state-owned enterprises that have installed their own autonomous generation facilities, the most effective engineering solutions, leading regions in the implementation of distributed generation facilities, as well as distribution system operators — in terms of the convenience and efficiency of connecting new generating capacities.
"Ukraine is effectively undergoing an accelerated transformation of its energy model — from highly centralized generation to a more distributed and flexible system. Today, hundreds of enterprises, communities and OSBBs are already investing in their own generation facilities and energy storage systems. However, the market lacks systematized information about which specific solutions have genuinely proven their effectiveness and who provides high-quality services for their implementation. We want not simply to compile a list of companies, but to showcase specific completed projects, their scale, technologies, economic impact and contribution to improving energy resilience," emphasized Oleksandr Holizdra, Head of the public organization League of Energy Development of Ukraine.
The ranking methodology will be based on a 100-point evaluation system. Participants will be able to receive up to 50 points for the scale of installed generation or Energy Storage capacity, and up to another 50 points based on an expert assessment of qualitative indicators.
For companies, the evaluation criteria will include reputation, comprehensiveness of the proposed solutions, number of implemented projects, price-to-service quality ratio, and innovation.
For businesses and individual facilities, the assessment will cover transparency of project implementation, level of autonomy and technological sophistication, economic impact and social significance. For communities, the main criteria will be the scale of implemented projects, level of energy independence and comprehensiveness of solutions, energy and social resilience, as well as practical benefits for the community.
Open online voting is also planned for certain nominations.
The jury of Energy Resilience Ukraine 2026 includes representatives of industry associations, energy experts, researchers, and representatives of the media and analytical centers. According to the organizers, this format is intended to ensure a comprehensive technical, economic, investment-related and social assessment of the submitted solutions.
As a result of the project, a TOP-50 ranking of distributed generation solutions and energy storage systems will be compiled, and an analytical PDF report, a printed magazine, a B2B catalog of participants and digital certificates will be prepared.
The results of Energy Resilience Ukraine 2026 are planned to be presented at a press conference attended by representatives of the energy market, businesses, communities and the expert community.
The organizers expect the ranking to become not only a tool for recognizing industry leaders, but also a practical database of proven solutions for enterprises and communities planning investments in their own generation facilities and electricity storage systems, as well as to contribute to the development of Ukraine's decentralized energy market.

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Authorities in France’s Haute-Savoie department placed a fifth river basin under the highest drought alert level Thursday as dry conditions persisted, according to the prefecture.
The middle Arve basin, known as Arve median, was moved to crisis level, the fourth and highest stage of the department’s drought alert system.
Authorities said the restrictions on water use already in effect across the department will remain in place until Oct. 30.
Five basins are now under crisis-level restrictions: the lower and middle Arve, the Dranses, the Cheran and the Usses.
The Fier and southwestern Lake Geneva basin remain under reinforced alert, while the Genevois and upper Arve basins are under alert.
Under crisis-level measures, only priority water uses are permitted, including drinking water supply, the survival of aquatic species, watering animals, civil protection and public health and sanitation needs.
The measures come amid persistent drought conditions in Haute-Savoie, where water levels have fallen significantly in several rivers, and some tributaries have dried up.

The Guardian view on Stormont: voters in Northern Ireland deserve more than an endless cycle of dysfunction | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:30:37 UTC
02:30:37 KST

Late last month, protesters deposited a sizable amount of foul-smelling green water on the steps of Stormont to draw attention to the appalling state of Lough Neagh, the largest freshwater lake in the British Isles. Years of agricultural pollution have created an environmental disaster in an area of huge ecological significance that once inspired the poetry of Seamus Heaney. Its plight should be a top priority for Northern Ireland’s devolved government. But the executive currently has other matters on its mind.
The sentencing of the former leader of the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) Jeffrey Donaldson, after he was convicted of child sexual abuse, dominated Thursday’s headlines. Meanwhile, a cross-party political crisis continues to play out. Halfway through the financial year, Stormont has yet to set a budget. The current deadlock in negotiations with the Northern Ireland secretary, Sir Chris Bryant, could lead to one being imposed from Westminster. Cuts are already being made by default amid an atmosphere of stasis and policy drift.
An unwelcome revival of sectarian tension on the streets is further undermining the fragile political institutions established by the Good Friday agreement. On Monday, Northern Ireland assembly members debated a motion of no confidence in the first minister, Michelle O’Neill. The move followed the Sinn Féin vice-president’s participation in protests against a proposed Orange Order march on the Garvaghy Road in Portadown, controversially sanctioned by the Parades Commission for the first time in 28 years.
A prolonged standoff between unionists and mainly Catholic residents ended peacefully, after Sir Chris banned the parade on police advice. The absence of violence was a silver lining, but the episode showcased the dangers of what one politician described as “negative nostalgia”. As those seeking to revive a route notoriously associated with loyalist violence surely anticipated, the bitter row has reopened old wounds and unleashed latent animosities.
The motion of no confidence in Ms O’Neill was a performative exercise, with no chance of obtaining the necessary cross-community support. But the combination of no budget and a renewed culture-war confrontation means that Northern Ireland now risks being governed by a zombie administration until elections next May.
Given the dismal recent track record of Stormont collapses and suspensions, that should prompt some hard thinking in London and Dublin as well as Belfast. The scandalous condition of Lough Neagh symbolises the deficiencies of a polity that now seems trapped in an endless cycle of dysfunction. The steady deterioration of public services such as healthcare, education and policing can partly be attributed to underfunding. But matters have been made much worse by the existence of a political vacuum and sectarian grandstanding where effective government should be.
Power-sharing designed to reassure nationalist and unionist communities remains indispensable. But a loveless-marriage model that allows the largest party on either side of the divide to routinely bring assembly business to a halt is in urgent need of reform. Otherwise, faith in Stormont’s ability to act in the name of the common good is in danger of evaporating. Huge strides have been made in civil society since the Good Friday agreement was struck nearly three decades ago. But Northern Ireland’s voters currently do not have the politics they deserve.

Britain still planning up to twelve new nuclear attack submarines
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:28:03 BST
02:28:03 KST

The Ministry of Defence has again said that it intends to procure up to twelve SSN-AUKUS submarines, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked the Secretary of State to set out the number planned following the 2027 spending review.
Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, answered in one sentence: “As set out in the Defence Investment Plan, we intend to procure up to 12 SSN AUKUS submarines.”
The question asked what the plan would be after the next spending review, and the answer restates the existing intention without saying whether the figure is secure against it. Up to twelve is a ceiling, not a commitment to a number.
SSN-AUKUS is the next generation nuclear powered attack submarine, designed in Britain around a British reactor and incorporating American technology under the first pillar of the AUKUS agreement. It will replace the seven boat Astute class, and will be built by BAE Systems at Barrow-in-Furness, with Rolls-Royce supplying the propulsion plant from Derby.
Australia is to build its own boats to the same design at Osborne in South Australia. The first British boat is expected to enter service in the late 2030s.

Netherlands opens nuclear deterrence talks with France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:26:45 UTC
02:26:45 KST

- The Netherlands and France held the first meeting of a bilateral Nuclear Steering Group on Oct. 14, discussing European nuclear and conventional deterrence.
- The talks follow Macron’s March offer of a strategic dialogue, which the Dutch government says complements NATO deterrence instead of replacing it.
The Netherlands and France held the first meeting of a new bilateral Nuclear Steering Group on Oct. 14, opening high-level talks on how French nuclear forces and European conventional forces could work together to deter attacks on Europe, the Dutch Ministry of Defence said.
The ministry announced the meeting in a statement on Oct. 15, saying it was the first time the two countries had held talks on the subject at this level. Senior French government officials attended, while the Dutch delegation was drawn from the Ministry of General Affairs, which is the prime minister’s office, along with the defense and foreign ministries. The two sides discussed ways to strengthen the European dimension of nuclear and conventional deterrence, according to the statement, which did not describe any specific decisions.
The talks follow an offer French President Emmanuel Macron made in early March to a group of European countries, including the Netherlands. The Dutch government accepted the French offer in line with its coalition agreement.
Macron set out the plan in a speech on March 2 at the Île Longue base in Brittany, home to France’s ballistic missile submarines. He said France would increase the number of its nuclear warheads and adopt what he called advanced deterrence, under which elements of France’s nuclear-capable air forces could be temporarily deployed to allied countries, Defense News reported. He named Germany as a key partner alongside Poland, the Netherlands and several other European states, and said partners could contribute early warning, air defense and long-range strike capabilities while their territory would gain a clearer link to French deterrence.
The Dutch government said Russia’s war against Ukraine has fundamentally worsened European security and requires Europe to take more responsibility for its own defense, and that the French offer fits that goal. It stressed that cooperation with France is meant to add to NATO’s collective defense and deterrence, and does not replace it.
France is the only nuclear-armed member of the European Union. Its arsenal is kept under exclusive national control, with the president alone authorized to order its use, and Macron has said that will not change under the new arrangements.
The Netherlands already takes part in NATO’s nuclear sharing arrangements, under which some allies provide aircraft and crews for the alliance’s nuclear mission while the United States retains control of the weapons.

The Guardian view on food security: we have just-in-time, we need just-in-case | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:25:36 UTC
02:25:36 KST

What’s worrying French supermarket bosses should be prompting British ministers to action. On Sunday, hackers forced up the temperatures of refrigerators in hundreds of food stores across France to as high as 50C, resulting in waste and fires. Beyond the immediate destruction and inconvenience, it raised the prospect of other malicious actors finding new ways to play havoc with the food chain.
Only weeks before, 150 experts together warned the British government that it does not have a plan to feed people in a crisis – and that the west is entering an era in which not only disruption but the weaponisation of food is a real possibility. “The public has been led to assume that food will simply be there,” they wrote. “It may not be.”
The Covid pandemic was a salutary reminder of how vulnerable modern systems are – a shock for consumers used to strawberries in October. Brexit, climate stress and the wars in Ukraine and Iran have underlined the risks and raised prices. One issue is overall supply in the UK, which imports about 40% of its food. But affordability, logistics, distribution and nutrition are also essential components of food security.
While food inflation has slowed, the cumulative impact has been severe. The Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit says that by September 2027, UK food prices are likely to be 50% higher than at the start of the cost of living crisis in mid-2021. That scale of increase previously took almost two decades. Food is a far smaller proportion of household budgets than it was 50 years ago. But the fifth of the population with the lowest incomes would need to spend 85% of their disposable income on food to meet governmental advice on healthy diets. Fruit and vegetables often give way to more filling but less nutritious options.
The government has encouraged households to stockpile several days’ worth of tinned goods and bottled water in case of an emergency. But outsourcing food security to individuals is a woefully inadequate response. Building civil food resilience will require more effort, including working with civil society.
Real improvement requires a structural shift away from the “leave it to Tesco” approach decried by Prof Tim Lang, a leading food-policy expert. As he points out, “framing markets is the job of politics”. Reliance on just-in-time last-minute deliveries and a few hubs makes economic sense for retailers, but is not conducive to national food security. Crises often winnow out smaller firms. But diversity is key to resilience. Geographical distribution – including relocalisation of food production – is also central. Almost 95% of retail food comes via 131 food-distribution centres. Disruption to just one supermarket chain’s infrastructure could have a mammoth impact.
Experts have rightly called for food supply shortages and disruption to be included as risks in their own right in the national security risk assessment. There is also a strong case for a dedicated national food council to focus on food security. The UK abandoned its strategic food stockpile in the 1990s. It should think again, as other countries around the world are doing.
Almost one in 10 households are already food-insecure. Others have become used to an age of abundance. None can count on food security without sustained action from the government, beginning with the recognition that this problem can’t be left to the market.

Army looks at off the shelf kit to stop drones over bases
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:25:32 BST
02:25:32 KST

An Army-led project called Halo Shield is examining how commercially available counter-drone technology could protect British military sites, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked for the full scope of the project.
Louise Sandher-Jones, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “Project HALO SHIELD is an Army-led initiative examining how commercially available Counter-Uncrewed Aircraft System (C-UAS) technologies can improve the protection of UK military sites from the growing threat posed by uncrewed aircraft systems.”
Halo Shield sits alongside Project PRESAGIUM, the £240 million enhanced counter-drone system the department described in a separate answer, which it says will provide detection and defeat of emerging drone threats.
Drone activity over British bases has moved from an irritant to an operational concern over the past two years, with incursions reported over sites including RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall, and the Prime Minister this week attributing the September incident at RAF Fairford to direction by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Counter uncrewed aircraft systems generally pair radar, radio frequency and optical sensors to spot and identify a drone with a mix of jamming, spoofing, nets, guns and directed energy to bring it down.
Protecting a fixed site is awkward because commercial quadcopters return almost no radar signature, because anything shot down has to come down somewhere, and because jamming radio transmissions over British soil runs into civil aviation and telecommunications law.

Pope Leo resumes work in hospital while recovering from surgery
Roman Catholic leader met top Vatican aide, as doctors say recovery proceeding after lung surgery to remove cancerous growth.
Vatican confirms Pope Leo’s surgery was successful
Pope Leo XIV has resumed work from hospital as the leader of the Roman Catholic Church recovers from surgery to remove a cancerous nodule.
Leo met Vatican chief of staff Archbishop Paolo Rudelli at Gemelli hospital in Rome, where he is being treated, the Vatican said on Thursday. The top aide handles much of the day-to-day administrative work of the Holy See.
An update from Leo’s personal physician, Dr Luigi Carbone and Dr Stefano Margaritora, the head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli hospital, said the pope’s post-operative tests remained within normal levels and his physiotherapy session on Thursday involved full mobility exercises.
Leo was going about his daily activities independently, doctors said.
“The chest X-ray revealed good recovery of the operated lung,” they reported. “Overall, his post-operative recovery is proceeding as expected.”
For a second day, the pope celebrated Mass with other priests in a special chapel set up near his room on the 10th floor of the hospital, spokesman Matteo Bruni said.
The 71-year-old had part of his right lung removed after a lengthy operation on Tuesday following doctors identifying a suspected cancerous nodule.
The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
Doctors are still awaiting the results of tests to understand the precise molecular makeup of the cancer, whether it has spread beyond the lobe and whether any further treatment is necessary.
Pope Leo attracted a following of almost one million people at a Mass in Paris during a four-day visit to France last month before announcing he was to undergo surgery.
It is unclear whether he will make his planned trip to South American countries next month.
Asked if any changes to Leo’s planned trip from November 6-17 were expected, spokesman Bruni pointed to Leo’s words on Sunday when he announced the discovery of the nodule and impending surgery.
“Thank you for your prayers for the pastoral visit I will make to Peru,” Leo said on Sunday in Spanish, in a greeting delivered to a Peruvian group. The trip is also scheduled to include Uruguay and Argentina.
Leo is expected to remain in hospital until at least next Tuesday.

Israel received Iranian, Russian weapons in secret transfer from Ukraine, fmr. ambassador says
Unknown

2026-10-15
17:24:15 UTC
02:24:15 KST

Security collaboration between Israel and Ukraine is expanding, particularly in the study of Iranian weapons and Russian drones, according to former Israeli ambassador to Ukraine, Michael Brodsky.
Brodsky discussed the growing security ties earlier this week during a meeting with a delegation of Ukrainian journalists. He confirmed that the two countries are working together to study weapons used in Russia's war against Ukraine and that Israel has received several weapons from Kyiv for examination. He did not specify which weapons or systems were involved.
According to Ukrainian media reports, Israel is examining samples of Russian attack drones provided by Ukraine, including newer models from the Geran family, which are based on Iranian-made Shahed drones.
Ukrainian officials also confirmed to Maariv that the cooperation is underway, saying one of its earliest stages involved Ukraine transferring an Iranian Shahed drone to Israel. Russia has used these drones extensively in its war against Ukraine.
Israel is actively developing defenses against drones, laser-based systems, other tech
Brodsky said Israel is actively developing defenses against drones, including laser-based systems and other technologies. However, he assessed that no effective solution capable of countering all types of drones has yet been developed.
"Unmanned aerial vehicles are the number one problem for the entire world today," he told Ukrainian media outlets. "Whoever is first to find an effective solution will gain a significant advantage, and that solution will subsequently be adopted by others as well."
Throughout the war, Russia has repeatedly modified its weapons, changed its tactics for penetrating air defenses, and adjusted the scale of its attacks. Ukraine has responded by developing and improving its drone detection and interception capabilities.
For Israel, Ukraine's battlefield experience is particularly relevant because Iran and its allies use weapons based on similar technology. According to Ukrainian reports, the samples provided to Israel could help researchers better understand the modifications Russia has made to its drones and develop ways to counter them.
Ukraine, meanwhile, could also benefit from Israeli expertise. Israel has extensive operational, intelligence, and technological experience in confronting Iran, including its missile and drone capabilities and other military threats in the region.
Sharing intelligence, threat assessments, and lessons learned from military operations could benefit both countries and further strengthen their security cooperation.

Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana slammed world leaders for accusing Israel of committing genocide, calling the allegations a “despicable lie” during a speech at the Council of Europe on Thursday.
“Israel is not committing genocide. Enough with this despicable lie. Israel is fighting genocide.”
“On October 7, there was no ‘collateral damage,’ civilians. Men, women, children, and even babies – were not caught in crossfire. They were the targets,” Ohana added.
Ohana criticized what he described as the hypocrisy of European countries accusing Israel of genocide, as well as the motives of their leaders.
“Today, we are facing a severe crisis of a lack of international courage. Many world leaders declare the importance of lofty values, but when the moment of truth arrives, it turns out that only a few are willing to defend them.”
“Worse still are those who knowingly choose to lie and cynically support false propaganda in order to secure fleeting electoral support and a false sense of calm in their simmering streets,” he said.
Ohana recalls October 7 Hamas massacre at parliamentary conference
Regarding the three-year anniversary of the October 7 Hamas massacre in 2023, Ohana said that “last week, we marked three years since October 7, the day thousands of bloodthirsty terrorists shattered the quiet along the border between the Gaza Strip and the neighboring Israeli communities.”
“They embarked on a campaign of murder, rape, and mutilation of bodies, burning people alive with medieval cruelty.”
Ohana also held up a copy of the book And Every Single One Was Someone, by Phil Chernofsky, before the parliamentary speakers. The book consists of 1,250 pages, on which the single word “Jew” is printed six million times in small letters.
“This book, which I brought with me and which is always on my desk, contains no words,” Ohana continued.
“This thick, heavy volume contains just one word: Jew – six million times. Each one represents an entire human life. Each line represents a classroom full of children. Every few lines represent an entire school. Each page represents a town. When you hold this enormous book and feel its weight, you begin to understand the scale of the loss suffered by the Jewish people, here, on European soil,” he added.
“This is what real genocide looks like,” Ohana continued.
“I keep this book on my desk so that I will never forget. So that the words ‘never again’ do not become an empty slogan. This is also the responsibility that the State of Israel has carried on its shoulders since October 7: to prevent genocide.”
Ohana calls on world leaders to stand with Israel
“This war is far from being merely a local conflict. It is a global confrontation between civilizations – a struggle between the forces of darkness, extremism, and fundamentalism, and the forces of liberty, freedom, and democracy. Some of the member states represented here have a particularly dark chapter in the pages of history,” he added.
“I call on you: This time, stand on the right side of history – alongside us,” Ohana said.
During his stay in Rome, Ohana is expected to hold meetings on the sidelines of the conference with parliamentary speakers and delegations from numerous countries, including Germany, Italy, Ukraine, Hungary, Romania, Lithuania, Montenegro, Cyprus, and Croatia.
These meetings would be held “with the aim of strengthening inter-parliamentary ties and presenting Israel’s positions,” the Knesset spokesperson’s office said.
