02:05:19 KST

Since her first appearance behind the podium this week, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia’s past has become murkier by the day.
A WIRED review of deleted social media and professional networking profiles has helped clear up at least one mystery. Zacharia’s online résumé shows a gap extending from 2013 to late 2023. For part of that time, she worked as an affiliate of Beachbody, a fitness company that ran a multilevel marketing operation she describes to WIRED as “sort of a pyramid scheme.”
Zacharia’s background prior to her emergence as a right-wing operative and pundit in recent years has been the subject of intense curiosity. Prior to joining the White House’s press team, she was a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, a communications adviser at President Donald Trump’s media company, and a commentator on Newsmax and Fox News.
Other parts of her professional background have come under scrutiny, particularly her legal work. According to her LinkedIn, Zacharia was an associate at the Zhong Lun law firm, known in China as a top-tier “red circle” firm, between 2011 and 2013. She also identifies herself on LinkedIn as having worked as general counsel for the nonprofit Fix California. Tax filings reviewed by WIRED, though, show that rather than working as general counsel for Fix California, Zacharia was in fact a fundraiser for the nonprofit.
On Tuesday, journalist Judd Legum reported that Zacharia—who, he noted, had been identified as an attorney in at least 18 appearances on Fox News—did not appear to have ever passed the bar. Since then, The Wall Street Journal has reported that she sat for the California bar exam but never passed—a finding WIRED independently confirmed. (On Wednesday, watchdog organization Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the State Bar of California seeking to investigate the veracity of Zacharia’s claims to be an attorney.)
WIRED was able to gain some clarity about other aspects of Zacharia’s professional history using a database of material leaked online and created by the open-source intelligence firm District 4 Labs. It contains details from a since-deleted LinkedIn account belonging to Zacharia, which listed Beachbody email addresses as two of her points of contact. A representative for the company told WIRED there was no record of her having worked there. In a phone call, Zacharia confirmed to WIRED that she had never been employed by the company.
Zacharia says she was, rather, an affiliate marketer for Beachbody, following her 2013 return from China. She recalls being brought in by a friend and promoting its Shakeology product, which is promoted as a “superfood nutrition shake.” She stopped using and promoting the product, she says, because of its vitamin A content, which she didn’t feel was good for her while pregnant.
Beachbody, now known as BODi, confirmed in a statement that Zacharia was among its 300,000 “independent Team Beachbody distributors” in 2013. A spokesperson added that they believed it would be “misrepresentation” to conflate Zacharia’s time at Beachbody with “BODi’s current business and operations.”
Perhaps unsurprisingly for a company that relied on a multilevel marketing scheme for decades, the company has run into a number of legal issues over the years. It's been accused of falsely advertising a revolutionary anti-aging treatment (the suit was voluntarily dismissed) and making false or misleading income promises to contractors. It got into a copyright battle with a company called Orderlegalsteroids.com, accusing it of stealing an image of Israeli bodybuilder Sagi Kalev from promotional materials for its “BODY BEAST” Program. (Beachbody won a default judgment.)
In 2017, Beachbody, without admitting any wrongdoing, settled a $3.6 million consumer protection lawsuit with the city attorney in Santa Monica, California. Prosecutors alleged that Beachbody made health-related claims about its products, including Shakeology, that were “false, misleading, and not backed by scientific evidence.” They also claimed in filings that Beachbody had been automatically charging customers credit cards for renewals of their products without their consent. As part of its settlement, Beachbody was ordered to pay $1 million to nonprofits that promote health and nutrition.
And in 2023, Beachbody was hit with a class action lawsuit accusing it of scamming its coaches. The lead plaintiff was a schoolteacher who alleged she joined Beachbody with the hope of making a supplementary income but ended up paying $20,000 in personal funds to cover expenses related to her coaching role—all while making about $50 per month for about 50 hours of work. The following year, the company dropped its multilevel marketing program in favor of a “single-level affiliate” one. In 2025, it reached a settlement in the class action suit that resulted in the dismissal of all claims, and the lawsuit was later formally dismissed.
In a statement to WIRED, BODi says, “Team Beachbody was a peer-to-peer sales and support network” and that the company “helped tens of millions of people pursue their health goals through in-home fitness programs like P90X, Insanity, and 21 Day Fix, and nutrition products such as Shakeology.”
This particular notch on Zacharia’s résumé puts her in good company with other high-profile Trumpworld personnel, a cadre of professionals who have a great fondness for supplement-related business opportunities. FBI chief Kash Patel previously promoted supplements that promised to help people “detox” from the Covid-19 vaccine. Nicole Saphier, Trump’s nominee for surgeon general, reported receiving nearly $300,000 in business income from her own company that owns a supplement line. And President Trump himself once oversaw a multilevel marketing company, The Trump Network, which sold an array of vitamins, home urine tests claiming to test for vitamin deficiency, and children’s snacks.

However, Israeli officials remain concerned that an Iranian provocation, an attack by Tehran's regional proxies or a military miscalculation could trigger a confrontation despite efforts to avoid one.
The prevailing assessment is that President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu are unwilling to risk a new military campaign ahead of the elections. Netanyahu is particularly concerned that renewed fighting with Iran could damage Likud's chances of remaining in power in the October 27 vote.
The possibility of an attack was discussed during a conversation between Netanyahu and Trump last week. Although Israeli officials generally consider a preelection strike unlikely, they still regard the possibility as significant.
One concern is that Iran or the Houthi rebels in Yemen could provoke an Israeli response through a limited operation or an attack carried out by one of Tehran's regional proxies.
Another is the possibility of a miscalculation, with each side interpreting the other's military preparations as evidence of an imminent attack and deciding to strike first.
Israel has conveyed a warning to Washington that if Iran makes such a move, it will face an exceptionally severe response, potentially unprecedented in scale, even after the thousands of Iranian targets struck by Israel and the United States during the war.
Israeli security forces are therefore maintaining a high state of alert and preparing for possible surprise attacks by Iran, Hezbollah or the Houthis.
Security officials have emphasized that any Israeli decision to attack Iran ultimately depends on Trump. Without the American president's approval, they say, Israel would be unable to carry out such an operation.
Trump does not appear to have reached a final decision and is continuing to weigh his options. Officials familiar with the matter said he blocked at least two planned Israeli strikes during the summer, both based on Israeli intelligence indicating that Tehran was rebuilding its nuclear program.

Israel's ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, issued a similar warning Thursday ahead of a Security Council meeting, saying he had delivered a direct message to Iran and Hezbollah.

"There is an understanding that without a ground operation by the Americans, there is no chance of achieving something different and new," the official said, adding that repeating previous military actions before the U.S. elections would be a political disaster for Trump.
The president has sent conflicting signals in recent days. During a campaign rally in Alaska on Tuesday, he threatened another major strike against Iran.
"Just wait and see what we do to Iran. We're going to hit them hard. Just wait and see what we do to Iran, because we're getting pretty fed up," Trump said.
Yet last week, Trump declared that he would not attack Iran again before the November 3 midterm elections.
For Israeli officials, the uncertainty means that while a deliberate strike before the elections remains unlikely, the risk of an unexpected escalation has not disappeared. The greatest concern is that an Iranian move, or an attack by one of its proxies, could force decisions neither Washington nor Jerusalem currently wants to make.

US: Somerville weighs Israel boycott over Gaza genocide
Lawmakers in Somerville, Massachusetts, are considering an ordinance that would bar the US city from awarding contracts to companies accused of complicity in Israel’s violations of international law, amid growing pressure to sever financial ties with firms linked to Israel's genocide in Gaza.
The proposal follows a November 2025 ballot measure backed by 55.7% of voters, calling for the city to end existing business with, and prohibit future contracts and investments in, companies linked to Israel’s “apartheid, genocide, and illegal occupation of Palestine”.
The City Council has delayed a decision to assess the ordinance’s scope and financial impact, with a vote expected on 27 October, according to local reports.
Following renewed discussions on Tuesday led by Somerville’s Legislative Matters Committee, councillors said more time was needed to assess which businesses would be affected and the potential financial implications for the city.
Two Jewish councillors have raised concerns about the proposal, particularly over which companies would fall within its scope.
If enacted, Somerville would join a growing number of US cities adopting divestment measures in line with the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement, which seeks to hold Israel accountable for its violations of Palestinian rights through economic pressure.
However, the passage of last year's ballot measure prompted a backlash from pro-Israel groups, which have been pressuring the city to reject the proposed ordinance, citing Somerville’s longstanding Jewish community, which is made up of around 84,000 residents.
Jewish opposition to Israel's policies has grown in the US, with many challenging attempts to portray criticism of Israel or support for Palestinian rights as inherently antisemitic.
An October 2025 survey, reported by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, found that 39% of American Jews believed Israel was committing genocide in Gaza.
More recently, a July 2026 Associated Press-NORC poll highlighted deep divisions within Jewish communities over Israel's military actions. Around four in ten religiously unaffiliated Jewish respondents believed Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, compared with around a quarter of religiously affiliated Jewish respondents.
A separate September 2026 survey by the Jewish Electorate Institute found that 61% of American Jewish voters held an unfavourable view of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, while 60% wanted him replaced.
The findings underline the diversity of Jewish opinion on Israel, even as pro-Israel groups continue to challenge divestment campaigns.
Somerville for Palestine (S4P), a local organisation that spearheaded both the ballot initiative and the proposed ordinance, has continued to press the council to implement the measure.
The group supports the BDS movement, which has long called for boycotts and divestment from companies it considers complicit in Israeli apartheid and genocide in Gaza.
Pro-Palestine activists have accused the city of maintaining financial ties with companies targeted by the BDS movement.
They point to city records showing that its pension fund has more than $500,000 invested in Lockheed Martin, a weapons manufacturer whose fighter jets and Hellfire missiles have reportedly played a significant role in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
Activists have also highlighted more than $1.7 million in contracts Somerville has awarded to Hewlett-Packard over several decades.
According to the BDS movement, HP-linked technology has been used in biometric surveillance systems at Israeli checkpoints in the occupied West Bank, which Palestinians and rights groups have condemned as part of Israel’s system of apartheid.
The ballot initiative and proposed ordinance have received backing from several Somerville councillors, including Ben Ewen-Campen, Ben Wheeler, Wilfred N. Mbah and Jon Link. Jewish Voice for Peace Boston has also voiced support for the measures, demonstrating that Jewish organisations are among those backing efforts to hold Israel accountable through divestment.
The campaign comes amid growing calls for local councils across the US, North America and the wider Western world to recognise the Gaza genocide and sever financial ties with companies accused of facilitating violations of international law.
Pro-Palestine campaigners are urging councils to divest from arms manufacturers supplying Israel with weapons and military technology, as well as companies involved in financing or constructing illegal Israeli settlements in occupied Palestinian territory.
Somerville’s debate follows a decision by Montreal’s city council in Canada to pass an amended motion in August expressing solidarity with the Palestinian people and civilians affected by hostilities across the Middle East.
The move followed a backlash from pro-Israel groups against an earlier proposal calling on the city to recognise and condemn “apartheid” and “genocide” in Palestine and immediately suspend institutional ties with the Israeli government, its institutions and municipalities.

According to the NYT, Russia could launch 70 missiles, 720 drones, and 150 aerial bombs at Ukraine over the course of a month. Three cities are reportedly being identified as targets.
Russia plans to launch approximately 70 ballistic missiles, 720 long-range drones and 150 guided aerial bombs at Ukraine within 30 calendar days, in order to cause the collapse of electricity, heating and water supply systems in Ukraine. UNN reports this, citing an article by The New York Times.
Details
The enemy's main targets could be Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa.
The publication's journalists analyzed data from Ukraine's Air Force and concluded that the indicated number of ballistic missiles and drones approximately corresponds to the average monthly number of such weapons that penetrate Ukrainian air defenses. Therefore, the NYT is convinced that Russia may attempt to inflict critical damage on Ukraine's energy system within one month—damage it failed to achieve during the previous four winters.
Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa are under the greatest threat
If Russia's scenario is implemented, the three largest cities identified as the main targets could face a large-scale disruption of municipal infrastructure. According to the enemy's plan, analyzed by the publication's editorial team, Russia seeks to reduce electricity supplies to Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa by 90%, and heating supplies by up to 90%. Missile and drone attacks could also cause serious disruptions to water supplies and sewerage systems.
Such a development would trigger a large-scale humanitarian crisis, especially in conditions of low temperatures, when the stable operation of power grids, boiler houses and pumping stations is critically important for ensuring the functioning of cities.
Why Russia's plan to black out three Ukrainian megacities could become reality
According to the publication, Ukrainian officials and analysts fear that Russia currently has significantly greater capabilities to carry out a large-scale air campaign against Ukraine's energy sector than in the previous years of the full-scale invasion. The reasons cited include the depletion of Ukrainian air defenses, a reduction in American military aid, and Russia's expansion of missile and drone production.
In addition, after several years of systematic Russian shelling, Ukraine's energy infrastructure remains vulnerable. Because of accumulated damage, even one successful strike may have consequences that previously required the enemy to carry out several attacks to achieve.
The shortage of interceptor missiles for American Patriot surface-to-air missile systems also "plays into the hands" of the Russian Armed Forces. These systems are among the most effective means of protection against Russian ballistic missiles, which pose a particular danger to critical infrastructure facilities.
In addition, the situation is complicated by the continuous improvement of Russian weaponry. Over the years of the war, Moscow has increased the number of missiles and drones in its arsenal and improved the effectiveness of their use. And Ukraine's "mirror" strikes on Russian energy facilities, including oil refineries, cannot inflict damage on Russia's economy on the same scale as the damage Russian attacks cause to Ukrainian infrastructure, officials and experts interviewed by the publication note.
What is known about Russia's plan to destroy the energy system
Earlier, The New York Times reported on a document that the Ukrainian side presented to European partners as an intercepted Russian plan for a large-scale campaign against Ukraine's energy system. According to the journalists, the plan envisages phased strikes on energy facilities, including electrical substations and hydroelectric power plants, with the aim of disrupting the operation of the entire energy system.
A separate threat is the possible disconnection from the power grid of three Ukrainian nuclear power plants that remain under Ukraine's control.
But it should be noted that the NYT editorial team emphasized that it was unable to independently verify the authenticity of the document. It is also currently unknown whether Russia will implement the described scenario and how successful such a campaign could prove to be.
We remind you
On October 14, Russian forces launched another massive attack on Ukraine, damaging dozens of energy facilities in Kyiv and Kharkiv. At least 600,000 people were left without electricity. Russian strikes also affected railway infrastructure in several regions of Ukraine.

Many American diets may not include enough of this essential nutrient
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

Many American diets may not include enough of this essential nutrient
Salt iodization was a public health victory that calls for renewed attention today
Grocery store shelves are bursting with fancy salts: Himalayan, kosher, sea salt and more. Considering these choices, it can be easy to forget about the public health victory found in basic, iodized table salt.
The nutrient iodine is a crucial component of thyroid hormones, necessary for fetal and early childhood brain development and health throughout life. At the start of the last century, iodine deficiency was a rampant and visible public health problem in the United States, with the telltale sign of enlarged thyroid glands, called goiters, especially prevalent in much of the north. A series of steps taken by a medical society in Michigan and U.S. salt producers brought iodized salt to tables across the country, and by the 1950s, occurrences of goiters had dropped precipitously.
But more recently, the United States appears to be backsliding on iodine nutrition. In 2017 and 2018, 24 percent of women and 30 percent of men, aged 14 and older, weren’t getting an adequate amount of the nutrient. That’s about twice as many as in 2001 and 2002, researchers reported in the Journal of Nutrition in 2025. Breaking the data down further, nearly half of pregnant women haven’t been getting enough iodine. The study reflects an estimated, short-term look at population iodine levels.
Long-term, a consistent dearth of iodine robs the body of the ability to produce sufficient amounts of thyroid hormones. If iodine levels in the population continue to trend down, that could eventually result in more goiters and harm brain development in children.
“The group that has the most severe potential consequences of iodine deficiency is pregnant women,” says Elizabeth Pearce, an endocrinologist at Boston University Chobanian & Avedisian School of Medicine. “Even mild degrees of iodine deficiency in pregnancy may be associated with measurably lower IQ in children.”
Yet women of reproductive age, at the U.S. population level, are on the cusp of mild iodine deficiency, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention stated in its 2026 Nutrition Report.
With all of the ways that diets, salt intake and noniodized options have changed over time, the importance of iodine nutrition may not be top-of-mind for the general public like it was a century ago. “Iodine deficiency is the leading cause worldwide of preventable developmental delay,” says Monica Serrano-Gonzalez, a pediatric endocrinologist at Hasbro Children’s and Brown University’s Warren Alpert Medical School in Providence, R.I. “People have kind of forgotten this is a risk.”
The “goiter belt”
When iodine deficiency keeps the thyroid gland from making enough hormones, the body calls for more, which stimulates and enlarges the gland. That supersized gland, called a goiter, bulges at the neck. In the United States, goiters were extremely common a century ago in the Northwest, Great Lakes and Appalachians; together, the area became known as the “goiter belt.” Iodine naturally occurs in seawater and soil. But in the noncoastal northern part of the country, soils and water sources have little iodine, so the crops produced in these inland areas lack the nutrient.
An examining physician for the World War I draft reported in 1918 that 30 percent of almost 600 men from a northern Michigan county had goiters, some large enough to be disqualifying. A 1922 Michigan Department of Health study of schoolchildren in four counties revealed that close to 50 percent had goiters. “It would have been a really visible public health problem at that time,” Pearce says.
In response to the state’s iodine issues, the Michigan State Medical Society recommended the addition of the nutrient to table salt. The minimal expense for iodization meant this common kitchen staple would remain affordable. Companies introduced iodized salt in Michigan in the spring of 1924. By the fall, the Morton Salt Company, a major producer, was selling iodized salt nationwide. Over time, the goiters of the “belt” dwindled.
Salt iodization has been linked to rising IQ in the United States. For example, for men born in areas without natural sources of iodine, there was a significant jump in World War II Air Force acceptances, based on a qualifying exam, after widespread salt iodization. The increase did not occur among men born in areas with adequate natural sources of the nutrient, researchers reported in the Journal of the European Economic Association in 2017.
Adding iodine to salt was never mandated by the U.S. government. But for a long time, the voluntary approach — combined with how most people consumed salt and other dietary habits — did the trick to get people enough iodine. Today, different meal practices and available food options are tearing holes in the iodine safety net. “Iodized salt is important, but it may not be reaching everybody anymore,” Pearce says.
There are many more noniodized salt options today, with one analysis reporting that only 53 percent of table salt sold in U.S. stores is iodized. People get much of their salt from prepared, processed and packaged foods, which generally are made with noniodized salt. Milk can provide iodine, due to iodine-supplemented feed and the use of an iodine cleanser on cows’ udders. But the amount of iodine in milk can vary greatly, a recent analysis found, probably because industry practices can differ. Diets that restrict dairy may also put people at risk of consuming too little iodine.
The U.S. recommended dietary allowance for iodine for adults is 150 micrograms per day, which rises to 220 mcg for pregnant people and 290 mcg for those breastfeeding. The amount of the nutrient that iodized salt contains can vary, but will be listed on the container’s label. Based on a 2023 federal report on food iodine content, one teaspoon of salt has around 300 mcg of added iodine. (The American Heart Association recommends a limit of 2,300 milligrams of sodium per day; one teaspoon of salt has 2,400 mg of sodium.)
The American Thyroid Association and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommend that pregnant and breastfeeding people, as well as those planning to become pregnant, take a daily supplement with 150 micrograms of iodine. Sufficient iodine is especially important in the first trimester of pregnancy, when a developing embryo relies solely on the mother’s supply.
When choosing table salt, “look for salt that’s iodized,” Pearce says. For people on a low-salt diet, it’s better to cut out packaged and prepared foods, Serrano-Gonzalez says. “We do want to have moderation with salt intake, but we need a little bit” of iodized salt, she says.
The consequences of too little iodine
People have largely forgotten why it’s important to choose iodized salt, Pearce says. It’s not a decision that many people have to make globally: One hundred and twenty-six countries mandate salt iodization, while only 21 have voluntary polices.
An observational study of an iodine crisis in Ethiopia indicates the catastrophic consequences of losing the nutrient. The country adopted a salt iodization policy in the 1990s, and by 1995, 80 percent of households reported using iodized salt. But the country’s stock came from Eritrea, and in 1998, a conflict between the two countries closed the border and interrupted the supply of iodized salt. By 2005, the Ethiopian population was severely iodine deficient, with up to 40 percent of school-aged children and 36 percent of women of reproductive age developing goiters. Ethiopia’s government was able to reinstate mandatory salt iodization in 2012, and household coverage climbed to 85 percent by 2015.
But the severe iodine disruption during the war had a devastating effect on the children born and raised in that period. In rural areas, which had very low soil iodine levels, mortality among children in the first two years of life reached 25 to 30 percent, compared with 10 percent in other areas, researchers reported in Nature Food in September. The children from rural areas who reached secondary school scored lower on national exams. The study team took other effects of the conflict into account, to focus on the impact of the iodine nutrition emergency.
In the United States, the worst manifestation of iodine deficiency was the long ago “goiter belt.” “There needs to be public health education,” Pearce says, “so people understand again what the dangers are if we don’t have adequate iodine nutrition, and how to just ensure that they’re protected.”

Ukraine at OSCE: Strikes on Russian oil refineries can stop only under mutual “energy truce”
Ukraine’s Permanent Representative to the International Organizations in Vienna, Yurii Vitrenko, said this during a meeting of the OSCE Permanent Council on Thursday, Ukrinform reports.
“We are ready for a ceasefire. We are ready to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries provided that Russia stops attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. This is fair,” the Ukrainian diplomat stressed.
He pointed out that Ukraine had repeatedly confirmed its readiness for various ceasefire arrangements, but instead of taking genuine steps toward peace, Moscow continued to intensify attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure.
Vitrenko informed OSCE participating States’ delegations that over the past week alone, Russia had carried out more than 200 strikes on electricity generation and transmission facilities in Ukraine, as well as 17 attacks on gas and oil infrastructure. In particular, on October 14, Russian forces launched a massive attack on critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv region and Kharkiv region, using 40 missiles. The attack damaged 30 energy facilities, including electricity and gas infrastructure, and left around 600,000 people without power. According to the State Emergency Service, 21 people were injured in Kyiv, while three were killed.
The diplomat stressed that Russia had continued attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure even after U.S. President Donald Trump announced an “energy truce” initiative on October 11.
“If Russia refuses reciprocal steps and continues to demonstrate complete disregard for peace efforts, there can be no meaningful progress toward a ceasefire,” Vitrenko said.
He emphasized that de-escalation must be mutual and backed by reliable guarantees, and that Ukraine’s exercise of its legitimate right to self-defense cannot be interpreted as unwillingness to achieve peace.
“The only obstacle remains Russia’s refusal to halt its attacks and engage meaningfully in de-escalation,” the permanent representative stressed.
According to him, until Moscow responds with concrete actions for peace, Ukraine’s Defense Forces will continue defending the country and degrading the aggressor’s military capabilities.
The Ukrainian delegation also called on international partners to increase sanctions pressure on Russia and ensure accountability for attacks on civilians, energy facilities and commercial vessels in the Black Sea.
As Ukrinform reported, on October 15, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine had resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries after Russia continued attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure despite the U.S. President’s “energy truce” initiative.

The UK's Green Party declare Zionism racism, exposing their double standards - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

In The Man of Destiny (1898), George Bernard Shaw gave Napoleon the definitive line on the English: “You will never find an Englishman in the wrong. He does everything on principle. He fights you on patriotic principles; he robs you on business principles; he enslaves you on imperial principles; he bullies you on manly principles; he supports his king on loyal principles, and cuts off his king’s head on republican principles.” Britain has spent a fortnight proving him right.
On October 4, in Brighton, the Green Party of England and Wales adopted a “Zionism is Racism” motion by 1,022 votes to 813. The party now “declares itself to be an anti-Zionist party,” resolves that Zionism “will be treated as any other form of racism,” and calls for “a single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine.”
An amendment to protect members of synagogues that identify as Zionist was defeated, 1,026 to 684. Outside, supporters chanted: “Say it loud, say it clear, Zionists are not welcome here.”
The motion’s brochure is franker still. It invokes “struggling by all available means, including armed struggle,” and asserts: “Only racists, genocidaires and supporters of apartheid can argue (and kill) for the continuation of Zionism.”
The lead author’s signed text ends with “Free Palestine, from the river to the sea!” – repeated on the endorsements page. The river is the Jordan, the sea the Mediterranean; between them lies Israel, which the slogan erases.
Zionism is nothing other than the right of the Jewish people to self-determination in the land where it became a people. By a grim twist of fate, the very same tireless champions of the right of return and of self-determination for every people deny both to the Jews alone.
And the “racism” Brighton denounces has a face: according to the Institute for Jewish Policy Research, 64% of British Jews identify as Zionists. The Board of Deputies and the Jewish Leadership Council called the motion “an attack on the Jewish community” and answered in three words: “Zionism is anti-racism.”
Brighton is no island. That same weekend, the Royal College of Nursing cut ties with Teva UK, the Israeli drugmaker’s subsidiary, after a Nurses for Palestine campaign.
Days earlier, The Sunday Times revealed Britain had granted asylum, then citizenship, to a former bodyguard of Hamas chief Ismail Haniyeh – accused by German prosecutors of helping prepare attacks on Jewish and Israeli targets in Europe.
A former Hamas bodyguard naturalized, an Israeli company shown the door, Zionism outlawed: each decision has its principle, and none is in the wrong.
Green Europe refused to follow. The European Green Party said: “As EGP we unequivocally distance ourselves from it” – while lambasting Israel’s government. German Greens co-leader Felix Banaszak called the motion “intolerable and unacceptable.” At home, a councillor, a former opposition leader in Richmond, and Amnesty International UK’s board chair have quit the party.
The J50, a forum of Diaspora Jewish leaders convened by Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, which declared in September that “Zionism is part of Jewish identity,” is working to keep the other Green parties apart from Brighton. Its aim is plain: Brighton must stand alone.
Israel has answered the Labour government – not Brighton. On October 8, Sa’ar confirmed the four measures announced on September 8 were implemented: British representatives removed from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat; British training of Palestinian Authority forces in Judea and Samaria terminated; 12 British elected officials and other Britons involved in antisemitic and anti-Israel activity denied entry; and the British Consulate in Jerusalem closed, its sign taken down.
'Labour Government brought us here'
London is saving face: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband says the building “will be known as the UK Mission, Jerusalem,” its staff only “temporarily withdrawn,” and pledges no “reciprocal action while such discussions are underway and credible.” The consul general and 19 diplomats are leaving all the same.
“We did not want to reach this point,” Sa’ar said, “but the actions of the UK Labour Government brought us here.”
Since July 2024, that government has recognized a virtual “Palestinian state,” restored UNRWA funding, suspended defense export licenses and free trade talks, sanctioned Israeli ministers, frozen military dialogue, kept IDF officers out of the Royal College of Defence Studies and, lately, imposed far-reaching sanctions on Judea and Samaria’s communities, amid accusations of “ethnic cleansing.”
Israel does not confuse a government with a nation. Sa’ar stressed that relations with Britain “are important and have repeatedly proven their value also in protecting the lives and interests of British citizens” – most recently with vital information in the RAF Fairford affair. Yet he warns: “any country that acts against Israel must know that there will be a price for doing so. … Israel will no longer turn its cheek to diplomatic attacks against it.”
That is how duplicity is sanctioned: not with invective, but with measured acts of state. The rest must follow – politically, at the ballot box; legally, wherever British equality and nationality law offers a foothold.
The self-determination of peoples is enshrined in Article 1 of the UN Charter; Britain’s Greens grant it to every people but one. Denying to Jews alone what is granted to everyone else has a precise legal name. That name is not “Zionism.” It is “discrimination.”
Shaw’s Englishman is never in the wrong. This time, he is simply wrong in law.
The writer is a Portugal- and Israel-based French entrepreneur, legal adviser, and expert in crypto assets, information security, and computer warfare. A former lecturer at the Institut des Hautes Études de Défense Nationale (IHEDN) on influence operations, he has participated in French parliamentary missions on economic intelligence and advised on digital threats facing France and European institutions. He regularly comments on French foreign policy and Middle East affairs.

Many American diets may not include enough of this essential nutrient
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

Many American diets may not include enough of this essential nutrient
Salt iodization was a public health victory that calls for renewed attention today
Grocery store shelves are bursting with fancy salts: Himalayan, kosher, sea salt and more. Considering these choices, it can be easy to forget about the public health victory found in basic, iodized table salt.
The nutrient iodine is a crucial component of thyroid hormones, necessary for fetal and early childhood brain development and health throughout life. At the start of the last century, iodine deficiency was a rampant and visible public health problem in the United States, with the telltale sign of enlarged thyroid glands, called goiters, especially prevalent in much of the north. A series of steps taken by a medical society in Michigan and U.S. salt producers brought iodized salt to tables across the country, and by the 1950s, occurrences of goiters had dropped precipitously.
But more recently, the United States appears to be backsliding on iodine nutrition. In 2017 and 2018, 24 percent of women and 30 percent of men, aged 14 and older, weren’t getting an adequate amount of the nutrient. That’s about twice as many as in 2001 and 2002, researchers reported in the Journal of Nutrition in 2025. Breaking the data down further, nearly half of pregnant women haven’t been getting enough iodine. The study reflects an estimated, short-term look at population iodine levels.
Long-term, a consistent dearth of iodine robs the body of the ability to produce sufficient amounts of thyroid hormones. If iodine levels in the population continue to trend down, that could eventually result in more goiters and harm brain development in children.
“The group that has the most severe potential consequences of iodine deficiency is pregnant women,” says Elizabeth Pearce, an endocrinologist at Boston University Chobanian & Avedisian School of Medicine. “Even mild degrees of iodine deficiency in pregnancy may be associated with measurably lower IQ in children.”
Yet women of reproductive age, at the U.S. population level, are on the cusp of mild iodine deficiency, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention stated in its 2026 Nutrition Report.
With all of the ways that diets, salt intake and noniodized options have changed over time, the importance of iodine nutrition may not be top-of-mind for the general public like it was a century ago. “Iodine deficiency is the leading cause worldwide of preventable developmental delay,” says Monica Serrano-Gonzalez, a pediatric endocrinologist at Hasbro Children’s and Brown University’s Warren Alpert Medical School in Providence, R.I. “People have kind of forgotten this is a risk.”
The “goiter belt”
When iodine deficiency keeps the thyroid gland from making enough hormones, the body calls for more, which stimulates and enlarges the gland. That supersized gland, called a goiter, bulges at the neck. In the United States, goiters were extremely common a century ago in the Northwest, Great Lakes and Appalachians; together, the area became known as the “goiter belt.” Iodine naturally occurs in seawater and soil. But in the noncoastal northern part of the country, soils and water sources have little iodine, so the crops produced in these inland areas lack the nutrient.
An examining physician for the World War I draft reported in 1918 that 30 percent of almost 600 men from a northern Michigan county had goiters, some large enough to be disqualifying. A 1922 Michigan Department of Health study of schoolchildren in four counties revealed that close to 50 percent had goiters. “It would have been a really visible public health problem at that time,” Pearce says.
In response to the state’s iodine issues, the Michigan State Medical Society recommended the addition of the nutrient to table salt. The minimal expense for iodization meant this common kitchen staple would remain affordable. Companies introduced iodized salt in Michigan in the spring of 1924. By the fall, the Morton Salt Company, a major producer, was selling iodized salt nationwide. Over time, the goiters of the “belt” dwindled.
Salt iodization has been linked to rising IQ in the United States. For example, for men born in areas without natural sources of iodine, there was a significant jump in World War II Air Force acceptances, based on a qualifying exam, after widespread salt iodization. The increase did not occur among men born in areas with adequate natural sources of the nutrient, researchers reported in the Journal of the European Economic Association in 2017.
Adding iodine to salt was never mandated by the U.S. government. But for a long time, the voluntary approach — combined with how most people consumed salt and other dietary habits — did the trick to get people enough iodine. Today, different meal practices and available food options are tearing holes in the iodine safety net. “Iodized salt is important, but it may not be reaching everybody anymore,” Pearce says.
There are many more noniodized salt options today, with one analysis reporting that only 53 percent of table salt sold in U.S. stores is iodized. People get much of their salt from prepared, processed and packaged foods, which generally are made with noniodized salt. Milk can provide iodine, due to iodine-supplemented feed and the use of an iodine cleanser on cows’ udders. But the amount of iodine in milk can vary greatly, a recent analysis found, probably because industry practices can differ. Diets that restrict dairy may also put people at risk of consuming too little iodine.
The U.S. recommended dietary allowance for iodine for adults is 150 micrograms per day, which rises to 220 mcg for pregnant people and 290 mcg for those breastfeeding. The amount of the nutrient that iodized salt contains can vary, but will be listed on the container’s label. Based on a 2023 federal report on food iodine content, one teaspoon of salt has around 300 mcg of added iodine. (The American Heart Association recommends a limit of 2,300 milligrams of sodium per day; one teaspoon of salt has 2,400 mg of sodium.)
The American Thyroid Association and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommend that pregnant and breastfeeding people, as well as those planning to become pregnant, take a daily supplement with 150 micrograms of iodine. Sufficient iodine is especially important in the first trimester of pregnancy, when a developing embryo relies solely on the mother’s supply.
When choosing table salt, “look for salt that’s iodized,” Pearce says. For people on a low-salt diet, it’s better to cut out packaged and prepared foods, Serrano-Gonzalez says. “We do want to have moderation with salt intake, but we need a little bit” of iodized salt, she says.
The consequences of too little iodine
People have largely forgotten why it’s important to choose iodized salt, Pearce says. It’s not a decision that many people have to make globally: One hundred and twenty-six countries mandate salt iodization, while only 21 have voluntary polices.
An observational study of an iodine crisis in Ethiopia indicates the catastrophic consequences of losing the nutrient. The country adopted a salt iodization policy in the 1990s, and by 1995, 80 percent of households reported using iodized salt. But the country’s stock came from Eritrea, and in 1998, a conflict between the two countries closed the border and interrupted the supply of iodized salt. By 2005, the Ethiopian population was severely iodine deficient, with up to 40 percent of school-aged children and 36 percent of women of reproductive age developing goiters. Ethiopia’s government was able to reinstate mandatory salt iodization in 2012, and household coverage climbed to 85 percent by 2015.
But the severe iodine disruption during the war had a devastating effect on the children born and raised in that period. In rural areas, which had very low soil iodine levels, mortality among children in the first two years of life reached 25 to 30 percent, compared with 10 percent in other areas, researchers reported in Nature Food in September. The children from rural areas who reached secondary school scored lower on national exams. The study team took other effects of the conflict into account, to focus on the impact of the iodine nutrition emergency.
In the United States, the worst manifestation of iodine deficiency was the long ago “goiter belt.” “There needs to be public health education,” Pearce says, “so people understand again what the dangers are if we don’t have adequate iodine nutrition, and how to just ensure that they’re protected.”

The Russian commentators living in Europe who justify Moscow's war against Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:59:46 UTC
01:59:46 KST

The Russian commentators living in Europe who justify Moscow's war against Ukraine
Yulia Latynina in an unnamed location, on Feb. 9, 2013. (Wikimedia Commons)
Latvia's decision last week to declare Russian-born journalist and blogger Leonid Ragozin persona non grata has drawn attention to a broader trend: Russians who once presented themselves as opponents of Vladimir Putin are now accused of echoing Kremlin narratives.
Some now live in Europe, taking advantage of the freedom and security that their adopted countries provide to broadcast their views.
Ironically, some of them blame the European Union for Russia’s war against Ukraine and most of the world's other problems while enjoying the liberties and safety provided by EU member states.
"Why are people who support Russia’s war or provide a justification for their country's actions welcomed in Europe?"
They span a wide spectrum, from self-styled impartial commentators who insist on hearing "both sides" to outspoken supporters of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine.
The Kyiv Independent has requested comment from Ragozin and will publish his response once it is received.
read also
A subtle promoter of Kremlin narratives
One of these commentators, Ragozin, has worked as a journalist for various English-language and Russian-language publications, including BBC, Newsweek Russia, Al-Jazeera, Bloomberg, the Guardian, Politico, the New Republic, Time, and the Washington Post.
In 2013, Ragozin moved to Latvia.
According to data from a leaked database obtained by the Kyiv Independent, Ragozin regularly visited Russia between 2014 and 2022. He left Russia on Feb. 17, 2022 – before the full-scale invasion began on Feb. 24 – and then returned there during the invasion. He again left Russia on March 3, 2022.
Latvia's Foreign Ministry announced on Oct. 6 that it had declared a Russian citizen persona non grata, without naming the individual. On Oct. 14, Ragozin confirmed that Latvia had referred to him and said that he had been notified of his expulsion from Latvia.
Ragozin said he was facing "political persecution" and argued that this was "revenge by far-right politicians for my investigation into their links to Russian neo-Nazis who found refuge in Kyiv" and "a punishment for my commentary on the Russian aggression in Ukraine."
Unlike some other critics of Ukraine, Ragozin has taken a more nuanced and subtle approach. He has never explicitly supported Russian President Vladimir Putin.
However, he has been repeatedly accused of promoting Kremlin-friendly narratives. Ragozin has written mostly in English and targeted an important audience — right-wing and left-wing commentators in the West, as well as the "Global South."
In 2021, Ragozin effectively blamed Ukraine for "provoking" an escalation with Russia by seeking NATO membership. He argued that Russia’s troop buildup around Ukraine's borders was reactive rather than aggressive.
Instead of criticizing the Kremlin, Ragozin has focused on lambasting nationalists and "neo-Nazis" in Ukraine.
Ragozin has effectively blamed the West for the war, arguing that it pushed Kyiv into an unwinnable conflict.
He also argued that "the war can only end on Moscow's terms" and accused Ukraine and Europe of sabotaging peace talks by seeking a compromise.
In a September interview, Ragozin said that he doesn't "think Russia has a deliberate policy of targeting civilians, but that can change." Over the past week, at least 150 Ukrainian civilians were killed by Russia, with the Kremlin targeting public transport in Kramatorsk, and apartment buildings in Pryluky and Zaporizhzhia.
Russia executed civilians in Bucha in 2022 and has deliberately destroyed cities in Ukraine's east — Avdiivka, Bakhmut, Siverskodonetsk, Pokrovsk, and Druzhkivka — to name a few.
Konstantin Eggert, who headed the BBC's Moscow bureau in the 2000s and was part of the board that selected Ragozin for the position of producer, commented on him for the Kyiv Independent.
Eggert said that several times he "heard the opinion that Ragozin is de facto equating the aggressor (Russia) with the victim of aggression (Ukraine), denying or downplaying atrocities committed by the Russian forces and portraying the Baltic States to his audience as irresponsible warmongers."
"I agree with this view," he added. "I believe that Ragozin or anyone else is perfectly entitled to hold and broadcast such views. But they should not be surprised if others describe such positions as chiming in with the Kremlin narratives."
InformNapalm, a Ukrainian open-source intelligence outfit, told the Kyiv Independent that "his recurring arguments effectively reinforce the Kremlin's preferred narrative about the causes of the war and the terms on which it could end, particularly among Western audiences."
Ragozin denied the accusations against him on X on Oct. 14.
"My stance on the war in Ukraine remains unchanged," he said. "I condemn the Russian aggression and support Ukraine's sovereignty over occupied territories…. But I'll continue to criticize Western countries for mishandling this conflict and not acting in the best interests of the Ukrainian people."
read also
A former liberal and pro-war propagandist
Yulia Latynina, a blogger, columnist, and writer, has gone much farther than Ragozin in the evolution of her views on Ukraine.
She used to be one of Russia’s most prominent anti-Kremlin liberal opinion leaders and called herself a "libertarian."
Latynina left Russia in 2017 following several attacks on her, as well as on her house and her car, that she blamed on people linked to the late Yevgeniy Prigozhin, then a trusted confidant of Putin.
According to media reports, since 2017 Latynina has been based alternately in Cyprus and Estonia. Her phone number is Cypriot, and several organizations founded by Latynina are based in Estonia.
Between 2014 and 2023, Latynina fully supported Ukraine and opposed Russia’s war.
But starting from 2024, she changed her views dramatically, turning into a harsh critic of Ukraine and the West. As Donald Trump was re-elected president of the U.S. in 2024, she increasingly aligned her views with the anti-Ukrainian rhetoric of Trump and his allies.
Now, Latynina fully supports Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine.
"If the project of Ukraine as an 'anti-Russia' cannot be destroyed completely, then it should be weakened as much as possible."
Latynina believes that Ukraine represents a "strategic threat" to Russia and that Russia had a right to invade Ukraine to defend its "strategic interests." Her views on foreign policy are now similar to those of Russian imperialists Alexander Dugin, Alexander Prokhanov, and Eduard Limonov.
Latynina has argued that it is in Russia’s strategic interest to ensure that the boundary between the Russian and Ukrainian languages is "as far west as possible."
"If the project of Ukraine as an 'anti-Russia' cannot be destroyed completely, then it should be weakened as much as possible," Latynina said in a 2026 interview.
When asked in 2026 about the war’s negative impact on Russians' living standards, she said that strategic interests should override their concerns, and average Russians "will always live like shit" regardless of the war.
Asked why she has shed her libertarian credentials and embraced something resembling Dugin's Eurasianism, Latynina told the Kyiv Independent that she had not read Dugin and had been influenced by U.S. foreign-policy realists George Kennan, Pat Buchanan, and Jeffrey Sachs.
"Russia could not allow a territory that had taken shape as a result of the Russian Empire's and the Soviet Union's westward expansion... to suddenly turn into Halychyna stretching from the river to the sea," she said in a reference to Halychyna (Galicia), a historic region in western Ukraine that, according to Russian propaganda, is the core base of Ukrainian nationalism.
She has opposed ending the war on terms that she thinks are "unfavorable" to Russia — such as freezing the front line.
In her attempts to justify Russia’s war, Latynina has gone as far as to claim that states "have a right to aggression."
Asked how this reconciles with the libertarian principle of the non-initiation of force, Latynina cited the Roman historian Livy in a comment for the Kyiv Independent, saying that "war is just for those for whom it is necessary."
In 2025, Latynina also shocked the audience by publishing an article trying to justify Russia’s actions by drawing parallels with Nazi Germany. She argued that Nazi Germany's expansionism was a result of the mistreatment of ethnic Germans abroad — similarly to alleged violations of Russian speakers' rights in Ukraine.
Like Ragozin, Latynina has also blamed Ukraine and Europe for the lack of progress in peace negotiations and accused them of perpetuating the war. She has repeatedly criticized what she sees as a stagnant European bureaucracy mired in a deep crisis.
Asked why she lives in the EU despite hating it, Latynina told the Kyiv Independent that "it's up to the bots and the nationalist decolonization advocates to explain why Latynina should be persecuted in a free country for refusing to toe the party line."
She now presents the Russian opposition as puppets of the West, saying that they will sell out Russia’s interests if they come to power.
Latynina's increasingly pro-Kremlin and pro-war narratives have prompted speculation that she is either working for the Kremlin or contemplating a return to Russia.
She has denied working for the Kremlin. Latynina said in a 2026 interview that the status of a foreign agent was impeding the publication of her books in Russia, and that she was thinking of the possibility of being stripped of that status.
However, she told the Kyiv Independent she had not contacted the Russian authorities about the issue so far.
read also
An ambiguous stance on Ukraine
Some other notable Russian commentators occupy a middle ground between Latynina and Ragozin.
Oleg Kashin, who had long been an independent journalist critical of the Kremlin, acknowledged that Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014 was illegal.
Despite this, he supported the annexation, arguing that it was a "restoration of historical justice."
"There is no doubt that it was annexed in violation of international law," Kashin, who is based in the U.K., told the Kyiv Independent. "But I don't believe that international law is taken seriously at all. There are simply no major players in world politics that genuinely abide by it… My Russian heart won't let me say that we should have made sure Crimea remained part of Ukraine."
Kashin also condemned the use of Russian troops in the Donbas in 2014. However, he blamed Ukraine for allegedly fueling tensions leading up to Russia’s invasion of eastern Ukraine.
On the eve of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, Kashin wished "Russian soldiers good luck and strength" in a future military conflict in Ukraine.
However, he eventually became a critic of Russia’s full-scale invasion, saying that it was at odds with Russia’s national interests.
He attributed his initial support for Russian soldiers in 2022 to his belief that Russia would only invade the unoccupied part of the Donbas, not the whole of Ukraine.
"When I realized that what was actually happening was an insane and suicidal march on Kyiv, I naturally spoke out against it immediately," he told the Kyiv Independent.
He said, however, that he believes that a limited Russian invasion of the Donbas in 2022 "would have been far more beneficial than the criminal regimes that had been established in the Donbas with Russia’s support" in 2014.
For Ukraine and its supporters, the question that arises is clear — why are people who support Russia’s war or provide a justification for their country's actions welcomed in Europe?
"When assessing information influence, what matters is not just how someone describes themselves — as an opposition figure or a critic of Putin — but also the specific narratives they consistently promote to their audience," InformNapalm said.

US lawmaker warns Colombia's president against interfering in House elections

Berk Kutay Gökmen
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
US Representative Gregory Meeks has warned Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella against involving himself in US House of Representatives elections, saying such actions could undermine decades of bipartisan support for relations between the two countries.
In a statement issued Wednesday, Meeks, the ranking Democratic member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, stressed that American voters alone should determine who represents them in Congress.
“A foreign leader interfering in American elections is unacceptable,” Meeks said, underscoring the importance of democracy in the relationship between Washington and Bogota.
The US lawmaker said the two countries shared “two centuries of friendship and partnership,” with democratic values serving as a central pillar of their alliance.
Meeks also expressed concern that the Colombian leader's remarks could weaken the bipartisan goodwill that has sustained bilateral ties for decades.

Two family-run British engineering firms have formed a joint venture to manufacture composite vehicle bodies in Tamworth, positioning themselves ahead of the British Army’s Land Mobility Vehicle competition, according to the companies.
North Strong brings together North Defence, the light mobility vehicle specialist founded by the former Royal Engineer Oliver North, and Strongs Plastic Products, the Midlands polymer engineering company founded in 1978 by the late Barry Strong and now run by his son James. The two have worked alongside each other since 2023, and the venture is incorporated at Companies House as North Strong Defence Limited.

Strongs has always prided itself on innovation in the use of polymers and we see this as another opportunity to develop and grow our capabilities in a new market sector with the help of North Defence.”
The announcement lands alongside the North Defence LMV MKIII, which the company says can be built on Toyota, Ford, INEOS Grenadier and Mercedes-Benz base chassis, all using the same North Strong body. The Land Mobility Vehicle programme is the Army’s effort to replace the ageing Land Rover-derived fleet that has carried infantry, engineers and support units for decades, and it has drawn a competitive field.

Over 70 rights groups urge Egypt to release Matsad2sh journalists

The organisations shed light on the escalating crackdown on the Matsad2sh platform (Arabic for ‘don’t believe’) and the six journalists who were detained following raids on their homes on 28 and 29 September.

An autism diagnosis, but where’s the treatment? | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:51:51 UTC
01:51:51 KST

Your coverage of the Fonagy review concentrates on children and on the risk of diagnosing too readily (NHS at risk of ‘system failures’ as demand for ADHD and autism care soars, inquiry finds, 9 October). I’d like to speak for those of us who were not diagnosed at all.
I first asked for help at 17. For 34 years I was treated for anxiety, depression and trauma. All were real; none were the whole story. I was diagnosed as autistic at 51. The same report identified ADHD, which until 2013 could not officially be diagnosed alongside autism.
I am still waiting for that ADHD assessment. ADHD is the one for which there is medication, but I cannot get to it. For autism there is nothing: you are given the diagnosis and sent home to deal with it.
The review asks for support based on need, not labels. I’d welcome that. But I have the label and the need, and neither has brought support. The diagnosis explained my life; it did not come with any help to live it.
 
Rebecca Hope Duncan
 
Southampton
Your editorial (11 October) correctly identifies the need for improved prevention and treatment of neurodevelopmental disorders, rather than rehearsing debates about diagnosis. Here are three additional suggestions.
First, neurodevelopment largely occurs during sleep: neuroplasticity is what sleep is for. Many infants and children are sleep-deprived, so a national public health programme on improving child sleep hygiene will prevent and ameliorate the severity of future neurodevelopment disorders.
Second, depression. Many young people with autism spectrum disorder and ADHD also fulfil criteria for depression, which is treatable at GP surgeries with combinations of exercise and pluralistic psychological therapy.
Third, work: to not work is bad for the mental health of young people with neurodivergence. If you can exercise, you can work, so the government could follow Dutch and Danish models and return to the supported employment and tax credits previously devised by Gordon Brown, undone by the political vandalism of Tory/Liberal Democrat austerity.
 
Jeremy Seymour
 
Retired consultant psychiatrist, Sheffield
Your editorial mentions that “the rises in psychological distress, and the need for support with neurodevelopmental differences, are real and tied to social changes”.
If the problems are tied to social changes, why is it primarily a healthcare issue? Wouldn’t we be better off calling out the “social changes” and addressing them?
It’s possible to do that while acknowledging the reality of the suffering of those involved, dignifying it in fact. By focusing entirely on the symptoms, we risk ignoring the root, and in doing so will allow more children to suffer.
 
John Bryant
 
GP, Bristol
 Given the alarming rise in childhood mental health problems, why do we allow our children to be fed on ultra-processed foods (UPFs)? Childhood anxiety is on the rise globally, but the UK is in the worst-performing group of wealthy nations in virtually every measure of child and adolescent mental health. Coincidentally, British children also have the equal worst diets in the world – along with the US – in terms of consumption of UPFs, which make up around two-thirds of their diet. A 2026 systematic review found a clear association between child and adolescent consumption of UPFs and mental health problems such as anxiety, depression, irritability, sleep disturbances and suicidal ideation. And a Canadian study of over 2,000 children found that as children ate more UPFs, they faced increasing risk of emotional and behavioural problems, and that replacing just 10% of UPF calories with minimally processed real food, lowered children’s behaviour problem scores. Until the government is ready to stand up to the powerful food industry and ignores the inevitable cries of “nanny state”, this won’t change.
 
Peter Deadman
 
Hove, East Sussex
The differing explanations for the huge rise in diagnoses for autism and ADHD arise, I believe, from a general problem in the diagnosis of mental health conditions. In physical medicine, diagnosis includes not just the description and classification of symptoms, but identifying the underlying pathology that gives rise to the symptoms, and where possible the cause of this pathology.
A symptom such as a headache, for example, can arise for a variety of reasons, and a diagnosis will determine what its origin is. The characteristics of the headache, such as severity, exact location and duration, will give clues as to the underlying cause, but this can only be determined accurately by medical tests. There are some conditions where a group of symptoms regularly occur together but where the underlying pathology is unknown; these are classed as syndromes, and the names for them are descriptive rather than true diagnoses.
In the area of mental health, there are few if any diagnoses in the strict sense, and the terms used are descriptive rather than truly diagnostic. Even for the most severe conditions, such as schizophrenia, the underlying pathology is unknown, and this is even more true of conditions such as depression and anxiety, where the distinction between normal reactions and conditions severe enough to be regarded as illnesses is unclear.
Nobody seriously questions that the phenomena of autism and ADHD exist; the question is whether the concept of diagnosis is appropriate. If not, the distinction between what is “normal” and what is a “disorder” is arbitrary, based on the severity of the problems experienced and how well someone is able to function. The criteria for autism have been broadened to include people on the “spectrum” with much milder difficulties than in the past, while ADHD is a condition that has only recently been recognised at all. It is therefore not surprising that many more have been diagnosed than in the past. However, it also raises the question of whether, in the milder cases, they should be regarded as “disorders” as opposed to differences in personality.
 
Steve Bamford
 
Littlehampton, West Sussex
It’s not just young people who have been let down by the lack of diagnosis and care available to those with ADHD and Autism. My 70-year-old wife has suffered from one of these conditions throughout her life, along with many others of her generation. Had she been diagnosed at an early age, she would have had a much easier, more successful and fulfilling life. However, National Institute for Health and Care Excellence and NHS guidelines in the UK did not recognise ADHD as a valid condition in adults until 2008, when she was aged 52 and her condition began to become more evident postmenopause.
Being born in the north of England in the 1950s meant there was little or no chance of her receiving a childhood diagnosis that would have made her life much more understandable. Today, living in Scotland where the NHS does not offer the “right to choose” for ADHD assessments, she would face a median wait time of 111 weeks, with some waits as long as 266 weeks and currently 8,886 adults in the queue. Not surprisingly she continues to remain undiagnosed along with many others.
 
Name and address supplied

The UK must have digital sovereignty | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:51:15 UTC
01:51:15 KST

The UK cannot become dependent on foreign AI technology that can be switched off at short notice, says George Williamson, head of the Alan Turing Institute (Report, 10 October). The growing opposition to Palantir, an American company, having government contracts that give it access to sensitive data are all part of the same issue. The UK does not have digital sovereignty.
This is not a theoretical problem. The US government imposed targeted sanctions on the international criminal court, stopping all digital services to certain individuals. This could happen to a country.
Even if you use European email and cloud services, our computer operating systems require constant software updates. This is not just to add new features. There is a constant race between the good guys patching the software bugs and the bad guys trying to gain entry to your computer using those same software bugs.
Recently, Holland and France took active steps to break the near monopoly of big Amercian tech by laying the foundations of a nationwide IT ecosystem that they would control. The UK needs to do the same.
 
Ian White
 
Cheltenham, Gloucestershire
The concern about the NHS’s dependence on Palantir (Palantir’s Tom Watson says ‘mob rule’ must not dictate awarding of government contracts, 9 October) is justified, but the £330m contract is a symptom of a wider habit. Whenever the government wants joined-up data, it buys one large platform from one supplier – and such projects have a long record of overrunning, costing far more than planned and locking the buyer in.
There is a working example of the alternative: the world wide web. It does not require everyone’s data to sit in one place or run on one company’s software. It simply defines how data is requested and transferred.
The NHS needs the same: an open specification for exchanging records, plus a registry of where each patient’s data is held. Any authorised clinician could then assemble the full picture of my treatment, while each hospital or practice chose its own software supplier. Specialist firms could still compete to analyse the data for planning and research – but none would own the plumbing.
The NHS already has the beginnings of this in its interoperability standards. Why do the money and political attention go to a single proprietary platform rather than to making open standards mandatory?
 
Bill Cawley
 
Ludlow, Shropshire

Venezuela’s Maduro and wife plead not guilty to US torture charges

Venezuela’s Maduro and wife plead not guilty to US torture charges
NEW YORK – Ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores pleaded not guilty on Oct 15 to a new US indictment accusing them of conspiring to torture political opponents.
The additional charges, brought on Oct 15, significantly expanded the US criminal case against Maduro, 63, and Flores, 70. They previously pleaded not guilty to charges that they abused their power to help drug traffickers ship cocaine.
Maduro and Flores, captured by the US military in a January raid ordered by US President Donald Trump and flown to New York, entered their pleas at an arraignment before District Judge Alvin Hellerstein in Manhattan federal court. They wore tan prison garb and were shackled at the ankles during the hearing.
When Hellerstein asked for his plea, Maduro said the accusations had been made previously and were false.
“I have seen it in its entirety, Judge Hellerstein,” Maduro said, referring to the indictment. “I reject this document in its entirety.”
The judge cut Maduro off as he spoke and said a plea of not guilty would be entered on his behalf.
Flores said: “I am completely innocent. I am not guilty.”
Maduro and Flores are not accused of personally carrying out any acts of torture. They would each face a mandatory minimum sentence of 50 years in prison if convicted on all charges.
Hellerstein postponed the trial start date by two weeks to June 14, 2027, due to the new charges.
‘Squeeze them harder’
Prosecutors with the Manhattan US Attorney’s office say Maduro directed Venezuelan officials to torture opposition politicians and military personnel accused of plotting against him to maintain power in the South American country.
In one alleged incident described in the indictment, Maduro in 2014 directed officials to kidnap military personnel to draw information out of them about possible dissidents, and told officials to “squeeze them harder” when some remained defiant.
Flores agreed with the plan in the meeting, and dismissed a suggested alternative plan to glean information by infiltrating the ranks, according to the indictment.
Relations between Maduro, a socialist, and the US were tense during his 13 years in power leading the oil-rich country.
Successive US administrations imposed sanctions on top Venezuelan officials and key state companies, citing alleged human rights violations, corruption and election-rigging. Maduro accused the US of seeking his ouster to gain greater control of the South American country’s natural resources.
Captured at home
The pressure campaign culminated in the Jan 3 raid, when the US military captured Maduro and Flores at their Caracas home and brought them to the US to face drug trafficking charges announced that same day. Since then, they have been held at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn.
Maduro’s former vice-president, Delcy Rodriguez, has led Venezuela since his capture and has ramped up cooperation with the US. Trump has touted Maduro’s capture and the reset of relations with Venezuela as a key foreign policy success heading into the Nov 3 midterm elections in which his fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress. Farmer's discovery in Egypt leads to pieces of statues for ancient king
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:51:08 UTC
01:51:08 KST

An Egyptian farmer found "an unusual stone." It led archaeologists to pieces of statues for an ancient king.
Cairo — Egyptian farmer Khaled al-Shahat was working on his land when he came across something he hadn't seen before. The unusual pink rock led archaeologists to unearth pieces of statues for King Ramses II, who ruled Egypt from 1279 B.C. to 1213 B.C.
"I was working on my land on Friday when I came across an unusual stone," al-Shahat told CBS News. "I informed the relevant authorities, and they came to examine it."
The stone turned out to be an ancient pink granite block measuring approximately 1.3 meters long (around 4.26 feet) and bearing two royal titles of Ramses II: "Nesw-Bity" (King of Upper and Lower Egypt) and "Sa-Ra" (Son of Ra, the sun god), the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities said.
Archaeologists began excavations, and near the block they uncovered a colossal head of a statue of Ramses II, measuring approximately 1.6 meters high (around 5.25 feet). The king is depicted wearing the double crown, a symbol of the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt around 3100 B.C.
On Wednesday, Minister of Tourism and Antiquities Sherif Fathy visited al-Shahat's hometown in Al Gharbia Governorate in the Nile Delta to honor him.
The minister presented al-Shahat and his wife with certificates of appreciation, and awarded them a trip to Saudi Arabia to perform the Umrah pilgrimage in recognition of his honesty and responsible conduct for not keeping the discovery to himself.
"The minister insisted that the citizen be honored in his village, on his own land, and among his family and fellow villagers, in recognition of his honesty, awareness, and sense of responsibility," the ministry said in a statement.
Archaeologists also unearthed the remains of the upper part of the statue's back pillar, bearing Ramses II's formal royal title, or Horus name: Hor Ka Nakht Mery Maat.
The size of the head suggests the complete statue was about 28 feet tall, according to archaeologists.
"I was surprised and happy when they discovered more antiquities," al-Shahat told CBS News. "They told me this might change the history of the area."
Most of a second royal statue, also believed to depict Ramses II, was uncovered. Measuring approximately 2.4 meters long (around 7.87 feet), it is missing its legs and base, as well as part of the upper section of its royal nemes headdress. Its head has clearly visible, well-preserved facial features resembling those of the first statue, the ministry said.
Excavations and archaeological studies are continuing on al-Shahat's land to learn more about the statues, the area's history and its architectural development in ancient Egypt.
