Forecasters watch progress of Pacific storm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:13 UTC
01:43:13 KST

Tropical Storm Champi formed yesterday and has the potential to increase in strength, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) said yesterday.
Forecasters are closely monitoring a Pacific high-pressure system that would dictate whether the storm turns north or moves toward Taiwan next week, the CWA said.
The most likely scenario is that it turns northward after passing the Ryukyu Islands, CWA forecaster Cheng Chieh-jen (鄭傑仁) said.
Photo courtesy of the Central Weather Administration
As of 8pm yesterday, Champi was east of Guam moving west-northwest at 20kph, CWA data showed.
It had maximum sustained winds near the center of 72kph and gusts of up to 101kph, the data showed.
If the Pacific high-pressure system weakens noticeably, the storm is likely to turn north earlier, but if it strengthens, the typhoon might be closer to Taiwan when it turns, Cheng said.
Champi is forecast to strengthen into a moderate typhoon by tomorrow and an intense typhoon next week, he said.
Rainfall could increase in northern and eastern Taiwan next weekend as the northeast monsoon or the outer circulation of the storm affects the region, Cheng said.
The Taiwan Typhoon Forum’s storm tracker forecasts suggest that Champi could begin turning north after Thursday next week as it approaches waters south of Okinawa, east of Taiwan and northeast of the Philippines.
Meanwhile, rain is expected to increase today, with isolated showers in coastal areas around Keelung, as well as Yilan, Hualien and Taitung counties and the Hengchun Peninsula (恆春半島), Cheng said.
From tomorrow to Tuesday next week, mountainous areas of central and southern Taiwan could have scattered showers in the afternoons, he added.
The next surge of the northeast monsoon is expected to strengthen on Wednesday next week, bringing localized brief showers to the greater Taipei area and Yilan, and isolated brief showers to eastern Taiwan and the Hengchun Peninsula, he said.
Isolated afternoon showers are also possible in mountainous areas of central and southern Taiwan, Cheng said.
The forecast for the latter part of the period would depend on Champi’s track and requires further monitoring, he added.
Until Tuesday next week, daytime highs are expected to be 32°C to 34°C in western Taiwan and 31°C to 33°C in the east, with overnight lows of 22°C to 25°C nationwide, he said.
Although the northeast monsoon is forecast to strengthen, accompanying cold air is expected to be weak, meaning daytime highs of 27°C to 31°C in windward areas, he said.

Belize prime minister urges deeper cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:43:13 UTC
01:43:13 KST

Belize Prime Minister John Briceno has called for deeper cooperation with Taiwan through investment, technology exchanges and people-to-people ties, saying that he hopes the links would contribute to his country’s development.
In an exclusive interview with the Central News Agency in Bangkok on Wednesday, Briceno spoke warmly of Belize’s close ties with Taiwan and highlighted areas such as shrimp farming and practical technology exchanges for potential cooperation.
Briceno, 66, said Belize’s young population was an advantage for technology cooperation.
Photo: CNA
“We have a young population, and they go to junior college on to university, and they learn quickly. So these are areas where we can collaborate,” he said.
In the field of artificial intelligence (AI) development, cooperation with Taiwan does not necessarily have to begin with the most advanced technologies, but instead could focus on practical solutions that meet Belize’s needs, Briceno said.
“For example, shrimp farming technology is one area where Taiwan could contribute,” he said.
He also emphasized the value of people-to-people exchanges, saying that Taiwanese students working in Belize could help strengthen ties between the two countries.
There are six Taiwanese exchange students working in government ministries and other fields in Belize.
For Belize, attracting business investment and building technological capacity are part of a broader effort to expand economic opportunities and improve living standards, its leader said.
Briceno is attending this year’s Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group in Bangkok as Belize’s finance minister and chair of the World Bank’s Small States Forum.
In the interview, he said that international financial institutions need to take into account the limited administrative capacity and resources of small countries.
He cited as an example the challenge his country faced in participating in a World Bank-funded project to help small farmers strengthen their resilience to climate change.
Briceno said that by the time Belize had completed the lengthy application procedure, it was close to the deadline, and he had to ask the World Bank to extend the timeframe.
Climate change is one of the issues affecting small nations, Briceno said.
Caribbean island nations and other coastal countries in the region are dealing with a massive influx of brown sargassum seaweed, which threatens tourism — a major economic lifeline, Briceno said, calling for regional solutions.
In Belize, another significant challenge is providing basic infrastructure and services to its widely dispersed population of about 420,000, given its limited tax base, he said.
“We have to constantly see how we can find that balance in providing basic services, access to water, access to electricity, and access to education and health,” he said.
Belize has 196 small communities and the government must balance residents’ needs against its limited resources while maintaining fiscal sustainability, Briceno said.
As a long-standing partner of Taiwan, Belize is committed to its relations with Taiwan, Briceno said, adding that China’s sanctions against Belizean Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Francis Fonseca would not change that position.
Belize is an independent country with the right to decide which countries it maintains relations with, Briceno said, condemning China’s sanctions as unreasonable, unnecessary, wrong and illegal.
That move by China would only serve to strengthen Belize’s resolve to support Taiwan, he said.
“We strongly believe in the right to self-determination,” he said, adding that Taiwan’s strengths in the economy, technology, AI, healthcare, education and climate research warrant recognition by the UN and other international organizations.
Briceno, who began his second term as prime minister last year, said he wants Belize to remain a free and democratic country with a vibrant economy capable of providing for its people.

Health ministry unveils dementia care 3.0 policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:10 UTC
01:43:10 KST

The Ministry of Health and Welfare yesterday unveiled its dementia care 3.0 policy to provide improved care, community resources and National Health Insurance (NHI) coverage for dementia medications.
The policy aims to achieve an 80 percent diagnosis rate, care service coverage and accessibility in public-facing venues, the ministry said.
The policy is effective from the time of the announcement to 2035, it said.
Photo courtesy of Hsinchu MacKay Memorial Hospital via CNA
The ministry said it is evaluating expanding NHI coverage for dementia drugs, subsidizing a larger range of specialist care, safety precautions, legal protections and efficiency in matching patients to medical care.
The package would include placing personnel at agencies and venues to recognize and help those with dementia, improve diagnosis rates and facilitate medical research, the ministry said.
Subsidies for dementia medicine and care would apply to people with the condition regardless of age to facilitate early medical intervention, which is crucial for alleviating the disorder’s symptoms, it said.
The policy aims to help people with early-onset dementia who could be working to support families, by providing early medical intervention, assistance in finding new jobs and community resources, it added.
It would also give dementia patients treatment, subsidies and help for family-related issues and specialized care appropriate to the disorder’s severity, it said.
People with early onset dementia who are working to support themselves or their families would receive occupational counseling in finding suitable jobs, the ministry said.
Dementia can debilitate a person’s memory, judgement and communication skills impacting their ability to have a normal life, it said.
Guidelines would be drafted for public-facing venues — including those related to finances, restaurants and food, transportation and cultural industries — to provide specialist services for people with dementia, the ministry said.
The ministry is in the process of establishing community resources at the district and township level, relationships with charity groups and training programs for “guardian angels,” and measures to protect dementia patients’ finances and physical safety, it said.
Increasing the number of certified trustees managing funds on behalf of dementia patients and the ability to find lost patients are also among the policy’s goals, it added.

A Thai influencer working illegally in Taiwan who was posting videos of her work and daily life drew the attention of National Immigration Agency (NIA) officers, leading to the arrest of 20 Thai nationals who had overstayed their visas and five people suspected of illegally employing them, the agency said yesterday.
The influencer, who had overstayed her visa, was working illegally at a farm in a remote area of Kaohsiung.
She posted TikTok videos of her work and of herself dancing, using them to recruit fellow Thai nationals, with one video drawing more than 100,000 views, the agency’s Southern Taiwan Administration Corps said.
Photo courtesy of a member of the public
The videos also helped officers track her down.
Investigators from the agency’s Kaohsiung City Specialized Operation Brigade pieced together clues about the farm’s surroundings and terrain from the footage, despite its secluded location, the brigade said.
After multiple stakeouts at suspected locations, officers arrested 20 Thai nationals and five people suspected of illegally employing them, the agency said, adding that it would investigate whether an illegal labor brokerage was involved.
Chao Chih-cheng (趙志成), captain of the Kaohsiung brigade, said employers who illegally hire foreign workers face fines of up to NT$750,000 (US$23,384).
Those who employ them illegally for profit face a prison sentence of up to three years, as well a maximum fine of NT$1.2 million, he added.

====================================================================================================

New life on Kaohsiung’s old cemetery slopes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:08 UTC
01:43:08 KST

Just 10 years ago, the site of Shuanghu Forest Park (雙湖森林公園) was a blight on the Kaohsiung landscape. Motorists on the nearby freeway were treated to a view of a weedy hill covered in scattered graves, with a few corrugated steel buildings thrown in for good measure. Things got worse before they got better.
It was decided to turn this public land into a park, but in order for that to happen, all the human remains had to be moved and the existing mess of weeds and patchy tree growth had to be landscaped. After nearly 30,000 burials were relocated to a nearby columbarium, the whole area was razed clean and the new park laid out. Old photos from 2018 show what looks like a desert landscape of bare earth, the unsightly chrysalis of the beautifully landscaped park that is still emerging today.
Thousands of trees were planted, and detention ponds were created, both for flood protection and to create a water ecosystem. Last year, as part of a major upgrade, nectar-producing plants were added to encourage butterflies to settle here, and even more trees were planted. Frogs, dragonflies and several butterfly species now call this place home, and there is more and more shade among the maturing trees.
Photo by Tyler Cottenie
Lastly, the entire slope leading up to the adjacent Kaohsiung Green Park, formerly the site of a golf course, has been transformed. Where a mishmash of tombs once lay, terraced pathways now run along the length of the hill, adorned with rows of trees, including Taiwanese golden rain trees, currently displaying their gorgeous pink fall color.
WALK, RUN, CLIMB
There are a few benches scattered throughout, but the park is, above all, a place for walking or jogging. If you want a large open space where you can sit down for a picnic or to let children run around, take a walk through Shuanghu Forest Park first and then hike up the hill along one of three trails to Kaohsiung Green Park for its open, grassy spaces.
Dingjin 1st Lane runs right through the length of the park from south to north and is its main transportation artery. It was recently widened and paved with asphalt, so it is also a nice lane for walking, especially thanks to the ample shade from the trees on either side.
Alongside Dingjin 1st Lane itself, there are five smaller parking lots, with spaces for cars and/or scooters. Right across from the first parking lot at the south end is the site of the Islamic burial section in the old cemetery. This was the last section to be cleared out, as the remains could not be cremated and moved to a columbarium, but had to await the opening of a new cemetery in far-away Shanlin District (杉林區) before they could be moved. Nowadays, the area is newly landscaped and there is no hint of its former function.
Wherever you start your walk in the park, check out one of the signs in these parking lots if you need a quick overview of the park’s layout. The “Sunset Walkway” is not a single trail but the interconnected walkways on the terraces going up the hill to Kaohsiung Green Park. These provide the best view of the surrounding city by far and are west-facing so they are a perfect spot to end your day around sunset. The “Green Hiking Trails” are newly built connectors providing access to Kaohsiung Green Park above.
The “Ecological Walkway” takes visitors around the new detention ponds that several egrets have already decided to call home, and among nectar-rich plants that have attracted numerous species of butterflies. The newly planted trees still have some filling out to do, but this area is already far more beautiful and ecologically diverse than 10 years ago. One final item worth noting on the sign is the “pavilion.”
It would be a grave mistake to visit the park without taking a walk over to this spot. Perched conspicuously up on a hill behind one of the detention ponds in the shade of two enormous banyan trees, this “pavilion” is actually a tomb dating back to 1938, and one of only three that was spared during the dismantling of the former cemetery.
THE TOMBS
Surrounded by a low, ornamented concrete wall, with a central staircase flanked by three pairs of stone lanterns, the tomb is distinctively Japanese in its style, and is likely one of the best-preserved examples still remaining in Taiwan.
It is visually stunning in its symmetry, beautifully framed by the banyans and provides an excellent view of the surrounding cityscape from the top, next to the tall stone monument. It was preserved not only for its aesthetic value but also for its historical significance.
Originally the tomb of Japanese businessman and longtime Kaohsiung (Takao) resident Sugimoto Otokichi, it later became the repository for the remains of approximately 3,000 Japanese. After World War II, Japanese graves scattered throughout the country were subject to abandonment and vandalism, so three locations were selected and the remains of Japanese from the colonial era were relocated to these locations.
The Sugimoto family, in keeping with Otokichi’s reputation as a man of justice, allowed his spacious tomb to become the designated repository for southern Taiwan. Over 50 years later, the remains were moved to a columbarium along with those in the rest of the cemetery, but the tomb’s structure was preserved.
Two other tombs of identical style were also preserved from the old cemetery and are easily accessible near the main road. One is right next to the second roadside parking lot from the south and belonged to Taiwanese businessman and local credit union co-founder Huang Ching-yun (黃慶雲). Much smaller in scale but equally well preserved, this tomb represents the inclination of some Taiwanese to adopt the customs and aesthetics of their colonizers.
The final tomb is directly east of the nearby incinerator’s smokestack, at a bend in the road. Slightly larger in scale, this one belonged to Japanese businessman Otsubo Yoichi and is notable for having been moved here from another location during the Japanese era.
GETTING THERE
Using public transit, take Bus Red 33 from the Aozihdi MRT stop, get off at the Benguan Rd. (Funeral Interment Management Office) stop, and walk north along the freeway to Dingjin 1st Lane, which takes you to the park’s south entrance. Alternatively, you can take Bus Green 2 from the Cultural Center or near any light rail stop on Dashun Road counterclockwise up to Minzu Road. Get off at the Jixian Park stop and walk south on Dafeng St. to the park’s north entrance. By scooter or car, approach from Benguan Road and then turn to follow the east side of the freeway to Dingjin 1st Lane to enter the park, or continue further north to a large parking lot and then walk up to the park entrance.
However, the easiest way may be to visit as a side trip from Kaohsiung Green Park, and it is recommended to combine these two into one excursion. Look for the marked trails down from Holes 13, 14 and 17.
Shuanghu Forest Park is open 24 hours a day but has no toilet facilities. The adjacent Kaohsiung Green Park has plenty, but the opening hours are 5am to 6pm in winter.

EDITORIAL: Beware Beijing’s expanding lawfare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:06 UTC
01:43:06 KST

China’s revised National Defense Mobilization Law took effect on Oct. 1, allowing the government to mobilize civilians and redirect resources for military purposes, and ensures a rapid transition from peacetime to wartime. It has a wide scope of “national interests” pretexts, which would likely be used against Taiwan.
The amendment incorporates Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) “Military-Civil Fusion” principle into law, and stipulates that once the state initiates national defense mobilization, “the people’s governments at or above the county level may expropriate and requisition civilian resources,” and “all organizations and individuals shall have the obligation to accept the lawful expropriation and requisition of civilian resources.” It massively expands China’s national mobilization, including drafting men aged 18 to 60 and women aged 18 to 55 into the armed forces, and allows it to legally and forcibly seize private property.
Given that most top Chinese political officials and military commanders have been purged under Xi’s corruption crackdown, the revised law was widely seen as a legislation to further consolidate Xi and his ruling clique’s control of public and civilian forces, paving the way for his five-year term or even to extend his leadership indefinitely.
As the new law aims to convert all peacetime resources, including energy, media and cutting-edge technologies, such as drones and artificial intelligence, into wartime supplies under government control, Taiwanese and international firms and assets in China could also be targeted. All cross-strait and cross-border business cooperation, supply chains, data flows and personnel could be incorporated into China’s national mobilization system, transforming them from commercial assets into warfare resources. Taiwan and other democracies should be vigilant and ensure Beijing is not using the law to expand its war preparations from just the military to the entire society.
The law has turned Xi’s aggressive and expansionary foreign policies into national legislation. While most countries’ military and social mobilization primarily focuses on crisis response, China’s law states that mobilization can take place if the nation’s sovereignty, unification, territorial integrity, security or development interests are threatened. This is the first time “unification” and “development interests” have been included in China’s legal framework for mobilization. The law also expands the discretionary power of the Chinese Communist Party, its government and military over what constitutes a threat.
The legislation could be used as “legal warfare” against Taiwan; Beijing could define an invasion of the nation as a “unification” mission to be safeguarded through defense mobilization. For example, the Chinese People’s Liberation Army could mobilize more civilian forces in its “gray zone” operations, cognitive warfare, cross-border repression or even a military conflict against Taiwan.
China could also use the law to send political signals, putting pressure on countries along the First Island Chain — including Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines — as well as Australia, the US and the EU.
American Foreign Policy Council Asian security senior fellow Larry Wortzel warned that “the wording of the legislation suggests a scope that is larger still,” as Beijing could invoke the law under the pretext of national development interests. It could mobilize warfare actions if it believes areas it “controls” — such as the South China Sea, East China Sea, or islands and territorial borders in dispute with other countries — are being threatened, or even just to secure overseas economic investments or foreign interests.
As Beijing strengthens its peacetime-wartime transition capabilities through legal and institutional adjustments, Taiwan must accelerate the enhancement of its national resilience and countermeasure capabilities. As a democratic country, it must consider how to integrate public and private “social powers” into collective “national resilience” based on democratic constitutionalism, cross-sectoral collaboration and social trust.
Dennis Blair, former US director of national intelligence and a retired commander of US forces in the Pacific, has praised the transformation of the annual Han Kuang military drill into a whole-of-society defense exercise, calling it a “great decision.” People and parties in Taiwan need to transcend political divisions, promote more social cooperation and shared determination to safeguard the security and sustainability of the nation.
Faced with China’s legalization of “military-civil fusion” for “national development interests,” which could pose a profound threat to regional stability and international order, democratic countries must foster more and stronger multilateral alliances to jointly counter Beijing’s aggression, and safeguard global democratic rules and peace.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:05 UTC
01:43:05 KST

China and North Korea yesterday officially opened their most significant land border crossing, aiming to rejuvenate trade and commerce.
Trucks festooned with the national flags of the neighbors drove across the long-delayed 3km New Yalu River Bridge, its towering pylons also decked in flags, linking the Chinese city of Dandong with North Korea.
Knots of spectators crowded a road on the Chinese side overlooking the cable-stayed bridge completed in 2014, but unused while North Korea left its approach roads and customs compound unfinished.
Photo: Reuters
Bilateral “relations are entering a new phase, embarking on a new chapter,” Chinese Premier Li Qiang (李強) said in a video address at the opening, the official Xinhua news agency reported.
The border crossing would “strongly promote” economic and trade cooperation, and further strengthen exchanges between their people, Li said.
It also offers an opportunity to improve border clearance procedures, boost connectivity and build cooperation in border areas, he said.
North Korean Premier Pak Thae-song also delivered a video address, Xinhua said, but North Korea’s state media were yet to report on the event.
The opening is the latest sign of warming ties between Beijing and Pyongyang after two summits between their leaders in the past year.
However, despite the potential economic boost from trade, analysts said North Korea remains cautious of greater dependence on China.
“The bridge is unlikely to lead immediately to a full-scale return to pre-sanctions trade,” said Lim Eul-chul at Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies.
The bridge will help move heavy equipment, raw materials and energy products that North Korea needs for development efforts, Lim said.
China is by far Pyongyang’s largest trading partner, even after a series of UN sanctions banned the flow of goods and workers with the North over the latter’s missile and nuclear weapons development.
China and Russia, permanent members of the UN Security Council that voted to approve sanctions resolutions until 2017, have since questioned the legitimacy and efficacy of such bans.
Russia is accused by countries such as the US and South Korea of supplying sensitive military assistance to the North in return for Pyongyang’s help in fighting the war in Ukraine.
The delay in opening the bridge was a setback for Dandong, whose economy thrived in the early 21st century as the primary trade gateway to North Korea’s isolated economy.
Until now, most goods have crossed about 10km upstream, using an 83-year-old bridge with a rail track and a single-lane road. That remains the busiest of about 15 crossing points along the roughly 1,350km shared border.
Dandong residents welcomed the opening.
“It’s been more than a decade since they first said the bridge would open ... but coming here today and seeing it for myself makes me incredibly happy,” said a 50-year-old resident surnamed He.
“Once the bridge opens, this place will become much livelier, attracting more tourists,” said another Dandong resident, surnamed Xie.
The bridge opening was “effectively the first visible case” of adoption of agreements struck at a June summit of leaders, a South Korean Ministry of Unification official said.

Navigating the strategic path ahead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:04 UTC
01:43:04 KST

Europe’s interest in strategic autonomy has been reignited as uncertainty surrounding US policy has reached a level that can no longer be covered up with diplomatic niceties. Repeated flip-flopping on tariffs, military aid, NATO and policy toward Russia have forced European countries to confront a harsh reality: Security frameworks dependent on a single provider are vulnerable to changes in political winds that can quickly translate into military, energy and industrial risks.
Increasing defense spending is the first step, not a complete solution. Europe has long struggled with fragmented weapons standards, lengthy procurement cycles, slow cross-border decisionmaking and insufficient defense manufacturing capacity. If countries increase their individual budgets, but continue purchasing and maintaining equipment independently, all that additional spending would only result in more variation in equipment models and higher logistical costs. Genuine European autonomy would require establishing shared requirements, joint procurements, interoperable components and wartime resupply mechanisms.
France’s proposal to link nuclear deterrence with European defenses mainly reflects Paris’ ambition to translate its existing capabilities into political leadership. Other member states have misgivings about concentrating decisionmaking power, as well as the possibility that France’s nuclear arsenal would ultimately serve French national interests. Such concerns cannot be dispelled by summit declarations alone. Europe must clarify who can initiate collective defense, who foots the bill, how non-nuclear states can participate in oversight and which institution takes command during a crisis.
Fiscal constraints present another major obstacle. Many European countries are grappling with aging populations, social welfare commitments, energy transitions and debt pressures. If defense budgets are financed solely through borrowing, their political support could be eroded within a few years. A more viable approach would be to integrate military procurement with industrial policy. Through joint financing, long-term contracts and regional specialization, additional spending could be converted into sustainable production capacity rather than one-off purchases.
European strategic autonomy should not be seen simply as a break from the US. It would minimize the potential fallout of any ally abandoning its commitments, while preserving NATO’s advantages in intelligence, nuclear deterrence and joint operations. Autonomy and alliance are not mutually exclusive. Indeed, a Europe capable of shouldering greater responsibility would be better positioned to coordinate with the US on equal footing.
Taiwan should draw two lessons from the debate in Europe.
First, rather than a weapons shopping list, increases in defense spending must meaningfully translate into production and maintenance capacity, ammunition supplies and personnel. Second, security cooperation commitments must be operable in peacetime, including intelligence sharing, supply chain contingencies, joint training and crisis communications.
If Europe turns strategic autonomy into nothing more than a budget race, its military system is likely to end up expensive and fragmented. Only by translating shared threats into common standards, pooled funding and joint decisionmaking can Europe develop genuinely effective security capabilities.
Similarly, Taiwan’s defense self-reliance does not mean producing everything domestically. It means ensuring that domestic capabilities are sufficient to sustain key operations even when external support is held up.
Taiwan must also be alert to the market changes that might result from Europe’s pursuit of strategic autonomy. As Europe looks elsewhere for defense procurements, it might toughen its requirements on local manufacturing, cybersecurity certifications and supply chain disclosures. Taiwanese manufacturers of drones, communications equipment and electronic components seeking to enter these markets cannot rely on competitive prices and delivery times alone. They must also be prepared to provide long-term maintenance, technology protections and establish local partnerships across Europe.
Security alliances are increasingly becoming a prerequisite for industrial involvement, and the government should help businesses understand the relevant standards and establish credible track records well in advance.
These steps are also a measure by which Taiwan can assess its strategic autonomy. The number of weapons procured is a single variable; the capabilities that can be sustained during a crisis are the real measure of success. Defense reform should include regular public reporting of non-sensitive indicators — such as equipment serviceability rates, training volumes and replenishment progress — so that the public can see what actual capabilities additional spending has delivered.
Edwin Yang is an associate professor at National Taiwan Normal University and chairman of the Central Taiwan Association of University Professors.
Translated by Gilda Knox Streader

What hope does Taiwan have? Quite a bit more, in fact, than Shuster lets on. Shuster points to genuine problems. The first Donald Trump administration had a mostly positive record on Taiwan policy. From that moment, the 10th day of the 10th month became a date of epochal significance, not merely in Chinese history, but in the broader arc of Asia’s encounter with modernity. Taiwan Blocks Coinbase, Kalshi Over Suspected Election Bets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:04 UTC
01:43:04 KST

Taiwan has blocked the websites of Coinbase Global Inc. and Kalshi Inc. over suspected election betting, weeks before local polls that will test support for President Lai Ching-te’s government.
A New Taipei court authorized the Taiwanese communications regulator and internet registry to bar domestic access to the platforms, according to a ruling seen by Bloomberg News. Some Coinbase users in Taiwan reported being unable to access the site since Wednesday.
The Criminal Investigation Bureau, which sought the order, said in response to questions from Bloomberg that the websites were suspected of violating the Public Officials Election and Recall Act. The law prohibits operating gambling for profit based on the outcome of an election or recall.
Photo: Reuters
Coinbase and Kalshi didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
The bureau said it requested the restrictions to protect election integrity and prevent “overseas interference,” without giving further details. Taiwanese authorities have separately warned that money from mainland China could enter the island through underground financial channels and be used to influence elections.
The government has stepped up scrutiny of illicit financial flows ahead of the Nov. 28 vote, including underground gambling operations. Authorities haven’t alleged that Coinbase or Kalshi handled funds from China.
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment sent outside normal office hours.
Taiwan is among the jurisdictions that criminalize election wagering. Under a 2023 amendment to the election act, bettors can face as long as six months in prison, while gambling operators can receive up to five years.
Authorities have increasingly targeted election wagering on prediction markets. Polymarket, the main rival to Kalshi, has also been blocked in Taiwan. Cryptocurrencies are often used to place bets on such platforms.
Taiwanese voters will choose local officials ranging from mayors and city councilors to village chiefs. The elections will be the first island-wide electoral test for Lai since he took office in 2024 and could offer an early indication of the political landscape ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

Trump cannot figure out peace in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:01 UTC
01:43:01 KST

US President Donald Trump’s deal to purchase diesel fuel from Russia is a moral outrage: It rewards an aggressor that is terrorizing Ukrainian cities with drones and missiles, while punishing the victim for fighting back. Its economic benefits for the US would be modest at best. Above all, the deal is sadly indicative of a deeper failing in Trump’s Ukraine policy. The president genuinely desires peace in that country, but his strategic blinders and indiscipline keep making that task harder.
The details of the deal are dispiriting. The US has agreed to temporarily lift sanctions so Russia can bring about 2 million barrels of diesel to market immediately (with about 13 million barrels committed in total), in hopes of driving down prices at the pump in the US before the midterm elections next month. The deal follows growing US frustration with Ukraine’s drone and missile strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, which have added to stress on global markets. It is not clear if the agreement would ease that pressure, given that the volumes involved are relatively small and the real problem in global energy markets is the president’s war with Iran.
However, the deal would have a strategic impact, by weakening the push to cut Western purchases of Russian energy. It threatens to undo a year’s worth of European efforts to convince Trump that Russia, not Ukraine, is the primary obstacle to peace. And it creates a perverse scenario in which Trump fills the coffers of a neo-fascist autocracy while penalizing Ukraine for targeting Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war economy in self-defense.
Illustration: Mountain People
A bipartisan group of senators has already condemned the deal. Trump has defended it and announced an “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia — a breakthrough more imagined than real.
Whatever comes of this episode, it illustrates how election-year incentives and economic blowback from the Iran war are affecting US foreign policy in theaters far beyond the Middle East. It is also a window into the frustrations of Trump’s bid to end the war in Ukraine.
Trump seems genuinely appalled by the killing. He has strong strategic incentives to seek a peace deal, amid a potential forever-war in the Persian Gulf and a rising Chinese threat in the Pacific — but his approach to peacemaking has done more harm than good.
To be fair, a realistic strategy would have included some of Trump’s initiatives, such as pushing the Europeans to take primary responsibility for aiding Ukraine. It would also involve quietly urging Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy’s government to accept that it would not recapture all the territory it has lost to Russia or become a member of NATO.
Yet the other half of this strategy would have involved a concerted effort to ratchet up sanctions pressure on Russia, consistent support for Ukraine’s punishing deep-strike campaign, and strong measures to convince Putin that he cannot simply outlast US support for Ukraine or wait for the Western coalition to fracture. Here, the record is bleak.
Since his Oval Office showdown with Zelenskiy in February last year, Trump has repeatedly feuded with the Ukrainian leader in public and threatened to withdraw US intelligence and military support. He has brawled with European allies not just in good causes (burden sharing), but also in bad ones (acquiring Greenland). His administration has sometimes taken Russia’s side in seeking to influence European elections; it might withdraw significant US forces from the continent just as Moscow’s hybrid warfare campaign intensifies. Trump and his aides also convey the strong impression that they want to get back to business with Moscow, once the pesky war in Ukraine is cleared away.
All this has surely encouraged Putin to think he can divide the US from Ukraine and from Europe if he shows enough bloody-minded patience. It gives him confidence he can win the war in Washington even if he cannot win it on the battlefield in Donetsk. Even when the administration seeks peace by offering up major Ukrainian concessions — as Trump did at his summit with Putin in Alaska last year — these efforts cannot satiate Moscow’s sweeping demands.
Trump’s Ukraine peacemaking has been a self-defeating experience that reflects two of his worst strategic flaws.
First, he has consistently misdiagnosed the source of the deadlock. He often seems more frustrated with Ukraine’s insistence on surviving as an independent nation than with Russia’s obsessive drive to snuff that independence out. He insists, against all evidence to the contrary, that Putin wants peace more than Zelenskiy.
That view might reflect Trump’s spheres-of-influence mentality, which holds that smaller powers must accommodate larger powers, but it blinds him to the fact that Putin seeks Ukrainian surrender as part of his larger geopolitical assault on the West. The Russian leader would only quit when the price of persistence becomes too high.
Second, a president who prioritizes quick fixes fails at the hard work of strategy. Peacemaking in Ukraine was never going to be easy. It demands deftly mixing pressure and diplomacy with Moscow; it requires sustaining Western solidarity while moving toward unsatisfying compromises.
However, Trump lacks the patience for careful, coordinated statecraft; he disdains consultation with allies. So he has repeatedly launched ill-considered peace initiatives that panic Kyiv and Europe, but fail to move Putin.
Now, Trump has struck a diesel deal that would have scant economic benefits and serious strategic costs. He is, reportedly, threatening to abandon Ukraine unless it drops its deep-strike campaign against Russian energy targets — that is, its best tool for making the price of Putin’s war prohibitive.
In the process, Trump is depleting US leverage, by encouraging Putin to continue his onslaught, and squandering US influence in Kyiv. Peace in Ukraine is a worthy destination. Alas, Trump has no idea how to get there.

What began as a regional uprising quickly ignited a chain reaction across the empire, toppling a dynastic order that had endured for more than two millennia and ushering in one of Asia’s first republics — the Republic of China (ROC). From that moment, the 10th day of the 10th month became a date of epochal significance, not merely in Chinese history, but in the broader arc of Asia’s encounter with modernity. GlobalFoundries gets US$21bn for plants in US-Japan deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:42:58 UTC
01:42:58 KST

GlobalFoundries Inc plans to build two new chip plants with the backing of as much as US$21 billion from the Japanese government, part of an arrangement that also includes the US taking a 4 percent stake in the company.
Under an agreement announced on Wednesday, GlobalFoundries will operate factories at its site in upstate New York that are jointly owned by the US and Japan. The facilities will be funded with money from Japan’s pledge to invest US$550 billion in the US.
The factories will make so-called essential chips, the vital yet less sophisticated semiconductors used in vehicles, industrial equipment and communications gear.
Photo: John Carl D’Annibale, The Albany Times Union via AP
The GlobalFoundries agreement is meant to boost American production of essential chips and reduce dependence on East Asian suppliers — addressing a national security concern for the US.
Under a broader arrangement with GlobalFoundries, the US Department of Commerce will take a roughly 4 percent equity stake in the company, “further enabling the American public to share in GF’s growth.”
GlobalFoundries will get to redirect funds from a previous US CHIPS and Science Act grant to invest in honing its manufacturing abilities. That includes advancing its work in fields such as silicon photonics, chip packaging and silicon germanium.
In a separate statement, the US Department of Commerce said it was reallocating US$955 million in CHIPS Act incentives to go toward GlobalFoundries’ factory expansion and modernization. As part of the agreement, the company will devote US$5 billion to capital investments at its plants in New York and Vermont.
The new Japan-linked factories will be operated in the same way that GlobalFoundries runs its current facilities, which serve customers such as Apple Inc and Japanese firms including Renesas Electronics Corp.
Profits will be divided among the owners and GlobalFoundries, following an approach laid out in last year’s US trade deal with Japan. US President Donald Trump touted the accord on his Truth Social site, saying it would help revitalize America’s industrial base and create jobs.
For GlobalFoundries, the arrangement will help the company meet surging demand for its products, chief executive officer Tim Breen said in an interview.
“We need to respond to what our customers need,” he said. “Right now, the whole industry is in short supply.”
The company has already begun work on the first plant, located by GlobalFoundries’ home base in Malta, New York. It expects to have the factory up and running in 2029. The second will go ahead as quickly as possible after the initial plant is completed. But that will depend in part on future demand, Breen said.
“Of course, it will be market-dependent,” he said. “We’re not going to do it if the market isn’t there, but every indicator I see today is flashing green around market demand.”
GlobalFoundries has taken a more conservative approach to spending on its factory network. That’s made it profitable but often resulted in anemic top-line growth.
Its annual budget for new plants and equipment was less than US$1 billion last year. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電), the biggest chip foundry, spent more than US$40 billion.
The US-Japan deal gives GlobalFoundries a chance to expand in a smart way, Breen said.
“It’s actually a pretty exciting win-win in terms of the economics of it,” he said.

Ministry passes bamboo forest carbon sink project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:42:58 UTC
01:42:58 KST

The first carbon sink project for bamboo forest management has passed review by the Ministry of Environment, marking a milestone in the development of Taiwan’s natural carbon sink policy, the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency said yesterday.
The environmental, social and governance (ESG) project by Chunghwa Telecom Co covers 34 hectares of makino bamboo grove in Taoyuan’s Fusing District (復興), the agency said.
The project was matched with Chunghwa Telecom through the agency’s Hsinchu branch two years ago and would run through the end of 2034, it said.
Photo courtesy of Chunghwa Telecom
Chunghwa Telecom prepared documents according to the bamboo forest management methodology and applied for the plan to be accredited as a voluntary emission reduction project, the agency said.
The project passed the review on Oct. 2 and became the first validated carbon sink project for bamboo forest management nationwide, it said.
That showed that Taiwan has not only established a calculation methodology for bamboo forest carbon sink, but has also put it into practice, marking a milestone in natural carbon sink development, the agency said.
Bamboo forest diebacks could occur if the plants are left unattended, it said, adding that proper management and human intervention are the key to maintaining bamboo forests’ carbon sequestration potential.
Bamboo forests renew about every four years and bamboo aged four years or older should be removed via selective cutting to create growing space for young bamboo, the agency said.
The agency set up the carbon sink and biodiversity ESG project matching platform in April 2024 to help match corporate investments with natural habitats or forests in need of conservation, it said.
Such projects can assist companies in acquiring carbon sinks or carbon credits while creating job opportunities for locals, the agency said.
For example, Chunghwa Telecom is to cooperate with an Atayal village as part of the project, it said.
Bamboo management requires substantial manual labor, the agency said, adding that the felled bamboo would be processed into products.
More bamboo forest-based ESG projects could be launched on the platform in the future, it said.
So far, the platform’s ESG projects are open only to companies or foundations that have registered and incorporated in Taiwan, it added.
The agency expects Chunghwa Telecom’s experience to encourage more companies to take on natural carbon sink projects via the platform based on their core technology and sustainability targets, the agency said.

16:42:57 UTC
01:42:57 KST

Taiwanese highly supported convenience stores’ efforts to reduce single-use items, but only 26.1 percent knew the significance of “refuse” in the “5R” sustainable living principle, a Taiwan Re-Think Environmental Education Association survey showed.
Results showed that people’s environmental knowledge and attitude have continued to improve over the years, association chief brand officer Sandra Wang (王滋鮮) said.
However, more than 70 percent did not know that refusing single-use items or unnecessary plastics is the first step of the 5R principle: “refuse, reduce, reuse, repair and recycle,” Wang said.
Photo: Lin Cheng-hung, Taipei Times
Only 26.1 percent knew the significance of “refuse” in the 5R principle, of whom more than 80 percent still ask for single-use items, she said.
This year, about 93.9 percent of respondents knew that paper coffee cups are recyclable, up from 84.6 percent last year, while people with knowledge of recycling plastics increased from 68.4 percent last year to 70.6 percent this year.
However, the percentage of people answering correctly to questions about kitchen waste recycling declined from 88.1 percent last year to 77.44 percent this year, likely because the rules were revised this year, the results showed.
The Ministry of the Environment also collaborated with the association and Taiwan FamilyMart Co on an environmental exhibition at Huashan 1914 Creative Park in Taipei.
The exhibition runs from today to Oct. 26, featuring a glass wall with more than 17,000 discarded cigarette butts, as well as thought-provoking environmental issues in daily life.
At a news conference yesterday, Minister of Environment Peng Chi-ming (彭啟明) thanked the association for helping promote environmental education with innovative ideas.
He also thanked FamilyMart for collaborating with the ministry on resource circulation, including a coffee grounds recycling program, which won a grand award in the Presidential Hackathon last year, he said.
As kitchen waste disposal fees surged due to the ban on feeding swill to pigs, proper management of kitchen waste has become a key issue, Peng said.
While kitchen waste disposal involves downstream management, reducing upstream waste is also important, he said.
The ministry has initiated communications with 20 major chain restaurants on the issue, Peng said, adding that the ministry has discussed food waste reduction with department stores and hotels, which produce kitchen waste mainly through food courts and buffets.
The ministry would establish an alliance to promote the “clean plate” campaign by the end of this year and launch a “cherish food Wednesday” campaign, Peng said.

Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) yesterday attended a Cabinet meeting to discuss his proposal to relocate Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport), a week after his re-election campaign unveiled the proposition.
Chiang and the Executive Yuan offered differing accounts of the meeting, with the former emphasizing progress in exploring the proposal and the latter expressing skepticism about the “significant reversal” in the city’s urban development policy.
Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport’s first and second terminals have a combined capacity of 48 million people a year, which is projected to expand to 70 million with the opening of the third terminal, Chiang said.
Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times
This increase is more than enough to replace Songshan airport, whose capacity is 5.6 million people, he said.
Asked why he did not make this policy request earlier during his term as mayor, Chiang said that he had filed a recommendation for the removal of Songshan airport to the central government in August last year.
Chiang declined to respond to questions about replacing the airport’s role as a logistics hub for Taiwan’s outlying islands and medical patients requiring air transport.
Executive Yuan spokeswoman Michelle Lee (李慧芝) said that this was the first time Chiang discussed relocating the airport with the central government.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) strongly hopes that Chiang would explain the significant developmental reversal and provide documentation on the city’s internal discussions to help assist with the project, she added.
Songshan airport is used for accessing the outlying islands, transporting medical patients by air, and international flights, a reserve for Taoyuan airport and doubles as a military airbase for the capital’s defense, she said.
Without Songshan airport, there would be a critical capability gap that is immensely challenging to fill, especially due to its role as the sole airport capable of accommodating E and F type aircraft, she said.
Taoyuan airport’s third terminal is not expected to be completed before 2030, or reach its full operational potential in less than 10 years, she said.

E-cigarettes collected at anonymous disposal points had reached 633kg since the scheme began on Sept. 8, equivalent to about 12,660 devices based on an average weight of 50g each, the Health Promotion Agency (HPA) said yesterday.
The six special municipalities accounted for about 70 percent of the total, while northern and central Taiwan combined accounted for 80 percent, the agency said.
On Sept. 8, the HPA set up 431 e-cigarette collection spots nationwide for people to anonymously dispose of e-cigarettes.
Photo: CNA
It added one more the following day.
The Tobacco Hazards Prevention Act (菸害防制法) prohibits the manufacture, import, sale, supply, display, advertisement and use of e-cigarettes.
The disposal boxes are positioned mainly at local health departments, health bureaus and public health centers.
The agency’s proposal to add “possession” to the list of e-cigarette prohibitions was passed by the Executive Yuan on June 25 and has been sent to the legislature for review, HPA Tobacco Control Division Director Lo Su-ying (羅素英) said.
Once it takes effect, there would be a one-month grace period in which the devices would be confiscated, but no fines would be issued. After the grace period, people found with the devices would face a fine of NT$30,000 to NT$100,000, as well as confiscation of the device, the HPA said.
Public support for the collection scheme was evident, HPA Deputy Director-General Lin Li-ju (林莉茹) said, adding that it would continue to provide the service and encourage people to properly dispose of their devices.
The program is expected to continue until one month after the revisions to the act take effect, with additional locations to be considered based on local demand, Lin said.

Stocks in Taiwan slumped to a four-week low yesterday as hotter-than-expected US inflation rekindled concerns over interest rates and a global sell-off in technology shares intensified.
The benchmark TAIEX fell 1,655.96 points, or 3.41 percent, to close at 46,969.87, on turnover of NT$1.319 trillion (US$40.9 billion), Taiwan Stock Exchange (TWSE) data showed.
Foreign investors led the sell-off with net sales of NT$302.56 billion, while proprietary dealers sold a net NT$95.82 billion, largely through hedging transactions.
Photo: CNA
Investment trusts were the only net buyers, purchasing NT$28.3 billion of shares, TWSE data showed.
The decline came after US consumer prices rose 3.7 percent year-on-year last month, exceeding economists’ 3.6 percent forecast and raising concerns that the US Federal Reserve might raise interest rate again later this month or in December, putting further pressure on technology shares, whose valuations are sensitive to borrowing costs.
US technology stocks fell on Wall Street overnight, extending a decline in semiconductor shares to a sixth consecutive session. The sell-off spread across Asian markets yesterday, with South Korea’s KOSPI plunging 7.57 percent and Japan’s Nikkei 225 falling 4.9 percent.
The Fed is due to review its monetary policy on Oct. 27 and 28.
Taiwan’s market was particularly vulnerable to the downturn because of its heavy reliance on technology stocks. The electronics sector came under pressure, with major companies including Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電), MediaTek Inc (聯發科), Nanya Technology Corp (南亞科) and Delta Electronics Inc (台達電) among the hardest hit.
Cheng-tung Security Investment Consultant Co (承通證券) analyst Cheng Lung (陳龍) attributed the sell-off across Asia largely to foreign investors pulling back from semiconductor and hardware stocks.
“Investors are more concerned about the sustainability of artificial intelligence [AI] spending, as rising financing costs heighten the risks of a recession,” he said, advising against drawing direct comparisons between Taiwan and South Korea, which have different industrial structures.
Memory makers might be posting strong profits, but competition from Chinese rivals could erode their edge, Chen said.
Young Cheng Asset Management Co (永誠國際資產) analyst William Chen (陳威良) urged investors to stay calm amid market volatility, advising them to focus on the fundamentals of AI-related stocks and avoid making hasty decisions.
Concerns have mounted following Broadcom Inc CEO Hock Tan’s (陳福陽) warning that many AI investors do not understand what they are buying, comparing their behavior to casino gambling.
The sell-off in technology stocks intensified, as bond yields at US AI cloud provider CoreWeave Inc surged past 15 percent overnight, fueling unease over the financing risks of the AI boom.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:42:49 UTC
01:42:49 KST

Seven years after COVID-19 put the brakes on Indonesia’s new women’s soccer league, Zahra Naqiyyah would finally return to the field with “high hopes” for the women’s game in the country.
Sunday’s matches in the Indonesia Women’s League (IWL) would be the first since 2019 and a new chapter for women’s soccer in the Muslim-majority country of 290 million people.
“I really believe that if Indonesia’s women’s football is properly managed we can become a powerhouse in Asia,” Zahra said at a training session in Bekasi, east of Jakarta.
Photo: AFP
“I have high hopes for women’s football in Indonesia,” she added, wearing a black hijab and the turquoise jersey of her club, Garudayaksa Women.
Indonesia has long been an outlier among soccer nations, including much smaller Asian ones, in not having a permanent league for women. That was until 2019, when the IWL was launched and Zahra, only 15 at the time, helped her team to victory and celebrated with a hero’s parade in her home city of Bandung — fulfilling a dream.
However, the league managed only one season because of the pandemic and subsequent financial problems, and has been on hold ever since.
Now, the Football Association of Indonesia has allocated 24 billion rupiah (US$1.34 million) to restart the league and pay salaries, albeit small ones, to players.
There would be six clubs to start in the five-year trial period, said association chairman Erick Thohir, former owner of Inter.
At 22, Zahra is still young enough to make a career of it. Others were not so lucky.
“Many of my friends ended up quitting because what else could they do? There is no league, and if they want to become coaches, who are they supposed to coach?” Zahra said.
While she learned to be a coach, others tried their luck with clubs abroad.
Nastasia Suci Ramadhani played last year in the Maldives.
The 20-year-old returned to Indonesia in January to play alongside Zahra.
Unsure about the league’s staying power, Nastasia is studying management and has also considered becoming a police officer or soldier.
“For men there’s a league every year, but for women there isn’t,” she said.
Garudayaksa coach Yopie Riwoe said the going will be tough if Indonesia wants to compete with top Asian nations.
Japan won the FIFA Women’s World Cup in 2011 and are the current Asian champions, while China and South Korea also boast women’s leagues and are competitive at international level.
“All this time they haven’t done continuous training like daily sessions with high intensity, so it’s been a bit difficult,” Yopie said of Indonesia’s women. “We’re trying to go slowly.”
Indonesia’s women have never been to the World Cup and failed to qualify for the Asian Cup last year, although they did reach the continental showpiece in 2022, losing all three games.
However, they won the regional ASEAN Football Federation Women’s Cup in 2024 and again this year.
They are currently ranked No. 105 in the world.
Hoping to join the national side one day, Azra Zifa Kayla is playing in the IWL for Persita Women, based west of Jakarta.
The 22-year-old would juggle afternoon practice with mornings teaching physical education to elementary-school students, afraid to stake everything, including a regular salary, on her passion for soccer.
“I am an athlete first,” she said on a soccer pitch in Tangerang, near the capital. “But to be an athlete — especially as a woman in Indonesia — can be limiting.”
“I should also focus on education because that’s the guarantee of my future,” said Azra, who studied health and sport science.
The IWL returns with about 200 players from clubs all from Greater Jakarta.
IWL boss Teddy Tjahjono said the long-term goal was to create a sustainable women’s soccer industry.
“If the industry is strong, then financially it will be good for the clubs, for the players and for the entire support system around women’s football, which will also continue to improve,” he said.

James, the NBA’s all-time leading scorer, in July announced that he had signed a two-year, US$8 million deal with the 76ers, ending weeks of speculation over where the four-time NBA champion would land as a free agent after eight seasons and one title with the Los Angeles Lakers. The 41-year-old, entering a record-extending 24th NBA season, won two titles with the Miami Heat, another with the Cleveland Cavaliers and a fourth

Montenegro changes temporary protection rules for Ukrainian men liable for military service

Unknown Publisher

Montenegro changes temporary protection rules for Ukrainian men liable for military service
Kyiv • UNN
New male applicants need a document confirming completion of or discharge from military service. The rule does not apply to those who already have protection.
The Government of Montenegro is changing the rules for temporary protection for Ukrainian men liable for military service in the country. From now on, to obtain protection, they must provide a document confirming completion of or exemption from military service. The restriction does not apply to Ukrainians who already have temporary protection status, the Government of Montenegro reports, according to UNN.
At its 142nd meeting, the Government adopted a decision amending the decision approving temporary protection for persons from Ukraine
The Government said that the decision complies with the provisions of Council Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/1912 of July 30, 2026.
The decision states that "temporary protection until March 4, 2027, is granted to Ukrainian citizens who, before arriving in Montenegro, actually resided in Ukraine and who have fulfilled their military duty in Ukraine or are exempt from military duty in Ukraine, subject to the submission of supporting documents, and who cannot return to Ukraine, which they were forced to leave because of the armed conflict".
The aforementioned restriction will not apply to persons from Ukraine who already enjoy temporary protection in Montenegro.
It will be recalled
On October 8, the period of temporary protection for Ukrainian refugees in Germany was extended until March 2028.

Albania’s PM dismisses calls to resign as student protests spread
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:41:30 UTC
01:41:30 KST

Albania’s PM dismisses calls to resign as student protests spread
Prime Minister Edi Rama condemns ‘chaos’ as protests continue for a third day in the capital and spread to other cities.
Albania’s prime minister has dismissed calls for his resignation as thousands of protesters clash with riot police in the capital for the third day in a row, leaving government buildings damaged.
“My responsibility is to listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward,” Prime Minister Edi Rama said in a written statement to the Reuters news agency, following protester demands for him to resign.
“The alternative would be a betrayal of the Albanians who gave me a strong mandate to complete negotiations on European Union membership,” Rama added on Thursday.
This comes as riot police used water cannons and tear gas against crowds of protesters in the capital, Tirana. Demonstrators have accused officials of corruption and neglecting education, expressing anger about the sale of parts of Albania’s southern coastline to a luxury resort development backed by United States President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
Tirana’s streets were littered with burnt-out rubbish bins, shattered bus stops and broken traffic lights. In the capital’s central Skanderbeg Square, police hit fleeing protesters with batons as tourists looked on.
Thursday’s protests also spread to several smaller cities as students joined university boycotts.
Rama, whose government denies corruption, said he would be ready to discuss rising education costs but rejected the calls to resign.
“Perhaps some forces, at home and abroad, do not want Albania to succeed as a forerunner for EU membership. But I will not allow violence to derail Albania’s European future,” Rama said in his statement to Reuters.
‘Everyone will certainly pay’
Rama earlier posted a video on his Facebook page showing him touring the burnt-out remains of an office at a university campus in Tirana.
“Until yesterday, this was the office of the College of Europe, the school of a united Europe,” he said in the video, his first public comments since the protests began.
“Everyone is responsible before the law, and everyone who has had a hand in this chaos will certainly pay.”
The prime minister was due to meet his party’s parliamentary group early on Thursday, when protesters circulated an “ultimatum” demanding his resignation by 1pm (11:00 GMT).
But even before the deadline passed, protesters had already begun clashing with police, building makeshift barriers and setting fire to bins.
‘Our prime minister is the meaning of the word corruption’
A student who gave her name as Kiara told Reuters the cost of living, poor job prospects and alleged corruption were the main issues for protesters.
“Our prime minister is the meaning of the word corruption. You can only find work in your field if you know a guy who knows a guy,” she said, her face covered by a mask, like many on the streets on Thursday.
The protesters demanded Rama’s resignation, saying no one had listened to their concerns during a summer of largely peaceful protests over the luxury resort development linked to Kushner.
Police said 65 people were arrested during Wednesday’s protests, suspected of “attacking police officers, institutions, public and private property”.
The Health Ministry said in a statement that hospitals in Tirana treated 89 people on Wednesday, including 61 police officers.
Four officers and two protesters remained hospitalised, with a demonstrator and two officers expected to undergo surgery.
“Attacking institutions, destroying public property and threatening public safety have nothing to do with the legitimate demands of students,” Rama said.

Trump Cancels Livestream of Fort Hood Firing Squad Execution Amid Bipartisan Pushback
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:41:09 UTC
01:41:09 KST

President Donald Trump on Thursday called off plans to livestream the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan following a wave of fierce bipartisan backlash.
In a post on Truth Social, the President said he thought streaming the execution “might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM,” but that “many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die.”
The families of victims may view the execution “if they so choose,” Trump added.
The execution remains scheduled for Dec. 3 and marks the first U.S. military firing squad execution since World War II.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced on Oct. 8 that the execution of Hasan would be livestreamed, sparking fierce backlash from both sides of the aisle.
Vice President JD Vance said earlier this month, “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen,” when asked about the livestream. He also said that he would not watch the livestream if it took place.
House Speaker Mike Johnson also said he would not watch the execution. In an interview with CBS News earlier this month, he said he had colleagues "who have concerns,” over the livestream, one of them being “that you would create a video that would be a recruiting tool for future terrorists."
In addition to many Democrats in Congress, several Republican lawmakers also expressed their disapproval over the plans..
“I absolutely support the sentence of death, but live-streaming executions is what jihadists do,” said Republican Rep. Austin Scott of Georgia, a member of the House Armed Services Committee, in a post on X. “America is better than that.”
Republican Rep. John Curtis of Utah said that “a civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment,” in a post on X in which he urged Hegseth to “reconsider” his decision. “Secretary Hegseth’s plan to livestream the Fort Hood execution risks feeding that appetite.”
Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, an outspoken GOP critic against Hegseth, called the livestream “beyond disgusting. Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America.”
Trump had reconsidered livestreaming Hasan’s execution this week after learning that he is paralyzed from the waist down, according to sources familiar with the matter who spoke to CNN.
Polling shows a majority of Americans disapprove of livestreamed executions
A majority of Americans also opposed the livestream of Hasan’s execution. According to an ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll, eight in ten Americans said the execution should not be livestreamed.
Majorities across party lines opposed the livestream, with 91% of Democrats, 83% of Independents, and 64% of Republicans, according to the poll.
Another YouGov poll found that 69% of respondents opposed broadcasting executions to the public, including 52% of Republicans, 67% of independents, and 87% of Democrats.
Among those who supported the death penalty, 55% opposed livestreaming executions.
In general, support for the death penalty has declined in the U.S. According to a Gallup poll, 52% of Americans supported capital punishment for convicted murderers in 2025, down from around 80% in 1994.
What was Hasan convicted of?
Hasan, a former U.S. Army major and psychiatrist, was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 in a mass shooting at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.
He opened fire inside a processing center where soldiers were preparing for deployments overseas, killing 12 soldiers and one civilian employee. Pvt. Francheska Velez, 21, was three months pregnant when she was shot and killed by Hasan.
Hasan said that he was motivated by opposition to U.S. operations in Afghanistan and support for the Taliban.
“I was on the wrong side but I switched sides,” Hasan said in 2013.

Russia builds massive new launch base for jet-powered attack drones in six weeks, satellite images show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:41:07 UTC
01:41:07 KST

Russia builds massive new launch base for jet-powered attack drones in six weeks, satellite images show
Russia has nearly completed construction of a major new facility for launching jet-powered attack drones near the Millerovo military airbase in Rostov Oblast in just six weeks, satellite imagery shows, with experts saying it could become operational within weeks.
Ukrainian open-source intelligence (OSINT) group Absolutely Reliable Source reported the construction on Oct. 13, citing satellite imagery. The analysts identified eight launch positions and 32 areas for preparing drones for takeoff.
According to the group, the facility is intended for launching Russia's Geran-5 jet-powered attack drones. Satellite images show that the site was an empty field on Sept. 1, while the first section of the complex was nearing completion by Oct. 12.
The analysts also reported that satellite imagery from Oct. 12 appeared to show drones being unloaded at the facility.
The group suggested that construction had been accelerated to expand Russia's drone attack capabilities following strikes on Kyiv in September. It also noted similarities between the new facility and Russia's existing Tsymbulova drone base in Oryol Oblast.
Later, on Oct. 15, Reuters published an investigation, revealing that the facility covers approximately 0.9 square kilometers and is located about 3.5 kilometers from Millerovo airbase.
Reuters' analysis found that two of the eight launch platforms already had launch rails installed, while rails were under construction on two others.
Mike Monnik, founder and CEO of the private intelligence company DroneSec, told Reuters that the facility could become fully operational within weeks, potentially sooner. He estimated that it could launch 100 or more jet-powered drones within 24 hours, depending on available supplies and operational needs.
Russia has significantly increased its use of jet-powered attack drones against Ukraine in recent months, with Kyiv and the surrounding region among the main targets.
Unlike older, propeller-driven models, Russia's newer jet-powered drones can reach speeds of up to 600 kilometers per hour, making them more difficult for Ukrainian air defenses to intercept.
Ukraine has been developing new interceptor drones to counter the threat. On Oct. 12, former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov announced that a new Ukrainian interceptor had shot down two Russian Geran-5 drones during its first week of deployment.

Trump scraps plan to livestream execution after global condemnation

Most Americans opposed

Syria announces arrest of Assad-era paramilitary leader
Syrian authorities on Thursday announced the arrest of a paramilitary leader who backed ousted ruler Bashar al-Assad during the country's civil war, and who is accused of being the main culprit in a massacre of nearly 250 civilians.
"The intelligence services have arrested Ali Kayali, who also went by the name Mihrac Ural, the main suspect in the Banias massacre of 2013, while he was attempting to flee across the border," state news agency SANA said.
It did not specify which country the man was trying to flee to.
In May 2013, government and forces and their allies killed at least 248 people in mass executions in the predominantly Sunni Muslim towns of Bayda and Banias, located in the coastal province of Tartus, according to Human Rights Watch.
The monitor had at the time described the killings as "one of the deadliest instances of mass executions in Syria's increasingly bloody conflict".
The arrest "sends a clear message: there is no room in Syria for impunity for criminals; the rights of victims will not be lost, no matter how much time passes," Syrian Justice Minister Mazhar Alwais wrote on X.
Syria's war began with pro-democracy protests in 2011 that were violently suppressed by the government, and quickly morphed into a complex armed conflict that drew in paramilitary forces, jihadists and foreign powers.
In a multiconfessional country, the war took on a sectarian nature, with the killings in Banias and Bayda often seen as a starting point of that shift.
It ended with the ousting of Assad in 2024 in a lightning offensive led by an Islamist rebel group that subsequently took power.
According to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights monitor, the death tolls in Banias and Bayda came to around 400.
Kayali fled from jail in 1982 in his home country of Turkey, before moving to Syria where he would end up founding a paramilitary force allied with Assad's government.
The new authorities in Syria have arrested dozens of former security officials. Their trials began in April.
President Ahmed al-Sharaa's media adviser Ahmed Zeydan welcomed Kayali's arrest, describing him as "a criminal... who committed massacres during the Syrian war, including those in Bayda and Banias. Every murderous criminal will be hunted down".

Quote: "The individual in question is Leonid Ryzhikov, a 36-year-old Russian citizen and resident of St Petersburg. He served in the 2nd Battalion of the 1009th Motorised Rifle Regiment, 68th Motorised Rifle Division of the 6th Combined Arms Army of the Russian Armed Forces, using the alias Yula.

Details: He fought against Ukraine in the Chuhuiv district of Kharkiv Oblast.

Armed with an AK-74 assault rifle, he fled the area and began walking towards the city of Kharkiv, hiding in forested areas.
Along the way, he burgled an abandoned house, stealing civilian clothes from it.
Quote: "On 13 October, near the village of Mykhailivka in the Kharkiv district, Ryzhikov unprovokedly shot dead a 60-year-old peaceful local resident, who was fishing at a pond, using his assault rifle. After killing the elderly man, he pushed his body into the water.

Nicolás Maduro insisted on Thursday during an appearance in a New York court that torture allegations in a rewritten drug trafficking indictment against the deposed Venezuelan president and his wife were “false accusations”.
Maduro, shackled at the ankles, was brought to court to face the new charges accusing the couple of leading a state-sponsored campaign of repression that tortured scores of victims, including three Americans.
Judge Alvin K Hellerstein entered a not-guilty plea on behalf of Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores. They were seized from their Caracas home by the US military in a night-time raid in January.
Hellerstein announced that he was entering the plea on behalf of Maduro after Maduro twice responded to the judge’s request to enter a plea by criticizing the indictment, saying it contained “false accusations and false testimony”. Maduro spoke through an interpreter.
Attorney Barry Pollack said when the charges were announced last week that Maduro, 63, denied them and “looks forward to his day in court”.
According to the rewritten indictment, Maduro oversaw a violent torture system that beat, asphyxiated and delivered electric shocks to its victims. He is accused of personally recommending torture methods, receiving updates on specific victims’ treatment and threatening to kill one prisoner’s child as a form of psychological torture.
Flores, 70, a former attorney general, helped develop the repressive system and ordered the torture of some specific people, the indictment alleges.
When she was asked to enter a plea, she said through an interpreter: “I am completely innocent. I am not guilty.”
Maduro, who served as Venezuela’s president from 2013 until his capture in January, has been under investigation for years by the international criminal court over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents. He has always denied wrongdoing.
Prosecutors told the judge during the hearing that lawyers on both sides want the trial date moved from 1 June to 14 June.
Torture is a crime under international law and can be prosecuted outside the country where the abuse occurred and regardless of the victims’ nationality. But the prosecution of foreign officials in the US is exceedingly rare, having been tried only a few times, including against the son of the former Liberian president Charles Taylor, Russians responsible for war crimes in Ukraine and a former prison warden in Bashar Assad’s Syria.
Earlier this year, Maduro and his wife pleaded not guilty in the US drug case, which said they conspired to flood the US with cocaine. Their attorneys say the case should be dismissed on immunity grounds because they were the leader and first lady of a foreign country.
The revised indictment covers allegations of torture stretching back to Maduro’s ascent to power in 2013, when he took over as president from his mentor Hugo Chávez, who died of cancer that year.
