UK Green member behind anti-Zionism motion ‘receives death threats’
Lubna Speitan, who has Palestinian roots, believes messages and emails are part of an effort to intimidate her.
London, United Kingdom – The British-Palestinian woman behind the Zionism is racism motion, passed by the Green Party of England and Wales earlier this month, says she has received death and rape threats since the vote.
In an interview with Al Jazeera on Thursday, Green member Lubna Speitan, an artist and activist, said she has received dozens of ominous social media messages and emails, which she has reported to the police.
“These threats were anticipated,” said Speitan, who believes they are a form of “intimidation” from pro-Israel agitators.
While “no one wants to be on the receiving end of death threats”, she said it is “necessary to confront these evils”.
The Greens passed the motion by 1,022 votes to 813 at their party conference in Brighton, but it has been criticised by virtually all other British political parties and has brought turmoil to the Greens.
Several of its left-wing MPs have criticised the move, and on Thursday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham ruled out partnering with the party, calling the motion “wrong” and “anti-Semitic”.
The motion defines Zionism, the belief that Jews have a historic claim to Palestine, as a form of racism, predicated on the dispossession and ethnic cleansing of Palestinians. Palestinians made up more than 90 percent of the population in 1917, when Britain declared its support for a Jewish state in the country.
The motion supports Palestinians’ right to self-determination and calls for the establishment of a single democratic state in historic Palestine for Muslims and Jews. It also says that anti-Zionism should not be equated with anti-Semitism.
‘Personally smeared’
Fifty-six members of Speitan’s family have been killed since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza three years ago.
“Zionism is defined clearly as an ethnonationalist settler-colonial project. The motion also recognises, correctly, that not all Jews are Zionists and not all Zionists are Jews,” she said. “It targets an ideology: Zionism.”
She added that she has been “personally smeared” by media outlets.
Recent headlines in the British press have claimed she was “friends” with an “al-Qaeda terrorist”, as she reportedly offered to testify in defence of Minh Quang Pham, a UK citizen who had planned an attack at Heathrow Airport.
“This tactic of guilt by association will not be dignified with a response,” Speitan said of the reports.
The Green Party of England and Wales told Al Jazeera that Speitan holds no party positions “other than being a member”.
“The Green Party takes all allegations of this nature seriously. Where members have expressed views that do not fit in with the party’s values, we have internal processes to investigate, and an investigation is under way,” it said.
Media watchdog NewsCord, which reviewed coverage of the motion, concluded that opponents of the resolution received 10 times more coverage than its supporters.
The Green Party is not the first Western political institution to classify Zionism as a form of racism. In 1975, the United Nations General Assembly passed a resolution declaring that Zionism was a racist ideology. Seventy-two countries voted in favour of the motion, while 35 opposed it and 32 abstained. The resolution was later repealed in 1991.

Lion Green Road by Mary Duggan Architects and RUFFARCHITECTS Wins RIBA Stirling Prize 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:35:00 UTC
01:35:00 KST

The RIBA Stirling Prize 2026 has been awarded to Lion Green Road, a housing development in Coulsdon, South London, designed by Mary Duggan Architects with RUFFARCHITECTS for Croydon Council. Comprising 157 homes across five residential blocks, the project combines privately owned and socially rented housing on a former car park. Presented annually by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA), the Stirling Prize recognizes a building considered to make a significant contribution to the evolution of architecture and the built environment. The 2026 winner was announced at a ceremony at Old Billingsgate in London on October 15, marking the prize's 30th anniversary.
Replacing a car park on a sloping site with an eight-meter difference in elevation, Lion Green Road reconsiders how higher-density housing can respond to suburban contexts. Rather than leveling the terrain or organizing the development around conventional residential streets, the architects used the site's topography to shape the arrangement of the buildings and their relationship to the surrounding landscape. The five blocks are positioned and rotated to respond to changes in level and take advantage of different views, including views toward a surviving fragment of the Surrey Iron Railway, recognized as the world's first fully independent public railway. The buildings form what the architects describe as a "living landscape," accommodating 635 residents while establishing a connection between Lion Green Road and the parkland beyond.
The five blocks share the same construction specification but vary subtly in height, orientation, and brickwork patterns. A palette of three brown brick tones relates the buildings to the surrounding greenery, while differences in brickwork give each block an individual identity. The development is organized around shared outdoor spaces, with a new public pathway connecting the street to the parkland. Children's play areas, a sensory trail, and residents' allotments provide spaces for recreation and everyday interaction, extending the landscape's use beyond the residential buildings and creating opportunities for engagement between residents and their neighbors.
Related Article
RIBA Reveals the Shortlist for the 2026 Stirling Prize
Within the apartments, dual-aspect layouts bring daylight into each home and provide views in more than one direction. Balconies are positioned to limit direct overlooking between neighboring homes, allowing the blocks to sit relatively close together without sacrificing privacy or access to outdoor space. This arrangement supports the project's approach to density, in which the positioning of buildings and the planning of individual homes are used to balance housing provision with daylight, views, and private outdoor areas. The project also incorporates measures to reduce its environmental impact, including efficient construction methods, simple finishes, and a streamlined building process intended to reduce carbon emissions. The landscape strategy further supports existing wildlife and biodiversity.
The 2026 Stirling Prize shortlist also included A House at Fairmead in Epping Forest by Sergison Bates, BEAM in Hertfordshire by Bennetts Associates, Paddington Square in London by Renzo Piano Building Workshop with Adamson Associates, Pembroke, Mill Lane by Haworth Tompkins, and River Wing at Clare College by Witherford Watson Mann Architects. Previous winners of the prize include Appleby Blue Almshouse by Witherford Watson Mann Architects (2025), The Elizabeth Line by Grimshaw, Maynard, Equation, and AtkinsRéalis (2024), The John Morden Centre by Mæ (2023), and The New Library at Magdalene College by Níall McLaughlin Architects (2022).

Israeli ad-tech firm helped place spyware on Al Jazeera devices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:32:03 UTC
01:32:03 KST

Israeli ad-tech firm helped place spyware on Al Jazeera devices
Citizen Lab investigation says dozens of Al Jazeera devices were infected by malware planted through advertisements.
Israeli advertising technology company Discover-Tech helped place spyware on dozens of devices used by Al Jazeera and other companies.
Al Jazeera Media Network on Thursday said it “condemns the spyware attacks targeting a number of its staff” and pledged to continue to “protect its employees and systems”.
The network said targeting journalists is an “assault on press freedom” and called for those responsible to be held accountable.
A Citizen Lab investigation, prompted by Al Jazeera’s initial internal probe into the issue, has confirmed that spyware from Candiru, an Israeli spyware firm blacklisted by the United States government in 2021 for its malicious cyber activities, was planted on these devices, using the first-known instance of “zero-click” targeted advertising.
The nature of installing this spyware means that once an infected advertisement appears on a device, that device, too, is infected – spying on, and feeding, all the data and information available on that platform to those stealing it.
The malicious software is designed to collect a wide range of sensitive data, including files, documents, and browser data such as cookies, bookmarks, and saved credentials. It can also capture keystrokes, take screenshots, record microphone and webcam input, and extract emails and messages from popular communication platforms.
To avoid triggering security mechanisms, the spyware often uses encrypted communication channels and breaks up stolen data into smaller chunks sent over time.
The particular tool used is understood to have cost several million dollars.
The incident highlights the sophisticated nature of threats posed by groups like Candiru, and their customers, who use techniques to bypass modern security defences.
The Citizen Lab, a research unit at the University of Toronto, concluded in its report that Discover-Tech purchased the advertisements with built-in spyware. It then directed devices to Candiru’s malware through these advertisements.
Al Jazeera journalists were among the millions whose devices were targeted – including several who reported on sensitive subjects.
Al Jazeera’s in-house technology team first discovered unusual patterns on devices used by some journalists in 2024. The pattern continued into 2025. Al Jazeera reached out to Citizen Lab for a more detailed investigation into its suspicions that spyware was responsible for the activity.
“Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera collected during the attack period provides a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed,” the University of Toronto-based team said in its report published Thursday.
Al Jazeera said that the cooperation “helped verify and publicly document these attacks”.
Meanwhile, New York-based advertising security firm Confiant said in a separate report that some of Discover-Tech’s advertisements also appeared in critical networks used by the Pentagon, the United Nations International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court.
Candiru’s spyware has previously been used to carry out surveillance on at least 100 journalists, dissidents and others in several countries.

Why are eight US states suing OpenAI?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:28:44 UTC
01:28:44 KST

Why are eight US states suing OpenAI?
They allege ChatGPT has caused harm to their residents, coaching its users — including teenagers — to harm themselves or others.
Eight US states have filed the most significant coordinated state action against tech giant OpenAI, adding to a wave of legal challenges that the firm is facing as it prepares for a public listing.
Recent legal and regulatory challenges have highlighted concerns about how AI chatbots and social media platforms are used and triggered discussions on policies for identifying and addressing user conversations that threaten violence.
Calls have been growing for AI companies to be held accountable for the impact of their digital platforms on users, specifically children, who are particularly susceptible to addiction and other harms.
What is this legal action about?
Florida filed the first lawsuit in June, alleging that the platform has harmed children by enabling information to be gathered by school shooters, providing access to guidance on self-harm and using addictive algorithms to keep young users hooked.
It cited a shooting at Florida State University in Tallahassee in April 2025, when a 20-year-old gunman shot dead two adults and wounded five others. According to the lawsuit, gunman Phoenix Ikner consulted OpenAI’s ChatGPT programme about what type of weapon and ammunition to use and at what time campus would be busiest.
On Wednesday, attorneys general from eight states – Iowa, Kansas, Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia – said they had also sued OpenAI in courts across the country.
They all claim ChatGPT has caused harm to their residents, alleging the chatbot has coached its users – including teenagers – to harm themselves or others.
Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said in a statement that OpenAI was “hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans.”
“OpenAI claims ChatGPT is safe while it’s giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide—all while pretending to be their fake friend,” she said.
West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey said the chatbot lacks adequate safeguards for sensitive conversations involving suicide, school shootings and self-harm. “We must do all we can to protect kids,” McCuskey said.
What are the allegations?
The legal action alleges that ChatGPT has been designed to be “agreeable and engaging to earn the trust of users”. In doing so, it reinforces delusions, encourages dangerous behaviour and assists users in planning violence like mass shootings.
Additionally, the suits accuse OpenAI of violating state consumer protection laws by misleading users about the safety of their AI tool, which in fact poses a danger to the health of the states’ residents.
The states are seeking orders forcing OpenAI to make substantial changes to how ChatGPT works, as well as measures barring the company from developing AI models that can improve themselves until it can ensure those models are aligned with human values.
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers said the lawsuit “simply holds OpenAI to the same standards under Nebraska law as any other company”.
How has OpenAI responded?
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri gave a statement to the media, saying that the company has “built industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack”.
“While no system can be perfect, we’ll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today,” Pusateri said.
“We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry, not just one company.”
What other lawsuits is the tech giant facing?
OpenAI is also facing dozens of lawsuits by private plaintiffs alleging ChatGPT helped users plan mass shootings or other violence.
A mother, whose two children use the chatbot, alleged in a proposed class action lawsuit filed on Tuesday in San Francisco federal court that OpenAI illegally profits from the personal information and data that minors share with ChatGPT.
The lawsuit claims the chatbot is designed to collect data and information from minors, which is then used to train OpenAI’s AI models. Minors can’t consent to the use of their data under California law.
In July, a Florida pastor sued OpenAI and its chief executive, Sam Altman, claiming ChatGPT’s inaccurate medical advice kept him from seeking treatment for recurrent dizzy spells, leading him to suffer a pulmonary embolism that nearly killed him.
OpenAI is also facing a series of lawsuits over its failure to alert authorities to threats made on ChatGPT in advance of one of the worst mass shootings in Canada’s history.
The province of British Columbia filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in a California court in September, seven months after 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar shot eight people in the small Canadian town of Tumbler Ridge, including his mother and half-brother, before dying by suicide.
The lawsuit alleges that OpenAI had failed to notify authorities about concerning user interactions on ChatGPT, accusing the company of “aiding and abetting a mass shooting”.
Victims of that shooting and their families filed 30 lawsuits against OpenAI in the Northern District of California in the San Francisco division at the start of September, alleging that “ChatGPT played a role in the mass shooting and OpenAI could have, and should have, prevented it”.
OpenAI said it had flagged a ChatGPT account linked to Van Rootselaar for abuse eight months before the shooting, and deactivated it, but did not alert police at the time because the user’s content “did not meet the higher threshold required for referral” – meaning the company did not believe it indicated a credible, imminent risk of a plan for violent acts.

The issue of imposing a preventive measure in the form of detention in custody is being considered.
The pretrial investigation is ongoing.

Ukrainian banks processed UAH 141 mln in bail payments to anti-corruption court in August-September – Pyshnyy
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
19:23:23 EEST
01:23:23 KST

Ukrainian banks processed 527 transactions to pay bail into the account of the High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC) in August-September, totaling more than UAH 141 million, National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) Governor Andriy Pyshnyy has said.
"It would be difficult to say that the system is not functioning," he said on the Follow the Money podcast hosted by the AML Hub civic organization.
Of the 527 transactions, 178 were cash payments totaling UAH 64 million, while 349 were non-cash transfers totaling UAH 77 million, Pyshnyy said.
As of October 10, banks had processed an additional UAH 4.5 million in payments to the HACC account.
"So to say that the system is not accepting payments today – it is accepting them," the central bank governor said.
Recent corruption scandals have brought increased scrutiny to such transactions, and some banks have strengthened their relevant monitoring systems.
Pyshnyy stressed, however, that this should not lead banks to abandon a risk-based approach to financial monitoring in practice.
"The National Bank neither authorizes nor prohibits anything in real time," he said.
Individual banks make decisions on specific transactions based on information about the customer, their transaction history, economic activity and risk level.
The NBU, in turn, assesses through supervision and inspections whether banks' internal control systems and application of a risk-based approach comply with legal requirements.
Pyshnyy said the central bank had increased its supervisory focus on this area in response to recent events to gather information and assess how such transactions were being handled in practice.
In September, Member of Parliament Vadym Stolar said banks had refused to transfer UAH 300 million for bail set by the HACC. Lawyers for Iryna Mudra, a former deputy head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, also reported that 15 banks had refused to accept payments for her bail.
On September 24, the HACC ordered the NBU to investigate the reported refusals.
The NBU said at the time that it had not instructed or recommended that banks automatically refuse transactions to pay bail.

Egypt becomes first country to retain WHO gold-tier Hep C status
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:23:16 UTC
01:23:16 KST

Breadcrumb
Egypt becomes world's first to retain WHO hepatitis C elimination status
Egypt has become the first country in the world to receive certification for maintaining the World Health Organization’s gold-tier status in its efforts to eliminate hepatitis C, following a review of its achievements in combating the virus between 2023 and 2025.
Until the 2010s, Egypt had the highest prevalence of Hep C globally, affecting roughly 10% of the population, largely due to historical public health campaigns involving unsterilised medical needles in the 20th century.
But on Wednesday, the country received the certificate from the WHO after the organisation confirmed that it had met the requirements for retaining the status, which it first obtained in October 2023.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus presented the certificate to Egyptian Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar during a news conference in Cairo, held on the sidelines of the 73rd session of the WHO Regional Committee for the Eastern Mediterranean.
The WHO said the recognition reflected Egypt’s continued progress in tackling Hep C. The review of the country’s efforts between 2023 and 2025 confirmed that it had fulfilled the requirements for maintaining the gold-tier status.
The decision had previously been approved in July 2026 by the WHO Regional Committee for the Validation of the Elimination of HIV, Hepatitis and Sexually Transmitted Infections.
Egypt's Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said the country’s achievements were built on the 100 Million Health campaign, launched in 2018. The campaign screened 68 million Egyptians and provided free treatment to around 4.5 million people living with the virus, using locally produced medicines.
In a statement, the WHO said Egypt had moved away from large-scale screening campaigns towards a sustainable and integrated approach to combating Hep C during the period in which it maintained its gold-tier status.
The approach includes strengthening routine screening, diagnosis, treatment, surveillance and prevention, while expanding access to services for people living with the virus.
The organisation highlighted Egypt’s expansion of screening, diagnosis and treatment services, as well as efforts to strengthen governance and oversight between 2025 and 2030.
Other measures include drawing up a national plan to sustain the elimination of Hep C and continuing to integrate hepatitis services into primary healthcare and the country’s comprehensive health insurance system.
Egypt has also worked to improve laboratory quality and disease surveillance systems, while maintaining high standards for blood and injection safety, according to the WHO.
The WHO first awarded Egypt gold-tier status in October 2023, making it the first country in the world to receive the recognition for its progress towards eliminating Hep C.
Over roughly a decade, Egypt, a country of more than 120 million people today, reduced the prevalence of the virus from 10% to 0.38%.
During that period, the country diagnosed 87% of people living with the virus and provided treatment to 93% of those diagnosed.
These figures exceeded the WHO’s gold-tier benchmarks, which require countries to diagnose at least 80% of people living with Hep C and treat at least 70% of those diagnosed.

Santa Ana Winds Trigger Wildfire Warnings in Southern California. Here's What To Know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:22:13 UTC
01:22:13 KST

Southern California towns are on high alert as the first Santa Ana winds of the season are set to arrive.
The red flag warning put out by the National Weather Service (NWS) Wednesday evening follows a relatively quiet wildfire season so far in California. Only 300,000 acres have burned since Jan. 1, compared to the over one million acres that fires have usually burned by mid-October.
Why are Santa Ana winds so dangerous?
Santa Ana winds blow in from the desert, typically between the months of September and May. The winds bring warmer temperatures and drier air to Southern California. They also greatly increase the risk of wildfires—warm winds coupled with summer drought can often make for a dangerous combination. The January 2025 fires that tore through the Pacific Palisades and Altadena were fueled by Santa Ana wind gusts that reached 100 m.p.h.
This week’s winds will not be as strong, according to NWS predictions. But that doesn’t mean the area is in the clear. The NWS has warned that, if any fires ignite, “conditions are favorable for extreme fire behavior.”
What areas of Southern California are under fire warnings?
The NWS has issued a red flag warning for the Los Angeles County San Gabriel Valley forecast zone that will stay in effect until Saturday evening. The most extreme conditions are expected in the Ventura and Los Angeles County valleys and mountains, particularly Santa Clarita, Thousand Oaks, and Simi Valley.
Southern California Edison is considering shutting off power to some 250,000 customers. Areas in Northern and Central California, including parts of Alameda county, Fresno County, and Napa County could also face power outages. Shutting down power helps stop downed power lines or aging infrastructure from sparking fires.
Recent rain means that San Diego and Orange County will face less of a fire risk, though the areas should still expect to see strong winds.
If you live in an impacted area, sign up for local emergency alerts, plan for power outages, and avoid any outdoor activities that might ignite sparks like BBQs, campfires, or improperly discarding cigarette butts.
One Southern California town is even encouraging residents to secure hallowed decorations—the giant skeleton and inflatable pumpkins haunting front lawns. High winds can turn Halloween decorations into hazards,” the city of Pasadena said in a Facebook post. “Secure them before winds pick up.”

Satellite imagery from Planet Labs and Airbus, reviewed by Reuters, shows the facility in Russia’s Rostov region expanding from an empty field on August 31 into a complex covering approximately 0.9 square kilometers, equivalent to roughly 126 soccer fields.

DroneSec assessed that the new facility likely benefits from the air defense systems protecting the military airfield, potentially complicating Ukrainian efforts to strike it, Reuters reported.

John Healey poised to raise taxes on banks in budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:17:05 UTC
01:17:05 KST

John Healey is poised to tax Britain’s banks in his 28 October budget, to help offset the damage inflicted on the public finances by war in the Middle East, the Guardian understands.
The chancellor is in Bangkok, where the International Monetary Fund has praised the UK’s progress towards balancing the books, urging him to “stay the course”.
To keep the Treasury’s deficit reduction plans on track in the face of rising government borrowing costs, the Guardian understands Healey has decided to tap the financial sector for additional revenue.
One option understood to be under discussion – reversing cuts to the bank surcharge made by Jeremy Hunt – would raise upwards of £2bn a year.
Lenders have been logging strong earnings on the back of rising interest rates, with the UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds Banking Group – alone having generated £200bn in pre-tax profits over the past five years.
Thinktanks and trade unions have repeatedly urged Healey to tax Britain’s banks more heavily, an option considered but rejected by his predecessor Rachel Reeves, who was wary of deterring future investment.
Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress (TUC), said: “Britain’s big four banks are making a billion pounds a week, while bonuses have hit a post-crash record. These are bumper profits, driven by high interest rates and households’ mortgage misery. It’s time to make sure banks pay their fair share.”
Speaking to journalists in Bangkok, Healey praised the banks as crucial to supporting economic growth. “People too often see them as big, distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects,” he said.
But he is nevertheless believed to be minded to increase the surcharge banks pay on their profits, over and above corporation tax. Industry figures believe that will probably mean raising the surcharge back to 8%, from 3% at present.
The UK’s cost of borrowing has risen sharply in recent weeks, alongside that of other big economies, as bond markets have responded to the prospect of higher inflation as a result of the Middle East conflict.
Analysts have suggested that could as much as halve the £24bn cushion Reeves had built up against Labour’s fiscal rules at the time of the spring forecast in March.
Healey is understood to be willing to accept a narrower “headroom”, but is also keen to convince bond markets he is wedded to deficit reduction.
Bank bosses have been lobbying intensively against tax rises since narrowly escaping higher levies during last year’s budget. UK bosses of lenders including HSBC, Lloyds, NatWest, Barclays and Santander met Healey last week but were given no reassurance that bank tax hikes had been ruled out.
 
Their lobby groups – including UK Finance and TheCityUK – wrote to Healey days later, saying that on top of “weakening investors confidence and damaging UK attractiveness”, higher taxes would force them to move staff and business out of the country.
 
That echoed warnings by the chief executive of JP Morgan, Jamie Dimon, who said in May he could scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquarters if the UK government became hostile towards banks. News of the tower – which will house more than half of the US investment bank’s 23,000 UK staff – was came days after Reeves spared the sector further tax rises in her 2025 autumn budget.
One industry source said banks were resigned to a rise in the surcharge. They believe Healey is minded to reverse Hunt’s cut – taking it back to 8% – but not go further. Such a move would raise £2.25bn a year, according to analysis by the TUC.
Another industry source said they were caught off guard by the change in messaging, having come just hours after Healey hailed banks as a “jewel” in the crown of the British economy. “We’re surprised to see this following earlier comments which appeared to be more supportive of the sector.”
When asked about how much the banking industry might be able to absorb in terms of tax rises, the head of policy at TheCityUK, John Godfrey, said banks “do not want to get into debating the menu of taxation. The fact is that we don’t want to eat in that restaurant.”
Healey has also been “listening to representations” from specialist banks, including Revolut and Shawbrook, that want the profit threshold at which the surcharge kicks in to be raised from £100m to £500m.
One government source said Labour was mindful of the UK needing to offer a positive environment for startup banks, especially the lending they offered to small businesses.
The TUC has lobbied for a much more punitive increase, to 16%, saying that could raise £24bn in tax revenues over the next four years.
Healey said he wanted his first budget as chancellor to give “breathing space” to both consumers and businesses in the face of rising energy prices.
There will be little additional funding for other Whitehall departments, however, which he stressed would have to stick to the budgets Reeves set out at her spending review in June 2025.
“It’s important that they do manage within what they’ve got, and it’s part of the job,” Healey said. “You have to reprioritise if you want to do fresh things, or more.”
The Institute for Fiscal Studies has said Reeves’s plans could result in real-terms spending cuts for some departments in the later years of the spending review period.
The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, used a visit to a financial services firm in Edinburgh on Thursday to caution against further banking tax rises, saying the sector already faced a higher effective tax rate than in many other big global financial centres.
Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: “Britain needs growth. But a raid on the financial services sector will stifle it. Labour should be backing businesses and wealth-creators, not making their lives even harder. Rather than hiking taxes yet again, Labour should cut spending.”
As well as an energy support package for households and businesses, Healey’s first budget is expected to set out more details of plans to devolve income tax to mayoralties, and explain how the government will fully fund the four-year defence investment plan announced by Keir Starmer before he stepped down as prime minister.
Healey is expected to duck the longer-term question of when the UK will spend 3% of gross domestic product on defence, the issue over which he resigned as defence secretary in June, contributing to Starmer’s downfall.

====================================================================================================

Time’s up for the leap second as scientists swap it for the leap hour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:16:10 UTC
01:16:10 KST

After decades of discussion, quibbling and worrying about clocks in computer systems, the world’s official timekeepers have voted to replace what many viewed as a tiresome correction: the leap second. It’s time, they say, for the leap hour.
Delegates from 69 countries cast their votes on Thursday at a conference in France of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, which ensures the world sticks to the same standards of time, weight, distance and more.
The decision to adopt the leap hour from next year aims to reduce the risk of computers and other technical systems tripping over as their software grapples with minutes lasting 61 seconds – and, worse, 59 seconds – instead of a round 60.
“After 30 years of debate, the leap second is making way for the leap hour,” said Dr Setnam Shemar, principal scientist in the time and frequency department at the UK’s National Physical Laboratory (NPL). “This will reduce the risks to the systems and national infrastructure that depend on accurate time while still preserving the fundamental link between our global time system and the rotation of the Earth.”
The vote at Versailles means that coordinated universal time (UTC) can drift up to an hour from astronomical time before a leap hour is needed, but that is unlikely to happen for thousands of years.
“We already have daylight saving where we change by an hour and no one gets bothered about that, apart from losing sleep or getting an extra hour’s sleep,” said Shemar, who sat on the international timekeeping expert committee that proposed the leap hour.
The more familiar leap year was introduced more than 2,000 years ago to ensure that the calendar year did not fall out of step with the time that the Earth takes to circle the sun. Adding a day to the end of February every four or so years does the job, because Earth orbits the sun every 365 and a quarter days.
Leap seconds are a much more modern invention. In 1955, Louis Essen and Jack Parry at the NPL built the world’s first practical, high-precision caesium atomic clock. The device revolutionised timekeeping, and in 1967 the astronomical definition of a second, based on the rotation of the Earth, was abandoned. Ever since, the formal definition of one second has been 9,192,631,770 vibrations of the caesium atom.
Atomic clocks are exceptionally stable and precise. Their timekeeping has become critical for modern computer systems, communications, satellites, trading systems and electricity grids. But the Earth’s rotation is far less reliable. Its spin is affected by the planet’s molten core, the shift of the oceans, global jet streams and other natural forces.
Broadly, Earth’s rotation is slowing down: when an asteroid doomed the dinosaurs, a day lasted about 23 and a half hours. Because of this, officials have added 27 leap seconds since 1972 to ensure UTC is aligned with astronomical time.
The strategy endured for more than 50 years until scientists spotted a fresh reason to fear technological mayhem. In the past decade, Earth’s rotation has sped up, meaning officials might have needed to add the first negative leap second, equivalent to lopping a second off UTC. The 30% probability of a negative leap second in the next decade brought the Versailles vote forward.
“Leap seconds can be tricky enough to deal with,” said Shemar. Telecommunications, electricity grids and navigation systems used high-accuracy timing, he explained, but software updates could apply leap seconds at the wrong time, knocking networks out of sync.
“After the leap second applied in 2012, there were some computer systems whose operating systems couldn’t cope with 61 seconds in a minute. The servers froze, they seized up. Systems went offline. And those are the sorts of failures that can happen with positive leap seconds,” Shemar said.
Among the crashed websites were Reddit and LinkedIn. Separately, Qantas flights were hit with delays. Negative leap seconds come with even greater risks. “There could be software out there that hasn’t been tested on negative leap seconds because we’ve never had to apply one before,” Shemar said.
To test all the computer systems that talk to one another around the world would cost companies a fortune. It was this concern that swung the vote.
Historically, the UK has grumbled about canning leap seconds because of the link with Greenwich mean time. Russia has also opposed the move, citing concerns of the impact on its Glonass satellite navigation system.
The IERS Earth Orientation Centre, in Paris, tracks changes in the Earth’s rotation and other movements that feed into UTC. The centre also issues notices when leap seconds must be added.
Dr Christian Bizouard, the director of the centre, approved of the vote, but said it passed the decision to people far in the future. “It’s kind of a philosophical discussion, because if a leap hour happens, it won’t be for a very, very long time,” he said. “What we are doing is pushing back the decision.”

School headscarf ban sparks rare protests in Azerbaijan and row with Turkey
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:15:06 BST
01:15:06 KST

School headscarf ban sparks rare protests in Azerbaijan and row with Turkey
- Published
"You are telling me, I can't come to school?" says a teenage girl in a navy blue Islamic headscarf, captured on video challenging a staff member at the entrance to her school.
The footage has been shared widely on social media, and shows a group of girls in hijabs standing behind her applauding as she continues: "Why should I have to give up my religion?"
Last Monday the education ministry in Azerbaijan began enforcing new uniform rules, turning away female pupils wearing hijabs. Protests began outside state schools in the capital, Baku, and in several southern districts including Masally and Jalilabad.
Protests are rare in this oil- and gas-producing country of 10.5 million people.
Azerbaijan is constitutionally secular and the government strongly enforces that.
President Ilham Aliyev has been in power since 2003 and has little tolerance for dissent. Opposition politicians and many independent journalists are in jail.
Azerbaijan is pulled between two neighbours, Turkey and Iran. Azerbaijanis belong to a Turkic group of nations, speaking a language close to Turkish, and Turkey is its closest ally.
But like Iran to the south, Azerbaijan is mainly Shia - over 60% of its people identify as Shia Muslims, while most Turks are Sunni.
The interior ministry said it had detained 37 people on Monday who tried to obstruct the rules and "grossly violate public order".
The rules, approved on 21 September, ban clothing which contradict "the principle of secularism in education" in state schools. They do not mention the hijab. Similar guidelines were extended to teachers on 6 October.
In one video, pupils outside School No. 69 in Balakhany, outside Baku, hold a banner reading: "The hijab does not prevent anyone from getting an education."
Shahiza Huseynova, a mother who was protesting outside a school in the Mashtaga district of the capital, was detained on Tuesday.
In an interview with Meydan TV, an independent Azerbaijani-language channel based in Germany, Huseynova's husband Agha said she had been given a warning: "Either you take off your child's hijab and send them to school, or you go to prison."
Friends have also lost contact with Ilkin Huseynov, an activist who on Tuesday launched an online platform called "Let Leyli Go to School". It offers free lessons from volunteer teachers to pupils barred from class.
According to a friend, Huseynov left his home in Baku with unidentified men at about 16:00 on Wednesday, and his phone has been switched off ever since.
The authorities have not commented, but friends believe he has been detained. On Thursday, the platform's Instagram page could not be accessed.
Since the protests began, users have reported problems accessing Instagram and TikTok without a virtual private network (VPN).
Most of the protests have been in religiously conservative neighbourhoods in Baku's outlying settlements and in southern districts near the 765km (475-mile) border with Iran.
The authorities have long been wary of religious influence from Iran, where more ethnic Azerbaijanis live than in Azerbaijan itself.
On the night of 13 October, Azerbaijan's State Service for Special Communications and Information Security said a "foreign hacker group" had attacked more than 100 state websites.
A pro-Iranian group calling itself the 313 Team (Cyber Islamic Resistance) claimed responsibility.
Azerbaijani officials have defended the rules. One MP, Nigar Arpadarai, told the 1news.az website that children did not choose to wear the hijab themselves but were influenced by their families.
"A child has no freedom to choose a religion. This is a conscious prerogative of adults," she said.
- Azerbaijan pardons Frenchman after EU lifts sanctions on Russian billionaire 
  - Published23 September
- Azerbaijan and Armenia sign peace pledge at White House summit with Trump 
  - Published9 August 2025
The row has now spilled over into Turkey, Baku's closest ally, which provided vital support during Azerbaijan's 2020 war with Armenia over Nagorno-Karabakh.
The two countries call themselves "one nation, two states".
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, a devout Muslim, has spoken of creating a "pious generation".
His chief adviser, Oktay Saral, has called the Azerbaijani restrictions "unacceptable" and urged Baku to "reverse this mistake".
"A headscarf is not an obstacle; it is a requirement of one's faith!" Saral wrote on X.
Several MPs from Turkey's governing AK Party joined in.
Small demonstrations were held outside Azerbaijan's embassy in Ankara, organised by Köklü Değişim, an Islamist movement linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir, and outside its consulate in Istanbul, organised by conservative Islamist group Özgür-Der.
President Aliyev's New Azerbaijan Party accused Turkish officials of an "openly defamatory" information campaign and of "baseless accusations", warning that Oktay Saral's comments risked harming ties, and cautioned against interference in Azerbaijan's internal affairs.
Earlier this month, Ilham Aliyev himself said no one should "stick their noses into our way of life".
Behind the dispute there may lie another source of friction. Turkish protesters have linked the headscarf rules to Azerbaijan's close ties with Israel, which sells weapons to Baku and buys Azerbaijani oil.
Turkey's relations with Israel have collapsed over Gaza, but Azerbaijan has tried to maintain relationships with both countries.
That is a difficult balancing act. On Thursday, when Israel's President Isaac Herzog addressed a regional security summit hosted by Azerbaijan in Baku, delegations from Turkey, Iran and other countries walked out of the hall.

Maduro, wife face minimum 50-year sentences if convicted on all charges
Flores agreed with the plan in the meeting, and dismissed a suggested alternative plan to glean information by infiltrating the ranks, according to the indictment.
Maduro and Flores are not accused of personally carrying out any acts of torture. Scheduled to go on trial starting on June 1, 2027, they would each face a mandatory minimum sentence of 50 years in prison if convicted on all charges.
Relations between Maduro, a socialist, and the United States were tense during his 13 years in power leading the oil-rich country.

Thames Water asks for £2.4bn more to avoid going bust this year or early 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:14:54 UTC
01:14:54 KST

Thames Water has asked its creditors for another £2.4bn as the embattled water company comes close to running out of cash.
The UK’s largest water company said on Thursday it needed another short-term cash injection because it would be unable to reach a longer-term deal to sort out its giant debt pile before running out of cash by “the end of 2026 or the start of 2027”.
Thames Water said in a statement to the stock market that it “does not expect to complete its recapitalisation process ahead of this date”, meaning it would run out of cash without creditors stumping up more.
The utility company serves 16 million customers in London and the Thames valley. However, it has been on the brink of collapse for several years after it became overwhelmed by a debt pile that is now about £20bn. Its shareholders walked away, leaving the company under the effective control of its creditors while they work out a deal to avoid bankruptcy.
The creditors gave Thames a £3bn lifeline in February last year to try to see it through negotiations on a deal to cut its debts and inject more money. The creditors, collectively called the London & Valley Water company, are led by a group of American hedge funds such as Elliott Management and Silver Point Capital, and institutional investors including BlackRock and M&G.
However, those talks have dragged on, and the water company has now drawn down £2.65bn of the £3bn, leaving it perilously close to running out of cash even as it carries out a series of expensive repairs and upgrades.
Thames said the extra cash would “extend […] liquidity into autumn 2027 and allow [it] to continue to deliver its capital programme and deliver improvements for customers and the environment”.
Thames Water’s creditors have drawn up detailed proposals for a rescue plan that would involve them writing off £9.6bn in loans. However, that plan hinges on Ofwat agreeing to let the company pay set penalties for several years upfront, and effectively creating a special regime for the company. That prospect has proven politically unpalatable for the Labour government.
Some Labour politicians and environmental campaigners called on Keir Starmer and then Andy Burnham to put Thames Water into special administration, a form of temporary government control while a new buyer is sought.
Burnham has pledged more public control of the UK’s water industry, and has said that public ownership for Thames Water “is what should be done”.
In addition, the change of prime minister has led to regulatory uncertainty for the broader water industry. Starmer’s government had committed to implementing recommendations on changes to the water system from the former Bank of England deputy governor Sir John Cunliffe, but Burnham’s government has not yet made clear what it plans to do.
Thames Water said it “continues to work closely with stakeholders to secure a market-led solution”.
Thames Water’s creditors are expected to vote on the proposals later in the month.

Yemen’s government needs weapons, but they can’t come from the US or Israel, expert tells 'Post'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:14:35 UTC
01:14:35 KST

The most effective way to defeat the Houthis and reverse their territorial gains would be to empower government forces to fight the group, though such support cannot come from the United States or Israel, an expert at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), the world’s oldest and the UK’s leading defense and security think tank, told The Jerusalem Post.
Speaking anonymously to protect his connections in Yemen, “A” said international forces need to view the war in Yemen differently from the fight against al-Qaeda, which struggled to hold territory and maintain control. He also advised against viewing the conflict through an international lens, framing it as purely a proxy war between Saudi and Iranian-backed groups rather than a local conflict between a legitimate but ill-equipped government and an armed group over domestic grievances.
“Locals who deal with local dynamics are there to stay, so they have a better understanding of how to navigate the complexities,” he reasoned, noting that international framing could also allow the Houthis to profit from the narrative that they are defending the Yemeni people against foreign aggression.
Empowering local forces also means more than supplying weapons, he stressed, noting that the Houthis have been able to exploit deprivation in Yemen. The civil war, drought and other natural disasters have contributed to one of the world’s most severe humanitarian crises.
Even before the latest escalation in the conflict, more than 17.1 million Yemenis were experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity, including five million on the brink of famine, according to the UNHRC.
Houthi support can be undermined by quality government
Support for the Houthis can be threatened if local populations can be offered a good quality of life in areas governed by the legitimate authorities, he said.
Pointing to the heavily populated city of Taiz, the war’s new front line, he noted that the siege 10 years prior was designed to systematically deprive civilians, spreading suffering as a means to apply pressure, and it was using the same strategy now.
The Houthis first attempted to take control of Taiz in 2015, seizing control of military bases, the local airport, and key government infrastructure. By August, the streets were overrun by members of the pro-government resistance and, unable to capture the city in full, it encircled the territory, blocking the entry of fuel, water, medicine, and commercial goods.
Though international truces occasionally diluted the impact of the siege, it wasn’t until 2024 that a main road opened, allowing the transport of goods and people.
Since early October, the Houthis have begun encircling the city.
Without arms, government can't counter Houthi threat
A warned that without arms, local authorities will be able to do little to break the blockade.
“The Houthis are being armed by the Iranians, and they’re not hiding that. They’re not denying it. The other side is still trying to convince the international community to give them access to what’s necessary,” he said.
He stressed that despite sharing a common enemy with the internationally recognized government of Yemen’s forces, Israel and the United States should not directly arm or fund them.
Instead, their role should be limited to disrupting Iranian weapons shipments to the Houthis. Any more direct involvement, A warned, could play into the Houthis’ hands.
Having built much of their support around portraying themselves as defenders of Gaza, the Houthis could exploit any perceived association between Yemen’s government and Israel to undermine its legitimacy and strengthen their own position.

Four Chinese sites added to World Heritage Irrigation Structures list
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
00:14:10 CST
01:14:10 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Four Chinese irrigation projects have been added to the World Heritage Irrigation Structures (WHIS) list, bringing the country's total to 46, the Ministry of Water Resources said Thursday.
The projects, located in Henan, Gansu, Jiangxi and Fujian provinces, were recognized during the 77th International Executive Council Meeting of the International Commission on Irrigation and Drainage (ICID) in Marseille, France, on Wednesday.
Dating back more than 2,200 years, a canal irrigation system in central China's Henan Province uses dam-free water diversion to irrigate about 34,000 hectares of farmland in Jiyuan and Jiaozuo. The irrigated farmland forms a major grain-producing area in the province.
In northwest China's Gansu Province, an oasis irrigation system in the Hexi Corridor, a key artery of the ancient Silk Road, dates back to the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644). It irrigates about 63,200 hectares of land and is a typical example of oasis irrigation in arid regions of Eurasia.
The project in Shangrao City, east China's Jiangxi Province, dates back to the Song Dynasty (960-1279). Its gravity-fed irrigation network consists of canals, weirs and ponds.
Another ancient irrigation system in Changtai District of Zhangzhou City, southeast China's Fujian Province, has a history of more than 800 years. Featuring low dams and a network of weirs, ponds and canals, it irrigates about 1,850 hectares of land.
China has a long history of irrigation engineering. The Dujiangyan irrigation system in southwest China's Sichuan Province, built in 256 BC, remains in use today and was added to the WHIS list in 2018.
Established by the ICID in 2014, the WHIS designation aims to protect and promote irrigation projects of historical value and scientific experience. ■

The current third round of inspections was launched in November 2023.
China's landmark Ecological and Environmental Code officially came into force on Aug. 15, strengthening the legal foundation for ecological protection. Adopted by China's top legislature in March, the code is China's second formal statutory code after the Civil Code.
The code comprises 1,242 articles in five chapters, covering pollution control, ecological protection, and green and low-carbon development, among other areas. The code also includes provisions on central ecological and environmental protection inspections. ■

Feature: Cross-border friendship takes root, grows into forest
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
00:13:50 CST
01:13:50 KST

ROME, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- "We do not speak the same language, we do not look the same, but we are brother and sister and we understand each other," said Ronald Sakolsky, a retired American history teacher, when describing his bond with Chinese desertification control expert Yin Yuzhen during a recent interview with Xinhua in Rome.
Through their friendship, Sakolsky hopes to encourage more people to cross national borders and work together to protect their common home, the Earth.
While in China on a teaching exchange program 27 years ago, Sakolsky raised 5,000 U.S. dollars to support Yin's tree-planting efforts in the Maowusu Sandy Land in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region.
After Sakolsky returned to the United States, the two lost touch for a while. They reunited in China in August this year, more than two decades after their first meeting. In the meantime, over 50,000 tree seedlings purchased with Sakolsky's donation had grown into a forest.
The two friends recently met again in Rome, where they were invited to attend the World Food Forum hosted by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO).
"When I was there in 2000, it was just sand. Now it is all green. It's beautiful," Sakolsky said, recalling his reunion with Yin in August.
He struggled to contain his emotion as he described returning to the land where they had helped plant the trees.
"When I went back this year, it was like a mother and father seeing their children. Our seeds had grown into big trees. I cried a lot," he said. "As Ms. Yin said, it was like our children waving hello to me in the forest."
The transformation of the Maowusu Sandy Land has given their cross-border friendship a deeper meaning. The growing trees have not only changed the landscape, but they also embody a broader shift in environmental awareness and hope for the future.
"I have learned that Mother Earth is alive. I heard her," Sakolsky said, recalling an experience in which he wore headphones in the forest and placed a microphone in the ground.
He said that if humanity failed to protect the Earth, the planet would no longer be able to provide people with fruit, vegetables, flowers and the oxygen they need to breathe.
In Sakolsky's view, countries should work together on environmental protection. He praised the Chinese government for paying increasing attention to combating desertification, and also applauded the Chinese people for actively participating in environmental protection.
"This is a concrete manifestation of a community with a shared future for humanity," he said.
Sakolsky described his donation over two decades ago as a simple act of kindness by an ordinary person.
"I wanted to help China. I did not expect anything back," he said, adding that Yin's perseverance over decades was what truly deserved recognition.
On Thursday, Sakolsky sat in the audience as Yin was honored for her inclusion among the FAO 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development, witnessing another milestone in his friend's life.
The seedlings the two friends helped plant have grown into a lush forest, while the bridge built through their friendship continues to carry the story of ecological restoration to a wider audience, inspiring more people to pay attention to environmental protection and land restoration. ■

Comprising 54 solar panels, three inverters and six batteries, the system is intended to support more than 1,800 students by providing a cleaner and more reliable electricity supply.
The "Yunnan Hand in Hand Program" comprises small-scale, practical and effective public welfare projects designed to benefit communities across South Asia, Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean region.
Since the launch of the program in 2022, 56 projects have been carried out in Myanmar in areas including infrastructure, clean energy, safe drinking water, agricultural technology, environmental conservation, educational support, cultural exchange, capacity building and healthcare. These projects have directly benefited communities in Yangon, Nay Pyi Taw, Mandalay, Sagaing, Shan and Kachin.

BEIJING, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- China's online literature market revenue more than doubled from 26.72 billion yuan (about 3.97 billion U.S. dollars) in 2021 to 57.47 billion yuan in 2025, according to a report released Thursday at a national online literature conference held in Beijing.
The report, released by the China Audio-video and Digital Publishing Association at the conference's opening ceremony, said the online literature sector had maintained steady growth during the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), with progress in content development, overseas expansion and industry governance.
Revenue from overseas online literature markets rose from 2.91 billion yuan in 2021 to 6.98 billion yuan in 2025, outpacing domestic market growth, the report said. The number of works distributed overseas, including original works created by overseas authors, increased from 314,600 to 933,100.
The report noted that the total number of authors registered on online literature platforms climbed from 23.41 million in 2021 to 33.73 million in 2025, while the user base expanded from 460 million to 646 million.
In 2025 alone, China's online literature market revenue grew 15.99 percent year on year, while overseas market revenue surged 45.03 percent, the report showed. The overseas expansion of adaptations across multiple formats, including films, television productions and short dramas, was a major growth driver.
In recent years, Chinese films, TV series, web novels and video games have gained growing popularity overseas. The country's online literature has reached hundreds of millions of readers in more than 200 countries and regions.
In the next five years, China will enhance copyright protection and transaction rules in online literature and arts, while also improving its international IP protection system and stepping up IP cooperation through multilateral international mechanisms, according to the country's 15th five-year plan for intellectual property protection and utilization.
The plan set the goal of making decisive progress in building China into an IP powerhouse by 2030, with its IP competitiveness ranking among the world's best by 2035. Another target is to raise the share of copyright industries' value added in GDP to 7.53 percent by 2030. ■

Lebanon insists on sovereignty and diplomacy

Lebanese official sources told The New Arab's Arabic-language sister publication, Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, that Beirut remained open to relations with Iran based on mutual respect and non-interference.

They also expressed concern over escalating rhetoric from Hezbollah and continuing Israeli threats, while stressing that Beirut remained committed to negotiations despite the difficulties involved.
"There is no solution except diplomacy, not war," the sources said.

Explainer-What does Alberta's referendum on separation from Canada mean?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:11:08 UTC
01:11:08 KST

Explainer: What does Alberta’s referendum on separation from Canada mean?
OTTAWA, Oct 15 - Alberta is holding a nonbinding referendum on Monday to ask residents if they want to remain part of Canada, marking the first time the oil-rich province has ever put the question of separation to the public. Polls have consistently shown most Albertans — about 70% — want to stay in Canada, with roughly a quarter of residents supporting an independent Alberta.
WHAT WILL RESIDENTS BE ASKED?
There are 10 questions, each with its own color-coded ballot. The last ballot voters see is question 10, on whether Alberta should remain a Canadian province or start the legal process required to hold a binding referendum on separation. A simple majority in favor of separation could trigger that process. There are nine other nonbinding questions about immigration, access to provincial services — including education, social care and healthcare — and voter identification requirements.
WHY IS ALBERTA HAVING THIS REFERENDUM?
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said in May it was “time to have a vote, understand the will of Albertans on this subject, and move on,” when she announced the government would add a question on separation. Smith’s decision followed months of campaigning by a small but vocal group of separatists, who argue Alberta’s energy wealth is subsidizing poorer parts of the country and that bureaucracy in Ottawa has stifled the province’s economy. Some members of the group had backed Smith's candidacy for premier. Smith says she voted for Alberta to remain in Canada during advance polling, according to a video she posted on social media on Wednesday.
HAVE THERE BEEN PREVIOUS SEPARATIST REFERENDUMS IN CANADA?
Yes, but not in Alberta. The majority French-speaking province of Quebec has had two referendums, in 1980 and 1995. Quebecers voted to remain in Canada both times, but by the slimmest of margins in 1995. The separatist Parti Quebecois won a provincial election earlier this month and has pledged to hold a third referendum, but only after US President Donald Trump has left office and if the party holds a majority. The PQ was elected with a minority government on October 5, meaning it will rely on smaller parties to pass legislation.
Canada is a federation of 10 provinces and three territories. While Ottawa is responsible for matters of national interest, such as defense, trade and foreign policy, the provinces and territories hold significant power over medical care, education and land rights.
WHEN WILL THE RESULTS BE KNOWN?
Polls are scheduled to close at 8 p.m. on Monday (0200 GMT on Tuesday). Elections Alberta says it will count ballots by hand and that the question on separation will be counted first.
It will publish results on the Elections Alberta website as they are received, and unofficial results are expected within 48 hours after voting ends.
WHAT HAPPENS IF MOST ALBERTANS VOTE TO START THE PROCESS OF LEAVING CANADA?
Smith has said she will respect the result and quickly begin the process to hold a legally binding referendum. But separation would not happen imminently. After the 1995 Quebec referendum, Canada's Parliament passed the Clarity Act in 2000, which says talks about secession can only be triggered if there is a clear majority from the public, without specifying the necessary threshold. The act also states provinces and territories have no unilateral right to leave Canada and that a constitutional amendment negotiated by provincial, territorial and federal governments is required.
First Nations groups have objected to the idea of an independent Alberta, as their land treaties with Canada predate Alberta's entry into Confederation. In May, an Alberta court judge ruled the province’s chief electoral officer was wrong to allow separatists to collect signatures requesting a referendum, because the process should have prompted a consultation with Indigenous peoples whose rights might be violated by separation. Alberta has appealed the decision.
WHAT HAS PRIME MINISTER MARK CARNEY SAID ABOUT THE REFERENDUM?
Carney, who was largely raised in Alberta, has previously said “the best place for Alberta is in Canada” and that the country cannot succeed if it's divided. He released a video on Canadian Thanksgiving, October 12, saying national unity is critical as Canada fights threats from abroad, including a trade war with the US. Carney has campaigned for Alberta to remain in Canada. REUTERS

Syrian men turn Assad-era military service booklets into art
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:09:51 UTC
01:09:51 KST

Breadcrumb
Just a Notebook: The Syrian project turning Assad-era military service booklets into works of art
Looking around the room, Syrian artist Yeser Berro saw a mix of anger, pain, and relief among the participants in his workshop in Damascus, Syria.
In front of him, some of the men were confronting their Syrian military conscription booklets for the very first time since the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime nearly two years earlier.
Then, they picked up pens and pencils and started to draw.
Amid the sound of focused scribbling and rustling papers, images soon started to take life across the aged pages: tombstones, fingerprints, caricatures of the overthrown dictator who had overseen a brutal 14-year war against the revolution in Syria.
"This document controlled their lives for many years," Berro explains about what the small paper booklet meant in some cases. "It was very therapeutic for everyone involved."
Mandatory military service had long been part of life for Syrian men, who were required to report for service when they turned 18 — at which point they would receive their military service booklets.
Under the Baathist state, this became further entrenched as a tool of state control written into the constitution that said: "Military service shall be a sacred duty and is regulated by a law."
Some were forced to remain in the military involuntarily for many years as the war raged on. Those who attempted to avoid conscription could be subject to severe punishment, be criminalised, and prevented from leaving the country.
"These notebooks, they symbolise the regime," the workshop’s host explained.
"It's basically an ideology book. It tells you who you're supposed to be as a soldier, what you're supposed to believe, what your duties are," Berro added.
"At the beginning of the notebook, there is a written rule, which says you cannot write anything on the notebook, you cannot delete anything, you cannot scratch anything."
The legacy of conscription
Acknowledging the potential historic role such documents may one day play toward accountability, the pens that Berro placed on the table that day were also erasable.
Wissam, one of those who took part in the recent workshop, tells The New Arab his military book previously "dictated my fate." His last name is being withheld for safety.
"It was essential for passing through military checkpoints, and I carried it in my bag wherever I went; if I ever left the house without it, I would be overcome with sheer terror."
While every man in Syria was expected to serve in the military, some were exempt if they were a family’s only son, temporarily if they were studying, or, in some cases, could afford to pay their way out.
Many fled, but many others were forced into service until the whole system collapsed along with the regime on December 8, 2024. Ahmed al-Sharaa's new government then abolished Syria’s mandatory military service.
Now defunct, many harbour complex feelings toward their old military conscription booklets — some even chose to burn them. But for those who didn’t, a creative outlet perhaps offered another option.
Held at Manzoul, a cultural space in Damascus, in February this year and hosted by the cultural initiative Nisaba, Just a Notebook invited young Syrian men to confront the document that had, for generations, reminded them of the power the Syrian state held over their lives.
The participants had made every attempt to evade military service: enrolling at university, becoming deserters, and some were even captured and forced to conduct desk work. Each had a different story, and a booklet uniquely chronicling their lived experience.
"It was kind of like breaking this taboo that has persisted not just throughout the war, but for decades of mandatory military service," Berro adds.
Working with erasable materials, 11 participants sat around a square table with free rein to tackle the book in whatever creative means they felt appropriate.
"Some people expressed their anger through drawing, others critiqued the contents of the booklet through writing," Berro says.
"Sometimes using humour, for example, by writing their own words into fields that were supposed to be filled by government officials."
For Wissam, the process involved drawing a recurring dream he had experienced, while confronting the names written within the booklet itself.
"I began to feel a desire for revenge against the notebook for the immense power it held; I vented my anger upon it, drawing on its pages and mocking the names written inside," he tells The New Arab.
"I also felt afraid, because it was not easy to anticipate such an act—being able to project my angry thoughts onto an institution that once governed my life but no longer existed. I drew a dream that had haunted me for a long time: standing on a hill while on guard duty during my military service, with a pack of rabid dogs advancing to kill me; behind the guard post, I drew a figure hanging himself," he continued.
"During my forced military service in the later years of the war, the only creature I had harmed was a rabid dog that had attacked me while I was on guard duty. Ever since, I feel guilty about it, and I cannot imagine how others were able to harm human beings, let alone their fellow Syrians."
Turning trauma into art
While the fall of the Syrian regime came and went almost two years ago, the collective process of healing a fractured nation is still in formative stages.
A 2021 study found 86% of respondents said the war was the main cause of mental distress, and further reporting by the World Health Organisation this summer stressed the importance of "communal healing" and the |activation of social networks" going forward.
While hosting the workshop, Berro observed the mood shift as the art progressed, with creativity allowing for deeper expression and understanding.
They turned to conversations about past ordeals, the lengths some had gone to defer conscription, and what it all means for looking ahead.
"Psychologically, it was one of the most cathartic experiences of my life," Wissam adds.
Just a Notebook is currently being scanned and developed ahead of a collective book launch anticipated for this month in Syria, featuring work produced during the workshop.
Berro is curating the collective book after participants selected which work they wanted to share, which Berro says will serve both as an archive and an "example of collective healing from an oppressive past."
The project marks a small but poignant shift in Syria’s creative landscape that Berro says is crucial to processing and rebuilding a collective Syrian identity, with artistic expression helping to "find a way out of survival mode and to process everything that we went through."
"If there's a time to begin new cultural projects, it's now," he states.
"There’s still a long way to go," he says. "But the first step to building a better future is to confront our complex past — and reconcile with it."
Tamara Davison is a British freelance journalist reporting across the Middle East on humanitarian issues, post-conflict resolution and migration
Follow her on Instagram: @tamaradavison_

The Government Media Office in the Gaza Strip on Thursday denied imposing taxes or fees on commercial trucks, accusing Israel of promoting allegations to justify restrictions on the entry of goods and demanding that Israel be compelled to allow 600 trucks into the enclave daily, Anadolu reports.
It came in response to allegations made Wednesday by Yoram Halevi, the Israeli government’s coordinator of activities in the Palestinian territories, regarding the imposition of financial charges on traders and measures regulating cash transactions in Gaza.
The media office accused Israel of waging a “disinformation campaign” and attempting to hold Gaza’s government authorities responsible for delays in allowing trucks to enter the enclave.
It said it sent messages to mediators and international bodies to clarify its position and warn against additional Israeli measures that could worsen the humanitarian crisis.
The media office stressed that “no government taxes or fees have been imposed on commercial trucks,” and that it had collected no taxes or fees on commercial activities in the last three years, given the enclave’s exceptional humanitarian and economic conditions.
Halevi alleged in a letter to international officials that the Palestinian resistance group, Hamas, was demanding traders pay 10,000 shekels ($3,225) for each truck entering Gaza, claiming that it had prompted the private sector to halt coordination for the entry of goods.
The media office said the amount was linked to a “voluntary community initiative” involving businesspeople, public figures, institutions and companies. It said the funds were allocated to support orphans, widows, children and students in need, as well as housing, sanitation and relief projects.
Halevi also alleged that Hamas was requiring traders to sell 30% of their goods in cash to control funds.
The media office said the 30% cash-transaction measures were introduced to address a severe cash shortage, the widespread circulation of worn-out banknotes, and the need to facilitate buying and selling.
It stressed that the Chamber of Commerce initiated the measures and agreed to them, rather than the government deciding unilaterally.
The media office said the “most urgent and highest priority is to ensure the regular and sufficient flow of goods into the Gaza Strip.”
It added that announced understandings, including those reached through the Sharm el-Sheikh track, required Israel to allow aid and supplies into Gaza, specifically 600 trucks daily.
The media office urged mediators, the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, the UN and international bodies to pressure Israel to honor its commitments and verify the facts through direct communication with authorities in the enclave.

Russia argues that the seizure was legitimate.
The territorial dispute has prevented the two countries from signing a peace treaty since World War II. Tensions have deepened in recent years amid Japan’s sanctions against Moscow over the Russia-Ukraine war.

Ukrainian Damba anti-drone EW systems to be produced in Lithuania for defence forces – photo
Ukrainian defence company December1 and Lithuanian company Pekkla have signed a memorandum to establish a joint venture in Lithuania.
Source: a press release from the manufacturer, as reported by Ukrainska Pravda
Details: The joint venture will manufacture Ukrainian Damba electronic warfare (EW) systems developed by December1. According to the Ukrainian company, the facility in Lithuania will operate as part of the Build with Ukraine initiative with the support of the local government, and the production of the EW systems is set to be launched in 2027.
The devices manufactured at the joint venture will be supplied to the Ukrainian defence forces.
Quote from Illia Kabachynskyi, Director of International Development at December1: "This is the first experience of its kind for December1, and we are delighted that Lithuania – a great and uncompromisingly reliable partner of Ukraine – has become our partner. The launch of the joint venture will allow us to scale up and provide the Ukrainian Defence Forces with even more of the necessary equipment."
Details: The press service for the manufacturer of the Damba EW systems explained that the Lithuanian company Pekkla operates in the field of unmanned aircraft systems and acts as a local partner in the project. The Lithuanian company will be responsible for infrastructure, regulatory support and recruiting local engineers, while the joint venture's technical expertise will remain with the Ukrainian manufacturer.
Quote from Martynas Andriejavas, CEO of the Lithuanian company: "This is an important partnership both for Pekkla and for each of the countries. It will allow Ukraine to obtain the necessary defence equipment, while Lithuania will be able to gain new experience, jobs and opportunities for development, and taxpayers' money will remain within the country".
Details: The Ukrainian Damba EW systems are used against Russian attack and reconnaissance drones. Specifically, on the front line, these systems can counter FPV drones and Shaheds at a depth of up to 50 km, and they are also used to protect critical infrastructure.
According to the company, Damba is one of the "most widely installed systems in Ukraine", with thousands of units operating across the country. December1 explained that a special feature of this EW system is precision jamming designed for specific types of Russian drones, as well as the system's directional action and its rotating platform, which can be controlled remotely.
Background: Earlier, Ukrainska Pravda reported that the Ukrainian Ai-Petri system for countering technical reconnaissance was showcased for the first time at the MSPO-2026 international exhibition in Poland in September 2026. The system is capable of jamming drone control signals as well as suppressing guided aerial bombs.
