How are Yemen’s Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia so effectively?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:06:03 UTC
01:06:03 KST

How are Yemen’s Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia so effectively?
LONDON, Oct 15 - Houthi militants who control northwestern Yemen have in the past week attacked Riyadh international airport and hit the headquarters of Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company, in air assaults that have laid bare Saudi Arabia's vulnerability to threats from its enemy next door.
The attacks are shattering the illusion of Saudi Arabia as a safe international investment hub as it tries to attract foreign money and diversify away from oil.
This nightmare scenario for a key US ally in the Gulf has been years in the making, weapons and regional experts say.
They attribute Saudi Arabia's vulnerability to a ragtag group of Yemeni fighters to a perfect storm of factors that include Tehran helping the Houthis reach near self-sufficiency in producing and deploying advanced weapons, and the impact of the US war on Iran that has depleted stocks of interceptors.
TRAINING TO SELF-SUFFICIENCY BY IRAN
Iran has been giving weapons, money and training to the Houthis, known formally as Ansar Allah, for more than a decade, although Tehran has officially denied arming the Houthis in violation of a UN arms embargo.
While Iran has come under its own financial and military strains due to war and sanctions, the Houthis have learned – with Iranian help – how to assemble their own weapons, including drones and missiles, the experts interviewed by Reuters said.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards and members of Iran's other ally, Lebanese Hezbollah, initially gave the Houthis knowledge of missile systems and their operation, said Andreas Krieg, senior security studies lecturer at King's College London.
"Former Yemeni military engineers and a growing generation of locally trained specialists have helped institutionalise these capabilities," he said.
"Tehran has not simply supplied the Houthis with weapons. It has helped create an indigenous military-industrial learning process that becomes progressively harder to dismantle, even if direct Iranian supply routes are disrupted."
Iranian analysts said that the Houthis have in this way become one of the most cost-effective and valuable military proxies of Iran.
"The Revolutionary Guards were forward-looking. They looked at what happened if the Houthis couldn't receive equipment or weapons directly (from Iran), or if these were seized by US-allied forces," said Hamid Nikou, a former political advisor to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Nikou said this strategy included teaching the Houthis how to assemble dual-use parts to make drones and even ballistic missiles.
"Iran has basically taught the Houthis how to fish," Nikou said.
The Saudi-led military coalition fighting against the Houthis in Yemen says it has intercepted a number of missiles fired by the Houthis at Saudi cities, and that it has destroyed 127 Houthi weapons storage facilities and launch platforms.
Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki told a press conference the Houthis had acquired advanced military technology with the help of "regional actors," including ballistic missiles, drones and explosive-laden fast boats.
DIVERSIFYING WEAPONS IMPORTS AND TECHNOLOGY
A key strength of the Houthis in building their own weapons is that they don't rely solely on Iranian-made equipment or imports coming from Iran.
The Conflict Armament Research organization said in a report this week that the Houthis were attempting to make advanced medium-range ballistic missiles using parts shipped from China, after Yemen's internationally recognised government seized one such shipment.
"China has emerged as a particularly important commercial source, while Iran continues to provide specialised military technology, technical expertise and components that are difficult to obtain commercially," Krieg said.
The Houthis have also experimented with artificial intelligence in efforts to improve their weapons' effectiveness.
Anthropic said last month that "a cell of threat actors based in northern Yemen" had used its Claude AI assistant to help develop software for a guided rocket, a planned ballistic missile with a range of more than 2,000 km (1,240 miles) and a missile variant incorporating a hypersonic glide vehicle.
WAR FATIGUE, DEPLETED MUNITIONS
While the Houthis have improved their weapons production, US allies in the region have seen their air defences stretched since the war that began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February.
The United States has used large amounts of the missile interceptors it deploys in the region to protect its bases and its allies, which include Israel and Gulf countries, leaving some vulnerable, Saudi Arabia in particular.
"Saudi Arabia, in terms of the sophistication of the military and the development of an integrated air defence network, is not really yet at the level of either Israel or Ukraine, and it just has a very tough job to do," said Farzan Sabet, a Middle East expert at the Geneva Graduate Institute.
Saudi Arabia's sheer size makes defence against air attacks harder than defending Israel or a US base, he said.
WAR EXPERIENCE
The Houthis have learned from the increased levels of violence in the region in recent years, Sabet said.
A Yemeni civil war, in which the Houthis battled Saudi-backed forces from 2014, settled into a shaky ceasefire in 2022. But after Israel’s assault on Gaza in 2023, which followed deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel, the Houthis began firing rockets at Israel and targeting shipping through the Red Sea.
The fallout from the US-Iran war this year reignited the Yemeni civil war, by which time the Houthis had developed new capabilities.
"They haven't been sitting still," Sabet said. "They were basically diversifying their supply chains... and as they gain operational experience, they're able to make those weapons more sophisticated." REUTERS

Obama warns Israel risks moral collapse over Palestinian violations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:06:00 UTC
01:06:00 KST

Former U.S. President Barack Obama criticized Israel’s approach, warning that military superiority alone cannot deliver lasting security and that denying Palestinians meaningful concessions risks eroding Israel’s moral credibility.
The former president made the remarks on Tuesday during a discussion with award-winning writer and journalist Susan McKay in Belfast, northern Ireland, according to the Belfast Telegraph.
Speaking about the Israeli war on Gaza, Obama said the violence should "pain everybody,” describing it as a destructive cycle driven by historical grievances, hardened attitudes and deep divisions.
He acknowledged the long history of persecution faced by Jewish people in Europe. However, he also stressed that Palestinians had suffered injustice through the loss of their land.
"That is undeniable. What is also undeniable is that they took land off people and they were excessive. And those people understandably said: ‘This is injustice and I want my land back,’” he said.
Obama argued that the stronger side carries a greater responsibility to help break the cycle of violence, rather than relying solely on its military and technological superiority.
"If the attitude of Israel is, now that we are the strongest, the most technologically advanced in the region, then our security will depend on us simply doing whatever we need and taking whatever we want, and not making any concessions to anyone,” he said.
"That may work short-term... but you have ceded moral ground if that is the position you take.”
He said the current Israeli government appeared to have adopted that approach and urged it to recognize that millions of Palestinians would remain in the region.
"I would say the current Israeli government appears to have taken that. It is incumbent on them to recognise that 7 million Palestinians are not going anywhere,” Obama said.
"It is not sustainable to press upon them a condition that no-one would accept for themselves.”
Earlier on Tuesday, Obama received an honorary doctorate from Queen’s University Belfast.

Venezuela’s Maduro pleads not guilty to US conspiracy to torture charges

Venezuela’s Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores have pleaded not guilty to new charges of ‘conspiracy to commit torture’, which were unsealed last week.
Maduro and Flores appeared in a New York City courtroom on Thursday after being abducted from Caracas in a United States military operation in January.
The pair had previously pleaded not guilty to several other charges, including narco-terrorism, cocaine importation conspiracy and possession of machineguns and destructive devices.
“I reject this document in its entirety,” Maduro said during the appearance on Thursday.
Flores, meanwhile, said she was “completely innocent”.
“I am not guilty,” she said.
US Attorney Jamie McDonald said last week that the couple had for more than two decades “engaged in a conspiracy to commit torture, including the torture of United States citizens, in addition to the narcotics trafficking and weapons offences already charged”.
The new indictment said that Maduro and Flores oversaw a system of torture, arbitrary detention, and violence as a means to target “individuals viewed as disloyal or a threat to their illegal narcotics activity” as well as a “means of repression against the political opposition”.
It pointed to several instances where Maduro and Flores are alleged to have specifically identified individuals to be targeted, asked for updates on the torture, or suggested techniques.
In one instance in 2014, Maduro urged his enforcers to work harder to extract information from detained military personnel, according to the indictment.
“Squeeze them harder,” he allegedly said. In another, Maduro is accused of suggesting sleep deprivation and pouring water on detainees.
Abuses committed under Maduro’s rule included beatings, electrocutions and threatening family members of detainees, the indictment said. US prosecutors did not accuse Maduro or Flores of directly taking part in the torture.
Maduro became president of Venezuela in 2013, and his re-elections, most recently in 2024, have been repeatedly contested by opposition figures and outside monitors.

“I am innocent. I am not guilty. I am a decent man. I am still president of my country,” Maduro said then, adding that he had been “kidnapped”.
Both Maduro and Flores have sought to have the charges against them dismissed, maintaining they have immunity as president and first lady of a sovereign country.

Brussels Drops ‘Urgency’ Language on Ukraine’s Next Accession Steps

2026-10-15
16:02:47 UTC
01:02:47 KST

The EU officials have removed the phrase “as soon as possible” from their draft conclusion for the Oct. 15-16 European Council summit regarding the opening of the remaining accession clusters for Ukraine and Moldova.
The change was reported Thursday by European Pravda, whose correspondent compared versions of the draft dated Oct. 13 and Oct. 14. in Brussels.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Accession negotiations cover 33 chapters grouped into six clusters that organize the legal and institutional reforms Ukraine must adopt and implement in order to formally join the EU.
So far, Ukraine and Moldova opened Cluster 1 – Fundamentals on June 15, and Cluster 6 – External Relations on July 14. Clusters 2 and 3 were opened on Tuesday, Oct. 13. after Hungary lifted its long-standing veto on Ukraine’s accession bid.
The two countries’ paths remain closely linked, and any decision regarding their accession requires unanimous support from all 27 states.
What changed
The softer wording comes as Ireland, which holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, said it aims to open Ukraine’s two remaining clusters – Cluster 4, on the green agenda and sustainable connectivity, and Cluster 5, on resources, agriculture and cohesion – before the end of 2026.
In the Oct. 13 version, the section on Ukraine said EU leaders looked forward to opening all other clusters as soon as possible, in line with the bloc’s merit-based approach.
Zelensky Seeks Greater NATO Support as Starlink Restrictions Strain US Ties
The updated draft keeps the expectation that the clusters will be opened under the merit-based approach but no longer includes any reference to timing.
The same edit was made to a separate paragraph on Moldova, which also previously called for the remaining clusters to be opened as soon as possible.
Clusters opened after months of stagnation
According to European Pravda, both paragraphs still welcome the intergovernmental conferences held on Tuesday, Oct. 13, at which Clusters 2 and 3 were opened for Ukraine and Moldova, following months of stagnation due to Hungary’s veto.
The breakthrough finally came through after Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, passed amendments expanding education rights for national minorities and introduced a special status for general secondary schools serving national minorities.
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar welcomed the move in a statement, saying that the amendments would make it fundamentally easier for Hungarian children in Ukraine’s Transcarpathia region to use their native language.
Hours after Ukraine adopted the law, Hungary dropped its long-standing veto and made it possible for the country to continue its path towards the EU.
“I can confirm that all EU member states have agreed to: open clusters 2 and 3 for Ukraine and Moldova,” Irish Minister of State for European Affairs and Defence Thomas Byrne said on Monday, Oct. 12, calling Oct. 13 another “Super Tuesday” for the candidate countries.
The European Commission previously proposed limiting Ukraine’s access to EU farm subsidies and markets for sensitive products even after accession, which Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi rejected on Tuesday, Oct. 5. by saying that Kyiv cannot accept permanent restrictions.
Hungary’s long-standing veto
Ukraine’s application had been largely stalled for years due to vetoes from Hungary’s former-leader Viktor Orbán. His defeat by Magyar in April removed the blockage, allowing talks to resume.
However, Magyar’s diplomatic stance on Ukraine continues to repeatedly shift, and Ukrainian authorities have linked it to that of Orbán for several times.
In June, President Volodymyr Zelensky and Magyar sealed what the Hungarian PM described as a “historic agreement,” formally securing the political, educational, cultural and linguistic rights of ethnic Hungarian communities in Transcarpathia.
Budapest later tied the opening of further clusters to Ukraine turning those commitments into law.
Around the same time in June, Magyar said he secured the removal of language accelerating Ukraine’s EU accession from the European Council summit declaration after four hours of negotiations.
The conclusion welcomed Ukraine’s accession process but omitted its speeding up.
By blocking the joint letter to the European Council and Commission outlining the EU’s common position on opening five remaining clusters, Hungary became the sole objector among all member states.
During a Council of the EU working group meeting on July 17, Hungary blocked the procedure. Although Budapest agreed to advance Cluster 3 for Moldova, other member states rejected the request decoupling the two candidate countries.
No conclusion was reached at the time.
Hungary then blocked Clusters 2 and 3 again on July 22.
“There are six clusters in total, and we don’t think opening them all at once is a good idea – partly because the ink on the first one isn’t even dry yet, and partly because it would send the wrong message to the countries of the Western Balkans,” Magyar told reporters at the Council meeting in Brussels.
On Sept. 8, Ukraine faced its fourth refusal from Hungary, as Kyiv said Budapest had yet to specify its demands in exchange for lifting its objection.
“For 17 months, the government of Viktor Orbán blocked the opening of clusters, although Ukraine has fulfilled all the conditions for this,” Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told European Pravda.
“But even having lost power, Orbán’s team continues to disrupt the normalization of Hungary’s relations with Ukraine,” he continued.
During his tenure, Orbán repeatedly cited concerns over the rights of the Hungarian minority as a reason Hungary had delayed opening the first negotiation cluster.
Hungary previously also blocked technical work on clusters 2 through 6 for Ukraine, later lifting its objection to Cluster 6, covering foreign and security policy, trade policy, and relations with third countries.

Pope Leo resumes some papal duties as he recovers from lung surgery, Vatican says
Pope Leo XIV has resumed some papal duties, the Vatican said Thursday, after he had a piece of his right lung removed and received a diagnosis of lung cancer earlier this week.
A spokesperson for the Vatican said the pope celebrated Mass around noon and began "a little bit of work activity," including reading documents. The pontiff also met with Archbishop Paolo Rudelli, undersecretary of state, on Thursday, the Vatican said.
Leo is set to be released from Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Oct. 20, one week after he was first admitted.
The Vatican spokesperson said Leo would like to lead the Angelus prayer from the hospital on Sunday, but it's not clear yet whether that will happen.
Leo also underwent routine checkups, including a chest X-ray, on Thursday, according to personal physician Dr. Luigi Carbone and thoracic surgeon Dr. Stefano Margaritora. Margaritora led the operation on the pontiff. The X-ray showed "good recovery of the operated lung," the two said in a statement, and the pope's "post-operative recovery is progressing as expected."
The pope has also had at least one physiotherapy session, Carbone and Margaritora said.
Candida Moss, the Edward Cadbury professor of theology at the University of Birmingham in England, told CBS News on Wednesday that it's typical for popes to stick to their schedules even amid health issues. Vatican protocols call for the pope's cardinals and aide to take over as many duties as possible, Moss said.
"We have a long tradition of popes — not just Pope Francis, but also Pope John Paul II, who had Parkinson's for 10 years — who continued to remain as active as they could, and as active in Catholic liturgies as they could, right up until the end of their tenures," Moss said.
The Vatican announced Leo had been diagnosed with lung cancer on Tuesday following his surgery.
Preoperative tests had indicated the potential presence of the cancer, the Vatican said earlier this week. During the 90-minute operation, a lobe of the pontiff's right lung that had a nodular lesion was removed, the Vatican said.
The Vatican has not shared any other details about Leo's cancer, such as its stage or genetic makeup.
Leo is expected to travel to South America next month. The Vatican pointed to comments the pontiff made Sunday, when he said he is looking forward to going.
The pope's audiences are canceled through Oct. 20.

====================================================================================================

Social freedom shapes whose version of reality you adopt, new research suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:00:09 UTC
01:00:09 KST

New research provides evidence that the culture or social environment we live in influences whose version of the world we adopt as our own. People in settings where relationships are easily formed and broken tend to align their worldviews more selectively with people who help them achieve their goals, partly by feeling less in sync with those who don’t. The findings were published in Social Psychological and Personality Science.
Human beings have an inherent need to make sense of the world, a process often shaped by the people around them. Psychologists refer to this merging of inner states, beliefs, and judgments as shared reality. As noted in a study covered by PsyPost in 2021, this psychological factor acts as an important bonding mechanism. It allows two people to experience the world through a common lens, deepening their connection.
People do not attempt to establish this deep mental connection with just anyone. They are often motivated to build shared reality with instrumental others, which refers to friends, family members, or colleagues who help them achieve specific personal or professional goals. In fact, a study covered by PsyPost in 2023 indicated that experiencing a shared reality with these helpful individuals is associated with greater academic and personal success. Sharing reality with helpful people has been linked to greater confidence in one’s own abilities and may help keep those relationships intact.
The research, led by Abdo Elnakouri, an assistant professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Houston and director of the Worldviews in Motion Lab, alongside Eli J. Finkel of Northwestern University and Abigail A. Scholer of the University of Virginia, explored how the broader cultural context might alter this dynamic. Specifically, the authors focused on a concept called relational mobility. This refers to the degree of freedom people have in a given society to form new relationships and end existing ones.
“Honestly this came as an idea to previous work our team had done on shared reality and goal success,” Elnakouri told PsyPost. “I came across the relational mobility variable through reading and going to conferences. Seemed like a possible cool extension.”
“Research finds those in high relational mobility contexts invest more in their relationships: they express more love, give grander gifts, and reveal deeper secrets,” Elnakouri said. “In these contexts, people don’t take their relationships for granted (the person can leave!), working harder to invest in them. So it made sense that this might extend out to shared reality as well.”
In low relational mobility contexts, social networks are more rigid, and people are largely tied to their existing connections. In high relational mobility settings, by contrast, people can easily choose new ties or walk away from current ones. Elnakouri and his team suspected that when people live in highly mobile environments where partners could leave, they might feel a stronger need to secure their most beneficial relationships.
“Specifically, I wondered whether relational mobility might push people to not only invest their hearts ❤️, but also their minds 🧠 in those they care about,” Elnakouri continued. “Might people be motivated to share reality, or ‘merge minds,’ with others when in a high relationally mobile context?”
To test this idea, the researchers first analyzed an archival dataset containing responses from nearly 17,000 participants across 39 countries. Participants completed questionnaires assessing the relational mobility of their local environment. They also reported on their relationship with a close friend or romantic partner, rating how much emotional support that person provided and whether they could count on the person in times of need. In addition, they rated how much they felt the person truly understood them, which served as a basic measure for shared reality.
People who lived in more relationally mobile settings tended to report more shared reality with their close partner. This association depended on how supportive the partner was. Comparing countries, the gap arose because people in high-mobility countries reported less shared reality with less supportive partners; when the researchers instead used participants’ own perceptions of mobility, the gap arose because people reported more shared reality with supportive partners.
To build on these initial patterns, the researchers conducted two social network studies with undergraduate students at a Canadian university, 353 in the first and 277 in the second. Both samples were composed mostly of women. Instead of focusing on just one close relationship, participants nominated people they had been in contact with during the past month (up to 30 in the first study and up to five in the second), rating each person’s helpfulness for their goals and their degree of shared reality.
When looking at these broader social networks, the researchers did not find that high relational mobility predicted an overall increase in shared reality. Instead, the effects centered on the relative difference between helpful and unhelpful members of their network. In both the 39-country dataset and the network studies, the scientists also measured other types of similarity, including shared personality traits, upbringing, and geographical background, but these did not follow the same pattern, suggesting the dynamic was specific to shared reality.
In three of four analyses, students who saw their social world as highly mobile showed a bigger gap between helpful and unhelpful people in their networks. In one analysis, this gap stemmed from lower shared reality with less helpful people; in the others, the shifts with helpful and unhelpful people were not statistically significant on their own. A measure of how free participants themselves felt to leave relationships showed no such pattern, which the authors interpret as a sign that concerns about others leaving drive the effect.
“I think the fact that people seem to primarily distance themselves from those who do not support their goal in high relationally mobile contexts was interesting,” Elnakouri explained. “So when people have choices, they look to more exclusively invest in those who are invested in them. It could have been the case that people only drew closer to those who helped them with their goal instead of distancing themselves from those that didn’t.”
Because the first three datasets relied on correlational data, the authors conducted an experiment to test whether shifting perceptions of relational mobility would directly alter shared reality. They recruited 590 adults and asked them to nominate three specific people in their lives: one who was helpful for their career goals, one who was not helpful for their career, and a third newer acquaintance unrelated to their career. In a separate pilot study of 102 people, the researchers confirmed that their experimental writing task shifted how freely people felt others around them could come and go.
In the main experiment, participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions. In the high relational mobility condition, they wrote about whether the third acquaintance might eventually drift away and leave their life. In the low relational mobility condition, they wrote about how that person might stay close and remain in their life.
Participants in the high relational mobility condition reported less shared reality with their less helpful career contacts (an average of 3.69 on a 7-point scale, compared with 4.04 in the low mobility condition). Shared reality with helpful contacts did not differ between conditions, suggesting that a sense of social fragility leads people to mentally distance themselves from less helpful ties.
“To answer that question, we find that the answer is ‘yes,’ but with one crucial caveat,” Elnakouri said, looking across the research program as a whole. “It looks like relational mobility pushes people to invest more in some relationships, yes, but also less in others.”
“The takeaway: cultures seem to shape how we see the world, but also who we look to in order to form our perceptions of the world/reality,” Elnakouri noted. “I think this is a cool connection between work on culture, shared reality, relationships, and self-regulation.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind regarding these findings. In the first study, participants were recruited through Facebook and 86 percent were women, which may limit generalizability. In addition, the social network studies relied on student samples at a single university, and the experiment manipulated perceptions by focusing on thoughts about a single acquaintance. Study 1 also measured shared reality with a single survey question, which captures only a narrow slice of the concept; the later studies used a more complete, validated questionnaire.
Social fluidity is also just one piece of the puzzle. “Effect sizes were what you’d expect from typical social psychology studies, so there is sure to be plenty of other factors shaping our worldviews!” Elnakouri pointed out.
There is also the question of how these selective alignments impact society at large. The authors suggest that if people in fluid social environments build shared reality more selectively with those who benefit their goals, they might form insular bubbles, leading to diverging views from those outside their immediate circles. Future research could test whether more relationally mobile cultures are more prone to defensiveness, polarization, and divided worldviews.
The research team plans to continue investigating how environmental contexts and personal goals interact. “I want to continue to explore how people’s worldviews are shaped by complex dynamics across multiple levels of analysis (e.g., self-regulatory needs, cultural context) that too rarely come into conversation with one another,” Elnakouri said.
The study, “Choosing Our Reality: Relational Mobility Shapes When and With Whom People Share Reality,” was authored by Abdo Elnakouri, Eli J. Finkel, and Abigail A. Scholer.

Lebanon's second airport opening delayed over security concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:00:02 UTC
01:00:02 KST

Breadcrumb
Why Lebanon's long-awaited second airport is still not open
The opening of Lebanon's second international airport has been delayed by incomplete security arrangements and additional work not covered by the original operating contract, with the government now targeting 15 November for the first commercial flight.
René Mouawad Airport in the village of Qlayaat, northern Lebanon, was initially scheduled to open for commercial flights in October, but several outstanding issues have pushed back the launch.
The original $10 million contract did not cover all the requirements set by security agencies, prompting Public Works and Transport Minister Fayez Rasamny to request an additional $6 million for further work, according to news site ASAS Media.
The installation of surveillance cameras alone is estimated to cost around $4 million, accounting for much of the additional funding. The work is expected to be put out to public tender through the Civil Aviation Authority, in accordance with Lebanon's public procurement law.
Responding to a request for comment from The New Arab, Sky Lounge Services, the company awarded the public tender to operate and invest in the airport, said it was committed to fulfilling its contractual obligations and supporting the government's efforts to prepare the airport for reopening.
In a statement issued on Wednesday, the company said its $10 million contract covered the construction of a new passenger terminal, which is being built from scratch and will be larger than originally planned, as well as the rehabilitation of the airport, infrastructure improvements and the installation of operational, technical and security systems.
However, Sky Lounge Services stressed that any additional work commissioned by the authorities outside the scope of its contract was not its responsibility. It said it had no role in decisions concerning the awarding, financing or implementation of such work.
The company added that it remained committed to completing all work and installing the equipment covered by its contract in time for the airport to be ready for operations on 15 November.
Questions also remain over which body will be responsible for securing the airport.
One proposal under discussion is to establish a separate security force, similar to the one overseeing security at Beirut's Rafic Hariri International Airport. Another is to extend Beirut airport's security command to cover Qlayaat, a move that would require an amendment to a 1978 law governing the body.
The security concerns come alongside legal and administrative obstacles, including procedures to transfer ownership of the airport from the Lebanese army to the Civil Aviation Directorate.
The airport served as a military airbase for decades before plans were revived to reopen it for civilian use.
MP Sajih Attieh, head of parliament's Public Works Committee, has also cited weather conditions as a factor affecting preparations.
Attieh previously said a new opening date, roughly a month later than originally planned, was being discussed, while Rasamny told Annahar that the airport would not open until it was fully ready, particularly in terms of security and logistics.
The minister said the aim was to begin operations before the end of the year, without committing to a firm date until the outstanding requirements had been met.
Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has since announced 15 November as the target date for the first commercial flight, which is scheduled to depart for Saudi Arabia, although questions remain over whether the airport will be ready by then.
Rasamny has said the additional security work could be carried out alongside airport operations and continue after flights begin.
The government has been holding meetings with the relevant departments and agencies, with weekly follow-ups covering the airport's legal, security, technical, operational and logistical requirements in line with civil aviation standards.
Preparations have included test flights to assess the runway's suitability and its ability to accommodate different types of civilian aircraft.
Two aircraft carrying technicians and employees from the Directorate General of Civil Aviation landed at the airport as part of the checks. The first aircraft belonging to the operating company also landed in August, ahead of the partial civilian operations initially planned for October.
The reopening was announced on 6 June after years of delays.
Salam said at the time that the Akkar district, where Qlayaat is located, should no longer remain outside the state's priorities, describing the airport as important to the national economy and to ending the isolation of impoverished northern areas.
Tripoli, Minyeh-Danniyeh and Akkar districts are among Lebanon's poorest regions.
Residents and politicians have long campaigned for the airport's reopening to create jobs and ease pressure on Beirut airport, which is already operating beyond capacity.
The airport is named after former Lebanese President René Mouawad, who was assassinated days after his election in 1989. Lebanon's national carrier, Middle East Airlines, used the airport for a limited period during the Lebanese Civil War, particularly between 1988 and 1990, operating domestic flights between Beirut and northern Lebanon.
Those services were later discontinued, partly after routes between different parts of the country reopened.

Why Lebanon's long-awaited second airport is still not open
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:00:02 UTC
01:00:02 KST

Breadcrumb
Why Lebanon's long-awaited second airport is still not open
The opening of Lebanon's second international airport has been delayed by incomplete security arrangements and additional work not covered by the original operating contract, with the government now targeting 15 November for the first commercial flight.
René Mouawad Airport in the village of Qlayaat, northern Lebanon, was initially scheduled to open for commercial flights in October, but several outstanding issues have pushed back the launch.
The original $10 million contract did not cover all the requirements set by security agencies, prompting Public Works and Transport Minister Fayez Rasamny to request an additional $6 million for further work, according to news site ASAS Media.
The installation of surveillance cameras alone is estimated to cost around $4 million, accounting for much of the additional funding. The work is expected to be put out to public tender through the Civil Aviation Authority, in accordance with Lebanon's public procurement law.
Responding to a request for comment from The New Arab, Sky Lounge Services, the company awarded the public tender to operate and invest in the airport, said it was committed to fulfilling its contractual obligations and supporting the government's efforts to prepare the airport for reopening.
In a statement issued on Wednesday, the company said its $10 million contract covered the construction of a new passenger terminal, which is being built from scratch and will be larger than originally planned, as well as the rehabilitation of the airport, infrastructure improvements and the installation of operational, technical and security systems.
However, Sky Lounge Services stressed that any additional work commissioned by the authorities outside the scope of its contract was not its responsibility. It said it had no role in decisions concerning the awarding, financing or implementation of such work.
The company added that it remained committed to completing all work and installing the equipment covered by its contract in time for the airport to be ready for operations on 15 November.
Questions also remain over which body will be responsible for securing the airport.
One proposal under discussion is to establish a separate security force, similar to the one overseeing security at Beirut's Rafic Hariri International Airport. Another is to extend Beirut airport's security command to cover Qlayaat, a move that would require an amendment to a 1978 law governing the body.
The security concerns come alongside legal and administrative obstacles, including procedures to transfer ownership of the airport from the Lebanese army to the Civil Aviation Directorate.
The airport served as a military airbase for decades before plans were revived to reopen it for civilian use.
MP Sajih Attieh, head of parliament's Public Works Committee, has also cited weather conditions as a factor affecting preparations.
Attieh previously said a new opening date, roughly a month later than originally planned, was being discussed, while Rasamny told Annahar that the airport would not open until it was fully ready, particularly in terms of security and logistics.
The minister said the aim was to begin operations before the end of the year, without committing to a firm date until the outstanding requirements had been met.
Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has since announced 15 November as the target date for the first commercial flight, which is scheduled to depart for Saudi Arabia, although questions remain over whether the airport will be ready by then.
Rasamny has said the additional security work could be carried out alongside airport operations and continue after flights begin.
The government has been holding meetings with the relevant departments and agencies, with weekly follow-ups covering the airport's legal, security, technical, operational and logistical requirements in line with civil aviation standards.
Preparations have included test flights to assess the runway's suitability and its ability to accommodate different types of civilian aircraft.
Two aircraft carrying technicians and employees from the Directorate General of Civil Aviation landed at the airport as part of the checks. The first aircraft belonging to the operating company also landed in August, ahead of the partial civilian operations initially planned for October.
The reopening was announced on 6 June after years of delays.
Salam said at the time that the Akkar district, where Qlayaat is located, should no longer remain outside the state's priorities, describing the airport as important to the national economy and to ending the isolation of impoverished northern areas.
Tripoli, Minyeh-Danniyeh and Akkar districts are among Lebanon's poorest regions.
Residents and politicians have long campaigned for the airport's reopening to create jobs and ease pressure on Beirut airport, which is already operating beyond capacity.
The airport is named after former Lebanese President René Mouawad, who was assassinated days after his election in 1989. Lebanon's national carrier, Middle East Airlines, used the airport for a limited period during the Lebanese Civil War, particularly between 1988 and 1990, operating domestic flights between Beirut and northern Lebanon.
Those services were later discontinued, partly after routes between different parts of the country reopened.

Hamas is preparing to launch a renewed international campaign highlighting hunger in the Gaza Strip, seeking to increase diplomatic pressure on Israel and derail efforts to disarm the terrorist organization under President Donald Trump's Gaza plan, according to Israeli security officials. The reported initiative comes as Hamas faces a severe financial crisis and imposes heavy taxes on merchants receiving humanitarian aid, contributing to rising prices and shortages in local markets, Israeli officials say.
According to Israeli security assessments, the organization needs approximately 90 million shekels every month to pay its estimated 30,000 personnel across Gaza, including administrative employees, lower-ranking operatives and members of its military wing. With average monthly salaries estimated at 3,000 shekels per person, Hamas is reportedly struggling to maintain its payroll and prevent its organizational structure from collapsing.
To raise revenue, Hamas has allegedly imposed steep taxes on Gaza merchants, including those receiving goods from outside the territory through humanitarian aid shipments. Israeli security officials say traders are required to pay thousands of shekels per truck, with charges reaching as much as 10,000 shekels. In addition, Hamas reportedly demands a cash payment equivalent to the sales value of 30% of each truck's cargo.
With approximately 300 trucks entering Gaza daily, the potential revenue from the per-truck charges alone could reach 3 million shekels a day if every shipment were charged the maximum amount. However, Israeli officials say the financial burden has become so severe that some merchants have stopped collecting shipments rather than pay Hamas, effectively abandoning goods intended for local markets.
The resulting disruption has contributed to rising prices and shortages in Gaza, according to the Israeli assessments. Security officials believe Hamas is now seeking to exploit those conditions by reviving the international publicity campaign surrounding hunger in the territory that gained prominence during the summer of 2025.
The planned campaign is intended to generate international pressure on Israel and encourage foreign governments to demand a halt to the Trump administration's Gaza plan, particularly provisions requiring the demilitarization of the territory and the disarmament of Hamas, according to Israeli officials.
Israeli security sources dispute claims that Gaza is currently experiencing starvation, maintaining that approximately 250 aid trucks a day would be sufficient to meet the population's needs if deliveries were properly monitored and prevented from reaching Hamas. That assessment reflects the Israeli security establishment's position and does not constitute an independent determination of humanitarian conditions in the territory.
Hamas, meanwhile, accuses Israel of obstructing merchants and commercial supply routes, placing responsibility for shortages and high prices on Israeli restrictions. Israeli officials contend that Hamas's own taxation policies are contributing to the disruption and believe the group intends to use the resulting economic hardship to win international support against Israel.
The renewed struggle over humanitarian aid therefore comes at a particularly sensitive moment for Hamas, as it seeks both to maintain its financial and organizational structures and to resist growing pressure to surrender its weapons under the US-backed plan.

Could this ancient shipwreck be the oldest ever found?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:58:39 UTC
00:58:39 KST

They don’t make ’em like they used to. A shipwreck believed to date to the early Bronze Age has been discovered at the bottom of the Mediterranean Sea, where it has remained sitting, complete with intact cargo.
The small boat was first found in 2024 by scientists at Türkiye’s Akdeniz University. A blip on their sonar screen led them to the remains, which were surrounded by three stone anchors.
While old shipwrecks in the area aren’t uncommon, most have dated to roughly 2,000 to 1,500 years ago, during the Roman or Byzantine eras. This ship, however, is far older, likely dating to the early Bronze Age, when the Hattian civilization was beginning to form. The scientists believe the remains are between 4,700 and 4,400 years old. That would make this the oldest shipwreck ever found, surpassing the previous contender by centuries.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Inside the ship, the archaeologists found around 18 remarkably intact, flat-bottomed containers called amphorae, which were commonly used to store and transport liquids such as olive oil and wine at the time. Some of the containers were marked with finely etched symbols, although what they mean is not yet clear.
The unfortunate crew of the doomed vessel were likely sailing to the west when disaster struck, the researchers wrote in a study about the wreck that was published earlier this year. The area where it was found has strong currents that can be treacherous when combined with wind, they noted.
Türkiye’s culture minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy posted a video of the underwater site on social media on Wednesday. In the post, Ersoy said the shipwreck sheds light “on the deep-rooted history of maritime trade along the Anatolian coasts.”
“We continue to illuminate Anatolia’s maritime history with new discoveries, preserving our underwater cultural heritage to pass it on to future generations,” he said.

Two 1960s London housing estates saved from demolition after decade-long battle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:57:50 UTC
00:57:50 KST

Two architecturally celebrated council estates in south London that have been under threat of demolition for more than a decade have been saved.
Residents of Cressingham Gardens and the Central Hill estate have campaigned tirelessly for their homes to be saved, saying the low-density 1960s developments are significant in design and popular with those living there.
Lambeth council argued that the estates were in poor repair and that razing them would create badly needed social and affordable homes.
The plans were pursued when Lambeth was controlled by Labour but the Greens won the most seats at elections in May and now run the council as a minority administration.
They oppose the demolition plans, which are expected to be reversed at a meeting of the cabinet next week.
The fate of the estates attracted wider attention, in part because of their design but also because of the many years of limbo faced by tenants and leaseholders as the council pursued demolition.
A 2022 review of Homes Lambeth, the now defunct body which managed housing for the council, questioned the redevelopment plans, saying the net number of social rent homes to be created was very small.
Sir Bob Kerslake, the former head of the civil service who led the review, said “feedback was uniformly negative”, with residents of estates earmarked for development citing inconsistent policy, delays and poor communication. He added: “As a consequence, levels of trust in the council are exceptionally low.”
Both threatened estates were designed by a team of Lambeth architects led by Ted Hollamby, who championed a move away from tower blocks toward lower-rise housing.
Cressingham Gardens, which adjoins Brockwell Park, was built to encourage neighbourliness, with front doors facing each other and green spaces for play.
The Central Hill project was led by Rosemary Stjernstedt when women were rare in social housing design. It was built on a sloping site near Crystal Palace, with homes maximising natural light.
Martin Abrams, the Green leader of Lambeth, said: “This is a decisive moment for Central Hill and Cressingham Gardens. It recognises the relentless work of my colleagues in securing the future for these communities without demolition. We can now focus on investing in residents’ homes and bringing empty properties back into use.”
Pete Elliott, the cabinet member for housing, said: “For over 12 years, we have fought for a better future for Central Hill and Cressingham Gardens. These proposals end years of uncertainty and put the focus where it belongs: repairing homes, supporting communities and filling empty properties.”

Israel says commercial goods no longer entering Gaza after merchants suspend coordination
JERUSALEM, Oct 15 - Israel said commercial goods were no longer entering Gaza over what it said was a dispute over taxes between local merchants and Hamas, shutting off a vital source of food and other goods in the territory where the population is dependent on aid.
COGAT, the Israeli military body that oversees humanitarian affairs in Gaza, made the announcement in a statement on Wednesday, citing what it said was a decision by Gazan merchants to stop coordinating with COGAT on the entry of commercial goods.
It said the Gazan merchants had told COGAT that they had made the decision in response to a 10,000 shekel ($3,220) fee imposed by Hamas on each truck entering Gaza and a demand for 30% of all of their sales in Gaza to be carried out in cash.
Hamas later said that the 10,000 shekel fee was a voluntary payment by wealthy Gazans to a national fund that seeks to provide for those in need such as widows and orphans. It also said that cash payments were encouraged due to what it described as an acute cash shortage in the war-torn territory.
A majority of Gazans are dependent on aid supplies, following three years of war, repeated displacement and severe restrictions imposed by Israel on aid deliveries.
A global hunger monitor in July warned that more than two thirds of Gazans could face acute hunger by the year-end. Around 2 million Gazans live in the territory, most in makeshift shelters.
Nahed Shhaibar, the head of the private transport union in Gaza, said that not a single truck carrying commercial products from Israel entered Gaza on Thursday. However, he said trucks carrying humanitarian aid had entered, as had trucks carrying commercial goods from Egypt via an Israeli-controlled crossing.
COGAT said the decision by Gazan merchants would cut the total number of trucks, which carry both humanitarian and commercial goods, entering Gaza each day to around 300 — or half.
Diplomats say that far fewer than 600 trucks normally enter Gaza each day. Shhaibar said the figure was closer to 300, with two thirds carrying commercial goods.
Israel is obliged under a US-mediated agreement to allow a minimum of 600 trucks carrying humanitarian aid to enter Gaza each day. However, it says it is required to allow only 600 trucks and that commercial goods are needed to supplement aid supplies. REUTERS

NEW DELHI: New Delhi: India needs to align power generation plans with the time required to build transmission infrastructure to meet future electricity demand reliably and affordably, energy sector experts said at RE: DIALOGUES 2026 in the capital.They flagged right-of-way constraints, the availability of transformers and the distance between renewable energy generation centres and consumption hubs as key challenges for power sector planning.The mismatch between renewable energy generation and transmission readiness has emerged as a major concern. Delays in transmission lines and substations can leave completed solar and wind projects unable to evacuate their full generation capacity.
The constraints are also leading to power curtailment. According to govt, 8,133 gigawatt hour of solar power was curtailed or restricted during April-June 2026 due to transmission constraints and to maintain grid security. The mismatch highlights the need to synchronise the commissioning of generation projects with transmission lines and substations to ensure electricity reaches consumption centres.

Repressive, secretive and highly militarised: Eritrea, the east African country facing UK visa ban threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:52:19 UTC
00:52:19 KST

Eritrea, the east African country embroiled in a row with the UK over its refusal to accept the return of rejected asylum seekers and criminals, is considered one of world’s most secretive and repressive states, with reports of arbitrary detention and severe restrictions on freedom of expression, opinion and religion.
Situated in the Horn of Africa and bordering Sudan, Ethiopia and Djibouti, it became a sovereign state after gaining independence from Ethiopia in 1993 following a 30-year war.
The country is run by an authoritarian regime under Isaias Afwerki, who led separatist forces to defeat Ethiopian forces in 1991 and became president in 1993. He has served as president since independence and heads the People’s Front for Democracy and Justice, the country’s only legal political party.
Eritrea has not held a national election since independence. A constitution that was ratified in 1997 by the constituent assembly has still not been implemented nearly three decades later.
In 2001, the government shut down all independent newspapers after the publishing of an open letter by senior ruling party officials calling on the government to implement the constitution and hold elections.
A highly militarised state, Eritrea runs a compulsory national service system that requires students to study at a military training centre in their final year of secondary school. They undergo military training and political education before working in either military units or civilian national service roles that can last decades.
The repression and conscription has forced many Eritreans to risk harsh punishment for evading, deserting or escaping the military by fleeing the country. It is estimated that up to one-third of the Eritrean-born population lives abroad.
Eritreans were the most common nationality arriving by small boat to the UK in the year ending June 2026. Earlier this year, Eritrea abruptly withdrew cooperation with the UK on migrant returns, and on Thursday the UK home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said all Eritreans could be stopped from coming to the UK unless the country agreed to accept more rejected asylum seekers and criminals.
Eritrea’s political, economic and social framework has been defined by a doctrine of economic self-reliance, with the country notably rejecting foreign aid.
It was an Italian colony and parts of the country feature early to mid-20th-century Italian modernist architecture. The capital, Asmara, was inscribed as a world heritage site in 2017, with Unesco describing it as “an exceptional example of early modernist urbanism at the beginning of the 20th century and its application in an African context”.
A multi-ethnic country, Eritrea is mainly made up of the Tigrinya people. Its extensive Red Sea coastline (1,388 miles) gives it a strategic position along the Red Sea corridor.
The country has been in the spotlight in recent weeks because of fears of war with Ethiopia. Both countries have accused each other of aggression. Ethiopia has claimed Eritrean troops crossed up to 60km (37 miles) into Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region, while Eritrea has said the accusation is a fabrication to create a pretext for war.
The escalation is linked to renewed fighting between Ethiopian government forces and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), an armed opposition group, in Tigray, which borders Eritrea.
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF, a claim that Eritrea has denied. On Tuesday, Ethiopian forces advanced to Zalambessa, a town on the border with Eritrea that was under Tigrayan rebel control.

The water disappeared after shelling or a blackout: how to find a safe source and properly store supplies
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:50:50 EEST
00:50:50 KST

The water disappeared after shelling or a blackout: how to find a safe source and properly store supplies
Kyiv • UNN
After emergencies, tap water must not be drunk without official confirmation. Experts advise boiling it and storing supplies properly.
Due to shelling, accidents, or power outages, Ukrainians may suddenly be left without water. In such situations, it is important not only to find an alternative source but also to make sure that the water does not pose a health risk. UNN explains where to get water during outages, how to determine that it cannot be used, and how to keep supplies clean at home.
Details
According to information from the Center for Public Health, water in a building may suddenly disappear as a result of a blackout, shelling, or damage to the water supply network.
People often act hastily in such situations: they collect the last water from the tap, use unverified sources, or grab the first container they find. However, the initial decisions determine whether the water will be safe for you and your family. After water supply systems are damaged, water may be contaminated with microorganisms or hazardous chemical substances. Most such contaminants cannot be detected by appearance, smell, or taste
Why water may be dangerous after accidents
During an accident, damage to the water supply network may allow groundwater, surface water, or wastewater to enter the system. As a result, the water may contain dangerous microorganisms capable of causing infectious diseases. At the same time, its appearance does not always indicate its actual quality.
Therefore, after accidents or prolonged outages, one should not automatically consider tap water safe to drink. First, check announcements from local authorities, the water utility, or the regional Center for Disease Control and Prevention; they can provide information about the cause of the disruption, the operation of water distribution points, and the rules for using the water supply system after its operation is restored. If the safety of the water has not been confirmed, it is better to use bottled water or water from official delivery points for drinking and cooking.
What water must not be used even after boiling
You cannot rely solely on the water’s clarity. If it has an unusual color, foreign impurities, smells of gasoline, solvents, paint, or sewage, is covered with a rainbow-colored film, or forms persistent foam, it should not be used.
It is especially important not to try to make such water safe by boiling it, because boiling helps destroy most disease-causing microorganisms but does not remove chemical contaminants, petroleum products, heavy metals, or nitrates. Moreover, as water evaporates, the concentration of nitrates may increase. If chemical contamination is suspected, you must find another source of water and report the situation to local government authorities or emergency services.
How to purify water if there is no other source
If there is no safe alternative and the water shows no signs of chemical contamination, it must be boiled: bring it to a vigorous boil and leave it to cool naturally. At the same time, do not rely solely on a household filter. It may improve the water’s taste and clarity but does not guarantee the removal of all bacteria and viruses, so filtration does not replace boiling when disinfection is necessary.
It is also important to remember that boiling does not make water safe if dangerous chemical contaminants are suspected. In that case, another source must be chosen.
How to store water at home so that it does not spoil
Even if water was collected from a safe source, its quality may deteriorate due to improper storage. That is why, before filling containers, you should wash your hands with soap, and use clean glass or food-grade plastic containers for supplies.
Containers marked HDPE 2 or PP 5 are suitable for storage - the corresponding numbers should be indicated on the bottom. Containers holding drinking water and utility water should be labeled so their purposes are not confused. Filled containers should be tightly closed and kept in a cool, shaded place. Do not add fresh water to leftover old water without first washing the container. These simple measures help reduce the risk of recontaminating the supplies.
How much water should you have in case of a prolonged outage
As soon as access to safe water is restored, you should prepare a household supply sufficient for at least 72 hours. The recommended minimum of drinking water is three liters per person per day. However, when planning your supplies, you need to take into account the needs of all family members. In particular, children, pregnant women, older people, and people with chronic illnesses require special attention. It is also important to think about neighbors who may find it difficult to get to a distribution point on their own or carry water home. If possible, you should help older people living alone, people with disabilities, and families with small children. The main thing is not to use water from unverified sources and to follow official announcements, as well as to store supplies properly. Advance preparation will help reduce the risk of infectious diseases and poisoning if the water supply suddenly stops.

Netanyahu did not say when exactly the call took place, but implied it had been during bloody clashes in southern Syria in July of 2025 involving Druze factions, Bedouin fighters and government security forces.
"I called al-Sharaa. It was a very short, very sharp conversation, and the slaughter stopped," Netanyahu said at an election rally with Israel's Druze community, according to footage aired by Israel's public broadcaster KAN.
The 2025 clashes erupted in Syria's Sweida province between armed Druze factions and Bedouin fighters, with government security forces and some tribal groups then intervening on the side of the Bedouins.
More than 2,000 people were killed, including 789 Druze civilians, according to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights watchdog.
A committee set up by the Syrian government said it had documented 1,760 deaths.
At the time, government forces and their allies were accused of executing civilians and other abuses.
Israel, which also has a Druze population, intervened militarily during the clashes, with strikes in Sweida and against government targets in Damascus, saying it was defending the minority community.
Government-aligned forces later withdrew from Sweida city, leaving a fragile ceasefire in place, and in July of this year Damascus said it had begun trying suspects over the violence.
Since the December 2024 ouster of longtime Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad, Israel has carried out hundreds of strikes in Syria and sent troops into a UN-patrolled buffer zone that had separated Israeli and Syrian forces in the Golan since 1974.
It has also carried out repeated incursions deeper into Syrian territory and has vowed to keep troops in a so-called "security zone" in southern Syria, where it seeks a broader demilitarised area.
Syria's new leaders have condemned Israeli military action in the country's south but have refrained from responding with force.
Despite the tensions, Syria and Israel have held several rounds of direct talks as they edge towards a security agreement.

Hezbollah acknowledged Thursday that a shipment of approximately half a ton of explosives seized by Lebanese authorities belonged to the Iran-backed group, in a rare public admission that directly challenges the government's efforts to disarm the terrorist organization.
The explosives were discovered last week in a vehicle traveling along the main highway connecting eastern Lebanon, near the Syrian border, with Beirut. According to a judicial source cited by AFP, the shipment included 250 kilograms of TNT and 250 kilograms of C-4, a powerful plastic explosive.
"The vehicle and its cargo belong to the resistance" against Israel, Hezbollah lawmaker Hassan Fadlallah said, demanding the immediate release of those arrested in connection with the seizure and the return of the vehicle and its contents. He insisted the explosives were intended exclusively for operations against Israel.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam had condemned the shipment and pledged that authorities would identify everyone involved in what he described as a criminal operation, including those who ordered it. He said the government would act firmly against weapons outside state control, citing public concern over the discovery of C-4, which has been used in several notorious political assassinations in Lebanon.
Hezbollah rejected suggestions that the explosives were intended for domestic attacks. Fadlallah accused Salam of conducting a campaign designed to deepen divisions among Lebanese citizens, insisting that the group's weapons were directed solely against Israel.
The dispute comes amid longstanding concerns about political violence in Lebanon. Members of Hezbollah were convicted by an international tribunal in connection with the 2005 assassination of former Prime Minister Rafic Hariri, who was killed in a massive bombing in Beirut.
Analysts described Hezbollah's unusually direct acknowledgment as a calculated political decision. Karim Bitar, a lecturer at Sciences Po Paris, said the group appeared to be trying to control the narrative after being caught with the shipment.
More significantly, Bitar said, the admission represents another rejection of Lebanon's August 2025 decision to task the military with disarming Hezbollah, placing the government in an increasingly difficult position.
David Wood, an analyst at the International Crisis Group, said Hezbollah was seeking to demonstrate that it remained committed to armed confrontation with Israel while denying accusations that its weapons could be used against political rivals at home.
Hezbollah has been weakened by two conflicts with Israel since 2023, including fighting that erupted in March 2026 in support of Iran. It has not claimed an attack against Israel since June 20, following a reduction in hostilities under diplomatic arrangements involving Washington, Tehran, Beirut and Jerusalem.
The collapse of Bashar Assad's regime in Syria also disrupted Hezbollah's traditional weapons supply routes from Iran through Iraq and Syria. Lebanese and Syrian authorities have since intensified efforts to combat smuggling across their shared 330-kilometer border.
Lebanon's military has seized two additional explosives shipments near the Syrian border this month, underscoring the difficulties facing efforts to enforce state control over weapons as Hezbollah continues to reject disarmament.

What is the ‘Mother of All Bombs’ US could use in Iran?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:46:41 UTC
00:46:41 KST

What is the ‘Mother of All Bombs’ US could use in Iran?
US media reports military considering plans to use GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB)
The United States has developed plans to strike Iran with the largest non-nuclear bomb in its military arsenal on Iran’s energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders renewed combat operations, according to US officials cited by CNN.
Deploying the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB), nicknamed the “mother of all bombs”, could significantly escalate the ongoing conflict at a time when fighting has lulled, experts say.
Concerns are also being raised, including within the Trump administration itself, over what such a move would even achieve. Officials familiar with military planning discussions told US news outlet CNN and Al Jazeera that deploying the MOAB would be unlikely to help the US achieve its stated strategic goals, including to destroy Iran’s nuclear capabilities.
Brussels-based military expert Elijah Magnier told Al Jazeera that using the MOAB would not even guarantee the destruction of Iran’s deeply buried underground nuclear installations and that such a strike would likely amount to little more than “political theatre”.
Here’s what we know:
What is the MOAB?
The GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB) is a massive munition containing about 8,500kg (18,000 pounds or 8.5 tonnes) of high explosives. It weighs 9,800kg (21,605 pounds or nearly 10 tonnes) – about the same as four saloon cars – and is as long as a small yacht at just over 9 metres (about 30 feet).
The MOAB is typically deployed from the Lockheed C-130 Hercules cargo aircraft because it cannot fit in a stealth bomber.
The bomb, which was first manufactured between 2002 and 2003, has undergone 12 detonation tests.
Its name is a reference to former Iraqi President Saddam Hussein’s comments during the 1991 Gulf War when he invoked the “mother of all battles”.
The US has only deployed the MOAB once before – during its 2017 attacks on an Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP) cave and tunnel complex in Afghanistan. Afghan authorities claimed that while 94 Islamic State-Khorasan Province (ISKP) fighters were killed in the blast, no civilians were hurt. However, there were unconfirmed, local reports of civilian casualties and many homes were destroyed.
- Released from the aircraft.
- Cradle separates; GPS and fins guide it.
- H6 explosives detonate.
- A powerful shockwave spreads.
- Hot gases, smoke and debris rise in a mushroom cloud.
What kind of damage can it cause?
Designed to explode a few feet above the ground, the MOAB sends out lethal waves of fire when it detonates, blasting away buildings, cave openings and other hard-surface structures.
“Its purpose is to generate an exceptionally powerful blast across a surface area,” Magnier said.
Military expert Colonel Nidal Abu Zeid told Al Jazeera the bomb does not require impact in order to detonate and that its massive blast will destroy everything above ground within a 1km (0.6-mile) radius.
It is likely that the US would aim to use the high-explosive MOAB to completely destroy Iran’s ground-force positions above ground, and to reach its underground facilities, including Pickaxe Mountain, which Trump has previously threatened to attack, Abu Zeid said.
However, Magnier said the bomb’s radius and level of destruction would depend greatly on the terrain it is used within and how populated the area is. He added that it may not be particularly effective against targets buried deep underground.
Some of Iran’s nuclear sites which the US may wish to target, such as the Fordow complex and an under-construction site at the Pickaxe Mountain, are heavily fortified and deeply buried.
“Its large explosive charge can produce devastating blast effects against exposed personnel, equipment and vulnerable structures,” Magnier said. “The Afghanistan operation demonstrates its intended application against a cave-and-tunnel position; it does not demonstrate an ability to destroy every kind of underground installation.”
While its blast can reach underground, the MOAB is not especially designed to punch through deep concrete or mountain rock in the way that a “bunker buster” bomb is. The US military’s most powerful bunker buster is the GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator. Weighing about 30,000 pounds (13,600kg), including a 2,700kg (6,000 pound) warhead, this precision-guided bomb is made of high-strength steel and built to penetrate up to 200 feet (61 metres) underground before exploding.
Would the US really use an MOAB?
It already has done – in Afghanistan in 2017.
However, besides not being guaranteed to hit underground targets effectively, Magnier told Al Jazeera it could be difficult to deploy the necessary aircraft in the regions of Iran where nuclear sites are located. Stealth bombers which are better suited to this terrain are not able to carry this size of bomb.
Using the bomb could also destroy infrastructure without inducing Iran to make any concessions, he added, noting that its deployment would risk turning “a spectacular event” into one that ultimately delivers few political results for Washington.
“The question I would put to any commander advocating its use is straightforward: What will this weapon accomplish that another available weapon cannot, and how will that result advance an achievable political settlement?,” Magnier said.
“If the answer centres on the spectacle of the explosion, the proposal is stronger as political theatre than as military strategy,” he added.
CNN reported that Trump, in private discussions, has been seeking a “definitive” end to the war that will prove Washington has been undefeated.
How might Iran respond?
A MOAB strike would likely prompt a major reaction from Iran, experts say, warning that Tehran could even invade its neighbours who host US military assets in response.
Iranian security officials have for months made comments regarding a possible invasion of countries like Kuwait to capture US troops and force Washington to surrender.
In May, during a pause in hostilities, Kuwait alleged that sailors from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) infiltrated its Bubiyan Island, leading to an exchange of fire between Iranian and Kuwaiti forces. One Kuwaiti was injured and four Iranian soldiers were captured.
Iran denied that it had invaded the island and said the troops’ navigation system had malfunctioned.
On Tuesday, IRGC security adviser Mohammad Reza Naghdi warned that Iran could capture troops if Washington were to launch ground attacks, although military experts have long dismissed Trump’s earlier threats of an invasion due to Iran’s mountainous terrain.
“If the United States launches a ground attack, so many of its troops will be captured that it will be forced to raise the white flag,” he said.
Experts say Iran has been preparing for another round of war by stockpiling weapons, fortifying key nuclear and defence locations, and rallying its supporters.
In a television broadcast on Sunday, National Security Council chief Mohsen Rezaei threatened that Iran would attack regional digital infrastructure, including communication cables, data centres and artificial intelligence facilities in the United Arab Emirates and others, if American strikes resume.

crafted from mycelium, hypha-lume pavilion maps human movement through light
what if a pavilion could remember every movement within it? hypha-lume combines reconfigurable mycelium modules with sensors, light, projection, and sound to transform human presence into an evolving spatial memory.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
MYCELIUM MODULES ADAPT TO VARIED SPATIAL CONFIGURATIONS
Hypha-Lume is an adaptive modular pavilion that uses reconfigurable mycelium components, sensors, projection, and sound to translate human movement into spatial data. Conceived as a responsive system, the structure incorporates three block types with curvatures of 20, 40, and 60 degrees. These tapered biomaterial modules connect around vertical supports for structural stability, allowing the shell to be reassembled into varied configurations depending on site requirements.
INTEGRATED SENSORS TRANSLATE HUMAN MOVEMENT INTO LIGHT
The pavilion, conceived by Darya Holub, Selin Ozasik, Pinak Bhapkar, Nikhil Narendiran and Baskar Bharathwaj Subramanian, functions as an interactive archive of site activity. Integrated sensors track visitor paths, pauses, and gatherings, converting occupant movement into real-time light patterns and audio. While the structure is defined by its organic geometry and modular rhythm during the day, nighttime illumination projects layered visual traces of previous human interactions directly onto the building envelope.

name: Hypha-Lume
designer: Darya Holub, Selin Ozasik, Pinak Bhapkar, Nikhil Narendiran, Baskar Bharathwaj Subramanian
