Moving Taiwan beyond Double Ten
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:26:35 UTC
00:26:35 KST

Last weekend, Taiwan celebrated Double Ten National Day, marking 115 years since the Wuchang Uprising.
An Army CH-47SD Chinook carried a massive 12-by-18-meter ROC flag across downtown Taipei, accompanied by two UH-60M Black Hawk helicopters, passing over vibrant celebrations in front of the Presidential Office Building.
The spectacle made global headlines, with Reuters even titling its report “Giant Taiwan flag flies from helicopter for national day, defying Beijing.”
Yet the irony is that the flag is not originally Taiwanese, and its display hardly represents defiance of Beijing given that ROC flags have filled Double Ten celebrations in Taiwan for decades.
There is a deeper paradox. Double Ten commemorates an event that did not take place in Taiwan and did not significantly involve Taiwanese people.
Double Ten commemorates the 1911 Wuchang Uprising in Wuhan, China. It took place while Taiwan was under Japanese rule.
A historical event fundamentally external to Taiwan’s own historical narrative and collective memory will inevitably struggle to resonate widely with Taiwanese.
The uprising helped overthrow the Qing dynasty and paved the way for the establishment of the Republic of China. It was not until 1949 that the ROC government relocated to Taiwan.
Although Double Ten distinguishes Taiwan’s national commemoration from the People’s Republic of China’s Oct. 1 National Day, it continues to tie Taiwan to an outdated pan-Chinese political ideology.
To solidify Taiwan’s identity, break free from historical constraints, and signal its separate sovereignty to the international community, the country should establish a new and genuinely Taiwanese national day.
More troubling is that the giant flags flown over Taipei last Saturday still serve as a stark reminder to many Taiwanese of the KMT’s authoritarian legacy.
The upper-left “blue sky, white sun” portion of the ROC flag is also used by the KMT as its party emblem. After the ROC took control of Taiwan in 1945 and the KMT government relocated there in 1949, the party-state embedded ROC institutions and symbols throughout Taiwan.
As a minority regime ruling over a largely local Taiwanese population, the KMT imposed martial law to maintain political control and suppress threats to its rule.
Its central narrative for justifying the suspension of constitutional democracy, freezing elections, and almost four decades of authoritarian one-party rule was that the ROC government remained the sole legitimate government of all China and Taiwan was merely a temporary base from which it would eventually launch a counteroffensive to recover the “mainland.”
No other day of the year displayed that narrative more vividly.
To project legitimacy, the authoritarian KMT government gathered foreign dignitaries and overseas Chinese delegates for grand Double Ten celebrations in Taipei.
Outside this elite circle, many of whom had little or no connection to Taiwan, many Taiwanese looked on with indifference or quietly shook their heads for fear of the repercussions of disrupting the regime’s manufactured narrative.
Many local Taiwanese also felt alienated by Double Ten celebrations during martial law, which centered on a China-focused national narrative expressed overwhelmingly in Mandarin.
This excluded Hoklo, Hakka, and Indigenous Taiwanese communities, many of whose members did not speak Mandarin. For many, authoritarian ROC governance represented language erasure and suppression of culture and identity rather than national liberation.
Although the holiday can counter Beijing’s narrative by emphasizing the distinction between the ROC and PRC, Double Ten nevertheless commemorates the founding story of a political system born in China.
Celebrating a national day with origins in the heart of China continues to tie Taiwan to a Greater China political framework. Beijing can exploit this ambiguity to bolster its narrative that Taiwan is an integral part of China that must ultimately be “unified,” by force if necessary.
It also reinforces the international ambiguity Beijing has worked to shape.
When international media report that Taiwan is celebrating a Chinese uprising as its national day, it can blur the reality of Taiwan’s current de facto independence and its existence as a sovereign political entity separate from China.
Breaking free of this Greater China framework will require a new national anchor.
Double Ten represents to many Taiwanese an imported historical narrative and a dark authoritarian past. Taiwan deserves better.
The country is no longer an authoritarian regime in exile, but a vibrant modern democracy. Celebrating a violent historical event that did not even take place in Taiwan sits awkwardly beside the democratic values that distinguish modern Taiwan so sharply from China.
While Taiwan’s government and civil society promote those values, celebrating a date tied to bloodshed in China more than a century ago risks confusing the story Taiwan tells about itself to the world.
A national day should also belong to the land and the people living on it. The Wuchang Uprising obviously did not take place in Taiwan.
Without the coercive machinery that once imposed a singular national narrative, it is difficult to expect Taiwan’s diverse communities to rally around a commemoration so distant from their own histories.
The national fabric would be better woven around a Taiwan-centered cause that people of different languages, cultures, backgrounds, generations, and newer immigrant communities can share. It would also help disentangle Taiwan’s statehood from the ROC’s founding history in China.
Taiwan needs a forward-looking national day that celebrates its democratic progress.
March 23 or May 20 could serve as alternatives. March 23 marks Taiwan’s first direct presidential election in 1996, while May 20 is the traditional inauguration day for Taiwan’s democratically elected presidents.
Either could serve as a reminder of the democratic mandate of Taiwan’s people and their collective journey toward self-government. May 20 could even allow national celebrations to coincide with presidential inaugurations every four years.
With China increasing pressure to distort Taiwan’s political reality, there is an even greater need for the country to step out of Double Ten’s Chinese shadow and tell the world that Taiwan is Taiwan.
A genuinely Taiwanese national day would make clear that Taiwan’s modern identity is rooted in the history, democratic choices, and political sovereignty of the people who live here.
Rath Wang is a political commentator based in Taipei focusing on Taiwan’s politics, media, civil society, and key issues influencing Taiwan’s future. He is a media producer and host of current affairs talk shows and podcasts and has worked on political campaigns and lived in Taiwan, Japan, Thailand, and the US.

El Nino a 'terrifying' threat to coral reefs: UN biodiversity expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:23:16 UTC
00:23:16 KST

El Nino a ‘terrifying’ threat to coral reefs: UN biodiversity expert
PARIS, France – A super El Nino fuelling record ocean temperatures poses a “terrifying” threat to the world’s fragile coral reefs, the chair of the UN’s expert nature panel told AFP.
Marine scientist David Obura said the exceptional El Nino pattern building strength in the tropical Pacific could drive vulnerable coral species even closer toward extinction.
Corals are heat sensitive and particularly vulnerable to climate change, which is heating the world’s oceans and increasing the frequency and intensity of damaging bleaching events.
But 2026’s El Nino layers “a terrifying level of additional risk”, said Obura, a Kenyan reef expert and chair of IPBES, the UN’s expert scientific panel on biodiversity.
The warming phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino events temporarily elevate global temperatures, altering cloud and wind patterns, and raise the risk of damaging weather.
Global forecasters expect this episode to be the strongest on record, and sea surface temperatures in parts of the Pacific have already hit all-time highs months before its expected peak.
That greatly concerns Obura, who recalled the damaging impact of a previous super El Nino episode in 1997/98.
“That this coming event is worse than that, after three intervening global bleaching events ... is a terrifying reality,” he said.
Significant worsening
Obura led a major reassessment of coral health published in Nature on Thursday that reported a sharp deterioration in reef-building species since the last global census in 2008.
“Our results show that by 2020, nearly half of coral species were at elevated relative risk of extinction” with climate change the main driver of this decline, wrote Obura and dozens of top scientists.
The review covered hundreds of species on the IUCN’s “red list” – icons like staghorn and table corals whose mineral skeletons give reefs their dazzling three-dimensional complexity.
This “indicates conditions for corals are worsening significantly... not at all surprising given the accelerated warming and lack of abatement of global drivers of coral decline”, said Obura.
But the study was completed in 2020 and the findings today would be even bleaker, he said.
Since then, global ocean temperatures have soared to unprecedented highs and the worst coral bleaching episode on record between 2023 and 2025 caused widespread mortality across reefs.
“It is entirely possible that reassessing the status of corals just after this coming El Nino may show them to have crossed the 50 percent mark of the proportion of species at elevated risk of extinction,” said Obura.
In 2025, scientists warned that warm-water coral reefs had almost certainly crossed a point of no return as oceans warm beyond a level most can survive.
The study in Nature said that projected rises in ocean temperatures and other pressures “primarily determined when and where, rather than if, conditions will become unviable for corals”.
“When they hit their threshold the collapse of reefs in that region could be precipitous and we don’t know if that is five, 15 or 30 years into the future, or maybe this year with the super El Nino ramping up,” said Obura. AFP

Man with suitcase full of snakes stopped at German airport
- Published
A man has been stopped at Cologne Bonn Airport in Germany after trying to smuggle in more than 90 lizards and venomous snakes.
Customs officials said the 45-year-old Mexican firefighter had looked "conspicuously nervous" as he tried to go through the green - nothing to declare - exit at the airport.
They conducted a drugs test on the man - which came back positive for cocaine - before proceeding to check his suitcase.
They did not find any drugs, but vipers, rattlesnakes and other species of snakes and lizards, including iguanas, hidden in shampoo and cream bottles, plastic containers and balls of socks.
"My colleagues at the airport are used to a lot when it comes to souvenirs in suitcases, but we've never had 37 live venomous snakes and 55 lizards from Mexico before," said Jens Ahland, spokesman for the Cologne Customs office.
Some were being kept "in inhumane conditions", Ahland said. Others had died during the journey from Mexico City via Istanbul.
The man, who has not been named, told officers that he had brought the animals back as a favour for a Brazilian acquaintance.
He was denied entry to Germany and flown back to Istanbul.
As for the surviving animals, they are being looked after at a snake farm in Germany.
"Last year, we had over 1,300 seizures nationwide involving more than 56,600 protected animals and plants or products made from them," the Customs spokesman said.
Six years ago, 26 rare reptiles - 10 of them dead - smuggled inside parcels of toys and sweets from Mexico, were found by customs officials at Cologne Bonn Airport.
They were destined for private buyers in Germany.

15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
The head of Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom said Thursday that a local ceasefire is being implemented near the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) to allow repairs at the facility under Moscow’s control.
Alexey Likhachev told reporters in Moscow that power supply to the ZNPP via the 330kV Ferosplavnaya-1 backup external power line is “extremely unstable and fraught with risks,” noting a “very high probability” of recurring loss of a stable power supply to the plant due to the “semi-destroyed state” of the nearby Zaporizhzhia Thermal Power Plant (ZTPP).
Likhachev said Russia began efforts to arrange a localized ceasefire days ago to facilitate repairs at the ZTPP, and that the plant’s switchgear is essential for ensuring safety and power supply, including for the ZNPP.
“By engaging the IAEA (International Atomic Energy Agency) and coordinating with our relevant ministries … we have successfully established a ‘regime of silence’ at the ZTPP today,” Likhachev was quoted by Russian media outlets, including state news agency Tass.
He went on to say that Rosatom specialists are heading to the site to begin repairing technical equipment, which he said will help strengthen power supply to the ZNPP.
The situation around the ZNPP, Europe’s largest nuclear power plant and one of the world’s 10 largest, remains tense amid persistent concerns about a potential nuclear disaster, as Moscow and Kyiv frequently accuse each other of carrying out attacks around the facility in southeastern Ukraine.
Since Sept. 1, 2022, IAEA personnel have been stationed at the plant, which Russia has controlled since March 2022.
IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi announced earlier this month that he was negotiating a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine to allow repairs at the ZTPP.

Syrian court sentences two to death over 2025 coastal violence

Unknown Publisher

15:19:18 UTC

Syrian court sentences two to death over 2025 coastal violence
Court rulings concern violence and killings during March 2025 uprising by pro-Assad forces, and retaliatory attacks.
A court in Syria has sentenced to death two supporters of the ousted Bashar al-Assad regime for inciting an uprising last year, and handed hefty sentences to members of the current government’s security forces for the killing of hundreds of civilians from the Alawite religious minority.
The Military Criminal Court at the Justice Palace in the northern city of Aleppo gave death sentences to Al-Waddah Ismail and Maher Ali, according to state media.
The Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA) reported that the pair were convicted of seeking to incite civil war and sectarian fighting and for leading armed gangs with the intent to attack public forces.
A third defendant, Maher Othman, was sentenced to 12 years in prison, the court also announced on Thursday without immediately specifying the charges on which he was convicted.
In separate rulings, the court sentenced Mohammed Bakour, a member of the Defence Ministry’s 82nd Division in the new government, to 20 years in prison after convicting him of intentional homicide.
It also sentenced Ammar Abdul Aal to three years for torture and acquitted Abdul Raouf Bakrjan and Mohammed Zarzouri, SANA said.
The rulings concern investigations carried out by a government committee into attacks in March last year. At least 1,426 people, mostly civilians, were killed in several days of sectarian violence in the predominantly Alawite areas of Syria’s coastal regions.
The defendants included loyalists to the former al-Assad regime and members of the new government’s security forces. It is the first time government-linked personnel have been put on trial for acts of violence.
The government committee said it had identified 298 suspects implicated in serious violations during the violence in the Alawite heartland.
The committee’s investigation documented “serious violations against civilians on March 7, 8 and 9 [2025], including murder, premeditated murder, looting, destruction and burning of homes, torture and sectarian insults”.
The committee said 238 members of the army and security forces were killed by pro-Assad fighters in the attacks in the provinces of Tartous, Latakia and Hama.
About 200,000 pro-government military reinforcements then converged on the area, carrying out alleged revenge killings.
Al Jazeera’s Heidi Pett, reporting from the Syrian capital, Damascus, said the uprising was started by individuals still loyal to the regime of al-Assad, who himself is from the Alawite religious minority.
“After the Assad regime fell and its leadership fled the country at the end of 2024, supporters including loyal soldiers from the ousted regime as well as militia members fled to the mountains from where they launched an uprising in March 2025 against the new government”, Pett said.
She added that forces loyal to the new government are accused of killing civilians from the Alawite minority group in revenge attacks.
“These trials are for seven men who took part in the initial pro-Assad uprising, and also seven members of the new government’s security forces who were subsequently deployed into the area and are accused of carrying out revenge attacks,” she said.
SANA reported that on September 17, the court issued verdicts in cases involving four other defendants accused of violations during the events in the coastal region last March. One was sentenced to death, one to life imprisonment and one to 20 years in prison; the fourth was acquitted.

Interview: Chinese desertification control expert calls for global unity to protect planet
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
23:19:11 CST
00:19:11 KST

ROME, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- A leading Chinese expert on desertification control has called for global unity to protect food security and the environment.
Yin Yuzhen, who has spent more than four decades restoring the Maowusu Sandy Land in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, said in a recent interview with Xinhua that she hopes to share her experience and inspire collective efforts to safeguard the future of the planet.
Yin was named one of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations' (FAO) 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development on Thursday.
Speaking to Xinhua in Rome, she said desertification control has not only transformed the local environment but also created new opportunities for rural residents to improve their livelihoods.
"I have spent more than 40 years transforming this desert, and now all kinds of food can grow here," Yin said.
Since planting her first tree in 1986, Yin has helped green over 70,000 mu (around 4,667 hectares) -- an area roughly the size of 6,500 standard soccer pitches -- of sandy land. Today, the area supports a greater variety of crops and plants, including cherries and roses, creating new opportunities for agricultural production and income growth.
For Yin, combating desertification is closely linked to food security. "If we cannot control the sand, how can we grow good crops when sandstorms come? How can we improve the soil?" she said, stressing that protecting the land is essential to producing quality agricultural products and ensuring that ecological restoration benefits local communities.
"The Maowusu Sandy Land has turned green, and now it is becoming a land of gold," she said, describing the transformation as an example of the Chinese concept that lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets.
Yin's work has also fostered a friendship that transcends national borders. In 1999, Ronald Sakolsky, an American teaching in China at the time, saw a television report on Yin's tree-planting efforts and raised 5,000 U.S. dollars to support her work.
Like the trees, their friendship has grown and endured.
"Although we come from two different countries and speak different languages, our hearts are connected," Yin said.
She sees their friendship as a reflection of the need for international cooperation in environmental protection.
"It is like the vision of a community with a shared future for humanity proposed by China. Although we come from different countries, we live on the same planet," she said. "We must unite to cherish nature and protect our planet."
Yin hopes to share her experience with communities facing land degradation, drought and desertification. Although conditions vary across regions, she believes that determination, and locally adapted approaches can help restore degraded land and improve people's lives.
The year 2026 has been designated by the United Nations as the International Year of the Woman Farmer. Yin said women play an important role in families and society and deserve greater support and opportunities in agriculture and rural development.
"They need not only equal status, but also more opportunities to put their abilities to use," she said. "Give them a little sunshine, and they will flourish."
Being named one of the FAO's 100 Women Heroes is both a recognition of Yin's past efforts, and an encouragement to continue her work, which shows that perseverance and cooperation can transform barren land into a fertile landscape.
"Like a Mongolian horse, I will keep pressing forward with perseverance and determination," she said. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang held talks in Beijing on Thursday with President of the Council of Ministers of Togo Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, who is on an official visit to China.
Li said that in recent years, under the strategic guidance of the leaders of the two countries, China-Togo relations have continuously reached new heights.
Chinese President Xi Jinping met with Faure on Tuesday, and the two leaders elevated bilateral relations to a China-Togo community with a shared future for the new era and made new plans for expanding bilateral cooperation, Li said.
No matter how the international landscape may change, China is willing to work with Togo to always remain good brothers and good partners who trust each other, carry forward the traditional friendship, consolidate political mutual trust, deepen cooperation in various fields, and better serve the modernization endeavors of both countries, he said.
Li noted that China is willing to deepen the synergy between their development strategies, explore and foster more growth areas for cooperation, and strengthen cooperation in such fields as infrastructure connectivity, agricultural modernization and finance, to jointly strengthen the driving forces for the development of the two countries.
China is willing to import more quality products from Togo, Li said, adding that Togo is welcome to make full use of policy facilitation measures provided by China, including the zero-tariff treatment and upgraded "green channel" for products exported to China.
The two sides can strengthen cooperation in such areas as healthcare, youth, culture, think tanks and subnational exchanges to enhance mutual understanding and friendship between the two peoples, Li said.
China is willing to work with Togo and other African countries to actively implement the 10 partnership actions between China and Africa and contribute to lasting peace, development and prosperity in Africa, he added.
Faure said the friendship between Togo and China has a long history, and China's rapid development has set an example for the world.
Togo firmly supports the one-China principle, and is willing to deepen practical cooperation with China in such fields as economy and trade, investment, agricultural products, customs quarantine science and technology, artificial intelligence, infrastructure, and education and training, to improve the well-being of the two peoples, he said.
Togo supports resolving differences and addressing hotspot issues in Africa through dialogue, and is willing to strengthen multilateral coordination with China to safeguard regional peace and stability, Faure added. ■

LISBON, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Thirty-seven participants in a housing rights protest in Porto were injured in the early hours of Thursday when police took action to end a sit-in encampment that had been occupying Praca D. Joao I since Saturday, two of them sustaining what the organizer of the protest described as serious injuries.
"At 02:56 (0156 GMT) on Thursday, police forces intervened at the housing encampment at Praca D. Joao I, Porto, in an operation aimed at ending the protest," the Movimento pela Habitacao said in a statement, adding that among those hurt was a person with a disability and that two people suffered fractures requiring hospitalization.

In Portugal, housing prices rose 17.8 percent year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026, the highest increase in the European Union, while median rents on new contracts grew 9.1 percent in the same period. ■

====================================================================================================

ACC Mulls Commercial Counter-Drone Services for Air Base Defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:15:36 UTC
00:15:36 KST

Air Combat Command is looking for defense firms capable of providing a private counter-drone service, complete with the personnel to operate it, for defending air bases across the Air Force.
ACC, which oversees the service’s Point Defense Task Force, is conducting a market survey to identify companies specializing in counter-small unmanned aerial systems defense technology that can provide “C-sUAS as a Service,” according to an Oct. 13 solicitation.
According to the solicitation, the intent of the service model is to:
- Provide organic, resilient, sustainable, and agile Point Defense capabilities across Department of the Air Force installations
- Implement a flexible, scalable architecture allowing installations to scale operational capacity up or down based on dynamic threat levels
- Leverage mature, commercially available or rapidly adaptable systems rather than initiating high-risk developmental programs
The market survey comes as the Air Force races to develop an arsenal of capabilities to defend its installations against drone threat.
“The Government envisions an initial prototype deployment at two designated Continental United States Air Force installations, with option mechanisms to scale across additional ACC installations upon proven performance,” the document states.
Interested firms have until Oct. 31 to respond to the solicitation. ACC is interested in companies that can provide technology for detecting, tracking, and identifying drones—ranging from small quadcopters to larger, Group 3 systems like the Iranian Shahed one-way attack drones that weight up to 1,320 pounds—at distances of up to five miles from a base perimeter, the document states.
Firms should also be capable of incorporating “government-approved kinetic and/or nonkinetic” effectors that range from radio frequency jamming to directed-energy such as lasers and high-powered microwave systems, the document states. Interested defense firms would also have to show they would continuously refresh software and hardware “within a multiyear service contract without frequent contract modifications,” according to the document.
ACC would also want a commercial capability to have the built-in logistical support to be self-sufficient for up to 96 hours, the document states.
The concept would require the contractor to “provide a complete, integrated, turn-key service solution covering materiel, personnel, training, sustainment, and ongoing modernization,” the solicitation states.
It’s unclear how this commercial service would align with the service’s intent to create a new point defense career field for enlisted Airmen, training and equipping them to defend air bases from drone and missile attack. The Air Force is slated to start designating Airmen with the new specialty within two years. As a short-term fix, the service has established point defense flights, specialized units of roughly 20 Airmen each, trained to rapidly deploy to hotspots and defend air bases against drone attacks.
Currently, the Air Force is equipping installations with the Small Unmanned Air Defense Systems, or SUADS, for countering drones. The system is capable of identifying and tracking enemy missiles or drones of multiple sizes, and downing incoming drones with an electronic warfare weapon. To stop missiles, it uses both electronic warfare and kinetic effectors. It can also interface with commercial counter-drone systems and other air defense systems, depending on the needs of a commander.
The service is also acquiring additional counter-drone systems through the Pentagon’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401. In the future, counter-drone technology will fall under the “point defense weapon system,” a classification to manage multiple counter-drone systems that range from sensors, radars, and command and control architecture to kinetic and non-kinetic effectors for disabling or destroying incoming drones.

Gökhan Ergöçün
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Istanbul Airport ranked as the busiest airport in Europe with an average of 1,530 daily flights last week. 
The European Organization for the Safety of Air Navigation (EUROCONTROL) released on Thursday its European Aviation Report covering the period of Oct. 5-11. 
Amsterdam Airport followed Istanbul Airport with an average of 1,386 daily flights, ahead of Paris Charles de Gaulle with 1,361, Frankfurt with 1,358, and Madrid with 1,305 flights.
Antalya Airport in southern Türkiye claimed the 10th spot among Europe's busiest airports, recording an average of 909 daily flights.

Ukraine has exhausted its stockpile of missiles for Patriot systems - media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:13:46 EEST
00:13:46 KST

Ukraine has exhausted its stockpile of missiles for Patriot systems - media
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine has exhausted its stockpile of Patriot missiles, CNN reports. Due to the shortage, nearly all ballistic missiles were not intercepted during the latest strike.
Ukraine is running out of Patriot air defense missiles, making it more vulnerable to Russian attacks. CNN reports this, according to UNN.
Ukraine has exhausted its stockpiles of missiles for the American Patriot air defense system, making it more vulnerable to attacks by Russian ballistic missiles
As noted, for several months, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly warned that Ukraine is running out of American Patriot interceptor missiles, which are one of the few types of defensive weapons capable of shooting down ballistic missiles.
However, these interceptor missiles are expensive, and there are not enough of them in the world, as other countries have depleted their stockpiles or are trying to strengthen their own defense systems amid the war in Iran.
A source told CNN that "almost all ballistic missiles during the latest strike were not intercepted due to a shortage of missiles."
It should be recalled
Greece and Spain have stockpiles of interceptor missiles for Patriot air defense systems whose service life is nearing its end. These missiles could be transferred to Ukraine, but the countries are so far refusing.

Houthis target Yemen gov't headquarters in Aden
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:13:25 UTC
00:13:25 KST

We're closing this live page now.
Join us back here from 0700 tomorrow for more live coverage of developments in the Middle East.
Thanks for following.
This live blog has now ended. Make sure to follow us for the latest news on Facebook, X, and Instagram.
You can follow developments from earlier on Thursday by visiting our previous live page here.
These were the key events on Thursday afternoon:
• Yemen's Houthis launched a missile attack on the presidential palace in the southern city of Aden. The government - which is headquarted at the palace - said that the prime minister and other ministers were unharmed by the attack.
•    Media affiliated with the group said it targeted the "headquarters of military operations, led by Saudi officers" at the palace.
•    Major fighting continues across multiple fronts in Yemen's Taiz, with significant casualties reported on all sides.
•    The Saudi-led coalition said it shot down a missile near Medina. The Houthis denied  launching the attack.
•    Two ships have sunk near the Strait of Hormuz, one hit by a projectile and the other by a sea mine, as ongoing attacks impact maritime traffic.
•    Iran says it is preparing for war amid US reports that the Trump administration is mulling using its largest munitions if it resumes attacks.
The UN Security Council issued a joint statement on Thursday condemning the "escalatory" attacks by Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia, including "reckless strikes" on Riyadh's airport.
The Saudi capital's international airport has been targeted by strikes 20 times since the beginning of the month, with an attack last weekend killing 13 people and wounding more than 300.
In a joint statement shared by the Security Council's president, Greece's Evangelos Sekeris, the 15-member UN body "condemned in the strongest terms continued and escalatory Houthi attacks against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia," as well as "continued Houthi attacks and threats against commercial shipping in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab (Strait)."
The statement also "affirmed the inherent right of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia of self-defence in accordance with international law."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Lebanon's president on Thursday that he should not return several hundred kilograms of explosives seized by Lebanese authorities from Hezbollah, a US official said.
"He urged President (Joseph) Aoun to hold accountable all those who ordered, financed, and directed the shipment, and underscored that returning explosives to Hezbollah should be out of the question," the official told reporters on condition of anonymity.
A Yemeni government minister said on condition of anonymity Thursday that a Houthi missile attack on the presidential palace in Aden had hit a command centre of the Saudi-led coalition fighting against the group.
The minister said the Houthis hit a command centre for Yemeni government "forces with three missiles and the headquarters of the Saudi-led coalition forces at the presidential complex with two missiles", adding that there were Yemeni and Saudi casualties, without providing a specific toll.
The prime minister of Yemen's internationally recognised government was present at the presidential palace in Aden on Thursday when the Houthis attacked the compound with missiles, though he was not hurt, a Yemeni minister told AFP on condition of anonymity
The minister said that premier Shaya al-Zindani "was not harmed in any way" in the attack.
The Israeli military said Thursday it had killed two Palestinians in Khan Younis the day before, claiming they were smuggling weapons into Gaza, without providing evidence.
Palestinian news agency WAFA reported that two men, identified as Basel Nabil Abd al-Rahman Kashta and Ahmad Raja al-Shaer, were killed in an airstrike targeting a vehicle in the southern city. The attack also injured a Palestinian woman.
A failure by the United States and Iran to agree within weeks on a UN-backed plan for moving fertilizer through the Strait of Hormuz could cause a food security crisis in parts of Asia and Africa, an official overseeing the proposed scheme said on Wednesday.
The United Nations set up a taskforce in March to facilitate passage of fertilizers through the strait. It is yet to implement the mechanism it drew up, but United Nations Under-Secretary-General Jorge Moreira da Silva said this could be activated within 7-10 days of an agreement between Washington and Tehran.
"It's absolutely crucial to get the deal in the next few weeks. Otherwise, we will miss the planting season," he said in an interview in Bangkok, on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings.
The Trump administration has issued fresh Iran-related sanctions targeting 16 individuals and 10 entities, according to a notice posted on the US Department of Treasury website on Thursday.
A Hezbollah MP acknowledged on Thursday that a 500-kilogram shipment of explosives seized last week by Lebanese authorities belonged to the group, a rare admission by the Iran-backed group.
"The vehicle and its cargo belong to the resistance" against Israel, lawmaker Hassan Fadlallah said.
He said Hezbollah also called for the immediate release of those arrested over the seizure.
Fadlallah demanded the return of the shipment, seized on a road linking eastern Lebanon to Beirut, saying it constituted "capabilities" used by Hezbollah against Israel.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has said the state will no longer tolerate any possession of "illegal weapons".
At least four people were killed and 10 more wounded in the Houthi missile attack on Yemen's presidential palace in Aden, three government military sources told AFP.
The forces of Yemen's internationally recognised government said Thursday that the Houthis had fired ballistic missiles at the central city of Marib, which sits in a strategic oil-rich region.
"Houthi terrorist militias fired several ballistic missiles at the densely populated city of Marib," the government forces said on X.
Yemen's information ministry is reporting that two guards were killed in the Houthi missile attack on the presidential palace in Aden.
Yemen's prime minister and other cabinet ministers were unharmed in the Houthi attack on the Al-Maashiq presidential palace in Aden.
Yemeni Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said that the group had fired five missiles at the palace, which is the headquarters of the internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government.
Houthi media have said that the group targeted a military headquarters at the palace.
Yemen's Houthis attacked a military headquarters at the presidential palace in Aden, which also serves as the seat of the internationally recognised government, media affiliated with the group reported Thursday.
The pro-Iranian fighters targeted "the headquarters of military operations, led by Saudi officers, at the Al-Maashiq Palace in Aden, as well as weapons depots belonging to them", according to the group's news agency.

Bundeswehr Orders 15 Watercat M18 AMC Combat Boats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:13:11 UTC
00:13:11 KST

The Bundeswehr has ordered 15 Watercat M18 AMC multi-purpose combat boats from the Finnish company Marine Alutech Oy Ab.
The contract was signed on October 12, 2026, by the Federal Office of Bundeswehr Equipment, Information Technology and In-Service Support (BAAINBw), according to Militär Aktuell.
The boats are intended for the German Navy’s Marine Corps battalion, which carries out missions in coastal waters and on land in the coastal zone.
In addition to the 15 boats, the contract covers personnel training, documentation, and additional equipment.
Delivery of all 15 Watercat M18 AMC boats to the Bundeswehr is scheduled for 2029–2031.
The procurement is intended to increase the tactical mobility of the German Navy’s marines and enable faster deployment of units between sea and shore in areas where the use of larger vessels is limited.
The Watercat M18 AMC is a high-speed armored combat boat developed by the Finnish shipbuilding company Marine Alutech Oy Ab.
Measuring 19.9 meters in length and 4.3 meters in width, the M18 can accommodate 30 people, 26 of whom are marines, for whom individual seats are provided.
The boat can reach a maximum speed of over 40 knots and maintain a sustained cruising speed of up to 35 knots when fully loaded. Its range is 370 kilometers.
The boat’s hull and superstructure are made of aluminum alloy and composite materials, which incorporate ballistic protection against light small arms fire. The vessel’s standard armament consists of a remotely controlled module equipped with a 12.7 mm machine gun.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that Lithuania and Latvia had signed a joint contract with Marine Alutech as part of the Common Future Multipurpose Attack Craft (CFMAC) program. The program involves the procurement of multipurpose combat boats based on the Watercat M18.

West Nile virus creeps north in record year for EU cases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:12:36 UTC
00:12:36 KST

Workers spray to combat the spread of mosquitoes in the municipality of Kordelio in Greece after the detection of West Nile virus, on Sept. 3, 2026. | Konstantinos Tsakalidis/SOOC/AFP via Getty Images
Greece, Italy and France are the worst affected countries, but the virus is spreading further north, authorities say.
Advertisement
"Recent detections in people and animals in Belgium and the Netherlands show that the virus is now circulating further north, a trend that is expected to continue in the coming years," the ECDC said.
The Netherlands has reported 59 human cases so far this year, while Belgium has reported 15.
The West Nile virus is asymptomatic in 80% of humans — but can lead to fever and, in severe cases, cause neurological diseases and become deadly.
Preventive measures against mosquito bites are recommended to reduce West Nile virus risks.
"Anyone living in or visiting areas where WNV is circulating can reduce their risk by using mosquito repellent, wearing loose-fitting long clothing in the evening and at night, and using window screens, mosquito nets, or air conditioning where appropriate," the ECDC said.

Just as Saint Nige thought it was safe to reappear, along comes pesky ITV | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:11:28 UTC
00:11:28 KST

Sometimes the world can be very unfair. As though life is just one cruel joke. How else to make sense of everything? For when the history books come to be written, Nigel Farage will go down as one of the century’s unluckiest politicians.
Poor Nige. All he has ever wanted is a better Britain. A country united in a shared vision where everyone gets along with one another. Where people of all faiths and none look out for each other. Where men and women of all colours are treated as equals. Where Nige can teach the world to sing in perfect harmony.
So why do so many bad things keep happening to such a good person? Where’s the justice in that? How come Nige has been given a lead role in the rewrite of Little Britain’s Book of Job. Nige as a latter day Old Testament prophet put on Earth to show us all the value of eternal suffering. Because Nige is a decent man. The very best of us. And yet time and again he is made to feel pain. No more so than in the last few months.
First there was the money. Few would have batted an eyelid if he had been given £5m by the RNLI. For all he has done to support the work that unpaid volunteers do in rescuing all people in trouble on the sea. Let’s face it, a modern day ministry doesn’t pay for itself and no demigod-like politician can expect to get by on less than £1m a year. Those houses and bottles of champagne aren’t going to pay for themselves. Yet because the £5m came from a Thai crypto-billionaire, suddenly everyone was asking difficult questions. Anyone would think Reform might have crypto-friendly policies.
Then there was the Channel 4 sting. And yet again our Messiah was the innocent victim of an establishment plot. Compared to Nige, Jesus had it easy in Holy Week. How could he be expected to realise that two associates whom he had barely known for years might allegedly be trying to secure an illegal donation from overseas? And what were the chances that Nige might be caught on camera giving considered responses as part of a conversation he hadn’t even been listening to? Some days you just can’t buy a break.
On Thursday morning, Farage had been scheduled to host a press conference near Southend where we were promised he would spread goodwill to all men with yet another major policy announcement. Only for the event to be cancelled late on Wednesday evening. The official reason given was that Reform didn’t want to clash with the fifth anniversary of the murder of the former Southend MP David Amess. Yet more bad luck for Nige. Imagine only being given five years’ notice to plan your schedule.
Or perhaps there was another reason for the cancellation. One related to another sting, this time by ITV, that had sent undercover journalists into the Reform operations room and uncovered the only bad apples in the entire organisation. Again, what were the chances of finding racists and misogynists attracted to a party that loved women and people of all colours?
How could this ever have happened? The chances were slimmer than winning the EuroMillions lottery. And surely had nothing to do with Nige’s would-be chancellor, Honest Bob Jenrick, saying he would consider allowing soldiers to be able to blow up migrants in small boats in the Channel. What’s wrong with killing a few thousand people for the sake of a greater good? The country is just too woke for its own good sometimes. Then there’s the wannabe home secretary Zia Yusuf, who is on a one-man mission to round up all immigrants – even women and children – and send them back to countries where they may be killed. So again we are left with the question. Why are so many racists attracted to Reform?
Let’s take Dean Miller. A vetted Reform councillor from Bromley who was filmed campaigning during the Makerfield byelection. Quite how extensive the vetting process was is anyone’s guess. “Tell us, Dean. Are you in any way prejudiced against people of colour?”. “Absolutely not. I just don’t want them anywhere near me.” “That’s great. Thanks Dean. Welcome to Reform.”
Anyway, Dean was caught on camera saying that it was kill or be killed with illegal immigrants. “They’re all fucking black and they’re like animals,” he said. “I’m not a racist, but you know what I mean.” Yes, Dean. We know exactly what you mean. And he couldn’t have been clearer about his intentions towards the king. Charles was a Muslim and deserved to be beheaded. It’s a view.
When Miller was asked for a comment before the film is aired this weekend, his defence was that he had been on heavy medication at the time. And suddenly that all made sense. Because I too am on regular medication both for my psyche and for my heart. So I chose to reread the common known side effects of one of my drugs. And there among the small print about causing faster breathing, fever, muscle stiffness and drowsiness, one thing stood out. “Never take in the presence of a black person or royalty. Can make you prone to racist outbursts and in extreme cases can provoke urges to kill the monarch.” I guess I must just have been extremely lucky so far.
Miller was not the only one to have been caught out this way. Others – also apparently vetted – declared that all foreigners were parasites, that the UK should have a 1% limit on all immigrants and made disgusting comments about a female Reform councillor. Raymond Dunning said he was so far-far right it was unbelievable. Then there were those who thought it best to try to sound moderate until after they had been elected. Then the gloves would come off and they could give foreigners hell.
And in the middle of all this we have the saintly Nige. Scratching his head and wondering why all this was happening to him again. He hadn’t come in to politics to stir grievance and division. He was the god of love, the man of peace. Others among the Reform elite knew exactly where the blame lay. And it wasn’t with the innocent men who had been caught saying the only racist and sexist words they had ever said. Dicky Tice and the former Tory MP Ben Bradley were pointing the finger at ITV for daring to do its job properly. It was outrageous they had recorded Reform councillors going about their everyday jobs. Every man and woman was entitled to be as racist as they like in the comfort of their workplace.
For now, Nige was determined to rise above it. He would survive. He was doing God’s work. Just a shame that God didn’t seem to like him much.

Is the AI mathocalypse coming for encryption next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:11:15 UTC
00:11:15 KST

Last week OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, dropped 722 mathematical manuscripts online in one go, every one of them penned by an artificial intelligence model unavailable to the public. The output was far from perfect: OpenAI withdrew three of the papers within a day, and mathematicians are still poring over the rest. But the scale of the research, and the incisiveness of its insights, has some worried.
Math powers cryptography. Every text you send and every bank log-in you submit is protected by a math problem that’s supposedly impossible to crack. The system rests on the assumption that no one will figure out how. And AI just showed it’s pretty good at math.
That worries Matthew Green, a cryptographer at Johns Hopkins University. In a social media post a few days after OpenAI’s massive math release, he suggested there was a 15 percent chance that we could lose confidence in existing public-key encryption algorithms—which allow computers to establish secure connections and verify digital identities without first exchanging a shared secret key.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
That confidence comes from decades of failed attempts to break those algorithms. Take elliptic curve cryptography, used across the Internet and by cryptocurrencies. Its security relies on the belief that there’s no efficient algorithm capable of reversing the mathematical operations at its core. But if AI can spot shortcuts that humans have missed, that belief could be proven wrong.
Humans have found such shortcuts before, Green says. An algorithm called the number field sieve made it far easier to crack RSA, another widely used public-key system, when it relied on 512-bit keys. Cryptographers responded by lengthening the keys, and 2,048 bits is now considered the minimum. Another advance on that scale “could potentially seriously reduce the security level of the schemes that we standardize,” he says.
Govind Pimpale, a research fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation, thinks AI could make the next one more likely. Public-key cryptography depends on relatively few mathematical problems, he says, each studied by a comparatively small community. Machines could throw vastly more effort at them and find flaws or faster algorithms that would let attackers work out secret keys from public ones. “Public-key cryptography is necessary for essentially all online commerce and secure messaging, so its loss would have dire consequences,” he says.
Plenty of others disagree that AI will break modern encryption. Yehuda Lindell, a professor at Bar-Ilan University in Israel and head of cryptography at Coinbase, wrote on X that there is “no evidence whatsoever” of a breakthrough against the mathematical problems underlying those systems. Nor does a single one of OpenAI’s 722 papers deal with cryptography, which Dan Boneh, a professor of computer science at Stanford University, calls “a little striking.”
Still, Green’s worry is not entirely hypothetical. In a recent preprint, Florian Tramèr, a computer scientist at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich, and his colleagues—three of them at the AI company Anthropic—pitted leading AI models against 191 code-breaking challenges. “It’s pretty clear that models’ ability in cryptanalysis is growing extremely rapidly,” Tramèr says. In summer 2025 the researchers weren’t even sure AI could reproduce relatively simple attacks. Months later, the models were turning up weaknesses no one had spotted before. Anthropic has also reported that its Claude model found a substantially improved attack on HAWK, a proposed digital signature scheme designed to withstand quantum computers.
But there’s a huge gulf between finding weaknesses in experimental cryptography and breaking the systems that secure large parts of our digital lives. “Today no currently deployed algorithm has been broken by AI,” Pimpale concedes. The bigger concern is a shortcut that cracks an entire family of mathematical problems at once, and with it every system built on them.
Public-key cryptography secures the connection between your browser and the sites you visit, and it produces the digital signatures that certify a software update or a cryptocurrency transaction. Crack it, and attackers could pose as your bank or listen in on your messages. Anyone who has stockpiled encrypted traffic could go back and read it years after the senders assumed it was safe.
Even then, it wouldn’t necessarily signal disaster. Bart Preneel, a cryptography professor at the Catholic University of Leuven (KU Leuven) in Belgium, says the consequences would depend on the scale of any breakthrough. A modest mathematical advance might dent the protection offered by existing systems but not break it. Even making an attack a billion times faster might still leave it requiring more computing power than anyone could realistically muster, AI or no AI. “I think there is, at least at this moment, no real reason to panic,” he says.
Even a modest advance would necessitate a defense upgrade, and Green thinks that that could do damage of its own. “The upgrade process itself is going to be a bit of a catastrophe,” he says. “We screw up the upgrade, and we end up with something insecure accidentally.”
Eyal Ronen, a researcher at Tel Aviv University, who co-authored the cryptanalysis study, is, like Preneel, cautious. AI is already very good at finding software vulnerabilities, he says, which presents a much more immediate threat than the hypothetical disappearance of encryption. And any hacker is more likely to take the easier route, such as hacking someone’s computer to steal their encryption keys, than to try breaking the mathematics protecting them.
Efforts to prepare for quantum computers, another potential threat, are already forcing governments and companies to rethink their encryption. Boneh says those efforts could help if AI discovers something unexpected, although the two threats aren’t identical. HAWK, after all, was built for the quantum era, yet AI found a way to weaken it.
For now, Boneh wants something relatively straightforward from AI companies: greater transparency about what their models have tried and how often they’ve succeeded. Green agrees. “We’re getting no signal whatsoever,” he says. If the labs have pointed their models at the mathematical problems underpinning cryptography, saying so would help reassure the people responsible for securing the Internet. “Please tell us what you have discovered when you tried some cryptography questions,” Boneh says. Until someone does, nobody can say whether AI has exposed something fundamental about the mathematics we rely on—or whether it’s simply getting better at solving problems that were always solvable.

What was going on at Shanidar? Another Neanderthal reported with fatal wound
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:10:04 UTC
00:10:04 KST

About 75,000 years ago, a Neanderthal was stabbed in the chest, almost certainly by somebody who meant it. He was about 45 when he died and was buried in Shanidar Cave in northern Iraq, and he wasn't even the first victim of possible hominin-on-hominin violence reported from Shanidar, he was the second.
Whether the implement of aggression against this Neanderthal, dubbed Shanidar A, was a sharpened wooden stick or a stone-tipped spear isn't clear. What can be said is that it slammed into his chest from the front, passed through a lung on a slightly upward trajectory and punched a round hole in his left shoulder blade, Emma Pomeroy of the University of Cambridge and colleagues reported in Nature on Thursday.
Nor was it Shanidar A's first rodeo. He had previously suffered facial injuries so severe that one of his front teeth had shattered and part of it had fallen out of his mouth. That painful mangling had been healing for about a year before he took the blow to the chest that killed him, according to the team's deductions.
But was poor Shanidar A merely unfortunate – could he have been the victim of a hunting accident by some myopic peer who mistook him for a gazelle or rabbit, and threw a spear? Or was this murder most foul, and if so, by what species exactly?
The find somewhat weakens hypotheses about the benignity of hominin hunter-gatherers, who wouldn't need to engage in snarling conflict with their peers but could move away, and here we have two victims of mayhem in Shanidar, albeit at a vast distance in time.
The first was a Neanderthal male dubbed Shanidar 3 who also died in his 40s following a fatal injury to the ribs around 50,000 years ago. The theory was posited that Shanidar 3 was murdered by a modern human, Homo sapiens, throwing a stone-tipped spear.
The common thinking was that Neanderthals used spears to thrust, but but didn't throw projectiles. Pomeroy clarifies that is no longer the thinking. Now it is that Neanderthals could throw a mean wooden spear just as well as we could. So there's no reason, really, to pick on our species.
We add that Shanidar 3 wasn't in the pink of health when he died either – he had a degenerative disorder of the foot that must have made ambulation painful.
What have we so far? Two dead Neanderthals buried in the cave around 25,000 years apart, who both survived injuries and illnesses that strongly indicate they were cared for by their peers; yet both died violently at the hands of their peers, and while our species Homo sapiens and Neanderthals were apparently both running around in the region both 75,000 and 50,000 years ago (including in Israel!), there's no particular reason to think we did it.
Home not alone
Shanidar is famed for being a "Neanderthal cemetery," a term that Pomeroy explains is all wrong. But the new research shores up the impression that Neanderthals engaged in mortuary rituals.
Shanidar is famed for being a "Neanderthal cemetery," a term that that Pomeroy explains is all wrong. But the new research shores up the growing impression that Neanderthals engaged in mortuary rituals.
Neanderthals definitely buried at least some of their dead in the cave, in two main phases; at least five in one cluster between 75,000 to 70,000 years ago; and a different group with three bodies around 50,000 to 45,000 years ago. Shanidar A and Shanidar 3 belong to the older cluster.
Regarding Shanidar 4, a romantic "flower burial" theory proposed in 1975 by the archaeologist Ralph Solecki, sadly turned out to be inaccurate. High concentrations of fossil pollen identified around the skeleton were suggested as meaning the body had been laid to rest on a bed of flowers. Later work favored burrowing bees transporting clusters of pollen, burrowing rodents disrupting the archaeological layers, and pollen blowing in with the wind.
The Neanderthals in the cluster were placed over years, though not over that much time, with evidence of new ones being put in before the body beneath had fully decayed, Pomeroy explains. But the living also used the cave for other things, not just to visit the dead like we do in today's cemeteries, she explains. So it isn't a cemetery per se.
Note that burying the dead inside the home isn't as weird as one might think. We did it too. Around 10,000 to 9,000 years ago, modern humans in the Neolithic Levant and Turkey would bury their dead under the floor of the home. In any case the Neanderthals seem to have used the cave sporadically, not for constant occupation. Among other things, the cave is in the Zagros Mountains where it gets snowy in winter.
Anyway, sequential burial at one spot suggests they attached meaning to the site as opposed to obeying pure practicality, the team says.
Further evidence of mortuary practices in Neanderthals is reported at sites in Europe, such as La Ferrassie, Le Regourdou and others in France. In Krapina, Croatia, archaeologists detected Neanderthal cannibalism, which could have been due to starvation, or maybe those Neanderthals ritually ate their dead. Some people do. "Recent populations do it as a kind of dominance over others – maybe they did that too," Pomeroy posits.
Murder Og wrote
The bottom line is that the evidence of caring for each other (or eating each other) doesn't actually contradict the implied evidence of interpersonal loathing, Pomeroy points out. Don't we humans evince the same two-facedness, or at least changeability? We do.
The brutal facial injuries Shanidar A survived show that somebody cared for him, and the manner of his death suggests not everyone felt the love. His scapula was preserved whole but for that telltale 1.5-centimeter-wide exactly round hole in it.
That hole could have been made by exactly the sort of Neanderthal spears found in the swamps of Schöningen in Germany, from 200,000 years ago. (The spears had been initially assessed at about 400,000 years ago, then 300,000 and now are believed to be 200,000 years old).
We assume the Schöningen spears were used to hunt animals, of which plenty were found, notably megafauna in the form of horses. There are no smoking spears in Shanidar but the shape of the scapular lesion is indicative of sharpened wooden spear. If the spear had a stone tip, the lesion would have been shaped like a lozenge but it's "extremely round," Pomeroy explains.
The team also deduced that the hole in his scapula couldn't have been made by a tree root or burrowing insects. In addition, remarkably similar lesions have been observed in the fossil skeletons of animals, from giants to small ones, at prehistoric sites.
What have we? Evidence that the guy went down like a hunted deer, presumably gnashing his healed teeth.
It's true that physical trauma was common among prehistoric humans and hominins, who hunted dangerous animals and maybe each other too. That is a suggestion that archaeologists tend to resist. But here we are.
"Neanderthals lived a precarious life so we do find healed fractures and bangs on the head but severe injury to the face is quite unusual," Pomeroy points out in respect to Shanidar's A smashed mouth, which healed over about a year. That kind of oral injury was atypical.
Is there any reason to connect the posited violence against Shanidar A and 3? Not over a time span of 25,000 years. Maybe it was coincidence. Or, early human lives were more violent than we thought, she answers and notes the case reported by archaeologists in Israel in July: of an early Homo sapiens in Qafzeh Cave who was smashed in the face with a rock about 100,000 years ago but was cared for, and survived.
"I think we have to see the same complexity in Neanderthals that we see in people today. Some are violent, some care," Pomeroy sums up. "We have contrasting stereotypes about hunter-gatherers – one where they are at one with nature, the other that life was nasty, brutish and short. But the story is more complex than that." And in Shanidar, the preponderance of the evidence is that they had deeply mixed feelings about each other.
