23:38:35 KST

The AI hub will bring selected Swedish start-ups and Nvidia staff under the same roof, alongside a biotechnology demonstration lab.
Nvidia is opening an AI hub in Stockholm, Sweden, to help start-ups tackle health and climate challenges.
The US chipmaker is partnering with Norrsken, a Swedish non-profit foundation established by Niklas Adalberth, co-founder of Swedish payments company Klarna. The foundation supports start-ups working on social and environmental problems.
Called Stockholm AI Lab, the hub is due to open in central Stockholm in 2027, according to Norrsken’s announcement.
It will bring selected start-ups and Nvidia staff under the same roof, alongside a biotechnology demonstration lab.
Nvidia will contribute computing infrastructure, software tools and connections to its international start-up network. The partners have not disclosed the size of the investment in the project.
What will happen inside?
The hub in central Stockholm will provide private offices and host events connecting founders with investors, researchers, industry representatives and policymakers.
“What these founders need now is what every great movement needs: a place. Somewhere to find each other, their investors, their first customers, and the conviction that they are not building alone,” Adalberth said in the announcement.
The demonstration lab will be run by Nvidia and Stockholm-based Root Bio, a start-up using AI to design molecules for biological applications, including reducing greenhouse gas emissions.
The partners say it will show how AI can help automate biological discovery. They also plan to select further demonstration partners working in robotics, climate, health and manufacturing.
Nvidia’s software tools will support work in robotics, simulation and life sciences
However, the announcement does not specify which equipment will be installed, how much computing capacity members will receive or what they will pay to use it.
Part of Nvidia’s wider European push
Nvidia has announced similar efforts elsewhere in Europe to help businesses and researchers use AI, although the projects take different forms.
In the United Kingdom (UK), the company announced a robotics research and development hub with technology trade association techUK in September 2025, working with training company QA to develop AI and robotics skills.
In June 2025, Nvidia also announced new or expanded AI technology centres in Germany, Italy, Spain, Finland, Sweden and the UK, supporting research, training and access to AI computing infrastructure.

Fico’s Slovakia Revives Moscow Ties With Energy and Trade Talks Set for November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15

23:36:33 KST

- Category
- World
Fico’s Slovakia Revives Moscow Ties With Energy and Trade Talks Set for November
Slovakia is preparing to revive a dormant cooperation forum with Moscow, with Russian energy supplies, nuclear fuel, and the treatment of Russian athletes expected to feature prominently, POLITICO reported on October 15.
According to a Russian government note obtained by POLITICO, Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár agreed during an August 20 video call to hold a meeting of the Russian-Slovak Intergovernmental Commission in Moscow. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico announced that the meeting is scheduled for November 25.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Slovakia under Prime Minister Robert Fico has repeatedly taken positions closer to Moscow than most EU governments, including halting state military aid to Ukraine, criticizing sanctions on Russia, and maintaining energy ties with Moscow. In May, Fico visited Putin, in Moscow and described himself as the EU’s “black sheep” for supporting dialogue with Russia.
The Russian-Slovak Intergovernmental Commission covers economic, scientific, and technical cooperation and has been dormant since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Its previous session was held in Bratislava in November 2021.
POLITICO reported that the Russian note was written by Science and Higher Education Minister Valery Falkov and dated September 10. The outlet could not independently verify the document but noted that it bore the hallmarks of a legitimate Russian ministerial communication.
Blanár had raised Slovakia’s opposition to the EU phaseout of Russian gas imports and requested that energy supplies be discussed at the Moscow meeting, according to the note.
Slovak representatives also emphasized continued Russian oil deliveries through the Druzhba pipeline and welcomed regular shipments of Russian nuclear fuel to Slovak power plants, POLITICO reported.
Fico has argued that ending Russian energy imports would increase costs for Slovakia, which remains heavily dependent on Russian oil and gas. During a May 9 meeting in Moscow, the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, stated that Russia would continue working to meet Slovakia’s energy needs.
The planned agenda extends beyond energy. According to POLITICO, the two sides are considering cooperation on culture, tourism, agriculture, and environmental protection, as well as the status of the Russian Center for Science and Culture in Bratislava.
The Russian note also recorded Blanár’s opposition to what it described as “discrimination against Russian athletes” in international competitions. That issue is expected to be discussed at the November meeting.
“We pursue a policy in all directions and maintain dialogue with all countries that are interested in pragmatic cooperation with us for the benefit of the Slovak Republic’s national interests,” Blanár stated after the August 20 call, POLITICO wrote.
The renewed Slovak-Russian dialogue follows Fico’s May visit to Moscow and comes after Viktor Orbán’s defeat in Hungary’s April election. POLITICO noted that Orbán had previously been one of Putin’s closest partners inside the EU.
Before leaving office, Orbán’s government had also revived Hungary’s own intergovernmental economic cooperation commission with Russia. Budapest and Moscow later agreed on a 12-point plan covering energy, trade, and cultural ties.
The Slovak initiative now mirrors parts of that approach, with energy cooperation serving as a central component of renewed ties with Moscow.
POLITICO also linked the effort to Russia’s broader attempts to expand energy relationships abroad.
After speaking with Putin, US President Donald Trump recently announced a deal under which Russia would supply diesel to US and global markets, potentially providing Moscow with additional revenue while Ukraine continues striking Russian oil infrastructure.

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Drone Attack on Lutsk Damages World’s Largest Painting—Ukraine’s 2,000-Square-Meter “Cosmogony”
Russia’s drone attack on the Ukrainian city of Lutsk on October 13 damaged Cosmogony, the largest work of painting in Ukraine and the largest painting in the world, after falling drone debris sparked a fire at the Adrenalin City entertainment complex, according to Suspilne on October 15.
The artwork was damaged after falling drone debris sparked a fire at the Adrenalin City entertainment complex, which houses the Museum of Modern Ukrainian Art.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Museum director Tetiana Repnytska told Suspilne that the fire damaged The Future, the final section of the six-part artwork, while the other thematic sections remained intact.
“By destroying art and culture, they are also trying to destroy Ukrainians. This is the largest painting in the world. Cosmogony covers an area of 2,000 square meters,” Repnytska said.
Despite the damage to the monumental painting, museum staff managed to protect much of the institution’s collection from the consequences of the attack.
According to art historian and the museum’s chief curator, Oles Tomakh, employees were forced to evacuate artworks during the fire, including pieces from an exhibition dedicated to Ukrainian artist Emma Andiievska .
“We had an exhibition of Emma Andiievska at Cosmogony, featuring more than 300 works. We began quickly removing them, but we couldn't get to some in time. However, only the glass was broken. Fortunately, all the other museum halls were undamaged,” Tomakh said.
The museum has yet to determine whether the damaged section of Cosmogony will be restored or replaced with a newly created segment.
Repnytska said the decision would be made by the artwork’s creators, emphasizing that the museum intends to continue its cultural activities despite Russian attacks.
“Despite the shelling, we will continue to develop contemporary Ukrainian art and preserve it,” the museum director said.
Cosmogony, by Ukrainian artist Petro Antyp, is one of Ukraine’s most ambitious contemporary art projects. Created over nearly two years at the Museum of Modern Ukrainian Art in Lutsk, the painting was officially recognized in September 2024 as the largest work of painting in Ukraine, surpassing the previous world record. Covering 2,086.5 square meters, the artwork exceeds the nearly 1,600-square-meter The Journey of Humanity, created by British artist Sasha Jafri in 2020.
The painting consists of six main thematic sections. These include The Beginning, depicting the origins of the universe; The Creation of Earth, illustrating the formation of the planet; The Creation of Nature, exploring the emergence of life; The Creation of Humanity, portraying human origins and development; The Creation of Society, examining the evolution of communities and civilization; and The Future, reflecting on humanity's relationship with the world and its future.
The project was launched in November 2022. Originally from Horlivka in the Donetsk region, Antyp relocated to the Kyiv region following the outbreak of Russia’s war against Ukraine in 2014 before settling in Lutsk after the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
While Ukrainian cultural institutions continue to face damage from Russian attacks, art is also being used internationally to support those affected by the war, including Ukrainian children.
In a separate initiative, Beatles musician Paul McCartney contributed a lyric from his 1973 song Band on the Run to inspire a charity exhibition and auction featuring original works by more than 60 contemporary artists. Proceeds will support children affected by armed conflicts worldwide, including Russia’s war against Ukraine.
According to The Art Newspaper on October 8, McCartney selected the line “Well the rain exploded with a mighty crash as we fell into the sun” from Band on the Run, the title track of the 1973 album released by McCartney and his band Wings.

Brazil’s Lula accuses Meta of favoring rival ahead of presidential runoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:35:31 UTC
23:35:31 KST

Berk Kutay Gökmen
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has accused the US technology company Meta of unfairly benefiting his right-wing rival, Flavio Bolsonaro, ahead of a closely contested presidential runoff, according to The New York Times on Thursday.
Lula’s campaign and independent watchdog groups allege that Meta’s platforms, including Facebook and Instagram, have restricted the visibility of progressive content while allowing material supporting Bolsonaro to circulate more freely.
The president’s campaign filed a complaint with Brazil’s electoral court on Saturday, demanding equal treatment online as the race enters its final stretch before the Oct. 25 runoff.
The complaint accused Meta of “algorithmic selectivity” during the presidential contest, arguing that videos critical of Bolsonaro were removed without explanation, searches failed to display progressive activists and posts praising Lula reached fewer users.
Meta has rejected allegations of political bias, saying it does not operate its systems to harm or favor any candidate. The company attributed some of the reported incidents to technical glitches and unintended errors, dismissing independent findings as anecdotal and difficult to verify.
“It is unfortunate that minor technical issues are being spun into a political narrative,” Meta said in a statement.
Lula’s campaign also cited a report by international watchdog Eko, which found that Meta approved political advertisements containing artificial intelligence-generated disinformation and deepfakes, although the ads were ultimately not published.
Some of the material reportedly included fabricated images of Brazil’s electoral court announcing a new election date and manipulated videos falsely showing US President Donald Trump endorsing Bolsonaro.
Meta said its safeguards would have flagged and blocked the advertisements before they reached voters.
Separately, Brazilian nonprofit CTRL + Z reported identifying 1,088 cases involving electoral censorship, account bans and reduced content visibility on Meta platforms. The group said content supporting Lula was disproportionately affected.

New: “Why Teach Philosophy?”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:34:35 UTC
23:34:35 KST

Why Teach Philosophy is a new series of interviews with philosophers known for their teaching, their research on philosophy pedagogy, or their work on curriculum design.
Created by Russell Marcus, professor of philosophy at Hamilton College, the interviews, he says, are “an offshoot of a larger research project about philosophical learning goals.”
Currently there are interviews with David W. Concepción (Ball State), Mo Janzen (Anoka Ramsey CC), László Kőszeghy (International Baccalaureate), Tommy Curry (Edinburgh), Rebecca Scott (Harper College), and L.A. Paul (Yale), with eleven more coming soon.
Professor Marcus says, “the interviews are tightly edited audio, typically under an hour, extracted from much longer (typically 3-4 hour) conversations that I had over the past year with renowned philosophy teachers. We’re not flashy, but I think the content is pretty good and the audience really should be philosophers.”
He adds, “I think that the podcasts could be especially good resources for grad schools to use in whatever teacher training they do. Typically, they do minimal such training. Listening to good teachers talk about their craft can be enlightening and useful.”
The Why Teach Philosophy interviews are available on YouTube, Spotify, Apple Podcasts, etc., and transcripts of the longer conversations are posted on the project’s site.

Top health civil servant urged to play no role in clampdown on ADHD clinics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:34:30 UTC
23:34:30 KST

A senior civil servant should play no part in ministers’ crackdown on private attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism clinics because of her recent ties to the industry, MPs have said.
Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs are demanding that Samantha Jones, the permanent secretary at the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC), steps away from any role in plans to toughen regulation of the booming market in private neurodiversity assessments.
They say Jones should not be involved because of her links to a company that is one of the biggest providers of NHS-funded neurodiversity assessments, which earned it £26m from the health service in England over the past six years.
Ministers are drawing up plans for how to better regulate the “wild west” of private clinics offering assessment, diagnosis and treatment of ADHD and autism that has grown rapidly in recent years as people have struggled to access care via the NHS.
The push comes after the government last week accepted the findings of a review by Prof Peter Fonagy, which raised concerns about the “consistency and quality” of assessments by private providers of neurodiversity services that had inbuilt “financial incentives” to diagnose and treat people.
Jones is responsible for overseeing the implementation of government decisions on health policy. She would therefore be expected to advise ministers on how best to strengthen the regulation of private providers of ADHD and autism services. Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, has vowed to introduce a much tougher regime.
Four MPs have called for Jones to recuse herself from any role in those decisions because of her previous ties to ADHD360, a provider of neurodiversity services. Her links to the private ADHD sector represent a serious conflict of interest, they claim.
Jones was appointed as the permanent secretary on 22 April 2025. A month later, she was still the chair of and a director of and shareholder in the private care provider Keys Group when, on 16 May, it bought ADHD360, a clinic that has increased its NHS income considerably in recent years.
At the time of the £22.5m purchase, Jones was also an operating partner in G Square Capital, the private equity company that owns Keys Group.
She sold her shares in Keys Group and resigned her roles there and at G Square Capital before she started at the DHSC on 16 June. Jones has already recused herself from involvement in the department’s decision over whether to extend Palantir’s £330m, seven-year contract with the NHS because of her past work for the lobbyists Carnall Farrar, which advised Palantir regarding the contract.
MPs believe her tenure at Keys Group could represent a conflict of interest. Ben Coleman, a Labour MP on the health and social care committee, said: “People will want to feel reassured that future regulation of private ADHD and autism assessments is beyond reproach. Given her recent close involvement with ADHD360, I would encourage Ms Jones to recuse herself from that work, as she has done over Palantir, to avoid any perception of a conflict of interest.”
In June, Jones apologised after she was reprimanded by the Civil Service Commission for breaching lobbying rules by failing to ask the (now defunct) Advisory Committee on Business Appointments for prior approval before undertaking work for four healthcare companies.
Helen Morgan, the Liberal Democrats’ health spokesperson, said: “Given Sam Jones oversaw the multimillion-pound acquisition of ADHD360 just weeks before entering the Department of Health, ministers must ensure she recuses herself immediately, just as she has over Palantir.”
Jones, 55, was widely admired in the NHS when she ran West Hertfordshire NHS trust in 2013-15. After a role with NHS England, she began working in private healthcare. Boris Johnson as prime minister handed her a key role in Downing Street in 2021. She returned to private health in 2023 and by 2023-24 had paid roles or shareholdings in 13 health or consultancy organisations.
Clive Lewis, the Labour MP for Norwich South, said Jones’s deep involvement in private healthcare meant she should not have been made DHSC permanent secretary in the first place, saying: “It just defies logic that anyone thought it was a good idea. Surely this must have come up during her recruitment process?”
Jones did not answer questions put by the Guardian. The NHS has paid ADHD360 just over £26m for its services since 2020, according to figures supplied by the Tussell public expenditure database. “When it comes to the government’s response to the [Fonagy] review, there should be no suggestion that the top NHS official is being influenced by any past or current links to a major private provider of NHS ADHD services,” said Stella Creasy, the Labour MP for Walthamstow. “This issue is too sensitive and complex to permit any conflicts of interest. As a result the permanent secretary should recuse herself from this area of policy.”
David Rowland, the director of the Centre for Health and the Public Interest thinktank, said: “The permanent secretary at the department which has responsibility for regulating private ADHD providers appears to have a conflict of interest in this area and so may struggle to remain impartial when it comes to implementing the recommendations made by Prof Fonagy.”
A DHSC spokesperson said: “There is no conflict of interest. The permanent secretary has appropriately declared all interests, in this post and when she was a non-executive director [of the DHSC]. She resigned from all her private sector posts before taking on the permanent secretary role at the department.”

U.S. Navy teaches drones to land on ships without GPS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:32:59 UTC
23:32:59 KST

- A U.S. Navy drone completed mission tasks and landed on a pitching ship without GPS or a pilot, using its own cameras and software.
- NAWCAD says the software is ready for fleet testing and is working to transition it to Navy drone programs, Collaborative Combat Aircraft and DARPA’s EVADE.
The U.S. Navy has flown a drone through mission tasks and landed it on a pitching ship at sea with GPS jammed or unavailable and no pilot at the controls, using only the aircraft’s own cameras, motion sensors and onboard software, the Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division said.
NAWCAD, the U.S. Navy’s main aviation test and engineering center at Patuxent River, Maryland, said the live-flight demonstration showed a tactical drone can carry out its tasks and recover aboard a moving vessel without satellite navigation. The software is now ready for operational testing on fleet platforms.
“In contested areas where satellites and communications are jammed, autonomy gives significant advantage to our sailors,” said Rear Adm. Todd Evans, commander of NAWCAD.
Landing a drone on a ship has usually depended on extra hardware. Shipboard recoveries rely on radar systems that cost millions of dollars, along with flight deck recovery gear and ship modifications that can take months to install. When the U.S. Navy’s RQ-8A Fire Scout made the service’s first autonomous drone landings on a moving ship aboard USS Nashville in 2006, it used a radar sensor on the ship to track the aircraft’s position relative to the deck.
NAWCAD’s approach moves that job into software. Engineers at the center’s Maritime Autonomous Guidance-Navigation-Control Intelligent Coupled Systems Lab paired the drone’s existing mission cameras with guidance, navigation and control algorithms. In flight, the aircraft recognizes the ship’s shape and visual cues and steers toward it much as a human pilot would, while the software predicts how the deck is rising and falling so the drone can time a smooth touchdown.
“In a high-end maritime conflict, GPS is the first operational link an adversary attempts to sever,” said Peter Arslanian, a NAWCAD aerospace engineer.
The system runs on commercial-standard cameras, motion sensors and electronics, and NAWCAD says the software works with nearly any drone flight computer. That means it can be added through a software upgrade instead of costly changes to ships with little spare room, and it can scale from small tactical quadcopters up to large combat drones.
NAWCAD plans to apply the technology next to larger uncrewed aircraft, including tactical resupply drones. The center is working to move the capability into the U.S. Navy’s Small Tactical Unmanned Aircraft Systems program office, the Collaborative Combat Aircraft program for drone wingmen, and DARPA’s EVADE effort.
EVADE, short for Early VTOL Aircraft Demonstration, is a DARPA project to field drones that can take off from and land on ship decks without launch or recovery equipment, with five companies including AeroVironment and Sikorsky building designs for it.
The Naval Innovative Science and Engineering Program and the Office of Naval Research funded the NAWCAD work, which now moves to operational testing on fleet aircraft.

 NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said on Thursday that the alliance would continue to work closely with its allies in the Black Sea region to strengthen deterrence and defense capabilities following a series of reported drone attacks on commercial vessels.
In a post on US social media platform X, Rutte said he held a meeting with Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev and Romanian President Nicusor Dan to discuss security in the Black Sea and the latest attacks on commercial shipping.

Bulgaria said it suspected Russia was behind the attack and summoned the Russian envoy.
Russia said two cargo ships carrying military cargo bound for Ukraine’s Odesa port had been hit during a sea crossing but did not identify the vessels.

Netanyahu says he spoke with Syria's al-Sharaa: ‘I threatened more strikes if Druze killings continued’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:32:23 UTC
23:32:23 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu revealed Thursday afternoon at a gathering with the Druze community in Yarka that he had spoken with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa.
"It was a very brief, very blunt conversation, and the massacre [of the Druze] stopped," he said. "I will do whatever it takes to protect our Druze brothers. There is still work to be done, and I can't reveal everything."
Netanyahu was the one who called al-Sharaa. His message was that if the massacre of the Druze did not stop, Israel would intensify its strikes against the Syrian regime. The killing eventually stopped.
In July 2025, between July 13 and 21, fighting between armed Bedouin groups and Syrian regime forces left more than 3,572 people dead. Hundreds of people were summarily executed by Syrian security forces, while approximately 225,000 were displaced from their homes.
Human rights organizations documented the abduction of more than 100 Druze women and girls by armed groups affiliated with the Syrian government and reported systematic rape and sexual violence. In at least three documented cases, women were raped before being executed.
A U.S.-brokered ceasefire was reached July 19 after an earlier attempt collapsed, but it proved fragile. Renewed clashes erupted in the following months, and in February 2026, the Syrian regime imposed a siege on Sweida, the center of the country's Druze community, blocking food and medical supplies to the entire province.
Many towns were left deserted, dozens of abducted men and women remain missing and no one has been brought to justice.
At the height of the clashes, Israel also intervened, striking Syrian regime targets in Sweida and Damascus to protect the Druze. Graphic footage from the fighting continued to emerge on social media for months, including videos showing executions, humiliation and religiously motivated killings.
Al-Sharaa condemned the massacres carried out by his forces against the Druze and said he considered the community "an integral part" of Syria.
He pledged to investigate the atrocities, saying that "criminal and unlawful acts" committed during the clashes were "completely contrary to the principles on which the Syrian state is being built."
He also promised that those responsible, "whether individuals or organizations operating outside the law, will be held legally accountable."

Supreme Court seeks Centre’s response on plea to hold protest organisers liable for damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:32:13 UTC
23:32:13 KST

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday sought responses from the Centre, Delhi Police and others on a plea seeking to hold organisers of protests personally or jointly liable for loss of life, injuries, damage to public or private property and the costs incurred by the authorities.A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi was hearing the petition, which also sought a direction that protests, dharnas, demonstrations, processions and public assemblies in the national capital should not be held without prior written permission from the competent authority.
The plea sought to make organisers, callers, leaders or convenors of protests liable for losses arising from unlawful acts or omissions, including when an assembly is held without permission or violates the conditions imposed for its approval.The bench issued notices to the Centre, Delhi Police and other parties, seeking their responses to the petition, according to news agency PTI.
Plea seeks designated protest sites in Delhi
The petition also sought directions to the authorities to identify and notify designated locations for protests, dharnas, demonstrations and public assemblies in Delhi. These sites, it said, should be situated away from densely populated, commercial and central areas.
It further proposed that every application seeking permission for a protest, demonstration, procession or public assembly should be accompanied by an affidavit from the organiser disclosing the source of funding.The declaration should also specify whether any part of the funds had been received, or was expected to be received, from a foreign source or an unidentified source, the plea said.According to the petition, a false or incomplete declaration should provide grounds for revoking permission, recovering compensation and costs from the organiser and those found to have financed the assembly, and initiating prosecution in accordance with the law.
Supreme Court hears multiple pleas linked to Delhi protests
The hearing came as the Supreme Court considered several petitions connected to protests in Delhi, including pleas concerning alleged assaults on journalists and lawyers, police action and restrictions on demonstrations.In a separate matter, the bench issued notices to the Centre and the Delhi government on a plea challenging the Delhi Police’s decision to de-notify Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site.The petitioner, advocate Swaty Malik, argued that removing the designation violated the fundamental right to protest. The plea maintained that demonstrations should be permitted at a location where protesters could make their grievances heard by the state administration.Justice Bagchi observed that the concept of being heard should also be considered in the context of technology.“The word ‘heard’ must be used in the perspective of technology also”, Justice Bagchi remarked.The court agreed to examine the petition and sought responses from the authorities.In other pleas linked to the protests, the Supreme Court sought responses from the authorities over allegations involving journalists and lawyers. It also directed law-enforcement agencies to preserve CCTV footage and other digital records relating to the demonstrations.The bench further directed that the order issued under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) be placed on record. The provision empowers authorised executive magistrates to issue urgent prohibitory orders to prevent public danger, disturbances or riots.The court indicated that the Union government would file a consolidated response to the batch of petitions while relevant material relating to individual cases was preserved.
Court also takes up pleas on voter roll revision
Separately, the Supreme Court issued notices to the Election Commission and chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar on a petition filed by Congress leader Rahul Gandhi and 12 other opposition leaders over alleged large-scale voter deletions and irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The bench also took note of submissions concerning the October 12 march to the Supreme Court by Rahul and other opposition leaders.“Nobody can browbeat us (judiciary),” CJI Surya Kant said during the hearing, adding that the court was aware of statements made both inside and outside the courtroom.
The court said it would ask one of the petitioners about his conduct at the next hearing, without naming the individual.The petition by Rahul and the other opposition leaders sought an independent audit of deletions and modifications made during the SIR, to be conducted by a committee headed by a retired Supreme Court judge and assisted by technical experts and other prominent citizens.It also sought safeguards against deleting voters’ names without notice and a reasonable opportunity to be heard, along with measures to allow eligible voters in Punjab and other poll-bound states to seek inclusion in electoral rolls within the time permitted by law.

Hurricane Trudy looms over Mexico’s Pacific coast, severe rainfall expected
MEXICO CITY, Oct 15 - Hurricane Trudy moved parallel to Mexico's western coast on Thursday, threatening further rain and strong winds in a region already battered in recent weeks by storms that left behind several deaths and severe flooding.
The storm, located about 480 km (298 miles) south-southwest of beach town Acapulco, packed maximum sustained winds of 120 kph (75 mph) and is moving northwest, the US-based National Hurricane Center said in a morning advisory.
• Trudy, a Category 1 hurricane, is forecast to rapidly intensify into a major hurricane on Friday.
• The storm is then expected to approach Mexico's Pacific coast with heavy rains forecast in the states of Colima and Jalisco, increasing the risk of life-threatening flooding and landslides, the NHC and Mexican authorities warned.
• Meanwhile, Tropical Storm Simon is nearly stationary farther northwest offshore, after dropping heavy rain along the coast earlier as a hurricane.
• Simon is forecast to move northwest, grazing the Baja California peninsula over the weekend, the NHC added. REUTERS

Apple consolidates smart-home capabilities in HomeView dashboard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:30:52 UTC
23:30:52 KST

Apple consolidates smart-home capabilities in HomeView dashboard
Technology company Apple has released a screen that consolidates the functions of its app products and its home-management software into one device.
HomeView is a seven-inch display meant to function as a centralised location for home controls, signalling a step forward in Apple's home integration and smart home services.
The screens come in two versions. One sits on its own, standing on a base with an integrated speaker, while the other is wall-mounted.
HomeView works similarly to other Apple touchscreen products, with a home screen, apps, widgets and a built-in front-facing camera. It has many of the same functions, including FaceTime video calling.
The product creates a physical dashboard for the Apple Home app, which was released in 2022 to control integrated functions such as smart locks, appliances, cameras and thermostats.
HomeView uses face recognition for up to six people per device in a household with personalised settings for each user, instead of the app sitting on personalised devices.
The product also includes an intercom system that can connect multiple devices within one household.
The tabletop version of the device has a distinct form, with a case and a thick base made from recycled aluminium. Its rounded base and movable screen evoke the design of the 2002 iMac G4 desktop computer.
Apple emphasised the device's potential as decor, calling it "the perfect addition to a kitchen counter, nightstand, or side table."
It comes in four colour options: silver, starlight, rose pink, and space grey.
The company also noted the integration of its next-generation AI, called Siri AI.
"HomeView features Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence and advanced Apple silicon," said Apple.
"Siri AI is a profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding and onscreen awareness."
The release also included a lineup of updated home products such as cameras, locks and thermostats.
HomeView comes after a slate of recent releases from Apple, including the brand's first foldable smartphone.
The imagery is courtesy of Apple.

15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Spanish prosecutors have reversed their earlier position and backed a court investigation into sexual assault allegations against singer Julio Iglesias, potentially reopening a case involving two former employees who accused him of abuse at his Caribbean properties.
The prosecutor's office now considers that Spain's National Court has jurisdiction to investigate the allegations, despite having dismissed an earlier complaint in January.
On Thursday, National Court Judge Antonio Pina gave Iglesias and the two women five days to submit arguments on whether the court has jurisdiction, according to Spanish news outlet El Diario.
The judge is expected to decide next week whether to open a criminal investigation, the daily reported, citing legal sources.
The case concerns allegations made by a former domestic worker and a physical therapist who worked at Iglesias' residences in the Dominican Republic and the Bahamas in 2021.
The women accuse the singer of sexual assault, human trafficking for forced labor, imposing abusive working conditions, physical injuries and degrading treatment.
They allege that Iglesias exploited his position of power and their vulnerability while they worked at his properties. One former employee alleged that she was pressured into sexual encounters, while the other reported unwanted sexual touching.
Iglesias has denied the allegations, insisting that the accusations are entirely false.
The allegations first emerged in a joint investigation by El Diario and Univision News, in which the women described alleged sexual abuse and degrading working conditions.
The women initially filed a complaint with Spanish prosecutors in January through the international women's rights organization Women's Link Worldwide.
However, prosecutors closed their preliminary investigation later that month, concluding that the alleged offenses occurred outside Spain and that the case lacked sufficient connections to the country.
In September, the women filed a new criminal complaint directly with the National Court, prompting Judge Pina to request a fresh assessment of the court's jurisdiction.

Trump cancels plan to livestream execution after global condemnation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:29:55 UTC
23:29:55 KST

Donald Trump has shelved a widely condemned plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people at a military base at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.
In a social media post on Thursday, Trump argued that broadcasting such an execution “might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan” but said that “many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device”.
“He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed,” Trump added. “That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose.”
Hasan, who was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot by law enforcement officers during the shooting at Fort Hood, now uses a wheelchair.
The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, said last week that the execution of Hasan would be a public event. Hasan’s sentence will be the first military execution in more than 60 years, and would have been the first in US history to be publicly broadcast.
In a statement to the Guardian on Thursday, a spokesperson for the Pentagon said Trump and Hegseth “spoke about the decision to not livestream Hasan’s execution” before Trump’s statement. Hegesth “supports the President’s decision, and they are completely aligned”, they added.
In an interview with Real America’s Voice last Thursday, Hegseth said he supported the public execution “because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things”.
But since then, the Trump administration has faced sweeping criticism, and comparisons to dictatorships in Iran and Afghanistan. Many US lawmakers, from across the political spectrum, have come out and condemned the announcement, and urged Hegseth to reconsider.
Yassamin Ansari, the first Iranian American Democrat elected to the US Congress, wrote in a post on social media: “In Trump’s America, we’re doing public executions now. WTF. This is what happens under brutal dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan. It’s all part of Trump’s authoritarian takeover of the United States.”
In another post, Lisa Murkowski, a Republican senator from Alaska, said that there was “no need to livestream any execution, including this one”, adding that she “would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America”.
The representative Rob Bresnahan, a Republican from Pennsylvania, said in a post on social media that “an execution shouldn’t be a live-streamed spectacle”, adding that “the focus should be on justice for the victims and their families, not turning an execution into entertainment”.
“Their pain deserves respect, not a public show,” he said.
On Friday of last week, the United Nations’ office of the high commissioner for human rights warned that broadcasting the killing would amount to a public execution and “breach the absolute prohibition of torture”, and the president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops also condemned the Pentagon’s plan, saying in a statement that “in no way can Hassan’s actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered”.
“The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people,” the statement added.
That same day, JD Vance appeared to cast doubt on whether the Pentagon would actually livestream the execution, telling reporters that “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen” when asked about the plans. The vice-president also said that if it were livestreamed, “I’m not going to be watching it.”
But over the weekend, Markwayne Mullin, who heads the Department of Homeland Security, stood behind the administration’s decision to livestream the execution.
Speaking with CBS News, Mullin said that “no one has to watch it” and said: “I follow President Trump. He’s the commander in chief of the country, and he does a phenomenal job. He leads this country with a very, very, very direct, forward, straight hand, and he’s restoring American values.”
Trump himself had made contrasting remarks in recent days on whether the live stream would happen. On Friday, he told reporters that he “absolutely” approved the plan to livestream the execution, but on Saturday he said that he had not yet made a final decision on whether to go through with it.
“There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show it” he said. “’Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but I’ll make a decision.”

Japan’s Nuclear Revival Has a Trust Problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:29:00 UTC
23:29:00 KST

When Tokyo Electric Power Company (TEPCO) brought Unit 6 at Kashiwazaki-Kariwa back online in January, it became the first TEPCO reactor to resume since the Fukushima Daiichi accident. An alarm halted the restart the next day; the unit resumed operation in February and entered commercial service in April. Unit 7 at Kashiwazaki-Kariwa, meanwhile, is not expected to restart before 2029–30, according to the EIA.
Clearly, the restart announcement in January was a bit of a false start. Still, the symbolism was unmistakable: The utility responsible for Fukushima is again operating a nuclear plant, the world’s largest by installed capacity.
The timing was also consequential. The Israeli-Japan strikes on Iran on February 28 and the resulting effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz exposed Japan’s reliance on imported energy. In 2025, the Middle East supplied 94 percent of Japan’s crude oil imports; 93 percent of the country’s crude imports passed through Hormuz, according to Reuters.
Japan’s exposure to Hormuz through LNG is much smaller: around 6 percent of total LNG imports, according to IEEFA. Yet Japan imports more than 97 percent of the LNG it consumes, and LNG generates about a third of Japan’s electricity, according to the government’s 2025 energy overview. The Hormuz shock therefore mattered both as a direct risk to Japan’s oil supply and as the cause of higher global gas and electricity prices.
The International Energy Agency reported that Japanese wholesale spot electricity prices in the second quarter of 2026 were more than 30 percent higher year on year. Futures in mid-July pointed to prices in the second half of 2026 nearly 40 percent above the same period a year earlier. These are wholesale-market figures, not household bills, but they show how a disruption to a relatively small share of Japan’s direct LNG supply can still transmit through global markets.
Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae has made it clear that the nuclear restart is part of the answer to Japan’s energy uncertainty. She said in March that the newly reopened Kashiwazaki-Kariwa Unit 6, combined with a temporary increase in coal-fired generation, could cut Japan’s LNG imports passing through Hormuz by about 40 percent.
That logic extends beyond the Gulf. A country dependent on LNG imports for a large share of its electricity is exposed to disruptions elsewhere in the Indo-Pacific, including scenarios involving shipping routes around Taiwan or in the East China Sea. For example, Japan’s continued reliance on Russian LNG has become a problem. The Sakhalin-II supply relationship has become a question of energy security, diplomacy, and policy autonomy.
The strategic case for nuclear power is therefore not just about decarbonization or energy bills. It is also about preserving Tokyo’s strategic autonomy by reducing its reliance on overseas energy providers.
Japan’s nuclear energy targets remain well ahead of the fleet it can count on today. The government’s Seventh Strategic Energy Plan set a target for nuclear power to supply about 20 percent of electricity generation in fiscal year 2040. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) estimated that meeting that target would require up to 30 reactors in operation. As of September 16, the latest date on the Nuclear Regulation Authority’s operating-status register, 11 reactors were classified as “Operation.”
On August 26, the Green Transformation Implementation Council adopted a package calling for the maximum use of nuclear power, with safety as a prerequisite, as NucNet reported. The plan set out plans to replace two to five reactors in the 2040s and a cumulative 11 to 14 by the 2050s, alongside investment in domestic supply chains for perovskite solar, next-generation geothermal, and offshore wind.
As Reuters reported, specific measures, including legislative steps, are expected by year’s end. The package is therefore more than a statement of intent, but key details – including the specific sites for nuclear plants – remain to be worked out.
Japan’s government may have a sense of political urgency, but its nuclear companies still lack institutional credibility. In September, an independent inquiry found that Chubu Electric Power, which operates the Hamaoka Nuclear Power Plant in Shizuoka Prefecture, had selectively used seismic-wave data to keep its estimates within internal parameters, despite earlier internal reports of irregularities. The inquiry also found that senior management had pressed staff to restart the reactors as soon as possible, according to Reuters. In response, Chubu said it would withdraw its applications to restart Units 3 and 4 at Hamaoka, and that its president and chairman would resign.
The episode shows what can happen when the commercial and political pressure for speedy restarts overtakes the discipline of safety review. It also gives opponents of restarts a concrete reason to doubt assurances from both utilities and government. Chubu says it may reapply after restructuring its organization and processes. Before it does, the company must show that its internal controls can withstand pressure to produce a favorable answer. Japan’s nuclear regulator, in turn, must be able to demonstrate that review standards are applied independently and transparently.
Public opposition, especially at the local level, is a related issue. Niigata’s governor approved the restart of Kashiwazaki-Kariwa, but a survey conducted before that decision found 50 percent of residents supported restarting Unit 6 and 47 percent opposed it. Nearly 70 percent said they were concerned about TEPCO operating the reactor.
The governor’s approval came with demands for clear safety explanations, evacuation planning, road improvements, and continued monitoring of TEPCO. In other words, local acceptance will require continued action on TEPCO’s part. A serious incident, a poor safety disclosure, or another data scandal at any plant can shape public opinion across the country.
Three tests will show whether Japan’s nuclear revival can provide a reliable source of energy – especially in large enough quantities to make a meaningful difference for Japan’s energy security. First, can the Nuclear Regulation Authority retain public credibility while the government presses for a faster energy transition? Second, can utilities with past governance failures repair their internal controls and earn the right to re-enter the review process? Third, will the August package’s promised legislation and funding arrive by year’s end, and will the longer-term replacement targets be matched by realistic project timetables and local consent?
Japan’s government can designate nuclear energy a security asset; it cannot legislate the public confidence required for the nuclear revival to proceed.

Iranian intelligence plot targeted prominent German Jewish leaders

Trump says Fort Hood shooter execution will not be livestreamed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:27:35 UTC
23:27:35 KST

Trump says Fort Hood US shooter execution will not be livestreamed
US president reverses Pentagon’s plan to publicly stream execution of Nidal Malik Hasan after outcry.
United States President Donald Trump has said that the execution of a man who killed several military personnel at the Fort Hood military base in 2009 will not be livestreamed.
The statement on Thursday represented a reversal for the administration, with the Pentagon saying last week the execution would be livestreamed and Trump saying he “absolutely” supported the plan. The public killing would have been the first of its kind in the US since 1936, with successive administrations criticising foreign governments for conducting such executions.
In his post, Trump called the convicted gunman, Nidal Malik Hasan, a “very bad and evil man”. He also accused the administration of former President Barack Obama of an “intelligence failure” ahead of the attack in Texas, which killed 13.
“With all of that being said, I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device,” the US president wrote.
“He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed,” Trump said, adding that immediate family members of victims would be able to view the execution.
US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth had announced last week that the execution would be “public”.
“Because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said in an interview with right-wing media figure Jack Posobiec.
He added that the execution would take place on December 3 at 1pm US Central Time (18:00 GMT), the same time that the 2009 shooting took place.
The announcement was met with condemnation from some lawmakers, including members of Trump’s own Republican Party.
In a post on X, Republican Senator Johyn Curtis warned that “a civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment”.
Trump’s own vice president, JD Vance, had earlier downplayed the likelihood the plans for a public execution would proceed, saying he would not watch if they did.
Some experts have said livestreaming the killing could violate domestic US law that prevents the transmission of obscene, indecent, or graphic material. They have argued it would be impossible to ensure minors were not able to access the livestream.
Critics have also questioned Hegseth’s claim that a public execution would serve as a deterrent, instead risking glorifying the attacker and inspiring copycats.
The US public also widely opposes the public execution, according to a ABC News-Washington Post-Ipsos poll released on Thursday.
Just 18 percent of respondents said the execution should be livestreamed, with 80 percent saying it should not be.

Liberman rejects Eisenkot's minority government plan, deepening opposition rift ahead of vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:26:24 UTC
23:26:24 KST

Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman on Thursday ruled out supporting a minority government after Israel's October 27 election, rejecting a proposal by fellow opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form a government even if the bloc seeking to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu fails to secure a parliamentary majority.
Speaking at a conference hosted by the Israel Democracy Institute and in a statement posted on social media, Liberman said: "We will not support any minority government, not even a temporary minority government. We need a Zionist majority government, period."
His remarks came a day after Eisenkot, chairman of the Yashar! party, said he would seek to establish a government even if the anti-Netanyahu bloc secured only 58 or 59 seats in the 120-member Knesset, with the aim of subsequently expanding it through support from additional mainstream Zionist lawmakers.
Liberman, whose party is among those Eisenkot would need to support such a government, ruled out joining a coalition with Arab or ultra-Orthodox parties. "Our position is clear and unequivocal: We will establish a coalition made up exclusively of Zionist parties. Without Ra'am, without the Joint List, without Shas and without United Torah Judaism," he said. He added that Likud could become a coalition partner if Netanyahu were no longer its leader, but insisted his party would never serve alongside the prime minister.
Despite the disagreement, Liberman expressed confidence that the opposition could secure a majority in the election, suggesting that some Likud lawmakers might be willing to join a coalition without Netanyahu. He said he knew lawmakers within the ruling party who understood the political situation and could provide the additional seats needed.
Eisenkot, who also attended the conference, avoided directly addressing Liberman's rejection of his proposal. Instead, he called for leadership that would bridge divisions within Israeli society. "My greatest challenge is preventing a situation in which one bloc defeats the other," he said. "This is a political struggle at the end of which every Israeli citizen should feel they have not been defeated." He also criticized Shas chairman Aryeh Deri over military conscription exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men.
Likud responded by accusing Liberman of hypocrisy, pointing to his participation in the previous coalition government alongside Mansour Abbas' Ra'am party. The party claimed Liberman had transferred 53 billion shekels to Islamic organizations that supported Hamas while serving as finance minister, an allegation presented without supporting evidence in its statement. "He talks right and acts left," Likud said, arguing that Eisenkot and Liberman could not form a government without Democrats chairman Yair Golan and the Arab parties.
Blue and White chairman Benny Gantz also weighed in, urging Eisenkot to pursue a broad Zionist unity government rather than a minority coalition. "Either Liberman is lying and will move to establish a minority government with the Arab parties under his leadership, or we're heading for another election," Gantz wrote on X. He pledged to support Eisenkot in efforts to form a national unity government.
Golan, meanwhile, rejected any possibility of joining a government with Netanyahu or Likud. "The only coalition that should be formed after October 27 is a coalition of the change bloc," he said, accusing Likud lawmakers of enabling the government's judicial overhaul, ultra-Orthodox military service exemptions and opposition to a state commission of inquiry into the October 7 Hamas attack. "We will not sit with Netanyahu, not with Likud and not with any party from the coalition of destruction," he declared.
The exchange exposed competing visions within the anti-Netanyahu camp less than two weeks before the election, with opposition leaders divided over whether a minority government, a broad unity coalition or an alliance excluding Likud entirely offers a viable path to power.

Trump says military execution will not be livestreamed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:26:02 UTC
23:26:02 KST

Trump says military execution will not be live-streamed
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump has cancelled the planned livestream of the execution of the former US Army major who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, saying on Oct 15 that he had overruled his defence chief who had intended it to be a public spectacle.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth had announced earlier in October that Nidal Hasan would be executed by a firing squad on Dec 3 at Fort Hood in Texas, the site of Hasan’s 2009 attack, surprising many by saying it would be broadcast live.
No other country is known to televise or livestream judicial executions.
“I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well-meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device,” Trump wrote in a social media post.
“He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed.”
The families of Hasan’s victims will be able to view the execution in person if they so choose, as is standard at US executions.
Some of Trump’s fellow Republicans, including Vice-President J.D. Vance, as well as religious leaders and international observers, had expressed doubts about the Pentagon’s livestream plan. Recent polls have also shown that a majority of Americans opposed live-streaming it.
Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the spiritual care of Catholic members of the US armed forces, also raised objections, while Pope Leo condemned capital punishment in all its forms.
Hegseth’s announcement came as capital punishment already faced renewed scrutiny after Christa Pike, convicted of murder in the 1990s, survived an execution attempt by Tennessee that left her badly injured and requiring hospitalisation.
Hasan, a former US Army psychiatrist, was found guilty in a military trial of fatally shooting 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.
Hegseth had said the broadcasting of the execution was needed to ensure people understand that “there’s serious consequences for these types of things”.
A spokesperson for the Department of Defense did not immediately respond to a request for comment. REUTERS

UK declares severe drought in southern England after record summer heat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:26:00 UTC
23:26:00 KST

A "severe drought" has been declared in parts of southern England by the UK government, which said it took the decision following an "unprecedented period of extreme weather".
The United Kingdom experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, featuring several heatwaves and an exceptional drought that resulted from a lack of rainfall not seen since records began in 1836.
More than 80 per cent of England is currently in a state of drought as it continues to experience below-average levels of rainfall into the autumn months.
"Record-breaking summer heat and severe drought have put our water resources under immense pressure," said Environment Agency head Philip Duffy on Thursday.
The "severe drought" status was declared in the English counties of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex. It is the worst stage triggered by "exceptionally low indicators over a long period of time".
The declaration came as two major reservoirs in south-west England serving nearly 400,000 properties were below 20 per cent of their storage capacity.
The Environment Agency said it "would expect reservoir storage to be around 75 per cent for this time of year".
South-east and south-west England have experienced their driest April to September period in more than a century, according to the government.
Scientists say climate change is intensifying weather events such as drought and heatwaves, resulting in records being broken more frequently.
As of last week, average reservoir levels across England stood at 54 per cent, with the nation receiving just 10 per cent of average October rainfall.
The government has urged water companies to monitor their water intake from natural resources and encouraged customers to cut their consumption, with usage restrictions already imposed in several regions.
"This level of drought is something we have not experienced for decades," environment minister Angela Eagle said.
Months of drought have piled pressure on everyone from farmers and anglers to firefighters who say tinder-dry conditions resulted in challenging wildfires this summer.
Since August, the government has convened a weekly National Drought Group, involving the weather agency, water companies, experts and farmers' representatives.

Haiti: Capoeira classes aim to promote peace

An association in Haiti is organising capoeira classes – an Afro-Brazilian martial art – in an attempt to reduce community violence and promote social reintegration. EU Eyes Starlink Alternative for Ukraine in Early 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:25:00 UTC
23:25:00 KST

The European Union is negotiating Ukraine’s access to its secure satellite communications program and could expand the system with commercial services in early 2027, the European Commission said on Wednesday, Oct. 14, following disruptions to Ukrainian military Starlink connections.
Speaking at a European Commission briefing, spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed that discussions concern Ukraine’s participation in GOVSATCOM.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We are currently in talks with Ukraine to fully associate Ukraine to Govsatcom,” he said.
However, Commission officials declined to compare European capabilities directly with Starlink or its military service, Starshield, leaving unanswered whether the proposed arrangements could support the same combat missions.
What Europe could offer
GOVSATCOM, short for Governmental Satellite Communications, pools satellite resources to provide secure connections for government users. Its hub began initial operations in January 2026, according to the European Union Agency for the Space Programme, or EUSPA.
At the time of its first operational deployment in March, the system brought together governmental satellite services supplied by France, Greece, Italy, Luxembourg and Spain. Cyprus became the first country to acquire and operationally use services through the hub.
The program supports communications for crisis management, surveillance and critical infrastructure, including situations in which terrestrial networks are disrupted.
Brussels Drops ‘Urgency’ Language on Ukraine’s Next Accession Steps
Rather than requiring each government to negotiate separately with several providers, the hub coordinates requests and allocates available satellite resources.
For Ukraine, that could provide another route to secure communications during Russian attacks on infrastructure and interruptions to conventional networks. It would also broaden the range of providers available to government users.
The diplomatic process predates the latest Starlink restrictions. On March 9, the EU Council authorized negotiations on an agreement governing Ukraine’s participation in GOVSATCOM and the Union Secure Connectivity Programme, including access to their governmental services. That authorization opened negotiations rather than granting access official itself.
Regnier said commercial capabilities could be added at the beginning of 2027, potentially supporting military needs.
He described this as an interim arrangement ahead of the planned IRIS² constellation of more than 300 satellites, which he said would be fully operational in 2029.
Why Ukraine needs another option
The European discussions have gained urgency after restrictions detected overnight on Oct. 13–14 disrupted Ukrainian drone operations.
Ukrainian Defense Ministry sources said units received no advance warning and reported connections dropping at different movement speeds, approximately 72 to 161 kilometers per hour.
The ministry contacted the United States, SpaceX and NATO partners while checking backup communications channels.
The disruption affected interceptor and medium-range strike drones, alongside reconnaissance, logistics and communications relay missions.
The reported speed limits concern how fast a terminal is moving, rather than its internet download speed.
Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said on Wednesday evening that connectivity at speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour was being restored, while calling for Starshield’s speed restriction to be removed entirely.
That partial restoration does not resolve every operational requirement. Two Ukrainian officials told RFE/RL that connections had improved below the threshold, but restrictions continued to complicate interception of Russia’s jet-powered drones.
One Ukrainian source said operating speeds needed to reach at least 450 kilometers per hour.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has accused those responsible of deliberately restricting the service during Russian attacks, saying the disruption weakened Ukraine’s defenses and endangered civilians. Who authorized the restrictions remains disputed.
Musk said Starshield systems are controlled by the US government and that their operational limits are determined by the US military and ultimately the president. A senior White House official, however, told Axios that the Trump administration was not involved.
Why switching networks will take time
According to Reuters, Europe has no ready-made replacement that Ukrainian troops can immediately attach to their drones.
Eutelsat already provides connectivity in Ukraine through its low Earth orbit and geostationary networks. But independent satellite consultant Christian Freiherr von der Ropp told Reuters that OneWeb faces capacity and performance constraints, while terminal cost, weight, size and power consumption limit frontline suitability.
Switching would also require replacing thousands of terminals: Starlink equipment uses proprietary technology and cannot simply connect to OneWeb.
European political pressure to develop alternatives is growing. In a statement on Thursday, Oct. 15, Renew Europe President Valérie Hayer urged EU leaders to strengthen support for Ukraine and address dependence on American satellite services.
“Recent days have also shown the urgent need for a European alternative to Starlink,” she said.

Scientists just voted to redefine how the world keeps time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:23:53 UTC
23:23:53 KST

Today an international group of scientists, diplomats and timekeepers voted to end the leap second, which has been keeping Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) aligned with the time according to Earth’s rotation (UT1) within one second of difference. The length of a day according to UTC is close to that of UT1 but not exactly the same because our planet’s rotation is irregular. We add a leap second every few years to keep them from drifting too far apart.
But soon the leap second will be replaced with a leap hour, added much more infrequently, which will extend the allowed difference between UT1 and UTC to an hour, or 3,600 seconds.
“After 30 years of debates, we are ready,” said Noël Dimarcq, a senior scientist at the French National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS) and president of International Bureau of Weights and Measures’ (BIPM’s) Consultative Committee for Time and Frequency, just before the vote, which took place at the General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) in Versailles, France.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
UTC is the world’s standard timescale. It’s the reference for how computers, phones, boats, planes, satellites and everything else tell time and for how navigation systems such as GPS function. It’s calculated via a weighted average of the time according to atomic clocks around the world and disseminated by the BIPM.
Shortly after UTC was first established in 1960, scientists noticed Earth’s rotation was ever so slightly slowing down, so it was not keeping pace with the count of the seconds according to atomic clocks. At the behest of astronomers and other experts, the first leap second was added to UTC in 1972 to realign the time standard with Earth’s rotation. Since 1972, 27 leap seconds have been added.
In the mid-2010s, however, Earth’s spin began speeding up. Scientists predicted that a negative leap second would be necessary soon, perhaps as early as 2029. Engineers say a negative leap second would be like a “mini Y2K” event because it would suddenly send the entire world one second backward in time, which could cause chaos in our digital infrastructure.
“Avoiding negative leap seconds is a very big driver to open the window” between UTC and UT1, says Nick Stamatakos, head of the Earth Orientation Department at the U.S. Naval Observatory, which manages the country’s GPS grid.
Since 2022 scientists, government officials, telecommunications professionals and others have been urgently trying to find a practical way to solve the leap second problem.
The BIPM, which is the official source of UTC, hosts CGPM every four years to discuss issues with member states. This morning officials at this year’s conference held the vote to end the leap second and make UTC continuous, with the change taking effect on May 20 (World Metrology Day), 2027. The resolution won by a majority vote.
Instead of using leap seconds, everyone has agreed that they will tolerate more drift between UTC and UT1 than they had in the past. And when things get really bad, we’ll add a leap hour instead. Although leap seconds have historically been added every few years, scientists predict that a leap hour won’t be needed for more than 1,000 years—effectively ending the BIPM’s procedure to link UTC with Earth’s position in the sky.
The change won’t be noticed by most of us, and switching to continuous time will be easier for our digital infrastructure—there will be much less risk of bugs or service outages arising from a leap second discontinuity. But the shift means that human civilization will even further diverge from our oldest way of telling time: by looking to the sky.

MOGADISHU, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- A global maritime watchdog on Thursday called for increased vigilance due to a recent resurgence in Somali piracy.
According to the nine-month report by the International Maritime Bureau (IMB), the threat of violence against crew members remains a major concern, prompting calls for timely incident reporting and strict adherence to Best Management Practices.
While overall piracy incidents remain at historic lows, the IMB recorded a surge in Somali piracy activity from January to September, with Somali pirates responsible for eight vessel hijackings and 94 percent of all crew members taken hostage globally.
"While incident levels are at their lowest in more than three decades, the recent uptick in Somali piracy activity is a reminder that the threat remains," IMB Director Michael Howlett said.
"Continued vigilance is essential to safeguarding seafarers and the vital trade routes on which the global economy depends," he added.
Despite some fatal incidents, the IMB noted that current activity remains far below the scale and deep-sea reach seen during the peak piracy era of 2008-2013. Meanwhile, only two incidents were reported in the Gulf of Guinea, with zero recorded in the most recent quarter.
Globally, the IMB reported just 51 incidents of piracy and armed robbery during the period, marking the lowest level recorded since 1992.
According to the report, 36 vessels were boarded, eight hijacked, four fired upon, and three subjected to attempted boardings.
Despite the historic decline in total events, physical threats to seafarers intensified, with 105 crew members directly affected, up from 72 in the same period in 2025. ■

‘Boiling point’: Why students are protesting against Albania’s Edi Rama
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:22:13 UTC
23:22:13 KST

‘Boiling point’: Why students are protesting against Albania’s Edi Rama
Experts say Albania’s protests reflect ignored student grievances and growing frustration.
Student protests against poor conditions in Albania’s education system have continued for a third day in the capital, Tirana, as Prime Minister Edi Rama insists he will not resign.
Demonstrators have called on Rama to quit in often violent protests since Tuesday. They have set fire to several buildings across the city, including the prime minister’s office, ministry buildings and branches of several banks.
Dozens of police officers and protesters have been injured amid attempts to disperse the crowds using water cannon and tear gas.
“What you are seeing is the boiling point of months of suppressed grievances,” Albanian journalist Arlis Alikaj told Al Jazeera.
Students have complained for months about the high cost of education and their limited employment prospects after graduation.
Afrim Krasniqi, a professor and researcher at the Institute for Political Studies in Tirana, told Al Jazeera that students and young people protested peacefully for nearly three months, “yet their demands were largely ignored, while the government often responded with discrediting campaigns rather than genuine dialogue”.
He added that the current escalation reflects “frustration not only with the government itself, but also with the lack of institutional accountability and responsiveness.”
The protests represent one of the most serious waves of public discontent directed at Rama, who won a fourth term last May but has since faced public anger over corruption allegations involving senior officials.
The unrest in Tirana coincides with a broader wave of student protests across Europe. In France, secondary school students have spent weeks protesting and blockading schools, demanding more teachers and better learning facilities. They have warned that deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms are undermining the quality of education.
Protests against Rama’s government began a few months ago, fuelled by plans to build a luxury resort along Albania’s largely unspoilt southern coast. Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son in law, is involved in the project.
Local media reported that the protests spread from Tirana to universities in Elbasan and Shkoder on Wednesday.
Albania is among the economies of the Western Balkans seeking to catch up with European living standards. However, the gap with the European Union average remains evident in purchasing power, wages, productivity and the quality of public services. Despite economic progress, the country continues to face challenges including emigration, regional inequalities and the need for stronger institutions and the rule of law.
After Montenegro, Albania stands out as one of the countries that has made the most progress towards full EU membership. However, behind the optimistic political rhetoric, frustration is growing among citizens over the slow pace of European integration and the lack of tangible improvements in their daily lives.
While opposition groups seek to support the demonstrators and capitalise on the moment to strengthen their own position, Alikaj said the protests are being driven by young people and students demanding systemic change.
On Thursday, Rama – who has been PM since 2013 – told Reuters, “As for calls for my resignation, governments change through democratic elections. Last year, we had elections, not a revolution.”
Sokol Lleshi, a lecturer at the University of New York Tirana specialising in political science, said social change is more likely to emerge from a broader coalition of different social groups, rather than mass mobilisation limited to university and secondary school students.
“Elite defection from the current ruling political elite could enable the institutional means to channel societal dissatisfaction or resentment into political and policy changes. Yet, the current student protest does not seem to replicate the December 2018 mass movement of university students and its effects”, Lleshi said.
The student protests that shook Albania in December 2018 began over rising education costs and forced Rama to dismiss eight ministers as part of a cabinet reshuffle and announce a package of measures known as the “Pact for the University”.
But some of the students’ demands remained unmet.
Lleshi drew some more positive conclusions from Albania’s past experience of social unrest.
Albanian society is polarised and unequal, “with hollowed intermediary political institutions”, he said, but the legacy of unrest and political confrontation will serve as a “warning to avoid destabilisation”, he said.
