Crown Prince Christian receives Denmark’s highest Dannebrog honor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:00:34 UTC
23:00:34 KST

King Frederik has marked his eldest son’s 21st birthday with a royal decoration and the release of new official portraits, while celebrations remain private.
Crown Prince Christian was awarded the Grand Commander Cross of the Order of the Dannebrog on Thursday, according to a statement from the Danish Royal House.
The decoration is the highest rank within the Order of the Dannebrog and is reserved for members of royalty who already hold the Order of the Elephant.
Christian received the Order of the Elephant on his 18th birthday, making him eligible for the distinction.
With his appointment, Denmark now has seven Grand Commanders of the Order of the Dannebrog.
The cross currently bears the monogram of King Frederik IX, who last awarded it. It will be updated with King Frederik’s monogram during restoration.
The Royal House also released portraits showing Christian wearing the Royal Life Guards’ red ceremonial uniform.
The photographs were taken several weeks earlier at Christian VII’s Palace at Amalienborg.
Christian currently serves as a second lieutenant and platoon commander with the Royal Life Guards at Høvelte Barracks.
He completed his compulsory military service in August 2025 before beginning officer training and is expected to remain in service until summer 2027.
The crown prince receives neither a military training salary nor a royal allowance.
His father also trained as a lieutenant, later qualifying as a naval frogman and serving four months with Greenland’s Sirius Patrol in 2000.
In a recent interview with Politiken, Christian said he would consider deployment after completing his lieutenant training.

Tiny parasitic wasp discovered in Denmark for the first time
A nature enthusiast searching beneath ferns in a North Zealand forest has identified an insect species never previously recorded in the country.
The discovery was made in mid-September at Gribskov National Nature Park during a bioblitz, a 24-hour event in which participants search for and document wildlife.
Around 70 people took part in the event, organized in collaboration with the Vores Vilde Natur project and biodiversity platform Arter.dk.
Nature educator Lars Holm Hansen discovered the wasp, measuring just a few millimeters, while shaking bracken ferns to examine the insects hiding underneath.
He collected several specimens using an insect aspirator but could not immediately identify them.
After posting a photograph on Arter.dk, he received help from experts who identified the species as Hemiptarsenus ornatus.
“It shows that if you put in a little effort out in the field, you can get lucky, and it is simply worth the effort,” Hansen said.
The Natural History Museum of Denmark confirmed the finding in a press release.
Museum insect curator Lars Vilhelmsen explained that the species has previously been recorded in Germany, Sweden and Norway.
“It has probably been here all along. It is already known from several countries around us, but it is so small that you do not just easily spot it,” Vilhelmsen said.
He added that relatively few people in Denmark study parasitic wasps, meaning many species may remain undocumented.
Hansen, who had participated in six bioblitz events this year, also suggested the insect’s Danish name: smykket dværgsnyltehveps.
He believes Danish names make unfamiliar species easier to discuss and remember.

Three Danish films shortlisted for Europe’s Oscars
Three Danish films have been shortlisted for the European Film Awards, often described as Europe’s equivalent of the Oscars.
The films are the dramas Kvinde ukendt by May el-Toukhy and Gæsten by Mads Mengel, and Sine Plambech’s documentary Rescue, the Danish Film Institute announced on Instagram.
A total of 45 films have been shortlisted in the fiction category.
May el-Toukhy’s Kvinde ukendt has already received international recognition. The drama was selected for the Venice Film Festival in September, where it won the main prize, the Golden Lion. Its lead actress, Mathilde Arcel, was named best actress.
The film has also been selected as Denmark’s entry for the Academy Awards in the Best International Feature Film category.
Set during the liberation of Denmark in May 1945, the drama follows a woman who has worked as a maid in the home of an elderly, respected widower she is now preparing to marry. She struggles to hide the fact that she has had a relationship with a German soldier.
Mads Mengel’s Gæsten has also attracted international attention. In July, the film received two awards at the Karlovy Vary International Film Festival in the Czech Republic.
It won the Special Jury Prize in the festival’s main competition, known as the Crystal Globe Competition, while Mengel was named best director.
The film follows Karl and Emilie, a couple preparing to host a naming ceremony for their son. Their plans are disrupted when an uninvited guest arrives: Karl’s mother, played by Trine Dyrholm, with whom he has not spoken for years.
The third Danish film on the shortlist is Rescue, a documentary by anthropologist Sine Plambech. It had its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival in September.
The documentary follows people fleeing across the Mediterranean and examines how the European Union’s border policies affect the lives and conditions of refugees.
Rescue is one of 15 films shortlisted in the documentary category.
Producers, distributors and other rights holders can submit films for consideration by the European Film Academy. The academy’s board and invited European experts then select films for the shortlist.
Members of the academy, which includes professionals from across the European film industry, watch the shortlisted films and vote to determine the final nominations. They vote again to select the winners once the nominations have been announced.
The final nominations will be announced on November 14. The awards ceremony will take place in Athens, the Greek capital, on January 16.

Liberal Alliance wants mindset interview for citizenship applicant
A debate in Denmark over a proposed law granting citizenship to 2,055 people has centered on whether the applicants have been checked well enough for anti-democratic opinions.
Liberal Alliance, a political party in Denmark, carried out its own check of the people listed in the citizenship bill. During this review, the party found a woman who had repeatedly praised Hamas and former Hamas leaders Yahya Sinwar and Ismail Haniyeh.
Following the discovery, Liberal Alliance wants the woman called in for an interview with Indfødsretsudvalget, the Naturalization Committee of the Danish parliament.
Alex Vanopslagh, the leader of Liberal Alliance, spoke about the matter to the Danish newspaper Politiken.
“As we see it, it just emphasizes the need to wait to grant more citizenships until a proper screening model is in place, so that we can specifically catch some types who, based on what we can see so far, appear strongly anti-democratic,” he told the newspaper.
Every six months, a new bill is introduced in Folketinget, the Danish parliament, to give people Danish citizenship. This happens after an application process that is often long and detailed. This process was also followed under the previous coalition government in Denmark.
The most recent round of citizenships was scheduled at the same time a parliamentary election was called in the spring. Because of the election, the bill that included citizenship for the 2,055 people was delayed.
The delay gave momentum to demands from opposition parties. They argued that officials must carry out a more thorough review of the people on the list to find out if any of them hold anti-democratic views. Socialdemokratiet, the Danish Social Democratic Party, supported this demand as well.
However, the new government decided to present the citizenship bill before a new screening system was ready. This choice led to a larger debate during the opening of the Danish parliament.
During that debate, Rasmus Stoklund, the political spokesperson for Socialdemokratiet, said that if opposition parties found a person on the bill who had anti-democratic views, they could inform the Naturalization Committee. Liberal Alliance has now acted on that suggestion.
Politiken also spoke with the woman identified by the party. She denied that she supports Hamas or any killings.
“I do not support anyone who kills anyone. Because I do not like anyone killing anyone, regardless of whether they are Israeli, Russian or anything else,” the woman told the newspaper.
She stated that she is ready to attend an interview with the committee to explain her position.
Other political parties have reacted differently to the proposal. Dansk Folkeparti, the Danish People’s Party, supports calling the woman in for an interview.
However, Enhedslisten, the Danish left-wing Red-Green Alliance party, strongly opposes the idea.
“It is deeply concerning that Liberal Alliance now to such an extent wants to begin exercising thought control,” Peder Hvelplund, the citizenship spokesperson for Enhedslisten, told Politiken.

Denmark’s minister for homeland security and emergency preparedness, Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen, says there is a clear need to talk with members of the Danish parliament about how to protect the country against cyberattacks.
Bech-Nielsen belongs to SF (Socialistisk Folkeparti), the Socialist People’s Party, which is a left-wing and green political party in Denmark. She spoke about the situation to the Danish broadcaster TV 2.
“The serious threat assessment and recent events are the reason why I have summoned the parties to a discussion of what initiatives can be set in motion,” she said.

Her comments came right after Sund & Bælt, the state-owned company in charge of major Danish bridge and tunnel links, announced on Tuesday afternoon that its construction site at Rødbyhavn was hit by what it called a cyber incident.
“Our contractor, FLC, has informed us that they have been subjected to a cyber incident,” said Jens Villemoes, the head of press at Sund & Bælt, in a statement published on the company’s website. FLC stands for Femern Link Contractors, the consortium hired to build the tunnel.
The local newspaper Lolland-Falsters Folketidende described the event as a hacker attack. According to the newspaper, the problems meant that workers were ordered not to connect to Wi-Fi, turn on their computers, or open emails from the contractor.

Bech-Nielsen had actually called for the political meeting before the problems hit the Femern project. That decision came after a recent leak of Danish CPR numbers, which are the personal identification numbers assigned to all citizens in Denmark.
The minister said it is still too early to draw final conclusions about the latest incident, but noted that “the authorities are investigating” it.

Kirsten Schwalbe becomes Denmark’s oldest person ever at 112
A woman from Struer has set a national longevity record, reaching 112 years and 218 days on Wednesday and surpassing the previous record held by Karla Lindholm Jensen.
Schwalbe also joins the list of Europe’s 10 oldest living people. The world’s oldest living person is Britain’s Ethel Caterham, who is 117.
The previous Danish record holder, Karla Lindholm Jensen from Herning, died in 2020.
Ahead of the milestone, Jyllands-Posten attempted to interview Schwalbe, but she needed a day of rest. Instead, the newspaper spoke with two of her three daughters.
Her daughter Hanne Jensen, 86, described how her mother sometimes struggles to understand that her children are now elderly themselves.
“She knows well enough that we are getting older, but she forgets that we can no longer withstand everything,” Jensen told the newspaper.
Schwalbe was born in Salling in 1914, just months before World War I began, and grew up alongside nine siblings.
She married her first husband in 1938, and the couple had three children.
Despite her age, Schwalbe continues to live in her own home in Struer.
Her life has previously been documented by regional broadcaster TV Midtvest in the television series “Kirstens vilde år,” which airs on TV 2.
Schwalbe has attributed her longevity partly to genetics. Four of her nine siblings also lived beyond 100, she told Berlingske in 2024.
She has also emphasized the importance of maintaining a positive outlook, previously telling TV Midtvest that a person’s mood plays an important role in living a long life.
Government party proposes mandatory helmets for e-bike riders
Rising numbers of serious traffic injuries have prompted Moderaterne, the Moderates, to call for stricter safety rules for people using electric bicycles.
Sten Larsen, the party’s health spokesperson, told regional broadcaster TV2 Østjylland that helmets should become a legal requirement for e-bike riders.
“E-bikes are both heavier and faster than regular bicycles,” Larsen said.
He pointed to an increase in serious injuries and deaths involving electric bicycles as justification for the proposal.
Currently, Denmark does not require helmets for ordinary bicycles or standard e-bikes, whose motors provide assistance at speeds of up to 25 kilometers per hour.
However, helmets are already mandatory for speed pedelecs, which can provide motor assistance up to 45 kilometers per hour.
According to the Danish Road Directorate, 200 e-bike riders were injured in traffic accidents in 2025, including 133 who suffered serious injuries. Another 11 riders died.
The number of seriously injured e-bike riders was the highest recorded in six years.
Larsen wants to discuss the proposed legislation with Transport Minister Signe Munk of Socialistisk Folkeparti, the Socialist People’s Party.
Ritzau sought a comment from Munk, but her ministry said she was unavailable.
Cyklistforbundet, the Danish Cyclists’ Federation, opposes making helmets compulsory, arguing that such a measure could discourage cycling.
“Our purpose is to get more people to cycle. So every measure that pulls in the opposite direction, we will oppose. But we warmly recommend that people use a bicycle helmet,” federation chair Jens Peter Hansen told TV2 Østjylland.
The proposal would introduce a helmet requirement for standard e-bikes, bringing their rules closer to those already applying to faster electric bicycles.

Denmark should maintain its current foreign aid budget but change where the money goes, according to Jacob Jensen, foreign affairs spokesperson for Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party.

Greenland moves closer to restoring former time zone and ending daylight saving time
Greenland’s three governing parties have agreed to support a proposal that would move the territory back to UTC-3 in 2028, reversing a decision made just a few years ago.
The parties, which hold a majority in Inatsisartut, Greenland’s parliament, announced their position during a debate Tuesday, according to Sermitsiaq.
The proposal would also abolish daylight saving time starting next year.
“We have decided that we should return to UTC-3 on the basis of the many people who have submitted a consultation response,” the governing parties said.
In 2022, Greenland’s parliament approved a move from UTC-3 to UTC-2 to balance the time difference with Europe and the United States. The change took effect in March 2023.
However, the decision has remained controversial, with 4,142 residents signing a petition calling for the previous time zone to return.
Opposition parties Naleraq and Siumut proposed reversing the change in May. The government initially opposed the move but supported ending daylight saving time.
Despite the government’s changed position, Greenlandic leader Jens-Frederik Nielsen of Demokraatit, the Democrats party, warned about potential consequences.
He said the change would increase the time difference with Europe by one hour in winter and two hours in summer.
Nielsen argued that reduced overlap with Danish medical specialists could lead to longer patient waiting times.
He also warned of higher costs for businesses, weaker flight connections with Europe and financial expenses associated with changing the time zone.
The proposal is scheduled for a final parliamentary vote October 21.

Greenland cancels 39.8 million DKK in benefit repayment claims
Greenland’s government has cancelled repayment claims totaling 39.8 million DKK against more than 19,000 residents who received excessive employment benefits because of government IT errors.
Naalakkersuisut, Greenland’s government, announced Saturday that recipients would not have to return the overpayments from the Suila-tapit program.
Suila-tapit is an employment tax allowance of up to 1,313 DKK a month for workers earning between 70,000 and 500,000 DKK annually.
The program was introduced on January 1, 2025, to encourage employment and reduce economic inequality.
Errors in the Greenlandic Self-Government’s IT systems caused some residents to receive excessive payments during 2025. The government initially demanded that the money be repaid.
“Some citizens were paid too much without having done anything wrong themselves, and that responsibility does not lie with the individual citizen,” Finance Minister Aqqaluaq B. Egede of Inuit Ataqatigiit said.
Residents who have already repaid the money will receive refunds.
“We cannot turn back time, but we can take responsibility and ensure that citizens do not have to pay for the mistakes made in the system,” Egede said.
The repayment demands had faced public opposition. A large demonstration was planned in Nuuk on Saturday but was cancelled shortly after the government announced it would withdraw the claims.

Copenhagen has far more municipal savings per resident than poorer municipalities
Danish municipalities differ significantly in how much readily available money they hold, according to an analysis by CEPOS, a Danish liberal think tank.
Copenhagen Municipality has the largest liquid holdings per resident, with savings equivalent to 31,685 DKK for each person.
At the other end of the ranking are Hjørring, Sorø, Thisted, Lolland and Aalborg municipalities. Their liquid holdings range from 3,127 DKK to 4,354 DKK per resident.
Liquid holdings can be viewed as municipal savings that have not been allocated to a specific purpose. Municipalities typically use the money to manage ongoing incoming and outgoing payments.
CEPOS said municipalities must always maintain a certain level of liquidity to cover their regular financial obligations.
Local authorities may also build up savings to finance future projects.
More than 500 marine mammals stranded along Danish coasts in 2025
A total of 538 marine mammals were recorded as stranded along Denmark’s coasts in 2025, according to a report from the Danish Environmental Protection Agency’s emergency service for stranded marine mammals.
The animals included 363 harbor seals, 38 grey seals and 137 harbor porpoises.
Most were found dead. Of the harbor seals, 310 were dead when discovered, while 136 of the 137 harbor porpoises were found dead.
The report identified disease, parasites, injuries and weakness as possible reasons for the strandings.
One animal from each of the three groups was recorded as having stranded after becoming caught unintentionally in fishing nets.
More unusual marine mammals were also found along the Danish coastline during 2025. These included a humpback whale and a striped dolphin.
Ambulances get deer whistles to avoid hitting animals
Ambulances and emergency medical vehicles in the North Denmark Region will be equipped with wildlife whistles to reduce the risk of collisions with animals.
The small plastic whistles are mounted outside vehicles and produce a high-frequency sound when air passes through them. The sound is intended to frighten animals away from the road.
“Unfortunately, we have a number of collisions with animals when we drive with emergency signals in forests and natural areas,” the region’s Prehospital Services wrote on Facebook.
“It is dangerous for the people in the car, it delays the driving, and is dangerous for the animals.”
The decision comes as Denmark faces a possible record year for deer collisions.
Dyrenes Beskyttelse, Denmark’s largest animal welfare organization, recorded 8,739 deer collisions during the first nine months of 2026. That compares with 7,994 during the same period in 2025.
The previous annual record was 11,870 collisions in 2025.
The risk of encountering deer is particularly high during autumn and around sunrise and sunset.
However, it remains unclear whether wildlife whistles effectively keep animals away from roads.
Two insurance companies previously gave the devices to motorists as part of separate trials. According to FDM, Denmark’s main car owners’ association, the companies could not reach a clear conclusion about whether the whistles reduced collisions.

Apartment prices in Copenhagen fell for the second consecutive month in September, while prices in Aarhus rose sharply.
The average sales price for owner-occupied apartments in Copenhagen Municipality declined by 1.0 percent from August to September, according to housing platform Boligsiden. Prices fell by 0.5 percent the previous month.

In Aarhus Municipality, apartment prices rose by 3.7 percent in September, the third-largest monthly increase since records began in 2011.

Prices in Aarhus have increased by 23.3 percent over the past year. Nordea housing economist Lise Nytoft Bergmann called the development “extraordinary” but warned that prices would eventually reach a limit.
Nationwide apartment prices were unchanged in September. Prices for houses and holiday homes increased by 0.3 percent overall.
Suspected hacker says AI created program used in Danish CPR breach
The suspected hacker behind the theft of nearly 8.75 million Danish CPR numbers says artificial intelligence created the computer program used in the attack.
“Any AI model launched within the past year or so would be able to do it,” the anonymous person told Danish newspaper Politiken.
Two experts reviewed the program, which contains more than 40,000 characters, and concluded that its code was generated by artificial intelligence, Politiken reported.
Danish authorities disclosed last week that unauthorized people accessed names, addresses and CPR numbers during approximately 10 days in September. CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The suspected hacker said the program accessed the national CPR register through a website operated by Odense-based company Pays ApS. Login details were allegedly obtained from a former employee’s leaked password.
Politiken reported that at least three Pays accounts used “123456” as their password, including the administrator account. Pays confirmed to Danish broadcaster TV 2 that it was the compromised company.
The suspected hacker denied having advanced technical skills. An error in the AI-generated code reportedly caused the program to search for people born in 1877 instead of 1977. Consequently, data for people born in 1977 was absent from material shared with Politiken.
The person said they did not intend to sell or publish the information. Pays’ director did not respond to Politiken’s inquiries about the company’s security.

Museums and animal parks are the most popular attractions among Danes planning activities during the autumn holiday.
One in five people spending the holiday in Denmark plans to visit a museum or animal park, according to a Norstat survey conducted for Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce and a major business association.

Number of disability pensioners under 40 falls for first time since 2020
The number of people under age 40 receiving disability pensions in Denmark has fallen for the first time in more than six years, according to figures from the Jobindsats.dk employment database.
In September, 43,229 people in the age group received disability pensions, 98 fewer than in August. It was the first monthly decline since early 2020.
Jesper Brask Fischer, head of welfare at pension company PFA, said it was too early to celebrate.
“The number of young people on disability pension is far higher than just a few years ago, and the development underlines the need for a strong effort toward prevention and early assistance,” he said.
The number of disability pension recipients under 40 has increased from 29,000 to more than 43,000 over the past decade. PFA has previously identified a possible connection between poor mental health and the increase.
Across all age groups, the number of disability pension recipients has declined for two consecutive months for the first time since late summer 2021.
Denmark had 261,418 disability pension recipients in September, down 487 from August.
Fischer said further consecutive declines could indicate that fewer people are entering the disability pension system. For now, however, he described the figures as only a cautious positive sign after years of significant growth.
Renovating all public concrete shelters could cost up to 3 billion DKK
Renovating Denmark’s 1,694 public concrete trench shelters and preparing them for use could cost between 2 billion and 3 billion DKK.
Public Security and Emergency Preparedness Minister Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen of the Socialist People’s Party provided the estimate in a response to the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, according to construction trade publication Licitationen.
The estimate remains highly uncertain and requires further assessment.
Renovating only the 831 shelters that already meet basic requirements and could be opened during an immediate emergency would cost between 500 million and 1 billion DKK.
Most of the shelters require treatment for mold and pests because they have not been used for many years, the parliamentary response said.
The Ministry of Public Security and Emergency Preparedness began inspecting Denmark’s shelter capacity and condition in May 2025. The review of concrete trench shelters is complete, while inspections of reinforced shelters are expected to continue until 2027.
Concrete trench shelters are public facilities intended for people away from home, including road users and residents of buildings without shelters.
Most Danish shelter spaces are in reinforced rooms inside residential and other buildings. Denmark also has supplementary shelters that offer some protection but do not meet full shelter requirements.
A 2024 inventory found about 3.4 million shelter spaces nationwide. Concrete trench shelters accounted for 113,018 of them.

Danish inflation rises to 2.2 percent as fuel prices increase
Denmark’s annual inflation rate rose to 2.2 percent in September, up 0.2 percentage points from August, Statistics Denmark reported Monday.
Higher fuel costs were the main reason for the increase, with transportation prices contributing significantly to inflation between August and September.
Mette Hørdum Larsen, chief economist at Lederne, an organization representing managers and executives, said similar developments were visible in neighboring countries.
“But in fact, the rising energy prices do not become quite as visible in Danish inflation because the electricity tax has largely been removed this year and next year,” she wrote in a commentary.
Lower prices for holiday home rentals, package holidays and food helped offset the increase.
Larsen said there was no reason for serious concern because inflation remained close to the two percent level generally associated with stable prices. She added that there were no signs that higher energy costs were spreading throughout the economy.
Søren Kristensen, chief economist at Danish bank AL Sydbank, reached a similar conclusion.
However, he said the reduced electricity tax was concealing a significant rise in underlying inflation during recent months.
“In fact, in recent quarters there has been a decline in purchasing power for the Danes because precisely during that period prices have run faster than wages,” Kristensen wrote.

Danish business emergency network grows to 223 members
The number of companies and organizations in Virksomhedsberedskabet, Denmark’s business emergency preparedness network, has risen from 63 to 223 in just over 10 months.
Together, its members represent about 350,000 private-sector employees.
The network coordinates resources from private companies so they can help maintain essential services during serious crises.
“It is about having this conversation about what one already has on the shelves, and how it can actually be repurposed for a crisis and support critical infrastructure,” director Maja Broløs said.
Fitness centers could provide shelter, baby stores could supply essential products and department stores could make their buildings available. Companies participating in the network include SATS Denmark, BabySam and IKEA.
Virksomhedsberedskabet is part of a broader effort to strengthen Denmark’s emergency preparedness. In February, the government launched a total defence preparedness initiative and allocated 1.2 billion DKK to the area.
Broløs said more members would be needed to respond effectively to a nationwide crisis.
“If it is a major regional crisis, we are in a pretty good position. But if it is nationwide, then those are completely different numbers we need to reach,” she said.
The network aims to exceed 1,000 members by 2029. By 2028, it plans to be capable of mobilizing members’ resources nationwide within six hours.

DTU Aqua, the National Institute of Aquatic Resources at the Technical University of Denmark, will establish 40 fish nurseries and spawning grounds near Bornholm over the next five years.

Bornholm is one of nine European islands participating in the EU-funded Isla Bonita project. Each island will establish a “Living Lab” where local groups will collaborate on nature restoration.

`123456’ password used in massive Danish CPR data breach
At least three accounts at the company linked to a major breach of Denmark’s CPR register reportedly used the password “123456”, including an administrator account.
At least three user accounts at the Funen-based IT company Pays used the password “123456” when hackers gained access to Denmark’s CPR register, Politiken reports.
One of them was the company’s administrator account.
The breach exposed information linked to around 8.8 million CPR numbers. The CPR system is Denmark’s central civil registration database and contains personal information on people living or previously registered in Denmark.
The newspaper Politiken reviewed data from the breach that the hacker allegedly used to gain access to the system.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor at Aarhus University’s Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, described the company’s password security as “hopeless”.
“There is really no security, it is an open door. A password like ‘123456’ is one of the very first things you would guess if you took a list of common passwords,” he told Politiken.
“I find it hard to see that you could have worse security. It was a matter of time before things went wrong.”
Pays ApS, based in Odense, confirmed to TV 2 on Friday that it was the company whose access had been compromised.
“We can confirm that we are the company that has been subjected to an attack where our legal access to search for information in the CPR system has been abused,” managing director and owner Sophie Laursen said in an email to TV 2.
The hacker had access to the CPR register from 10 September for a total of 21 days and 17 hours.
An anonymous hacker told Politiken on Thursday that they were behind the attack and claimed gaining access had not been particularly difficult.
According to the hacker, access was initially obtained using a leaked password belonging to a former employee of a small Danish company. The hacker then allegedly created two computer programs to retrieve information from the CPR system and store it externally.
The hacker told Politiken that there were no plans to sell or publish the information.
Private companies and associations can be granted access to information in Denmark’s CPR register when they have a legitimate need, for example to obtain address information about customers or members.
According to Denmark’s Central Business Register, Pays ApS had two employees as of July 2026.
One in four Danish driving penalty points linked to mobile phone use
Danish motorists received almost 21,000 penalty points for using handheld mobile phones while driving last year – the highest number in four years.
Mobile phones are playing a growing role in traffic offences in Denmark.
In 2025, motorists received 20,910 penalty points on their driving licences for using a handheld mobile phone behind the wheel, according to figures from the police case management system POLSAS.
That means mobile phone use accounted for roughly one in every four of the 84,056 penalty points issued for traffic offences during the year.
The number of mobile-related penalty points increased by 7.5 percent compared with 2024 and reached its highest level in four years.
On average, police issued 57 penalty points every day for handheld mobile phone use.
Britta Bjerregaard, claims director at insurance company Alm. Brand, described the development as deeply concerning.
“Most people know full well that the phone should stay put while driving. Still, it can be tempting to just answer a call, reply to a message, or change the song,” she said.
“Traffic does not pause while you look at the screen.”
89 metres without watching the road
The Danish Road Safety Council considers inattention one of the major risks on Danish roads, with mobile phones posing a particular problem.
“The mobile phone takes an incredible amount of attention if you use it behind the wheel,” deputy director Karina Petersen said.
“If you look at the screen for four seconds at country road speed, you are driving 89 metres blind.”
However, Petersen cautioned that the increase in recorded offences does not necessarily mean that more drivers are using their phones.
The rise could also reflect more police checks or improved camera equipment used for traffic enforcement.
What are the rules in Denmark?
Using a handheld mobile phone while driving in Denmark results in a DKK 1,500 fine and a penalty point on your driving licence. An additional DKK 1,000 contribution to the Victims’ Fund is also charged.
The rule applies even when the car is stationary in traffic or waiting at a red light.
Drivers may briefly operate a phone if it is securely mounted, and using a vehicle’s built-in screen is also permitted.
The ban on handheld mobile phone use also applies to cyclists, electric scooter users and drivers of other motorised vehicles.

IEA members to accelerate release of 100M barrels as oil markets remain tight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:00:34 UTC
23:00:34 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
International Energy Agency (IEA) members agreed Thursday to accelerate the release of around 100 million barrels of remaining emergency oil stocks, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel as soon as possible amid continued tightness in global energy markets.
The agency's Governing Board said its latest assessments pointed to persistent tightness in oil markets, particularly diesel, following a meeting on energy markets and security.
Approximately 330 million barrels have already been released under the collective action launched in March in response to the Strait of Hormuz crisis.
Total releases will exceed the original commitment of 400 million barrels, as some members have released more than initially pledged and others intend to do so, the board said.
Members agreed to take all necessary steps to complete the remaining releases in a timely manner consistent with national circumstances, with specific acceleration plans already in place.
The board also encouraged members with oil production and refining capacity to boost supplies of crude and refined products, particularly diesel, and emphasized the importance of the free flow of energy trade.
Reaffirming their commitment to international energy security, members expressed willingness to take further action to address global energy market challenges, building on the G7 statement of Oct. 2.
The IEA Secretariat will monitor progress and inform G7 leaders and the Governing Board of further action needed, drawing on an updated oil market assessment focused on diesel.

Nordea shares plunge 7.3 percent after earnings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:00:28 UTC
23:00:28 KST

The Nordic region’s largest bank reported third-quarter earnings broadly in line with analysts’ expectations, but uncertainty surrounding regulatory assessments weighed on investor confidence Thursday.
Nordea shares fell 7.3 percent by 12:50 p.m., making the bank the worst performer in Denmark’s C25 stock index.
The decline followed the publication of Nordea’s quarterly financial results, which showed a profit of 1,181 billion euros and total income of 2,968 billion euros.
Both figures were broadly consistent with analysts’ forecasts.
However, the bank announced it would suspend a planned share buyback program while awaiting clarification from the European Central Bank (ECB) regarding its risk assessments.
The regulatory process is not expected to conclude until 2027.
Share buybacks allow companies to return money to shareholders by purchasing their own shares, often reducing the number available and potentially increasing the value of those remaining.
According to Danish financial newspaper Børsen, Nordea had planned to repurchase approximately 500 million euros worth of shares.
Martin Munk, senior equity adviser at Jyske Bank, said the market reaction reflected regulatory uncertainty rather than disappointing financial performance.
“It is not the financial statements that are creating noise. Rather, it is the uncertainty about where they land with the ECB,” Munk told MarketWire.
Nordea CEO Frank Vang-Jensen acknowledged that the regulatory review was taking longer than anticipated.
“It has proven to be a long process,” he told Børsen.
Vang-Jensen said the bank considered pausing repurchases appropriate while uncertainty remained over its future risk-weighted assets, a measure used to determine how much capital banks must hold against potential losses.

Tiny parasitic wasp discovered in Denmark for the first time
A nature enthusiast searching beneath ferns in a North Zealand forest has identified an insect species never previously recorded in the country.
The discovery was made in mid-September at Gribskov National Nature Park during a bioblitz, a 24-hour event in which participants search for and document wildlife.
Around 70 people took part in the event, organized in collaboration with the Vores Vilde Natur project and biodiversity platform Arter.dk.
Nature educator Lars Holm Hansen discovered the wasp, measuring just a few millimeters, while shaking bracken ferns to examine the insects hiding underneath.
He collected several specimens using an insect aspirator but could not immediately identify them.
After posting a photograph on Arter.dk, he received help from experts who identified the species as Hemiptarsenus ornatus.
“It shows that if you put in a little effort out in the field, you can get lucky, and it is simply worth the effort,” Hansen said.
The Natural History Museum of Denmark confirmed the finding in a press release.
Museum insect curator Lars Vilhelmsen explained that the species has previously been recorded in Germany, Sweden and Norway.
“It has probably been here all along. It is already known from several countries around us, but it is so small that you do not just easily spot it,” Vilhelmsen said.
He added that relatively few people in Denmark study parasitic wasps, meaning many species may remain undocumented.
Hansen, who had participated in six bioblitz events this year, also suggested the insect’s Danish name: smykket dværgsnyltehveps.
He believes Danish names make unfamiliar species easier to discuss and remember.

Denmark’s decision comes despite the general principle of open borders under the Schengen Agreement, which allows people to travel between participating European countries without routine border checks.
However, regulations introduced in 2024 allow countries to extend existing border controls when the security threats that originally justified them remain in place.
Wammen said Denmark continues to face threats involving terrorism and sabotage.

Save the Children received 4,069 reports of suspected artificial intelligence-generated sexual abuse material involving children and young people during the first six months of 2026, according to figures obtained by Kristeligt Dagblad.
The international children’s rights organization recorded 6,558 reports throughout 2025, compared with 2,770 in 2024, an increase of approximately 140 percent.
The figures reflect reports submitted by people who believe they have encountered such material online, rather than confirmed cases.
Lea Wermelin, justice spokesperson for Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, expressed concern about the growing numbers.
“The technology makes it much easier to make, but we must never get used to it just being something encountered online,” she told Kristeligt Dagblad.
Pernille Spitz, Save the Children’s head of protection against abuse, warned that greater exposure to such content could make it appear more acceptable.
“The more of it there is, and the easier it is to come across, the more legitimate it may seem,” Spitz said.
Save the Children’s reporting service, AnmeldDet, reviews submissions from the public and assesses whether they should be forwarded to authorities.
During 2026, the service has referred 377 reports to police.
Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit, known as NSK, told Kristeligt Dagblad that it could not determine what proportion of child sexual abuse material involved artificial intelligence.
However, the agency said it believed AI was increasingly being used to produce such content.
Denmark amended its criminal code in 2025 to make realistic AI-generated child sexual abuse material punishable by law.
Denmark restricts land registry searches after 17 million queries in days
An unusually high volume of requests for publicly available property information has prompted authorities to introduce new safeguards following disruptions to a government database.
The Danish Court Administration said 17.2 million searches were recorded in the Digital Land Registration System over several days, compared with fewer than two million in a typical week.
The activity was discovered after the system experienced repeated disruptions during week 41.
Rikke Holler, president of the Land Registration Court, emphasized that the searches were legal and involved only information available without logging in through MitID, Denmark’s digital identification system.
“It is the number of lookups that gives cause for attention,” Holler said.
The system provides limited public information about properties, cooperative housing and vehicles.
Authorities have not identified what caused the surge in activity.
Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen, a member of Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, said he had informed the Danish Parliament about the incident.
Although the searches were permitted, Wammen said their unusual volume warranted serious attention.
The Danish Court Administration warned that publicly available information could potentially be used to make fraud attempts appear more convincing.
It also referred to a recent leak involving 8.8 million CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
Wammen urged people never to share passwords or confidential information through phone calls or emails, even when someone contacting them knows details they consider private.
The Land Registration Court has introduced additional limits on searches to maintain system stability.
Officials did not specify the measures but reported that the number of queries had decreased following their introduction.

Three Danish films shortlisted for Europe’s Oscars
Three Danish films have been shortlisted for the European Film Awards, often described as Europe’s equivalent of the Oscars.
The films are the dramas Kvinde ukendt by May el-Toukhy and Gæsten by Mads Mengel, and Sine Plambech’s documentary Rescue, the Danish Film Institute announced on Instagram.
A total of 45 films have been shortlisted in the fiction category.
May el-Toukhy’s Kvinde ukendt has already received international recognition. The drama was selected for the Venice Film Festival in September, where it won the main prize, the Golden Lion. Its lead actress, Mathilde Arcel, was named best actress.
The film has also been selected as Denmark’s entry for the Academy Awards in the Best International Feature Film category.
Set during the liberation of Denmark in May 1945, the drama follows a woman who has worked as a maid in the home of an elderly, respected widower she is now preparing to marry. She struggles to hide the fact that she has had a relationship with a German soldier.
Mads Mengel’s Gæsten has also attracted international attention. In July, the film received two awards at the Karlovy Vary International Film Festival in the Czech Republic.
It won the Special Jury Prize in the festival’s main competition, known as the Crystal Globe Competition, while Mengel was named best director.
The film follows Karl and Emilie, a couple preparing to host a naming ceremony for their son. Their plans are disrupted when an uninvited guest arrives: Karl’s mother, played by Trine Dyrholm, with whom he has not spoken for years.
The third Danish film on the shortlist is Rescue, a documentary by anthropologist Sine Plambech. It had its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival in September.
The documentary follows people fleeing across the Mediterranean and examines how the European Union’s border policies affect the lives and conditions of refugees.
Rescue is one of 15 films shortlisted in the documentary category.
Producers, distributors and other rights holders can submit films for consideration by the European Film Academy. The academy’s board and invited European experts then select films for the shortlist.
Members of the academy, which includes professionals from across the European film industry, watch the shortlisted films and vote to determine the final nominations. They vote again to select the winners once the nominations have been announced.
The final nominations will be announced on November 14. The awards ceremony will take place in Athens, the Greek capital, on January 16.

Liberal Alliance wants mindset interview for citizenship applicant
A debate in Denmark over a proposed law granting citizenship to 2,055 people has centered on whether the applicants have been checked well enough for anti-democratic opinions.
Liberal Alliance, a political party in Denmark, carried out its own check of the people listed in the citizenship bill. During this review, the party found a woman who had repeatedly praised Hamas and former Hamas leaders Yahya Sinwar and Ismail Haniyeh.
Following the discovery, Liberal Alliance wants the woman called in for an interview with Indfødsretsudvalget, the Naturalization Committee of the Danish parliament.
Alex Vanopslagh, the leader of Liberal Alliance, spoke about the matter to the Danish newspaper Politiken.
“As we see it, it just emphasizes the need to wait to grant more citizenships until a proper screening model is in place, so that we can specifically catch some types who, based on what we can see so far, appear strongly anti-democratic,” he told the newspaper.
Every six months, a new bill is introduced in Folketinget, the Danish parliament, to give people Danish citizenship. This happens after an application process that is often long and detailed. This process was also followed under the previous coalition government in Denmark.
The most recent round of citizenships was scheduled at the same time a parliamentary election was called in the spring. Because of the election, the bill that included citizenship for the 2,055 people was delayed.
The delay gave momentum to demands from opposition parties. They argued that officials must carry out a more thorough review of the people on the list to find out if any of them hold anti-democratic views. Socialdemokratiet, the Danish Social Democratic Party, supported this demand as well.
However, the new government decided to present the citizenship bill before a new screening system was ready. This choice led to a larger debate during the opening of the Danish parliament.
During that debate, Rasmus Stoklund, the political spokesperson for Socialdemokratiet, said that if opposition parties found a person on the bill who had anti-democratic views, they could inform the Naturalization Committee. Liberal Alliance has now acted on that suggestion.
Politiken also spoke with the woman identified by the party. She denied that she supports Hamas or any killings.
“I do not support anyone who kills anyone. Because I do not like anyone killing anyone, regardless of whether they are Israeli, Russian or anything else,” the woman told the newspaper.
She stated that she is ready to attend an interview with the committee to explain her position.
Other political parties have reacted differently to the proposal. Dansk Folkeparti, the Danish People’s Party, supports calling the woman in for an interview.
However, Enhedslisten, the Danish left-wing Red-Green Alliance party, strongly opposes the idea.
“It is deeply concerning that Liberal Alliance now to such an extent wants to begin exercising thought control,” Peder Hvelplund, the citizenship spokesperson for Enhedslisten, told Politiken.

Kirsten Schwalbe becomes Denmark’s oldest person ever at 112
A woman from Struer has set a national longevity record, reaching 112 years and 218 days on Wednesday and surpassing the previous record held by Karla Lindholm Jensen.
Schwalbe also joins the list of Europe’s 10 oldest living people. The world’s oldest living person is Britain’s Ethel Caterham, who is 117.
The previous Danish record holder, Karla Lindholm Jensen from Herning, died in 2020.
Ahead of the milestone, Jyllands-Posten attempted to interview Schwalbe, but she needed a day of rest. Instead, the newspaper spoke with two of her three daughters.
Her daughter Hanne Jensen, 86, described how her mother sometimes struggles to understand that her children are now elderly themselves.
“She knows well enough that we are getting older, but she forgets that we can no longer withstand everything,” Jensen told the newspaper.
Schwalbe was born in Salling in 1914, just months before World War I began, and grew up alongside nine siblings.
She married her first husband in 1938, and the couple had three children.
Despite her age, Schwalbe continues to live in her own home in Struer.
Her life has previously been documented by regional broadcaster TV Midtvest in the television series “Kirstens vilde år,” which airs on TV 2.
Schwalbe has attributed her longevity partly to genetics. Four of her nine siblings also lived beyond 100, she told Berlingske in 2024.
She has also emphasized the importance of maintaining a positive outlook, previously telling TV Midtvest that a person’s mood plays an important role in living a long life.

“E-bikes are both heavier and faster than regular bicycles,” Larsen said.
He pointed to an increase in serious injuries and deaths involving electric bicycles as justification for the proposal.
Currently, Denmark does not require helmets for ordinary bicycles or standard e-bikes, whose motors provide assistance at speeds of up to 25 kilometers per hour.
However, helmets are already mandatory for speed pedelecs, which can provide motor assistance up to 45 kilometers per hour.

The number of seriously injured e-bike riders was the highest recorded in six years.

Cyklistforbundet, the Danish Cyclists’ Federation, opposes making helmets compulsory, arguing that such a measure could discourage cycling.
“Our purpose is to get more people to cycle. So every measure that pulls in the opposite direction, we will oppose. But we warmly recommend that people use a bicycle helmet,” federation chair Jens Peter Hansen told TV2 Østjylland.
The proposal would introduce a helmet requirement for standard e-bikes, bringing their rules closer to those already applying to faster electric bicycles.

Copenhagen has far more municipal savings per resident than poorer municipalities
Danish municipalities differ significantly in how much readily available money they hold, according to an analysis by CEPOS, a Danish liberal think tank.
Copenhagen Municipality has the largest liquid holdings per resident, with savings equivalent to 31,685 DKK for each person.
At the other end of the ranking are Hjørring, Sorø, Thisted, Lolland and Aalborg municipalities. Their liquid holdings range from 3,127 DKK to 4,354 DKK per resident.
Liquid holdings can be viewed as municipal savings that have not been allocated to a specific purpose. Municipalities typically use the money to manage ongoing incoming and outgoing payments.
CEPOS said municipalities must always maintain a certain level of liquidity to cover their regular financial obligations.
Local authorities may also build up savings to finance future projects.

A total of 538 marine mammals were recorded as stranded along Denmark’s coasts in 2025, according to a report from the Danish Environmental Protection Agency’s emergency service for stranded marine mammals.
The animals included 363 harbor seals, 38 grey seals and 137 harbor porpoises.

Ambulances get deer whistles to avoid hitting animals
Ambulances and emergency medical vehicles in the North Denmark Region will be equipped with wildlife whistles to reduce the risk of collisions with animals.
The small plastic whistles are mounted outside vehicles and produce a high-frequency sound when air passes through them. The sound is intended to frighten animals away from the road.
“Unfortunately, we have a number of collisions with animals when we drive with emergency signals in forests and natural areas,” the region’s Prehospital Services wrote on Facebook.
“It is dangerous for the people in the car, it delays the driving, and is dangerous for the animals.”
The decision comes as Denmark faces a possible record year for deer collisions.
Dyrenes Beskyttelse, Denmark’s largest animal welfare organization, recorded 8,739 deer collisions during the first nine months of 2026. That compares with 7,994 during the same period in 2025.
The previous annual record was 11,870 collisions in 2025.
The risk of encountering deer is particularly high during autumn and around sunrise and sunset.
However, it remains unclear whether wildlife whistles effectively keep animals away from roads.
Two insurance companies previously gave the devices to motorists as part of separate trials. According to FDM, Denmark’s main car owners’ association, the companies could not reach a clear conclusion about whether the whistles reduced collisions.

One in four Danish driving penalty points linked to mobile phone use
Danish motorists received almost 21,000 penalty points for using handheld mobile phones while driving last year – the highest number in four years.
Mobile phones are playing a growing role in traffic offences in Denmark.
In 2025, motorists received 20,910 penalty points on their driving licences for using a handheld mobile phone behind the wheel, according to figures from the police case management system POLSAS.
That means mobile phone use accounted for roughly one in every four of the 84,056 penalty points issued for traffic offences during the year.
The number of mobile-related penalty points increased by 7.5 percent compared with 2024 and reached its highest level in four years.
On average, police issued 57 penalty points every day for handheld mobile phone use.
Britta Bjerregaard, claims director at insurance company Alm. Brand, described the development as deeply concerning.
“Most people know full well that the phone should stay put while driving. Still, it can be tempting to just answer a call, reply to a message, or change the song,” she said.
“Traffic does not pause while you look at the screen.”
89 metres without watching the road
The Danish Road Safety Council considers inattention one of the major risks on Danish roads, with mobile phones posing a particular problem.
“The mobile phone takes an incredible amount of attention if you use it behind the wheel,” deputy director Karina Petersen said.
“If you look at the screen for four seconds at country road speed, you are driving 89 metres blind.”
However, Petersen cautioned that the increase in recorded offences does not necessarily mean that more drivers are using their phones.
The rise could also reflect more police checks or improved camera equipment used for traffic enforcement.
What are the rules in Denmark?
Using a handheld mobile phone while driving in Denmark results in a DKK 1,500 fine and a penalty point on your driving licence. An additional DKK 1,000 contribution to the Victims’ Fund is also charged.
The rule applies even when the car is stationary in traffic or waiting at a red light.
Drivers may briefly operate a phone if it is securely mounted, and using a vehicle’s built-in screen is also permitted.
The ban on handheld mobile phone use also applies to cyclists, electric scooter users and drivers of other motorised vehicles.

Puberty may mark a turning point for sex differences in the brain’s emotion and memory centers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:00:08 UTC
23:00:08 KST

Differences between males and females in the fine-grained tissue structure of deep brain regions are minimal at ages 9 to 12 but emerge and widen during adolescence, according to a new brain imaging study. The timing coincides with puberty and with the period when sex differences in conditions like anxiety and depression begin to appear, though the study could not determine what drives the brain changes. The findings were published in Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience.
Deep gray matter refers to a collection of structures located beneath the outer layer of the brain. These areas include the amygdala, which processes emotions, the hippocampus, which is central to memory, and the nucleus accumbens, which plays a role in reward and motivation. The study also examined the thalamus, a relay hub for sensory signals, and the caudate and putamen, which help control movement and habits. In human populations, many mental health conditions tied to these brain functions show different rates of diagnosis between men and women, but the biological reasons behind these differences remain poorly understood.
Animal research points to puberty as a key period for these changes: a 2008 study in rats found that sex hormones during puberty drive the addition of new cells to brain regions that differ between the sexes. In humans, a 2014 study that followed young people over time found that pubertal development was linked to the size of these deep brain regions in both boys and girls, independent of age.
While overall volume provides part of the picture, scientists have sought to understand the microscopic layout of brain tissue. Earlier work by the same research team, covered by PsyPost in 2024, found large differences between young adult men and women in measures of tissue microstructure, with men showing signs of more densely packed cells in regions like the hippocampus. The new research, led by Christopher G. Filippi of The Hospital for Sick Children and Richard Watts of the University of Canterbury, aimed to pinpoint when those microscopic differences first develop.
The research team examined brain scan data from 1,643 individuals aged 9 to 35. The participants were drawn from two large public databases: the Human Connectome Project Development dataset for children and teens, and the Young Adult dataset for older participants. In their analyses, the scientists statistically controlled for age and body mass index, and they accounted for family relationships among the many twins included in the adult sample.
To evaluate tissue microstructure, the researchers used an advanced magnetic resonance imaging technique called Restriction Spectrum Imaging. This method measures how water molecules diffuse through brain tissue. Water trapped inside a cell encounters barriers, producing a restricted diffusion signal that reflects cell packing. Water in the spaces between cells encounters fewer obstacles, producing a hindered diffusion signal that reflects the extracellular environment.
For the youngest participants, aged 9 to 12, the researchers observed no statistically significant differences between boys and girls in these diffusion measures. Across the deep gray matter structures, the tissue composition in childhood appeared similar between the sexes.
However, differences began to emerge between ages 13 and 16, first in the hippocampus, amygdala, and thalamus. Restricted diffusion rose with age in both sexes, but from puberty onward it was consistently higher in males, a pattern the researchers suggest may reflect more densely packed cells or larger cell bodies. By ages 17 to 21, sex accounted for roughly 13 to 33 percent of the variation in restricted diffusion across all six regions, and in adults it explained 32 to 37 percent in the hippocampus and amygdala.
Females, in turn, showed a larger hindered component, meaning a greater share of the water signal came from the spaces between cells. Because both measures are expressed as shares of the total signal, the two patterns largely mirror each other.
In regions such as the nucleus accumbens, caudate, and putamen, females showed a slowing in development in their late teens before accelerating again in their early 20s, while males followed a more steady progression. By the mid-20s, the size of the sex difference in the hippocampus and amygdala had leveled off, though the measures themselves were still changing in both sexes. In the thalamus, the divergence between the sexes continued to widen up to age 35.
“Sex differences in the brain have so far been primarily investigated at the macro-structural level (i.e., differences in overall brain size or differences in the size of specific regions),” said Yumnah Khan, a doctoral scientist at the Autism Research Centre at the University of Cambridge who was not involved in the research. “What is interesting about this work is it provides evidence for differences in brain microstructure (i.e., what is happening at a finer level within brain tissue), which gives us a more detailed picture of sex differences in the brain.”
Marco Balducci, a senior researcher at the University of Turku who was not involved in the study, said the findings build on earlier work. “Earlier studies had identified sex differences in subcortical brain structure and, more recently, in diffusion-derived microstructure in young adults,” Balducci told PsyPost. “This study extends that work by showing that the differences emerge during adolescence rather than simply being present in adulthood.”
The timing of these changes aligns with the pubertal transition, leading the study authors to speculate about biological drivers. Earlier animal work indicates that sex hormones can influence synapses and dendrites, the connection points and branching extensions of nerve cells. Because these adolescent brain shifts occur alongside the emergence of sex-biased mental health conditions, identifying typical developmental paths could help clarify underlying vulnerabilities.
Khan told PsyPost that considering human imaging alongside animal research helps connect biology to observation. “Animal studies can provide much stronger evidence about causality and specific mechanisms, while human studies are generally observational and correlational,” she said. “However, when both of these lines of research are considered and interpreted together, we get a better picture of the mechanisms underlying sex differences in brain development.”
Balducci noted that the broad descriptive findings appear well-supported. “The main descriptive finding appears robust because the study uses a large combined sample, finds a consistent developmental pattern across several brain regions, and applies correction for multiple comparisons,” he said. “However, the reasons for these differences remain uncertain because the data are cross-sectional, and in this setting it is difficult to distinguish age-related changes from pubertal development or establish a hormonal cause.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relied on cross-sectional data from different individuals at each age, rather than following the same individuals across their development. Additionally, puberty was measured using ratings of physical development, which rose so closely with age that the researchers could not separate the effects of puberty from those of getting older, and hormone levels were not measured. The researchers did find an association between a girl’s first menstrual period and a specific measure in the thalamus, but they describe any role of sex hormones as speculative.
The researchers also had to combine two projects that used different scanners and imaging settings. Because one covered ages 9 to 21 and the other ages 22 to 36, the statistical adjustments for those differences fall at the same point as the transition into adulthood, so features of the age trajectories near that point, such as the slowdown seen in females, should be read with some caution. Comparisons between males and females within each age group are less affected.
“I think the biggest risk is interpreting these findings as showing that male and female brains are fundamentally different,” Khan said. “In reality, sex differences in the brain tend to be relatively small, with a lot of overlap between the sexes.”
She added that the timing of differences depends on which ages a study covers. “It is also important not to assume that adolescence is when these differences necessarily begin,” Khan noted. “Although the study found minimal differences early in childhood, sex-by-age effects can be highly sensitive to the particular age range that is being studied. As such, the findings do not necessarily mean that differences are entirely absent earlier in development.”
Balducci also cautioned against reading too much into what the scans can show.
“The findings do not show that differences in water diffusion directly cause differences in behavior or mental health,” Balducci pointed out. “Diffusion MRI provides an indirect measure of tissue microstructure.”
“Also, as with many sex differences, males and females vary on average,” Balducci added. “However, when multiple small differences are considered together, the overall profiles of males and females can become considerably more distinct.”
To address these remaining questions, both outside researchers point toward the need for investigations that capture earlier and more detailed developmental data.
“The most important next step would be a longitudinal study that repeatedly scans the same individuals before, during, and after puberty, while also measuring pubertal hormones and developmental phases,” Balducci told PsyPost. “That would help determine whether the observed diffusion changes track individual pubertal development and whether they are related to later mental-health outcomes.”
“It would be very interesting to see this approach being used in earlier stages of development, such as the prenatal period,” Khan said. “The prenatal period is another critical window for the emergence of sex differences in the brain. Moreover, male and female fetuses are exposed to different levels of sex hormones, which may contribute to differences in early brain development.”
The researchers say the sex-specific trajectories they describe could serve as a reference point for future studies exploring how departures from typical development might relate to mental health conditions.
The study, “Sex Differences in Human Deep Grey Matter Microstructure Emerge During Adolescence,” was authored by Christopher G. Filippi, Jay N. Giedd, Aziz M. Uluğ, and Richard Watts.

Ukrainian experts bring home responsible gambling practices from SBC Summit 2026 in Lisbon
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:56:14 EEST
22:56:14 KST

Ukrainian experts bring home responsible gambling practices from SBC Summit 2026 in Lisbon
Kyiv • UNN
In Lisbon, Ukrainian specialists studied international responsible gambling practices and technologies for the early detection of risky behavior.
The Responsible Gambling Center organized the Ukrainian delegation’s participation in SBC Summit 2026 with partner support. Three days of industry sessions in Lisbon gave the delegation a detailed look at how other countries put responsible gambling tools into practice, reports UNN.
The summit draws government agencies, market operators, technology companies, and civil society organizations each year to discuss where the industry is heading and how players are protected. The program runs from payment solutions and technology to government gambling policy, and that breadth has long made the summit one of the main professional gatherings for the sector.
For RGC, the trip continued the international work the organization carries out to study current methods of preventing gambling addiction and bring the most effective of them into Ukraine’s responsible gambling system. Specialists from government institutions and the expert community made up the delegation, spending three days in panel discussions and professional sessions alongside the Center’s team.
The Player Protection Symposium drew the delegation’s greatest interest — a dedicated series of sessions devoted entirely to player protection and reducing gambling harm. Much of the discussion there centered on artificial intelligence and data analytics, which can track player behavior automatically and catch the first warning signs before gambling stops being entertainment. That kind of monitoring flags changes in a person’s behavior early, so they can be acted on while the risks are still moderate.
Participants also discussed at length how responsibility for player protection is shared among the state, regulators, operators, and players themselves. Speakers returned repeatedly to mechanisms for cooperation between all parties, and to the role independent organizations and the expert community can play in building an effective responsible gambling system.
"One of the important takeaways from SBC Summit for me was that the modern player protection system rests increasingly on prevention. New technologies let us not only respond to a problem that has already taken shape, but see changes in player behavior, and the risks that come with them, much earlier. For Ukraine, it is especially important to study such practices and understand which of them can be effectively adapted to our own system," said Maryna Slobodnichenko, founder of the Responsible Gambling Center.
A separate part of the program covered communication with players and risk prevention. Experts shared their experience of explaining the possible consequences of gambling to consumers and fostering responsible behavior, so that players can set their own limits in time. Advertising ethics came up alongside it, since marketing campaigns noticeably shape how audiences behave. Advertising messages therefore call for a measured approach, particularly where vulnerable groups are concerned.
The Compliance Tech track introduced the Ukrainian participants to the technology used for oversight in the industry. One example was affordability checks, which assess whether a player’s spending threatens their financial position, so the risk can be addressed in time. Speakers also covered digital identification and KYC procedures, along with risk assessment systems that help prevent fraud and abuse.
The delegation also paid close attention to how other countries build gambling policy. The summit examined how different jurisdictions have approached market reform and licensing, action against illegal operators, and the creation of transparent rules for everyone involved. The discussion addressed tools that let the legal market grow while keeping state oversight effective and strengthening player protection. The trip also gave representatives of different Ukrainian government institutions a chance to talk to one another, opening the way to closer interagency cooperation back in Ukraine.
Participants singled out two practices as most relevant for Ukraine: technology for early detection of risky behavior and mechanisms that help players set limits. Also worth considering are approaches to financial risk assessment and digital identification, responsible advertising practices, and the groundwork laid for cooperation between the state, the regulator, civil society, and responsible business.
"Professional dialogue at the international level lets us analyze systematically how approaches to regulatory policy, responsible gambling, and player protection are changing around the world, and identify practices that could be useful for Ukraine. It is important that international experience does not remain merely a subject of discussion, but helps shape practical solutions, improve the regulatory environment, and prevent gambling addiction," said Zoriana Toporetska, Head of the Project Office for the Review of Scientific Recommendations and Expert Consultations on State Policy in the Gambling and Lottery Sector at the Ministry of Digital Transformation.
The visit gave the Ukrainian specialists a first-hand view of where the world is heading on responsible gambling and player protection technology, and a chance to talk with international experts across a range of sectors. With support from its partners, RGC will continue to study international work on preventing gambling addiction and protecting players, in order to adapt the most effective of those approaches to Ukraine’s own circumstances.

‘Severe drought’ declared in parts of southern England

- The government has urged water companies and customers to save water. Farmers, anglers and firefighters face strain, while officials say climate change is making droughts and heatwaves worse.
AI generated
LONDON – A “severe drought” was declared in parts of southern England on Oct 15 by the British government, which said it took the decision following an “unprecedented period of extreme weather”.
The United Kingdom experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, featuring several heatwaves and an exceptional drought that resulted from a lack of rainfall not seen since records began in 1836.
More than 80% of England is currently in a state of drought as it continues to experience below average levels of rainfall into the autumn months.
“Record-breaking summer heat and severe drought have put our water resources under immense pressure,” said Environment Agency head Philip Duffy.
The “severe drought” status was declared in the English counties of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex. It is the worst stage triggered by “exceptionally low indicators over a long period of time”.
The declaration came as two major reservoirs in south-west England serving nearly 400,000 properties were below 20% of their storage capacity.
The Environment Agency said it “would expect reservoir storage to be around 75% for this time of year”.
South-east and south-west England have experienced their driest April to September period in more than a century, according to the government.
Scientists say climate change is intensifying weather events such as drought and heatwaves, resulting in records being broken more frequently.
As of last week, average reservoir levels across England stood at 54%, with the nation receiving just 10% of average October rainfall.
The government has urged water companies to monitor their water intake from natural resources and encouraged customers to cut their consumption, with usage restrictions already imposed in several regions.
“This level of drought is something we have not experienced for decades,” environment minister Angela Eagle said.
Months of drought have piled pressure on everyone from farmers and anglers to firefighters, who say tinder-dry conditions resulted in challenging wildfires this summer.
Since August, the government has convened a weekly National Drought Group, involving the weather agency, water companies, experts and farmers’ representatives.

2026-10-15
