US producer inflation hits 6.3% in September, exceeding expectations of 5.3%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:12:29 UTC
22:12:29 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
US annual producer inflation reached 6.3% in September, exceeding expectations of 5.3%, as surging energy costs drove a sharp increase in prices, according to data released Thursday.
The Producer Price Index for final demand rose 1.3% from the previous month, the largest monthly increase since March 2022, said the US Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The increase followed gains of 0.5% in August and 0.2% in July.
Prices for final demand goods climbed 2.6% in September, while services prices advanced 0.8%.
Energy prices jumped 10.8%, accounting for more than 80% of the monthly increase in goods prices. Gasoline prices surged 20.3%, contributing half of the overall rise in goods prices.
Diesel fuel, jet fuel, residential electricity, and crude petroleum prices also rose.
Food prices climbed 1.2%, while goods prices excluding food and energy increased 0.3%. Prices for chicken eggs, however, plunged 39.7%.
Services prices also accelerate
The 0.8% increase in services prices was the largest since April, with nearly half of the gain attributable to a 1.4% rise in trade services margins, which measure the difference between wholesalers’ and retailers’ selling and purchase prices.
Transportation and warehousing services prices climbed 3.4%, while services excluding trade, transportation, and warehousing rose 0.3%.
Margins for machinery and vehicle wholesaling increased 3.9%, accounting for more than one-fifth of the rise in services prices.
Meanwhile, producer prices excluding food, energy and trade services increased 0.5% in September, following a 0.3% gain in August.
That metric rose 5% over the 12 months through September.

- Atom adds stronger anti-tamper checks and aims to tap bigger markets in security phones, tokenisation and AI identity verification, said CEO Pascal Gauthier.
AI generated
LONDON – Crypto hardware wallet maker Ledger is launching a smartphone-like device for users seeking extra protection for their digital assets and online activity, in the wake of a security incident involving some of its products.
The US$899 (S$1,150) Ledger Atom – available from next summer – will run Android apps and a separate operating system for sensitive tasks such as crypto transactions, encrypted messaging and actions carried out by artificial intelligence agents.
It is aimed at individuals and businesses that may already use a separate smartphone for sensitive activities, offering a device designed specifically with those security needs in mind, Ledger’s chief executive officer Pascal Gauthier said in an interview.
The market opportunity will be significantly larger than that of Ledger’s traditional hardware-wallet business, Gauthier added, with about 200 million security phones sold annually.
“It’s not trying to replace your iPhone,” he said. “It’s a separate category.”
Atom’s launch takes Ledger beyond its core business, as the Paris-based company deals with the fallout from fund losses reported by users who had bought some of its wallets from a Malaysian reseller.
The total amount lost in the incident – first disclosed on Oct 9 – has been estimated at more than US$90 million across hundreds of cryptocurrency addresses, according to research published by Galaxy Digital.
An investigation of the breach by Ledger, published on Oct 15, found that attackers had bought genuine devices, fitted them with hidden spyware implants designed to capture users’ passwords, and returned them to circulation through resellers in South-east Asia.
Ledger’s own systems and devices were not compromised, the company said. It did not confirm the total number of users affected or total losses.
The Atom will include additional protections against physical tampering, including new methods to help detect if the enclosure surrounding the device’s secure element has been opened or the display removed, the firm said.
Those protections, which will continue to run even when the device is off, will explicitly block the kind of spyware implants discovered by users earlier in October, it added.
The incident marks the latest in a series of breaches involving makers of crypto hardware wallets, which have long been considered one of the safest ways for users to safeguard their digital assets.
The surge comes as cryptocurrency hacks soared in 2026, with advances in AI making it easier for online criminals to identify flaws in company code that can be exploited.
“Perfect security doesn’t exist,” Gauthier said when asked about the recent incident. “It’s a reminder that the fight between good and evil never stops. We’re not taking it lightly.”
Hardware wallets store the private keys needed to access and move cryptocurrency, keeping them separate from everyday devices connected to the internet. While that adds a layer of security, it can also make transactions more cumbersome by requiring users to switch between multiple devices.
The Atom aims to combine the security functions of Ledger’s hardware wallets with a smartphone’s apps and touchscreen functionality, allowing users to initiate and approve transactions on the same device in a secure environment.
The Atom device runs two operating systems: an open-source version of Android for everyday apps, and Ledger OS, the company’s own system running on a secure chip for sensitive activities. It can switch between these modes automatically, the company said.
Through the Atom, users will be able to send and receive crypto and access some services from third-party platforms such as digital-asset exchange Kraken to transact with their holdings, Ledger said.
The device can also be used to manage AI agents through OpenClaw, and users will be able to encrypt private messages before sending them through a messaging app of their choice. Ledger will not be able to see the unencrypted text, it said, while recipients can decrypt and read the message via another Atom device in secure mode.
Through the new device, Ledger is also betting on growth in tokenisation, where everyday assets such as stocks are represented on a blockchain, creating a need to securely store them and prove their ownership.
The company also sees an opportunity in AI, as people increasingly use autonomous agents to act on their behalf and will need ways to verify who controls them and their own identity online.
“How do you prove tomorrow, in a world of AI, that you online is actually you?” Gauthier said. BLOOMBERG

Maldives Opposition Eyes Sweeping Constitutional Overhaul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:09:00 UTC
22:09:00 KST

The Maldives’ main opposition party, the Maldivian Democratic Party (MDP), held its fifth National Congress from October 1 to 3.
The congress, which is the party’s highest decision-making body, adopted significant changes to the MDP’s internal structure. It abolished the posts of party president and vice president, consolidating leadership under the chairperson, a position currently held by former President Mohamed Nasheed. Yet its most consequential decision was the overwhelming endorsement, by 520 of the 563 delegates present, of a sweeping constitutional reform program titled Bodu Badhalu (meaning “Big Change” in Dhivehi).
Formally submitted by former Economic Development Minister Fayyaz Ismail, the program seeks to address perceived weaknesses in the constitution adopted during the country’s transition to multiparty democracy in 2008. It argues that, despite the formal separation of powers, the president can exercise excessive authority, particularly when backed by a parliamentary majority. It further contends that constitutional safeguards for fundamental rights, including freedoms of expression, assembly, and the press, offer inadequate protection against executive overreach.
To remedy this, its central proposal is to split the executive into two separate offices: head of state and head of government. The latter would be directly elected by voters in a national election but could be removed by parliament. The head of state would instead be appointed by a special assembly comprising parliamentarians and elected local councilors.
The program also proposes several changes to the legislature, including setting a fixed limit on parliamentary seats, whose number currently increases with population growth; introducing preferential voting; reserving seats for women; and exploring a bicameral system. Citizens would gain the power to recall elected officials, while the removal of Supreme Court judges would require approval through a public referendum. The program further proposes reforms to the appointment and oversight of independent constitutional bodies to reduce political interference.
Regardless of its merits or prospects for implementation, the program’s overwhelming endorsement marks a dramatic shift in the MDP’s internal politics. Most notably, it reflects Nasheed’s renewed grip on a party that, until recently, had treated him as a pariah. Although formally proposed by Fayyaz, the program also advances Nasheed’s longstanding ambition to change the Maldives’ system of government, an ambition he now pursues alongside Fayyaz, with whom he has forged an unlikely political alliance.
Nasheed has long championed a parliamentary system, having backed it unsuccessfully in a 2007 referendum before winning the presidency under the new constitution in 2008. Following his controversial ouster in 2012, he narrowly lost the disputed 2013 presidential election to Abdulla Yameen. A controversial terrorism conviction subsequently barred him from contesting the 2018 election, which was won instead by his erstwhile close ally Ibrahim Mohamed Solih. Nasheed went on to win a parliamentary seat in 2019 and became speaker, eyeing a return to executive power as prime minister under a parliamentary system.
However, Solih resisted Nasheed’s efforts to hold a referendum on replacing the presidential system with a parliamentary one. Nasheed sought to advance the proposal at the MDP’s fourth National Congress in August 2022 but faced opposition from Solih and Fayyaz, then party chairperson and economic development minister in Solih’s cabinet. Nasheed subsequently shelved the proposal.
Relations with the party deteriorated further after Nasheed challenged Solih during the MDP’s January 2023 presidential primary and lost. He subsequently vowed to “destroy” the MDP and left to join The Democrats, a new party formed by his loyalists. Ahead of the presidential runoff, The Democrats demanded a referendum on the system of government as a condition of their support. Although the MDP agreed to hold one after the election, The Democrats withheld their endorsement.
Following Solih’s defeat to current President Mohamed Muizzu, the MDP’s National Council voted overwhelmingly against a parliamentary system, reflecting widespread resentment toward Nasheed, whom many blamed for contributing to Solih’s electoral defeat.
Yet Nasheed has since made a remarkable political comeback, reclaiming leadership of the very party he once threatened to dismantle. After a two-year hiatus from Maldivian politics, during which he served as secretary general of the Climate Vulnerable Forum, he rejoined the MDP in 2025. Strikingly, his return to the party’s helm was aided by former Solih loyalists, most notably Fayyaz. It was Fayyaz’s resignation as chairperson that created the vacancy Nasheed subsequently contested.
For now, the partnership serves both men’s political ambitions, with Fayyaz having supported Nasheed’s return to the MDP leadership and Nasheed, in turn, backing Fayyaz’s presidential ambitions for 2028. Bodu Badhalu was unveiled in April 2026 as the centerpiece of Nasheed’s chairperson campaign. It culminated in his landslide victory over a Solih-backed candidate, reflecting a profound shift in the party’s internal balance of power. The congress’s subsequent endorsement of Bodu Badhalu demonstrates that Nasheed has, at least for now, brought the party behind his constitutional vision.
Although that vision differs significantly from the traditional Westminster-style parliamentary system Nasheed has long championed, it nevertheless offers him a potential path back to high office. While Nasheed has repeatedly pledged not to contest the presidency in 2028 and reaffirmed his support for Fayyaz, he has nonetheless expressed interest in serving as head of state under the proposed arrangement, with Fayyaz as head of government. The precise powers and titles of the two offices, however, remain unclear.
Whether their alliance will endure remains an open question. Nasheed’s previous partnership with Solih fractured once the latter secured the presidency and asserted his political independence from Nasheed. Although Fayyaz formally proposed Bodu Badhalu, he had previously opposed Nasheed’s efforts to amend the constitution, and his embrace of reform now serves the purpose of securing Nasheed’s support for his presidential bid. Should Fayyaz win the presidency, it is unclear why he would pursue reforms that could curtail his own powers and establish a rival center of authority.
Even if sincerely pursued, Bodu Badhalu faces several challenges. Fayyaz must first win a competitive MDP primary against contenders including former Foreign Minister Abdulla Shahid and former Vice President Faisal Naseem, who claims to have Solih’s backing (although earlier reports suggested Solih himself was considering a bid). Should another candidate secure the nomination, the congress’s endorsement offers no guarantee that the party would remain committed to the program.
Beyond the primary lies the 2028 presidential election. Even if the MDP returns to power, it would initially face a hostile parliament in which Muizzu’s People’s National Congress holds a two-thirds supermajority. The composition of the next parliament, to be elected in 2029, remains uncertain. Meanwhile, constitutional amendments require a three-quarters majority.
Public approval would present a further hurdle, as changes to the nature of presidential elections require a referendum. Indeed, despite commanding a parliamentary supermajority, President Mohamed Muizzu failed to secure public support for his own constitutional reform proposal in April 2026, when voters rejected his plan to merge presidential and parliamentary elections.
For now, Bodu Badhalu underscores Nasheed’s remarkable political comeback. Barely three years after vowing to dismantle the MDP, he has reclaimed its leadership and secured its backing for reforms that could return him to high office. The question remains whether he can translate that influence into electoral victory and bring the program to fruition.

15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Half of UK adults say there are no circumstances in which they would go to war for Britain, a new poll suggested Thursday.
Despite rising security concerns over Russia, China, and Iran, the figure for those unwilling to go to war for the UK remained unchanged since April 2025.
The poll, conducted by Ipsos among 1,090 British adults between Sept. 29 and Oct. 1, also found that half of respondents were reluctant to fight for Britain, even as they backed increased defense spending.
Of those who supported higher spending, 37% said it should be paid for with spending cuts elsewhere, while 36% backed increasing the taxes they personally pay, Sky News reported, citing the figures.
Although those who support increasing defense spending were split on how to fund it, by far the most popular way of raising money for defense was increasing income tax on those earning more than £125,000 ($165,000) a year, with 46% supporting such a move.

Lula or Bolsonaro: Why Brazil's presidential election matters for Brics and India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:08:21 UTC
22:08:21 KST

When 
Brics
 leaders met in New Delhi last month, Brazil’s President Lula da Silva was conspicuously absent from the Bharat Mandapam. He was campaigning for the crucial fourth term back home, so his foreign minister Mauro Vieira arrived in the capital for the "non-West" summit.
That absence could now highlight the Brics' road ahead, at least for the time US President Donald Trump occupies the White House.
Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability. This is what Brics stood for when India hosted it on September 12. However, the real B of Brics, which is Brazil, has the world's attention.
(From left) Egyptian president Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Russian president Vladimir Putin, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Chinese president Xi Jinping and South African president Cyril Ramaphosa during a joint tree plantation initiative during the 18th Brics Summit, at the Bharat Mandapam, in New Delhi.
On 25 October, Brazilians will choose between Lula and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of jailed ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, and the winner will decide how deeply one of the bloc’s founding members keeps investing in it.
Flávio Bolsonaro leads the race into the runoff (second round of voting) after securing 47 per cent of the first-round vote, against Lula’s 45 per cent. Brazil mandates a second round of voting if no candidate secures a majority (more than 50 per cent) in the first round. Therefore, for a grouping already stretched by its own expansion, the result matters well beyond South America.
Results after first round of voting in Brazil.
A bloc pulled in three directions
Brics began with five members and grew to eleven after the 2024 expansion, with Indonesia the newest, joining in 2025. 
Brazil opposed the enlargement, particularly because of the one nation. Iran. It feared that adding the avowedly anti-West Islamic Republic would cost the group its cohesion. Like India, Brazil wants Brics to be reformist and not revolutionary, thereby limiting it to a body that argues for change inside the existing order rather than one that tries to replace it.
Vieira, putting the Brazilian view plainly in the run-up to the 2026 summit, said that “a multipolar world that promises peace and prosperity must not be confused with a world of spheres of influence.” In other words, Brasília wants rules that bind the strong as well as the weak.
Brazil had some success as the New Delhi declaration reaffirmed support for the United Nations system and the Paris climate agreement, going further than the G7, whose latest declarations did not mention the climate pact.
However, these are words and not actions, and Russia, a Brics member, has ignored the UN Charter in recent years. Even so, agreeing to acknowledge the UN’s legitimacy was a better outcome than blocking any mention of it.
Brics continues to expand unlike the West-dominated G7.
Those gains on paper may not last, as Brazil’s place in the bloc will depend largely on its next president. The world’s two biggest powers have very different visions for what Brics should become. Both Washington and Beijing are seeking to tilt the balance in their favour.
The United States, under Donald Trump, has made clear what it wants from Brazil. The Trump administration imposed heavy trade duties on Brazilian exports in July 2025, in retaliation for what it called a judicial “witch hunt” against former President Jair Bolsonaro, who Trump see as his "ally".
It has sanctioned the Supreme Court justice who prosecuted him and revoked the visas of several justices. It also accepted Flávio Bolsonaro’s appeal in May to designate two Brazilian criminal groups as foreign terrorist organisations, while Lula’s alternative proposals went unanswered.
Beyond one man’s fate
A Bolsonaro win would help realign Latin America behind an America First agenda of militarised approaches to crime, crackdowns on migration and preferential access to critical minerals and energy. Brazil holds the world’s second-largest rare earth reserves, and Washington wants to reduce its dependence on China for them.
On the trade and commerce front, Bolsonaro has criticised non-dollar initiatives, which is exactly the kind of de-dollarisation talk that makes some Brics ideas unwelcome in Washington. His platform does not mention Brics at all, and he has entertained the idea of leaving the group.
Beijing sits on the other side of the ledger, and its leverage is economic. China has been Brazil’s largest trading partner since 2009. It buys nearly 30 per cent of Brazil’s total exports, including soybeans, crude oil and iron ore, and it has become a major investor in electricity, mining, cars and oil.
The Brics has outperformed G7 over the last two decades.
A Brics that China hopes to make firmer and more assertive is difficult to build without Brazil, the largest economy in Latin America. That is why a Brazilian drift towards Washington would be felt in Beijing, even if it never became a formal exit.
Nevertheless, the challenge with China is intricate, as even under Jair Bolsonaro, anti-Beijing rhetoric did not stop bilateral trade from reaching record levels, and Brazil resisted US pressure to exclude Huawei from its 5G rollout. Flávio Bolsonaro’s own programme envisages continued commercial engagement with China. A withdrawal from Brics, in short, is possible but far from inevitable.
Therefore, a Bolsonaro government could stay inside the main multilateral bodies while withdrawing from the effort to give them energy, shifting from coalition-building among middle powers to a transactional, bilateral relationship with Washington.
Lula, by contrast, has pursued what officials call “multi-alignment”, keeping a working relationship with the United States, expanding trade with China and using Brics, the G20 and UN climate talks to widen Brazil’s room for manoeuvre.
Brics constitutes 40% of the global GDP.
A state under strain
The foreign policy debate is real, but it is not what most Brazilians say drives their vote. Crime is a central worry, and Bolsonaro’s “mano dura”, or iron fist, approach appeals to voters tired of violence in their neighbourhoods.
Education is another concern, as a recent poll found that 71 per cent of Brazilians are weighing it in their vote, and 83 per cent believe it should be among the next government’s top three priorities.
Only 66 per cent of Grade 2 children met basic literacy requirements in 2025, well short of the 80 per cent target for 2030.
On the US relationship, voters appear to lean towards Lula. Polls show his popularity rose after his frequent disagreements with Trump over trade and security, and other surveys found Brazilians blamed Bolsonaro more for the tariffs imposed in July.
A woman at a voting centre in US to participate in Brazil's general election. (Reuters photo)
The Brazilian Association of Institutional and Governmental Relations says the same pressure would follow Bolsonaro into office.
Its president, Jean Castro, said: “He cannot adopt a stance that could be mistaken for subservience.”
Behind these campaign themes lies a harder question. Can Brazil actually deliver on what it promises abroad? Brasilia's influence depends on partners believing that today’s deals will survive tomorrow’s politics, and that this belief is eroding.
More than 90 per cent of the federal government’s non-interest spending is mandatory, leaving little room for infrastructure, which Brazil needs if it is to make use of its mineral reserves.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) projects that government debt will reach about 98 per cent of GDP by the end of 2026. Real interest rates sit near 10 per cent, so servicing that debt consumes funds that could strengthen security forces or support strategic goals.
Adding to that, criminal networks operate across more than 1,500 clandestine airstrips in the Amazon basin and move drugs, gold and weapons across borders with Brazil’s ten neighbours.
Responsibility for fighting them is split among federal police, highway police, an intelligence agency, police forces in 26 states and the federal district, the armed forces and prosecutors. Efforts to bring them under one authority have failed in Congress. The result is that decisions about gangs operating from Brazilian soil are increasingly taken elsewhere, as Washington’s terrorist designations show.
The third problem is trust in the courts because since late 2025, the public has learned how far parts of the judiciary became entangled with the Banco Master affair.
The bank’s owner is alleged to have made side payments and awarded lucrative contracts to families of Supreme Court justices, and to have lent his private jets to justices.
Flavio Bolsonaro is himself under investigation over alleged links to the bank, and figures close to Lula’s government have also been drawn in.
The winner will appoint at least three of the court’s 11 justices, reshaping the institution that is meant to hold the next government to account.
The neighbourhood also offers little relief. Brazil once led the creation of regional institutions such as Mercosur, but it is now increasingly isolated in South America. Its relationship with Argentina, which helped underpin four decades of regional stability, has deteriorated to the point that neither country has an ambassador in the other’s capital.
Where India stands
India could probably be the member with the most to lose from a Brics that becomes either a Chinese-led counterweight to the West or an empty shell.
India has a significant interest in Brazil's political direction, given its economic ties with the Latin American nation. Bilateral trade exceeded $15 billion in 2025, making Brazil India's biggest trading partner in Latin America. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva have set a target of taking bilateral trade to $20 billion by 2030.
Brazil's importance also extends to the steel sector, as the country is a major global supplier of iron ore and has substantial reserves of minerals used in steel production. Stronger cooperation could help India secure vital raw materials and access technologies needed to support the long-term expansion of its steel industry, according to a government statement.
One in every four overseas Indians lives in Brics nation.
Flavio Bolsonaro, meanwhile, has indicated that he would not align himself exclusively with any side, naming India among the countries with which he would maintain engagement.
India and Brazil have shared a strategic partnership since 2006, with collaboration covering areas such as defence, energy, agriculture, healthcare, critical minerals, technology and digital infrastructure.
Beyond trade, the two countries coordinate on several international issues, including reform of the United Nations, climate change and counter-terrorism. Brazil is also India's largest trading partner across Latin America and the Caribbean.
India hosted this year’s summit, where the Iranian and Emirati presidents both turned up, and it shares Brazil’s view that the bloc should push for reform rather than confrontation.
ALSO READ | Bombs without brakes? Why the US-China AI race may be harder to control than the nuclear one
The two countries also sit together in Partners for Multilateralism, launched on 21 September alongside Canada, Australia, Barbados, the European Union and Kenya.
The framework is meant to support international law and institutional reform, and it links western and Global South middle powers without forcing any of them to pick a camp.
That makes Lula a natural partner for New Delhi, and a Bolsonaro victory a quiet setback that could probably interrupt the bloc's ambitions.
India would lose a like-minded voice for a measured, rules-based Brics, leaving it with partners who are either more radical or more distant. Its own position, balancing Washington and Beijing, depends on a bloc that can talk to both.
However, whichever way Brazil votes, nobody expects an immediate revolution in its foreign policy.
Rubens Ricupero, a former Brazilian diplomat, calls Bolsonaro’s approach a “blank slate”, while Lula’s is well established. The market for Brazil’s minerals, the weight of its trade with China and the limits on its finances will constrain either man. The pressure will come from outside.
Rubens Barbosa, a former Brazilian ambassador to the US, warns that “the Americans may prove reluctant to yield anything to Lula, preferring to wait and negotiate with Bolsonaro.”
Economist Monica de Bolle argues that a re-elected Lula facing a right-leaning Congress would feel “a lot of pressure” to give in “to some US demands regarding natural resources, as well as other issues.”
That is the real stake for Brics on 25 October. The bloc’s future will turn on whether Brazil stays a champion of its reformist wing or becomes a member that merely turns up.

Could the US exit from Iraq fuel an Islamic State resurgence?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:06:56 UTC
22:06:56 KST

Breadcrumb
Could the US exit from Iraq fuel an Islamic State resurgence?
Erbil, Iraq - The US completed its planned troop withdrawal from Iraq by 30 September, with the last of the remaining anti-Islamic State (IS) coalition troops leaving Iraqi Kurdistan’s capital, Erbil, ahead of that deadline.
The withdrawal, however, has renewed anxieties in Iraq that IS could exploit the inevitable power vacuum and regional crises to reorganise and regroup, threatening the region and its peoples once again.
In late September, veteran Kurdish leader Masoud Barzani warned that the withdrawal reopens the risk of another IS resurgence. He recalled how the previous 2011 American withdrawal led to the infamous IS invasion of Iraq in mid-2014. “I fear the same scenario will happen,” he said.
Barzani isn’t the only one concerned about IS. Former Iraqi Interior Minister Baqir Jabr, a veteran Shia politician, claimed in early October that IS remnants in Syria have increased to as many as 10,000 fighters since the former regime of Bashar Al-Assad collapsed in December 2024.
IS initially seized territory in Syria and expanded by invading northern Iraq in June 2014, declaring a caliphate on those vast swathes of territory it conquered and symbolically dismantling the Iraq-Syria border.
While a restoration of that self-styled caliphate isn’t imminent today, analysts warn that multiple factors must be addressed to prevent a significant IS resurgence.
Obstacles
“IS is definitely trying to make its presence known in Iraq with the US withdrawal, but it is still small and relegated to mostly rural areas of northern Iraq with very little support,” Joel Wing, author of the Musings on Iraq blog, told The New Arab.
“There are no signs that Sunni Arabs are backing the group once again,” he said. “During the war, the government forces carried out widespread Sunni cleansing and still occupy many Sunni areas, making it far too costly for people to back the insurgents again.”
Mohammed A. Salih, a non-resident senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, noted that conditions in Iraq and Syria are markedly different from those in 2012-14.
“Iraqi Sunnis participate in the political process despite ongoing grievances, while security forces are more capable, particularly with the presence of the ideologically driven Popular Mobilisation Forces,” Salih told The New Arab.
“Syria also has a generally functioning government rather than a full-scale civil war.”
The PMF consists of several mainly Shia militias mobilised in 2014 to help combat IS. Many powerful Iran-backed groups operate within the state-sanctioned paramilitaries and have refused recent efforts by incumbent Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to disarm them.
Despite the significantly different circumstances between today and 2014, Salih still sees a significant risk of an IS resurgence. Stopping it will very much depend on continued support from the US-led coalition and security cooperation between Iraqi and Kurdish forces.
Across the border, Syria's new security forces must also show the “willingness and capacity” to contain IS.
“Ideological overlap between some elements of Syria’s security apparatus and IS could also create openings, especially amid economic hardship and growing public frustration over the government’s approach to dealing with Israel,” Salih said.
To Iraq’s east, any collapse or substantial weakening of the regime in Iran could undermine Iraq’s ruling Shia elite, potentially creating opportunities for IS.
“Some regional actors might also be tempted to support a Sunni insurgency if Iran-backed Iraqi militias continue attacking neighbouring countries, further increasing the risk of instability,” Salih said.
Security gaps
In 2014, the Iraqi Security Forces (ISF) infamously failed to prevent a comparably small number of IS militants from swiftly seizing Mosul.
Today, Wing believes the ISF are “far more competent,” noting that they are no longer reactive and are “mostly carrying out pre-emptive raids and operations”.
After losing all of the territory it captured in Iraq in 2017, IS remnants were still able to operate within security gaps in the disputed territories between federal Iraq and Iraqi Kurdistan, such as Kirkuk.
IS benefited from the lack of cooperation between the ISF and the Kurdish Peshmerga, particularly in the aftermath of Iraq’s forceful seizure of Kirkuk from the Peshmerga in October 2017.
Iraqi lawmaker Mazen Gharib warned this October that the group is once again doing this following the coalition’s withdrawal, pointing to increased movements in Kirkuk province and the existence of “active detachments.” On 10 October, Iraq’s security forces and IS clashed in Kirkuk’s Hawija district.
According to Wing, the gap between the Iraqi forces and the Peshmerga continues to be a security concern in Iraq.
“There are some areas where the space between the two forces is quite large, and IS has exploited this for years,” he said.
“The problem is this is in the disputed territories and the Kurds want to move back into them after they were forced out following the 2017 Kurdish independence referendum and Baghdad does not want them to return,” he added.
“This dispute has resulted in the security gap between the two sides.”
Sectarian fault lines
FPRI’s Salih concurs that the ISF is more prepared than before. “At the federal level, the presence of the PMF, as an ideologically driven and predominantly Shia force, has strengthened the ISF’s overall capabilities,” he said.
“However, effective coordination between federal and Kurdish forces remains critical to denying IS the operational space it needs in the disputed territories.”
Security coordination between Iraq and Syria is also “hugely important” for containing IS. Such cross-border cooperation is essential since the “predominantly Sunni Arab borderlands” between them have served as a “core breeding ground and operational hub” for IS for several years.
Wing noted that the two neighbours are trying to cooperate on border security for the first time in decades. “How thorough that is remains to be seen, but it can’t do anything but help,” he said.
Still, some of the forces deeply distrust one another. Iran-backed PMF groups entered Syria during the civil war to fight for President Bashar Al-Assad while the former militias that make up the new Syrian armed forces fought against Assad.
“The two definitely don't like each other, but there have not been reports of the two clashing,” Wing said.
“I think with everything else going on in the region such as the Iran war, Prime Minister Zaidi demanding the PMF to disarm, etc., the distaste for the new Syrian government has simply not been a priority.”
Independent Iraqi analyst Lawk Ghafuri noted that while IS was militarily defeated in Iraq in 2017, its ideology was never eliminated.
“Since December 2024, Syria has become an increasingly concerning environment, with foreign extremists, including individuals with IS and al-Qaeda backgrounds, potentially embedded within the new security structures,” Ghafuri told The New Arab.
“The presence of the PMF in Iraq and hostile forces across the Syrian border creates a dangerous sectarian fault line.”
Islamic State prisoners
Iraq presently holds thousands of suspected IS militants and their families in its prisons. Thousands of them were airlifted by the US military from Syria in January, including from the infamous al-Hol camp.
These militants previously attempted a well-planned, coordinated jailbreak in Syria’s Hasakah in January 2022, which took local Kurdish-led security forces more than a week to suppress.
Human Rights Watch released a report in early September charging that these detained IS suspects in Iraq face abuse, unfair trials, and executions.
The report also noted that dozens of countries are stalling on repatriating their national suspects, pledging aid instead. Baghdad rejected a Syrian request to repatriate 4,000 Syrian suspects in Iraqi custody, declaring that any of those Syrians who committed crimes in Iraq will be tried there under Iraqi law.
FPRI’s Salih argued that it is critically important for countries with nationals among the IS prisoner population in Iraq to repatriate them, noting that Iraq is already “overwhelmed by the sheer number” of these inmates.
“Iraq should not be treated as a dumping ground for unwanted IS elements and prisoners,” he said.
“In the event of major instability or chaos in Iraq, particularly as a consequence of the Iran-US-Israel war, these prisoners could become a readily available pool of battle-hardened and highly motivated manpower for IS,” he added.
There are concerns in Iraq that these prisoners could return to the battlefield in the event of a prison break, or if regional tensions spill into Iraq, Salih notes.
“That said, it is important that other countries repatriate their nationals held among IS prisoners and help alleviate some of the enormous burden Iraq is shouldering.”
Ghafuri pointed out that the US-Iran war has undoubtedly shifted regional attention further away from counterterrorism, giving IS elements a potential “opportunity to regroup” and prepare for their next phase.
“IS may no longer face the same international military pressure, while regional governments are preoccupied with Iran, oil, and wider geopolitical rivalries,” he said.
“The greatest danger is not simply that IS could return, but that the regional conditions that once enabled its rise are beginning to re-emerge.”
Paul Iddon is a freelance journalist based in Erbil, Iraqi Kurdistan, who writes about Middle East affairs.

Violating oil tanker catches fire in Sea of Oman

Why you should visit Sigulda, the autumn capital of Latvia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:04:46 UTC
22:04:46 KST

The banks of the Gauja River are transformed into a sea of orange during the cooler months.
New England is synonymous with autumn, but while there’s too much orange in the White House, many of us will be looking elsewhere for our leaf-peeping fix.
Thankfully, there’s somewhere with plenty of golden hues much closer to home: Sigulda.
Regarded as Latvia’s autumn capital, the town is just over an hour away from the capital Riga by train and boasts an abundance of trees that turn shades of yellow, orange and red when there’s a chill in the air.
Best of all, you’ll likely have the scenery all to yourself as you won’t find any tourist crowds here – other than those who read Euronews Travel’s autumn bucket list, which included Sigulda as a must-visit.
I first visited Sigulda last summer, and made it my mission to return in the autumn to see it for myself, which is exactly what I did earlier this month.
Here’s what you should do while you’re there.
What to do in Sigulda
While the town itself is very pretty in autumn, the best scenery can be found around the Gauja River, which you can cross via cable car.
The seven-minute ride passes over the Gauja Valley, and along the way you’ll spot several castles.
After passing to the other side of the river, you can take a short walk through the woods to Gutman's Cave.
The largest cave in the Baltics, the walls are covered in carvings from lovers who have visited here over the centuries.
The cave is associated with the legend of the “rose of Turaida”, a girl named Maija who was abandoned during the Swedish-Polish war and grew up in Turaida Castle (more on that in a moment).
Maija fell for the castle’s gardener, Victor Heil, and the pair would meet in the cave. Unfortunately, army deserter Jakubowsky also fell for Maija, and lured her to the cave by pretending to be Victor before murdering her after she tricked him into attacking her by saying she had a magic scarf that would protect her from all injuries.
From Gutman’s Cave, it’s another short walk to Turaida Castle. From the top of the main tower, you’ll have views all around, with each window offering a vista prettier than the last.
The castle itself dates back to 1214, and you’ll be able to learn about its history through several exhibitions on site, while the gardens are home to numerous sculptures from Indulis Ranka.
There are a number of castles scattered around Sigulda, including the New Castle, which is home to several creative businesses which occupy the old manor buildings.
Here, you can buy your very own Sigulda walking stick, with the patterned cane serving as a symbol of the town.
Sigulda is seen as the gateway into Gauja National Park, so there are plenty of hiking trails where you can put your walking stick to good use. Your best source for trails is Enter Gauja, the official tourism website for the region.
Another popular town to visit within the Gauja region is Cēsis, which is home to a medieval castle dating back to the 13th century.
How to get there
Both Sigulda and Cēsis are accessible by train, which takes around an hour and 10 minutes from Riga for the former and an hour and 20 minutes for the latter.
You can grab a ticket in the station, or book through the Vivi website.
If you don’t want to walk, there are buses from Sigulda to Turaida Castle, but they run just once per hour, so you may be left waiting a while. Tickets can be bought directly from the driver with cash or card.

Chicory: how it benefits digestion and who should consume it with caution
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:04:01 EEST
22:04:01 KST

Chicory: how it benefits digestion and who should consume it with caution
Kyiv • UNN
Inulin from chicory nourishes beneficial gut bacteria and helps increase fiber intake. People with irritable bowel syndrome should monitor their body's response.
Chicory is often used as an alternative to coffee, but this plant can be more than just the basis for a beverage. Dietitian Oleksandr Kushch told UNN journalist more about the value of chicory root, how it affects the microflora, and who should be cautious about consuming it.
What are the benefits of chicory root
According to the doctor, chicory belongs to the aster family, and its root contains inulin — a type of fiber that beneficial gut bacteria like to consume. The expert notes that a lack of certain types of fiber is one of the common problems of modern nutrition. Incidentally, chicory can be used not only to prepare a beverage, but also added to various dishes.
First of all, I want to say that this root contains a lot of inulin. Inulin makes up as much as 75% of its content. It is added to fruit teas, side dishes, and salads
Oleksandr Kushch explained that the body needs a sufficient amount of fiber for the digestive system to function properly. However, getting the required amount solely from individual foods can be difficult, so it is important for the diet to include various sources of dietary fiber.
The daily fiber intake for an adult is somewhere around 35–45 grams per day. Modern people generally do not consume enough fiber. It may seem like 35–40 grams is not much, but to put it into perspective, 150 grams of salad, for example, provides only approximately 5 grams of fiber. In other words, there is an overall fiber deficiency among modern people. There is also a small nuance: fiber should be divided into two types
How chicory affects the gut microflora
Thus, the inulin in chicory feeds beneficial bacteria that participate in the functioning of the intestines. At the same time, its breakdown produces biologically active substances, including short-chain fatty acids. According to the doctor, nutrition and the condition of the gut microflora are also connected with other processes in the body.
Inulin is food for bacteria. When bacteria feed on this fiber, they produce many biologically active substances, such as serotonin — the happiness hormone, which passes through the blood–brain barrier into the brain and directly affects our mood. So, instead of chasing chocolate, you can improve your fiber intake. Short-chain fatty acids are also produced, which our mitochondria like to consume as they produce our vital energy
The dietitian also advises paying attention not only to chicory but to other root vegetables as well. According to him, they can be an important addition to the diet, especially during the cold season.
Useful properties of pistachios and recommendations for their selection27.02.25, 10:38 • 52083 views
Modern people consume quite few roots. I mean not only chicory, but also parsnips, parsley, and celery roots. Especially during the winter, they can be a very good source of beneficial substances, plant protein, and fiber
Who should consume chicory with caution
According to the dietitian, chicory can be included in the daily diet, and he does not specify a separate universal daily intake. At the same time, Oleksandr Kushch noted that people with irritable bowel syndrome should monitor their body's reaction to foods high in fiber, and if such foods intensify discomfort, the amount of these products in the diet should be adjusted.
The only category of people whom I strongly advise to consume roots with caution is people with irritable bowel syndrome. An overload of fiber can lead to additional irritation. Such people should consume these products carefully
Thus, chicory can be one way to diversify the diet and increase fiber intake. The most important thing is to maintain a balanced diet and take into account the body's individual reaction to foods.

Jeffrey Donaldson arrives at Newry Courthouse in Northern Ireland as his trial reaches its conclusion on June 22, 2026. | Charles McQuillan/Getty Images
NEWRY, Northern Ireland — The former leader of Northern Ireland’s main pro-British party, Jeffrey Donaldson, received a 15-year prison sentence Thursday for sexually abusing two schoolgirls.
Donaldson, 63, kept his hands clasped together but offered no visible reaction as Judge Paul Ramsey said the former Democratic Unionist Party leader must serve an 11-year sentence for raping one girl and a further 4-year term for sexually abusing another.
Donaldson has been behind bars since June, when a jury found him guilty of 18 counts of sexually abusing the two women — identified in court only as Victim A and Victim B — when they were children. The listed offenses ran from 1985 to 2008.
Advertisement
Ramsey, addressing a packed Newry Crown Court, read from the two victims’ statements, which described abuse that began when they were 7 or 8 years old. One of the victims described recurring nightmares: “I wonder what it is like not to be afraid at night.”
The judge noted how Donaldson, who is appealing the conviction, had “doubled down on his denials” over what he called the veteran politician’s “catastrophic descent into disgrace.”
Donaldson’s former party, which denounced him immediately after his 2024 arrest and scrubbed him from the DUP website, said in a statement Thursday that Donaldson “deserves every day of the lengthy prison sentence he has to serve” for what it described as “vile and disgusting crimes.”
“Our first thoughts are again with the innocent victims who, having suffered such evil, were retraumatized through giving evidence at the trial. They deserve our compassion, support and respect,” the DUP statement said.
Donaldson was an MP representing Lagan Valley from 1997 to 2024, first for the moderate Ulster Unionist Party and then — after belatedly breaking with the party over its support for the Good Friday peace accord of 1998 — as a member of the hard-line DUP.
Donaldson became DUP leader in 2021, when he oversaw the collapse of Northern Ireland’s power-sharing government in a bitter dispute over the region’s peculiar post-Brexit trade rules. Just weeks before his arrest, he again played a key role in reviving the coalition, the cornerstone of the Good Friday peace deal he had once rejected.

In March 2024, Donaldson was arrested in his secluded County Down home and charged alongside his wife, Eleanor. She was subsequently deemed by the Newry judge not mentally fit to stand trial on charges of aiding and abetting his crimes.
The U.K. government in July removed Donaldson from membership in the Privy Council, a body of parliamentary advisers to King Charles III. The king also stripped him of his knighthood.
Donaldson has been placed in an isolated hospital wing at Northern Ireland’s Maghaberry Prison, alongside other convicted sex offenders, to protect him from potential assaults from other prisoners. He reportedly is spending much of his days behind bars doing puzzles and reading the Bible.

UK threatens visa ban on Eritreans over migrant returns dispute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:03:27 UTC
22:03:27 KST

Aysu Bicer
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
- Fast-track visas for senior officials and other VIPs to be suspended
The UK government has threatened to ban all Eritrean nationals from entering the country unless Eritrea agrees to accept the return of more of its citizens who arrive in the UK by small boats or have been convicted of crimes, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said Thursday.
Starting Thursday, Eritrean diplomats will face restrictions on their movements outside London, while fast-track visas for senior officials and other VIPs will be suspended, according to the government.
Under the new measures, Eritrean diplomats will be prohibited from travelling more than 60 kilometers (37 miles) outside London without permission. The Home Office said the restrictions mirror those imposed on British officials in Eritrea’s capital, Asmara.
Speaking to The Telegraph, Mahmood said Eritrea had repeatedly refused to cooperate with the return of individuals who have committed crimes or have no legal right to remain in the UK.
“Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused,” she said, adding that she would consider further measures against countries that refuse to cooperate.
The UK government accused Eritrean authorities of abruptly withdrawing cooperation earlier this year. London has previously used the threat of visa restrictions to pressure other countries into accepting the return of their nationals.
Eritreans were the largest nationality group among small-boat arrivals in the UK in the 12 months to June, accounting for 18% of arrivals, according to figures cited by the House of Commons Library.
Eritrea, a one-party state, has seen many young people attempt to leave the country to escape military conscription, which can last for decades.
The UK government earlier this year threatened visa restrictions against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Restrictions imposed on the Congo last year were lifted after cooperation on returns improved, according to the Home Office. Angola and Namibia agreed to changes before the threatened restrictions were introduced.
In November, Mahmood announced plans to reform the UK’s asylum system, warning that visa penalties would be imposed on countries that failed to cooperate with the return of their nationals.
The proposed measures included an “emergency brake” on visas for countries with high numbers of asylum claims, which would remain in place until they agreed to take back citizens living in the UK illegally.

Bring a bottle: Viennese dog owners told to rinse pets’ urine from trees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:01:29 UTC
22:01:29 KST

A neighbourhood in Vienna has introduced guidelines for dog walking, including the use of bottled tap water to rinse away urine and protect vulnerable trees.
Neubau, an up-and-coming, densely populated district dotted with cafes and galleries, rolled out the Schönes Gassi (nice dog walk) campaign this week.
The project addresses the impact of the area’s 600 dogs on greenery, including about 250 trees planted over the past decade to help mitigate the effects of the climate crisis.
Using the slogan Das Flascherl zum Sackerl (the bottle to go with the bag), the guidelines say animal urine corrodes tree bark, weakening its protective layer and potentially letting corrosive pathogens and fungi penetrate the trunk.
“While marking territory is a form of communication for dogs, it causes stress for urban trees,” said Grätzllabor, a community group that takes its name from the Viennese slang for quarter or neighbourhood. “This results in rot and, in the worst case, compromised stability.”
The group said the campaign had been launched in concert with “concerned citizens” in the Austrian capital. It also asks owners to carry plastic bags to clean up after their pets.
Owners can pick up a free 270ml water bottle at the town hall to rinse areas used by their dogs. The voluntary scheme could be expanded to other districts.
Fresh canine urine is highly water-soluble and dilution significantly reduces the concentration of ammonia and other harmful substances seeping into the soil, while also softening the smell.
Grätzllabor said the rinsing strategy should not be interpreted as a “licence” for dogs to mark trees or green space but rather as an action owners could take to minimise harm caused by their pets.
Conny Sporrer, who is a dog trainer, said the Schönes Gassi campaign could help head off more drastic calls to mitigate problems linked to animal waste.
“In Vienna, we don’t need a city full of dog bans, or a city where dogs are just allowed to urinate anywhere they please,” she told reporters, saying most pets could be taught where to relieve themselves. “What we need is consideration, education and sufficient suitable facilities for dogs.”
Similar schemes have been introduced in Japan, Italy, Switzerland and Spain, which has the highest share of dog-owning households in the EU at 70%. Austria has relatively low levels of ownership, at just 17% of households.
Berlin, where more than 100,000 dogs are kept as pets after an increase in ownership during the pandemic, has also begun addressing the problem by stopping the planting of black locust trees in some areas because they are particularly sensitive to urine.
In the spring, the western district of Charlottenburg-Wilmersdorf began installing “pee stones” for dogs to use as a target, instead of trees.

Ukraine passes key laws to help unlock billions in aid from EU, IMF
KYIV, Oct 15 - Ukraine's parliament passed a package of legislation on Thursday to advance the implementation of key demands from the European Union and the International Monetary Fund to unlock billions in foreign aid.
As the war with Russia is in its fifth year, Ukraine faces a budget crisis driven by a huge military funding deficit, stalled economic growth, and domestic revenue shortfalls due to intensified Russian strikes on businesses and infrastructure.
Lawmakers approved bills to raise taxes on foreign parcels, increase e-commerce transparency, and amend financial monitoring rules for politicians.
"The laws approved today establish a modern model for the taxation of e-commerce, which is in line with the European Union’s approach and is fair to domestic businesses," said Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko.
"The reform is also part of the cooperation programme with the IMF and a condition for macro-financial support from the EU."
As the war gets more expensive and demand for weapons, drones and ammunition continues to grow, Ukraine is struggling to cover its defence spending with domestic revenue and crucially depends on financial aid from its Western allies.
Last month, the government was forced to delay some of the budget spending – like reconstruction work and preparations for winter – due to a budget liquidity crisis. Domestic tax revenue fell by 32 billion hryvnias ($711 million) in August and September as Russia intensified its strikes on the Ukrainian infrastructure, logistics and businesses.
Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said that the results of this week's parliamentary work gave the government cause for optimism, but there was still a lot of work to do to meet all the requirements of the country's lenders.
For the remainder of this year, Ukraine has around $29 billion available in EU financial support waiting for continued disbursement.
The finance ministry said that the new rules for foreign parcels, introducing a 20% value-added tax, would take effect no earlier than July 2027. It was expected to generate an additional 20-30 billion hryvnias in budget revenue, lawmakers estimated. REUTERS

‘Fantastically special’: all 10 Victoria Crosses awarded to Royal Marines go on show for first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:00:13 UTC
22:00:13 KST

They tell tales of bravery under fire, may lead to conversations about the UK’s place in the world and could prompt visitors to reflect on what they might have done if faced with the same perilous circumstances.
All 10 Victoria Crosses (VCs) awarded to members of the Royal Marines are going on display together for the first time along with tales of courage during conflicts such as the Crimean and both world wars.
“It’s fantastically special,” said Matthew Sheldon, the chief executive officer of Royal Navy Museums. “The Royal Marines have only ever been awarded 10 Victoria Crosses. We have all 10 of them. The originals have never been seen together before. They’ve been in secure storage, not visible to the public, which seemed like a crying shame.”
The medals will go on permanent display at a new £15m “Royal Marines Experience” at Portsmouth Historic Dockyard telling 360 years of marines’ history.
Sheldon said the marines awarded VCs tended to be “youngish” and not from very senior ranks. Like modern marines, who usually work in small, agile teams, they tended to find themselves in very close quarters to the enemy.
He said the stories could lead to debate about the role the UK played in global conflicts.
“When we look at the world now and we look at our military, it’s not about large set pieces – it’s often quite small incidents below the level of full-out declared wars. I think the medals ask questions about the world we live in now.”
Earlier this month, the Royal Marines returned to the Faroe Islands for the first time since the second world war as part of security efforts in the strategically vital Greenland-Iceland-UK Gap. This autumn, commando engineers have been practising digging underground hospitals that offer protection against drone attacks.
Sheldon said he thought the medals could prompt visitors to ask questions of themselves. “They are about a moment in time and somebody’s choice in that moment. They are powerful because they make you think: ‘What would I have done in the same incident.’”
Staff at the museum say it is hard to pick out a favourite story but when pressed, Sheldon said he was very keen on that of Sgt Norman Augustus Finch, born in 1890.
Finch was awarded the Victoria Cross during the Zeebrugge Raid on 23 April 1918. While serving onboard HMS Vindictive, Finch was stationed on a high lookout platform.
During the battle, his position was hit by shells, killing or wounding everyone around him. Although he was severely injured, Finch remained at his post and continued to fire on enemy positions until another shell finally put him out of action.
Because of the bravery shown by the entire battalion, the marines were allowed to vote for who should receive the VC. Finch was chosen by his peers.
Mark Berry, the assistant curator of artefacts, said he liked the story of L/Cpl Walter Richard Parker. During the Gallipoli campaign, Parker served as a stretcher bearer.
On the morning of 1 May 1915, Parker was a member of a party tasked with taking aid to men in an isolated frontline trench. To reach the trench, Parker crossed 365 metres (400 yards) of open ground under intense enemy fire.
He was the only person to successfully reach the trench. Having aided the wounded, he helped them evacuate the next morning, and himself was severely injured in the thigh and chest.
Berry said: “It’s a really good example of the multilayered role of the marines. It’s not just fighting. It’s also trying to save lives, trying to help people.”
- The Royal Marines Experience opens at Portsmouth Historic Dockyard on 24 October.

Brain implants are helping people who’ve lost their voice
