Brain implants are helping people who’ve lost their voice
The technology could get those with ALS, Parkinson’s disease and brain injuries “talking” again
This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)
On paper, my interview with Casey Harrell looks like any other.
I ask the questions, he answers them. He tells me about his background as a climate activist, his Southern roots and his daughter, who as a preschooler loved to dress up like a cheetah and roar around the house. “My daughter was incredibly cute in her cheetah outfit,” Harrell says.
The transcript tells the story of our conversation. But between the lines is an entirely different story — the story of where Harrell’s words come from.
Harrell started losing his ability to speak in his early 40s, nearly six years ago. He talked to me using a brain implant that can decode his words directly from his thoughts. The device, called a brain-computer interface, is experimental. But it has transformed Harrell’s life. And it could soon transform others. Advances in computing power and AI, lessons gleaned from patient experience and investments from neurotechnology companies are starting to yield real progress on brain-computer interfaces for people who can no longer talk. In other words, Harrell’s new voice might not be so singular in the future.
“There’s a lot of excitement and hope in the field right now,” says Matthew Willsey, a neurosurgeon and biomedical engineer at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, who recently implanted a new type of speech interface in a woman’s brain. For years, Willsey says, scientists didn’t know whether attempts to decode speech would be successful; now, a body of research results points clearly to yes. “They’re thinking, ‘Wow, this is actually a usable technology that addresses a real problem that people suffer from.’”
Harrell has amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS. The progressive neurodegenerative disease, which affects an estimated 35,000 people in the United States, kills nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord that control muscles. As the neural connections between Harrell’s brain and body began to falter, he gradually lost his ability to move his muscles, leaving him confined to his bed or a wheelchair. Some of those dropped signals directed the muscles in his throat and mouth, the ones that allow him to speak.
“I began to lose my ability to talk shortly after my diagnosis in 2020,” Harrell says. After that, it was “a slow-motion car crash” as fewer and fewer people could understand him. “[My voice] is the most important thing I have lost in this whole disease,” he says.
In a stroke of luck, Harrell learned through a family member about a clinical trial happening at the University of California, Davis — one that attempted to restore speech with a brain-computer interface. In 2023, Harrell had four small devices implanted on the left side of his brain. These grids of electrodes reside on Harrell’s speech motor cortex, a stretch of brain along the precentral gyrus that controls the movements required for speech.
Today, Harrell uses his system for about 10 to 14 hours daily, making him, as he puts it, “the world’s biggest power user of the brain-to-computer interface known to man.” Hard data suggest he’s right. A recent count shows that Harrell has used his system to communicate nearly 2 million words, the scientists working with him reported in June in Nature Medicine.
The very existence of Harrell’s words shows it may be possible to restore speech for people with ALS, as well as for those whose speech is impaired by stroke, paralysis, cerebral palsy and Parkinson’s disease. “This kind of technology has the potential to dramatically change the conversation,” says David Brandman, a UC Davis neurosurgeon and neuroscientist who works with Harrell.
Harrell’s interface still has room for improvement. It’s bulky, relatively slow and limited in what sorts of nonword sounds it can decode.
But it is a “beginning,” says Leigh Hochberg, a neuroscientist at Brown University who works with Harrell. “It’s still early days. There’s a lot of research to happen, and it’s going to be very exciting.” The end game, Hochberg says, is a world in which people could use a device to communicate seamlessly, quickly, clearly — and in their former voices.
Success would mean restoring more than just people’s words, Brandman says. It would mean restoring their ability to connect in all the ineffable ways that make us human. “Speech is so fundamental to who we are,” he says. “Imagine living in a world where you couldn’t tell someone you’re in pain, or you couldn’t say that you love them … It’s not hard to imagine how devastating that would be for your quality of life.”
The voice inside
On the path to a technology that enables fast, natural speech, scientists first had to answer a more basic question: Could the brain’s electrical chatter be decoded and translated into action outside of the head?
Nerve cells speak to each other with tiny pulses of electricity, signals that can be picked up with electrodes. The existence of this electrical language raised the tantalizing idea that electrical messages could be decoded straight from where they originate in the brain, bypassing damaged links to the rest of the body.
“This has really started as early as the 1950s, the first time scientists put electrodes into brains to record neural activity,” says Sergey Stavisky, a neuroscientist and neural engineer at UC Davis. “You can record the electrical activity of brain cells or parts of the brain. And that’s really when modern neuroscience started trying to study, how does the brain compute? How does it allow us to move our muscles?”
Figuring out how to decode simple neural commands was the first step. Animal studies paved the way, including experiments in which rhesus monkeys consciously controlled the movements of a robotic arm using only brain signals detected by implanted electrodes.
The Deep End podcast explores what makes your voice yours
What if you lost your voice? Today, AI can re-create it, and brain implants can turn thoughts into speech. This season of The Deep End follows people living through these vocal transformations — and asks what these remarkable technologies can teach us about why our voices matter in the first place.
By 2004, scientists had enough confidence in the approach to launch a clinical trial in humans called BrainGate. Researchers implanted a grid of electrodes in the brain of a paralyzed man named Matthew Nagle. A former star athlete, Nagle was able to control a computer cursor with his thoughts alone. “That was really the starting gun of the modern version of the brain-computer interface field,” Stavisky says.
From there, attempts to link brain activity with some physical outcome — such as moving a computer mouse, a wheelchair or a robotic arm — blossomed. Some of these efforts focused on the brain signals and regions that controlled movements of the hands and arms. Others focused on a very tricky version of the same basic problem: talking.
A brain-computer interface that could detect the intention to say a word and bypass the muscles needed to say it would be a powerful workaround for people with diseases like ALS or brain injuries. And it is no small thing to people who can no longer talk. “Losing their speech is way more devastating than losing their mobility,” says Jessica Pietrowski, a speech and language pathologist at UC Davis who has worked with many such patients. “Speech is how they maintain their identity in their relationships.”
Harrell emphasizes this point. “What does my voice mean to me? It means so much,” he says. “It is the ability to parent my daughter. It is the ability to connect with my wife. It is the ability to make a wry joke with my friends.”
Looking for a cheetah
Talking feels effortless to most of us, but just saying hello involves a sweeping array of actions — and upwards of 100 muscles. “It’s incredibly complex and intricate, and really, an incredible human feat,” Pietrowski says.
Consider the “h” sound in “hello.” Known as a glottal fricative, it involves an orchestra of tiny movements. First, the diaphragm contracts to fill the lungs with air. Chest and abdominal muscles push air up through relaxed vocal cords and surrounding tissues. This puff of air then travels to the mouth, where lips, jaw and tongue execute complex sequences of movements that create the rest of the sound. Finally, air waves, perfectly shaped, ripple from the mouth. Then, and only then, “you have speech,” Pietrowski says.
But the beginnings of this nearly miraculous transformation start in the brain, where tiny electrical nerve pulses command the body to speak. In Harrell’s trial, he would attempt to speak words, prompting his motor cortex to send signals to his body. The implanted electrodes would detect the patterns and send them to a computer to interpret. With this work-around, it didn’t matter that Harrell’s muscles didn’t get the message; the computer would.
After Harrell recovered from surgery, researchers began testing the system in his home. They collected his neural data and streamed it to computers on a nearby cart, where machine learning algorithms attempted to match Harrell’s brain activity patterns to those that predictably occur with certain sounds. Called phonemes, these sound units are the building blocks of words. The algorithm assembled the phonemes into words, as it made its best guess about what Harrell was trying to say. To limit the computational power required, the algorithm used a vocabulary of just 50 words.
When the system was plugged in and ready to go, scientists asked Harrell to try and say a specific, random sentence built from that library: “What good is that?”
Harrell got to work. His eyebrows shot up as he saw the words appear on a screen in front of him in response to his thoughts. The decoder worked.
Everyone paused. Some of the researchers started to cry. Harrell and his family became emotional. Being in the room when the switch was flipped on was “incredible,” Brandman says. “The majority of my adult life was working up to that moment, and to see it come to fruition was an incredible experience. But more than that was seeing what impact it immediately had for Casey and his family.”
Harrell remembers his feelings that day, too: “Pure joy.” Even though he wasn’t choosing his words for that first test, “it was a profound moment,” he says. “The possibilities for the near future for me and the rest of humanity were overwhelming to realize.”
The second day of testing was even more profound, but in a personal way. This time, the system’s algorithm was using a vocabulary of over 125,000 words. This would be more challenging for the decoder, but it would give Harrell more autonomy to say what he wanted.
Harrell started the session with a joke, Hochberg recalls, along the lines of, “Is this thing on?” But his next line was a real puzzler: “I’m looking for a cheetah.”
Hochberg, who had joined remotely on a video call, was sure it was a mistake. “There’s no way that the second sentence on the second day of using a brain-to-computer interface is going to say anything about a cheetah,” Hochberg says. “That’s obviously a decoding error.”
But there was something the scientist couldn’t see. Harrell’s 4-year-old daughter had bounded into the room, dressed as a cheetah.
The discovery was big scientifically, but it was bigger for what it represented to Harrell. Brain technology could restore not just his words, but also the spontaneous exchanges that had once made up his everyday life.
“It was so amazing to be able to be understood right from the get-go and to be able to talk and respond to my daughter,” Harrell says, “especially because that was lacking completely from my life.”
Hochberg says moments like that represent the promise that brain-computer interfaces hold. “To me, seeing it work that quickly and that powerfully really, really emphasized that these are technologies that are going to be able to restore not only activities of daily living,” he says, “but they’re going to restore communication between parent and child.”
From thoughts to words
Casey Harrell’s brain-computer interface extracts neural signals from his brain and, through a few key steps, transforms them into
words. Electrodes implanted in Harrell’s speech motor cortex detect neurons’ electrical signals (1), generating raw neural data (2). Advanced machine learning efforts (3) map chunks of the data to phonemes, the building blocks of words (4). Those phonemes are then assembled into sentences by a predictive language model, or LM (5), and put on a screen where they can be read or spoken.
Harrell uses his interface to send email and Slack messages and play Wordle with his wife and child. He uses it to work; in fact, he’s just getting started on a new climate consultancy project. Harrell’s interface has connected him to the world in a way that would have been impossible even a few years ago.
But the system is still a research device. And like any early design, it comes with limitations. First, it isn’t portable; Harrell has wires coming from a port that sits on the top of his head, and he can use it only at home. And it is slow by the standards of typical conversation. You can’t tell from the written transcript of our interview, but our conversations always came with built-in delays.
For example, as we chatted, we discovered that we had both worked in the same part of Washington, D.C. I asked him if he remembered his old address. The answer came some two minutes later.
“I make a very simple analogy where I talk about having the brain-to-computer interface being akin to trying to catch a train, running to get the last car before it leaves the station,” Harrell says. With the current interface, “if people are patient and wait for my sentence correction, I can [catch the train and] be a part of the conversation.”
Harrell’s system translates his neural activity into words on a screen. If he chooses to do so, he can then use a computerized voice to say the words out loud. “It is brain-to-text, and then it gets translated to the voice,” Harrell says. A brain-to-voice system, in which a person’s thoughts are translated directly into spoken words, he adds, “is the holy grail of what this will become.”
More than words
Harrell and the scientists working with him are getting closer to this very type of real-time communication. Last year in Nature, they debuted a new algorithm that attempted to turn Harrell’s brain signals straight into sounds. The results: He could speak his mind with a delay of just 10 milliseconds. That’s very close to a real-time conversation. But the sounds Harrell made were hard to understand, with just over half of them being intelligible to listeners.
The next generation of devices aims to do better. Willsey, the University of Michigan neurosurgeon, is working on one such device, a fully implantable array. In June, he implanted what’s called the “cortical module,” about the size of a dime, in the brain of a 68-year-old woman. Like Harrell, the woman could no longer talk in a way that most people could understand.
Unlike the BrainGate system, this new device — made by Austin, Texas–based neurotechnology company Paradromics — is portable. Surgeons implanted it in a stretch of brain tissue that made up the woman’s speech motor cortex, along the precentral gyrus. The cortical module collects neural data and sends it to another device implanted in the chest called a transceiver. From there, signals shoot to a receiver on her chest, where the data gets transformed into sounds — spoken words that play out of speakers on a nearby computer.
Paradromics’ priority is to test whether the implant is safe. If so, scientists can turn to the goal of restoring speech in real time. “The moment that you’re thinking the words, you don’t have to wait for the sentence to complete,” says Willsey, who, like Brandman, is a site investigator for the Paradromics clinical trial. “You can let the words kind of flow out as they would in a normal conversation.”
Scientists also want to decode more than words. Qualities of voice, such as pitch, are important for marking questions, says Vikash Gilja, a Paradromics neuroscientist. Speakers can also alter or pace their conversation to show sarcasm or concern. These sounds are all made by moving muscles, Gilja says, and can therefore be decoded from the brain.
“Our near-term goal right now is just to restore speech,” says Paradromics neurosurgeon Stephen Ryu. “But eventually, we’re hoping that we can actually restore someone’s ability to be fully involved in a conversation, to basically decode things like their timing, their emotions, their personality.”
Other researchers are trying to incorporate the gestures that many of us use to communicate.
“Some gestures can substitute for speech entirely, like nodding yes, shaking your head no, waving, shrugging, giving a thumbs up,” says bioengineer Samantha Brosler of the University of California, San Fransico. Gestures can also change the meaning of words; a “maybe” with a head nod is close to a yes, for instance. “I think of gestures and body movements as an additional communication channel that can work together with speech,” Brosler says.
In a new study, Brosler and colleagues enabled two people with paralysis who had lost their speaking ability to instead use their brain signals to control both the words and gestures of digital avatars. The advance, reported in September in Nature Neuroscience, adds to the repertoire of signals that could be decoded and turned into action.
And as all this is happening, scientists are creating smaller, more stable types of electrodes to embed in the brain; more powerful computational algorithms to handle larger amounts of data; and better models of how those signals relate to sounds, words and gestures, Gilja says. “We can see all the pieces coming together.”
There are many reasons to be optimistic about the future, says Brandman, who is an investigator for the clinical trial led by Paradromics. “I think I’m about five years away from being able to meet a patient with ALS and having the following conversation,” he says. “‘Ms. Smith, I’m sorry you’ve been diagnosed with ALS. I don’t have a cure for you, but I do have a device that I can implant that can help you communicate.’”
That conversation is tantalizing. But there are no guarantees that these systems will work as hoped, or that they will be widely available. Such implants would probably come with hefty price tags, invasive brain surgeries and perhaps more demand than the few capable clinicians and technologists could meet.
And there are underlying questions about the brain itself. One concern is that changes to the brain over time might render neural signals unreliable, especially as diseases progress. If that happens, a person’s interface might produce a scrambled message — or be left without enough neural data to decode.
“These are real challenges, and the field is working on them,” Stavisky says. “But they’re not solved yet.”
Despite these hurdles, the push for voice-restoring technology can’t come soon enough for people who have lost theirs. In September, researchers reported that the woman with the Paradromics implant had a message for them. “OK,” she used her brain-computer interface to tell researchers. “I have a lot to say.” With her system, she was able to call her grandchildren on the telephone.
And Harrell is now living a life that looks very different from the one he might have imagined six years ago. Although his disease keeps him close to home, he can now share his thoughts with the world — and his family — instead of locking them away inside.
“The ability to scream when you are running and want to get out some stress, the ability to say sweet nothings into your partner’s ear,” Harrell says. “These are the things that life is all about, and when you are robbed of those times, you want them back at all costs. And this is why this is good enough for now.”
But he too has a vision, a day when these devices are commonplace, “when I am one of many, instead of being one of one.”
For more about the human voice and to hear from Casey Harrell himself, listen to The Deep End podcast Season Two, called Talk to Me. It’s free wherever you get your podcasts.

7 sailors missing as two ships off Romanian Black Sea coast catch fire amid drone incursion

7 sailors missing as two ships off Romanian Black Sea coast catch fire amid drone incursion
Seven sailors are missing from one of two tanker ships that caught fire in Romania's Black Sea overnight amid drone incursions into the country's airspace, Romanian officials said on Oct. 15.
The San Marino-flagged "Wine Trader," a chemical tanker, reported a fire aboard and eight people missing at 07:00 a.m. local time near the Romanian city of Sulina, a press release by Romania's naval authority said. The authority has since updated the numbers to seven missing.
Search and rescue operations were continuing, it added.
On the evening of Oct. 14, Romanian defense minister Radu Miruta said the country's authorities were also investigating a reported drone attack on an chemical tanker, the "Yara J," Romanian media Digi24 reported.
The Romanian Agency for the Rescue of Human Life on the Sea (ARSVOM) received a call for a rescue mission for the Comoros-flagged ship after it had caught fire.
The sailors from Syria, India, and Iran were all safe aboard, but said the ship was hit by a drone at about 08:25 p.m. local time, Digi24 said.
The leader of the Romanian Seafarers' Free Union, Adrian Mihalcioiu, considered the incident an intentional attack of a ship in Romanian territorial waters en route to Ukraine, Digi24 said.
Miruta said that no drone was seen approaching the ship on the defense ministry's radars, but at the same time pointed toward two drones that entered Romania's airspace at 10:26 p.m. local time, according to Digi24.
"Whether it was struck by a drone or not, an investigation is currently underway," he said. "It is a matter of significant gravity, as long as such incidents occur in Romanian territorial waters."
On Oct. 13, two cargo ships were struck by drones near Bulgaria's Black Sea coast overnight, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.
Radev called the attacks "absolutely unacceptable" and said Bulgaria had informed its permanent representatives to NATO and the European Union. Sofia is seeking assistance to strengthen surveillance of the air and maritime domains and improve its response capabilities.
Attacks by Ukraine and Russia in the Black Sea intensified over the summer.
In July, Ukraine launched Operation Molochka, a campaign targeting Russia's shadow fleet in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov in an effort to tighten the noose around Russian-occupied Crimea.
Turkey called on Moscow and Kyiv in August to impose a moratorium on attacks against vessels, following a series of strikes in the region that involved Turkish-flagged ships.
While Kyiv has said it is ready to accept a moratorium on attacks in the Black Sea, Moscow has shown no interest in de-escalating the situation.
Ukraine established its own Black Sea maritime corridor in August 2023, after Russia withdrew from a U.N.- and Turkey-brokered grain deal. Since then, Russia has regularly targeted ports and civilian shipping.

Taiwan's ITRI and eJoule improve drone battery manufacturing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:57:44 UTC
21:57:44 KST

TAIPEI (TAIPEI NEWS) – Hsinchu-based Industrial Technology Research Institute said Thursday that it has partnered with local battery maker eJoule to make high-capacity batteries for drones and electric vehicles.
Medium-and high-lithium ternary batteries use nickel, cobalt, and manganese. Higher lithium content means greater storage capacity, making them suitable for drones, robotics, and electric vehicles.
According to a press release, drones and EVs are driving demand for lighter, longer-lasting batteries. Although ternary batteries are valued for their capacity, there are lifecycle and safety bottlenecks that need to be addressed before commercialization.
ITRI and eJoule co-developed a solution using single-crystal structures, electrode fabrication, and power cell certification to speed commercialization for drones, robotics, and storage applications. The project also aims to achieve production and supply chain self-reliance.
Electrode fabrication combines raw materials with metal foils to create the positive and negative charges required for batteries to function. The common method involves mixing the materials with additives and solvents such as water for coating onto the foils, which are then vacuumed and pressed into batteries.
ITRI Material and Chemical Research Laboratories Director Chiu Kuo-chan (邱國展) said eJoule provided the material while ITRI designed battery specifications and conducted performance tests. He noted that the material proved stable after extensive, repetitive cycles of charging and discharging, making it a suitable candidate comparable to lithium iron phosphate batteries in terms of lifespan as well as safer than traditional ternary materials.
ITRI said eJoule’s patented dynamic crystallization process yields simple, high-performing structures without using toxic precursors. eJoule Vice President Liu Min-tuan (劉敏端) said the initiative would combine ITRI's battery expertise to speed material applications from laboratory settings to commercially viable products.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Delta Electronics Chair Cheng Ping (鄭平) said Thursday that power infrastructure is failing to keep pace with the rapid expansion of AI data centers.
Four major US cloud service providers are expected to spend 4.7 times as much on capital expenditures this year as in 2022, while investment in power systems has grown only 1.8-fold, Cheng said at a forum, per CNA.
Cheng said global electrification stands at about 21%, compared with 30% in Taiwan, and electricity demand will continue rising as transportation, industry, and data centers expand. He projected that EV power consumption could increase fivefold over the next decade, while data center electricity use could triple from last year’s level by 2030.
Citing estimates, Cheng said US data centers are expected to add 44 GW of electricity demand by 2028, while the power grid is projected to add only 25 GW in supply capacity, leaving a 19 GW gap. He attributed the infrastructure lag partly to regulations, equipment lifespans, and investment returns.
Cheng said improving energy efficiency is essential to stable power supplies. He noted that Delta has invested in solid oxide fuel cells, which generate electricity using hydrogen or natural gas and can achieve overall efficiency of up to 85%, per Anue.
Cheng said the company is also developing solid-state transformers that convert medium-voltage alternating current directly into 800-volt direct current, reducing conversion losses in data centers. He added that the company’s new prefabricated power solution can cut on-site deployment time by 50%.

In response, aircraft, naval ships, and coastal-based missile systems were deployed. Thirteen of the People’s Liberation Army aircraft crossed the Taiwan Strait median line in the country’s northern, central, southwestern and eastern air defense identification zones, according to the ministry.
So far this month, Taiwan has tracked Chinese aircraft 96 times and ships 164 times. Since September 2020, China has increased its use of gray zone tactics by incrementally increasing the number of military aircraft and naval vessels operating around the country.
Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

Euro area industrial output unexpectedly falls 0.5% in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:56:35 UTC
21:56:35 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Industrial production in the euro area fell 0.5% month-on-month in August, against expectations of stagnation, according to Eurostat data released Thursday.
The decline followed a 0.3% contraction in July and a 0.1% drop in June, marking the third consecutive monthly fall.
Across the EU, seasonally adjusted industrial output decreased 0.3% in August, following a 0.4% drop in July.
Euro area production of non-durable consumer goods saw the sharpest monthly decline among the main industrial groupings, down 2.7%. Intermediate goods output decreased 0.8%, while energy production slipped 0.6%.
Capital goods production, however, rose 0.4%, and durable consumer goods output climbed 0.2%.
Across the EU, non-durable consumer goods production fell 2.3%, energy output declined 0.5%, and intermediate goods production dropped 0.3%. Capital goods output rose 0.7%, while durable consumer goods production remained unchanged.
Among member states, Belgium saw the largest monthly decline at 5.1%, followed by Ireland at 3.1% and Portugal at 2%.
Sweden posted the strongest increase at 6.5%, followed by Estonia at 4.3% and the Netherlands at 2.6%.
Among the bloc’s largest economies, industrial output rose 0.4% in Germany but fell 0.3% in France, 1.3% in Italy, and 0.8% in Spain.
On an annual basis, industrial production declined 1.1% in the euro area and 0.2% across the EU.
Euro area non-durable consumer goods output dropped 9.1% from August 2025, while intermediate goods production fell 0.4%. Energy, capital goods, and durable consumer goods output climbed 3.1%, 3%, and 0.4%, respectively.
Ireland saw the steepest annual contraction at 15%, followed by Belgium at 7.1% and Bulgaria at 5.4%. The Netherlands saw the largest jump at 9.8%, ahead of Hungary at 8.8% and Denmark at 8.3%.

Obama says Israel has ‘ceded moral ground’ in Middle East conflict
Unknown

Berk Kutay Gökmen
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Former US President Barack Obama has criticized Israel’s handling of the Middle East conflict, warning that military strength cannot guarantee lasting security and that refusing concessions to Palestinians risks undermining its moral standing.
The former president made the remarks on Tuesday during a discussion with award-winning writer and journalist Susan McKay at Belfast, northern Ireland, according to the Belfast Telegraph.
Speaking about the Israeli war on Gaza, Obama said the violence should “pain everybody”, describing it as a destructive cycle driven by historical grievances, hardened attitudes and deep divisions.
He acknowledged the long history of persecution faced by Jewish people in Europe. However, he also stressed that Palestinians had suffered injustice through the loss of their land.
“That is undeniable. What is also undeniable is that they took land off people and they were excessive. And those people understandably said: ‘This is injustice and I want my land back,’” he said.
Obama argued that the stronger side carries a greater responsibility to help break the cycle of violence, rather than relying solely on its military and technological superiority.
“If the attitude of Israel is, now that we are the strongest, the most technologically advanced in the region, then our security will depend on us simply doing whatever we need and taking whatever we want, and not making any concessions to anyone,” he said.
“That may work short-term... but you have ceded moral ground if that is the position you take.”
He said the current Israeli government appeared to have adopted that approach and urged it to recognize that millions of Palestinians would remain in the region.
“I would say the current Israeli government appears to have taken that. It is incumbent on them to recognise that 7 million Palestinians are not going anywhere,” Obama said.
“It is not sustainable to press upon them a condition that no-one would accept for themselves.”
Earlier on Tuesday, Obama received an honorary doctorate from Queen’s University Belfast.

Photos: China and North Korea open new border bridge amid deepening ties
The New Yalu River Bridge connects Dandong, China, and Sinuiju, North Korea, enhancing regional trade and collaboration.
The opening of a long-delayed bridge linking China and North Korea underscores the deepening ties between the two neighbours as Pyongyang courts both Beijing and Moscow to ease its economic isolation.
China’s official Xinhua news agency said a launch ceremony was held on Thursday for the New Yalu River Bridge, which connects the northeastern Chinese city of Dandong with the North Korean border city of Sinuiju.
Video from state media showed trucks decorated with the national flags of both countries lined up on the four-lane span, which itself was festooned with Chinese and North Korean flags.
In a video address, Chinese Premier Li Qiang hailed the bridge as a “new landmark” of the countries’ “traditional friendship” and urged both sides to use the opening to deepen connectivity and explore new cooperation in border areas, Xinhua reported. North Korean Premier Pak Thae Song also delivered a video message.
The 3km (1.8-mile) road bridge is expected to ease pressure on the ageing Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, a decades-old structure on the same route that carries a railway line and vehicles but can accommodate only one-way traffic at a time.
More than 70 percent of official trade between the two countries currently goes through that crossing, according to Chinese data. The South Korean government has counted at least 17 active road and rail links along the 1,400km (870-mile) North Korea-China border.

Mysterious brain activity under anesthesia challenges what we know about consciousness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:52:05 UTC
21:52:05 KST

Mysterious brain activity under anesthesia challenges what we know about consciousness
- Date:
- October 15, 2026
- Source:
- Baylor College of Medicine
- Summary:
- Even under general anesthesia, the human brain can analyze language, recognize different types of words, and predict what comes next in a story, according to a surprising discovery by Baylor researchers. The findings challenge our understanding of consciousness and suggest that the unconscious brain is far more capable than scientists previously realized.
- Share:
Even when a person is fully unconscious under general anesthesia, their brain may still be doing something remarkable: processing language, recognizing patterns, and even anticipating which words will come next.
Researchers at Baylor College of Medicine have discovered that the brain retains surprisingly sophisticated abilities during anesthesia, despite the absence of conscious awareness. The findings, published in the journal Nature, challenge traditional assumptions about the relationship between consciousness and thinking. They could also provide new insights into how the brain processes memories and language, potentially leading to advances in technologies that help people communicate after neurological injuries.
"Our findings show that the brain is far more active and capable during unconsciousness than previously thought," said Dr. Sameer Sheth, professor and Cullen Foundation Endowed chair of neurosurgery and a McNair Scholar at Baylor. "Even when patients are fully anesthetized, their brains continue to analyze the world around them."
Recording Brain Activity During General Anesthesia
To investigate what happens inside the unconscious brain, Sheth, who is also a neurosurgeon at Baylor St. Luke's Medical Center, and his colleagues studied patients undergoing epilepsy surgery while under general anesthesia.
These procedures offered an unusual opportunity to examine the hippocampus, a brain structure deeply involved in learning and memory. Located within the brain's temporal lobe, the hippocampus helps organize information and plays an important role in forming new memories.
The researchers used advanced recording devices called Neuropixels probes to monitor electrical signals from hundreds of individual neurons in the hippocampus. These tiny probes can detect activity from many nerve cells simultaneously, providing a detailed picture of how groups of neurons respond to information.
According to the researchers, this technology had not previously been used to investigate this particular brain region in this way. It allowed the team to examine how the hippocampus responds to sounds and language while patients are unconscious and unable to report what they experience.
The first experiment involved playing a series of repeating tones, occasionally interrupted by a sound that differed from the others.
Although the patients were under anesthesia, neurons in their hippocampus responded differently to the unexpected sounds. Even more surprisingly, the brain cells became better at distinguishing these unusual tones as the experiment continued.
This improvement suggested that the hippocampus was showing signs of neural plasticity, the brain's ability to change its responses through experience. In other words, some of the basic processes associated with learning appeared to remain active even without conscious awareness.
The Unconscious Brain Can Process Language and Predict Words
The researchers then tested whether the unconscious brain could handle something more complicated than simple sounds.
They played short stories to the anesthetized patients while continuing to record activity from neurons in the hippocampus.
The results revealed a surprising level of language processing. Distinct patterns of neural activity contained information about different categories of words, including nouns, verbs, and adjectives. This suggested that the hippocampus was responding to meaningful features of language rather than simply detecting that sounds were occurring.
But the most intriguing discovery went a step further.
The researchers found that neural activity also carried information that could be used to predict upcoming words in a sentence. Even though the patients were unconscious, their brains appeared to anticipate how the language unfolding around them might continue.
"The brain appears to anticipate what comes next in a story, even without conscious awareness," said Sheth, who is also Director of The Gordon and Mary Cain Pediatric Neurology Research Foundation Laboratories within the Duncan Neurological Research Institute at Texas Children's Hospital.
This ability is related to a process known as predictive coding. Rather than passively receiving information, the brain continually uses patterns and previous experience to anticipate what might happen next. When listening to someone speak, for example, the brain can use the words already heard to form expectations about what is likely to follow.
Scientists have typically studied this kind of sophisticated prediction in people who are awake and paying attention. Finding evidence of it during general anesthesia suggests that at least some of the underlying neural processes can operate independently of conscious awareness.
"This kind of predictive coding is something we associate with being awake and attentive, yet it's happening here in an unconscious state," said Dr. Benjamin Hayden, professor of neurosurgery at Baylor.
What Does This Discovery Mean for Consciousness?
The findings raise important questions about what consciousness actually contributes to the brain's ability to process information.
Consciousness is generally associated with subjective awareness, including the experience of hearing, thinking, and understanding the world around us. Yet the study suggests that some neural processes involved in interpreting language and predicting future information can continue even when that awareness is absent.
This does not necessarily mean that the anesthetized patients consciously understood the stories being played to them. Instead, it indicates that the brain can carry out surprisingly complex aspects of language processing without a person being aware of doing so.
The distinction could help researchers better understand how consciousness emerges.
One possibility is that awareness depends not simply on whether individual brain regions remain active, but on how information is coordinated and shared across larger networks of brain regions.
Under this view, a structure such as the hippocampus might continue analyzing information even when the broader communication between brain regions needed for conscious experience is disrupted.
A Surprising Connection Between the Brain and Artificial Intelligence
The discovery also highlights an intriguing similarity between human brain activity and artificial intelligence (AI).
Large language models, the technology behind many modern AI chatbots, generate text by using patterns learned from enormous amounts of language data to predict what should come next.
The researchers observed a related predictive ability in the hippocampus, where neural signals reflected information about upcoming words even during unconsciousness.
Although biological brains and AI models operate in fundamentally different ways, both can use patterns in language to anticipate future information. Studying these similarities may help scientists better understand how prediction works in natural and artificial systems.
The findings could also have practical implications for brain-computer interfaces, which use signals recorded from the brain to communicate with external devices.
One potential application involves speech prosthetics, technologies designed to help people communicate when injuries or neurological conditions have impaired their ability to speak.
If scientists can reliably identify meaningful language signals in the brain, those signals might eventually be used to support communication technologies for patients who have lost speech abilities.
"Can we use these signals to deploy and run a speech prosthetic for some of the parts of the brain that are damaged by stroke or injury? These are questions that we can now consider in relation to this part of the brain," said Dr. Vigi Katlowitz, first author and a neurosurgery resident with Baylor.
Scientists Are Rethinking the Limits of the Unconscious Brain
Despite the striking results, the researchers emphasize that several questions remain unanswered.
The experiments were conducted under one particular type of general anesthesia, so the findings cannot automatically be extended to other anesthetic methods or states of unconsciousness.
It is also unclear whether similar language processing occurs during sleep or coma, two conditions that differ significantly from medically induced unconsciousness.
Another important limitation is that the researchers focused on the hippocampus. Further studies will be needed to determine whether comparable abilities persist in other brain regions and how these areas interact when consciousness is absent.
Nevertheless, the results provide compelling evidence that unconsciousness does not necessarily mean the brain has stopped performing sophisticated information processing.
Instead, the brain may continue analyzing patterns, responding to unexpected events, and anticipating language even when a person has no conscious awareness of the surrounding world.
"This work pushes us to rethink what it means to be conscious," said Sheth. "The brain is doing much more behind the scenes than we fully understand."

UAE royal sentenced for child neglect after London cocaine binge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:48:34 UTC

Breadcrumb
Abu Dhabi royal sentenced for child neglect after cocaine binge in London
A member of Abu Dhabi's ruling royal family has been sentenced for child neglect after being found unconscious on a busy London street following cocaine use, while a three-year-old child in her care wandered barefoot near moving traffic.
Mahrah Al Nahyan, 32, admitted one count of child neglect at Southwark Crown Court on Tuesday and was handed a two-year community order requiring rehabilitation, according to The Times.
The court heard that Al Nahyan, who is connected to the ruling dynasty of Abu Dhabi and the United Arab Emirates through marriage, had been taking cocaine in the days leading up to the incident on 13 June.
Members of the public discovered her slumped against railings in west London beside an unconscious man, while the toddler played nearby with a scooter and a toy plane.
The child, who was not wearing shoes, was seen approaching moving traffic, prompting passers-by to intervene and contact the police at around 1.50pm.
Rio Pahlavanpour, prosecuting, told the court that the child had been left unattended and was at serious risk of harm.
"They noticed the child was unattended, without shoes on the street with a scooter and members of the public intervened as he seemed to be in close proximity to moving traffic," he said.
Al Nahyan reportedly remained unconscious for around 30 minutes before waking and behaving erratically.
"This is not a slaughterhouse, why do you care so much? Why are you so worried?" she allegedly shouted at those who had intervened.
Video footage recorded by a member of the public showed Al Nahyan slumped against railings with her head bowed and arms crossed, while the unconscious man lay on his back in a nearby doorway.
Police subsequently discovered drug paraphernalia in her bags, although no illicit substances were recovered.
Sentencing Al Nahyan, Mr Justice Johnson KC condemned her conduct, saying she had shown a serious disregard for the child's welfare.
"By leaving [the child] to play barefoot in the street while under the influence of drugs, you showed a recklessness and disregard for [the child’s] safety," he said.
The judge described how the toddler had run towards the road while chasing a piece of paper before being stopped by a member of the public.
"But for the intervention of strangers there was a serious risk they would be seriously injured or worse," he said.
"They could have run away, become lost. They could have been taken or harmed by a stranger and could have become distressed seeing you and your friend unconscious in the street."
Royal family ties and drug rehabilitation
Al Nahyan is connected through marriage to the House of Nahyan, the dynasty that has ruled Abu Dhabi for generations and from which UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan comes.
The family, which controls vast oil wealth and holds extensive international investments, is estimated to be worth more than £250 billion, according to The Times.
The court heard that Al Nahyan receives a monthly allowance of £8,000, although details of her marriage and her precise relationship to members of the ruling family were not disclosed.
Her defence lawyer, Stephen Vullo KC, told the court that she had not taken drugs on the day of the incident but was exhausted after using cocaine beforehand.
He said she had demonstrated "significant remorse and resolve to overcome her addiction" and had not used drugs since entering the Priory rehabilitation centre in Woking, Surrey, in July.
"The immediate future is she intends to complete all of the steps of a three-month programme which will come to an end at the end of this month," he said.
Her lawyer added that she intended to move to the Guildford area following her treatment and continue attending rehabilitation sessions and Narcotics Anonymous meetings.
"She made a grave mistake that day and she knows it," he told the court.
Al Nahyan was sentenced to a two-year community order with a rehabilitation requirement and ordered to pay a £5,000 fine and £1,000 in prosecution costs.

Dr. Khaled Mohammed Batarfi is an assistant professor at Saudi Arabia’s Al-Faisal University.
For Israel’s neighbors, the central question in the approaching election is whether its next government will change the policies that make their region less secure. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s departure could create an opening. It would not, by itself, constitute a peace initiative. Regional capitals should distinguish between welcoming a less confrontational interlocutor and believing that a change of leadership will resolve conflicts rooted in occupation, contested sovereignty, and denied Palestinian rights.
The electoral arithmetic counsels caution. A recent poll reported by Anadolu placed both Netanyahu’s bloc and the opposition below the majority required to form a government outright [1]. Coalition bargaining will therefore matter as much as the identity of the leading candidate. A prime minister’s room for compromise depends partly on which partners can bring down the government. Winning an election against Netanyahu does not necessarily mean winning a mandate for Palestinian statehood.
The region is not a monolith. Cairo and Amman both have immediate interests in preventing Palestinian displacement and further instability along their borders. Beirut and Damascus need sovereignty and space to rebuild. Riyadh seeks a durable settlement that reconciles regional integration with Palestinian rights. Ankara views developments through the dual lenses of the Palestinian question and Syrian security. Their priorities overlap, but their exposure to Israeli decisions differs.
Measures of change
For Gaza, a successor could make consequential decisions: facilitate humanitarian access, honor ceasefire commitments, permit reconstruction and negotiate withdrawal arrangements. Such changes would save lives and should never be dismissed as merely cosmetic. Yet reconstruction without a political settlement risks merely financing temporary recovery between recurring rounds of destruction. September’s joint statement by eight Arab and Muslim-majority countries demanded implementation of existing commitments and linked Gaza’s future to a sovereign Palestinian state [2]. That is a substantive test for any incoming government.
The West Bank provides an even sharper measure. Will the next government stop settlement expansion, confront settler violence, and reverse measures that fragment Palestinian territory? Or will it preserve those policies while describing them more diplomatically? A quieter approach to the same territorial outcome would offer little reassurance. Netanyahu’s opponents should be judged by what they are prepared to change, rather than by their opposition to him.
On the Lebanese and Syrian fronts, a change in Israeli leadership could influence the frequency of military action, willingness to negotiate, and respect for agreements. A government less dependent on permanent confrontation might offer practical opportunities for de-escalation. But Israel’s neighbors cannot build security on an Israeli leader’s temperament. They need verifiable arrangements, respect for sovereignty, and an end to the assumption that Israel can indefinitely determine its neighbors’ security conditions through unilateral force. Israeli civilians also deserve security; durable agreements must protect civilians on every side.
Red lines for Saudi Arabia and Türkiye
For Saudi Arabia, normalization remains conceivable as part of a credible peace settlement. It cannot substitute for one. Riyadh has publicly tied diplomatic relations to Palestinian statehood. Changing the Israeli prime minister does not remove that condition, nor does it erase the political and moral consequences of Palestinian suffering [3]. Any prospective government would need to demonstrate that its offer goes beyond improved messaging or another open-ended negotiating process.
A Netanyahu-led coalition dependent on opponents of Palestinian sovereignty would face an obvious contradiction in pursuing normalization. A successor coalition might have greater flexibility, but its composition and program would remain decisive. Saudi Arabia should keep the diplomatic door open while requiring measurable commitments. Regional acceptance is valuable precisely because it can help secure a just settlement; offering it without substantive movement would diminish that influence.
Ankara’s reading is likely to be similarly conditional. The intensity of its confrontation with Netanyahu gives his departure potential diplomatic significance. Yet Türkiye’s concerns extend beyond personal hostility. Its October statement condemning Israeli actions in Syria reaffirmed support for Syrian sovereignty and territorial integrity. A new Israeli government could lower tensions, but rapprochement would require changes in conduct in both Syria and the Palestinian territories [4]. A different tone could start a conversation; it could not by itself repair bilateral ties.
If regional capitals conclude that the election offers limited practical change, their response should be coordinated diplomacy, not resignation. They should agree on benchmarks, link further integration to compliance, strengthen Palestinian institutions, and press Washington and European partners to support enforceable commitments. Existing diplomatic channels can serve those purposes.
The election matters because governments make choices, and different choices can prevent suffering. But the region cannot put its interests on hold until Israeli politics produces an ideal partner. Regional states must test whichever coalition emerges, reward genuine progress, and resist attempts to substitute a more acceptable public image for genuine policy change. The decisive question is what the next government will do with power.

A German court has convicted two men of working for Iran and planning attacks against pro-Israel figures in the country.
The Higher Regional Court in Hamburg sentenced a Danish citizen of Afghan origin to 8 1/2 years in prison and an Afghan national to 4 1/2 years. Judges followed the demands of federal prosecutors, while defense lawyers had sought acquittals.
The court found it proven that the men, who lived in Denmark, scouted pro-Israel figures for an assassination plot and worked on an arson attack against a kosher food store in Berlin.
The prime suspect received orders directly from officers of the Quds Force, the foreign operations unit of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, according to German authorities.
Both suspects were arrested in Denmark last year after tips from Danish intelligence and later transferred to Germany.
The 54-year-old was detained in Aarhus in the summer of 2025, while the 43-year-old was taken into custody in November.

Should we turn the Red Planet green?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:45:54 UTC
21:45:54 KST

What if we could turn the Red Planet green?
The idea of Mars made verdant with grasses, trees and other Earthly life-forms may sound like science fiction, but at least one small group of scientists and engineers is working to make it a reality. Pioneer Labs, a nonprofit research organization led by CEO Erika DeBenedictis, recently announced what it calls “the first microbe for Mars”: a microorganism adapted to Martian conditions that might someday help humans survive there, too.
Such bioengineered bugs could, in principle, allow astronauts to better “live off the land” on Mars by converting the planet’s raw resources into building materials for habitats, fertilizers for crops, and other products. But the broader vision of Pioneer Labs is far more audacious and fraught: to use biology to help transform Mars into a more habitable and Earth-like world. Terraforming remains a distant and deeply speculative prospect beset by enormous scientific and engineering challenges. It also raises fundamental questions about whether and how humans should ever deliberately unleash Earth life on an alien world.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Scientific American sat down with DeBenedictis to explore the scientific promise, technical hurdles and ethical dilemmas of sending bioengineered terrestrial microorganisms to Mars. What could such organisms realistically accomplish? How close are we to deploying them beyond Earth? And what obligations do we have to preserve a world where the past or present existence of indigenous life remains uncertain? The answers to these questions could ultimately help shape a larger debate about humanity’s extraterrestrial future—and whether the impulse to make other worlds more like our own should be tempered by any obligation to leave them undisturbed.
[An edited transcript of the interview follows.]
Hey Erika, thanks so much for taking the time to talk. I know you’ve been busy!
Hey! And, yeah, you could say that. On September 22 we announced the first microbe we made for Mars, which was a really cool milestone. It’s a useful and safe thing for us to send to Mars and to use to prepare for the first human mission. It’s the very first step toward this bigger picture—this really inspiring vision of terraforming Mars and making it a habitable, beautiful place.
So this microbe—what’s so special about it, and what exactly is it supposed to do?
What’s cool about it is that we’ve engineered it so that it can directly use the nutrients in Martian regolith, water and processed atmosphere—which is really useful! The idea is that you can go to Mars, and you can feed it dirt, water and air, and use it to build bioplastic houses for astronauts.
Bioplastic?
Yeah. This is a derivative of a terrestrial bacterium called Cupriavidus necator, which naturally produces bioplastic kind of for the same reason that when you eat too many doughnuts, you put on weight in your hips. When this organism has too much carbon around, it creates these big vacuoles of bioplastics, which is a class of materials we’re all familiar with in everyday life. We use them to make everything from compostable cups to 3D printing filament—and that’s essentially how we’d like to make houses on Mars.
So the astronaut houses would have these 3D-printed panels that hold up the structure, and then it would have this plastic lining that holds in the pressure so that you can breathe and that also shields you from radiation.
We’re calling this engineered microbe sPL.001—a special strain made by Pioneer Labs, and the very first of several, in fact. We’ve got plans for four more.
Something to help you build houses seems like a pretty good first step. You mentioned there are more microbes in the works. Presumably they’d do other things—because if we’re trying to build some kind of self-sustaining habitat on Mars, we need obviously more than just big domes made of bioplastic, right?
Absolutely. So let me give you some context first: we’re called Pioneer Labs, and that name is referring to this ecological idea of a pioneer species. On Earth, nature is really good at taking hostile environments—like after a volcanic eruption or a forest fire—and rebuilding a complex ecosystem one step at a time, and the very first steps are executed by really hardy organisms called pioneer species.
They’re often lichens. My favorite, though, is dandelions. They can grow in these really harsh environments, and their presence makes that environment more hospitable for a wider diversity of organisms.
I need to be clear, though: this very first microbe, sPL.001, can’t grow outside on its own on Mars, and that’s important because we don’t want to contaminate Mars accidentally. Yet it’s useful for making these habitats that more stuff can grow in. We think there are four other microorganisms that could complement this first one; altogether we think this could scale up to let us make arable land that’s suitable for agriculture—growing beautiful green plants and making food.
So we’ve talked about this first one for helping to build shelters on Mars. What about the others?
We have candidates for the others now, so nothing is finalized yet, but the idea is each additional microbe type can be another step in this ecological succession for Mars. So consider this a sneak peek.
About half the team is now working on windows. Because if you want to make greenhouses, for instance, you need transparent materials to let the sunlight in. And ideally you’d be able to manufacture those at scale with biology. Imagine growing microbes in a pond that secrete something that floats to the surface, and then you can peel what will become a nice big greenhouse panel right off the top.
And the other half of our team is working on getting rid of the perchlorate in Martian regolith. Perchlorate is a compound that’s poisonous to humans, and there’s so much of it there that Mars dirt can be poisonous to humans, too, as it is now. But there are microbes we’ve found that are able to eat that toxin and degrade it. We’ve found some actually that can eat it directly out of simulated Mars dirt—just add water! So now we just have to push the concentrations up, because Mars has more perchlorate than any organism on Earth has ever experienced naturally. And just like with all our other work, we’re using evolution to try to make an organism that can tolerate it.
Okay. And so the whole idea is that by growing these things locally—by living off the land, so to speak—you’re able to be more efficient and cost-effective, and ultimately self-sustaining, because you don’t have to bring everything from Earth?
Yeah. The reason we haven’t already done a human mission is that humans, with all our radiation shielding and food and so on, are just so heavy. And it’s just so hard to get that much mass to Mars to allow people live for a period of time, and then it’s even harder to bring them back. So it’s incredibly helpful to use resources that are on-site. And indeed, that’s what frontier civilizations have always done.
I want to be upfront about my own biases here: I think this is such a cool idea. But as with pretty much every other aspirational project related to human spaceflight, let alone otherworldly settlement, this one has its critics, too. And I think if I could summarize the sorts of criticisms I’ve seen, it would be three interlinked questions: Why terraforming? Why Mars? And why now?
That is, assuming these bioengineered bugs could also be really useful on Earth, why not just focus your efforts here?
You and I and everyone who’s ever lived is really lucky to live on the one planet we know of that has a functional biosphere. That’s why we’re here breathing, right, because we have a whole planet worth of photosynthesis that’s cranking out oxygen for us all the time. We just call it “nature” and tend to take it for granted.
When we go to space, nature is the one thing that we’re missing. It’s the thing we leave behind when we go away from Earth. Well, I love the biosphere, and I think we should bring it with us. I would love for any future humanity that ventures off into the stars to have more interaction with all sorts of delightful types of life rather than less.
This runs counter to typical visions for the future, I think, where there’s this tendency to think that progress means less nature and fewer trees and we all live in cities with big skyscrapers. That makes me sad, and I don’t think it has to be that way, and so I’m trying to fix it.
Mars specifically is this fascinating world in part because it’s almost like a long-lost twin of Earth. Four billion years ago, both planets had liquid water. And Mars, to this day, even after its climate has been substantially altered, still has all the raw materials for life in abundance in a way that the moon doesn’t and that even Venus doesn’t. Venus doesn’t have a lot of water left, and Mars does—it’s got a whole northern hemisphere that’s permafrost, with huge amounts of buried ice. If only we could warm it up, Mars might become a pretty nice place to live.
And I think that the instinct to go searching outward is just a thing people have. Not everyone wants to be an explorer, but for people who do, Mars is this incredibly intriguing target. And whoever goes first, I’d love for them to have flowers when they live somewhere that’s not Earth.
Flowers on Mars! Maybe it’ll be a dandelion, even.
That would be Pioneer species number six, ha.
Your announcement of sPL.001 made quite a splash, of course. I’m wondering, though, outside of the millions of people who saw your social media post or watched the slick promotional video introducing Pioneer Labs, what the reactions have been from some of your peers in bioengineering, planetary science, astrobiology, and so on. Has it been mixed?
So far, the reaction has been overwhelmingly positive. And I think that’s partially because we took our time preparing for this. We didn’t just announce that we’d engineered the first organism for Mars. We also released a paper showing how we did it, a second paper about a proposed planetary protection framework for thinking about the risks of actually sending such things to Mars and a third paper offering a complete techno-economic analysis for the use cases.
We’ve shown sPL.001 would be extremely dead if it gets outside on Mars, so, in many ways, this is less risky than sending a human complete with a diverse and complex microbiome on her skin and in her gut. And we’ve shown how this could actually be useful, right—not just how to grow the organism but all of the equipment that has to surround it in order to feed it, heat it, purify products from it and actually build houses. We’ve quantified how much all that mass is, how many launches you’d need to get it to Mars and the total footprint it would have.
So we really put our best work into trying to introduce this idea to people in a way that shows why it’s so cool and valuable but also is thoughtful about the ethics. This work has value even if we never terraform Mars. Practically speaking, this is just a good thing to do for the first human mission.
And so—especially on X, where this really went viral—I think there were more people who applauded the fact that we had also released a paper about the ethics than there were people who were like, “Er, we should never go to Mars.”
You’d have to go over on Bluesky to see more of those reactions, I think.
Yeah, exactly.
Let me try to “both sides” this a bit. I want to double down on the very valid point you’re making: if we’re trying to weigh risk and potential impact, landing a single human—or even a single piece of human excrement, let’s say—on Mars, that’s an orders-of-magnitude bigger deal than landing an enclosed bioreactor.
But I also inquired about the reactions of your peers because peer review is important in science, and it’s not clearly something that’s happened for any of those three papers you mentioned. There’s a disclaimer near the end of each one that basically says this has not and will not be submitted for peer-reviewed publication because that goes against the “open science” policy of the Astera Institute, a billionaire-backed nonprofit for incubating transformative science and technology that partly funded the work.
So with that in mind, I have to ask: Who is independently evaluating this stuff? You’re saying that it’s safe to send sPL.001 to Mars, and in the second paper that you mentioned, yes, you’re proposing a protocol for ensuring that nothing bad can happen in terms of biocontamination. But who’s validating these assertions? That seems like a pretty important step in the process, so I’m wondering why you’re skipping it.
My hope is for us to get to share the science we’re doing openly and very quickly. And I should say that we at Pioneer Labs don’t make NASA policy—and that NASA, in fact, isn’t the only organization that makes policy for the whole world, either. There are a lot of discussions that have already been happening about how to update things like planetary protection frameworks for the upcoming new era of human interplanetary spaceflight.
We clearly need new frameworks. Historically, NASA policy has been to stringently sterilize everything that goes to Mars, and you obviously can’t do that for a living human! So we’ve decided to throw our hat in the ring and make suggestions about what that new framework could look like. The goal of the Planetary Protection paper we released is for it to be discussed by COSPAR [the Committee on Space Research], which is the main body that makes policy suggestions to the world. My co-founder Una Nattermann will also be on NASA’s newly convened M-FORCE tiger team, which will make recommendations to COSPAR. Our goal here is to participate in the discussion.
And similarly, we’ve made suggestions about what it could look like to do the first biomanufacturing on Mars. We call this a “reference architecture,” which is a type of paper or engineering document that the space science community often uses. These aren’t usually published in a traditional science journal. I think space science is a discipline that certainly sometimes uses peer review to great effect, but not all of the science happens specifically through journals.
We do currently have funding from the Astera Institute, which believes very strongly that the current peer review journal system is incredibly toxic for science and for innovation. I don’t think anyone really disagrees with that. But as you say, there is this downside to being forced not to participate in traditional journals, which is getting this question about who certifies it. We have, ahead of time, already shared these papers with various colleagues, some of whom are acknowledged in them for the feedback they provided.
Also, there’s no stamp of approval, including from a journal, that means something is definitely right, which means even if we did send it to a journal, that doesn’t mean it’s better. We’re just trying to do the best science we can, and part of the challenge is we have to chart new territory about what it looks like to do this without this kind of crutch of journals dictating what is correct—which we all know to not be true anyway.
I should say the question doesn’t necessarily come from an adversarial place. You’ve stated elsewhere that Pioneer Labs is hopeful to hit the 2031 launch window for Mars. And that’s practically tomorrow, as far as developing a payload and securing a rocket ride is concerned, right? So it would seem in your best interest to try to bring everybody on board, so to speak, as quickly and fully as possible by addressing any significant concerns that exist.
Relatedly, maybe, I wonder if there’s anything you could tell me about what that 2031 mission would notionally look like?
Yeah, I agree. Flight testing is incredibly difficult in terms of the amount of prep that needs to go into it and the magnitude of engineering that needs to go right. That’s even more true for a Mars mission because Mars is so far away. So we’ve released that third paper, the reference architecture, in part because we’re interested to see how the space science community reacts, especially to different possibilities for what the first flight test could look like.
Here’s one example of what the first flight test could be. Wouldn’t it be so cool to go to Mars and do a search-for-life experiment there, where you take a scoop of Mars dirt, you add water, and you incubate it and see if anything grows? Because Mars had nice liquid water back when there was very nascent life on Earth, and there seem to have been giant impacts ping-ponging around the solar system—so maybe one of those impacts sent something to Mars, and maybe today it’s not growing because Mars is too harsh. Maybe it’s dormant in the soil or the ice. One way to find it would be an “enrichment”-type search-for-life experiment. You could sample some dirt or ice, see if it grows anything under more hospitable conditions and do the same after adding fertilizers to see if it’s nutrient-limited.
Now in order to do that experiment correctly, you do need a positive control, so you need to know that your device worked and that stuff can grow in it, and here is where the first microbe we engineered comes in. You could bring sPL.001 as your positive control and confirm that, yes, this organism that’s been carefully selected to die if it gets outside on Mars can in fact grow in a sealed container using the nutrients in Mars dirt.
I think this would be great for everyone. Like, the best-case scenario is you find life on Mars—but even if you don’t, by testing this organism’s growth on Mars you’ve now derisked this big thing that would allow you in the next test to actually use it for engineering and biomanufacturing.
So this is one possible example of a pretty small first step toward deliberately sending terrestrial life to Mars. It’s safer than sending a human. It has some basic science benefit. And it can be scaled up to do things like testing a larger bioreactor—depending on how big a step the space science community feels comfortable taking and which scientific risks we want to address and eliminate.
Speaking of scientific risks, the loudest critics I’ve seen of this work are astrobiologists interested in finding life on Mars who worry that something like sPL.001, if sent there, still poses unacceptable chances for contaminating the planet and irreparably sabotaging the search. Then there’s the more extreme ethical criticism of possible terraforming, perhaps best summarized by the late, great Carl Sagan: “If there is life on Mars..., Mars then belongs to the Martians, even if the Martians are only microbes.”
Yeah, I don’t agree with that second one.
In general, human astronauts on Mars would massively expand our ability and flexibility to search for life. The search for life doesn’t end because you’ve sent humans. Here on Earth, we still go out and look for dinosaur bones even though we already know they’re there. On Mars, the search could and would continue, which reflects something good about humans. We’re curious about our surroundings and we want to know more, and I think that’s something we should encourage.
It’s really complicated, of course, but here are some simple facts to think about. Here on Earth, we have a word for being vegetarian. But we don’t even have a word for trying not to eat microbes, because it’s totally infeasible! There are many different types of life deserving of our respect, but that doesn’t mean a very simple life-form on Mars should unduly eliminate any possible benefit humans could gain by going there.
I think we’re overdue for a big-picture shift in our approach to Mars, which we’ve been treating solely as this object of scientific study, with incredibly strict protocols for what you can send there and how sterile it needs to be—because this isn’t the only relationship that we could have with Mars, right? Like, humanity could live on Mars, and in that scenario, you then have to weigh the potential value of the scientific knowledge of the planet’s history and its former or extant life against the value of humanity having another home.
And just practically speaking, I do think humans are gonna go to Mars someday, so we have to figure out how to do it in a thoughtful way that sets us up for success in living there, as well as in understanding the planet and its history. I don’t think the answer is to get totally tied in knots and paralyzed by the ethics.
That brings me to my final question. You’ve stated in various places that you hope within your lifetime to look up at the little red dot of Mars in Earth’s sky and see that it’s slightly tinged with green—presumably from imported terrestrial life. What do you think is the biggest hurdle to overcome for that? Would it be scientific, technical, political, ethical?
If you had asked me this question two years ago when we began, I would say the biggest hurdle is a technical one. That’s why I was excited to work on sPL.001—because I perceived myself as someone who knows how to solve science problems, and I was looking for a big juicy target to sink my teeth into.
And now when you ask me, I actually do think maybe the hurdle is more social and political in a similar way to how on Earth we struggle to figure out the collective action puzzle of who pays for addressing climate change. Part of why I like working on the Mars case is that I think in some ways it’s much simpler. There’s no NIMBYism on Mars. And I’m hopeful that together, both the technical and the social things that need doing to make humans on Mars happen could be useful right here on Earth, too.

Hungarian PM Magyar hopes that meeting with Zelenskyy in Brussels will help ‘open new chapter’ in relations

21:45:27 KST

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar hopes that a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, scheduled for Friday morning in Brussels, will "open a new chapter" in their relations. However, he does not anticipate Ukraine’s accession to the European Union in the near future, noting that the entire process could take 15–20 years.
He made these remarks to journalists in Brussels on Thursday upon his arrival for a meeting of the European Council.
"On Friday morning, I am set to have a brief meeting here, at the Council building, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy... We shall see what we can discuss in more detail during those 10–15 minutes. I hope we reach a point where a new chapter [in our relations] truly opens, and we might be able to meet in Berehove, where a Hungarian-speaking majority resides," Magyar stated.
When asked whether there is a specific date for Ukraine’s EU accession, the Hungarian Prime Minister noted that "no such date exists." "Look at the Western Balkan countries—they have been trying to join for 15 years. They have begun accession negotiations, yet one could argue they are not much closer to joining now than they were at the start. I don't believe it is possible to determine [an accession date]," he emphasized.
Magyar stressed that he "believes in accession negotiations based on merit." "We do not believe in 'greater' or 'stronger' membership, in passive membership, or in parallel membership; we believe in genuine membership. But that could take 15 or 20 years," he said.
The Hungarian prime minister also pointed to the example of Turkey: "Look at Turkey—it wanted to join for decades, but now it doesn't really want to anymore. The mere fact that someone begins negotiations means nothing in itself. I think this is a good thing for us; everyone can see the historic success we have achieved in just a few weeks—namely, that we have been able to strengthen the rights of the Hungarian minority living there in the Carpathians—or the rights of a future Hungarian minority—regarding education, the use of language, and official procedures. From this perspective, it is a positive outcome for us. That is diplomacy. We asked for guarantees, and it seems we have received them from the Ukrainians," said the Hungarian leader.
