Algeria approves sweeping expansion of death penalty laws
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:28:31 UTC
21:28:31 KST

Breadcrumb
Algeria approves sweeping expansion of death penalty laws
Algeria has officially expanded the death penalty to cover various crimes, including forest arson and child kidnapping, following amendments to the penal code, the state-run Algeria Press Service reported on Wednesday, triggering human rights concerns.
The amendments, which were discussed after forest fires swept through northern Algeria in August, killing 12 people, were approved by both houses of parliament last week.
The law now provides capital punishment for a range of offences, including forest arson, certain acts of incitement on social media and child abduction.
It states that anyone who “deliberately” sets fire to forests, wooded areas, fields, trees or public or private property could face the death penalty. It notes that this also applies to anyone who commits arson at the instigation of or for the benefit of a foreign state or party, or in connection with treason or collusion with an outlawed or organised criminal group.
The law also targets acts deemed to threaten security and public order, national unity, institutional stability or the national economy. It further covers acts involving damage to the environment, ecological balance, and animal and agricultural resources.
People accused of using social media to incite, encourage, finance, plan, contribute to, or prepare for any of the specified acts could also face the death penalty.
Child kidnapping is another key focus of the law, with capital punishment prescribed for those convicted of abducting, torturing, sexually assaulting or subjecting a child to brutal treatment.
Anyone convicted of these offences will not be eligible for mitigating circumstances.
Human rights concerns
The development marks a significant expansion of capital punishment in Algeria, which has not carried out an execution in more than three decades.
It has raised concerns among rights activists, who warn that the legislation's vague wording could leave it open to broad interpretation, potentially exposing more people to the death penalty.
Earlier this month, Amnesty International's deputy regional director for the Middle East and North Africa, Diana Eltahawy, described the decision as a “devastating blow for human rights”. She added that it was also at odds with Algeria's international human rights obligations.
Some experts have also highlighted UN General Assembly resolutions calling for a moratorium on executions with a view to abolishing the death penalty.
Other rights commentators have noted that Algeria is a party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which restricts the death penalty to the “most serious crimes”, generally understood to involve intentional killing.
The covenant also prohibits states from expanding the scope of the death penalty in ways that violate its provisions.
“The amendments, which were rushed through parliament in a process devoid of meaningful consultations with relevant stakeholders, including human rights NGOs and lawyers, introduced the death penalty for broadly worded actions such as inciting, encouraging or facilitating arson, including on social media, as well as the abduction, torture and sexual assault of children,” Eltahawy said.
“While the devastating wildfires demand thorough investigations and accountability, the tragic loss of life they caused must not be used to justify further loss of life,” she continued.
Algeria's President Abdelmadjid Tebboune called for the move in August, when he accused criminals of being behind the blazes in the Jijel, Bejaia and Tizi Ouzou regions.

‘Appalling’: Actor Omar Sy joins public figures criticising French authorities’ response to student protests

The student protests have been building since late September, sparked by complaints of staff shortages and dilapidated schools. A major strike action is planned for this Saturday, and more public figures are expressing their support for the students’ demands.
Protests in France rage on, as students and teachers continue to raise awareness of staff shortages, poor school infrastructure, defective equipment, and deeper anxieties over diminishing prospects and the cost-of-living crisis.
This week, on Tuesday, more than 480,000 protestors took to the streets across France (according to the inter-union of high-school and university group), with placards which read: “Nos lycées tombent en ruines, comme nos espoirs” ("Our schools, like our hopes, are falling into ruin”) and “Diplômés aujourd’hui, précaires demain” ("Graduates today, insecurity tomorrow").
Since the nationwide movement began in September, acts of violence have been reported, with one teenager losing their hand and more than 6,800 youngsters taken into temporary police custody.
According to the government, 147 National Education staff members have been injured, and nearly 40 investigations have been launched into alleged acts of violence committed by the police against protesters.
Public figures have been expressing their support for the protests, including environmental activist Greta Thunberg, NBA star Victor Wembanyama, singer Louane, and celebrated actor Vincent Lindon, who stars in the recently released Victor Hugo adaptation, Les Misérables. The actor praised the movement in French outlet Le Parisien: “These are young people who want chairs to sit on […] decent, functional sanitary facilities, and the fair distribution of resources – and therefore opportunities.”
Lindon added: “I have children who went through middle school, high school, and so on, and it is true that this is one of the first times the younger generation is legitimately asserting demands and rights in the face of a state that currently lacks the funds to buy social peace.”
Before a major countrywide mobilisation takes place this Saturday, with more than half a million people expected to take to the streets, further public figures have been speaking out. The latest is French actor Omar Sy.
During a guest spot on France Inter, the star of The Intouchables, Jurassic World: Dominion and the hit Netflix show Lupin, criticised the authorities’ handling of the protests and called for the demands of students to be listened to, first and foremost.
“These are our kids; it is the future of our country that is speaking out to a nation that is completely adrift,” said Sy.
The actor condemned the violence surrounding the protests, adding: “When I see that there’s no response to this, and that the immediate instinct is to stop them from speaking out, or to beat them up, or even to pit them against one another in childish brawls, I find it appalling.”
Sy added: “I ask myself: where are the adults in charge? What is our role, as adults, as parents? What are we actually doing to our children? Instead of jumping straight to reprimanding, punishing, or correcting them, or forcing them to face off against one another, we aren’t listening to them at all."
"In fact, it’s even worse. We tell them to be quiet, and then we expect them to reach an agreement on their own. We don’t even know what they have to say.”
The police response to the protests has also drawn criticism from human rights organisations, with Amnesty International denouncing a "disproportionate" use of force, while the UN Human Rights Office has expressed concern, calling for de-escalation.

Palestinian farmers petition High Court over three years of blocked access to Nahalin land
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:28:10 UTC
21:28:10 KST

Six Palestinian farmers have petitioned the High Court of Justice to restore access to agricultural land around Nahalin in the West Bank, saying soldiers and settlers have prevented or severely restricted their work since October 2023 without presenting orders authorizing the restrictions.
The Association for Civil Rights in Israel (ACRI), which submitted the petition on their behalf, is seeking an urgent hearing as the olive harvest begins. The farmers say they face a fourth harvest under restrictions that have damaged crops, deprived families of income, and left cultivated land vulnerable to encroachment.
The petition, dated Wednesday, targets the IDF commander in the West Bank, the head of the Civil Administration, and the commander of the Israel Police’s Judea and Samaria District.
Its central argument is the no legal basis for the restrictions has been disclosed. Rather than asking the court to overturn a particular closure order, the farmers say no such order has been shown to them, their lawyers, or local Palestinian authorities despite repeated requests.
They describe overlapping obstacles: agricultural roads blocked with earth and stones, soldiers ordering farmers off their plots, settler threats and violence, and a checkpoint where passage allegedly depends on an unexplained list of approved residents.
Petition says criteria for inclusion on Etzion checkpoint list left unexplained
According to the petition, farmers have been turned back at the Etzion checkpoint since April 2024 because their names were absent from that list. They say neither the criteria for inclusion nor the legal authority for denying passage has been explained, and attempts to add names through Palestinian liaison officials have failed.
The land comprises olive groves, vineyards, fruit trees, and seasonal crops around Nahalin, southwest of Bethlehem. Some petitioners claim ownership through family holdings; others cultivate leased land, including property belonging to the Muslim religious trust Wakf.
One farmer says he worked a plot for approximately 50 years before worsening harassment and military instructions prevented him from continuing. The petition acknowledges that access varies: Cultivation has stopped on some plots, while farmers continue trying to reach others despite the threat of expulsion or violence.
In one incident described in the filing, on June 23, a farmer said settlers brought sheep into his olive grove, damaging trees. He called the police, who he said did not arrive. Soldiers who subsequently reached the site allegedly detained him, threatened him at gunpoint, and ordered him to leave, instead of removing the settlers.
The petition also describes a September 14, 2025, visit accompanied by the farmers’ lawyer, during which soldiers allegedly claimed a closure order existed but did not produce it.
The filing includes photographs and mapped locations of roadblocks and cites affidavits, land records, and police complaints. It lists four written approaches to the authorities between October 2025 and August 2026, which it says received no response.
High Court ruling from 2006 says Palestinian farmers should not be kept off land
The legal argument draws on the High Court’s 2006 Morar ruling, which held that keeping Palestinian farmers off their land to protect them from attacks was disproportionate. Authorities should provide protection and act against those responsible for the threats. The ruling nevertheless preserved narrowly limited emergency powers to impose temporary closures.
ACRI argued that such exceptions cannot justify restrictions continuing for years without a disclosed order. It also said that the damage extends beyond missed harvests: Trees and soil require regular care, and prolonged absence exposes plots to takeover and threatens the farmers’ interests in the land.
“The state and the army are obligated to protect Palestinian residents, their property and their livelihoods,” ACRI attorney Reut Shaer said in the accompanying statement.
The petition asks the court to order the removal of unlawfully placed barriers, ensure access wherever no valid, duly published restriction applies, and instruct troops not to demand prior coordination without legal authority. It also seeks passage through the checkpoint for residents accessing their farmland, a short deadline for the authorities’ response, and an urgent hearing.

Student protests spread in Albania as demonstrators call for PM resignation
Clashes broke out between demonstrators and police for the third consecutive day on Thursday in Albania, with Prime Minister Edi Rama condemning the “chaos” that caused damage to government buildings. Thousands of protesters are calling for Rama's resignation and better studying conditions for Albanian students.
Protesters and police clashed in Albania's capital on Thursday, the third straight day of violence, with Prime Minister Edi Rama condemning the "chaos" that has left government buildings badly damaged.
Thousands of demonstrators are demanding Rama's resignation and more support for students, citing poor university conditions and high tuition fees.
On Thursday protests had also spread to several smaller cities, as students joined university boycotts.
Read moreAlbania protests turn violent as protestors demand PM Rama's resignation
The escalation comes after months of anti-government demonstrations in the country, originally sparked by a controversial resort development linked to US President Donald Trump's family.
"We demand real change, not empty promises. We want a government that works for its people, not against them," journalism student Teftalia Papa told AFP.
"We want a better Albania, where healthcare provides the basic standards every citizen deserves, education provides decent conditions and equal opportunities, and students can afford to study and live without being crushed by rising costs," she said.
Protesters in Tirana on Tuesday and Wednesday smashed their way into several government buildings and set at least one ablaze.
As protests again began on Thursday, police pushed back crowds trying to approach the education ministry and the parliament, while demonstrators hurled stones at officers, according to an AFP reporter.

Euro slides to fresh lows against US dollar and British pound despite ECB rate hikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:25:34 UTC
21:25:34 KST

The euro slid this week to its weakest level against the US dollar since mid-May 2025 and the British pound since early June 2025, as an energy shock, France’s debt crisis and a resurgent US dollar outweigh two interest rate hikes by the European Central Bank.
Europe’s single currency fell on Wednesday to lows against the US dollar not seen since mid-May last year, and against the British pound since early June last year, as soaring energy costs, a bond market revolt over French public finances and a stronger US dollar weigh on it.
The slide comes even though the European Central Bank (ECB) has raised interest rates twice this year, which would normally support a currency.
The euro traded at roughly $1.111 on Wednesday, its weakest since mid-May 2025 and below the low it first hit earlier this month, before rebounding slightly to around $1.121 in early trading on Thursday.
It is down more than 5% since late August, completely reversing the recovery it staged over the summer.
Against the British pound, it hit roughly £0.842 on Wednesday, the lowest since early June 2025, and edged back to around £0.846 on Thursday. That leaves it down roughly 2% since late September, wiping out the gains it had made since mid-July.
An exchange rate has two sides, so the euro’s slide also reflects a stronger US dollar.
The US dollar index, which tracks it against major currencies, hit an 18-month high on Wednesday after US inflation rose to 3.7% in September, above forecasts.
Rate hikes offer no shield
The US inflation data roughly doubled traders’ bets that the Federal Reserve will raise rates on 28 October. Its benchmark rate already stands at 3.75-4%, well above the ECB’s current 2.5%.
The ECB raised its deposit rate by a quarter point to 2.5% on 10 September, its second hike this year, to counter the energy shock from the Iran war as Europe imports most of its energy, leaving it more exposed to the oil price spike than the US.
Eurozone inflation has since climbed to 3.8%, a three-year high.
Traders are currently betting the ECB will keep rates on hold on 29 October before raising them again in December.
"We are probably going to have to hike again," Belgian central bank governor Pierre Wunsch told Bloomberg on Wednesday.
Bundesbank president Joachim Nagel struck a more patient tone, saying earlier this month that "there are so far no clear signs that inflation has fed through to price and wage setting."
In the UK, robust economic data has fuelled bets that the Bank of England will also raise rates in November, supporting the British pound.
French debt crisis
The extra yield investors demand to hold French rather than German 10-year debt, a gauge of nerves, rose above 150 basis points earlier this month, the most since the euro debt crisis around 2011.
The French government’s 2027 budget, which aims to save some €54 billion and narrow the deficit to 5% of economic output from an expected 5.4% this year, faces a rocky ride through a divided parliament, where debate began on Tuesday amid student protests revindicating additional public funding for the education system.
France's public debt reached a record 119% of GDP at the end of June 2026, according to INSEE data. This represents about €3.59 trillion and is double the official EU threshold for public debt-to-GDP which is 60%.
ECB President Christine Lagarde has dampened hopes of the central bank helping.
"The primary and first solution lies at home in France [...] and it has to do with fiscal policies," Lagarde stated on Wednesday on the sidelines of the annual meeting of the IMF and the World Bank Group in Bangkok.
Spain, meanwhile, heads to a snap election on 29 November, adding to the political turmoil that is rattling European markets.
Investors will next look to final eurozone inflation figures on Friday, followed by interest rate decisions from the Federal Reserve on 28 October and the ECB a day later.

Why South Korea has fallen out with Ukraine but seeks reconciliation with North Korea: Korean expert explains
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:25:00 EEST
21:25:00 KST

Why South Korea has fallen out with Ukraine but seeks reconciliation with North Korea: Korean expert explains
Just two weeks ago, relations between Ukraine and South Korea seemed almost trouble-free. Russia and North Korea were deepening their military cooperation, North Korean soldiers were fighting against Ukraine, and Kyiv and Seoul appeared to have an increasing number of shared security interests.
On 23 September, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha met his South Korean counterpart Cho Hyun in New York. They discussed strengthening political dialogue, trade, investment, Ukraine's reconstruction, and the common threats posed by military cooperation between Russia and North Korea.
The meeting was a continuation of an eventful year in bilateral relations. In July, Volodymyr Zelenskyy met South Korean President Lee Jae-myung for the first time. Seoul announced an additional US$100 million in non-military assistance to Ukraine. Economic cooperation also held considerable potential: a framework agreement between the two countries provided for up to US$2.1 billion in preferential South Korean loans for Ukraine's reconstruction by 2029.
But on that very same day, 23 September, relations between the two countries began to deteriorate rapidly.
During his address to the UN General Assembly, Zelenskyy announced that Ukraine had transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea. Both soldiers had been captured by Ukrainian forces in Russia's Kursk Oblast in January 2025.
On the face of it, this should have been seen as an example of successful cooperation between Kyiv and Seoul. After all, South Korea had previously advocated the transfer of prisoners to its territory, where they could live in safety.
Instead, on 24 September, President Lee Jae-myung publicly accused Ukraine of violating a confidentiality agreement. According to Seoul, the transfer was supposed to remain undisclosed to protect the prisoners themselves and their families still living in North Korea. Ukraine denied that any such agreement existed.
South Korea demanded an official explanation and an apology. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described the situation as a diplomatic misunderstanding. His South Korean counterpart, Cho Hyun, later confirmed that he had received a letter of apology but said it fell short of Seoul's expectations.
On 2 October, Lee Jae-myung threatened Ukraine with further measures unless Kyiv acknowledged its breach of the agreement and issued a public apology. He also criticised Ukrainian statements about the threat of a military conflict between North and South Korea, accusing Kyiv of using rhetoric that could push the Korean Peninsula towards war.
On 8 October, the diplomatic crisis escalated to the recall of an ambassador: South Korea's Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced its decision to bring its ambassador to Ukraine, Park Ki-chang, back to Seoul.
Ukrainian–South Korean relations had thus entered one of their most serious political crises since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion.
All this is happening as President Lee Jae-myung seeks to ease tensions with North Korea and restore inter-Korean dialogue. Pyongyang, however, has shown little interest in reciprocating.
Quite the opposite. On 7 October, Kim Jong Un sent Vladimir Putin a birthday message in which he called the Russian president his "dearest friend", reaffirmed his commitment to developing the strategic alliance with Moscow, and once again expressed support for Russia's "sacred war".
While Seoul is looking for ways to reconcile with Pyongyang, North Korean troops are gaining combat experience in Russia's war against Ukraine, and Moscow is helping North Korea develop its military technologies.
Why did the transfer of two prisoners of war provoke such a strong reaction from South Korea? Does Seoul's policy of reconciliation with Pyongyang stand any chance of success? What is North Korea gaining from its involvement in Russia's war against Ukraine, and how could this change the balance of power on the Korean Peninsula?
Ukrainska Pravda spoke about these issues with Sangmin Shim, Senior Research Fellow at the Center for Foreign Policy and National Security at the Asan Institute for Policy Studies, who specialises in international law and security affairs. His analytical articles and commentary on security and environmental issues in East Asia have appeared in international publications, including the American magazine The National Interest, as well as leading South Korean newspapers such as Chosun Ilbo and JoongAng Ilbo.
Although Shim is critical of certain policies and approaches pursued by the current South Korean administration, he is not a political opposition figure. His perspective is primarily that of an independent policy expert, shaped by his background in international law, diplomacy and national security. He previously taught international law at the Korea National Diplomatic Academy and has advised the government on legal and foreign policy issues.
The crisis in Ukrainian-South Korean relations
Ukrainian-South Korean relations are experiencing their first political crisis since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. South Korea recently even recalled its ambassador from Ukraine. Why has the issue of the two North Korean prisoners become so sensitive for President Lee Jae-Myung's administration?
Well, this is my personal take, but I believe the South Korean government is so pro-Russian that anything potentially sensitive for bilateral relations between North Korea and the Russian Federation is largely discounted. That is what we are seeing today. Even though Ukraine has graciously sent those North Korean prisoners to South Korea, the South Korean government is not really appreciative of it. South Korea is so preoccupied with normalising relations with the Russian Federation that the many gestures the Ukrainian government approaches us with do not really count from the South Korean perspective. This is a truly sad matter, in my view.
Did the situation with those two North Korean prisoners create any domestic debate in South Korea?
In the general public's view, it is great that these prisoners have been transferred to South Korean territory to live in a free state. But the current South Korean government is extremely worried about the consequences of having these North Korean prisoners on its territory.
They fear the possible negative effects of holding them in South Korean custody, which makes them highly sensitive about their presence. This is completely irrational from my perspective. South Korea has always strongly argued for the transfer of Korean prisoners of war to its territory, as the government deems these POWs to be its own citizens.
There is a total inconsistency in logic between the South Korean government's general policy and what they are doing in this specific situation.
Inter-Korean tensions
What we see in the news now is that the South Korean president wants to ease tensions and restore inter-Korean relations and dialogue. But how realistic is this when there appears to be very little interest in dialogue from North Korea?
This might be my personal judgement, but looking at the South Korean government's attempts to ease tensions with North Korea, I don't think it is going to happen. The North Korean government is completely focused on differentiating the two regimes. Pyongyang believes that any ties it might have with South Korea will not bring any real benefit to the prosperity of the North Korean regime. Therefore, the North Korean regime has decided to totally sever ties with South Korea, and that is exactly what they are doing. Unfortunately, the South Korean government is not ready to give up its hope for reconciliation with North Korea. This is where the real tragedy begins.
We also see that North Korea has physically reinforced the separation. They are building barriers, laying mines, and fortifying the border with South Korea. From your point of view, is this just another period of rising tension, or has Kim's "two hostile states" policy changed these relations?
From what I can see, North Korea is highly focused on differentiating between the South Korean and North Korean regimes. They started by laying mines to prevent South Korean troops from crossing into North Korean territory. This is extremely unfortunate, and as you know, it has led to unnecessary casualties among South Korean soldiers. I do not know how this issue can be resolved between the governments of South Korea and North Korea, but I really hope it will be smoothed over. I hope we can find common ground to talk to each other, with the understanding that this issue should not destroy us. There are still many factors that can influence a hopeful outcome in the future.
President Lee's opponents accuse him of being overly cautious about provoking North Korea. How strong is this criticism inside South Korea, and does it explain the unusually sharp reaction to Ukraine?
There is a deep political divide between the progressive and conservative fronts. The conservative front argues that any engagement with North Korea is basically a concession. Meanwhile, the progressive front believes it is a necessary step toward reconciliation. So, there is a huge divide regarding how they want to move forward in the current situation.
President Lee also criticised Ukraine's statement regarding a possible future conflict between North and South Korea, saying such rhetoric could push the peninsula towards war. Why is this topic particularly sensitive for him?
This is anyone's guess, but as I perceive it, a high-ranking official from the Ukrainian Presidential Office stated that ignoring the ties between North Korea and the rest of the world would have a ripple effect on South Korea's security. But is South Korea ready to accept that?
They believe that through peaceful inter-Korean relations, we will have better relations with every country south of the Korean peninsula. But this is unproven. So we will continue to have contentious relations with both the Ukrainian and North Korean governments.
The role of the North Korean military in the war in Ukraine
North Korea has already sent roughly 15,000 troops to Russia, and thousands of them have reportedly been killed or wounded. Before this, North Korea lacked military experience in such a large-scale war. How different is the North Korean army today because of its experience in Ukraine?
After sending their forces to defend or take over the Kursk region, those North Korean troops have gained valuable battlefield experience in modern warfare — particularly combining drone warfare with conventional warfare. From a South Korean perspective, this is not something we can easily discount. South Korea now needs to prepare for potential provocations from North Korea. However, the current government is not taking this seriously. Because this administration leans pro-Russia, pro-China, and pro-North Korea, they do not see these signs of provocation as something to truly worry about. I am sorry to criticise my government, but this appears to be the reality.
And have you already seen evidence that the lessons learned by North Korean soldiers have been incorporated into North Korean training or doctrine at home?
What I can see from the collaboration between North Korean and Russian forces is that the Russians have been sharing technical advice to further develop North Korea's military expertise — particularly in military tactics and drone warfare. Because of this, North Korean forces are in a better position. I do not know how else to put it, but those North Korean forces are now superior to South Korean forces in terms of dealing with drone warfare and other non-conventional forces involvement.
So, could you say that soldiers returning from Russia will eventually form a new, combat-experienced elite within the North Korean military?
First of all, the initial group sent to Russian territory consisted of combat troops from their special operations forces. They sent about 10,000 of their best elite troops, and the results speak for themselves. The involvement of these forces has genuinely contributed to retaking territories crucial to the Russians from Ukrainian control. This has had a major effect. I do not know if this trend can continue, because the North Korean government will also face difficulties with the continuous mobilisation of its armed forces. We do not know how the next stage will play out.
Let us look at the evidence the North Korean government is presenting. They are doing everything they can not to reveal the presence of their personnel on the battlefield. They want to limit their manpower to factories and other workforces – helping Russian forces and industries build stronger weapon systems. So, from what I perceive, North Korean personnel are not going to be seen anywhere near the front lines. But what I really want to emphasise in this case is that North Korea is collaborating with the Russian government and military to build up Russian stockpiles, ensuring the Russian military is prepared for incoming attacks from Ukraine or other countries.
We have a fairly good picture of what is moving from North Korea to Russia: soldiers, ammunition, and missiles. But we know much less about what is moving in the opposite direction and so from your point of view, what's North Korea actually getting in return from Russia?
I mean, what North Korea really hopes to gain from the collaboration with the Russian regime is that they will get military expertise in terms of ballistic missiles development and other top-notch military development. And in turn those current regimes will provide war forces in the form of manual labour and everything to provide the help necessary for the Russian Federation to rebuild their drone systems. So, then they will be able to compete with Ukraine in terms of non-conventional forces engagement.
The Russian government is seeing that the Ukrainian government will not be able to provide all the necessary supplies for all the necessary equipment for forever. And then this is going to be a kind of a war of attrition between Russia and Ukraine in which both will be subject to having to pay the highest consequences from this military conflict. This is so sad but this is also a fact.
If North Korea is developing the capacity to mass produce Shahed-type drones with Russian assistance, how would that change the threat facing South Korea and is South Korea prepared for the kind of mass drone warfare we have seen in Ukraine?
I mean, we have heard the most recent report from the National Security Advisor of the Korean Republic that if North Korea has been engaging too much in this Russia-Ukraine conflict, this would be the best opportunity for Korea to start taking over the northern part of the Korean Peninsula and making the whole Korean Peninsula as a unified nation. But this is not going to be the case that I have been seeing because this is not going to involve the political discussions between the major powers and basically the military aspect will not resolve the matters as we see it.
So what I perceive to be the case is that whatever happens in the territories between Ukraine and Russia will not have any consequences for the inter-Korean relations.
Inter-Korean relations will have to be dealt with by their own dynamics. Meaning that Russia, the United States, Japan, Korea and both North and South Korea will have to be sitting at the same table to negotiate away the differences. This is not going to be a short-term matter but it has to include the case of negotiations.
How Ukraine іs perceived in North Korea
Maybe you know how North Korean propaganda explains Ukraine to its own population? What have North Koreans been told about why their soldiers are fighting and dying thousands of kilometres from home?
I mean the North Korean government is ready to just decorate their lost lives as their national heroes. But this is not going to be the case if the loss of the lives and casualties continues to accrue for the North Korean regime. We have a report that records those current casualties at around 3,000 soldiers who have lost their lives and then another 33,000 soldiers who have basically lost their capability to re-engage in the world.
But with the intensification of the war and tensions within Russia and Ukraine, this will lead to more casualties for North Koreans. And I don't know if the North Korean government will be able to continue to persuade their general public with this loss of life as an unavoidable matter.
I don't know, but the North Korean government is not a democratic nation but they will not be subject to national approval or to answering the questions of the people but they will still feel the pressure from the North Korean populace about the loss of life that has been the consequence of the involvement of North Korean troops in the Ukrainian military conflict.
Is Ukraine portrayed as an enemy in its own right or is it simply as part of a larger confrontation with the United States and the West?
This is a really interesting question. Between the US and Ukraine, they don't seem to have much differences. But by just looking at the recent episode between the Ukraine and Republic of Korea, they seem to have some impending conditions to be dealt with between these two nations.
But from my perspective, these would be only diplomatic matters and if these matters were to be entrusted with both countries' foreign ministers, these differences will be easily negotiated away. What matters to Korea for now is that the current president of the administration. He's so active in voicing criticism about the Ukrainian government. This is not going to be helpful for settling the battle between Ukraine and South Korea. I really hope that the South Korean president will stay silent for at least for the next two weeks for the two ministers to be able to reach a mutually satisfactory agreement.
And from your point of view, how much do the average North Koreans actually know about the scale of their country's involvement in Russia's war?
From the conservative people's point of view, this government is so pro-North Korea and they suspect that North Korea has a huge influence over the matters of the South Korean government, but I don't believe this. But whatever is the case with the North Korean and the South Korean government, I suspect that the South Korean government needs to be in a better position to fight away the incoming threats from North Korea.
Basically in terms of cybersecurity and maritime security. But without those concerns, we have to see that the South Korean government is going to live their lives as if nothing has happened. This is not going to be a very positive case for the South Korean population.
And what happened with thousands of soldiers who return home with direct experience of Russia, of modern warfare, of modern technologies which are most likely not represented in North Korea?
I mean, these North Korean soldiers who have been sent back to the North Korean territories have returned with better experience with drone warfare and better experience with modern warfare. So they may have something to say to their military leadership. But what are considered to be the barricades with these North Koreans, they have been so exhausted with the too-stressful battlefield conditions. So, they may be the key. I mean, this is my hopeful suggestion, but these people will be the driving forces for asking for more changes regarding the South Korea and North Korea territories. And then, if the current administration fails to address these questions then there will be more political decisions, moving forward.
And could these people potentially be a problem for the regime now?
This is another matter that we don't really know the answer to. Military and civilian society have been in co-existence for a long time. But what I perceive in that case is that the military, they are taking the upper hand with the civilian structures. So whatever situation may arrive, it's going to be down to the hands of the military that will take the final decisions.
How South Korea іs helping Russia and what the consequences could be
What we see in the recent investigation by Reuters is that South Korean petroleum product experts have reportedly helped Russia with fuel shortages caused partly by Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries. How is this issue perceived in South Korea or is it even discussed there?
There are two different opinions about this matter. For conservative people, this is a really serious matter because it seems to be the case that the South Korean government is basically just looking away in the case of helping the Russian economy by support with petrochemical fuels.
But at the same time, from a purely technical perspective, the South Korean government is not prohibited from providing petrochemical products to the Russian Federation because this is not going to be subject to any country's sanctions regimes. So this is kind of revealing a kind of difference between many different countries' sanctions regimes.
From my perspective, it should be right to tighten the grip upon the differences in the different countries' sanction regimes. But at the same time, we have to hold our countries to settle out the differences between many unlike-minded nations to achieve the core missions of these sanctions which is to weaken the fighting ability of the Russian Federation in terms of the battlefield between the Russian Federation and Ukraine.
From the Ukrainian perspective this trade could be the next major source of tension between Seoul and Kyiv. From your perspective, how could these South Korean-Ukrainian relations be mended?
I mean, we have current issues between Ukraine and the Republic of Korea, but I strongly believe that this case will be settled away between the diplomatic negotiations between these countries.
What I perceive to be the more worrisome outcome is if the South Korean president Lee Jae-myung continues to press hard on the relations between Ukraine and the Korean Republic. And if that would be the case, then there's not going to be a case for these two bilateral regimes to be reconciled pretty much soon. Because as long as the president's mandate is not going to be met, there's not much that the South Korean foreign minister will do proactively to settle the differences. So all it might come down to is the president changing his position between Ukraine and the Republic of Korea.
In a way, the revealing of the identity of the prisoners, those North Korean soldiers, would not be so much to disrupt the bilateral relations between these countries. It's really important that the South Korean government is so aware of this importance and also about the importance of not being too far away from these two government's positions.

Kyiv’s 3 Main CHP Plants Stop Producing Power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:23:42 UTC
21:23:42 KST

Kyiv’s three main combined heat and power plants are no longer producing electricity, leaving the capital more dependent on supplies from elsewhere in Ukraine, according to a report published on Thursday, Oct. 15.
Ekonomichna Pravda reported, citing sources at an energy company, that CHP-5, CHP-6 and the Darnytsia plant, also known as CHP-4, had lost their ability to generate electricity. Their contribution previously could reach approximately 1.3 gigawatts.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The report concerns the capital’s largest plants rather than the disappearance of every source of electricity within Kyiv. It also identified smaller distributed generating facilities already operating in the city.
Russian forces targeted all three plants again overnight on Oct. 13-14, Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky said on Wednesday. Energy infrastructure supplying the capital and central Ukraine was also attacked.
Emergency crews began firefighting, clearing debris and carrying out priority repairs at the affected facilities.
Kyiv depends on power reaching the city
The loss of major local generating capacity leaves Kyiv more exposed to damage along the transmission network bringing electricity into the capital.
The city remains connected to Ukraine’s national grid, but available generation elsewhere cannot compensate for damaged delivery infrastructure unless sufficient power can reach consumers.
Lawmaker Serhiy Nahorniak told Kyiv24 on Oct. 13 that Kyiv’s electricity consumption reaches approximately two gigawatts during peak winter hours. He identified damage to transmission infrastructure as a major risk alongside problems at the city’s power plants.
6 Injured After Russian Drone Lands Near Pechersk Residential Building in Kyiv
DTEK Kyiv Grids explains that national grid operator Ukrenergo determines restrictions based on the condition of the wider system.
Distribution companies then deliver the available electricity to households and businesses and implement those restrictions.
Damage can also leave neighboring buildings with different supply conditions because they are connected to different lines or substations.
Restoring one connection therefore does not necessarily restore service throughout a district.
Longer winter cuts remain a risk
Ekonomichna Pravda described outages of up to 20 hours a day as a worst-case winter scenario involving severe cold, further major attacks and restrictions on electricity deliveries.
That is a conditional assessment, rather than an announced timetable for the capital.
Earlier this month, Oleh Popenko, head of Ukraine’s Union of Utility Consumers, warned that further attacks could leave Kyiv facing 14-16 hours without electricity daily.
“Further strikes could result in Kyiv already facing schedules of 14 to 16 hours without electricity in October,” he said.
The length of future outages will depend on additional damage, repairs, available generating capacity, imports and the ability to move electricity through the grid.
On Thursday, DTEK’s official outage page said scheduled stabilization cuts were operating in Kyiv under Ukrenergo’s instructions.
The company warns that emergency restrictions can interrupt published schedules when operators need to balance the system urgently. Such cuts can occur without the advance notice associated with scheduled outages.
Electricity disruption also affects water supplies
The consequences extend beyond household lighting. Water pumps, heating equipment, hospitals, transportation, and communications all need reliable electricity.
Following Wednesday’s attack, Kyiv authorities reported water supply disruptions in several districts, saying reduced voltage prevented pumping equipment from operating normally.
Some facilities stopped in an emergency, leaving residents with reduced pressure or no running water.
The electrical operating status of the three CHP plants should also be distinguished from the availability of heating across the entire city.
Kyiv’s heat supply includes other facilities, while electricity is needed to operate equipment that moves water and heat through distribution networks.
Backup systems support essential services
In an Oct. 14 update on emergency preparations, city authorities said Kyiv had prepared approximately 700 generators for water and heating facilities, together with 70 mobile boiler units.
Three diesel power stations with a combined capacity of 16 megawatts had been built to provide backup electricity for water supplies.
Authorities said another 40 megawatts was planned by the end of the year.
The city also reported 480 generators at healthcare facilities and independent water wells at 15 hospitals.
More than 6,000 generators, inverters and batteries had been purchased for residential buildings through municipal energy-resilience programs.
These systems are intended to sustain individual facilities and essential services during interruptions. They provide a smaller reserve alongside the capital’s connection to the national grid, rather than replacing the output previously available from its largest power plants.

Merlin helicopters head to Scotland to protect sub force
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:21:25 BST
21:21:25 KST

Four Merlin Mk2 submarine hunters and around ninety sailors moved at short notice from Cornwall to Prestwick to work over the approaches to the Clyde, tracking a new attack submarine on her dive trials and screening the waters around Britain’s submarine base, according to the Royal Navy.
The deployment, run under the name Operation Iceblast, took crews and aircraft from 824 and 814 Naval Air Squadrons out of Royal Naval Air Station Culdrose and set them up at HMS Gannet for a fortnight of operations.
Captain James Hall, the commanding officer at Culdrose, said: “Operation Iceblast demonstrated exactly what Culdrose and Merlin Helicopter Force are designed to do. That is to deploy at short notice and deliver warfighting readiness from a forward location with a world-class anti-submarine warfare capability, whenever and wherever it is required.”
The crews oversaw the arrival of HMS Agamemnon, the newest Astute class boat, into His Majesty’s Naval Base Clyde, then used their dipping sonar to track her while she carried out dive trials. Hunting a friendly submarine of the latest type is about as demanding a target as a Merlin crew will get.
Alongside that, the detachment worked with NATO partners including Norwegian and German forces during Exercise Strike Warrior, the large workout for the UK Commando Force that has just finished in Scotland. That included standing search and rescue watch while Royal Marines practised boarding operations with the German supply ship FGS Berlin. Further sorties went into monitoring strategic areas of the North Atlantic.
A drone team from Culdrose’s 700X Naval Air Squadron worked in parallel, providing additional security around the Clyde to protect the submarine force.
Captain Hall said: “This exercise tested our ability to operate across multiple sites simultaneously. Together, these activities demonstrated the agility, readiness and professionalism of our personnel.
“The strategic environment demands constant vigilance. Operational deployments such as Iceblast ensure that our people, aircraft and support teams remain ready to protect the UK’s interests, contribute to NATO security alongside our Norwegian partners, and provide the capabilities required to support the nation’s nuclear deterrent.”
He said the exercise was built to test whether the air station could deploy and sustain anti-submarine warfare operations away from its home base near Helston, and that working from Gannet gave a realistic rehearsal of dispersed operations with the logistics and command and control complications that come with them. Lessons from the fortnight will be folded into future procedures and training.

Explainer: What is the ‘hospital of the popes’ where Leo is recovering from surgery?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:21:03 UTC
21:21:03 KST

Explainer: What is the ‘hospital of the popes’ where Leo is recovering from surgery?
ROME, Oct 15 - Rome's Gemelli Hospital, where Pope Leo is recovering after surgery for lung cancer, is known as the "hospital of the popes".
The hospital, with a suite especially for popes, has become the preferred medical facility for modern pontiffs since the time of Pope John Paul II.
WHAT IS THE GEMELLI?
Located some 5 km (3 miles) from the Vatican City, the Gemelli hospital offers every major medical speciality under one roof. It also serves as the teaching hospital of the Catholic University of the Sacred Heart and has more than 1,600 beds.
There is a dedicated suite for popes on the 10th floor, including a private chapel. However, this is currently under renovation, meaning Leo is staying in a different set of rooms.
In the 2026 Newsweek-Statista "World's Best Hospitals" rankings, Gemelli was named as Italy's top hospital and ranked 33rd globally among more than 2,500 hospitals assessed across 32 countries.
HOW DID IT BECOME THE POPES' HOSPITAL?
Popes were traditionally treated by doctors summoned to their residence. For example, Pope Paul VI underwent prostate surgery in 1967 in a specially equipped operating room set up inside the Vatican's Apostolic Palace.
Everything changed during the pontificate of John Paul II. He was rushed to the Gemelli after a 1981 assassination attempt, undergoing emergency surgery that saved his life.
He returned repeatedly to the hospital over the following decades for treatment, spending more than 150 days there during his pontificate. He dubbed the place "Vatican III", after the official residences at the Vatican itself and Castel Gandolfo.
Benedict XVI was never admitted during his pontificate.
By contrast, Francis, who died in April 2025, was hospitalised several times, including for colon surgery in 2021, respiratory problems and abdominal surgery in 2023, and for bilateral pneumonia in the weeks before his death.
IS GEMELLI OWNED BY THE VATICAN?
The Gemelli hospital was built on land originally owned by the Vatican that was donated by Pope Pius XI in 1934 to the body that oversees the Catholic University. Opened in 1964, it is named after Agostino Gemelli, the Franciscan friar, physician and psychologist who founded the university.
However, despite its close association with the papacy, Gemelli is not a Vatican institution. It operates as a private non-profit academic medical centre within Italy's healthcare system, with most patients treated through the country's publicly funded health service.
The Vatican owns the Bambino Gesù hospital in Rome, but that facility specialises in paediatric care. REUTERS

Chemicals giant Covestro to axe 309 jobs in the Port of Antwerp
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:19:42 UTC
21:19:42 KST

The German chemicals firm Covestro plans to cut 309 of the 976 jobs at its Antwerp site. The news means that 260 people will be made redundant. The company intends to reorganise the site given global overcapacity. Staff were informed this morning. “The staff have reacted with surprise and dismay; this affects 25 per cent of the workforce,” says Patrik Collier of the Christian ACV union.
Chemicals giant Covestro to axe 309 jobs in the Port of Antwerp
According to trade union representative Collier, the management is closing a BPA plant and five of the six production lines at the Makrolon plant. As a result, only the Aniline plant and the Polyether plant will remain. Management cities 2027 as the deadline. “When you have 970 employees and they’re talking about 260 redundancies, which amounts to 25 per cent of the workforce – and, above all, the families who depend on them,” says Collier.
Covestro produces polycarbonate plastic pellets at the Makrolon plant. This material is used in items such as car headlights. The management points to global overcapacity in the market and that new sites have been established in Asia.
According to the management, this is putting pressure on prices and means that the grades produced in Antwerp are no longer profitable. In Europe, the company only intends to produce profitable polycarbonate grades in future.
The remaining plants form part of the MDI chain. Collier says there is certainly potential for future growth and profit here. However, capacity utilisation at the polyether plant has fallen in recent years. “So, the question is what will remain and how viable that is,” he says. The industry uses polyether and aniline for foams in mattresses, sofas and cars.
Structural crisis in the chemicals sector
The company points to a structural crisis in the European chemicals sector. “It is becoming increasingly difficult for Covestro to sell materials produced in Europe competitively and profitably, particularly in the segment of lower-cost standard polycarbonates. Failing to take action today would undermine the long-term economic viability of our Antwerp site,” Susanne Buchholz, managing director at Covestro, said.

Govt issues clarification on 'unconditional apology' in SC over internet shutdown

2026-10-15

The SC had issued contempt notices to govt on Oct 11 over alleged violation of its earlier order.
NEW DELHI: The Union home minister on Thursday clarified that the unconditional apology submitted by home secretary, the commissioner of police and other officials in their affidavits before the Supreme Court was part of the procedure followed in contempt proceedings.In a statement, the government reacted to the media reports that the Union home secretary Govind Mohan had tendered an unconditional apology to the Supreme Court in response to a contempt notice.It said whenever the Supreme Court issues a contempt notice, the party responding to it is required to begin its affidavit with an unconditional apology, followed by the presentation of other facts and arguments.“This is mandatorily followed in every contempt petition,” the statement said.
It added that the affidavits subsequently provided detailed particulars to establish that the actions taken by the government and the police were in accordance with the law and that no case of contempt was made out against them.Mohan, in his affidavit filed late on Wednesday night, said the suspension of cellular internet services within a four-kilometre radius of Raisina Hills from 10 pm on October 9 to 10 pm on October 10 was necessary to prevent a disturbance of public order and maintain peace.
He said the Delhi Police's request for the suspension “was found to be a proportionate measure, having regard to the magnitude of the situation and the need to prevent any disturbance of public order in the national capital.”The Supreme Court had issued contempt notices to Mohan, Delhi Police Commissioner and Delhi Metro Rail Corporation chairperson on October 11 over the alleged violation of its earlier order. The court had directed that “internet facilities should function unhindered”.
Mohan said the suspension was limited to cellular internet services and did not cover Wi-Fi, broadband or other non-cellular internet services. He argued that suspending internet services for a limited period and within a defined geographical area, subject to statutory safeguards, was a recognised measure to maintain public order in appropriate circumstances.The home secretary also requested the Supreme Court to modify its October 11 order “to the extent necessary to permit the suspension of internet services in situations of necessity, strictly in accordance with law and subject to applicable statutory requirements and safeguards”.

A torrential downpour hit Istanbul: homes and cars were flooded, three people died
Kyiv • UNN
A powerful downpour flooded parts of Istanbul, roads and homes, sweeping away cars. Three people died, four are missing, and 2,727 people were evacuated.
Heavy rain struck Istanbul, Turkey. Roads turned into lakes, and vehicles were flooded. The flooding claimed the lives of three people. UNN reports this, citing TRT Haber.
Details
The heavy rain that began in Istanbul yesterday morning, October 14, and continued intermittently throughout the day intensified considerably in the evening.
A residential complex in the Küçükçekmece district in the European part of Istanbul was flooded, and the lower floors of apartment buildings were submerged. In this area, the water level in the Ayamama stream - an important waterway in the European part of Istanbul - rose due to the heavy rain.
In Ayazağa, one of the districts hardest hit by the rain, vehicles were swept away several meters by floodwaters. Many buildings were flooded.
After the heavy rains, Istanbul's Golden Horn (Haliç) turned brown.
A statement from the local governor's administration said that the number of people killed by the rain had risen to 3, while the number of people currently missing stood at 4.
In particular, it stated that the body of another victim - a man - had been found near Sadabad Park in the Kağıthane district, and that identification procedures were ongoing.
Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi announced that rainfall in some areas of Istanbul had reached 272 kilograms per square meter due to the heavy rain. Çiftçi said that a total of 9,588 reports had been received from the provinces where warnings about adverse weather conditions had been issued, with 8,815 of them coming from Istanbul.
In Istanbul, 2,727 people trapped by floods and inundation were evacuated through the efforts of AFAD (the Disaster and Emergency Management Authority), the coast guard, the gendarmerie, and municipal teams.
Çiftçi urged citizens to exercise caution regarding the risk of floods and inundation and to avoid going outside unless absolutely necessary.

The Navy destroyed four Su-34 aircraft, with two more hit — what is known about the carrier of guided aerial bombs used to terrorize Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
The Ukrainian Navy struck the Borisoglebsk airfield in Voronezh Oblast with a Neptune missile. Four Su-34s were destroyed and two more damaged.
The Naval Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine destroyed 4 Russian Su-34 bombers, and two more were damaged on the territory of the "Borisoglebsk" airport. This aircraft is a deeply modernized version of the basic Su-34 frontline bomber, which russia began producing serially in 2020. Thanks to its new hardpoints, this aircraft is the main carrier of KAB guided aerial bombs and precision-guided missiles with which the enemy attacks Ukraine’s frontline regions, UNN writes.
Details
On the morning of Thursday, October 15, the Naval Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported the destruction of 6 Russian Su-34M fighter-bombers during the night of October 15.
During the night of October 15, the Naval Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine struck the "Borisoglebsk" military airfield in russia’s Voronezh region using a Neptune coastal missile system. As a result of the strike, six Su-34M bombers were destroyed. Technical equipment supporting aviation operations was also destroyed, while secondary detonations and a fire were recorded on the airfield grounds

What is known about the Su-34M
The Su-34 (under NATO codification: Fullback (Крайній захисник) is a Soviet/Russian all-weather, two-seat fighter-bomber developed by the Sukhoi Design Bureau.
The Su-34 was designed to carry out precise missile and bomb strikes against enemy ground targets at operational and tactical depths, as well as to engage enemy air targets. It can reach speeds of up to 1,900 km/h at altitudes of up to 14.6 km.
The Su-34 prototype made its first flight in 1990. The aircraft was designed through extensive modernization of the Su-27 fighter.
The Su-34M (also known as "Sych" or Su-34 NVO - Navigation and External Equipment) is a deeply modernized version of the basic Russian Su-34 frontline bomber. The contract for its serial production and delivery to the armed forces was signed in 2020, after which it completely replaced the basic modification on the production line.
Following modernization, the Su-34M received more advanced navigation equipment, powerful reconnaissance systems, and a targeting system with a target-designation system. This expands the range of weapons used, increases the crew’s ability to detect targets, and improves firing accuracy.
For the Su-34 NVO version, three variants of unified suspended reconnaissance pods were developed: electro-optical, electronic intelligence, and radar.
With their help, the aircraft will be able to independently detect ground, sea, and air targets in any weather at a greater distance than before.
The bombers received new radar, targeting, and communications systems, and their missile and bomb armament was expanded. Onboard radio-electronic equipment and electronic warfare systems were improved.
The Su-34M gained the ability to use the latest range of precision-guided munitions (air-to-surface missiles, new guided aerial bombs, and so on), which increased the range and effectiveness of engaging targets without entering the zone of dense enemy air defenses.
In particular, the bomber has 12 hardpoints and can carry up to 8,000 kg of various weapons. At the same time, the aircraft is the main carrier of aerial bombs equipped with UМПК modules (Universal Planning and Correction Module), which turn conventional free-fall bombs into precision-guided glide weapons with a release range of 40–80 km.
What is a guided aerial bomb: range, speed, and countermeasures23.09.26, 07:10 • 58106 views
These are the very aircraft that are "terrorizing" Ukraine's frontline regions. The bomber can be equipped with high-explosive bombs of various calibers — FAB-250, FAB-500, FAB-1500, FAB-3000 with UMPK, as well as KAB-500 and KAB-1500.
It can also be equipped with air-to-surface missiles such as the Kh-38, Kh-29, Kh-59MK2 and Kh-69, as well as anti-radiation missiles: Kh-31P / Kh-31PD, and anti-ship missiles: Kh-31A and Kh-35U.
In addition, the bomber can be equipped with missiles "for self-defense," that is, air-to-air missiles, including medium-/long-range missiles with active radar homing, the R-77, and short-range missiles with infrared homing heads for close-range maneuvering combat, the R-73.
It is not known exactly how many of these aircraft the Russian Federation may have. However, as reported by Russian media, since 2012 the Russian Ministry of Defense has received more than 120 Su-34 aircraft. By 2027, the military agency planned to receive at least 76 upgraded Su-34M aircraft. In 2021, the first six aircraft entered service with the Russian Aerospace Forces.
Russian Federation losses
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Russia has lost 443 aircraft since the beginning of the war. It has been visually confirmed that the Russian Federation lost only one Su-34M aircraft. This occurred in July 2022. The bomber was shot down near Alchevsk, Luhansk region, and it was the Russians themselves who did so as a result of "friendly fire."
Overall, Ukraine has destroyed 43 Su-34 aircraft.

Cyberscams have dominated headlines and authorities’ attention across Southeast Asia for over a year as the leading criminal enterprise worth tens of billions of dollars annually.

Russian investigators question Novaya Gazeta editor after raiding his home
Oct 15 - The editor-in-chief of Russian independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta was taken in for questioning by investigators in Moscow on Thursday, the outlet said, after authorities searched his home.
The TASS state news agency, citing law enforcement sources, said Sergei Sokolov was being questioned in a case regarding the "unlawful use of personal data" following a search at his home.
Novaya Gazeta, one of Russia's best-known investigative media organisations, said staff lost contact with Sokolov around noon local time, shortly before an editorial meeting was due to begin.
Sokolov was taken to the offices of the state Investigative Committee, the newspaper said, adding that a lawyer had been despatched to meet him there.
Russia has tightened its censorship laws and increased pressure on independent media since it launched its war in Ukraine in 2022. Media watchdog Reporters Without Borders says 50 journalists and media workers are currently imprisoned in the country.
Russian authorities on Tuesday detained a Japanese journalist on suspicion of espionage, the most high-profile detainment of a foreign reporter since the 2023 detention of Wall Street Journal journalist Evan Gershkovich.
Founded in 1993, Novaya Gazeta is known for its investigations into corruption and its critical coverage of Russian politics.
One of its journalists, Oleg Roldugin, was arrested in April on allegations that he misused personal data - an offence that carries a prison term of up to 10 years. He is currently under house arrest awaiting trial.
Former Novaya Gazeta editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize and dedicated the award to six colleagues who were killed because of their work. REUTERS

Israeli firm’s digital ads enabling installation of ‘zero-click’ spyware, researchers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:15:22 UTC
21:15:22 KST

An Israeli advertising agency has been serving millions of online adverts that allow “zero-click” spyware to be used against targets, researchers at a Canadian university have said.
Citizen Lab, a digital investigations research unit at the University of Toronto, said it believed dozens of devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera had been compromised by spyware delivered through ads run by Discover-Tech, which describes itself as a specialised digital advertising agency.
According to Citizen Lab, Discover-Tech operates a software platform called Controlium that allows its clients to “mass-profile and deanonymise” internet users then covertly hack targets with third-party spyware. Unlike infections that rely on people interacting with links or files, the spyware requires no interaction from the victim to be installed, making it a new delivery technique, Citizen Lab says.
The infections happen without a user’s knowledge, and in a matter of seconds, according to Citizen Lab.
“[The online advertising] ecosystem is being weaponised at a massive scale to profile millions of users, then silently infect targets with zero-click mercenary spyware,” the report says.
According to the report, Controlium is able to harvest a user’s identity and IP address when the user is shown a seemingly benign custom-created ad – for example, for a digital game or a telecoms service. If the user has been selected as a target for hacking, a mercenary spyware firm can then send a malicious code containing spyware to their device, the researchers say.
They say that millions of users worldwide have been served ads by Discover-Tech since 2024, including in Yemen, Brazil, Mexico and Czechia.
Related work by the research group Confiant also suggests that Discover-Tech’s ads have been shown to users of the networks of government entities in Europe and the US, as well as the UN, Nato, the international criminal court and the International Atomic Energy Agency.
“It’s disastrous that major ad vendors and organisations apparently were neither able to detect nor prevent the company’s malicious advertising operations for years,” said Wolfie Christl, a researcher at Citizen Lab. “The way the online advertising ecosystem works today is a security threat for states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike.”
According to Citizen Lab, Controlium acts as a “facilitator” for third-party spyware firms that have targeted “government officials, journalists, businesspeople, activists, academics and embassy workers”. Citizen Lab claims it can deliver spyware that can access everything on the device of a target, extracting messages, photos and emails, recording calls and secretly activating microphones.
The full extent of the targeting allegedly enabled by Discover-Tech is unknown. Citizen Lab’s findings join mounting evidence that the opaque arrangements underpinning the world of online advertising can be leveraged for surveillance.
“There has been a lot of buzz that online ads can be used to identify and automatically hack targets with pinpoint precision, but now for the first time, we have concrete technical evidence showing this process in action,” said Bill Marczak, a researcher at Citizen Lab.
Discover-Tech has been approached for comment.
When a user navigates to a website that shows advertisements, their details become part of a split-second programmatic auction involving dozens or hundreds of companies. These companies bid automatically to place an ad in front of that user.
These bids are based on the user’s profile, which can include information about their device and data compiled on them by tracking their activity across the web. For example, companies given the profile of a 35-year-old interested in sports betting and crypto might bid to show that individual an advertisement for an energy drink.
There is little regulation on this automated online market, and there is growing evidence that it is being exploited by malevolent actors.
Reuters has reported that billions of dollars’ worth of Meta’s ad revenue comes from ads for scams, illegal gambling, pornography and other banned content. In the US, ICE and other government agencies have bought software that uses ad tech data to track people’s movements.
“Cybersecurity agencies, regulators and lawmakers in the US, Europe and other regions must urgently step in. They must investigate the involved companies and fix the systemic risks that enable malicious ad targeting,” said Christl.

Israeli forces have arrested more than 2,000 Palestinian children since the onset of its genocidal Gaza war, with at least 350 remaining in custody under severe conditions, the Palestinian Prisoners Society said Wednesday.
The non-governmental organization that the Israeli army arrested six children overnight in the towns of Sa'ir and al-Shuyukh in the Hebron governorate of the occupied West Bank.
Monitoring and documentation indicate that "more than 2,000 children have been arrested since the start of the genocide on October 2023, while at least 350 remain in detention under harsh conditions," it said.
The group warned of an escalation in the targeting of Palestinian children through practices including intimidation, arrest, torture, starvation, isolation and denial of health care.
It added that information on the number of children detained from the Gaza Strip since the start of the war remains unclear, particularly amid the presence of thousands of missing people in the enclave, including children, and the continued practice of "enforced disappearance."
The group said Israel’s administrative detention policy, under which Palestinian detainees are held without a publicly stated charge or a clear timeframe for release, leaves children facing an uncertain future and deprives them of family and educational stability.
It also said Israeli courts contribute to the continuation of violations against children amid the absence of effective accountability.
The Palestinian Prisoners Society cited the case of child Walid Khaled Ahmad, who "died in Megiddo Prison in March 2025, amid medical findings at the time indicating severe emaciation and signs of malnutrition and dehydration."
The group raised questions about accountability for his death, noting that the investigation into the case had been closed.
It also highlighted the case of 15-year-old Mohammed Hamid, who it said developed scabies while detained in Ofer Prison, leading to a deterioration in his health and serious infections affecting vital organs.
Hamid underwent heart surgeries and was admitted to intensive care in critical condition before one of his legs was later amputated, the group said.
It added that Hamid has continued receiving treatment for about three months since Israeli authorities released him following the deterioration of his health, a move the group described as "an evasion of responsibility for his medical care."
The group called for international action to secure the release of children held arbitrarily, end administrative detention and coercive interrogations, and stop torture, starvation and the denial of medical treatment.
It stressed the need to move beyond documentation and condemnation toward concrete measures that end the violations and bring impunity to an end, saying that "protecting Palestinian children requires firm international intervention to ensure respect for their rights, lives and dignity."
Since October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured in Gaza in the Israeli genocide since October 2023, while around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed.
Israeli army raids and attacks by occupiers against Palestinians and their property have intensified in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since the start of Israel’s genocide against the Gaza Strip in October 2023.
