Ukraine: Critical health supplies destroyed in ongoing Russian attacks
Ongoing and deadly Russian attacks across Ukraine are causing serious healthcare disruption, with more than $1.5 million-worth of medicines and supplies destroyed in four separate strikes on warehouses used by the UN there since July.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), 21 warehouses have been targeted this year, out of a total of 400 incidents, almost all involving heavy weapons which is classified as firearms, tanks, missiles, bombs and mortars.
Speaking to UN News, WHO Communications Officer Sarah Tyler described what WHO witnessed at hospitals and warehouses that had come under attack: “When you stand in those places, you really understand what the numbers mean.
“In just three months, four warehouses used by WHO were hit and three were destroyed…The health workers I met keep caring for patients under extraordinary pressure; protecting health care means protecting them.”
Growing toll
The development comes amid a large wave of large-scale attacks by Russian forces across Ukraine this week. Strikes overnight into Wednesday killed at least three people in Kyiv and left hundreds of thousands without power.
This was despite the announcement by President Trump last Friday of an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine.
Over the weekend, other Russian attacks included one in Zaporizhzhia that killed more than 20 people including four children.
Following the bombing, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) highlighted the “unimaginable loss” for families, insisting that the violence “must not become the new normal”.
WHO has verified more than 3,300 attacks on healthcare since the full-scale Russian invasion in February 2022. A total of 247 people have been killed and more than 1,090 health workers and patients have been injured, according to data compiled by the agency.
The agency underlined that the consequences of attacks extend well beyond damage to individual buildings. “When warehouses and other humanitarian installations are hit, medicines, medical equipment, laboratory reagents and other essential supplies can be lost, disrupting the support that health facilities need to treat patients,” explained Dr Ihor Perehinets, WHO Regional Emergency and Health Security Director.
Under pressure
He stressed that Ukraine’s health workers face “extraordinary pressure” while continuing to deliver care.
“Protecting health services means protecting the people who provide them, as well as the medical supplies, equipment and humanitarian infrastructure on which their work depends,” Dr Perehinets added.
The agency’s support in Ukraine includes emergency response, assistance with trauma care, medical supply provision, energy resilience and developing the capacity to manage chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear incidents.
WHO’s 2026 Ukraine appeal seeks $42 million to support 700,000 people.
Continued funding is important to sustaining emergency health operations, maintaining access to essential services, replenishing medical supplies and strengthening preparedness.

WHO urges vigilance after Kenya confirms second Ebola case

WHO urges vigilance after Kenya confirms second Ebola case
The World Health Organization (WHO) continues to support Kenya’s efforts to contain Ebola after a second person tested positive for the Bundibugyo virus, the UN agency’s representative in the country said on Thursday.
The patient, a 39-year-old man, is a relative of Kenya’s first case – related to the ongoing deadly outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) – who died in hospital on 5 October.
He was among contacts who were placed in quarantine and developed symptoms on 13 October.
‘We all have a role to play’
“I congratulate the Government for taking this important step to ensure that contacts are listed and quarantined,” WHO Representative Dr. Neema Rusibamayila Kimambo told UN News in Nairobi, a day after the Ministry of Health confirmed the new case.
“But to defeat this disease, it's not about the Government, it is not about partners It is about everybody,” she insisted. “We all have a role to play and if each one of us plays our part, then we should be able to contain the disease and stop community spread.”
Casting a wide net
Kenya’s first Ebola patient and fatality was a local man who had been living in the DRC, where the record outbreak continues to spread in the east.
He arrived in Nairobi via Uganda on 3 October and died in hospital two days later.
Dr. Kimambo commended health authorities who “cast the net very wide” to identify people who had come into contact with him – whether in the air or on the ground.
The more than 40 people included airline passengers and crew, airplane cleaners, airport workers, baggage handlers and immigration officials, as well as health personnel and family members.
Most are in quarantine, while a few low-risk contacts have self-quarantined and are being monitored. Meanwhile, every effort is being made to reach six passengers who have been difficult to locate because they have foreign phone numbers.
Stepping up preparedness
Even before the first case , WHO and the Kenyan Government were stepping up Ebola preparedness after the outbreak was declared in the DRC in May. Neighbouring Uganda also confronted the disease, with any outbreak officially ruled out in late August.
Teams are working across all areas, including surveillance and contact tracing. WHO has also brought in a senior incident manager who participated in the Ebola response in Uganda, as well as other experts.
“We are building on the work that we started during the preparedness phase, so case management and IPC (infection prevention and control) are critical at this time in the quarantine centres,” Dr. Kimambo said.
WHO also continues to provide assistance to Kenya in various other ways. The UN agency has donated some $70,000 worth of supplies, including IPC and laboratory items, since the first Ebola case was identified.
Additionally, more than 4,000 health workers have been trained, including for screenings at ports of entry.
Keep borders open
While Dr. Kimambo said there still is no need to impose travel restrictions or close national borders, she underlined the importance of appropriate screening to identify travellers who may pose a health risk.
Preventing Ebola begins with understanding how the disease is transmitted, she said, which is through contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person.
She reiterated the advice to practice regular handwashing, use hand sanitizer and avoid shaking hands.
As Ebola symptoms include fever, vomiting and diarrhoea – which mimic symptoms of malaria and other diseases – she stressed the need to seek medical care quickly. In the interim, Kenyans are urged to keep calm and stay safe.
“I think one is not to over panic and be very fearful because we do not have community spread,” she said. “But two, let us be responsible. Whoever is sick, let’s make sure we go to a health facility and get care. And also, let us ensure that we take IPC measures.”

World losing ground in ‘war on nature’ as progress on biodiversity targets lags
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

The world is waging a ‘war on nature’ as progress on biodiversity targets lags
Fewer than half of the national targets set to protect the world’s plants, animals and ecosystems are on track, the UN warns in a new report, days before countries gather in Yerevan, Armenia, for the COP17 biodiversity conference.
The landmark deal struck in Montreal in 2022 – the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework – set out a vision of “living in harmony with nature” by 2050, with urgent action needed by 2030.
The new report suggests the world is falling behind.
“Biodiversity underpins life on Earth,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres wrote in the report. “Safeguarding biological diversity is essential to the health of our planet, the resilience of our economies and the wellbeing of all people.”
Trailing behind
One of the deal’s flagship goals was to protect at least 30 per cent of the world’s land, inland waters, coasts and oceans by 2030.
Yet even if current commitments are met, only 26 per cent of land and 12 per cent of the ocean would be protected by that deadline, the report finds.
Progress is also lagging on money, skills, cooperation and data, as well as on economic incentives that reward protecting nature rather than destroying it.
“This bad news means that the war on nature has not yet ended,” Mr. Guterres said at the report’s launch in Yerevan.
He warned that the world is still caught in three interlinked crises: climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution.
Glass half full
There has been some progress since 2022, however.
Nearly 90 per cent of countries that are parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity have set national targets, and more than half have drawn up their own plans to deliver them.
More than 70 per cent have measured and reported on their results.
Indigenous Peoples, local communities, regional and city authorities, charities and businesses have also made some 5,000 commitments – though the report warns of a serious gap between ambition and action.
The road ahead
Closing that gap will require money and expertise for developing countries on a far bigger scale, the report says.
Governments need to scrap subsidies that harm nature, strengthen social protection, redirect spending towards protecting nature and work with businesses on strong disclosure rules.
Better coordination is also needed between governments, business, civil society, young people, women and Indigenous Peoples to strengthen accountability, enforcement and cooperation.
“Biodiversity must be part of every decision being made – across policies, regulations and budgets,” Mr. Guterres said.
“Nature won’t thrive on good intentions.”

AI, green energy and economic transitions risk leaving vulnerable communities behind, UN warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

AI, green energy and economic transitions risk leaving vulnerable communities behind, UN warns
Rapid transformations – from artificial intelligence and digital technologies to renewable energy and demographic shifts – are reshaping economies worldwide, creating new opportunities but also threatening to deepen socio-economic inequalities, a new UN report warned on Thursday.
Benefiting from these changes often requires specialised skills and access to the latest technologies, putting disadvantaged groups at risk of being left behind.
Women, young people, older persons, persons with disabilities, migrants, Indigenous Peoples and low-income communities are particularly vulnerable, the report stresses, outlining recommendations for governments to ensure these transformations benefit everyone.
Inclusion is a priority
Social inclusion is a moral imperative, but it is also an economic necessity, the report from the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs (DESA) underlined.
It found that expanding opportunities to marginalised groups enlarges the productive workforce, strengthens human capital, increases innovation and entrepreneurship, improves labour allocation and spreads productivity gains more widely.
“Inclusive societies are more productive, resilient, and prosperous,” Secretary-General António Guterres summarised in a video message for the launch of the report.
Measures towards social inclusion should also be taken urgently, as those left outside key systems face steeper barriers to catching up later, the report emphasised.
What to do
As artificial intelligence transforms labour markets, the report urges governments to invest in continuous training and reskilling for workers whose jobs may be replaced or transformed, rather than focusing solely on creating new jobs.
Similarly, the shift to renewable energy must include support for workers and communities reliant on fossil fuels, through retraining, alternative employment opportunities and social assistance.
To bridge the digital divide, governments should also expand affordable access to the internet, digital infrastructure and technology training – particularly in disadvantaged communities.
One last major recommendation is to stop relying mainly on GDP to evaluate growth, and to also assess progress through poverty reduction, access to education and healthcare, employment security, inequality and environmental protection.
Economic growth that benefits only a small share of the population, it argues, cannot be considered genuinely inclusive.
Funding these investments
Importantly, these investments require resources and many developing countries are facing financial constraints that could hamper the transition.
Nearly half of the world’s poorest countries are either in or at high risk of debt distress, with interest payments relative to revenue at their highest levels in a generation, the UN Secretary-General warned.
He called on leaders to live up to the commitments made through last year’s Doha Political Declaration on Social Development and the Sevilla Commitment on financing for development.
He also pushed for reform of international financial institutions to better represent and serve developing countries.
“Transformations are inevitable. Inequality and exclusion are not,” the UN Secretary-General said.
“Let’s work together to ensure that the profound transformations reshaping our world help build societies rooted in justice, dignity and opportunity for all.”

Afghanistan faces record hunger levels amid rampant rights violations

Afghanistan faces record hunger levels amid rampant rights violations
Acute malnutrition and hunger in Afghanistan have reached the highest levels ever recorded, with 15.9 million people facing acute food insecurity and conditions set to worsen in the coming months, according to a global hunger monitor report released on Thursday.
UN agency heads are calling for emergency support to stem the crisis, as a separate report details serious human rights violations – from public floggings to a new ban on demonstrations.
Key points
- 15.9 million Afghans are facing acute food insecurity
- 3.4 million are experiencing emergency food insecurity conditions, which precedes famine, and conditions are expected to worsen
- New UN report on human rights in Afghanistan reveals serious violations, from public floggings to a fresh ban on demonstrations
Crisis-level hunger
Record acute malnutrition levels for the August–October period have seen hunger levels grow for millions of Afghans – according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), a global initiative aimed at informing decisions based on five phases of food security.
Economic pressures are straining households nationwide, contributing to more than 32 per cent of the population facing crisis-level acute food insecurity phase three or above, including 3.4 million people experiencing emergency phase four conditions.
The current deterioration is driven by disease outbreaks and inadequate water, sanitation and hygiene conditions, compounded by sharply reduced access to nutrition services, the report found.
Set to worsen
The situation is expected to worsen from November to April during the winter lean season, when nearly 19.2 million people are projected to face phase three or above, including five million people in emergency food insecurity conditions.
Acute malnutrition is also set to grow significantly, with 4.04 million children under age five projected to need treatment between January and December 2027.
“Although improved rainfall and better agricultural production have supported food availability, declining humanitarian assistance is reducing households’ ability to cope,” the report warned.
‘A window to act’
The World Food Programme (WFP) and Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) issued a stark message on Thursday, calling for urgent funding to scale up food assistance, emergency agricultural support and malnutrition prevention and treatment.
“We still have a window to act, but it is closing fast,” WFP country director John Aylieff said. “With urgent support, families can get through the winter with dignity. Without it, many will face impossible choices no parent should have to make.”
FAO representative Richard Trenchard said families need opportunities to earn a dependable living that “helps them withstand the next shock” and support to get through this winter.
Crackdown on women, media, civic space
The UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) on Thursday reported the continued erosion of basic human rights across the country between July and September, with women and girls bearing the brunt of restrictions imposed by Taliban authorities.
Key observations
Girls’ school ban: Girls remain barred from formal education beyond grade six. Asked about the ban, a Taliban spokesperson said that “problems and considerations” had to be taken into account from the perspective of Sharia law.
Women arrested, detained or cautioned: UNAMA documented more than 50 cases related to the hijab, mostly in Herat and Kabul. In one case, a 13-year-old girl was held overnight. Women were also blocked from entering health clinics and markets without a male guardian, or mahram.
Arbitrary arrests and detentions: The mission recorded at least 443 cases and 97 incidents of ill-treatment by virtue and vice inspectors over offences including hijab violations, trimmed beards, skipped prayers and listening to music.
Judicial corporal punishment: While the de facto Supreme Court stopped publicly announcing such cases on its social media account and website in April, UNAMA documented public lashings of 22 men and six women on charges including theft and adultery, and the arrest of 14 former security force members, with at least four others killed.
Media and civic freedom curtailed: Several outlets were suspended without clear reasons or appeal procedures. A journalist arrested in July 2025 remains in custody without conviction. A new police law, published in August, bans all demonstrations.
Cross-border violence: Since October 2025, 512 civilians have been killed and 1,236 injured, with 33 casualties in the latest quarter, including children killed in Pakistani airstrikes on homes in Kunar and Helmand.

Could your brain data be used against you? UN calls for limits on neurotechnology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Could your brain data be used against you? UN calls for limits on neurotechnology
Brain signals recorded by a gaming headset or a wellness gadget could one day be used as evidence against you in court, according to a new UN report which warns that neurotechnology is outpacing the laws meant to protect human rights.
Presenting the Secretary-General’s report to the General Assembly on Thursday, senior human rights official Claudia Fuentes Julio said the technology could threaten privacy, freedom of thought and the right to a fair trial, particularly for marginalised people.
Key points
- The new report examines the growing use of neurotechnology in justice systems and the risks arising from its convergence with artificial intelligence (AI)
- Data collected through gaming or wellness devices, for instance, could be used in a court of law, impacting fundamental human rights, including the right to a fair trial
- The report calls for prohibiting coercive and abusive applications of neurotechnology and establishing stronger legal and ethical safeguards
When high-tech meets the law
Neurotechnology was once exclusively used for medical diagnoses or treatment, measuring, monitoring, analysing, predicting or modulating the nervous system.
The new tech gathers neural data – defined as qualitative and quantitative data about the structure, activity and function of the nervous system.
“Neurotechnology accesses, measures and analyses brain signals,” the UN chief wrote in his report. “If these signals are treated as direct indicators of thoughts, intentions or truthfulness, the use of neural data points could undermine how we understand and value each of us as human beings.”
Once confined to clinical or research environments, these devices are now entering, or may enter, consumer markets, workplaces, schools, public services, law enforcement and justice systems, the report found.
Gaming to wellness
UN Assistant Secretary-General for Human Rights Claudia Fuentes Julio highlighted a range of risks when introducing the report to Third Committee members, including the growing commercialisation of neurotechnology and the collection of large volumes of neural data by technology companies.
Marketed for wellness, gaming and productivity, wearable, so-called electroencephalography devices are now increasingly available.
As such, neural data collected through these devices could be accessed by governments or introduced as evidence in legal proceedings without adequate recognition of its highly sensitive nature, the report warned.
From privacy to fair trial rights
While these new technologies hold significant promise, particularly for medical and assistive applications, Ms. Fuentes Julio said the report “warns of risks to dignity, privacy, freedom of thought, fair trial rights, liberty and protection from ill-treatment, especially for marginalised groups”.
Indeed, when applied in the courtroom these technologies serve different purposes and pose distinct legal and human rights risks, especially as tools and data developed for medical use are repurposed without appropriate safeguards, the report argues.
Ms. Fuentes Julio said the report calls for “prohibitions on coercive and abusive uses, and stronger safeguards, informed consent, scientific validation, oversight, accountability and protection of neural data.”
The report emphasises that neural data, as “uniquely sensitive personal data,” demands heightened protection.

Points deduction, relegation or stripped titles: What could happen to Manchester City?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:59:24 UTC
20:59:24 KST

Findings of financial misconduct against Manchester City have set the stage for a potentially landmark case that could reshape both the club’s future and the way English football polices its richest clubs.
The independent commission’s conclusions span nine seasons and open the door to sanctions that could reach far beyond a conventional financial penalty.
Sports law expert Jan Zglinski said the scale of the case is unlike anything previously seen, with possible consequences ranging from a heavy points deduction and compensation claims to questions over titles won during the period under scrutiny.
“I really hope this case will in a few years’ time be seen as a turning point, because this is a breach of unprecedented scale,” Zglinski, an associate professor of law at the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE), told Anadolu.
“It’s been systematic, and the financial volume of it is something we haven’t seen yet in English football or in world football,” he added.
The Premier League announced in late September that an independent commission had found City guilty of serious financial rule breaches spanning nine seasons, from 2009-10 to 2017-18, following charges brought against the club in February 2023.
The commission found that City used “sham” contracts with commercial partners as part of schemes that artificially inflated revenue and reduced reported costs by more than £900 million ($1.2 billion), concealing the true state of the club's finances from auditors and football regulators.
It also found that City had significantly breached Premier League and UEFA spending limits and failed to cooperate fully with the league's investigation.
The Premier League confirmed City's appeal on Oct. 2, with the club rejecting the commission's findings and maintaining its innocence.
“The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case,” City said in a statement.
Potential sanctions have yet to be determined.
Zglinski said approximately £830 million of the nearly £950 million in sponsorship revenue recorded by City had been funded by the club's ownership rather than the sponsors themselves, describing the scale as “quite shocking.”
He explained that sponsors paid only a fraction of the amounts recorded as revenue, with the club's owners covering the remainder.
“And this is how we get to the situation where there was on the books a really large sum of money that was coming into the club. But in reality, very little of that was paid by the sponsors themselves. Most of it was footed by the club ownership,” he said.
Zglinski said the distinction between funding provided by the club's ownership and money originating from the UAE government would not change the Premier League's findings on sponsorship revenue.
“Now, one way in which I don't think it's going to matter is that the Premier League's financial rules clearly stipulate that the club itself must be earning the sponsorship rights,” he said.
However, he said the origin of the money could become relevant in potential proceedings involving individuals in City's leadership, particularly where questions of state immunity arise.
“So the origin of that money indeed will have a consequence,” he said. “They shouldn't, though, impact the Premier League's findings in this matter.”
Asked how City could challenge the findings, Zglinski pointed to the club's previous legal proceedings against UEFA, suggesting it could again question whether the evidence met the required standard.
“Back then, the basis of the appeal was that Manchester City thought the standards of evidence hadn't been met,” he said. “It said that UEFA didn’t have quite the right information to justify a sanction. I am sure that in this case, they will try that as well.”
Unlike City's previous UEFA case, which reached the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS), the Premier League proceedings follow a separate appeals process.
“Here we're now going to have the appeal by the Premier League Appeal Board,” Zglinski said.
“From that, there might be a further step to the High Court here in England, but that allows an appeal only on quite narrow grounds,” he added.
Zglinski warned that City could face a substantial points deduction, potentially accompanied by a fine.
“Realistically, I think we’re looking at the very least at a very heavy points deduction, possibly combined with the fine,” he said.
Zglinski said a sufficiently heavy points deduction could effectively relegate City, while a separate decision to force the club out of the Premier League would create practical difficulties because the English Football League (EFL) would need to accommodate it.
“The EFL would need to accept Manchester City as part of these clubs,” he said.
He explained that accommodating City could require another EFL club to drop out or the league to temporarily expand, an option he believed the EFL would be reluctant to consider.
Previous points deductions imposed on Everton and Nottingham Forest offered some guidance on how the Premier League applies its financial rules, but Zglinski cautioned that City's case involved breaches on a far greater financial scale.
“These are, of course, in some ways valuable precedents because they show how the Premier League's handbook is applied,” he said.
“However, they, of course, concern a completely different order of magnitude,” he added.
The possibility of stripping City of titles won during the period covered by the findings was another issue.
“There’s a strong argument to be made that Manchester City should not in the history books carry on the honor of having won the Premier League or the FA Cup in a period where they systematically and significantly breached the financial rules of this country,” Zglinski said.
However, he said awarding those titles to rival clubs would be more complicated.
“Whether that means that other clubs will be reinstated in their position, whether Liverpool finally gets to lift that trophy, I don’t think is quite as straightforward,” he added.
Beyond potential sporting sanctions, Zglinski said rival clubs that believed they had suffered financial or sporting harm could pursue compensation claims against Manchester City.
He cited the dispute between Burnley and Everton, in which an independent Premier League commission ordered Everton in June to pay Burnley £26 million ($35 million) in damages, plus £9.1 million in interest, over financial-rule breaches linked to the 2021/22 season.
The commission found that Everton's breaches had given the club a sporting advantage that contributed to Burnley's relegation that season. Everton appealed the compensation ruling, arguing that the decision was flawed in law and fact.
However, Zglinski warned that the unprecedented scale of City's case could make it difficult to establish a workable compensation framework.
“Because of the unprecedented scale, we don’t really know how that will practically happen,” he said.
As for possible consequences beyond English football, Zglinski considered further action by UEFA unlikely. He noted that CAS overturned City's two-season European competition ban in 2020, with some of UEFA's claims in those proceedings found to be time-barred.
“I would not be expecting, in the first place, UEFA to take action now,” he said.
He added that FIFA had no official role in the Premier League investigation and was not in a position to impose sanctions at that stage.
Beyond the potential sanctions, Zglinski criticized the length of the Premier League's investigation, saying football authorities needed to respond more quickly to financial misconduct.
“It also needs remembering that this investigation took very, very long,” he said, referring to the years that had passed since City's early successes during the period covered by the breaches.
“That’s way too long and that cannot be the way forward,” he added.
Zglinski urged the Premier League to review its procedures to prevent similar delays in future cases.
“So I'm very much hoping that the Premier League will take a hard look in the mirror and try to find ways of making the system more effective,” he said.
“Because one thing that no one wants, not the clubs, not the fans, is to discuss titles and championships a decade later in the courtroom instead of on the pitch,” he said.

Belarus Modernizes Infrastructure for Russian Aggression Near NATO Borders by 2027
Belarus could be ready for full-scale participation in a wider Russian war by spring or mid-2027 as military infrastructure and arms production expand toward NATO borders, Centrum Europy reported on October 14.
The report, prepared by the Belarusian democratic forces’ analytical center BELPOL together with the underground Association of Belarusian Railway Workers, was presented in Warsaw. Centrum Europy noted that its authors relied on open sources, leaked documents, and information they claimed was obtained after “bribing Russian generals.”
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Centrum Europy, BELPOL identified a secure military communications network being built across Belarus from east to west, rather than radiating outward from Minsk. The group argued that its layout is designed to support the movement of Russian forces from the Russian border toward Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, and Ukraine.
“This network is being built from east to west, along Belarus’s largest roads and highways,” BELPOL representative Maćwiej Kuprejczyk told Centrum Europy. “The center of this system is not in Belarus.”
Centrum Europy also detailed Russian-funded railway modernization connecting Belarus with Ukraine and NATO states, including stronger tracks, new unloading ramps, sidings to ammunition depots, and infrastructure for underground fuel storage.
BELPOL assessed that these upgrades could allow Russian divisions and heavy equipment to move rapidly toward NATO borders without first concentrating forces in eastern Belarus.
Particular attention was given to routes leading toward the Suwałki Gap, the narrow area connecting Poland and Lithuania that links the Baltic states with the rest of NATO.
Centrum Europy reported that BELPOL representatives claimed Russian commanders had described the infrastructure as potentially useful for an operation aimed at seizing the corridor and cutting Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia off from Poland.
BELPOL also identified around 120 Belarusian companies producing or preparing to produce for the Russian Armed Forces. The report described new defense plants and civilian factories being converted for military output, including a facility expected to assemble 122 mm rockets for BM-21 Grad launchers.
“The preliminary date when everything will be ready is the beginning or middle of 2027,” Kuprejczyk stated.
He added that most facilities were expected to reach maximum production capacity by March 2027, with the remainder reaching full capacity by midyear.
Asked by Centrum Europy whether that meant Belarus could be ready for war by spring 2027, Kuprejczyk answered affirmatively.
BELPOL maintained that the buildup could support Russian operations not only against Ukraine but potentially against NATO’s Baltic members.
Centrum Europy noted that BELPOL had already warned in 2024 that Belarus under Alexander Lukashenko was preparing for deeper involvement in Russia’s war and potentially for operations against NATO states. The group now argues that the continuing expansion of railways, communications networks, and military production has made that scenario more concrete.
Days earlier, masked individuals crossing from Belarus damaged Latvian border surveillance equipment and stole cameras before retreating back across the frontier.
Latvian authorities also reported that armed masked individuals had accompanied migrants toward the border, describing the episode as part of continued provocations and hybrid activity targeting Latvia and NATO’s eastern flank.

What to know about Starshield, SpaceX's military-focused Starlink service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:54:43 UTC
20:54:43 KST

Uncertainty over who controls SpaceX's military satellite system, Starshield, has drawn renewed attention, as restrictions on the technology hinder Ukraine's defenses.
Ukraine has accused SpaceX-owned Starlink of restricting its military-grade services, known as Starshield, as Russia intensified attacks on Kyiv.
Officials in Kyiv said SpaceX had imposed restrictions on Starshield without advance notice, disrupting military operations and hampering efforts to protect civilians amid intense Russian attacks this week.
In response, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk appeared to shift responsibility for any changes to Starshield's use in Ukraine to the U.S. government and President Donald Trump. He said that Starshield systems are owned and controlled by Washington, with the U.S. military and ultimately the president determining any limits on their use. The White House and the Pentagon didn't immediately reply to CNBC's request for comment.
Here's what to know about Starshield, and how it differs from Starlink.
What is Starshield and how does it work?
Starshield is SpaceX's satellite network designed for government and national security use, building on the technology developed for Starlink. On Tuesday, Ukrainian officials reported that their Starlink communication systems were no longer working for terminals moving at speeds above 100 miles per hour, or about 160 kilometers per hour.
Ukraine relies on this connectivity to track and intercept incoming threats. Ukraine's military also uses the commercial Starlink technology, according to media reports, but it is not clear which of its terminals operate under the commercial arm versus those provided through Starshield.
Speaking to Piers Morgan on Wednesday, Zelenskyy lamented that "Starlink was switched off."
He said connectivity in the middle of the night, disrupting Ukrainian drones used to intercept Russian attacks, and that restrictions had prevented Ukraine from intercepting some Russian drones, contributing to civilian deaths. He also criticized the lack of advance warnings about incoming Russian ballistic missiles.
"Often when we destroy jet shaheeds, we use drones with Starlinks," he said.
"It's not about attack. It's also about defending the lives… People were killed because not enough destroying, not enough interceptors, including interceptors with Starlink, which didn't work."
"They knew what they did," Zelenskyy said, referring to SpaceX and the U.S. and describing the Starlink restrictions as particularly troubling given Ukraine's reliance on the U.S. as a strategic partner.
Mykhailo Fedorov, who was until recently Ukraine's defense minister, said Wednesday that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h was being restored, and that "removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense."
According to SpaceX, Starshield currently focuses on Earth observation, secure global communications for government users, and so-called "hosted payloads," which refers to hosting specialized equipment aboard satellites for customers.
Unlike Starlink, which serves consumers and businesses, Starshield offers enhanced security features, including high-assurance cryptographic capability designed to handle classified information. It says its satellites can handle a range of equipment and connect with other satellites through laser communications technology.
SpaceX was awarded over $6 billion in multi-year U.S. government contracts for Starshield, primarily from two major Space Force contracts for low Earth orbit-based communications and sensing constellations, SpaceX said in its latest earnings report.
Musk on Wednesday distinguished Starshield from SpaceX's commercial Starlink service, which he said was restricted to civilian and defensive purposes and could not be used for offensive military operations.
How does Starshield differ from Starlink?
Although Starshield serves a different purpose from Starlink's commercial internet service, which provides high-speed connectivity to regular people, the two are closely connected.
Starlink is SpaceX's general satellite internet service, sold for consumer, civilian, and defense purposes, and offers internet access in remote areas where it has traditionally been limited.
Starshield uses stronger encryption and specialized terminals for secure communications, but relies on Starlink's extensive satellite network to operate.
According to SpaceX, Starlink operates in more than 160 countries, territories and other markets, offering residential plans starting at $55 per month. The company says its service can deliver download speeds exceeding 400 megabits per second in most locations.
Why does Starshield matter to Ukraine?
On Tuesday, Ukrainian officials reported that their Starlink communication systems were no longer working for terminals moving at speeds above 100 miles per hour, or about 160 kilometers per hour.
Ukraine relies on this connectivity to track and intercept incoming threats. Ukraine's military also uses the commercial Starlink technology, according to media reports, but it is not clear which of its terminals operate under the commercial arm versus those provided through Starshield.
Speaking to Piers Morgan on Wednesday, Zelenskyy lamented that "Starlink was switched off."
He said connectivity was cut off in the middle of the night, disrupting Ukrainian drones used to intercept Russian attacks. Those restrictions prevented Ukraine from intercepting some Russian drones, contributing to civilian deaths. He also criticized the lack of advance warnings about incoming Russian ballistic missiles.
"Often when we destroy jet Shaheds, we use drones with Starlinks," he explained.
"It's not about attack. It's also about defending the lives… People were killed because not enough destroying, not enough interceptors, including interceptors with Starlink, which didn't work."
"They knew what they did," Zelenskyy said, referring to SpaceX and the U.S. and describing the Starlink restrictions as particularly troubling given Ukraine's reliance on the U.S. as a strategic partner.
Mykhailo Fedorov, who was until recently Ukraine's defense minister, said Wednesday that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h was being restored, and that "removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense."

Anthropic thinks your fridge could one day hide a rogue AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:54:42 UTC
20:54:42 KST

Everything is a computer these days. Fridges, washing machines, televisions, and more are now outfitted with computer chips to give them new capabilities, and manufacturers called them “smart” even before ChatGPT came out. Now, though, researchers have strung 15 cheap TV boxes together to run an artificial intelligence model, raising the possibility that the computers inside these everyday gadgets could someday help spread autonomous, AI-powered malware.
On Monday Anthropic released a blog post exploring this sort of attack. Researchers at the company tested how AI models might act as computer worms, programs that move between devices and leave copies of themselves behind, among everyday household gadgets. A worm that runs on smart devices instead of relying on a data center could prove difficult to shut down. Anthropic’s experiments suggest how that might happen—though they stop short of demonstrating the full threat.
Typically, large language models (LLMs) are trained and run in data centers, which can contain hundreds of thousands of specialized chips called graphics processing units, or GPUs. “Just because you don’t have a big GPU doesn’t mean that you can’t be a host to one of these models,” says Jeffrey Ladish, founder and executive director of Palisade Research, a California-based AI safety nonprofit that studies the risk of AI systems slipping beyond human control, past malware to rogue behavior.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In recent months, researchers have experimented with various types of computer worms, stapling AI models onto them to make them adaptive and harder to kill. Here, though, the researchers explored whether an AI model itself could be distributed as the worm, spreading its weights to new devices and running across even weak chips.
"Anybody with an open-weight model, with the right prompts and by brute-force luck, can find these worms," says computer scientist Vyas Sekar.
Specifically, researchers working on Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team showed two key capabilities. First, they were able to split up a relatively small model—one from Google DeepMind’s open-weight Gemma line—across 15 TV boxes they had bought and networked themselves so that they could run the entire model by chaining these boxes together. Each individual box was too weak to run the model on its own. But LLMs can be split into layers, an arrangement in which each layer manipulates the data it receives and passes that revised data to the next layer. By giving each box the job of handling just a couple of these layers, the team was able to run Gemma entirely and get responses back from just the weak chips in these boxes.
After that, the researchers tested how an AI worm might spread across devices in a virtual sandbox. A larger model—from the Chinese start-up Z.ai—managed to get a smaller model—one of Meta’s Llama models—running on the targets. But the larger model was too large to run on those weak devices itself, and it still relied on a separate server. This means the team did not show an AI worm capable of spreading and running itself on such devices. Anthropic argues that as small models become more capable, one could eventually use both methods.
The research also raises the prospect of adaptation and improvement by suggesting that AI models could subsist on low-power devices and drift through the Internet, getting better at spreading as they go. Anthropic makes this clear in its blog post about the work, concluding that AI systems could soon be “passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves.”
Ladish believes the main lesson from the research is in how AI models could divvy up work across computers of all shapes and sizes. “Basically, compute is a resource that these models can use,” he says, pointing to everything from Apple MacBooks to data centers to everyday objects like smart TVs as possible sources of computing power if attackers can hack them.
Not everyone thinks that the experiments amount to a new kind of threat, however. “I think there’s some caution that’s needed here to make sure we talk about what capabilities are new and transformative,” says Michael Bailey, a professor studying computer systems security at the Georgia Institute of Technology. He emphasizes avoiding “fearmongering” with the lessons taken away from this kind of work. Researchers already know how insecure devices like TV boxes can be. “We already had self-replicating malware,” says Bailey. “We had botnets.”
“All of these are classical computer security threats,” adds Vyas Sekar, a professor of computer engineering at Carnegie Mellon University. According to Sekar, the bigger problem is that more people might be able to launch such attacks—a “democratization of being evil,” as he calls it. Sekar thinks this makes monitoring and restricting data flow between smart devices even more important.
Even the risk of hijacking raw computing power on chips is not new. Hackers have long taken over other people’s computers to mine cryptocurrency. So while smart devices could face new attacks of the kind Anthropic describes, the underlying weakness is an old one: plenty of our gadgets are already easy to commandeer.

Syrian intelligence authorities have arrested Ali Kayali, also known as Mihrac Ural, the chief suspect in the 2013 Baniyas massacre who has also been implicated in the deadly twin bombings in Türkiye’s Reyhanli district, state media reported on Thursday.

Kayali, a former militia leader loyal to Syria’s ousted regime leader Bashar al Assad, has long been accused of involvement in mass killings in Baniyas and the nearby village of al Bayda during the early years of the Syrian uprising.

Trump could lose Congress and still expand the US war on Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:53:16 UTC
20:53:16 KST

President Trump has promised that the United States will not attack Iran before the 3rd November midterm elections. That statement sounds like restraint and at the same time also be read as a warning. By tying military restraint to election day, Trump has made the period after the vote more dangerous.
The Iran war is making the election harder for the Republican Party. As of now, prediction markets give Republicans roughly a one-in-ten chance of retaining both chambers of Congress.
An October AP-NORC poll found that 69 per cent of Americans believed the war was not worth fighting, while only 28 per cent approved of Trump’s handling of Iran. For many voters, the war is no longer a distant foreign-policy issue. They feel it through higher fuel prices, inflation, and the fear of another open-ended conflict.
A Republican defeat, however, would not remove Trump’s military power the next morning. He would remain Commander-in-Chief, and the outgoing Congress would remain in office until 3rd January 2027. This leaves a two-month gap between the election and the arrival of a new Congress. During that period, Trump would face less pressure to protect Republican candidates, but Democrats would not yet control the congressional machinery needed to challenge him.
That is the main danger. Americans may vote against the party that owns the war, but their votes would not immediately change who controls military decisions. The election could reject the war politically while leaving Trump free to expand it militarily.
Trump would not need a special executive order or advance approval from Congress to begin a limited operation. Like other presidents before him, he could rely on a broad interpretation of his Commander-in-Chief powers, claim that an attack was needed to protect American personnel or interests, and use forces and funds that Congress had already approved.
Congress would then be responding to a war that was already under way.
The War Powers Resolution offers some restraint, but not enough to prevent the opening attack. It requires the President to report the use of US forces in hostilities within 48 hours and sets a timetable for ending an operation that Congress has not authorised. In practice, this gives Congress a way to contest a campaign after it begins. It does not reliably stop the first missiles from being launched.
A further attack would also face serious questions under international law. Unless Washington could show Security Council authorisation or a genuine case of self-defence, the use of force against Iran would be difficult to justify under the UN Charter. Yet this is another example of the gap between law and action: a strike can take place before courts, international organisations or legislatures are able to respond.
READ: Axios: Netanyahu discussed joint strike on Iran with Trump before Israeli election
This does not mean that a Democratic victory would be meaningless. Democratic control of both chambers would make a prolonged war harder to sustain.
Congress could investigate the administration, subpoena officials, expose the real military and financial costs, and attach conditions to future funding. It could also demand the withdrawal of US forces and force the White House to defend its war aims in public.
But congressional power has limits. Trump could veto legislation restricting the campaign, and Democrats would need a two-thirds majority in both chambers to override him. The administration could also continue using previously approved funds while Congress debated what to do. The important distinction is simple: a Democratic Congress could make the continuation of war more difficult, but it might not prevent Trump from starting the next phase.
The Pentagon’s preparations make this risk more credible. Recent US reporting indicates that Central Command has been asked to prepare options for renewed operations against Iran. Military planning is not proof that Trump has decided to attack. It does mean that the machinery is being put in place so that he can act quickly if negotiations fail. After election day, the immediate political cost of such action will be lower.
The consequences would be felt far beyond Washington. Iran can retaliate against US forces and partners across the region and can disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. A new round of attacks could raise energy and insurance costs, expose countries around the Persian Gulf to retaliation and place even more pressure on governments trying to stay outside the conflict. American military superiority may win individual battles, but it has not produced a stable political settlement or removed Iran’s ability to impose regional costs.
The timing also matters for Palestine. Every new escalation with Iran allows Israel to present the region mainly as a security threat and draws diplomatic and media attention away from its actions in Occupied Palestine. A wider US-Iran war would therefore not only deepen regional instability. It would also give Israel more space to avoid pressure over Gaza and the continuing dispossession of Palestinians.
Regional governments should not wait for the American election to solve this crisis. An election can change the political price of war, but it cannot produce peace by itself. Pakistan and Qatar, which are facilitating indirect communication, should use the period before 3 November to press for an immediate and lasting ceasefire. Other regional states should support an agreement that protects navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, prevents further attacks and restores a credible diplomatic path on the nuclear issue.
The real question is therefore not only whether Democrats will win Congress. It is whether diplomacy can produce an agreement before the last electoral restraint on Trump disappears. If it cannot, the period after 3rd November may become more dangerous, not less.

Sally Rooney's books withdrawn in U.K. over author's support for designated terror group Palestine Action
London — World-renowned Irish author Sally Rooney's books will no longer be supplied to booksellers in the United Kingdom due to her public support for Palestine Action, a group banned as a terrorist organization in Britain.
Rooney, the bestselling novelist behind "Normal People" and "Conversations with Friends," both of which have been adapted into television shows, and her publisher Faber have agreed to halt the supply of her books to British retailers, according to a statement from Faber.
"Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher," Faber said.
Rooney previously said she intended to use proceeds from her work to financially support Palestine Action, potentially exposing her and her publisher to prosecution under British anti-terrorism laws.
In an article published in The Irish Times in August 2025, Rooney wrote: "I want to be clear that I intend to use these proceeds of my work, as well as my public platform generally, to go on supporting Palestine Action and direct action against genocide in whatever way I can."
What is Palestine Action?
Founded in 2020, Palestine Action is a British direct-action group that has targeted arms manufacturers and other companies it accuses of supplying weapons to Israel with protests and sabotage.
The group describes itself as a "movement committed to ending global complicity with Israel's genocidal apartheid regime."
The British government designated Palestine Action as a terrorist organization in July 2025, citing the group's history of criminal damage and escalating attacks on defense infrastructure, including a factory belonging to U.S. defense company Teledyne Technologies in 2022.
The 2025 decision came after the group claimed responsibility for breaking into a major air base, RAF Brize Norton, northwest of London, and damaging aircraft. The Associated Press and other outlets cited British police as putting the cost of the damage at around $9.4 million, though authorities have not publicly confirmed that figure.
Under U.K. law it is a crime to be a member of a designated terrorist group, or to publicly support one.
The ban on Palestine Action has prompted widespread protests and thousands of arrests across the U.K. According to the latest figures from Britain's Home Office, which oversees all domestic law enforcement, the average age of those arrested on suspicion of supporting Palestine Action is 59, compared to 28 for other terrorism-related arrests.
The legality of the ban remains the subject of a Supreme Court challenge.
"Sally Rooney is finding out that she can't have her cake and eat it," a spokesperson for the U.K. activist group Campaign Against Antisemitism told CBS News, adding that it had reported the author to counterterrorism police over her vow to financially support Palestine Action.

Former leader of Northern Ireland’s largest party sentenced to 15 years for sexual offenses against children
Kyiv • UNN

The former leader of Northern Ireland’s largest unionist party, Jeffrey Donaldson, was sentenced on Thursday to 15 years in prison for historical sexual offences against children. The judge called the case “a catastrophic fall from grace.” Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
The 63-year-old Donaldson was found guilty in June of one count of rape, 13 counts of indecent assault of a sexual nature and four counts of gross indecency involving two women. The crimes were committed between 1985 and 2008. It is one of the highest-profile court cases in the British-administered region in recent years.
Donaldson was one of Northern Ireland’s best-known politicians and served longer than any other representative from the region as a member of the British Parliament. He was arrested and charged in March 2024.
The judge called the case “disturbing and deeply unpleasant” and assessed Donaldson’s risk of reoffending as moderate.
Donaldson, who had been in prison awaiting sentencing since June, denied all the charges and intends to appeal his conviction.
Prosecutor Rosemary Walsh said during last month’s pre-sentencing hearing that one of the victims described the abuse as “the worst moment of her life” and said it had affected all her subsequent relationships.
The other victim felt that her childhood had been stolen and had felt “shame” ever since. Both victims, whose names cannot be disclosed for legal reasons, gave evidence during the trial.
The judge said he had no doubt about the indelible mark the crimes had left on the lives of both victims. He noted that the duration of the abuse and the victims’ ages were aggravating factors in determining the severity of the sentence.
Donaldson immediately resigned as leader of the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), founded by Protestant clergyman Ian Paisley at the height of three decades of sectarian bloodshed that ended after the 1998 peace agreement was concluded.
In 2016, Queen Elizabeth II knighted him for political service. Two months before his arrest, Donaldson played a key role in negotiations on a major post-Brexit trade deal.
Two days after being found guilty, Donaldson asked to be stripped of his knighthood.
The jury also found that Donaldson’s wife, Eleanor, assisted her husband and facilitated the commission of the crimes. She also denied the charges.
Last month, the court found her unfit to stand trial because of mental health problems, and therefore she could not be criminally convicted.

Study identifies immune cells that can attack deadliest lung cancer
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
19:47:57 CST
20:47:57 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have identified a previously overlooked type of immune cell that can recognize and kill small cell lung cancer (SCLC), revealing a new immune pathway for fighting the deadliest form of the disease.
The study, led by Australia's Walter and Eliza Hall Institute of Medical Research (WEHI), found that patients with higher levels of gamma delta T cells in their tumors tended to live longer, uncovering a hidden immune defense that could be exploited to attack these hard-to-treat tumors, according to a WEHI statement released on Thursday.
Researchers also showed two existing drugs could be repurposed to boost the cancer-killing abilities of these immune cells, potentially paving the way to enhance therapies for a disease with limited treatment options.
SCLC has a five-year survival rate of less than 7 percent. Although immunotherapy has improved outcomes for several cancers, only a small proportion of SCLC patients experience long-term benefits, partly because these cancers are often invisible to the conventional immune cells that treatments rely on, according to the study published in Cancer Cell.
The study found that gamma delta T cells could detect and attack these lung cancers that are able to evade conventional cancer-fighting immune cells, overcoming a major treatment challenge.
The researchers created miniature tumors in the laboratory using patient samples and found that gamma delta T cells taken from the patients' blood could effectively recognize and kill SCLC cells.
"This could open an entirely new avenue for personalized treatment approaches in SCLC and other solid cancers that are often missed by conventional immune cells," said Jin Ng, first author of the study at WEHI. ■

KATHMANDU, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Remittance inflows and foreign exchange reserves in Nepal increased in the first two months of the 2026-27 fiscal year, the central bank said on Thursday.
In its monthly report, Nepal Rastra Bank said remittance inflows rose 13.5 percent year on year to 2.85 billion U.S. dollars between mid-July and mid-September.
The increase in remittance inflows came despite a slight decline in the number of Nepalis leaving the country for foreign employment.
A total of 130,483 Nepalis, including first-time workers and those renewing their work permits, left for foreign employment between mid-July and mid-September, compared to 136,084 during the same period in the previous fiscal year.
Likewise, gross foreign exchange reserves rose 4.6 percent to 26.48 billion dollars in mid-September from 25.31 billion dollars in mid-July, according to the report.
"Based on the imports of the two months of 2026-27, the foreign exchange reserves are sufficient to cover the prospective merchandise imports of 20.9 months, and merchandise and services imports of 17.8 months," the report said. ■

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Malaysia's information and communication technology (ICT) economy grew 5.6 percent in 2025, contributing 476.8 billion ringgit (about 116.8 billion U.S. dollars), or 23.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), official data showed on Thursday.
The ICT economy, comprising the ICT industry and e-commerce, accelerated from 5.2 percent growth in 2024, the Department of Statistics Malaysia said in a statement.
The ICT industry generated 288.1 billion ringgit in gross value added, with ICT services accounting for the largest share at 40.3 percent, followed by ICT manufacturing at 38.2 percent.
The two segments grew 7.6 percent and 6.4 percent, respectively, while ICT trade, content and media accounted for the remaining 21.5 percent.
E-commerce generated 267.6 billion ringgit in gross value added, equivalent to 13.2 percent of the economy, growing 3.7 percent in 2025.
Manufacturing accounted for 50.5 percent of e-commerce gross value added, expanding 1.3 percent, while services contributed 47 percent, with growth accelerating to 7.2 percent from 5.1 percent in 2024.
Exports of ICT products rose 14.8 percent to 513.6 billion ringgit, while imports increased 24.2 percent to 405.3 billion ringgit, resulting in a trade surplus of 108.3 billion ringgit. ■

Players walk into the pitch at Xinjiang Special Education Vocational Secondary School in Changji Hui Autonomous Prefecture, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, Oct. 14, 2026. Xinjiang's first blind football team is known as the "Wei Wei Wei" team. It takes its name from the call players shout to locate teammates and avoid collisions. This call is the communication code of this special sport.
In blind football, players wear light-blocking blindfolds throughout the match. They track the ball by the bell inside it and keep calling "wei, wei, wei" to gauge teammates' positions, enabling them to dribble, pass and shoot without sight. In training, they run, collide, feel the boundary boards, and build muscle memory through countless falls and getting back up. For visually impaired teenagers who rarely dare to sprint at full speed in daily life, this enclosed pitch is a place where they can run freely.
"We cannot see the world, but we strive to make the world see us." In the darkness, guided by their calls and the sound of the ball, these young athletes break through barriers and shine brightly on the green pitch. (Xinhua/Ding Lei)

China releases probe results on formamide-related safety issues in infant diapers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
19:47:41 CST
20:47:41 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- A joint investigation team comprising four Chinese government departments on Thursday released findings of a probe into safety concerns over formamide in infant diapers, concluding that no formamide was detected in tested diaper products.
The joint investigation was conducted by the State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR), together with the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, the National Health Commission, and the National Disease Control and Prevention Administration, following recent public discussions over the issue.
The investigation team carried out spot checks on 168 domestic baby diaper manufacturers, including contract manufacturers, covering 368 batches of finished diaper samples from 180 brands, according to a statement released by the SAMR.
Testing was entrusted to authoritative institutions, including the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention and the Chinese Academy of Quality and Inspection & Testing. No formamide was detected, the statement said.
All inspected enterprises met the hygiene requirements for the production of disinfection products, and no addition or presence of formamide was found in production processes or raw materials.
The investigation confirmed that several testing entities at the center of the public concern, which claimed to have detected formamide in baby diapers, were found to have deficiencies, including unclear principles for qualitative determination, failure to conduct blank and parallel sample tests, flawed testing procedures and criteria for determination, and the deletion of raw data, making it impossible to reach a conclusion that formamide was detected.
The joint investigation team also commissioned academicians and experts to develop a blood sample formamide testing method through repeated verification. Using this method, a re-test of the blood samples tested by an institution of public concern found no formamide.
Based on current investigation and test results, no formamide-related health hazards from baby diapers have been found, the statement said.
Testing for formamide in baby diapers is a rigorous and professional activity, and research into formamide-related health hazards, in particular, should be conducted in a prudent and objective manner, the statement said.
The statement added that relevant authorities will continue to strengthen supervision of infant products and welcome public participation to jointly create a safe and reassuring consumption environment. ■

Swedish parliament rejects Andersson's PM nomination amid coalition deadlock
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
19:47:40 CST
20:47:40 KST

HELSINKI, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Sweden's parliament on Thursday rejected Social Democratic Party leader Magdalena Andersson's nomination as new prime minister (PM), prolonging a political deadlock over government formation following last month's general election.
Andersson, who served as Sweden's PM from 2021 to 2022, received 99 votes in favor and 248 against in the 349-member Swedish parliament, the Riksdag, according to Swedish Television (SVT).
Following the vote, Andersson told SVT that the Riksdag was facing a difficult situation and that several rounds of voting might be needed before a new government could take office.
The vote came after Parliament Speaker Andreas Norlen nominated Andersson on Tuesday to lead a single-party Social Democratic government, despite the failure of negotiations among four parties that together secured a narrow parliamentary majority in the September election.
The Social Democratic Party, Left Party, Green Party and Center Party won a combined 176 seats, but remain divided over the composition of a new government.
According to SVT, coalition talks have been hampered mainly by disagreements between the Center Party and the Left Party, with the latter insisting on joining the government and securing cabinet posts, while the Center Party refuses to serve in the same government.
The Left Party, Green Party and Center Party all announced ahead of Thursday's vote that they would oppose a single-party Social Democratic government.
Andersson acknowledged Tuesday that although progress had been made in coalition negotiations, conditions were still not in place to form a government capable of securing sufficient parliamentary support.
The former PM was first tasked with exploring the formation of a new government on Sept. 18, after outgoing PM Ulf Kristersson requested to be relieved of his duties following the election.
However, she returned the mandate on Sept. 28 after the Left Party backed the Moderate Party's candidate rather than the Social Democratic Party's candidate in the parliamentary speaker election. Norlen subsequently reassigned her the task in early October, but negotiations remained inconclusive.
Under Sweden's system of negative parliamentarism, a PM candidate can take office unless at least 175 of the 349 lawmakers vote against the nomination.
Following Thursday's rejection, Norlen will have to put forward another candidate. Under Sweden's constitution, if parliament rejects four proposed PM candidates, an extraordinary election must be held. ■

France's CPI climbs more than 3 pct in September

PARIS, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- France's consumer price index surged 3.1 percent year on year in September 2026, accelerating from 2.4 percent in August, according to data released by the French National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies on Thursday.
The annual inflation rate was revised up by 0.1 percentage point from the provisional estimate published on Sept. 30. According to French news channel BFM TV, the CPI reached its highest level since January 2024.
The acceleration was mainly driven by faster increases in energy prices, which surged 21.3 percent year on year in September, up from 16.7 percent in August. Service prices also accelerated, rising 2.4 percent from 1.9 percent in August, while food prices increased 1.4 percent, up from 1.1 percent.
The decline in manufactured goods prices narrowed to 0.3 percent from 0.4 percent in August. Tobacco prices rose 3.3 percent year on year, unchanged from the previous month.
On a monthly basis, the CPI fell 0.3 percent in September, following a 0.7 percent increase in August. Seasonal drops in service prices drove the decline, which fell 1.4 percent after a 0.1 percent decline in August.
Energy prices rose for the third consecutive month, increasing 3.9 percent month on month in September, compared with 3.4 percent in August and 2.3 percent in July. Manufactured goods prices rose 0.5 percent, slowing from 1.6 percent in August, while food prices increased 0.1 percent, down from 0.4 percent. Tobacco prices remained stable for the second consecutive month.
Core inflation stood at 1.5 percent year on year in September, up from 1.1 percent in August, the statistics organization said. ■

Frozen Russian Assets: Europe Rejects US Control Plan – FT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:46:58 UTC
20:46:58 KST

The US proposed that European countries unfreeze some Russian sovereign assets and place them under Washington’s oversight to help revive negotiations over Russia’s war against Ukraine, according to a report published on Thursday, Oct. 15.
The Financial Times reported, citing four people briefed on the discussions, that US envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner presented the idea during talks in Miami. European representatives rejected it.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“They were told that this was just simply not going to happen,” one person told the newspaper.
The proposal involved transferring some immobilized reserves into a new financial vehicle overseen by Washington. A US official told the FT that possible uses of the assets were being discussed as part of a comprehensive peace agreement, with the mechanisms for releasing and spending the money still under consideration.
The Miami talks brought together representatives of Ukraine, Britain, France, Germany, the European Commission, and NATO alongside American negotiators. The meeting ended without an announced breakthrough.
Europe opposes surrendering control
European officials at the meeting opposed both handing control of the assets to another party and returning any of the funds to Moscow, according to the report.
Western countries immobilized roughly €260 billion ($291 billion) in Russian sovereign assets after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Around €210 billion ($235 billion) remains blocked in the EU, with much of it held through the Brussels-based securities depository Euroclear.
Military Starlink Service Restored in Ukraine, Defense Sources Say
These are Russian central bank reserves, distinct from the private property of sanctioned businesspeople. EU restrictions prohibit transactions involving the management of those reserves, preventing Moscow from freely accessing them.
European leaders have repeatedly said the assets should remain immobilized until Russia ends its war and compensates Ukraine. In December 2025, the EU adopted additional emergency measures prohibiting transfers of the central bank’s assets or reserves back to Russia. Those measures strengthened the freeze without transferring ownership of the underlying reserves to Ukraine.
European governments nevertheless remain divided over how far they should go in using the funds. Belgium has raised legal and financial concerns about proposals to mobilize the principal, while Ukraine has pressed its partners to use Russian reserves more broadly to finance its needs.
The assets already help finance Ukraine
The EU currently channels extraordinary earnings generated by the immobilized reserves toward assistance for Ukraine, while keeping the underlying assets frozen.
According to the Council of the EU, the assets have generated €8 billion ($9 billion) in windfall profits. Of that amount, €3.8 billion ($4.2 billion) has reached Ukraine, while €4.2 billion ($4.7 billion) has contributed to repayment of EU-G7 loans or been set aside for that purpose.
Under the current distribution rules, 95 percent of those revenues goes through a mechanism helping Ukraine repay approximately €45 billion ($50 billion) in EU-G7 loans. The remaining five percent support the European Peace Facility, which finances military assistance.
A separate €90 billion ($101 billion) EU support loan for 2026-27 is financed through European borrowing backed by the EU budget. European leaders agreed that Ukraine would repay that loan once it receives Russian reparations, while reserving the EU’s right to use immobilized Russian assets for repayment in accordance with international and EU law.
The dispute therefore concerns more than the location of the reserves: European governments have already tied them to Ukraine’s financing and eventual compensation for war damage.
Washington has floated economic incentives before
The latest proposal follows earlier discussions about offering Moscow economic incentives for a limited ceasefire.
Those discussions included releasing some frozen Russian reserves, authorizing a transaction involving Lukoil’s foreign assets, and easing restrictions on Belarusian potash exports. The incentives were reportedly presented as measures that could encourage a partial halt to fighting, including attacks on energy infrastructure or maritime routes.
Ukrainian negotiators sought safeguards in those discussions, including matching financial releases for Ukraine and guarantees of faster military assistance if Russia violated a prospective truce.
Frozen reserves also featured in a 28-point US-backed draft peace plan published in 2025. That draft proposed investing $100 billion in Russian assets in US-led reconstruction efforts in Ukraine, with Washington receiving 50 percent of the profits. It also envisaged a separate US-Russian investment vehicle.
The new asset proposal comes amid a broader disagreement over sanctions relief. European governments have opposed following Trump’s Russian diesel agreement, arguing that pressure on Moscow should remain in place while Russian attacks continue.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said earlier this week that following Washington’s diesel decision was “out of the question” for Germany and Europe, while maintaining that European governments remained in contact with the US over a common approach to ending the war.
