A fungus is threatening the world’s food supply. Scientists just found a new defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:45:43 UTC
20:45:43 KST

A fungus is threatening the world’s food supply. Scientists just found a new defense
- Date:
- October 15, 2026
- Source:
- John Innes Centre
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a potential new weapon against a devastating fungus that threatens rice, wheat, and barley worldwide. By engineering a special type of plant immune receptor, researchers created defenses capable of recognizing multiple fungal threats at once. The breakthrough could eventually lead to crops with powerful, long-lasting disease resistance, helping protect a global food supply increasingly threatened by spreading infections and climate change.
- Share:
Scientists have uncovered a promising new way to protect some of the world's most important food crops from a destructive fungus that threatens global food security. By engineering the natural immune defenses of plants, researchers have developed an experimental approach that could eventually help wheat, rice, and barley resist fungal infections more effectively.
The international research team, led by scientists at the John Innes Centre in the United Kingdom, investigated a recently discovered group of plant immune receptors. They identified how these proteins recognize invading pathogens and demonstrated that they can be modified to detect multiple fungal threats. The findings could open the door to crops with stronger, more durable disease resistance.
"We've discovered something that could lead to a potential intervention on what is the worst fungal disease of cereals," said Professor Mark Banfield, a research group leader at the John Innes Centre and an author of the study, which involved collaborators at Kobe University in Japan.
A Devastating Fungus Threatens the Global Food Supply
The target of the research is Magnaporthe oryzae, the fungus responsible for blast disease. It causes the most serious fungal disease affecting cultivated rice and has also become a major threat to wheat and barley in parts of Asia and Africa.
The damage is enormous. Each year, rice blast destroys enough rice to feed approximately 60 million people. As the fungus spreads into additional agricultural regions, developing effective ways to protect crops has become increasingly important for global food security.
The fungus infects plants through a sophisticated biological strategy. It delivers specialized molecules known as effectors into cells in the leaves and stems. These molecules interfere with normal plant functions, allowing the pathogen to establish an infection and promote disease.
Plants, however, have evolved their own defense systems. Specialized immune receptors can recognize these foreign molecules and trigger a protective response. One important mechanism involves causing infected cells to die in a controlled, localized area, helping prevent the pathogen from spreading farther through the plant.
Scientists Discover a Hidden Plant Immune Defense
For more than three decades, much of the research into plant immunity has centered on proteins called Nucleotide-binding and leucine-rich receptors (NLRs). These receptors have played a central role in understanding how crops recognize and defend themselves against blast disease and other infections.
More recently, scientists have begun investigating another group of immune proteins found in cereal crops, known as tandem kinase proteins (TKPs). Although researchers are still learning how these receptors operate, they appear to offer additional opportunities for strengthening plant defenses.
Earlier studies revealed that some TKPs contain a specialized region called a Heavy Metal Associated (HMA) domain. Similar regions are also found in certain NLR receptors, where they help recognize pathogen effectors and initiate immune responses.
This shared feature attracted the attention of Banfield and his colleagues because it suggested that scientists might be able to redesign the receptors to recognize additional fungal threats.
"This piqued our interest," said Professor Banfield. "If we can engineer these integrated HMA domains for new properties by making amino acid protein changes where effectors bind, we can gain what we call novel recognition specificities - and potentially a new frontline for defense of plants against disease."
Turning Fungal Attack Molecules Into Targets
In the study, published in Science Advances, researchers examined precisely how HMA domains interact with the molecules released by the blast fungus.
Using biophysical techniques and crystallography, a method that allows scientists to determine the detailed three-dimensional structure of molecules, the team obtained a high-resolution view of how these plant receptors bind to fungal effectors.
The results revealed that HMA domains can function as biological bait. By binding to molecules the fungus uses during infection, these regions help plants recognize the presence of an invading pathogen and activate their defenses.
Armed with this structural information, the researchers modified TKP immune receptors so they could recognize two different fungal effectors associated with infections in wheat and barley.
This ability to detect multiple targets, known as dual specificity, is unusual in naturally occurring immune receptors. Demonstrating that it can be introduced through protein engineering suggests a promising way to expand the range of threats that crop immune systems can recognize.
The findings also provide a foundation for investigating other recently identified TKPs in different cereal crops. Scientists may eventually be able to design customized immune receptors that detect several fungal effectors simultaneously, potentially making plants more difficult for pathogens to infect.
Engineering Crops With Stronger Disease Resistance
Although the findings are encouraging, the technology remains at an early experimental stage.
The researchers conducted their initial tests using protoplasts, individual wheat cells that serve as a simplified model for studying how plant tissues respond. The next step is to determine whether the engineered receptors can provide effective protection in whole plants grown under controlled greenhouse conditions.
"Our study indicates that this new class of resistance proteins is amenable for engineering purposes. We now know that the previous tools we used in engineering NLR receptors may also work with this new class," said Dr. Daniel Yu, the first author of the study.
Understanding exactly how fungal effectors attach to plant immune receptors could also help researchers take advantage of other technologies. Precision breeding and artificial intelligence may provide additional ways to redesign HMA domains, allowing them to recognize pathogen molecules that previously escaped detection.
One particularly promising possibility involves combining different types of immune receptors within the same crop.
Because NLRs and TKPs appear to activate plant defenses through different mechanisms, using them together could create several layers of protection. This might make it harder for fungi to evolve ways around a plant's immune system.
"We think these two classes of immune receptors, NLRs and TKPs, are probably activated in different ways," said Professor Banfield. "That gives the potential for more robust immunity in the field because you are not putting all your eggs in one basket. Further down the road, we may be able to use techniques to stack genes encoding TKPs and NLRs together against the same disease, making a super-resistant crop. They will have different ways of activating immunity, so it is likely to be more difficult for a pathogen to evolve away from," he added.
A Growing Threat to Wheat, Rice, and Barley
The need for better protection is becoming more urgent as blast disease continues to threaten major food crops.
Wheat blast was first identified in Brazil during the 1980s and has since spread to parts of Asia and Africa. Although the disease has not been detected in the United Kingdom, climate change could eventually create conditions that allow it to threaten cereal production in northern Europe.
For farmers, the emergence of blast disease in new regions presents a serious challenge, particularly because the fungus can threaten crops that are essential to feeding large populations.
By revealing how a previously underexplored class of plant immune receptors can be engineered to recognize multiple fungal threats, the researchers have identified a possible new strategy for protecting future harvests.
Further testing will be necessary to establish whether these modified defenses work effectively in whole plants and under agricultural conditions. If successful, combining different immune receptors could eventually help scientists develop crops with more resilient protection against one of agriculture's most destructive fungal diseases.

Ukrainians fear US intelligence cuts as Russian strikes intensify

Ukrainians fear US intelligence cuts as Russian strikes intensify
Reduced missile warnings increase threat to civilians as Trump pushes an ‘energy ceasefire’ and peace negotiations.
Kyiv, Ukraine – The supernova-like blasts of exploding Russian ballistic missiles are followed by thunderous thumps, shockwaves, fires and deaths – and the staccato of Ukrainian air defence systems.
This week’s nightly attacks on Ukraine that killed at least 15 and wounded dozens resembled hundreds of previous raids – with one exception.
The air raid sirens began howling just seconds before or after yet another wave of missiles struck apartment buildings, power plants and warehouses.
But Ukraine’s partners did not provide the country with intelligence data from NATO’s early-warning satellites, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday, as tensions between Washington and Kyiv rise.
He did not name the United States and President Donald Trump has denied that Washington has stopped sharing intelligence.
The constellation of military satellites detects Russian ballistic missile attacks by the rockets’ thermal flames seconds after launch.
The warnings give Ukrainians up to 10 minutes – precious, life-saving time to sound air raid sirens and send emergency text messages to prompt evacuations to bomb shelters.
“That’s what helps prevent the killings,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine’s ground radars can only detect the incoming missiles as their speed ranges from 6,000 to 12,000km/h (3,730 – 7,260 miles per hour).
‘Trump pressures our president’
Despite Trump’s denial, Ukrainian observers have a simple yet harrowing explanation – the US president wants to help Republicans win more congressional seats in upcoming midterm elections by pressuring Kyiv into declaring an “energy ceasefire” with Moscow that would drive global oil prices down.
“Trump pressures our president, pressures Ukraine” as he strives to “get advantage by any means necessary in the election campaign,” Lieutenant-General Ihor Romanenko, former deputy head of Ukraine’s general staff of armed forces, told Al Jazeera.
The lack of intelligence data “significantly affects the effectiveness of air defence, we don’t have time to respond,” he said.
Without the satellite data, Ukrainian drones and missiles also “lose precision when striking targets deep in Russia,” he said.
On Sunday, Trump announced the ceasefire that envisages no mutual strikes on energy infrastructure – from Russian oil refineries and fuel depots to Ukrainian power and heating stations.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Trump wrote on social media.
Kyiv said the announcement was a surprise, while Moscow declined to say whether it backs the idea – and kept on hitting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
The pressure goes beyond the refineries as Trump wants to quickly reopen, arbitrate and complete peace talks between Kyiv and Moscow – even if they benefit the Kremlin.
“He needs peace talks to succeed. Ideally, it is a certain unblocking of the peace settlement process, when Kyiv shows more willingness to agree with Russia’s demands,” Kyiv-based analyst Igar Tyshkevych told Al Jazeera.
The pressure will continue until “Kyiv shows readiness for a compromise and concessions towards Russia,” he said.
Moscow “simply abuses” the pressure and the suspension of air raid warnings to escalate attacks on Ukraine, he said.
Kyiv’s ‘priority’: The destruction of oil refineries
The suspension of data-sharing was especially shocking, given that Kyiv did stop hitting Russian refineries for three days.
It was only on Wednesday that its drones attacked refineries in Saratov and Ryazan regions, said Russia’s Deputy Prime Minister, Aleksander Novak.
However, Kyiv’s focus on striking oil refineries is ineffective and counterproductive, another observer said.
“Kyiv’s strategic priority is still the destruction of oil refineries,” Nikolay Mitrokhin of Germany’s Bremen University, who has penned hundreds of authoritative analyses of the hostilities, told Al Jazeera.
However, Russia overcame the initial shock by transporting gas from refineries in Siberia and exporting it from neighbouring Belarus and Kazakhstan.
No economic collapse, massive joblessness or public protests followed the strikes, while Moscow continued its air raids, adding jet-powered drones that resemble cruise missiles and are hard to down with Ukraine’s existing air defence system, he said.
“What is the basis for Kyiv’s and its backers’ conviction that strikes on oil refineries and depots will lead to Russia’s strategic defeat before Ukraine is defeated? I don’t understand,” he said.
However, Ukrainian attacks on data centres, bridges and factories where drones are assembled are far more effective, he said.
Recent strikes on data centres of Russian online giant Yandex and the state-run Sberbank resulted in disruptions of services in Russia and even former Soviet republics where Yandex operates its online payment, food delivery and taxi services.
Trump “didn’t ask him to stop the war, to give away cities or stop striking Russian rears in general,” Mitrokhin said.
Kyiv has repeatedly reiterated that it was ready to start peace talks if they are preceded by a ceasefire, but Moscow wanted to continue ground assaults and air raids until the peace terms were finalised – which could take months or even years.
‘We’re ready for any turn of events’
On Wednesday, Ukraine’s drone czar accused Elon Musk’s SpaceX of throttling Starlink satellite terminals that are part of the military-grade Starshield system.
Serhiy Beskrestnov said that SpaceX abruptly and without any warning limited services for terminals placed on drones flying over 160km/h (100mph).
The limit affected crucially-important interceptor drones and followed Trump’s request, presidential adviser Serhii Sternenko said.
Musk said that the White House owns and controls the Starshield systems and that any limits on speed are decided by Trump.
Some military analysts warn that the limit may be followed by a total shutdown of Starlink for Ukraine that could damage the quality of all military communications.
“But we were getting ready for everything,” Andriy Pronin told Al Jazeera. “We already know it may happen, that’s why we’re ready for any turn of events.”
In September 2022, Musk secretly ordered engineers to switch off Starlink coverage in the Russia-occupied Kherson region, effectively thwarting Kyiv’s push to retake it, Reuters reported.
In 2023, Musk threatened to cut off Ukrainian military access to Starlink unless the US defence department took over the costs.
Later, the Pentagon, Poland and other European allies took over the costs.

Millions of phones exposed to Israeli spyware operation through online ads, researchers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:45:37 UTC
20:45:37 KST

Rather than persuading victims to click a malicious link, attackers can exploit advertisements to identify and potentially infect devices without any interaction from the user. | Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
An Israeli surveillance technology firm has run a large-scale operation to infect mobile phones with spyware using online advertisements to hack the devices, researchers said on Thursday.
An investigation by the University of Toronto's Citizen Lab and cybersecurity firm Confiant Threat Intelligence laid bare an ad-based infection technique developed by an Israeli company that researchers named "AdFection." The hacks weaponized legitimate online ad systems for espionage purposes, allowing spyware manufacturers to connect to millions of devices and identify, track and target victims.
“Plugging into the online ads ecosystem provides the mercenary spyware industry a stealthy delivery system,” said Bill Marczak, senior researcher at The Citizen Lab. He said the findings were “surely just the tip of the iceberg” of how online ads are abused for espionage.
Advertisement
Researchers discovered critical details of the hacking tools by analyzing devices belonging to journalists and staff at the Al Jazeera media network, finding that 45 devices of journalists and staff were targeted and some infected with Israeli-made spyware known as Candiru.
At the heart of the hacking campaign is the Israeli company Discover-Tech that describes itself as an advertising business. Citizen Lab researchers said the company facilitated surveillance for commercial spyware operators. Its platform, called Controlium, allegedly allowed spyware makers like Candiru — which in 2025 was acquired by Integrity Labs — to identify, track and target devices by loading advertisements on websites and apps.
Discover-Tech and Integrity Labs did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The scale is striking: An analysis of four billion advertising records found that Discover-Tech's ads appeared across nearly 200,000 websites and mobile apps in dozens of countries over four months. Among the websites that featured the ads were institutional sites of NATO, the United Nations, the European Parliament, European Commission and Council of the EU.
The technique exploits real-time bidding — the automated system used by platforms such as Google to sell advertising space and target users. Rather than persuading victims to click a malicious link, attackers can exploit advertisements to identify and potentially infect devices without any interaction from the user — a technique known as "zero-click" infections.
Discover-Tech's advertisements directed millions of devices to servers associated with Candiru, potentially enabling large-scale surveillance and reconnaissance, researchers said. That does not mean all those devices were infected.
The findings triggered calls for further investigation on Thursday. “The possibility that EU institutions have been exposed should set off alarm bells across Brussels," said Hannah Neumann, a German European Parliament lawmaker of the Greens group. Neumann herself was the victim of a cyber-espionage operation by an Iranian hacking group.
"Europe cannot claim to defend democracy while leaving its own democratic institutions vulnerable to spyware,” Neumann said.

Türkiye prepares local climate action projects for COP31 Climate Change Conference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15

Fatma Zehra Solmaz
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
The Ankara Climate Transition Forum, held in the runup to next month’s COP31 UN Climate Change Conference, to be hosted in the southern Turkish city of Antalya, kicked off on Thursday in Ankara, the nation's capital.
The forum aims to showcase local climate action initiatives for Antalya, in line with the COP31 Presidency’s goal of delivering a conference focused on implementation, with participation from EU representatives, the UN Development Program, municipalities, international financial institutions, and scientists.
Halil Hasar, head of climate change at Türkiye’s Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Ministry, said at the forum’s opening that tackling climate change requires collective action.
Stressing the importance of early warning systems and data, Hasar said: “One neighborhood is facing a heat wave, while another is dealing with rain and flooding. We are living in a different era where even normal conditions are changing.”
Hasar said 2024 was Türkiye's hottest year on record, while 2025 was its driest.
He said long-term precipitation levels have fallen 28%, adding that rainfall of 300 kilograms (661 pounds) per square meter in a single day reflects the consequences of the climate crisis rather than ordinary precipitation.
Hasar stressed the importance of local climate action and science-based planning, saying preventive measures could reduce costs.
He said Türkiye would showcase pilot projects at the conference in Antalya, adding: “We will try to demonstrate these efforts to everyone through a pilot project in Antalya at COP31.”
COP31, the UN Climate Change Conference, is due to be held on Nov. 9-20 in Antalya on the Turkish Riviera, with Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Minister Murat Kurum serving as president.
According to the UN, the conference “is where the world comes together to agree on the actions to address the climate crisis, such as limiting the global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7F), helping vulnerable communities adapt to the effects of climate change, and achieving net-zero emissions by 2050.”
The conference will bring together world leaders and negotiators from the member states of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) to further global progress, with business leaders, young people, climate scientists, Indigenous peoples, and civil society “sharing insights and best practices to strengthen global, collective, and inclusive climate action,” the UN added.

Gaza's patients face death as Israel restricts Rafah crossing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:43:07 UTC
20:43:07 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza's patients face death as Israel restricts medical evacuations via Rafah
Khitam Doghmosh, a Palestinian cancer patient in Gaza battling lymphoma and breast cancer, fears she will die before getting any chance to seek treatment outside the war-torn enclave.
Despite receiving an urgent medical referral, the 45-year-old mother of five remains stranded in the besieged territory, where shortages of medicines and medical equipment have left her without the treatment she needs because of Israeli policy.
On 5 February 2024, the Israeli army killed Doghmosh's husband in an airstrike. Two months later, in April, she was diagnosed with lymphoma and breast cancer and spent more than two months in hospital without receiving adequate treatment.
"The doctors did everything they could, but there are no medicines or treatments available for my condition, which is why they issued an urgent medical referral," she described to The New Arab. "Since that day, I have been waiting in vain. Only a small number of patients manage to leave Gaza, and there are others ahead of me in the queue. I am terrified I will die before my turn arrives."
Doghmosh has lost more than 40 kilograms because of her illness. "I am in my forties, yet I look like I am in my sixties as if I was an elderly woman worn down by disease," she said, sharing fears about what would happen to her children if she died.
Her ordeal reflects the plight of thousands of patients awaiting medical evacuation as Israel continues to prevent sick and wounded Palestinians from leaving through the Rafah crossing, which has remained closed to patient evacuations for more than two weeks, according to Gaza's Ministry of Health.
Mohammed Abu Afash, director of Medical Relief in Gaza, told TNA that 2,027 patients had died while awaiting treatment and medical evacuation since October 2023, amid the continued Israeli closure of crossings and restrictions on the entry of medicines and medical supplies.
"More than 21,000 patients require medical evacuation," Abu Afash said, adding that no patients had left through Rafah in the preceding five days.
"Those awaiting travel include cancer patients, people with kidney failure and heart disease, and others with chronic illnesses requiring specialised care unavailable in Gaza. Delays can worsen their conditions and lead to potentially fatal complications," he explained.
The healthcare system is also struggling with severe shortages of medicines, medical supplies and diagnostic services, including laboratory tests, radiology and operating theatres.
Out of more than 574 healthcare centres operating before the war, only 227 remain functional, many with limited resources, undermining services for pregnant women, children and other patients, he explained.
Thousands face years-long wait
Beyond the illegal Israeli closure itself, the scale of the waiting lists and the limited number of patients permitted to leave have deepened the crisis.
Gaza's Medical Referral Committee at the Ministry of Health warned that evacuating the more than 21,000 patients and wounded people currently awaiting travel could take four years under the existing mechanism, even if no new cases were added.
With new medical referrals continuing to be approved each month, clearing both the accumulated backlog and incoming cases could take approximately eight years, the committee said.
For patients whose conditions require urgent intervention, such delays could prove fatal.
In a press statement, the Ministry of Health said the closure of Rafah was depriving patients and wounded people on approved travel lists of access to medical treatment, while adding to the burden on hospitals already struggling to accommodate critical cases.
The closure also prevents patients from departing on the three days each week designated for coordinating medical evacuations, disrupting travel schedules and prolonging waits for those who have already completed medical and security procedures.
The ministry called on international, UN and human rights organisations to pressure Israel to ensure the sustainable reopening of Rafah and other crossings and facilitate the immediate departure of critically ill patients and those with severe injuries.
War survivors stranded without care
The crisis also affects Palestinians wounded during the war who require specialised treatment abroad, including survivors who have lost entire families and are now struggling to secure care for themselves and their children.
Tamer Mahmoud was injured in an Israeli strike on his home in al-Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza in May 2024. The Israeli army attack killed his mother, sisters, nieces and nephews, wife and three children. He survived alongside one of his children and his father.
Mahmoud requires treatment abroad for his injuries, while his surviving child, who is already a disabled child, requires spinal cord-related therapy that was unavailable in Gaza even before the war.
"I survived alongside my child, who has special needs. I used to travel with him constantly to Egypt for spinal cord treatment therapy that wasn't even available in Gaza before the war, let alone now," he told TNA.
Both have received medical referrals, but neither has been able to travel.
About two weeks ago, Mahmoud received a call from the World Health Organisation telling him to prepare for travel, reviving his hopes of obtaining treatment for himself and his child.
The crossing's closure soon dashed those hopes, leaving him uncertain about when they could leave.
"A few days ago, I felt that relief was near and that I would finally be able to travel and receive treatment, but the crossing was shut," he said. "Today, I do not know whether we will travel or not."
The wait continues for Doghmosh, Mahmoud and thousands of others as their health deteriorates and treatment remains out of reach due to Israeli restrictions.
With more than 21,000 people awaiting medical evacuation and thousands of patients facing conditions that cannot withstand prolonged delays, the continued Israeli closure of Rafah threatens to turn the wait for treatment into a death sentence.

US-Iran stalemate: What are Trump’s next military options?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:41:05 UTC
20:41:05 KST

US-Iran stalemate: What are Trump’s next military options?
Trump has ruled out attacks before the midterms. Analysts weigh what he could do next, and at what cost.
United States President Donald Trump has stated on his social media platform Truth Social that he will not attack Iran before the November 3 midterm elections.
But he also told a Republican convention in September that the conflict “is going to end immediately after the elections”, and the US military has been sending more forces to the region in recent weeks.
Meanwhile, Iranian attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have surged to their highest level since the war began, with an Iranian official telling the Reuters news agency that Tehran has begun using different offensive tactics against vessels it considers to violate its restrictions.
As control of the Strait of Hormuz remains central to the US-Iran conflict, what military options does Trump have left, and what would each cost?
Al Jazeera spoke to military analysts to find out more:
Where does the US-Iran war stand?
Deadlocked.
The US and Israel first launched an attack on Iran on February 28, triggering counterattacks by Iran against US military assets and other infrastructure in Gulf countries and Jordan in the following months.
Iran also closed the Strait of Hormuz, which carried at least 20 percent of global crude and liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies before the war, sending global energy markets into chaos. The price of Crude Oil – the global benchmark – rose from about $72 a barrel the day before the war began to a high of nearly $120 a barrel earlier this year. On Thursday, it was trading at about $104.
A June ceasefire agreement collapsed over control of the strait, and Washington has kept up a naval blockade on Iran’s southern ports while Iran has continued to attack ships attempting to pass through. Indirect talks via Pakistan and Qatar continue – along with the exchange of various proposals from each side – but Trump rejected Iran’s latest offer to reopen the strait last month.
The US has “enormous military capability that Iran can’t match”, but it has not delivered the outcomes Washington wants, Afzal Ashraf, a visiting fellow in international relations and security at Loughborough University in the United Kingdom and a former senior Royal Air Force officer who served in Iraq, told Al Jazeera.
What forces does the US have in the Middle East right now?
It has at least three aircraft carrier strike groups in the Gulf, or heading towards it.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group, carrying about 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines, is sailing to the Middle East to join the carriers already there.
The US also maintains a host of military assets and about 50,000 soldiers at different bases in Middle East countries.
What are Trump’s military options?
Keep squeezing Iran
The US naval blockade on Iranian ports and the naval escorts for commercial ships it has been providing through the Strait of Hormuz are the status quo, which it can continue. This is the most likely course of action, Patrick Bury, a senior associate professor at the University of Bath and former NATO research analyst, told Al Jazeera.
Before the war began, the Strait of Hormuz typically handled about 125 large commercial vessels a day, carrying an average of 17.1 million barrels of oil. This collapsed with the closure of the strait in March.
In recent weeks, with the help of US Navy escorts, Gulf oil flows through Hormuz – excluding Iran’s – had recovered to more than 81 percent of pre-war levels in September, according to maritime tracking firm Kpler. However, this has again reversed with Iran’s recent stepping up of attacks on ships in the strait. According to Kpler, only 2.9 million barrels of oil were carried through the waterway on October 11, the lowest level this month.
Washington is trying to maintain patrols and surveillance over the southwestern side of the strait, “enough to give ships some sort of protection to get out”, Bury said. Increasingly, drones do the grunt work of feeding intelligence and carrying out attacks, which is cheaper than keeping aircraft on long sorties. “I mean, it’s been somewhat effective,” he said, adding that high oil prices and crew bonuses mean “people are willing to take some risk.”
But now, Iran has changed tactics.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre recorded 15 attacks on ships between October 6 and 14. Iran appears well prepared, Bury said, pointing to “the asymmetry of costs”. “By dint of its geography”, he explained, Iran still enjoys “a kind of easier starting point.”
Resume air and missile attacks
This is another option.
Trump has said it may be “possible” to ramp up bombing after the elections, but has not given details.
If the situation does escalate, however, Bury said he expects “further strikes in fairly limited packets” against targets on Iran’s coastline and further inland.
A new campaign could “actually achieve a lot less” than the hits earlier this year, Ashraf said, because Iran has adapted. “They have fewer, but they can conceal them better,” he said of its weapons.
The costs would also be high for the US, which has already depleted much of its stockpile of very expensive defensive missile systems.
Each relatively cheap Iranian drone or missile can force the US to fire “an interceptor of a million [dollars] or more”, he said, and “the United States is running out of missiles for its own defence.”
Furthermore, the US has fired more than 1,000 Tomahawk cruise missiles at Iran during the course of the war. Fully restoring its pre-war inventory could take until the end of 2030, according to estimates from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).
Getting back to pre-war levels across key munitions would take “three to four years”, Bury said. “The problem is to solve that issue takes a long time, even when you press Go with the money.”
Tehran has also promised to hit back harder. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf declared last month that the era of “proportionate responses” was over.
Renewed attacks could also cost Washington access to some Gulf bases, Ashraf said.
Iran’s recent retaliation has targeted Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain, sparing other Gulf states that Ashraf said may have reached an understanding with Tehran to stay out of the fighting.
Could a US ground operation against Iran be an option?
It is very unlikely, experts say.
One target could be Kharg Island, 26km (16 miles) off Iran’s coast, which handles about 90 percent of Iran’s exports.
Joseph Votel, a former US Central Command (CENTCOM) commander, has said 800 to 1,000 soldiers could take it, but they would be highly exposed to fire from the mainland, according to Reuters.
Ashraf said US forces could launch a limited invasion, likely preceded by electronic warfare to blind Iranian defences.
But Iran would then attack the island itself. “They don’t need very much in the way of targeting information, once they know the island is occupied by American forces,” he said. “And the appetite for casualties is low in a war that is already very unpopular.”
Iran could also hit oil infrastructure across the Gulf in return, he warned, concluding that the seizure of Kharg Island would be “the most irrational of the irrational decisions”.
Is a full-scale US invasion of Iran possible?
This is also highly unlikely.
Trump has largely ruled out a ground offensive, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in March that ground troops would not be needed to achieve the administration’s goals.
“I don’t think they’re going to do it anyway,” Bury said, adding, “I don’t think they can do it, to be honest with you.”
Why does the timing matter?
This war is deeply unpopular with the US public, and Trump is facing mid-term elections in a matter of weeks.
About 65 percent of Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of it, according to the Pew Research Center.
Bury argued that the bigger question is whether the US can rebuild its military strength in a short amount of time. “Can America over the next few years regenerate that as a military power?” he said.
The task would outlast Trump’s term, he added, as “the next president would need to do the same thing anyway.”
The longer the war goes on, Ashraf warned, the greater the risk of unrest across the region, arguing that “we should not divorce the military options from the enormous capacity for political instability.”
On Sunday, Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei said Tehran had been striking vessels in the US-backed shuttle through the Strait of Hormuz every night for weeks.
“You are smuggling,” he said, “but the strait is under Iran’s control.”

My autumn of comfort TV and comfort food
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:40:11 UTC
20:40:11 KST

After a summer spent travelling here, there and everywhere, I am welcoming more time at home and bingeable telly with open arms. And, like a lot of the nation, I am obsessed with this season’s Celebrity Traitors. It is my achilles heel; so much so that, earlier this year, I politely declined an invite to a hot industry party because it clashed with the final, and there is no amount of free champagne or hobnobbing that would’ve got me off my sofa. The beauty of such shows is that they are on early enough to make an evening of it. Strictly has become our Saturday night family ritual, while my eldest will usually join us for Tuesday nights watching Bake Off. There are bowls of food, eaten by the spoonful, mugs of tea and endless biscuits. It’s a small, cosy ritual that makes the passing of summer feel a little less bleak.
For ease, I try to live by the rule of one meal for everyone. On nights when we eat on the sofa, I like to make something in advance that the girls can eat after school and that we can return to later on. Nigella Lawson’s chicken barley, for instance, is a firm favourite and, importantly, if a little less glamorously, it reheats well. The same goes for Laura Goodman’s mac’n’cheese, a surefire hit and a fixture in our house.
Essentially it’s all about batch cooking, comfort and being prepared. I also love to make big pots of congee and dal, which I freeze in portions for a rainy day. Both are perfect for feeding a range of appetites, too, with toppings and accompaniments added to suit. Ravinder Bhogal’s seasonal pumpkin and miso variation is firmly on my to-make list, as is pe hin, a Burmese dal recipe from Amy and Emily Chung.
Sofa food isn’t all savoury, of course. If you’ve ever watched Bake Off, you’ll know that doing so without a sweet treat to hand is a form of torture. A mug of tea and a plate of biscuits will usually do that trick, particularly if those biscuits are homemade. Current favourites in our house are Ana Ortiz’s alfajores de dulce de leche and Rebecca Bishop’s brown butter nutmeg shortbread. If something more substantial is required – because, let’s be honest, sometimes only a warming bowl of pudding will do – my first port of call is Felicity Cloake’s sticky toffee pudding (pictured top) with her proper custard on the side, naturally. And, being autumn, I’m also a sucker for Nigel Slater’s apple and blackberry crumble, ideally with more of that custard, too. Nothing says, “hello, autumn”, like a hedgerow-inspired crumble after all.
My week in (sweet) food
A slice of Jamaica | I was recently lucky enough to be on the receiving end of one of Doreen’s homemade Jamaican rum cakes, and I cannot stop thinking about it. I’m looking for any opportunity I can to send one as a gift. You can select a variety of shapes and sizes, but I do think the heart one is particularly endearing, as well as a gorgeous sentiment. Set up by Jackie Christian, the recipe was passed down to her from her Jamaican-born mum, Doreen. It’s a beautiful story and a stunning gift, and I’m already planning on buying myself another.
Malt loaf magic | Friend and fellow food writer Nicola Miller recently introduced me to Wooster’s Bakery, a 30-plus-year-old family business that takes bread and baking seriously. Based in Suffolk, it’s not somewhere I can frequent regularly, but luckily for those of us who aren’t local, you can order their incredible malt loaf online. Mail-a-malt is divine: a delicious, sticky, plump and rich loaf that comes in a glorious circular box.
Sweet innovation | Hello, my name is Georgina Hayden and I am a full-blown chocoholic. And, fortunately for me, one of my favourite pastry chefs, Philip Khoury, has created an online shop where his chocolate creations can be enjoyed by everyone. They are all outstanding, but his latest ingenious creation may be my favourite to date: namely, fig chocolate. Made in the style of white chocolate, it’s packed with fresh figs, fig leaves and a little almond. Elegant yet playful, it feels like a more grown-up chocolate orange. Just don’t wait until Christmas.

Russia detains independent outlet Novaya Gazeta editor Sergei Sokolov

Russia detains independent outlet Novaya Gazeta editor Sergei Sokolov
Sergei Sokolov, the editor-in-chief of Russia's independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta, was detained and taken for questioning on Thursday after authorities searched his home, the newspaper said.
The chief editor at Russia's independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta, Sergei Sokolov, has been detained and taken to Moscow's Investigative Committee, his newspaper said Thursday.
Novaya Gazeta, historically a bastion of Russian independent journalism, is classed as a "foreign agent" by Russian authorities.
Read morePolitkovskaya 'predicted' Russia's turn under Putin, editor says on 20th anniversary of her death
"Sergei Sokolov, the editor-in-chief of Novaya Gazeta, is being taken to the Investigative Committee following a search of his home," Novaya Gazeta said on social media.
The newspaper said it lost touch with its editor-in-chief around noon Thursday "just before the editorial meeting he was due to chair".
It said it knew authorities searched his home and that a lawyer was on his way to Sokolov.
Read moreMusk says Zelensky should 'go' as doubts grow over US support for Ukraine
Sokolov is a veteran editor at the newspaper, whose offices are far smaller than they were before Moscow's 2022 offensive in Ukraine.
Russia has introduced strict censorship laws since sending troops to Ukraine, with many independent journalists in exile.

Hezbollah admits explosives shipment, defies Lebanon weapons ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:38:17 UTC
20:38:17 KST

Breadcrumb
Hezbollah admits seized explosives shipment is its own, demands return
Hezbollah has admitted ownership of a massive explosives shipment seized by Lebanese security forces, insisting the materials were intended for use against Israel while openly rejecting a government ban on its military activities.
Hezbollah MP Hassan Fadlallah confirmed on Thursday that the vehicle and its cargo belonged to the group, demanding the immediate release of two detained men and the return of the confiscated explosives.
The admission marks a significant escalation in the confrontation between Hezbollah and the Lebanese government, which has launched an investigation into the shipment amid fears that the materials could be used in political assassinations.
Speaking from parliament, Fadlallah said Hezbollah had contacted security and judicial authorities immediately after the vehicle was intercepted at the Dahr al-Baidar checkpoint, along a major highway connecting Beirut to the Bekaa Valley and Syria.
He said the group had informed authorities that "the vehicle and its cargo belong to the resistance" and demanded "the immediate release of the detainees and the return of the vehicle and its contents".
Fadlallah insisted that the explosives were intended exclusively for use against Israeli forces occupying Lebanese territory, rejecting suggestions that they could be used to carry out political assassinations inside Lebanon.
He accused Prime Minister Nawaf Salam of exploiting the seizure to fuel internal divisions, describing suggestions that the explosives were intended for assassinations as a politically motivated campaign.
The Hezbollah lawmaker claimed that elements within the government were using the incident to serve Israeli and American interests, warning that the group would not tolerate attempts to undermine what it considers its right to resist Israeli occupation.
He also accused the Lebanese authorities of abandoning their responsibility to protect the country and its people.
Fadlallah went further by rejecting the Lebanese government's 2 March decision banning Hezbollah's military and security activities, describing it as unconstitutional and imposed under foreign pressure.
He said the group did not recognise the decision or its consequences on the ground, accusing the government of abandoning southern Lebanon to Israeli occupation.
The lawmaker warned authorities against exploiting Hezbollah's commitment to civil peace and stability to undermine the group or its supporters, arguing that such actions could threaten Lebanon's internal security.
Explosives shipment raises assassination fears
The admission follows the seizure of approximately 500 kilograms of explosives from a grey Dodge Caravan intercepted at the Dahr al-Baidar checkpoint.
Interior Minister Ahmad Hajjar said on Tuesday that security personnel became suspicious of the vehicle because it appeared to be carrying an unusually heavy load.
A search uncovered explosive materials, prompting officers to arrest the driver and a passenger. Both suspects, along with the seized cargo, were handed over to military police on the instructions of judicial authorities.
Salam previously revealed that the vehicle was travelling from the Bekaa Valley towards Greater Beirut and was carrying hundreds of kilograms of explosives, including the powerful military-grade explosive C4.
He warned that similar materials had been used in some of Lebanon's most notorious political assassinations.
Sources familiar with the investigation previously told The New Arab that the explosives were of a type used in past political killings, raising concerns about their possible intended use.
"The case is sensitive, and the quantity of materials seized was not small. These materials have been used in political assassinations in Lebanon," the sources said.
However, investigators have not publicly established that the shipment was intended for assassinations, and Hezbollah has insisted that the materials were destined for use against Israeli forces.
The Lebanese army's intelligence directorate and the Internal Security Forces' Information Branch have been instructed by the public prosecutor to expand their investigations and identify everyone involved in transporting the explosives.
Salam has called for the investigation to continue until all those responsible are identified and referred to the judiciary.
He also praised security forces for uncovering an additional quantity of explosives in the Qasr-Hermel area near the Syrian border.
Justice Minister Adel Nassar has called for the case to be referred to the Judicial Council, a special court responsible for cases involving serious threats to national security.
Nassar previously warned that storing explosives in densely populated areas would constitute a serious crime regardless of their intended use.
He also cited concerns over reports that explosive materials had been transported towards Beirut's southern suburbs, warning that the quantities involved could cause devastating destruction.
Pressure mounts over Hezbollah's weapons
The seizure has intensified Lebanon's internal dispute over Hezbollah's arsenal, with opponents of the group urging the government to accelerate efforts to bring all weapons under state control.
On Wednesday, a committee pursuing legal action against Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem held an emergency meeting at the office of MP Ashraf Rifi.
The committee said the explosives seizure could not be treated as a minor security incident and pledged to continue pursuing its criminal complaint against Qassem as new information emerges.
It called on judicial and security authorities to establish the shipment's origin, intended destination and the identities of those involved, while demanding that the investigation remain free from political interference.
The committee also urged authorities to keep investigations into past political assassinations open and ensure that those responsible are held accountable.
The developments come amid mounting international pressure on Hezbollah to disarm, with Washington linking billions of dollars in reconstruction assistance to the group surrendering its weapons.
A US State Department spokesperson said this week that Washington was working with Gulf and European partners on a reconstruction assistance package for Lebanon but insisted that Hezbollah must first give up its arsenal.
The confrontation unfolds against the backdrop of Israel's continuing military campaign in Lebanon, which has caused widespread destruction and displacement.
Israeli forces have continued demolishing buildings and damaging infrastructure and agricultural land in southern Lebanon, while occupying parts of the border region.
Hezbollah maintains that its weapons remain necessary to confront Israeli occupation and attacks.

Frankfurt Airport facing kerosene shortage: Reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:36:55 UTC
20:36:55 KST

Oliver Towfigh Nia
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Frankfurt Airport is facing a kerosene shortage, forcing Lufthansa aircraft to carry additional fuel before arriving at the airport, according to German media reports and statements from the companies involved.
According to Lufthansa, one reason for the tight kerosene supply situation at Germany’s largest airport is reduced capacity in the pipeline connection.
Frankfurt Airport operator Fraport said routine maintenance is currently underway on a pipeline that also supplies the airport with jet fuel. However, no disruptions are expected from the maintenance, as alternative supply routes and sufficient fuel storage capacity are available.
“The airport’s operations will therefore not be affected,” Fraport said.
Meanwhile, daily Bild cited the low water level of the Rhine River as another possible factor affecting supply, as tankers can navigate the river only with limited cargo.
Lufthansa has responded to the situation by taking precautionary measures to maintain flight operations. These include having aircraft on select routes take on additional fuel before departing for Frankfurt.
The practice, known as “tankering,” is intended to reduce the need for additional refueling in Frankfurt. The report said short- and medium-haul routes are primarily affected, while long-haul flights are also increasingly being included.
According to Bild, guidelines for aircraft in the Airbus A320 family set an upper limit of eight metric tons of additional fuel. At the same time, flight planning should ensure that the added weight does not result in restrictions on the transport of passengers or cargo.
Lufthansa emphasized that the measures are intended to ensure reliable flight operations. They will remain in effect until further notice and be adjusted as the situation evolves, the report said.

Ukraine bins 'energy cease-fire' with attacks on Russian refineries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:36:00 UTC
20:36:00 KST

Ukrainian drones struck an oil refinery in Russia's Ryazan region early Thursday, hours after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy declared the end of a brief, unreciprocated truce amid growing rift with Washington.
The drone strike started a fire at the refinery about 300 kilometers (180 miles) southeast of Moscow, Russia’s Defense Ministry and Ryazan Gov. Pavel Malkov said. Russia’s Astra online news outlet posted what it said was a photograph of the blaze.
A senior Ukrainian official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to speak publicly confirmed that Ukraine had hit the refinery.
The strike could further complicate Kyiv’s relations with U.S. President Donald Trump, which have soured again in recent days.
Zelenskyy was outraged by Russia’s continuing aerial bombardment of his country’s energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump’s demand Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks.
The Ukrainian government said that it was heeding the cease-fire, but Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that Ukraine never stopped its strikes on Russian refineries. It wasn't possible to independently verify each side's claims.
Zelenskyy complained that, despite going along with Trump’s demand for a truce, Ukraine in recent days was denied the usual Western intelligence on Russian ballistic missile strikes and limits were placed on its use of U.S.-made Starlink communication terminals. Both are vital for Ukrainian defenses and attack operations.
The Ukrainian leader said that his patience had run out. He said in an interview with the Financial Times published Thursday that Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries would resume. "We’re done," he was quoted as saying.
Trump made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, despite international efforts to sanction Russia for its invasion and diplomatically isolate Putin.
Zelenskyy slammed the agreement, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than 4 1/2 years ago. U.S. efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress.
Zelenskyy said in an interview late Wednesday with Piers Morgan on the British journalist’s YouTube show that he felt betrayed by Trump’s deal with Putin, the energy cease-fire announcement and the Starlink operational issues.
"Really, yes, between us," Zelenskyy told Morgan when asked if he felt betrayed by the American president. "Our country has to survive, and we count on our real partners, strategic partners, the United States and President Trump."
He said that the U.S. behavior "was really strange and what was not like between partners but that they switch off Starlink, so some actually crazy steps between us."
In the same interview, Zelenskyy said that "we are losing a strong partner" in the United States.
He said that "it’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side. But we are OK that he’s in the middle."
Zelenskyy said someone is pushing Trump into a stance that is "not the right side of history."
The Starlink speed limits choked Ukrainian efforts to defend itself and hit back against Russia, Kyiv officials said.
Elon Musk noted on X that the military version of Starlink, called Starshield, is controlled by the U.S. military and Trump.
The absence of Western intelligence leaves Ukraine more vulnerable to Russian ballistic missiles. Trump has said the U.S. hasn't stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
Amid fears that the Trump administration may be withdrawing support for Ukraine, Zelenskyy was due in Brussels for talks with European Union leaders attending a summit.
He was traveling to Belgium after visiting London, where he won pledges of more help from U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Asked whether the EU still trusts Trump, the bloc’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, replied: "We definitely have a different approach to this war. We see that we have to pressure the aggressor to stop the war, not the victim to surrender."
"Squeezing Ukraine is not the right approach, and that is why Europe is standing beside Ukraine," Kallas told reporters at the summit, which Zelenskyy is scheduled to attend on Friday.
Three people were killed and six others injured after the Kirovohrad region of central Ukraine came under a Russian drone attack lasting more than 10 hours, Ukraine’s Emergency Services said Thursday.
Zelenskyy said on X that between midnight and Thursday morning Russia launched more than 850 drones at Ukraine, adding that the barrage came "precisely at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted."
Russian aerial attacks hit 15 Ukrainian regions, he said.
"It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine," Zelenskyy said.
"It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war and guarantee security," he added.
Ukrainian air defenses stopped 536 Russian drones during a large-scale overnight attack, the Ukrainian Air Force said, but impacts were recorded at 31 locations.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said that air defenses downed 166 Ukrainian drones overnight. It said that its forces hit two vessels carrying military cargo.

In line with the government’s transparency and open data initiative, the Military Court Service is to publish the court listings for the military court centres.
Each court listing covers the next one or two week assize period. This will be published on the internet by the last working day in advance of the assize period.
In addition to this, the court listings are published using digital signage technology within the reception areas of both military court centres.
Please be aware that the court listings are subject to change after publication, if you wish to find out more please contact the relevant military court centre. Details can be found at the bottom of each court listing.

John Healey vows to give ‘breathing space’ to consumers and businesses in first budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:33:08 UTC
20:33:08 KST

John Healey has promised to use his first budget in a fortnight’s time to offer consumers and businesses a “breathing space” while sticking to Labour’s fiscal rules.
Speaking to journalists in Bangkok, where he has been attending the International Monetary Fund annual meetings, the chancellor said he was conscious of rising costs.
“I want the budget to be a budget that gives Britain a bit of breathing space – but also reinforces the strength of our fiscal plans and the strength of our resilience and our economy for the future,” he said.
The government has already cut VAT on electricity bills, but Healey is expected to announce a further package of energy support at his 28 October tax and spending statement, before what is expected to be a sharp rise in the energy price cap in January.
He said: “The prime minister’s talked about recognising the cost of business, not just the cost of living.”
Healey also reiterated his insistence that he would be sticking to the spending plans set out by his predecessor Rachel Reeves at last year’s spending review – and that cabinet colleagues would have to find any additional resources within their existing budgets.
“When the second half of a spending review is in place, there are pressures on departments, and colleagues are doing a good job of managing with what they’ve got,” he said, adding: “You have to reprioritise if you want to do fresh things.”
The UK has been praised by the IMF this week for setting out a plan to tackle its deficit, with the fund’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, urging the government to “stay the course”.
Healey stressed he would stick to the rules set out by Reeves. “We will meet those fiscal rules, and I think one of the hallmarks of the IMF’s backing of our fiscal plans is recognition that there isn’t just a forecast for the future, but there’s some evidence of performance already.”
He declined to say whether he would increase taxes on banks, or raise capital gains tax, to offset the expected pressure on his budget from higher energy prices and government borrowing costs.
“If you think back to the run-up to previous budgets, the speculation about what was set to be in those budgets was actually deeply damaging,” he said. “It led to people cashing in their pensions early when they didn’t need to. It led to people holding back or not investing in their businesses when they didn’t need to. So I’m just not going to get drawn into any speculation.”
Healey, a former defence secretary, also hinted he was working on an additional package of support for Ukraine, to be announced at the budget.
He said: “I’m working on different ways we can step up support for Ukraine: military, diplomatic and economic, and you know, if anybody needed any reminder of that, it’s what we see coming out of Ukraine, with [Vladimir] Putin targeting these energy systems with thousands without power, as we’ve got a harsh winter approaching.
“The step back from this is that the future of Ukraine is the future of European security, and that’s why it’s so crucial that Putin doesn’t prevail.”
Healey and the Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, chaired a meeting of G20 policymakers on Thursday morning, in the absence of the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent.
The chancellor will fly back to London on Thursday evening to put the finishing touches to the budget.

Former OpenAI engineer booked flight to Saudi Arabia before arrest in bugging case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:32:21 UTC
20:32:21 KST

Dilara Hamit
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
A former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a recording device at the company’s San Francisco office booked one-way tickets to Saudi Arabia for himself and two family members before his arrest, according to a newly unsealed US court filing.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, his wife and another family member were scheduled to fly from San Francisco via Istanbul on Oct. 12, prosecutors said.
The FBI arrested Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national and US permanent resident, three days before the planned departure.
Prosecutors disclosed the bookings in an Oct. 8 motion requesting that the criminal complaint, arrest warrant and related documents remain sealed until his arrest.
“The defendant has the means – and will have an incentive – to flee the United States sooner if he learns about this case before he is arrested,” Justice Department lawyers wrote.
Alfozan is charged with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications. He faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine if convicted.
He had worked as an OpenAI engineer since July 2025 and was dismissed on the day of his arrest, the Justice Department said.
According to the complaint, OpenAI personnel discovered an audio recorder on Sept. 30, wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into a USB port behind a television in an executive conference room. Its stored files appeared to be encrypted.
The conference room was frequently used for confidential discussions about research, product plans, business opportunities, government engagements and company strategy.
Security footage allegedly showed Alfozan near the room on several occasions despite not being authorized to attend meetings there. Footage from Oct. 5 also appeared to show him looking behind the television, according to the complaint.
Prosecutors alleged that he used an internal productivity tool to search for building addresses, conference-room capacities, meeting calendars and locations used by executives and external partners.
A chatbot account associated with his wife also allegedly submitted prompts about building, concealing and remotely accessing an audio recorder, including continuous recording, live listening, encrypted storage and Wi-Fi connectivity.
The complaint does not accuse Alfozan’s wife of committing an offense or allege that she personally submitted the prompts.
OpenAI security personnel later found a similar recorder in a bag containing Alfozan’s wallet and identification, prosecutors said.
The Justice Department has not publicly identified a motive or alleged that he acted for the Saudi government or another foreign entity. He has not been charged with espionage or stealing trade secrets.
Alfozan remains in federal custody, with a detention hearing scheduled for Oct. 19, according to the US Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of California.

'It melts all sides': Slovenia takes drastic measures to stop its last glacier from vanishing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:31:14 UTC
20:31:14 KST

Locals say ‘unique ecosystems’ are vanishing and rivers are losing water as Slovenia’s last glacier melts away.
Drop by drop, Slovenia is losing its ice. The Skuta Glacier is now the last glacier left in the country. Its other glacier on Mount Triglav, Slovenia’s highest peak, has almost completely melted away.
Mountain guide Andrej Slak has watched Slovenia’s glaciers shrink for 35 years. Climbing over rocky terrain toward what remains of Skuta, he says the change has been especially noticeable over the past decade and that its impact on the local community has been devastating.
"We are standing next to Slovenia's last remaining glacier and just look at what is left of it – nothing but a small patch of ice covered in grit and debris; the change is striking.
"These glaciers serve as vital water reservoirs for us in the valley throughout the year. Shepherds used to utilise icy hollows like this to store and preserve meat, but they can no longer do that as such ice pockets are nowhere to be found in the mountains anymore."
What remains is a patch of ice on the surface of the mountainside, and the rest buried under stones, with a narrow opening leading into a crevasse.
How quickly is Slovenia’s last glacier shrinking?
In Ljubljana, scientists have been gathering data on the glaciers.
This year marks 80 years since the Anton Melik Geographical Institute at the Research Centre of the Slovenian Academy of Sciences and Arts began monitoring both glaciers.
"When we started, there were about two and a half to three hectares of ice under Skuta. Now it has shrunk to 1.5 hectares, and ice has mostly thinned out. On Skuta, it has thinned from several tens of metres to just a few metres. Back when we started, the Triglav Glacier covered a little over 14 hectares. Later, five or 10 years ago, we were still talking about half a hectare to one hectare. In recent years, it has been less than 0.2 hectares, but the ice, as I said, has now completely disappeared," explains Miha Pavsek.
Pavsek says the change is due to a combination of two factors.
"The turning point comes when we have a combination of very little snow, meaning a very low maximum seasonal snow depth, followed by a very warm summer,” he says. “And those two factors coincided very well this year.”
On Skuta, a marker painted on a rock shows how high the glacier reached in 1994. The ice has pulled back from this point since then.
“Skuta is following the same path as the Triglav Glacier. The ice is now protected. We were in the mountains a week ago, and about 80 to 90 per cent of the ice surface is covered by gravel, which provides additional protection, but it melts from all sides," says Pavsek.
Glacier melt has knock on effects on rivers and groundwater
Gravel gives the ice’s surface some protection from the sun, but inside the cave beneath the ice, water falls from the ceiling.
The effects reach well beyond the mountains.
"The waters from the glaciers feed our great rivers, including the Drava, in Croatia, as well as the Mura, which originates in Austria. There, according to the latest forecasts, all glaciers below 3,500 metres will disappear by 2050. So, these rivers will have much less water. And normally, these rivers feed the groundwater, where we have wells and pumps for drinking water," explains Pavsek.
For hikers who still come to the mountain, the loss is easy to see.
"I am concerned about this from a broader perspective, specifically regarding climate change in general, because glaciers serve as a vital reserve of Earth's water," says Tanja Plavec, a local hiker. "As they disappear, that reserve disappears with them. Furthermore, glaciers host a unique ecosystem that also vanishes as the perennial ice disappears."
This year, Europe sweltered under an exceptionally hot and arid summer, the intensity of which scientists say would have been "virtually impossible" without climate change from humans' burning of fossil fuels.
The continent is the world’s fastest-warming, with temperatures increasing twice as fast as the global average since the 1980s, according to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service.

Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, on his way to the EU summit on October 15, said that if you "want to help Ukraine? — then drink less beer," Politico reports, writes UNN.
Details
"One less beer per European per year" would help cover the costs of the war effort, he said.
"This one beer is simply a cost [for EU citizens]. For them, it is a cost of living. We drink less, their lives are saved," he said. "It's that simple."
Supplement
He said this ahead of the EU leaders' summit, which aims to bring the bloc closer to reaching an agreement on the EU's next seven-year budget. Leaders have two days of talks, covering everything from energy prices and trade with China to Ukraine, maritime security, and migration.

Scientists discover a surprising danger in smaller cancer cells
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:27:40 UTC
20:27:40 KST

Scientists discover a surprising danger in smaller cancer cells
- Date:
- October 15, 2026
- Source:
- Virginia Tech
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that unusually small cancer cells carrying extra chromosomes can be far more aggressive than larger ones, growing faster, spreading more readily, and resisting common treatments. The surprising finding could help explain why some tumors are especially dangerous and provide a new way to predict cancer outcomes.
- Share:
Some cancers grow faster, spread more aggressively, and respond less effectively to treatment than others. Researchers at Virginia Tech are uncovering surprising reasons behind these differences, including how abnormal cancer cells recruit healthy tissue to support tumor growth and why the size of certain cancer cells could help predict their danger.
The discoveries emerged from years of painstaking laboratory work, including the careful examination of tumors grown in mice.
Graduate student Megan Sweet, who studies biological sciences at Virginia Tech, spends much of her time preparing extremely thin slices of tumor tissue. Working inside a refrigerated metal chamber, she carefully adjusts a mounted tumor, roughly the size of a pinkie fingernail, toward a sharp cutting blade.
"It's all about fine-tuning and making sure it's going to be an even slice," said Sweet, who studies biological sciences.
As the blade moves through the tissue, it produces a steady, rhythmic chopping sound.
"This is the hardest and most time-consuming part," Sweet said. "But it's also kind of meditative."
Each section is cut so thin that light can pass through it. Sweet carefully transfers the delicate tissue onto a glass slide, where selected cellular structures are stained to make them easier to distinguish under a powerful microscope.
The process involves repeated rounds of cutting, staining, examining, and comparing samples. Although painstaking, this work is helping scientists piece together why certain tumors become much more dangerous than others.
The Virginia Tech team has published findings that shed new light on how cancer develops and progresses. Their research was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, with additional findings published earlier this year in Cancer Research.
How Chromosome Errors Can Fuel Cancer
Most healthy cells in the human body are diploid, meaning they contain two complete sets of chromosomes, with one inherited from each parent.
Under normal conditions, these cells divide to produce new cells with the same chromosome arrangement. Occasionally, however, something goes wrong during division, leaving cells with an abnormal number of chromosomes.
When these errors are passed on during subsequent cell divisions, they can accumulate over time. Such changes are one of the ways cancer can develop.
For the past five years, Sweet and fellow graduate student Mat Bloomfield have worked with cell biologist Daniela Cimini to investigate cells carrying abnormal numbers of chromosomes, a common characteristic of cancer.
To study the consequences of these abnormalities, Cimini's team manipulated diploid cancer cells so they would duplicate their chromosomes without completing cell division.
The result was a type of cell known as a tetraploid cell, which contains four complete sets of chromosomes rather than the usual two.
These cells are not limited to laboratory experiments. Tetraploid cells can also emerge during the development of human tumors, and their presence has been associated with cancer progression and poorer outcomes for patients.
Cancer Cells Recruit Healthy Cells to Fuel Tumor Growth
Scientists have long recognized that tetraploid cells can make tumors more aggressive. What remained unclear was exactly how they contributed to cancer growth.
To investigate, Sweet and Bloomfield compared tumors that developed from ordinary diploid cancer cells with those formed from tetraploid cancer cells.
The experiments produced an unexpected result.
As tumors grew in mice, the proportion of tetraploid cells actually decreased. Despite this decline, the tumors continued expanding rapidly and reached substantial sizes.
The researchers discovered that tetraploid cancer cells were encouraging the recruitment of stromal cells, which are noncancerous connective tissue cells that help provide structural support.
These additional cells appeared to create an environment that favored further tumor development.
"The presence of even a small fraction of these tetraploid cells can promote the recruitment of extra non-cancerous cells that support further tumor progression," Sweet said.
The finding revealed a previously unrecognized mechanism through which abnormal cancer cells can promote tumor growth, even when they account for only a small portion of the tumor.
Smaller Cancer Cells Reveal a Surprising Danger
A separate investigation uncovered another unexpected connection between tetraploid cells and cancer aggressiveness.
Bloomfield was initially examining the physical characteristics of tetraploid cells. After producing tetraploid cells from human cancer cells and establishing colonies derived from individual cells, he noticed that the resulting groups were not all the same size.
Because tetraploid cells contain twice the usual number of chromosome sets, the researchers expected them to be approximately twice as large as diploid cells.
Instead, some of the cells were 25 to 30 percent smaller than anticipated.
Even more surprisingly, those smaller cells proved to be more capable of forming aggressive tumors than their larger counterparts.
"The smaller clones are more aggressive," Bloomfield said. "They grow faster, are more invasive, and more tolerant of common anti-cancer and stress-inducing drugs."
Further experiments in mice supported these observations. Tumors containing smaller tetraploid cells frequently grew more quickly than those containing larger ones.
The pattern was not restricted to a single type of cancer. Researchers observed similar results in both colorectal and breast cancer cells, suggesting that the relationship between tetraploid cell size and tumor aggressiveness may extend across different cancers.
Cancer Cell Size May Help Predict Patient Survival
The researchers next examined whether the same relationship could be found in human cancers.
They analyzed information from the Cancer Genome Atlas, a large collection of detailed data from thousands of cancer patient samples.
The results revealed that smaller tetraploid cells were associated with worse prognoses and lower survival rates across several cancer types.
This suggests that measuring the size of these abnormal cells could provide valuable information about how aggressively a tumor might behave.
"We already knew that tetraploidy can make cells more tumorigenic, but now we know that if you incorporate the size of the cells, it can be more predictive of tumorigenic potential," Cimini said.
The findings add an important dimension to scientists' understanding of cancer. Abnormal chromosome numbers have long been linked to dangerous tumor behavior, but the new research indicates that cell size may offer additional clues about a cancer's potential to grow and spread.
The team now plans to investigate the biological mechanisms responsible for these effects in greater detail while continuing to examine human cancer data.
For Sweet, that means more hours at the laboratory bench, carefully cutting and analyzing tiny sections of tumor tissue in the search for answers to one of cancer biology's most important questions.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Virginia Tech. Original written by Kelly Izlar. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal References:
- Megan L. Sweet, Mathew Bloomfield, Nicholas Keen, Nazia Bano, Xiang Pan, Nicolaas C. Baudoin, Barath Udayasuryan, Raffae N. Ahmad, Eva Riddervold, Erica Klaiber, Scott S. Verbridge, Eva M. Schmelz, Jing Chen, Daniela Cimini. Oxidative stress and serum deprivation influence the evolution of newly formed tetraploid cells during tumorigenesis. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2026; 123 (22) DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2522077123
- Mathew Bloomfield, Sydney M. Huth, Daniella S. McCausland, Ron Saad, Nazia Bano, Tran N. Chau, Megan L. Sweet, Nicolaas C. Baudoin, Andrew McCaffrey, Kai Fluet, Eva M. Schmelz, Uri Ben-David, Daniela Cimini. Cell and Nuclear Size Is Associated with Chromosomal Instability and Tumorigenicity in Cancer Cells That Undergo Whole Genome Doubling.
