Security costs at Netanyahu's residences top $41 million, quaduple previous prime ministers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:27:31 UTC
20:27:31 KST

Israel's Prime Minister's Office paid 127,432,277 (about $41 million) shekels for security and protection projects at prime ministerial residences between 2023 and October 2026, during Benjamin Netanyahu's current term, more than four times the approximately 29 million shekels (about $9.4 million) paid in the preceding three years, according to newly disclosed government figures.
The figures, released Wednesday by the Prime Minister's Office Freedom of Information Unit following a petition filed by the Givat Mordechai Community Association with the Jerusalem District Court, reveal a sharp increase in security spending at properties under the office's responsibility.
The properties include the official prime ministerial residence on Balfour Street in Jerusalem, Netanyahu's private residence on Gaza Street in Jerusalem, which was designated an alternative official residence, and his private home in Caesarea.
However, the Prime Minister's Office stressed that the figures cover all residences under its responsibility, including official and private properties belonging to serving and former prime ministers. The disclosure does not specify how much was spent at each property.
According to the figures, 10.9 million shekels (about $3.5 million) was paid in 2023, rising to 27.8 million (nearly $9 million) in 2024. Spending then surged to 72.5 million (about $23.4) shekels in 2025, approximately six times the amount paid in 2022. A further 16.2 million shekels (about $5.2 million) was paid between January and October 2026.
By comparison, approximately 29 million shekels was paid during 2020–2022. The two totals cover periods of different lengths, with the latest figures spanning nearly four years and the earlier figures covering three.
The Prime Minister's Office attributed much of the increase since 2024 to changes in the security threat level that required substantial investment in protecting the official residence. The explanation appears to refer, at least in part, to the threat posed by explosive drones following the October 2024 drone strike on Netanyahu's private residence in Caesarea.
The attack highlighted the vulnerability of highly secured locations to aerial threats and prompted renewed scrutiny of security arrangements around the prime minister and his family. Despite releasing the overall figures, the Prime Minister's Office has refused to disclose how much was spent at individual residences, arguing that such information could compromise national security.
The disclosure has renewed scrutiny of Netanyahu's previous criticism of his predecessor, Naftali Bennett, over spending on security arrangements at Bennett's private residence in Ra'anana.
In 2022, Netanyahu shared a television report and accused Bennett of using public funds to renovate his home at a cost of 50 million shekels (about $16 million). "At the expense of Israeli citizens: Bennett renovated his private home in Ra'anana for 50 million shekels. Watch Ayala Hasson's investigation," Netanyahu wrote at the time.
However, the latest government disclosure comes alongside official figures showing that the cost of security and protection work at Bennett's home was approximately half the amount Netanyahu had publicized. According to the State Comptroller, the cost of security work at Bennett's Ra'anana residence totaled approximately 24.9 million shekels (about $8 million). 
During 2021 and 2022, when Bennett and Yair Lapid served as prime ministers for most of the period, approximately 22.7 million shekels ($7.3 million) was paid for security projects across all prime ministerial residences combined. The figures do not necessarily represent the full costs incurred during those years, as some payments for projects undertaken at the time may have been made in subsequent years.
Kobi Eisen, chairman of the Givat Mordechai Community Association, which filed the petition, told the court that the earlier report concerning Bennett had been false and argued that Netanyahu had amplified its claims. "That is why it is critical for the public to know how much money was invested in private homes," Eisen said.
Government: Spending figures could expose security weaknesses
The Security Division of the Prime Minister's Office opposed releasing a breakdown of expenses by property, saying the information could help hostile actors identify vulnerabilities and assess the level of protection at different residences.
"Publishing security expenditures for the prime minister's residences and offices could reveal the extent of the security investment allocated to them and make it possible to draw conclusions about the level of protection and security priorities," the division argued.
It warned that publishing expenses for individual properties could create security risks. According to the division, hostile actors routinely collect publicly available information, including photographs, intelligence obtained through agents and drones, and other sources.
Such information, it argued, could be combined with spending figures to identify preferred targets, potential weaknesses and possible methods of attack. The division stressed that Israel is currently facing a security threat level that is among the highest since the establishment of the state, if not the highest. Under those circumstances, it said, the requested detailed disclosure could not be permitted.
Alon Halva, the Prime Minister's Office deputy director general for security, emergency preparedness, information and cyber affairs, who is considered close to Netanyahu and his wife, also opposed releasing the figures.
Speaking during the court hearing, Halva argued that even the amount allocated to each property could provide valuable intelligence.
An adversary examining the figures alongside information gathered from other sources, he said, could compare the sums invested at residences associated with Lapid, Bennett and Netanyahu and use them to assess their respective levels of protection.
‘A number that reveals nothing’
Eisen rejected the government's arguments, maintaining that disclosing spending totals would not expose actual security arrangements or technical details. "Disclosing quantitative information does not harm security," he told the court. "There is no problem showing how much money was invested in the building on Balfour Street. The information does not allow a third party to know what the money was spent on, only how much was spent."
He argued that the figures were important primarily because they would enable voters to assess the use of public funds. "It is a number that reveals nothing, other than allowing voters to know how much was invested," Eisen said.
He again referred to Netanyahu's earlier criticism of Bennett, arguing that transparency was particularly important given the public controversy surrounding the former prime minister's residence. "The prime minister amplified the false report about Naftali Bennett concerning investments in Bennett's home. That is why it is critical for the public to know how much money was invested in private homes," he said.
Eisen emphasized that his association wanted the information released before the October 27 election. "We want the information to reach voters before voters reach the ballot box," he said. "There is a kind of limbo here. They say the voters should decide, but they are not giving voters the information they need."
Jerusalem District Court Deputy President Judge Arnon Darel ordered the Prime Minister's Office to provide an additional breakdown by Thursday, distinguishing between private and public residences and separating the figures according to periods or governments.
The order represents a further step in the legal dispute over how much information the public should receive about security expenditures at properties used by Israeli prime ministers. The court's next hearing is scheduled for Sunday, October 18, when it is expected to decide whether the more detailed figures should be made public.

King Charles III's 42-year-old younger son and Meghan, 45, who left Britain and quit royal duties in 2020 amid a bitter royal family feud, were greeted with cheers before they chatted and joked with well-wishers in the central city of Nottingham.
The royal-style visit puts the pair at odds with Buckingham Palace after the king made it clear in a letter released last month that their position was "akin to private citizens" rather than public figures and that they should not be addressed as his and her royal highness.
The couple are due to spend the day in the city visiting three charities that support young people and local communities through music, film, sport and tackling food poverty.
Known formally known as the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, they posed for selfies, hugged members of the crowd and accepted flowers.
Following a spectacular falling out with the rest of the royal family, Harry and Meghan have built bridges with the king they remain estranged from Harry's older brother and heir to the crown Prince William.
The couple settled in California six years ago but in a surprise move in August they returned to live in the United Kingdom with their two young children, Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five.
Private citizens
The late Queen Elizabeth made it clear to Harry and Meghan before her death in 2022 that there was no "half-in/half-out" option under which they could pursue commercial ventures while being working royals.
A letter issued last month by the Lord Chamberlain, the most senior official in the Royal Household, said that following the couple's relocation there had been "a number of requests for guidance".
"It is well known that in January 2020 the Duke and Duchess stepped down from undertaking representative duties on behalf of the sovereign and are no longer working members of the royal family," it said.
"This position, distinct from the state and royal duties undertaken by the working royal family, and with the personal latitude it brings the couple in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish, will continue to be fully respected."
"Working royals" are members of the royal family who carry out official duties on behalf of the monarch. They receive administrative and other support from the Royal Household to do so.
There are currently seven senior working royals, King Charles and Queen Camilla; son and heir Prince William and his wife Catherine, Princess of Wales; Charles's sister Princess Anne, brother Edward and the latter's wife Sophie.
Others working royals include several of the late Queen Elizabeth's cousins.

Don&#8217;t let Britain shelve Sally Rooney
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:25:47 UTC
20:25:47 KST

This week, something happened in Britain that should worry every reader, every writer and everyone who believes in free speech.
Faber, the publisher of the Irish novelist Sally Rooney, announced that it will no longer supply her books in the United Kingdom, in any format. Her novels, Normal People, Conversations with Friends, Beautiful World, Where Are You and Intermezzo, will slowly disappear from British bookshops.
Faber said that current UK law means it cannot pass on UK earnings to the author. It said that selling a writer’s work without paying her is not acceptable for any publisher. It will continue to sell her books in every other country.
Think about that for a moment. A British publisher can sell its own author’s books all over the world, but not in Britain.
How did we reach this point? In July 2025, the government banned the direct-action group Palestine Action under the Terrorism Act. A month later, Rooney wrote openly in The Irish Times about her position and said she would direct the proceeds of her work accordingly. The group is not banned in Ireland, where she lives. In Britain, however, she says that fulfilling her publishing contracts could now be a serious criminal offence.
She warned the High Court last year that this could happen. She also won the Sky Arts Award for literature for Intermezzo, but she could not come to London to receive it because she feared arrest.
This week, she said she had tried to be honest with the public about her beliefs, and that she was ready to accept the consequences. Many public figures hide their views to protect their careers. Rooney did the opposite. She told the truth and accepted the price.
It is fair to state the government’s position too. In June, the Court of Appeal ruled that the ban is lawful. Ministers say people can always oppose the ban by lawful means. The case is not finished, and it is expected to go to the Supreme Court. The courts will decide what is legal. But what is legal is not always what is wise.
No court has convicted Sally Rooney of any crime. No jury has heard her case. Yet the result is clear: a novelist is being separated from her readers in a democratic country because of a view she expressed. When this happens in other countries, Britain is quick to criticise it. We should hold ourselves to the same standard.
Since the ban began, thousands of people have been arrested across Britain, most of them for holding signs. Many were older people, teachers, faith leaders and former soldiers. Now the effect of the law has moved from the streets into the bookshops. Jeremy Corbyn described the decision as more proof that the ban is absurd. The band Kneecap expressed their solidarity.
Many writers and readers are now asking a simple question: if this can happen to one of the most famous writers of her generation, what is happening quietly to the writers, artists and academics we never hear about?
READ: UK removes signage from East Jerusalem consulate as Israeli closure deadline expires
For me, as a Palestinian, this is personal. My father was born in Majdal Sadiq, near Ramla. In 1948, he left with my grandfather and never returned. Our story as Palestinians has often been told by others, cut by others, or kept off the shelf completely. So when a writer with Sally Rooney’s voice refuses to stay silent, it means a great deal to us.
This is not the first time she has paid a price. In 2021, she refused to sell the Hebrew translation rights of her third novel to an Israeli publisher that would not distance itself from apartheid. Two major Israeli bookshop chains removed her books. At the same time, a Palestinian bookshop in occupied East Jerusalem ordered more copies, because readers were asking for them. Today, her books are leaving the shelves of another country.
So what can we do? We can do a lot, and all of it within the law.
First, buy the copies that are still in shops. Waterstones has confirmed that its existing stock can still be sold. Ask for her books at your local bookshop while they are still there.
Second, look for second-hand copies. Charity shops, Oxfam’s online shop, World of Books and AbeBooks all have copies already in circulation.
Third, use your public library. Borrow her novels, reserve them, and ask your library to keep them on the shelves. Librarians notice what readers ask for.
Fourth, read her and share her. Choose one of her novels for your book club. Lend your copy to a friend. A book only truly disappears when people stop reading it.
Fifth, write to your MP. Ask a simple question: why is Britain the only country where her own publisher cannot sell her books? Ask whether a law made to stop violence should end up removing novels from bookshops.
You do not have to agree with every view Sally Rooney holds to stand with her. You only need to believe in something Britain has always said it values: that writers should not lose their readers because of what they believe and say.
Her novels are about ordinary people trying to speak honestly to each other. It would be very sad if the country that made her famous became the one place where her honesty cost her a voice.
Britain can still change course. Until then, the least we can do is keep her books in our hands, and keep her voice on our shelves.
OPINION: What next after Tel Aviv closed London’s consulate—one older than the State of Israel itself?

====================================================================================================

Water scarcity and costly imports threaten food security in landlocked countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:22:36 UTC
20:22:36 KST

As one of only two doubly landlocked countries globally, Uzbekistan faces unique water and food security challenges.
Almost 57 per cent of people living in the world's 32 landlocked developing countries cannot afford a healthy diet, according to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). Around one in six faces hunger.
Home to nearly 600 million people, these countries face additional obstacles in securing food supplies and reaching international markets. Their dependence on transport routes through neighbouring states can increase costs for farmers, businesses and consumers.
A 2025 UN study quantified that disadvantage. Logistics costs per tonne of imported goods are 75 per cent higher in landlocked developing countries than in transit developing countries – the coastal nations through which exports flow. For exports, the difference is 63 per cent.
The findings provided context for discussions at the Global Technical Forum on Food Security, organised at the beginning of October by the FAO and Uzbekistan's Ministry of Agriculture in Tashkent.
Transport costs affect food security
The impact of geography extends beyond the cost of shipping agricultural products. Food imports, fertiliser and fuel can become more expensive when goods must cross additional borders or travel longer distances.
"The countries that will always be the most affected are the poorest countries, because those are the ones that import food, and their food import costs will increase," Máximo Torero, the FAO's chief economist, told Euronews.
For agricultural exporters, delays also create risks. Fresh fruit and vegetables can lose quality or spoil before reaching buyers, reducing farmers' earnings and increasing losses along supply chains.
Torero also identified climate change and population growth as long-term pressures on food production. He cited disruptions affecting the Black Sea and the Strait of Hormuz, alongside drought-related restrictions on shipping through the Panama Canal, as examples of risks to international agricultural trade.
Uzbekistan: High production, but continued reliance on imports
Uzbekistan is one of only two doubly landlocked countries in the world, alongside Liechtenstein. Neither country has direct access to the sea, and all their neighbours are also landlocked.
Agriculture, forestry and fisheries accounted for approximately 19 per cent of Uzbekistan's GDP in 2024, according to the FAO.
Despite its geographical constraints, Uzbekistan has significantly reduced hunger. The FAO estimates that the prevalence of undernourishment has remained below 3 per cent over the past decade, compared with approximately 20 per cent in 2000.
The FAO's July 2026 assessment forecast an above-average cereal harvest of approximately 9 million tonnes, including 7.3 million tonnes of wheat.
Despite that production, Uzbekistan's wheat and wheat flour import requirements are forecast at 4.2 million tonnes for the 2026-2027 marketing year. Demand for high-quality wheat, particularly from neighbouring Kazakhstan, remains significant.
The figures illustrate why domestic agricultural output alone does not eliminate the need for reliable cross-border trade.
"We are telling the world that we have moved from being 'landlocked' to 'land-linked'," Uzbekistan's Agriculture Minister Ibrokhim Abdurakhmonov told Euronews. "But this connectivity does not happen on its own. First and foremost, we need to work together to address our common challenges."
Water management and agricultural innovation
Transport connectivity is only one part of the challenge. Agriculture across Central Asia depends heavily on irrigation, while several countries share limited water resources.
"Our common challenges are particularly visible in Central Asia. First and foremost, there is the issue of water," Abdurakhmonov said.
Uzbekistan is proposing a regional initiative bringing together natural resource management, agricultural research and new technology. The minister also outlined plans to strengthen knowledge-sharing and support the adoption of new farming methods.
The FAO has identified water scarcity, land degradation and climate change among the main challenges facing Uzbek agriculture. Its cooperation programme with Uzbekistan includes initiatives covering digital agriculture, biodiversity and natural resource management.
However, increasing production does not automatically guarantee access to nutritious food.
The FAO's global food security research highlights how processing, transport and distribution costs influence the prices consumers pay. But access to nutritious food also depends on household incomes and the support available when prices rise.
"On food security, I think it's not a standalone goal but it's really part of a larger picture," Sabine Machl, the UN Resident Coordinator in Uzbekistan, told Euronews.
She highlighted education, healthcare, social protection and equal opportunities as essential parts of that wider picture. Social protection, in particular, can help vulnerable households maintain access to food when rising prices put pressure on their incomes.

IISc, Samsung open quantum lab to advance research in next-gen technology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:22:16 UTC
20:22:16 KST

BENGALURU: The Indian Institute of Science (IISc) and Samsung Semiconductor India Research (SSIR) on Thursday inaugurated a Quantum Research Lab at IISc, aiming to strengthen India's research capabilities in quantum technologies and advanced semiconductors.Supported by Samsung's corporate social responsibility (CSR) funding, the lab supports research into quantum devices, cryogenic electronics (electronics operating at extremely low temperatures), and materials that could help develop future technologies.Quantum technologies exploit the unusual behaviour of matter at the scale of atoms and subatomic particles. Unlike conventional computers, which use bits representing zero or one, quantum computers use quantum bits (qubits), which harness quantum effects to perform certain calculations in fundamentally different ways. Building reliable qubits and the systems to control them remains a major challenge.The new facility will focus on qubit characterisation, cryogenic electronics, quantum-device reliability, and single-photon sources and detectors. Single photons are individual particles of light that can carry quantum information, making them important for quantum communication and other applications.Researchers will also investigate two-dimensional (2D) materials, which are extremely thin and can have properties different from their bulk counterparts.
The work includes exploring 2D-material-based quantum devices under cryogenic conditions.A key objective of the collaboration is to make specialised research infrastructure accessible to students and researchers beyond IISc. Such equipment can be expensive to acquire and operate, limiting opportunities for institutions without dedicated facilities. The lab aims to address this gap through structured training and research exposure.The partnership will also connect quantum research with semiconductor skills development through the India Semiconductor Workforce Development Program (ISWDP), which addresses gaps in device physics, process development, modelling, simulation, characterisation and reliability. Selected modules will cover quantum materials and devices, cryogenic electronics and qubit technologies.Prof Mayank Shrivastava, chair of IISc's Department of Electronic Systems Engineering and lead for the two initiatives, said the aim was to build capabilities spanning semiconductor education and advanced research. He said the workforce programme was giving thousands of learners practical exposure to semiconductor workflows, while the new lab was advancing research into 2D-material-based quantum devices, including qubits and single-photon detectors.
Samsung Semiconductor India Research managing director Rajesh Krishnan said semiconductors and quantum were poised to be the next wave of innovation, making talent critical to India's technology ambitions, and industry-academia collaboration could create lasting impact through infrastructure, education and access.IISc director Prof Govindan Rangarajan said Samsung's support had enabled IISc to strengthen frontier quantum research and semiconductor workforce development, complementing its larger role in advancing national capabilities in quantum computing and next-generation semiconductor technologies.The initiative comes as India seeks to expand domestic expertise in semiconductors and quantum technologies. By combining specialised facilities with wider access to training, the collaboration aims to strengthen research while developing talent for these emerging fields.
Chethan Kumar is a Senior Assistant Editor with the Times of India. Aside from specialising in Space & Science, he has reported extensively on varied topics, with special focus on defence, policy and data stories. He has covered multiple elections, too. As a young democracy grows out of adolescence, Chethan feels, there are reels of tales emerging which need to be captured. To do this, he alternates between the mundane goings-on of the Common Man and the wonder-filled worlds of scientists and scamsters, politicians and soldiers. In a career spanning nearly 18 years, he has reported from multiple datelines — Houston, Florida, Kochi, Hyderabad, Chennai, Sriharikota (AP), NH-1 (J&K Highway), New Delhi, Ahmedabad, Raichur, Bhatkal, Mysuru, Chamarajanagar, to name a few — but is based out of Bengaluru, India’s science capital that also hosts the ISRO HQ.

Switzerland plans tougher social media rules to protect minors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:21:50 UTC
20:21:50 KST

Ilayda Cakirtekin
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Switzerland plans to introduce stricter rules for major communication platforms and search engines to strengthen the protection of minors online, the Federal Council said Wednesday.
Under the proposed legislation, major platforms and search engines, including those powered by artificial intelligence, would be required to assess the risks their services pose to minors and take measures to mitigate them.
Providers would also be prohibited from displaying advertisements to minors based on profiling, which involves analyzing users’ online behavior and personal characteristics.
The Federal Council said the draft legislation had received broad support during the consultation, including from a majority of political parties represented in the Federal Assembly, cantons and national associations.
The proposed bill aims to strengthen users’ rights and increase transparency among major communication platforms and search engines, as “people increasingly rely on” them to access information.
It would also require communication platform providers to establish procedures allowing users to easily report content they suspect is illegal.
The legislation would apply to very large communication platforms and search engines, while smaller services would remain outside its scope.
The Federal Council also said it would consider whether additional measures to protect minors should be included in the legislation.

Netanyahu has headed the current government since December 2022, leading a coalition widely described as the most right-wing in Israel’s history, as well as drawing international criticism for its actions in Gaza, the West Bank, and elsewhere.
Netanyahu also faces charges of corruption, bribery and breach of trust in three cases.

====================================================================================================

Flydubai hijacking attempt exposes major gaps in Israel's aviation security, experts warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:16:50 UTC
20:16:50 KST

A bomb scare aboard a Delta Air Lines flight at Ben-Gurion Airport on Tuesday morning prompted a security search that found no explosives, less than two weeks after an attempted hijacking of a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv exposed serious questions about Israel's aviation security arrangements.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Passengers were evacuated after the Delta flight arrived from New York, and the aircraft was moved to an isolated area for inspection. Authorities found no explosives, and preliminary assessments suggested the anonymous threat might have been a hoax.
The September 30 flydubai incident presented a different and potentially more dangerous threat: An airline employee allegedly attempted to turn the aircraft into a weapon.
According to prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates, a co-pilot aboard flydubai flight FZ1073 attacked the captain with an emergency axe and attempted to seize control of the aircraft. Investigators said he intended to crash the plane into the passenger terminal at Ben-Gurion Airport, causing mass casualties.
The aircraft plunged thousands of feet before the wounded captain, passengers, and other crew members managed to subdue the attacker. Two additional pilots aboard the flight helped bring the aircraft safely to an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
Brig.-Gen. (res.) Dr. Mena Bacharach, an international aviation security expert and former senior aviation security official with Israel's Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), said the attack demonstrated the need for additional technological safeguards inside aircraft cockpits.
Bacharach proposed installing remotely activated, Wi-Fi-based cockpit cameras that would allow authorized personnel on the ground to observe what was happening during an emergency. The cameras would remain off during normal operations and activate only after a distress signal had been triggered, potentially allowing ground personnel to assess a crisis and coordinate a response.
Such a system would require careful consideration of operational reliability, secure communications, privacy, and protection against unauthorized access.
“A serious problem needs creative solutions, and there is need for a whole range of them,” aviation commentator Aharon Lapidot told The Media Line. “Any solution, especially the technological ones, brings with it a host of new challenges, such as privacy issues and vulnerability to cyberattacks.”
The suspect, identified as 29-year-old Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, had passed professional and security checks before joining flydubai in January. UAE investigators said he had developed extremist views years earlier and had deliberately pursued a career in aviation to carry out an attack inspired by the September 11, 2001, attacks in the United States.
The disclosures have intensified scrutiny of how airlines assess their employees and whether existing safeguards adequately address threats originating inside the cockpit.
“In professional terms, this is an ‘insider threat,’ and it forces us to re-examine the fundamental beliefs that aviation security is built on,” Yossi Amrusi, a former senior officer in the Shin Bet security agency and a researcher at the Misgav Institute for National Security and Zionist Strategy, told The Media Line. “It highlights the importance of having additional protection mechanisms in case one of the crew members, not necessarily the pilot, turns out to be a threat.”
Security screening must include ground crews, non-pilot flight personnel
He said security screening must extend beyond pilots to include other flight personnel and ground crews responsible for maintaining and servicing aircraft.
“This is a major earthquake,” Lapidot told The Media Line. “It opens a whole new perspective and a wide range of possibilities for terrorists to carry out attacks.”
UAE Attorney General Hamad Saif al-Shamsi said on October 9 that the co-pilot's radicalization began in 2017 while he was studying in Australia. Investigators said he had consumed extremist material, adopted beliefs advocating violence, and made preparations for an attack.
The suspect had previously worked for Oman Air and Royal Air Maroc before joining flydubai. According to reporting by The Wall Street Journal, his employment history included concerns about extremist interests that had affected his prospects at those airlines. Flydubai reportedly did not consult his former employers about those concerns before hiring him.
The revelations have raised questions about whether airlines should be required to share more information about employees whose conduct or expressed beliefs have prompted security concerns.
“You can check a person’s history, his training and his professional abilities, but it is much harder to predict his future intentions,” Amrusi told The Media Line.
The incident recalls the March 2015 Germanwings disaster, when co-pilot Andreas Lubitz deliberately flew a passenger aircraft into the French Alps, killing all 150 people aboard.
French investigators subsequently found that Lubitz had experienced serious mental health problems and had concealed information about his condition from his employer.
Although the Germanwings crash was not a terrorist attack, both incidents demonstrate how dangerous it can be when a person entrusted with operating an aircraft deliberately endangers those aboard.
“There are far more terrorists than people with suicidal tendencies who wish to commit suicide while killing other people,” said Lapidot, explaining why the flydubai incident is being viewed as a turning point in the aviation industry.
Bacharach said the flydubai incident exposed weaknesses in Israel's aviation security arrangements that had already been highlighted in a 2024 State Comptroller's report.
The report called for a comprehensive examination of civil aviation security, including flights departing Israel, Israeli aviation operations abroad, and foreign aircraft entering Israeli airspace. It recommended that the National Security Council work with relevant government and security agencies to reassess responsibilities, oversight, and the allocation of resources.
Following the report, the security cabinet ordered an interagency review of security arrangements for international commercial flights to Israel. The National Security Council was tasked with coordinating the work of the Transportation Ministry, Civil Aviation Authority, Shin Bet, Mossad, and Finance Ministry.
According to subsequent Israeli media reporting, disagreements emerged over which agency should bear responsibility for security checks on foreign airlines and whether the Transportation Ministry had the personnel and resources to carry out the task.
The ministry ultimately retained responsibility, but reporting following the flydubai attack indicated that important screening requirements had not been consistently enforced.
Bacharach said the attempted attack illustrated the need to translate security recommendations into practical safeguards.
“Israel spends billions of dollars on security; it shouldn’t be left to the hands of a brave pilot, courageous civilians and a miracle to thwart attacks,” said Bacharach. “Someone didn’t do their job and fell asleep while on guard.”
Omani co-pilot allowed on flight to Israel despite lack of diplomatic relations
One of the most immediate questions concerned how the Omani co-pilot was allowed to operate a flight to Israel.
Oman does not maintain formal diplomatic relations with Israel. Israeli security regulations restrict the participation of crew members holding citizenship in certain countries on flights to Israel, including countries without diplomatic relations.
According to an internal security directive reported by Israeli media, foreign airlines were responsible for checking crew members against a list of restricted nationalities. However, the Transportation Ministry had not consistently enforced those requirements or verified crew lists.
Following the attempted hijacking, the ministry tightened restrictions on foreign airline crews, barring people holding citizenship in countries without formal diplomatic relations with Israel from operating or traveling aboard Israel-bound flights, according to Channel 12.
The change has already affected airline operations.
Israeli media reported that an Ethiopian Airlines cargo flight traveling from Addis Ababa to Tel Aviv was forced to turn back overnight Sunday after Israeli authorities discovered an Indonesian national among the crew.
Indonesia has no diplomatic relations with Israel. According to reports by Channel 12 and The Jerusalem Post, the crew member was a pilot.
Channel 13 reported that the crew list was transmitted to Israeli authorities only after the aircraft departed Ethiopia. The plane subsequently resumed its journey after the crew member was replaced.
The incident illustrated the operational difficulties of enforcing restrictions when authorities do not receive and check information about flight crews before departure.
But Bacharach warned against treating nationality as a sufficient measure of risk.
“The problem is not only pilots from hostile countries,” Bacharach told The Media Line. “With the massive migration waves into Europe in recent years, even a pilot from a country that has relations with Israeli could undergo radicalization.”
Israel has also established a legal framework to collect and analyze passenger and crew information to help identify potential security threats.
A 2023 law provided for the establishment of the National Center for Passenger Data Analysis within the Israel Tax Authority. The legislation authorizes the creation of a database containing passenger and crew information and specifies how authorized agencies may access and use that information.
The legal framework is intended to support aviation security, counterterrorism, border control, and other authorized activities. However, the current operational status of the center, and whether it played any role in screening the flydubai crew, has not been established.
The attempted attack has raised broader questions about whether existing information systems are adequately integrated with airline screening procedures and whether relevant intelligence reaches officials responsible for approving foreign flight crews.
“This isn’t just an Israeli problem,” Amrusi said. “An ‘insider threat’ is relevant to all airlines. A person’s nationality isn’t necessarily the main motivator once someone has decided to use their position in order to target the plane.”
Aviation security has changed significantly since the September 11 attacks, with tighter passenger screening, reinforced cockpit doors, and stricter access controls.
Those measures were largely designed to prevent unauthorized individuals from bringing weapons aboard or gaining control of an aircraft.
The flydubai incident demonstrates the different challenges posed by an authorized crew member who already has access to the cockpit and the aircraft's controls.
“Airlines have to conduct much more thorough and frequent background checks and psychological evaluations,” Lapidot said. “Peer reviews must also be more frequent.”
Such measures could help identify concerning behavior, changes in circumstances, or information unavailable during initial hiring.
Expanded screening would require clearer guidelines on information sharing
But expanded screening raises questions about privacy, employment rights, the reliability of intelligence, and the possibility of unjustified suspicion based on nationality or personal beliefs.
Airlines also operate across numerous jurisdictions, each with different legal requirements governing background checks, professional licensing, and the sharing of security information.
Establishing a coordinated approach would require clearer rules governing what information should be exchanged, who may access it, and what action should follow when a potential warning sign is identified.
Lapidot warned that additional security requirements would also carry financial consequences.
“All of this is going to raise prices for the consumers,” Lapidot added.
Amrusi said screening improvements alone would be insufficient because no system can reliably predict every person's future behavior.
“We need to be honest though - there is no test that can predict with certainty the malicious intentions of a person,” Amrusi said. “Therefore, we need a system that can handle the situation once a person has managed to evade the testing.”
That approach would place greater emphasis on safeguards capable of limiting the damage if an authorized crew member attempts to seize control of an aircraft.
Flydubai suspects Tel Aviv flights, Miri Regev declines resumption of service
The flydubai incident has already produced operational consequences. The airline suspended its Tel Aviv flights following the attack, and Transportation Minister Miri Regev subsequently declined its request to resume service pending further scrutiny of its security procedures.
According to published reports, flydubai has conducted an internal investigation, dismissed several employees, and sought discussions with Israeli authorities about measures needed to restore service.
The case has renewed pressure on governments and airlines to reconsider how they identify potential insider threats and how aircraft can be protected when prevention fails.
Any new safeguards will have to balance security requirements with the realities of international aviation. Yet the questions raised by the attack extend beyond screening technology or the nationality of individual crew members to the effectiveness of coordination among airlines, regulators, and intelligence agencies.
For the passengers aboard flight FZ1073, the existing defenses were insufficient to prevent a violent cockpit attack. Their survival ultimately depended on the wounded captain, other pilots, and passengers who intervened before the aircraft could be brought down.

Chios airport to close from 15 November to 15 March amid strong local opposition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:15:48 UTC
20:15:48 KST

Four-month suspension of runway operations at Chios State Airport "Homer" aims to complete works by 28 February 2027 and boost flight safety.
The State Airport of Chios "Homer" will temporarily suspend operations from the evening of Sunday 15 November 2026 until 15 March 2027, as part of works to extend and upgrade the take-off and landing runway, according to an announcement by the Hellenic Civil Aviation Authority (HCAA).
The Authority considers the suspension necessary for the safe execution of the works, which include extending the runway to the north and an overall improvement of the airport's operational infrastructure.
As the HCAA points out, the planning takes into account the particularities of an airport with a limited runway length, the winter weather conditions and the need to ensure smooth air links to the island during the 2027 tourist season.
Shorter timetable for the works
Under the updated schedule, the works in the second and third phase will be completed in four months, instead of the five months foreseen in the original approved timetable.
At the same time, the contractor has pledged to make every effort to speed up the works, with the aim of completing them by 28 February 2027. The HCAA notes that its goal is to limit the runway closure to the shortest possible period.
For the duration of the shutdown, a relevant NOTAM has already been issued so that all parties concerned are informed and can adjust their planning in good time.
What applies to emergency flights
During the works, emergency flights will be able to operate with helicopters, landing and taking off directly to and from the airport apron.
This provision covers, among others, air ambulance transfers, search and rescue missions, firefighting operations, humanitarian and state missions, as well as other flights of national character.
It is noted that at this stage the airport remains operationally available, as the works are still in their first phase. Flights are being served by turboprop aircraft with a limited number of passengers, due to the temporary reduction in the available runway length.
1,799m-long runway once the works are completed
The upgrade provides for the extension of the runway to the north, bringing its total length to 1,799 metres.
The aim is to further enhance operational safety and to enable the airport to serve larger types of aircraft, a development expected to strengthen Chios's air connections and bring benefits both to passengers and to the local economy.
The HCAA calls on passengers, airlines and all stakeholders to take the planned suspension of operations into account when arranging their travel between 15 November 2026 and 15 March 2027.
Reactions from the local community – protests and request for a meeting with the minister
Local organisations on Chios are warning of protest action, including the possibility of shutting down shops to keep the airport open over the holidays, reacting to the plan for an earlier suspension of the island's airport operations.
At the same time, they are requesting a meeting with the Minister of Infrastructure and Transport in order to clarify the timetable for the works and avoid last-minute changes.
Representatives of local bodies express their strong opposition to the prospect of the airport closing on 15 November instead of 15 January, as they say was initially agreed. They describe such a development as a blow to the economic and social life of Chios and call for the original schedule to be respected.
The president of the Chios Chamber of Commerce, Pantelis Legatos, warned of the impact that the interruption of air links will have, especially during the festive period, when many residents have already planned journeys, family visits and medical appointments.
He stressed that the geographical position of Chios, about five nautical miles from the Turkish coast, makes the air link with Athens particularly important for residents' access to health services, as well as for their personal and social needs.
Doubts over completion of the works
Reservations about the timetable were also voiced by the regional governor of the North Aegean, Kostas Moutzouris, who took part via teleconference from Mytilene. He raised questions as to whether the airport will be ready to resume operations before Easter 2027.
At the same time, he underlined the need for a substantive upgrade of the airport's infrastructure, noting that he will take part in the decision-making procedures on the issue.
'No decision without the local community'
The mayor of Chios, Giannis Malafis, stressed the need to maintain the island's air connection during the major festive periods.
The mayor asked for the airport to remain in operation at Christmas, New Year and Easter, while also insisting that any decision on the future of the project should be taken in consultation with local bodies and Chios society.
The timetable for the works remains at the heart of the reactions, with the island's representatives seeking clear answers on the duration of the shutdown and its impact on residents' daily lives and on the local economy.

Syrian authorities arrest main suspect in 2013 Baniyas mass killings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:12:00 UTC
20:12:00 KST

Syrian authorities arrest main suspect in 2013 Baniyas mass killings
Syrian officials apprehended Ali Kayali, also known as Mihrac Ural, as he tried to cross the border, SANA reports.
Syrian authorities have arrested a suspect accused of involvement in the mass killing of civilians in the coastal city of Baniyas in 2013, according to state media.
Intelligence officials apprehended Ali Kayali, also known as Mihrac Ural, “while he was attempting to flee across the border”, state news agency SANA reported on Thursday. It did not say which country he was trying to flee to.
Kayali has long been suspected of playing a leading role in the killing of mostly Sunni civilians in the villages of Bayda and Ras al-Nabaa in the Baniyas region of western Syria in 2013.
At the time, he led an armed group loyal to then-President Bashar al-Assad.
At least 264 civilians, including 36 children and 28 women, were killed in the massacre at Bayda, whereas 195 people, including 56 children, were killed in Ras al-Nabaa by Kayali’s militia, according to figures from the Syrian Network for Human Rights (SNHR), quoted by SANA.
Human Rights Watch in 2013 described the killings as “one of the deadliest instances of mass executions in Syria’s increasingly bloody conflict”.
Militias affiliated with Kayali are also accused of committing massacres in the Latakia, Aleppo and Idlib countrysides, leaving hundreds of people dead or wounded.
Turkiye’s state-run Anadolu news agency reported that Kayali is also the main suspect in the 2013 twin bombings in the Turkish border town of Reyhanli, in which at least 52 people were killed.
Named Mihrac Ural at birth in 1956 in Hatay, Turkiye, Kayali fled to Syria in 1982. SANA said he is married to Malak al-Fadel from the country’s Alawite community, a religious minority to which former leader al-Assad belongs.
Earlier this month, Kayali’s deputy Jamal Tarabulsi was arrested by Syrian security forces, as authorities intensify efforts to capture former regime officials and militia commanders accused of crimes against civilians during the country’s civil war.
Syria’s war began with pro-democracy protests in 2011, and quickly morphed into a complex armed conflict that drew in paramilitary forces, armed groups and foreign powers.
In a multiconfessional country, the war took on a sectarian nature, with the killings in Baniyas and Bayda often seen as a starting point of that shift.
It ended with the ousting of al-Assad in 2024 by a rebel group that took power in a lightning offensive.

No Kings protest across the US aims to get voters to the polls for midterms
The upcoming No Kings mass demonstrations this weekend aim to mobilise voter turn-out for the upcoming 3 November US midterm elections.
On Saturday 17 October, cities across the US will be holding demonstrations to get Americans to the polls ahead of the 2026 midterm elections–what many see as key to preserving the country's democracy.
"No Kings Vote Early is the next step in reclaiming our power after a year of mass mobilisations," reads a statement on the No Kings website.
"It's a day of non-partisan voter participation, being in community with each other, and making sure every eligible voter has a plan, knows their options and is ready to make their voice count," the statement continues.
The midterms will take place on 3 November. Early voting has already started in multiple states, and many advocates are urging for people to cast their ballots as soon as possible to ensure their vote is secured.
According to polls, Democrats are expected to bring in a blue wave by reclaiming the House and possibly the Senate. US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly accused the Democrats of rigging the elections, has said that he will be sending election monitors to polling sites. He has also suggested sending in the military to the polls, which many critics see as voter intimidation.
The last several months have seen internal debates among protest organisers over whether or not they should continue holding mass demonstrations or focus on voter turnout. This event is brings together both camps.
"Voting early means your vote is locked in and safe, days before anyone else can decide what happens next," reads the demonstration's website. "No matter what the laws look like where you live, preparation is universal."
To date, three No Kings protests have taken place across the US, each having its own theme. The first one, in June 2025, was to compete with Trump’s America 250 concert that was also a celebration of his birthday. The demonstrations were a response to the suggestion that Trump was ruling as a king.
Previous No Kings protests, which serve as an umbrella of multiple coalitions have seen record turnouts, with the last one in March seeing at least 8 million attending nationwide.
"A blue wave could be a result of this mobilisation. They seem to be funneling all of these themes into policy," David Frank, a professor of rhetoric and political communication at the University of Oregon, told The New Arab. "I think it's a wise move by the organisers."

DPP’s Puma Shen pushes compassionate governance for Taipei

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) is campaigning for better public services, stronger community support, and safer streets.
Shen is challenging incumbent KMT Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) in the Nov. 28 local elections. The legislator has made childcare, housing, transport, and services for older residents central to his campaign.
Liberty Times reported that Shen unveiled a five-part policy platform called "HEART" in August. The plan aims to improve public spaces, create opportunities, strengthen community support, and make daily life easier for residents.
Shen has proposed more housing for young people and families, additional green spaces, and improvements to aging apartment buildings. He also wants to expand services for older residents and make their homes more accessible, per PTS.
Shen plans to expand childcare support across Taipei's 12 districts. He wants to establish a single contact point where parents can seek advice and assistance for children up to age 18.
He has also proposed four hours of free temporary childcare each week for children under 6, per CNA. Shen said the service would give parents more time to rest and manage daily responsibilities.
On transport, Shen wants safer routes to schools, better bus services, and more bicycle lanes, per Rti. He has also proposed including shared electric scooters in Taiwan's TPASS public transport program.
Shen has also pledged to help young people develop skills and improve their financial security. His proposals include a youth development fund, artificial intelligence training, and support for overseas study and entrepreneurship, per Newtalk.
Shen grew up in Taipei and attended Taipei Municipal Jianguo High School before studying law at National Taiwan University. He later earned a master's degree from the University of Pennsylvania and a doctorate from the University of California, Irvine.
Before entering politics, Shen taught criminology at National Taipei University. He became known for his research into Chinese disinformation and its impact on Taiwan's democracy.
Shen founded Doublethink Lab, which studies disinformation, and helped establish Kuma Academy, which provides civilian emergency preparedness training. He was also involved in human rights advocacy and served as vice chair of the Taiwan Association for Human Rights.
Shen entered the Legislative Yuan in February 2024 as a DPP party-list legislator. He has served on the Foreign and National Defense Committee, focusing on national security and foreign affairs.
His involvement in civil defense has drawn criticism from political opponents. In June, questions arose over Kuma Academy's fundraising, while DPP Secretary-General Hsu Kuo-yung (徐國勇) rejected attempts to link the organization's finances to Shen personally.
The DPP formally nominated Shen for Taipei mayor in May, marking his first mayoral bid. At the nomination event, Shen said he would focus on meeting residents and listening to their concerns rather than following a fixed campaign strategy.

EXPLAINER - Why higher oil prices cannot shield Gulf economies from Hormuz shock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:03:41 UTC
20:03:41 KST

- Saudi Arabia, UAE also expected to shrink as production and export disruptions outweigh gains from higher prices
- IMF forecasts point to a strong rebound in 2027, but recovery depends on restored production and trade
Gulf economies are expected to shrink sharply this year as long-term disruptions to energy production and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz outweigh the benefits of higher oil and gas prices, according to the International Monetary Fund’s latest forecasts.
The October World Economic Outlook points to particularly severe declines in economies most exposed to interruptions in hydrocarbon output and transport, with Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain facing double-digit contractions.
The deterioration highlights a central feature of the regional shock: higher global energy prices offer limited protection when producers cannot maintain production or deliver exports to customers.
The damage also extends beyond hydrocarbons, as weaker trade, higher costs and uncertainty weigh on business activity and complicate efforts to diversify Gulf economies.
Smaller Gulf producers face steepest declines
The IMF projects Kuwait's economy will contract 16.7% in 2026, while Qatar is expected to shrink 15.6% and Bahrain 11.3%, according to published accounts of the October report.
Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are also forecast to contract, although by smaller margins, reflecting differences in economic structure and exposure to disrupted export routes.
Saudi Arabia's economy is projected to shrink 3.3% this year, a sharp reversal from the 1.7% growth forecast in July. The change represents a five-percentage-point downgrade in just three months.
The IMF expects Saudi growth to rebound to 7.9% in 2027, compared with its previous projection of 5.5%, indicating that part of the activity lost this year could return as conditions improve.
The UAE is forecast to contract 3.9% in 2026 before expanding 7.7% next year. Outside the six-member Gulf Cooperation Council, Iraq faces a projected 16% contraction, underlining the broader exposure of regional energy exporters to the disruption.
These figures are projections for annual real economic output, rather than confirmed full-year outcomes, and remain sensitive to the course of the conflict and the restoration of trade.
Outlook deteriorates as disruption persists
The new forecasts mark a substantial deterioration from the IMF's spring assessment.
In April, the fund still projected 2% growth for the Gulf Cooperation Council as a whole in 2026. Its country forecasts included contractions of 8.6% for Qatar, 0.6% for Kuwait and 0.5% for Bahrain.
That earlier outlook assumed a relatively short-lived conflict, with trade resuming and production normalizing by the middle of the year.
The persistence of disruption has therefore undermined a central assumption behind the earlier projections, leaving economies exposed to a longer period of reduced output and impaired logistics.
The geographical differences are important. In its April regional briefing, the IMF highlighted that Oman faced a more limited downgrade because its access to the sea lies outside the Strait of Hormuz.
That distinction illustrates why the availability of alternative export routes can influence economic outcomes alongside the size of financial reserves or the level of global oil prices.
Higher prices cannot replace lost production
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned Gulf finance ministers and central bank governors on Oct. 1 that the regional economy was expected to contract as hydrocarbon production fell sharply and growth outside the sector slowed.
She identified the near closure of Hormuz, disruption in the Red Sea and damage to energy facilities as constraints on exports and production capacity.
Reduced trade, weaker business confidence and rising prices for essential goods were also restricting non-hydrocarbon activity, she said.
For energy producers, the distinction between prices and volumes is critical. A higher price per barrel can support receipts from the oil that is sold, but it does not restore barrels that cannot be produced or shipped.
Real GDP measures production after accounting for price changes. Consequently, an increase in export prices does not automatically prevent an economy from contracting when physical output falls.
This also helps explain why an energy shock can simultaneously raise import costs elsewhere and reduce economic activity in the countries supplying those commodities.
Strong rebound would not erase every loss
The IMF's projections envisage substantial recoveries in several of the hardest-hit economies next year as production, exports and logistics normalize.
Qatar is forecast to grow 18.8% in 2027, Kuwait 17.1% and Bahrain 13.9%. The broader Middle East and Central Asia region is projected to expand 6.3% after contracting 0.3% this year.
However, large percentage rebounds partly reflect the lower starting point created by this year's contractions.
Applying the projected annual changes illustrates the distinction. Kuwait's output would fall from an index of 100 in 2025 to 83.3 in 2026, then recover to approximately 97.5 in 2027. It would therefore remain about 2.5% below its 2025 level despite double-digit growth.
Qatar's projected contraction and rebound would bring output approximately back to its 2025 level. Neither calculation captures the additional production that might have occurred had the disruption never happened.
Financial buffers and logistics shape resilience
Georgieva said government measures and investment in energy and logistics infrastructure had helped contain the wider fallout, including through rerouting supplies and supporting firms and banks.
She nevertheless stressed that financial buffers cannot substitute for physical resilience to trade shocks.
The IMF has highlighted the potential for the GCC Railway and Saudi Landbridge projects to reduce losses from a Hormuz closure by improving alternative transport connections.
Its policy advice calls for temporary, targeted support where needed, while avoiding broad stimulus when the principal constraint is disrupted supply.
As conditions normalize, the fund recommends rebuilding financial buffers and maintaining investment in diversification and economic security.

Russia Keeps Attacking Ukraine’s Frontline but Has No Verified Gains to Show, ISW Says
Russian forces continued offensive operations across several sectors of the frontline on October 13 and 14 but failed to achieve confirmed territorial gains, according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW).
In its October 14 assessment, ISW reported that Russian troops attempted to advance in the Kharkiv, Donetsk, and Zaporizhzhia regions, although Ukrainian forces prevented confirmed breakthroughs.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In northern Kharkiv region, Russian troops continued offensive operations on October 13 and 14 without achieving verified advances. Meanwhile, Russian officials and military bloggers circulated claims that Ukrainian units had been encircled in the northeastern part of the region.
On October 13, Russia's Defense Ministry claimed on the Max social media platform that Russian forces were eliminating allegedly surrounded Ukrainian troops in Mykolaivka, Varvarivka, and Nefedivka, located east of Vovchansk.
The following day, a Russian military blogger published a map suggesting that Russian forces had closed an encirclement between Vovchansk and Velykyi Burluk, surrounding Varvarivka and the area between Chorne and Nefedivka.
However, ISW analysts rejected these claims as unsupported, emphasizing that there was no verified evidence of Ukrainian forces being encircled in the area.
Russian troops also conducted limited offensive operations along the Kupiansk and Borova axes on October 14 but failed to achieve confirmed advances.
Further south, Russian forces launched attacks northeast and southeast of Lyman on October 13 and 14, although ISW reported no confirmed territorial gains. Similar attempts were recorded east of Sloviansk, particularly near Kryva Luka, Mykolaivka, Piskunivka, and Kalenyky, where Russian troops continued offensive operations without making verified progress.
In the Kostiantynivka sector, Russian forces maintained offensive pressure in and around the city throughout October 13 and 14. However, ISW found no evidence of confirmed Russian advances in the area.
Meanwhile, in western Zaporizhzhia region, Russian sources reported continued offensive operations over the same period amid Ukrainian counterattacks. Despite these claims, ISW said it had not observed evidence of Russian territorial gains in this section of the frontline.
The latest assessment follows reports of Ukrainian territorial gains in the Sumy region, where Ukrainian forces recently advanced southeast of Yunakivka, northeast of the city of Sumy.
According to ISW's October 13 assessment, geolocated footage published on October 12 confirmed the Ukrainian advance, marking a verified change in frontline positions in the area.

Honeybees deemphasize potential ‘misinformation’ in their waggle dances
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:01:38 UTC
20:01:38 KST

When a bee wants to tell its hive mates how to find a scrumptious field of flowers, it wiggles its rear end. A complicated combination of figure eight–like movements known as a waggle dance tells nearby bees what direction to fly in and how far to go. But what happens if a waggling bee is unsure of its directions?
A study published in Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology earlier this year shows that bees amplify their communication based on how certain they are that their information is true. It seems the more confident a bee is in what it’s conveying, the more emphatically it communicates with the hive, says study lead author Karmi Oxman, a behavioral ecologist at Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
“Confidence is sort of a human-y word, but it’s useful in this context,” Oxman says. Confidence reflects the communicator’s belief in a message’s relevance or reliability, “and the dance is a self-report of the situation in the field.” This extra information also prevents the bee from accidentally misleading the hive.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The experiment started with one bee flying to a specialized feeder. This first bee, also known as the focal bee, was always met with a sugar solution. The researchers then manipulated the scenario by changing what happened after the focal bee returned to the hive and gave directions to the feeder. In the “honest” scenario, the feeder remained full, and all the bees following the directions got a sugary treat. In the “liar” scenario, the feeder was found empty. And in the “unverified” scenario, all the bees were caught before they could return to the hive and report what happened.
When given the chance to communicate the feeder’s location to the hive again in a later experimental stage, the focal bee in the honest scenario tried harder to convince its fellows to visit the sugar source by performing more waggle dance circuits—suggesting the bee could assess the reliability of its own signal. Unverified and “liar” bees did not show that same increase; in fact, unverified bees decreased their recruitment efforts.
“For me, the big takeaway is that bees are not little robots,” says James C. Nieh, a behavioral ecologist at the University of California, San Diego, who was not involved in the study. “They’re getting information from their environment, and that [information] also includes how successful they are in communicating to their nest mates.”
Both Oxman and Nieh say they wonder what other types of communication beyond what we can see—such as chemical signals or vibrations—could be playing a role in waggle dances. Further research into how bees communicate can help with efforts to “maintain the world in a way that they can still thrive,” Nieh says.

2,000 Palestinian children arrested by Israel since 2023: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:01:25 UTC
20:01:25 KST

Israel has arrested more than 2,000 Palestinian children since the start of its genocidal war on Gaza, with at least 350 still in detention under harsh conditions, the Palestinian Prisoners Society said in a report on Wednesday.
The non-governmental organisation added that the Israeli army arrested six children overnight in the towns of Sa'ir and Al-Shuyukh in the Hebron governorate of the occupied West Bank.
The organisation’s monitoring and documentation indicated that “more than 2,000 children have been arrested since the start of the genocide in October 2023, while at least 350 remain in detention under harsh conditions,” it said.
The group warned of an escalation in the targeting of Palestinian children through practices including intimidation, arrest, torture, starvation, isolation and denial of health care.
It added that information on the number of children detained from Gaza since the start of the war remains incomplete, particularly amid the presence of thousands of missing people in the enclave, including children, and the continued practice of “enforced disappearance.”
The group said Israel’s administrative detention policy, under which Palestinian detainees are held without charge or a clear timeframe for release, leaves children facing an uncertain future and deprives them of family life and educational stability.
It also said Israeli courts contribute to the continuation of violations against children amid the absence of effective accountability.
Detention conditions
The Palestinian Prisoners Society cited the case of child Walid Khaled Ahmad, who “died in Megiddo Prison in March 2025, amid medical findings at the time indicating severe emaciation and signs of malnutrition and dehydration.”
The group raised questions about accountability for his death, noting that the investigation into the case had been closed.
It also highlighted the case of 15-year-old Mohammed Hamid, who it said developed scabies while detained in Ofer Prison, leading to a deterioration in his health and serious infections affecting vital organs.
Hamid underwent heart surgeries and was admitted to intensive care in critical condition before one of his legs was later amputated, the group said.
It added that Hamid has continued receiving treatment for about three months since Israeli authorities released him following the deterioration of his health, a move the group described as “an evasion of responsibility for his medical care.”
The group called for international action to secure the release of children held arbitrarily, end administrative detention and coercive interrogations, and stop torture, starvation and the denial of medical treatment.
It stressed the need to move beyond documentation and condemnation towards concrete measures that end the violations and bring impunity to an end, saying that “protecting Palestinian children requires firm international intervention to ensure respect for their rights, lives and dignity.”
Since October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured in Gaza in Israel’s genocidal war, while around 90 percent of the enclave’s infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed.
Israeli army raids and attacks by illegal Israeli settlers against Palestinians and their property have also intensified in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since then.

Swedish Parliament votes against Social Democrats leader as PM, as expected
STOCKHOLM, Oct 15 - Sweden’s Parliament on Thursday rejected Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson’s bid to form a minority government, as widely expected, extending a period of uncertainty over who will become prime minister after last month’s general election.
Four centre-left opposition parties, which have all said they favour Andersson as prime minister, on September 13 won a majority of seats in Sweden’s Parliament, the Riksdag, but do not agree on who should be part of a new government.
The opposition in September won 176 seats to 173 for Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s right-wing bloc. Thursday’s ballot was the first of up to four votes before a new election must be called.
“It’s been clear to me since the election night that it will take some time and that several ballots would likely be necessary to appoint a prime minister,” Andersson told reporters after the vote in Parliament.
Only the Social Democrats voted in favour of Andersson, while the other parties voted against.
The Parliament Speaker is widely expected to next ask Kristersson of the Moderates – the second-biggest party after the Social Democrats – to have a go at forming a government.
There is little indication so far that Kristersson would be able to secure a majority, and the task of government formation could thus revert to Andersson at a later time. REUTERS
