Revealed: Serbian ruler’s secret role in ‘illegal’ effort to help Trump business
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:00:11 UTC
20:00:11 KST

Serbia’s authoritarian ruler personally intervened to advance an allegedly illegal scheme to hand over a protected site in Belgrade for a Trump tower, the Guardian can reveal.
Aleksandar Vučić summoned officials to a meeting at his presidential offices about the project, which has culminated in a landmark indictment of senior figures from his regime on charges of abuse of public office.
The criminal case is believed to be the first resulting from the Trumps’ global moneymaking campaign, described by critics as a “pay to play” arrangement where everything from sanctions relief to cutting-edge chips is available to those who enrich the first family and their associates.
The alleged scheme to override the protected status of a historic building in the Serbian capital looms over an election scheduled for 25 October, when Vučić will seek to extend his 12 years in power in the face of a mass protest movement spurred by government corruption.
A nationalist former propaganda chief under Slobodan Milošević, Vučić hosted the US president’s son Donald Trump Jr and son-in-law Jared Kushner in Belgrade as they developed plans for a $500m hotel and residential tower to add to their global property portfolios.
After the abuse of power charges were brought last December, Kushner’s company announced the project would not proceed “at this time”. Vučić threatened reprisals, calling the prosecutors “corrupt gangs” who “fabricated cases”.
“We have lost an exceptional investment,” the Serbian president said. “I will personally ensure that everyone who participated in causing this damage is held accountable.”
Vučić’s culture minister is among those charged with abuse of power. But a Guardian investigation, drawing on interviews and leaked documents, reveals that the Serbian president himself led the initial meeting where the alleged scheme was discussed. This crucial meeting is not mentioned in the indictment, raising questions about what information the prosecutors are holding back and why.
Representatives of the Trumps and Kushner said they had no part in the removal of the building’s protected status and that it would be “false” to say the Belgrade project was part of a “pay to play” scheme.
Vučić did not respond to requests for comment. His decision to call a snap election means that a hearing at which witnesses might reveal details of his involvement will not take place until after the vote.
A free 99-year lease
On 6 February 2024, Dubravka Đukanović, a Serbian conservation professor in her 60s, arrived for a meeting at the presidency, a domed former royal palace. For three years, she had been the director of the country’s institute for the protection of cultural monuments.
The topic was the General Staff building, the former Yugoslav ministry of defence in central Belgrade. The building, an architectural gem seen as an emblem of resistance to the Nazis, was already cherished when Nato forces bombed it in 1999 during its campaign to force Milošević to withdraw from Kosovo, deepening its resonance.
Vučić himself had reaffirmed the General Staff building’s legally protected status in 2016. Now, the president said he wanted Đukanović to rescind it, according to two people with knowledge of the meeting. Some unspecified “foreign investor” was keen on the site.
Under Serbian law, stripping the General Staff building of its protected status was not in Đukanović’s gift. Her institute would have to commission an expert opinion, which would have to conclude that there were good reasons why protected status was no longer merited.
But the president wanted it done. At 6ft 6in and intolerant of dissent, Vučić can be intimidating. His tone towards Đukanović and another heritage official present was unpleasant, the sources said. He told them they were lazy and incompetent. The message was clear: do what I want or resign.
A plausible explanation for Vučić’s forceful intervention came the following month, when an agreement between the Serbian government and Kushner’s real estate company leaked.
Married to Trump’s daughter Ivanka, Kushner had been an influential White House aide during his father-in-law’s first term. Since Joe Biden’s victory in the 2020 election, Kushner had been concentrating on his investment fund.
By early 2024, Trump was storming to the Republican nomination and was favourite to win the coming election. If Trump took back the White House, Kushner would once more be one of the most influential people on the planet.
The leaked agreement showed the Serbian authorities had granted Kushner’s company a 99-year lease over the General Staff site, free of charge.
Kushner, whose spokesperson said he had been looking at the project since 2021, posted an image of the design on X, professing himself “excited”.
The news was not universally welcomed in Belgrade. “Serbia is not a buffet, and Vučić is not a waiter,” said Aleksandar Jovanović Ćuta, an environmental activist who revealed the agreement. “This is not his private property.”
Yet Vučić’s regime proceeded to sign a contract, dated 13 May 2024 and seen by the Guardian, undertaking that the “cultural heritage designation” of the site would be removed “to the satisfaction” of Kushner’s company.
Comply or resign
The week after the contract was signed, Đukanović was summoned to another meeting. The president was not there this time. Siniša Mali, his finance minister and right-hand man, took charge.
Mali urged Đukanović and Olivera Vučković, Belgrade’s top heritage official, to cancel the General Staff site’s protected status, according to the indictment’s summary of testimony the two women would later give prosecutors. It makes no reference to the earlier meeting with the president but indicates that the subject had previously been broached.
“Mali asked them if they had given it any thought,” the indictment says, “and if they would initiate the procedure to remove the building’s protected status.”
The women refused, “believing that the legal conditions for it were not met”. In that case, Mali told them, repeating his boss’s ultimatum from February, they should resign. They did.
In her resignation letter, which the Guardian has seen, Đukanović wrote that she could not agree “to inappropriate interventions that would permanently destroy all the values of the complex, which testifies to the highest achievements of contemporary Serbian architecture and is of incalculable importance for preserving enduring creative values, the education of future generations, and the strengthening of the cultural identity of the Serbian people”.
Approached by the Guardian, Đukanović and Vučković confirmed the accuracy of this account. Đukanović added: “I prefer not to make any statement on this matter while the court proceedings are ongoing.”
Little was heard of the General Staff plan for months. In November, Trump beat Kamala Harris to win re-election. Ten days later, Vučić’s government announced that the General Staff site had been stripped of its protected status.
Keeping it in the family
One of the first things Trump did upon regaining the presidency was to ditch the pledge he made in his first term that his family business would refrain from doing deals abroad while he was in office.
“The scale of corruption will be orders of magnitude greater than what we saw in the first Trump administration,” Kathleen Clark, a government ethics lawyer at Washington University School of Law, warned at the time. Trump had made it much easier, she said, to buy his favour.
The family business remained officially under the control of his two oldest sons, Don Jr and Eric. In January 2025, four days after their father’s inauguration, Eric spoke about some new projects. The Trumps and the Kushners, New York real estate families united by marriage, had decided to embark on their first venture together: Kushner’s Belgrade hotel and tower would bear the Trump name.
“It’s going to be fun to bring the family together,” Eric told the New York Times. “Serbia is one of the fastest-growing countries in Europe, and we’re incredibly honoured to be there.” Kushner, who had travelled to Belgrade for what Vučić called an “inspiring” meeting with the Serbian leader, added: “Our research showed that the Trump brand would be the best for this market.”
That brand has enjoyed a surge in demand around the world during Trump’s second term, accompanied by allegations that it comes with a quid pro quo.
In Vietnam, Eric was showered with confetti at the groundbreaking ceremony for a £1.5bn golf resort, the permits for which were granted with unusual speed. Then Trump halved Vietnam’s tariffs. The Saudis poured money into Kushner’s fund, and plans emerged for a Trump plaza in Jeddah. Then Trump agreed to sell the kingdom new US fighter jets. A cryptocurrency baron’s company and senior Emiratis cut a lucrative transaction with World Liberty Financial, the digital currency venture Don Jr and Eric founded. Trump gave the crypto baron a pardon and the Emiratis access to restricted US chips.
Asked about such deals last year, Kushner, now a presidential envoy to Russia, Israel and elsewhere, said: “What people call conflicts of interests … I call experience and trusted relationships that we have throughout the world.”
Those who strike up “trusted relationships” with the Trumps, even if there is not an obvious quid pro quo, gain something less tangible but maybe still more valuable: the aura of friendship with a president who is happy to wield his superpower to make or break smaller nations and their leaders.
Vučić has plenty in common with Trump. Both are friendly with Vladimir Putin and contemptuous of the EU – in Vučić’s case, despite his country having applied to join. A shared disdain for Nato may help explain why the one part of the General Staff building’s heritage that the redevelopment pledged to retain was a memorial to the alliance’s “aggression” against Serbia.
And there is a lot that Vučić could use US help with, not least the fate of Kosovo, which he says is still part of Serbia.
Not long after his father returned to office, Don Jr landed in Belgrade. Vučić said that during their meeting he “emphasised the importance of the economic and political relations between Serbia and the USA and stressed the importance of strategic cooperation between the two countries and joint projects in the years to come”. When Don Jr returned the following month, Vučić fed him a choice sucking-pig.
For Vučić, the support of the first family was timely. Days before his regime stripped the General Staff site of its protection, the collapse of a canopy at Novi Sad railway station, which killed 16 people, triggered rolling protests against graft. The student organisers’ slogan has become “Serbia or mafia”.
Don Jr’s visit came on the eve of the biggest demonstration in Serbia’s history. He invited Vučić on to his podcast, Triggered, and declared that the Serb ruler’s opponents were “weaponising” the Novi Sad disaster, just as Trump’s had done with the Capitol riots after his 2020 election defeat.
But the protesters maintained their momentum, and began to rally against the Trump tower. In May 2025, Vučić went to the US, hoping to visit Trump at Mar-a-Lago, his Florida members’ club. He got to see Rudy Giuliani, Trump’s disgraced lawyer, but not the president. State media reported this was because Vučić fell ill.
No sooner was Vučić home than police arrested Goran Vasić, the man who had been installed as head of the heritage institute to replace Dubravka Đukanović following her resignation. To achieve the cancellation of the General Staff building’s protected status, prosecutors said, Vasic had forged a supportive expert opinion.
More arrests followed. In December 2025, Vučić’s culture minister was indicted for abuse of office for his alleged part in the General Staff scheme. Within days, Kushner’s company announced the project was off.
Coup or cover-up?
Vučić’s threat of reprisals was not idle.
His allies attacked Đukanović, claiming that she had tried to profit personally from her time as a heritage official. Her deputy, who received a visit from the state security service after she went on television to denounce the cancellation of the General Staff building’s protection, has been accused of unrelated misconduct. The Serbian conservators’ industry body said this had “the obvious aim of discrediting her”. Both are expected to give evidence in the criminal proceedings.
For the specialist unit of organised-crime prosecutors who brought the charges, this is a watershed case. Never before has a serving Serbian minister been indicted.
Vučić accuses the prosecutors of staging a coup. Others, though, fear they are pulling their punches. That concern increased when Nikola Selaković, the indicted culture minister, used a court appearance in April to reveal that, while police were raiding his ministry, he was in his office sipping plum brandy and smoking cigarettes with Mladen Nenadić, the head of the organised-crime prosecutors’ unit. The unit’s spokesperson said there was “no discussion regarding the course of the case”.
“In everything that happened regarding potential investments, I saw a chance for our country and citizens,” said Selaković, who faces three years in prison if convicted.
Vučić has not been charged. Neither has his lieutenant, Mali. Both deny wrongdoing.
The indictment refers to evidence from witnesses who were present at the Vučić meeting in February 2024 but does not mention it, raising questions about the apparent decision to omit what would appear to be a key part of the narrative.
The spokesperson for the organised crime prosecutors’ unit said that it had evidence regarding Vučić’s February 2024 meeting with the heritage officials. Beyond those already indicted, prosecutors were “conducting pretrial proceedings in this case to determine potential criminal liability of other persons as well”, the spokesperson added.
Vučić has stepped down and cannot seek another term but is expected to retain his control over the regime if he is elected prime minister on 25 October. In one of his last acts as president, he issued 49 pardons. Some of the recipients have not been identified and it is not clear whether they include defendants in the General Staff case.
The White House referred questions to the Trumps’ company. Its representative said: “The Trump Organization has no plans to develop any project in Belgrade, was never, at any point, involved in any discussions or negotiations to acquire any site in Belgrade and denies any involvement in or knowledge of the alleged claims.”
Kushner’s spokesperson said: “The suggestion that Jared Kushner pursued the Belgrade project as part of any political arrangement or ‘pay to play’ scheme is categorically false.” Rather, it was “an opportunity to transform a site associated with a painful chapter in Serbia’s history into a symbol of healing and reconciliation, while bringing substantial private investment, jobs and economic opportunity to Belgrade”.
The spokesperson added: “Jared had no involvement in the Serbian government’s internal processes concerning the site’s protected status.”
For all Vučić’s difficulties, the tale of the Trump Tower Belgrade does not appear to have put others off doing business with the first family. Trump retains stakes in dozens of his companies, even if his sons nominally run them. In July, he released his financial disclosure for his first year back at the White House. It showed he had made $2bn.

Kids’ Content Is Deeply Broken. A New Platform Wants to Fix It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

If you have young kids or if you know somebody who does, then you know about YouTube’s AI slop problem.
Videos targeted at children on the platform are often filled with bizarre and hyperstimulating content that’s AI generated. Not all of it is age-appropriate. These videos autoplay on endless, algorithmically curated streams punctuated by ads.
Maka, a new streaming app for kids aged 0 to 6, is positioning itself as an antidote to that concern. The platform has zero ads and doesn’t allow autoplay or endless scrolling, and its algorithms intentionally do not maximize watch time.
The company’s cofounder and chief product officer, Tanyella Leta, tells WIRED the platform is purposely abandoning the mechanisms that “turn children’s media into an engagement machine.”
Maka’s CEO and cofounder Isabel Sheinman adds that a lot of the streamers were built to serve adults, not children. “Kids were really the afterthought,” she says. Sheinman wants to set a much higher bar for what quality looks like in children’s media, which she says has been warped by harmful incentives. “Maka was built with child development science and children's behavior first and foremost.”
Launching today, Maka’s programming slate is a mix of licensed content from global studios and independent creators. It features 25 shows in its curated catalog, including Franklin, The Wiggles, Pocoyo, Vida the Vet, and Sesame Street. The platform runs on a subscription service, with a $15 monthly plan and a $107 annual plan.
It was during the Covid pandemic that Sheinman and Leta became obsessed with thinking about how to redesign kids' media. The solution? Every episode streamed on Maka is evaluated by child development experts through Imprint, a framework created with researchers at the Yale Child Study Center. The evaluation process, which examines everything from scene cuts to how fast-paced content is, maps child development across seven core domains. It looks for things like emotional regulation, kindness, how child-caregiver relationships are modeled in a story, and how a story might support critical thinking or language development.
AI-generated content has only added a new wrinkle to kids’ entertainment: videos are incoherent, have no plot, or contain outright misinformation but are packaged to look like learning. Some of it, as WIRED has previously reported, is disturbingly sexualized, featuring gore and other fetishes.
Michael Robb, head of research at the media literacy nonprofit Common Sense Media, says that on a platform like YouTube, slop videos that have the veneer of education sit side by side with carefully designed educational shows. Robb believes YouTube and other kids’ streaming platforms have not done enough to distinguish educational content from slop, which has only made filtering content harder for parents. “Platforms have taken steps to reduce kids’ exposure to age-inappropriate content, and that matters. But ‘not inappropriate’ is a very low bar. There’s a big gulf between that and media created intentionally with kids in mind.”
A 2020 study by Common Sense Media on YouTube videos watched by young kids found 75 percent had “weak or no educational value.” Kids also frequently ended up watching ads and content intended for older audiences.
According to its policy for YouTube Kids, which lets parents approve specific content themselves, YouTube excludes videos that are “deceptive, sensational, or clickbait” but acknowledges that not every video has been manually reviewed. YouTube also makes clear that automated filtering cannot guarantee every video will be appropriate. “There’s a chance that your child will find content that you don't want them to watch,” the company notes in its support docs.
Earlier this year, in an effort to encourage better digital literacy among kids, the American Academy of Pediatrics updated its guidance beyond screen time recommendations, urging children to avoid “AI-generated content,” “AI chatbots,” “short-form videos,” and “highly sensationalized content or clickbait.” The guide prioritized quality content and coviewing with parents rather than passive watching.
Tiffany Munzer, a developmental-behavioral pediatrician and digital media researcher at the University of Michigan, was the lead author on Academy of Pediatrics’s “Digital Ecosystems, Children, and Adolescents” policy statement, and tells WIRED in an email that the proliferation of low-quality content has led kids to “miss out on important, slower learning opportunities that promote critical thinking, generate new ideas, and practice stretching their attention spans.”
In April, child advocacy group Fairplay sent a letter, signed by more than 200 organizations and individual experts, asking YouTube to address the spread of AI videos on its platforms, saying AI slop “harms children’s development by distorting their sense of reality, overwhelming their learning processes and hijacking their attention.”
A YouTube spokesperson tells WIRED that on YouTube Kids, which is meant for kids 12 and under, AI content is limited to a small set of high-quality channels, and parents have the option to block channels entirely. The platform has stricter standards for content made for younger viewers, the company says.
For Maka’s business model to succeed, its shows will need to entertain and educate kids while also establishing confidence in parents. “The value that parents want is relief, knowing that what their child is seeing has been vetted by child development experts and everything on Maka they can trust is good for their kid,” Sheiman says.
Yalda Uhls, a former film executive at Sony and MGM who is now a researcher at UCLA focusing on how media affects the social learning of young children, worries that as AI revolutionizes kids’ streaming content, people who study child development are being left out of the process. “When I was a studio executive, every story meant for children passed through layers of accountable adults,” she says. “But today, algorithms, anonymous creators, and AI tools shape what kids see, and people who study child development are rarely in the room.”
“The gatekeepers have been replaced by a metric: minutes watched,” Uhls says. “Nobody in that chain is required to ask what a child is actually learning.”
One of Maka’s core features is a timer that parents set at the start of every viewing session to help the child wind down off the screen. As the show concludes, a character Maka developed named Scoot appears on the screen to get the child ready to detach from their device. Features like that are the difference between capturing a child’s attention versus earning it, Sheinman says. “So it becomes less of a moment of tension in a family and a moment that the child is prepared for.”
The founders ultimately want Maka to help change the perception of kids' relationship to screens.
“We’re seeing a really big challenge around the judgment of parents,” says Leta, explaining that one problem with screen time is the demonization of parents who rely on it. “We have all judged parents who bring out the screen on the train or at a restaurant. Let's be real, most parents will reach for the screen at some point. We don't think that they should be judged for that choice.”
Whether any of this will work is unclear. One question at the core of Maka’s mission is whether it can build a successful streaming company without adopting the same incentives that created the problems it is trying to solve.
Robb from Common Sense Media calls competing with YouTube a Herculean task. “YouTube is free and already on the devices within their homes. Moving them away can be tricky,” he says. The real test for Maka, Robb says, “will be whether it can grow with kids and stay sustainable without being pulled back toward the engagement metrics that drive the rest of the industry.”
Leta, one of Maka’s cofounders, admits that it’s easy to be cynical when it comes to children and screens. “But TV also gave us Sesame Street. It gave us Fred Rogers, who believed that the space between the child and the screen was sacred ground.”
“One of the dads in our beta told us that with other platforms, when his kid is watching, it feels like ‘a race to the bottom of my kid’s brainstem,’” Leta says. “It doesn't have to be like that.”

LinkedIn shared its 2026 ranking of the best Israeli startups on Wednesday, with the newly unveiled identity security firm Oak, which was launched publicly in July with a $60 million seed investment, leading the ranking.
Greylock Partners, Accel, and CRV led Oak's seed funding, and Shai Morag, who has already founded two cybersecurity companies acquired by market giants such as Palo Alto Networks and Tenable, co-founded the company with Tal Marom.
"Our annual LinkedIn Top Startups list surfaces the 15 emerging Israeli companies growing fast, gaining attention and recruiting top talent right now," said LinkedIn in a statement.
The three-year-old AI development firm doubleAI placed second, AI operating system developer Wonderful placed third, open software platform Kela Technologies was fourth, and business-to-business (B2B) cybersecurity firm Kela Technologies placed fifth.
LinkedIn explained that it identified companies working on pioneering cybersecurity solutions, AI "expert intelligence," and automation of workflows, while only data from LinkedIn was used to develop the ranking.
The full ranking includes Cyera (Private network security), Notch (AI automation), Mate Security (Cybersecurity), Eon (Cloud data protection), Port (Workflow automation), Encore AI (AI data analysis), Limitless Labs (AI for precision manufacturing), Adaptive6 (Spending control), Dream (AI cybersecurity), and FINQ (AI fintech firm).
How is the LinkedIn ranking made?
The professional social networking platform explained that the ranking focused on five sections of data available on LinkedIn: employee growth, engagement, job interest, and attraction of top talent.
It also specified that engagement was measured with "views and follows of company pages by non-employees, as well as non-employees’ views of startup employees’ profiles."
The "job interest" ranking used views of and applications to advertised roles, while the acquisition of top talent was measured by ranking the company's ability to hire workers from LinkedIn’s global Top Companies lists.
LinkedIn also explained that companies included in the ranking were required to be no more than seven years old, privately held, fully independent (and not owned by larger firms), and to have at least 30 employees employed from July 2025 to June 2026.
It also clarified that startups that laid off 10% or more of their workforce during July 1, 2025, and the list’s publication were ineligible for the ranking.

Online ads helped deliver Israeli spyware to devices visiting Al Jazeera, 120,000 websites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:59:33 UTC
19:59:33 KST

Israeli digital advertising agency Discover-Tech spied on internet users through a sprawling network of online ads that it used to track targets and help hack their devices, two research groups said on Thursday.
Its services gave Israel's Candiru, a spyware company blacklisted by the US government, and other Israeli surveillance firms access to advertising platforms run by Google, Comcast, Russia's Yandex, and others, according to separate reports from the Canadian cyber watchdog group Citizen Lab and New York advertising security firm Confiant.
The reports show how the online advertising business, long a subject of privacy concerns, can also serve as a channel for sweeping espionage campaigns.
"The way online advertising works today is a systemic security threat," Wolfie Cristl, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab, told Reuters. "For states, the private sector, civil society, and everyone else alike."
Discover-Tech's online ads, often for ordinary products such as phones or earpods, reached more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps through its various partnerships, Citizen Lab said.
Discover-Tech could identify and track users who visited sites or used apps with the malicious ads, and it would sometimes also try to extract phone numbers from some smartphone users, the researchers said. Ads only needed to load on a website for the spying to occur.
Some ads would be used to help plant spyware from Candiru on users' devices, both research groups said, though Confiant said that ads it tied to Candiru were a tiny fraction of Discover-Tech's overall volume.
Confiant cofounder Jerome Dangu said Discover-Tech was pumping out at least 10 million ads per day all around the world and that data-sharing arrangements - called cookie matching - allowed it to track people even beyond the reach of its advertisements.
"Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," Dangu said.
Discover-Tech, which was founded in 2020, did not return messages left via its contact form. A LinkedIn message and emails sent to its chief executive, Dekel Boni, were not returned.
Reuters' attempts to reach Candiru's owners were not successful. The US Commerce Department blacklisted Candiru in 2021 for allegedly supplying spyware that was used to maliciously target government officials, journalists, activists and academics.
Candiru spyware used to compromise Al Jazeera devices
Citizen Lab said a powerful form of Candiru spyware delivered through Discover-Tech's ads had been used to compromise 45 Windows devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera between 2024 and 2025, something it said it was able to confirm because the media group had shared its network logs with the group. Al Jazeera did not return messages seeking comment.
In a statement, Al Jazeera said it "condemns the spyware attacks targeting a number of its staff" and that it was taking steps to protect its employees and its systems. "Those responsible must be held accountable," it said.
Dangu of Confiant said that the malicious ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive categories," including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court. He also said that some regions, such as Gaza and the West Bank, were particularly saturated by the Israeli firm's ads.
"You go to almost any site in Palestine - any site - you find a Discover-Tech ad. It gives them a very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country," he said.
Citizen Lab also said it had similar evidence showing the malicious ads were shown to people in the United Nations, NATO, the European Commission, and more than a dozen other national governments. Other networks the ads appeared in included chip-related firms such as Nvidia, Sandisk, Broadcom, and Micron, as well as several media organizations in Mexico, Israel, and Europe that were not identified.
In addition to identifying Candiru and a couple of other surveillance vendors, Citizen Lab said it was able to glean some details about where Discover-Tech's users might be based because the firm inadvertently exposed its authentication logs to the internet, showing people logging in from internet protocol addresses in Israel, Europe, and the Gulf.
Discover-Tech being frozen out of online ad market
Discover-Tech is now being frozen out of parts of the online ad market.
Google said in a statement that it had collaborated with Citizen Lab and Confiant on the investigation and kicked Discover-Tech off its ad platforms "for systematically violating our policies."
IAB Europe, the European-level association for the digital marketing and advertising ecosystem, said in an email that it suspended Discover-Tech from its list of globally approved vendors last week after an audit identified policy violations.
Comcast ad tech subsidiary Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its platform "following recent activity," Comcast said in a statement. Yandex did not return Reuters messages seeking comment.
Advertising-driven surveillance is increasingly being seen as a national security threat. Earlier this year, the Pentagon said it had received reports that US forces deployed to war zones had been targeted using location data harvested by ad tech firms and data brokers. Branches of the military have since disabled ad tracking on some devices.

Ukraine Seeks 450 Kph Starlink Limit to Counter Jet Drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:59:16 UTC
19:59:16 KST

Ukraine is seeking to remove speed restrictions on military satellite terminals after disruptions on Wednesday, Oct. 14, hampered drone missions. Ukrainian sources say the system must support movement at speeds of at least 450 kilometers per hour (280 miles per hour) to help counter Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.
Journalist Alex Raufoglu wrote on X, citing a source in Kyiv, that Ukraine wants unrestricted service restored, rather than simply a modest increase in the current threshold.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“A Kyiv source tells me Ukraine needs unlimited speed restored,” he wrote.
According to Raufoglu’s source, the service previously operated without speed restrictions and is funded by Germany under a contract running through April 2027. The source said the current limit of about 160 kph (99 mph) is insufficient to counter jet-powered Shaheds.
A government source separately told RFE/RL that Ukrainian forces need connectivity at speeds of at least 450 kph (280 mph), with the broader aim of returning to unrestricted operation. The distinction matters: raising the threshold would address some operational needs, while removing it would restore the conditions Ukraine says existed before the disruption.
Partial restoration leaves the speed cap in place
Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said on Wednesday evening that connectivity was improving for terminals moving below the existing threshold.
“Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h [99 mph] is being restored,” he wrote on X.
Ukraine’s Privatized Air Defense Project Sees First Successes
Fedorov added that completely removing Starshield’s speed limit remained critical for Ukraine’s defense. His announcement concerned service below the threshold and did not mean restrictions on faster-moving terminals had been lifted.
According to DW, Fedorov also said strike drones and interceptor drones should be able to fly again as connectivity recovered. DW noted that he no longer holds the defense minister’s post.
The defense ministry subsequently told RFE/RL that the formal restriction remained approximately 161 kph [100 mph], although connection quality below 160 kph [99 mph] had improved. During the day, some units had experienced interruptions at considerably lower speeds. The ministry said it was continuing discussions with partners and SpaceX about stable service conditions and preventing sudden restrictions.
What stopped working
The reported restriction concerns the speed at which a terminal is moving, rather than the speed of its internet connection.
When a drone or vehicle carrying a terminal crosses the permitted movement threshold, it can lose its satellite connection. That can interrupt communications needed to control the aircraft or relay information during a mission.
Defense ministry sources said military Starshield users began experiencing disruptions overnight on Oct. 13-14, without advance warning. Units reported connection losses at different speeds, ranging from approximately 72 to 161 kph (45 to 100 mph).
The interruptions affected interceptor drones, medium-range strike operations, reconnaissance, communications relays, and frontline logistics. The ministry said it was gathering reports from units, contacting the US, SpaceX, and NATO partners, and checking backup communications channels.
The reports concern restrictions on moving terminals, rather than a nationwide shutdown of all Starlink connections.
Musk points to US control of Starshield
SpaceX owner Elon Musk responded to Fedorov by distinguishing commercial Starlink from the military-grade Starshield service.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” Musk wrote on X.
He said decisions about speed and usage limits were made by the US military and ultimately the US president. Musk described commercial Starlink as a separate SpaceX-controlled service intended for civilian or defensive activities.
His statement did not explain who authorized the latest restrictions or why Ukrainian forces received no advance warning. A senior US official separately told Axios that the Trump administration had not been involved, leaving conflicting accounts of responsibility.
Faster Russian drones increase the pressure
The demand for a higher operating threshold comes as Ukraine adapts its air defenses to Russia’s growing use of jet-powered drones.
These aircraft fly faster and higher than conventional propeller-driven Shaheds, giving defenders less time to react and making interception harder for mobile fire groups and slower counter-drone aircraft.
Ukraine is developing dedicated interceptors alongside other defenses, including fighter aircraft and small missiles. President Volodymyr Zelensky said earlier this month that Ukraine was testing five high-speed interceptor models, with one potentially reaching production of around 400 units by the end of October.
Reliable communications are another requirement for interceptors using satellite links. Restoring connections below 160 kph (100 mph) can help some missions, but it does not resolve the problem for aircraft that must fly substantially faster to reach their targets.

Chaos in Tirana: Violent Student Protests Surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:59:00 UTC
19:59:00 KST

Reported by
Prime Minister Edi Rama addressed youth protesting in Tirana on Thursday for the first time after three days of violent demonstrations, calling them the country’s future and urging dialogue, while insisting that genuine students were not responsible for the widespread destruction.
Speaking in a video message recorded inside the damaged offices of the European Union-backed College of Europe in Tirana, Rama drew a sharp line between student concerns and the street violence that has paralyzed parts of the capital.
"Students are the future... and for them, we are always ready to sit down, speak, discuss, and find solutions," Rama said. However, he accused political opponents of hijacking the demonstrations, calling the attacks on public institutions the work of "an opposition which, hiding behind blind masks, seeks with fire and iron to drag Albania back into the abyss". Warning that the law applies to everyone, Rama vowed that anyone responsible for the devastation "will pay".
His address came as tens of thousands of students—aged between 15 and 25—abandoned their schools and universities on Thursday to pour into central Tirana's square and surrounding streets. Heavy police deployments actively moved to prevent the crowds from spreading further into the city's major thoroughfares.
According to an OCCRP correspondent on the ground, the explosive student uprising is the latest and most volatile phase of a 100-day siege of Albania’s political center, mounting the most formidable challenge in years to Rama's government. Demonstrators rallied near local high schools this week to mobilize students into the broader movement, dubbed by organizers as the “Flamingo Revolution.”
The movement originally began months ago as a localized environmental campaign. It was sparked by government plans to allow Affinity Partners, an investment firm backed by U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, to construct high-end tourism facilities on the uninhabited Sazan Island and within the protected Vjosa-Narta wetland ecosystem—a habitat for the flamingos that gave the protests their name. While Rama framed the investment as a key catalyst for tourism and European Union integration, environmentalists fiercely opposed the privatization of pristine reserves.
In September, an OCCRP report provided the catalyst that broadened the protests into a national anti-corruption revolt. OCCRP revealed that Rama had backed a 2023 law relaxing environmental restrictions on protected areas shortly before the Kushner project advanced. The report also revealed that the project’s ownership structure was concealed behind a cascade of offshore shell companies stretching to Amsterdam and Doha, and that Albania's anti-corruption agency had unfrozen $127 million in related assets after facing political pressure.
During the initial two days of the current protests on Tuesday and Wednesday, demonstrators hurled stones, flares, and Molotov cocktails, and erected flaming barricades out of rubbish bins. Police deployed tear gas and water cannons to hold back the crowds.
More than eight public institutions were attacked, including the Prime Minister’s Office, the Constitutional Court, the Bank of Albania, and three government ministries.
According to a detailed statement from the Albanian State Police, the violence initially began around 2:00 p.m. on Tuesday outside the Ministry of Education, where masked individuals threw concrete slabs and explosives at police and the building itself, damaging its walls and windows. Protesters later broke into Tirana City Hall on Ded Gjon Luli Street, smashing a door and setting a fire on the ground floor.
Elsewhere, protesters smashed the entrance doors to the Speaker’s Office of the Parliament, starting another fire inside the building. At least four commercial banks and several private businesses—including a microfinance institution and a business near the city's Twin Towers—were damaged, vandalized, or looted.
The unrest brought central Tirana to a standstill for hours. Police officially stated that six officers were injured by stones, hard objects, and explosives. Under the direction of the Tirana Prosecutor's Office, police arrested 16 individuals—ranging in age from 23 to 59—in connection with the violence, while another 49 face criminal proceedings. Authorities urged peaceful demonstrators to distance themselves from masked agitators, noting that arson and property destruction carry penalties of up to seven years in prison.
The scale of the violence prompted immediate international concern. The U.S. Embassy in Tirana issued a security alert on Wednesday, noting that the protests on Durres Street next to Skanderbeg Square had turned violent due to rock throwing and could expand to nearby government buildings. The embassy advised personnel to avoid demonstrations and urged American citizens to remain vigilant.
The European Union Delegation in Albania also strongly condemned the escalation of violence and the destruction of public and private property. Calling on protesters to exercise restraint and avoid all acts of violence, the EU stressed that "violence has no place in democracy". While emphasizing that freedom of assembly and expression are core European values that must be exercised peacefully, the delegation added that constructive dialogue between all parties is the only way forward to address legitimate concerns.
Albania's President Bajram Begaj reacted via a statement on Facebook, calling on the youth to exercise restraint. He emphasized that the right to peaceful protest is a fundamental part of democracy, but warned that "violence cannot be a means of expressing dissatisfaction, nor should the use of force by the police exceed the limits of the law and proportionality."
"The Constitution and the law must remain the limit for everyone, without exception. I remain ready to listen to all concerns," Begaj added.
In a separate video address on Thursday, Education Minister Mirela Kumbaro appealed directly to parents, teachers, and civil society as tensions spread across school networks. Speaking as both a minister and a mother, Kumbaro urged families not to let their children become victims of the chaos or be manipulated by "dark hands" seeking to destabilize the country. While defending the right of youth to protest legitimately, she insisted that dialogue—not destruction—is the only way forward, emphasizing that schools must remain protected places of learning.

There is no need to destroy what works: the Aerospace Association warns of risks to the aviation industry due to changes to the reservation rules
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:57:59 EEST
19:57:59 KST

There is no need to destroy what works: the Aerospace Association warns of risks to the aviation industry due to changes to the reservation rules
Kyiv • UNN
Changes to the reservation rules could deprive the aviation industry of key specialists and derail defense contracts. Businesses are calling for the current rules to be preserved.
The changes proposed by the government to the rules for reserving conscripts and defining critically important enterprises could lead to the loss of qualified specialists, a reduction in production, and the failure to fulfill defense orders. Such decisions could be particularly dangerous for the aviation and aerospace industries, which are already operating amid closed airspace, a personnel shortage, and limited funding due to the full-scale war. Volodymyr Semenov, Director General of the Aerospace Association of Ukraine, said this in an exclusive comment to UNN.
Restrictions for critically important enterprises
On October 13, the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine considered amendments to Resolution No. 76, which regulates the procedure for reserving conscripted employees. According to media reports, during the meeting the government did not make a final decision on reducing reservation quotas for critically important enterprises.
The draft resolution proposed reducing the percentage quotas for reservations for enterprises in the defense-industrial complex and energy sector—from 100% to 85%, and for the utilities sector—from 75% to 60%. The relevant amendments are planned to be finalized within 5 days.
The document removed the provision excluding employees who have a deferment (students, parents of many children, and others) from the calculation.
The government decided to establish a Coordination Center involving the Security Service of Ukraine, the Main Intelligence Directorate, the Foreign Intelligence Service, and the National Police, with the relevant decision to be further finalized.
At the same time, business representatives pointed out that the proposed amendments had not been discussed with them, and businesses had received no official explanations regarding the decisions adopted.
The aviation industry risks losing specialists who cannot be quickly replaced
According to Volodymyr Semenov, Director General of the Aerospace Association of Ukraine, constant changes to the reservation procedure have already become a serious problem for enterprises, which are forced to spend resources not on developing production but on preserving their personnel potential.
Changes to the reservation rules will negatively affect not only the aviation industry but the entire defense-industrial complex of Ukraine. It is already difficult for enterprises to retain their people, while constant changes to the reservation rules create additional problems. Figuratively speaking, changes to the procedure for reserving employees take place every three months
He emphasized that staffing is particularly painful for aviation enterprises. Training qualified specialists in narrow fields in the aviation and aerospace industries takes years, while replacing an experienced engineer or designer within a short period is practically impossible.
It is impossible simply to snap your fingers and find a new qualified engineer, designer, or other narrow-field specialist. There are already very few such specialists left, and their training takes years
According to him, the existing reservation percentages should be maintained depending on the category of the enterprise. Today, critical enterprises have already been divided according to the relevant criteria, and specific working conditions have been established for them. The Aerospace Association sees no need to change the rules in a way that would deprive enterprises of the ability to retain the specialists they need.
Therefore, our main request is simple—there is no need to destroy what is already working. This is one of the basic principles of engineering and management. If the system allows enterprises to confirm their critical status and reserve the employees they need, it should be improved where this is truly necessary, rather than creating new problems for the industry
At the same time, the industry has already faced a reduction in the volume of civil air transportation, difficulties in production, and a shortage of qualified personnel because of the war. Airlines were forced to relocate their operations abroad and continue to contribute to the Ukrainian budget.
Speaking specifically about the aviation industry, the situation is already difficult. Aircraft are hardly flying at all or are flying very little, production remains an extremely complex process, and there is a shortage of qualified specialists. Against the backdrop of all these problems, enterprises are once again forced to adapt to new rules
In his view, another tightening of restrictions could deepen the personnel crisis and call into question the ability of some enterprises to continue operating.
Aviation and aerospace enterprises involved in fulfilling defense orders are particularly sensitive to such changes. The loss of even a small number of key specialists could disrupt production processes, delay the fulfillment of contracts, and affect the supply of necessary products for defense needs, warns the director general of the Aerospace Association.
Industry representatives are also particularly concerned about the tight deadlines being discussed for reviewing the sectoral criteria for criticality.
According to Semenov, enterprises may find themselves in a situation where delays in completing the new procedures create a risk of losing employee reservations.
Semenov warns that for the aviation industry, where a significant portion of production processes depends on highly specialized professionals, even temporary uncertainty regarding employee reservations could have long-term consequences.
We have already been working under wartime conditions for the fourth year, and enterprises are once again forced to prove their criticality. How many more times must we confirm what should have long been obvious? The industry needs stable rules, not the constant revision of procedures that are already working. Therefore, our position as the Aerospace Association is quite specific. First, it is necessary to preserve the current procedure for confirming the criticality of enterprises and reserving employees. If the mechanism works, there is no need to create additional obstacles and complicate it
Aviation enterprises may cease operations
In Volodymyr Semenov's opinion, the issue of employee reservations cannot be considered separately from the other difficulties facing the aviation industry. One of the most acute problems at present remains the lack of funding. According to him, the funds allocated for carrying out the relevant production tasks do not always arrive on time or in the necessary amounts.
As a result, enterprises are forced to address several problems simultaneously: fulfilling orders, finding working capital, retaining personnel, and undergoing new administrative procedures to preserve employee reservations.
We may be promised funding, for example, in December, but how is an enterprise supposed to produce goods until then? How can orders be fulfilled if there is insufficient working capital? Without funding, it is impossible to organize production steadily, purchase the necessary materials, and ensure the work of specialists
The combination of financial difficulties with the risk of losing qualified employees could jeopardize the continued operation of some enterprises.
If they are unable to retain key employees, ensure production, and obtain the necessary funding, the question will arise of how they can continue operating at all. In the worst-case scenario, enterprises may be forced to scale back their activities or cease operations altogether
At the same time, the consequences of such a development would extend far beyond individual companies. A reduction in the activities of aviation industry enterprises would mean the loss of jobs and production expertise, while the state would also lose tax revenues. For enterprises involved in defense production, an additional risk would be delays in fulfilling government orders.
In addition, additional pressure on Ukrainian aviation enterprises will complicate the recovery of civil aviation after the airspace is reopened. After all, returning the sector to full operation requires preserving not only aircraft and production facilities, but also the specialists capable of ensuring their operation, maintenance, and repair.
The government is introducing an additional approval level
Volodymyr Semenov is critical of the initiative to establish an additional approval body—the Coordination Center—whose powers and responsibility, in his opinion, remain insufficiently defined.
In fact, another level of approvals is emerging, on which the ability of enterprises to retain employee reservations will depend. At the same time, a question arises: who will be responsible for the consequences if, due to delays in approvals, an enterprise loses reservations for its specialists?
He explained that the Aerospace Association is already involved in communication with the Ministry of Defense. In particular, under the leadership of Deputy Defense Minister Hanna Hvozdiar, a platform for regular meetings with representatives of industry associations is operating and serves as a coordination center.
These meetings take place every week, and we are trying to convey our position to state authorities. But the problem is that even regular meetings do not guarantee that all business proposals will be heard and taken into account. It is very difficult for one association to achieve the necessary changes independently. A systematic dialogue is needed between the state, enterprises, and industry associations, within which business will not simply express its position but will also have the opportunity to influence decisions
According to him, the Aerospace Association will insist on participating in consultations with the authorities regarding changes to the reservation rules and the determination of critical status. After all, the loss of qualified employees may become irreversible for some enterprises, since restoring human-resource potential will require significantly more time than reducing it. This is especially dangerous at a time when enterprises are trying to preserve their production potential, fulfill defense orders, and prepare for the future resumption of civil flights.
The Verkhovna Rada is already ready to respond to the Cabinet resolution
Yaroslav Zhelezniak, First Deputy Chairman of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Finance, Taxation and Customs Policy, said that he plans to submit to the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine a draft resolution to repeal the Cabinet's decision.
"This morning I sent all members of parliament a draft resolution for signature regarding the government's latest decision on employee reservations. The draft recommends:
-  repealing the Cabinet's decision of October 13; 
-  holding consultations with business; 
-  including representatives of business associations in the Coordination Center; 
leaving this Center exclusively with an advisory function—with no right to adopt decisions binding on enterprises", – Zhelezniak reported.
He noted that Parliament would hardly have time to consider this initiative during the current plenary week.
But tomorrow there will be Question Time with the Government. And the presence of dozens of members of parliament who support this position will clearly signal to the Government that the decision needs to be reconsidered

Israeli ad firm helped spyware target Al Jazeera journalists
Israeli digital advertising agency Discover-Tech spied on internet users through a sprawling network of online ads that it used to track targets and help hack their devices, notably Al-Jazeera offices in Doha, two research groups said on Thursday.
Its services gave Israel's Candiru—a spyware company blacklisted by the US government—as well as other Israeli surveillance firms access to advertising platforms run by Google, Comcast, Russia's Yandex and others, according to separatereports from Canadian cyber watchdog group Citizen Lab and New York advertising security firm Confiant.
The reports show how the online advertising business, long a subject of privacy concerns, can also serve as a channel for sweeping espionage campaigns.
"The way online advertising works today is a systemic security threat," Wolfie Cristl, a senior researcher at Citizen Lab, told Reuters. "For states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike."
Discover-Tech's online ads—often for ordinary products such as phones or earpods—reached more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps through its various partnerships, Citizen Lab said.
Users who visited sites or used apps with the malicious ads could be identified and tracked by Discover-Tech, which would sometimes also try to extract phone numbers from some smartphone users, the researchers said. Ads only needed to load on a website for the spying to occur.
Some ads would be used to help plant spyware from Candiru on users' devices, both research groups said, though Confiant said that ads it tied to Candiru were a tiny fraction of Discover-Tech's overall volume.
Malicious ads
Confiant cofounder Jerome Dangu said Discover-Tech was pumping out at least 10 million ads per day all around the world and that data-sharing arrangements—called cookie matching—allowed it to track people even beyond the reach of its advertisements.
"Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," Dangu said.
Discover-Tech, which was founded in 2020, did not return messages left via its contact form. A LinkedIn message and emails sent to its chief executive, Dekel Boni, were not returned.
Reuters' attempts to reach Candiru's owners were not successful. The US Commerce Department blacklisted Candiru in 2021 for allegedly supplying spyware that was used to maliciously target government officials, journalists, activists and academics.
Citizen Lab said a powerful form of Candiru spyware delivered through Discover-Tech's ads had been used to compromise 45 Windows devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera between 2024 and 2025, something it said it was able to confirm because the media group had shared its network logs with the group. Al Jazeera did not return messages seeking comment.
Dangu of Confiant said that the malicious ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive categories," including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court. He also said that some regions, like the Palestinian territories, were particularly saturated by the Israeli firm's ads.
"You go to almost any site in Palestine—any site—you find a Discover-Tech ad. It gives them a very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country," he said.
Citizen Lab also said it had similar evidence showing the malicious ads were shown to people in the United Nations, NATO, the European Commission, and more than a dozen other national governments. Other networks the ads appeared in included chip-related firms such as Nvidia, Sandisk, Broadcom, and Micron, as well as several media organizations in Mexico, Israel, and Europe that were not identified.
In addition to identifying Candiru and a couple of other surveillance vendors, Citizen Lab said it was able to glean some details about where Discover-Tech's users might be based because the firm inadvertently exposed its authentication logs to the internet, showing people logging in from internet protocol addresses in Israel, Europe, and the Gulf.
Measures against Discover-Tech
Discover-Tech is now being frozen out of parts of the online ad market.
Google said in a statement that it had collaborated with Citizen Lab and Confiant's investigation and kicked Discover-Tech off its ad platforms "for systematically violating our policies."
IAB Europe, the European-level association for the digital marketing and advertising ecosystem, said in an email that Discover-Tech had been suspended from its list of globally approved vendors last week after an audit identified policy violations.
Comcast ad tech subsidiary Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its platform "following recent activity," Comcast said in a statement. Yandex did not return Reuters messages seeking comment.
Advertising-driven surveillance is increasingly being seen as a national security threat. Earlier this year, the Pentagon said it had received reports that US forces deployed to war zones had been targeted using location data harvested by ad tech firms and data brokers. Branches of the military have since disabled ad tracking on some devices.

China's FDI equity stock ranks second globally: commerce ministry
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:54:43 CST
19:54:43 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- China's foreign direct investment (FDI) equity stock reached 26.8 trillion yuan (about 3.98 trillion U.S. dollars) in 2025, ranking second globally and marking six consecutive years of growth, the Ministry of Commerce said Thursday, citing the latest annual reports from foreign-invested enterprises.
A total of 461,000 foreign-invested enterprises filed annual reports last year, up 5.7 percent from 2024, according to data compiled by the ministry and other government departments.
China's vast market offers foreign businesses opportunities to generate tangible returns, ministry spokesperson He Yadong told a press conference, adding that China welcomes foreign companies seeking to expand their presence in the country and share in its development opportunities.
The reporting companies posted an average profit margin of 8.7 percent in 2025. In the manufacturing sector, their profit margin was 2.2 percentage points higher than that of China's major industrial enterprises, the data showed.
Foreign-invested enterprises accounted for one-third of China's total goods trade and one-seventh of the country's tax revenue in 2025. They also provided an average of more than 30 million jobs annually over the past five years, the ministry said.
High-tech industries have become a bright spot for foreign investment in China. FDI in the sector rose 35.1 percent year on year to 200.26 billion yuan in the first eight months of this year, official data showed.
China has stepped up efforts to stabilize foreign investment and direct more capital into advanced and high-value-added sectors. A 15-measure action plan unveiled in June this year aims to expand market access, streamline investment procedures, strengthen investment promotion and improve services for foreign investors.
A new version of the Catalog of Encouraged Industries for Foreign Investment also took effect on Feb. 1, encouraging foreign investment in advanced manufacturing, modern services, high-tech industries, energy conservation and environmental protection, as well as in China's central, western and northeastern regions. ■

World Insights: Xi's principles on settling Africa's hotspot issues resonate across continent
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:54:29 CST
19:54:29 KST

NAIROBI, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The four principles proposed by Chinese President Xi Jinping for resolving Africa's hotspot issues have resonated across the continent, with diplomats, scholars and media professionals hailing them as timely and practical guidance for promoting peace and development in Africa.
The four principles -- adhering to the principle of "Africa-led," upholding fairness and justice, promoting ceasing hostilities for peace, and addressing both symptoms and root causes -- were put forward on Tuesday in Beijing during Xi's meeting with Faure Essozimna Gnassingbe, president of the Council of Ministers of Togo, who is on an official visit to China.
Noting that the proposal comes at a time when conflicts across the continent are compounded by external interference and intensifying geopolitical rivalries, African experts said they support its emphasis on building lasting security through African ownership, international fairness, peaceful dialogue and sustainable development.
AFRICAN OWNERSHIP
At the heart of the four principles is the "Africa-led" approach, under which the African people are the true masters of Africa, and should play a central role in regional affairs.
Claudio Rabenja, a Malagasy economist and international affairs expert, said the principle is "relevant and particularly important in the current geopolitical context," as crises in Africa stem from complex local factors that outside actors often fail to understand.
"Solutions imported from or imposed by external actors do not always provide lasting answers," he said, adding that Xi's approach responds to Africa's aspiration to stop being a battleground for major-power rivalry and is consistent with China's tradition of non-interference.
Similarly, Etienne Bankuwiha, a Burundian sinologist, said Xi's proposal "consolidates the fundamental principle of African solutions to African problems," affirming that African countries are entitled to choose their own partners and development paths while rejecting externally imposed governance agendas.
Emmanuel Yenshu Vubo, dean of the Faculty of Social and Management Sciences at the University of Buea in Cameroon, said Africa "is not and cannot be reduced to mere spheres of influence or former colonial units that have only nominal independence ... Africa should be its own master."
FAIRNESS AND JUSTICE
The principle of upholding fairness and justice calls on all parties to abide by the principles of the UN Charter and respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the countries concerned.
Rabenja said respect for sovereignty and the UN Charter helps safeguard territorial integrity, curb destabilizing interventions and promote the peaceful settlement of disputes.
"It is essential that African countries be able to resolve their disputes without being subjected to pressure that runs counter to their national interests," he said, noting that China's consistent stance gives African governments greater freedom to make their own choices.
Gerard Njoya, editor-in-chief of Actu Chine Cameroon, said the principle reinforces the African Union (AU)'s Agenda 2063 by opposing unilateral sanctions and arbitrary interventions, addressing the long-standing demand for "an end to interference and double standards."
Balew Demissie, a senior consultant at the Policy Studies Institute of Ethiopia, said the principle's call for consistent application of international law underscores the need to treat African countries fairly and with dignity.
PEACE THROUGH DIALOGUE
Noting that wars and unilateral sanctions cannot fundamentally resolve conflicts, experts said the principle of promoting peace through a cessation of hostilities calls for mutual respect, extensive consultations, seeking common ground while setting aside differences, and fostering mutual understanding and accommodation.
Moutlakgola Masire, a journalist at Radio Botswana, said multi-stakeholder consultations and ceasefire commitments can prevent further civilian suffering and open the way for sustainable settlements.
Rabenja said military confrontation without a credible political process often fails to eliminate the root causes of violence.
"Mutual concessions do not mean abandoning fundamental principles," he said. "They recognize that lasting peace often requires arrangements acceptable to all parties."
China's diplomatic experience and relations with African countries can help support mediation, complementing the efforts of the AU, subregional organizations and the United Nations, he said.
Njoya said ending hostilities through dialogue aligns with the AU's Silencing the Guns initiative, offering an approach to conflict resolution rooted in African values.
SECURITY AND DEVELOPMENT
As the principle of addressing both symptoms and root causes calls for tackling immediate security threats while pursuing long-term development, experts said China can help Africa address its challenges, citing its contributions to infrastructure construction, scholarships and vocational training across the continent.
Rabenja called security and development "two inseparable dimensions of stability."
Beyond protecting civilians in the short term, he said, the underlying causes of conflict -- poverty, youth unemployment, inequality and weak institutions -- must be addressed through investment in education, agriculture, energy, infrastructure and industrialization.
"Security creates the conditions necessary for investment, while development reduces some of the vulnerabilities that can fuel conflict," he said.
Njoya said addressing root causes is essential to achieving the goals of Agenda 2063, adding that the principle "endorses the AU's integrated approach, which seeks to tackle poverty, youth unemployment and inequality -- the underlying causes of instability."
Bankuwiha said China-Africa cooperation in agriculture, industrialization, poverty alleviation, green transition and infrastructure provides the economic empowerment needed to address the structural drivers of conflict in regions such as the Horn of Africa and the Lake Chad Basin.
Observers said the four principles forge "a new framework of equal partnership" that respects Africa's independent choices.
"Taken together, these four principles can serve as a practical reference guide for settling past, present and future hotspot issues in Africa," Demissie said. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- An article by Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, on advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance with higher standards and more concrete measures, will be published on Friday.
The article by Xi, also Chinese president and chairman of the Central Military Commission, will be published in this year's 20th issue of the Qiushi Journal, a flagship magazine of the CPC Central Committee.
It calls for upholding and strengthening overall Party leadership and persistently advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance to turn the blueprint drawn up at the fourth plenary session of the 20th CPC Central Committee into reality.
It stresses that the Party Central Committee's major policy decisions and arrangements must be implemented with stronger determination and vigor.
It also demands strengthening concrete, targeted and regular oversight of the implementation of strategic initiatives, such as applying the new development philosophy, promoting high-quality development, and accelerating the building of a new development paradigm.
The article requires more scientific and effective efforts to confine power to an institutional cage. It highlights that everyone is equal before laws and regulations, with no exemptions or special privileges when observing and enforcing these rules.
The article says that the fight against corruption must be pursued with greater sobriety and resolve. It describes the anti-corruption campaign as a high-stakes struggle that cannot be lost, requiring an unswerving high-pressure posture to be maintained.
It further demands the timely detection, accurate identification and effective resolution of all forms of corruption, with refined anti-corruption mechanisms that align oversight actions across all sectors. ■

Fighting in Yemen intensifies: What’s the latest on the battlefield?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
10:52:12 UTC
19:52:12 KST

Fighting in Yemen intensifies: What’s the latest on the battlefield?
Houthis attempt to raise the cost of the Yemen war for Saudi Arabia as attacks, fighting intensify.
Forces aligned with Yemen’s government on Thursday said that they had intercepted a drone headed towards Medina in Saudi Arabia, and a missile fired towards Riyadh, amid escalating fighting between them and Yemen’s Houthi group.
Fighting between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iran-aligned Houthi rebels has intensified along the country’s western Red Sea coast, along with expanding Houthi attacks on oil facilities and airports in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
On Wednesday, Yahya Saree, the military spokesman for the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah or Supporters of God, said the group’s forces had conducted “a high-quality military operation targeting Aramco in Dhahran”, as well as strikes on Riyadh airport and a refinery in the capital.
He added that operations “will continue in the coming days, targeting Saudi enemy airports and oil facilities”.
A Saudi Ministry of Energy official confirmed that a building belonging to Aramco in Dhahran was hit, resulting in a “limited fire” but “no casualties or fatalities”. Dhahran is home to Aramco’s headquarters, a vast complex comprising numerous buildings and residential compounds.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition launched strikes against the Houthi stronghold in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, which the armed group seized in 2014 and has held ever since. The coalition fought the Houthis, who also seized large quantities of Yemen’s military assets, until a ceasefire was agreed in 2022. That ceasefire has broken down in recent months.
Reporting from Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said the war has become a tit-for-tat exchange of blows. The Iran-backed group “will continue to launch these air strikes and … its goal is to meet fire with fire – air strike for air strike, capital for capital, airport for airport, and energy facility for energy facility”.
Which sites have the Houthis targeted in Saudi Arabia?
Recent Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have mainly targeted key infrastructure on the outskirts of Riyadh, but they appear to be edging closer to the city centre.
Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport over the weekend killed 14 people and wounded more than 300 others. Houthi attacks have also been reported on other airports, including Abha international airport in southern Saudi Arabia, where two people were killed, and on Saudi Aramco energy facilities.
Authorities say Riyadh airport will remain shut at least until Saturday as several airlines cancelled flights, emptying the skies over the kingdom’s capital.
Al Jazeera’s Mawry said Saudi Arabia “has much more to lose” from tit-for-tat attacks disrupting air traffic, as Sanaa international airport has been closed for many years due to the damage it has sustained over the years of civil war. There are currently no Yemeni airliners at the airport.
Additionally, by disrupting security, the Houthis are signalling that Saudi Arabia will suffer mounting economic costs for its involvement in Yemen. Earlier this year, the Houthis similarly began launching strikes on Saudi-linked shipping in and around the Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea. Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on this shipping route for oil exports since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in March, under fire from the United States and Israel.
The kingdom is set to host a major investment conference in Riyadh later this month, dubbed “Davos in the desert”, but it is now unclear whether the event will go ahead amid the attacks.
Organisers of the Six Kings Slam tennis tournament, originally slated to begin next week in Riyadh, have announced the event will be pushed to December.
Saudi Arabia is also preparing to host the FIFA World Cup in 2034.
Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi, reporting from the Qatari capital, Doha, said, “These military hits by the Houthi forces are meant to create a pressure campaign that is also having knock-on economic effects.”
“The Gulf Cooperation Council has become a place where these enormous events have been playing out over the past year, and if they carry on, the international implications for the global economy will continue to be negative,” he added.
What’s the situation on the ground in Yemen?
Yemeni government forces are currently engaged in a major counteroffensive operation, called “Dawn of Yemen“, to retake coastal territory seized in recent weeks by the Houthis near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a vital maritime trade chokepoint.
The Saudi cabinet pledged in a meeting led by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman this week that it “will not allow its security or freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb strait to be threatened”.
On Wednesday, Yemeni government forces said they had carried out 2,309 “targeting operations” against the Houthis as part of their “Dawn of Yemen” military campaign.
The forces’ spokesperson, Majeed al-Nuzaili, said the operations were conducted using combat aircraft, drones, artillery and rocket launchers, and destroyed 460 Houthi military vehicles.
Government forces say they have retaken areas in Sabr al-Mawadim and al-Sarari in Taiz governorate and have repelled a large Houthi attack west of Taiz city in southwest Yemen, a government-held city that was besieged by Houthi fighters earlier this month. Taiz governorate includes the flat, western coastal region on the Red Sea, which contains the port city of Mocha and the Bab al-Mandeb. Much of the governorate also lies within Yemen’s highlands while its capital, Taiz, is nestled between mountains.
Al Jazeera’s Mawry said fighting has been so intense in the area because of its strategic value. “Whoever controls the altitude and gains control of the mountains controls the landscape. They control the Red Sea coastlines and even the city of Taiz,” he said.
The internationally recognised Yemeni government has been calling for more reinforcements as well as Saudi air attacks on the positions recently taken over by the Houthis, mainly in the district of al-Misrakh, south of Taiz, and the district of at-Turbah, which are the gateways to the city of Taiz.
Mawry reported that while the Saudi-led coalition’s aerial strikes are forcing the Houthis to withdraw and retreat, allowing government forces to advance, they have not been able to gain a full hold over some of those positions.
“It is then followed by another counter-military offensive by the Ansar Allah group to retake the area. And this is sort of the routine that we have been seeing since early September,” he said.
The Houthi siege of Taiz has resulted in civilian casualties and severe shortages of fuel, gas and other supplies. On Wednesday, the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) reported that wheat flour stocks have been nearly exhausted.
The Red Cross said front-line hospitals in areas including Marib, Taiz and Yemen’s Red Sea coast are registering unprecedented numbers of weapon-wounded patients, with some facilities admitting more than 700 casualties in a single week.
