Netanyahu vs Bar: Who called who is fascinating, but both ignored writing on the wall - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:45:31 UTC
18:45:31 KST

The latest broadside from former Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) director Ronen Bar against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu includes some fascinating new revelations and sparks new discussion.
The majority of the focus has been on whether Bar had Netanyahu’s phone number and whether the prime minister in the past had always taken Bar’s calls or sometimes ignored them.
These anecdotes are compelling, and the fight over them shows the depth of miscommunication and enmity between the men.
While The Jerusalem Post will take them apart to explain what they really mean, the main point is that all of this is a sideshow.
Netanyahu wants the debate to focus on the night before the invasion, but that is a straw man.
The October 7 disaster was a decade or more in the making, contributed to by failures of the political leadership and the entire defense establishment after the 2021 war with Hamas, and during the internal Israeli fight over the judicial overhaul.
The phone call that wasn't
More on that in a moment, after explaining the phone drama.
Presidents and prime ministers do not have their phones attached to their brains while they sleep.
Therefore, they have national security staff nearby, who are designated to receive middle-of-the-night calls to wake them if needed.
In Netanyahu’s case, as I wrote in my new book, In the War Room, a Shin Bet official, under orders from Bar, called Netanyahu’s wake-up staff at 6:13 a.m., 16 minutes before the invasion started.
The head of the wake-up staff, Netanyahu’s personally selected military secretary, Maj.-Gen. Avi Gil decided not to wake him up.
This is not the fault of the Shin Bet.
Gil was Netanyahu’s personal appointee, empowered to make exactly this type of decision: when to wake the prime minister up in the middle of the night.
In that sense, Bar did not need to complain that Netanyahu had not given him his personal phone number because Netanyahu would not have picked up such a call while sleeping.
Bar’s unnecessary attack on this issue was made because of Netanyahu’s unnecessary defense: They did not call me on October 7.
No one called Netanyahu personally because the procedure was to call his staff, which was followed.
Nevertheless, it is somewhat disturbing if Netanyahu was actually withholding contact information from the Shin Bet chief, and it could indicate that he never trusted him because Bar was appointed by Naftali Bennett.
When push comes to shove, who is responsible for October 7?
But that is immaterial to the question: Who is responsible for October 7?
Netanyahu, the IDF, the Shin Bet, and all officials in their positions going back 10-15 years are responsible because they all participated in propagating the idea that Hamas was contained and deterred.
They did not push to see whether cutting a peace deal with Fatah in the West Bank would sufficiently weaken Hamas to cause it to be less of a threat, neither did they attack Hamas in a stronger way to topple it militarily, nor did they leave enough soldiers on the border to defend against a ground invasion which they were sure would never come.
These were the true October 7 failures of Netanyahu, the IDF, and the Shin Bet.
Additionally, they all misread the 2021 war as an Israeli win, when Hamas chief Yahya Sinwar viewed it as a validation of his strategy to ignite a multi-front war against Israel.
Moreover, they all mishandled the judicial overhaul internal fight in a way that led to the country being seen as vulnerable to attack by Hamas. Relations between Netanyahu and top defense establishment figures were so bad in July 2023 that he refused to receive certain critical intelligence briefings lest they expose him to various potential criticisms after the fact.
At the end of the day, whatever happened on the eve of October 7 was a tiny part of the story; whether Netanyahu gave his cell phone number to Bar or not does not impact the bottom line. And the person whom the prime minister chose to decide whether to wake him up decided not to, because he, like everyone else in Israel, could not imagine that Hamas would actually do what they did a very short while later.

Ukraine Strikes Ryazan Oil Refinery After Announcing Resumption of Attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:45:17 UTC
18:45:17 KST

The Ukrainian Defense Forces attacked the Ryazan oil refinery in Russia overnight on October 15.
Pavel Malkov, governor of Russia’s Ryazan region, confirmed the attack.
The drone strike sparked a fire at the oil refinery.
The Ryazan oil refinery is owned by Rosneft, one of Russia’s largest oil companies. It is one of the country’s largest refineries, with a capacity of around 17 million tonnes of crude oil annually.
The refinery has four primary oil processing units, plus equipment to refine crude oil into fuel and other petroleum products.
The oil refinery has been targeted by Ukrainian attacks several times.
On the morning of September 6, 2026, Ukrainian drones struck the Isomalk-2-LIN-800 low-temperature isomerization unit, which processes pentane-hexane fractions.
This unit is critical to the Ryazan oil refinery’s production process. It converts low-octane straight-run petroleum fractions into a high-octane gasoline component.
This allows the refinery to produce high-grade, environmentally compliant motor fuels, including Euro-5 gasoline, without adding harmful additives.
The attack came after Ukraine observed a three-day energy truce proposed by Donald Trump and refrained from striking Russian oil refineries. However, Russia continued to attack Ukrainian energy infrastructure, prompting Ukraine to resume its strikes.
President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that Ukraine is no longer bound by any restrictions on such attacks.
Meanwhile, the President said Ukraine could agree to another pause in strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, even if Russia continues attacking Ukrainian facilities. Syrian court sentences two to death over 2025 coastal massacre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:41:23 UTC
18:41:23 KST

Breadcrumb
Syrian court sentences two to death over torture, killings during 2025 coastal massacre
Two men have been sentenced to death and several others handed prison terms over the deadly violence that swept Syria's coastal region in March 2025, when more than 1,400 people were killed amid widespread attacks on civilians.
The sentences were handed down on Thursday by a military criminal court in Aleppo as part of ongoing proceedings against suspects accused of involvement in the violence, according to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA).
The rulings included death sentences for Al-Waddah Ismail and Maher Ali, a 20-year prison sentence for Mohammad Bakour, and a 12-year sentence for Maher Othman.
The court sentenced Bakour to 20 years in prison after convicting him of intentional murder, while Ammar Abdul Aal received a three-year sentence for torture, SANA reported.
The court also convicted Captain Mustafa Shannan and Khaled Muhaimid, both members of the Defence Ministry's 54th Division, of complicity in torture and sentenced them to two years in prison.
Abdul Raouf Bakrjan and Mohammad Zarzouri were acquitted, while Mahmoud Shaheen, another Defence Ministry member, received a two-month prison sentence for assault.
In a separate case linked to the massacre in Syria's coastal region, Ismail and Ali were sentenced to death after being convicted of offences involving acts intended to incite civil war and sectarian fighting, as well as leading armed groups formed to attack government forces.
Othman was sentenced to 12 years in prison after being convicted of complicity in the same offences.
The latest rulings form part of ongoing judicial proceedings aimed at holding those responsible for the March 2025 massacre to account.
The unrest involved armed clashes, military operations and widespread abuses against civilians, prompting calls for justice and accountability for perpetrators regardless of their affiliations.
On 17 September 2026, the military criminal court in Aleppo issued earlier verdicts against defendants involved in the same events, including death sentences, life imprisonment and 20-year prison terms, alongside the acquittal of one defendant.
The trials have attracted considerable attention as a major test of Syria's efforts to address abuses committed during the coastal violence.
Syrian authorities face the challenge of establishing individual criminal responsibility and ensuring that those implicated in abuses are held accountable through transparent judicial proceedings.
The violence erupted in Syria's coastal region in March 2025, beginning with attacks by armed groups linked to the former Assad regime against security and military positions.
The attacks were followed by military operations during which widespread violations against civilians, particularly from the Alawi community, were reported.
A national fact-finding committee investigating the coastal massacre previously documented the deaths of 1,426 people, including 90 women, and identified 563 suspects allegedly involved in abuses committed by different parties.

For him, advancing Ukraine's EU membership bid is one of those things.

‘Each country goes its own way’: How Balkan politics shape ties with Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:35:01 UTC
18:35:01 KST

‘Each country goes its own way’: How Balkan politics shape ties with Israel
Balkan countries’ ties with Israel reflect domestic politics, defence deals and strategic interests rather than a united regional position.
Throughout Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, Europe’s position has, to an extent, been aligned.
Outliers such as Spain and the Republic of Ireland have long been more vocal in condemning Israel, but overall, the shift from unconditional solidarity with Israel to concern over its conduct has taken hold in much of the continent.
Across the Balkans, divergent policies towards Israel reflect domestic calculations, transactional diplomacy, and unresolved identity politics rather than a shared vision for the Middle East, according to experts.
“The Balkan countries have almost no common positions at all, and so it’s not surprising their positions towards Israel and Gaza are all over the map,” Marko Prelec, analyst at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera. “Each country goes its own way.”
Prelec noted that while there is genuine revulsion towards Israeli policy in Gaza and sympathy for Palestinians – particularly among Bosnian Muslims – most countries in the region take their positions based on unrelated interests.
Florian Bieber, professor of Southeast European history and politics at Austria’s University of Graz, said regional consensus is nearly impossible.
“The position towards Israel is strongly shaped by domestic politics and also national narratives, which makes a regional or even a country-specific position unlikely,” Bieber told Al Jazeera.
Bosnia and Herzegovina: Differences from one entity to another
Nowhere is this fragmentation more evident than in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where the war in Gaza has deepened existing ethno-national divisions.
Bosniak political representatives and much of the public in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina have expressed strong solidarity with Palestinians, while leaders in Republika Srpska have been openly pro-Israel, and some Croat political figures have also adopted a more sympathetic tone towards Israel.
“Bosniak solidarity with Palestinians is often seen not just through an ideological lens, but also from the perspective of war and being a victim of Serb nationalist aggression, comparing the Palestinian experience with the Bosniak experience in the 1990s,” Bieber explained.
Conversely, leaders in the Serb-majority entity, Republika Srpska, led by former President Milorad Dodik, have openly embraced Israel.
Foreign policy analyst and journalist Bosko Jaksic told Al Jazeera that for Dodik, “The enemy of my enemy is my friend – Jews and Orthodox Serbs against Muslims. This religious and ethnic factor allows him to maintain an Israeli connection parallel to his closeness with Russia, while simultaneously performing a new American flip by glorifying [US President] Donald Trump.”
Prelec added that Bosnian Serb outreach to Israel and specifically Likud, the ruling Israeli party, represents “an attempt to find allies for its internationally unpopular flirtation with separatism, and an indirect way to strengthen ties with parts of the MAGA [Make America Great Again] movement and the Trump administration”.
Serbia: Arms sales and multi-vector balancing
In Serbia, the approach to Israel blends defence economics with foreign policy.
Despite historically friendly relations with Palestine and voting in favour of Palestinian membership in international bodies, Belgrade has exported ammunition and arms to Israel since October 2023.
The relationship has also moved beyond exports. In September, Serbia opened an Israeli-linked drone assembly plant, underlining the growing practical dimension of bilateral defence cooperation.
Vuk Vuksanovic, lecturer in foreign policy and grand strategy at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera that Serbia’s defence industry “has not been particularly picky when it comes to its customers, and the desire for profit has been one of the factors”.
However, he emphasised broader geopolitical ambitions.
“In the past three years, there has been a tilt towards Israel regarding security cooperation, while diplomatically Serbia tries to be cautious in multilateral institutions due to its ties with the wider Islamic world,” he said.
Vuksanovic noted that Belgrade views Israel as a partner to “acquire the protection of Israeli lobby groups and access to the Trump administration in the US”, especially as the Serbian government faces domestic political opposition.
Meanwhile, Jaksic warned of the international risks involved.
“Due to the significant increase in ammunition exports to Israel during the war in Gaza, Serbia risks being accused of complicity in genocide,” he said. “Beyond financial calculations, the Serbian president attempts to use closeness with his ideological, authoritarian, and nationalist ally, [Israeli Prime Minister] Benjamin Netanyahu, to get closer to Trump.”
Kosovo, Albania, and the Washington anchor
For Kosovo and Albania, foreign policy regarding Israel remains anchored to security alliances with Washington.
Under the 2020 Washington Agreement, Kosovo recognised Israel in exchange for Israeli recognition of Kosovo’s independence, subsequently opening its embassy in Jerusalem. Serbia, which had pledged in 2020 to move its embassy to Jerusalem, ultimately did not do so.
Pristina opened its Jerusalem embassy “defying the stance of the wider international community”, said Jaksic.
“Israel’s growing influence in the Western Balkans is evident,” he noted. “That includes investments, and in the case of Serbia, especially military cooperation. This absolutely does not exclude personal attempts to buy political impunity from American sanctions, or to ease diplomatic pressure.”
In neighbouring Albania, Prime Minister Edi Rama’s government has preserved warm political ties with Israel.
Driven partly by operational defence needs, Albania deepened cooperation with Israeli cybersecurity companies after cyberattacks, while aligning broader diplomacy with Washington and Brussels.
Executive rifts and ideological turnarounds
In Croatia, foreign policy on Gaza has been paralysed by a sharp executive rift between conservative Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic and President Zoran Milanovic of the Social Democratic Party.
Plenkovic’s government has followed a cautious, mainstream European Union approach, while Milanovic has openly condemned Israel’s military conduct in Gaza, labelling it disproportionate and creating a public fracture in the country’s foreign policy leadership.
Further north in Slovenia, there are ideological shifts.
The previous centre-left government adopted firm measures against Israel – such as an arms embargo, a ban on imports from illegal settlements, and a ban on the entry of top officials like Netanyahu – as well as recognising Palestinian statehood.
Conservative forces under Prime Minister Janez Jansa have sought to reverse these policies.
“In Slovenia, we can see the classic left-right division where populist and far-right parties support Israel because of Netanyahu as a similar political actor,” said Bieber. “They recognise him as ideologically aligned, which helps reinforce their view of Islam as a threat, fitting their own narratives.”
Quiet alignment and strategic alliances
Smaller NATO members like Montenegro and North Macedonia have chosen a path of quiet alignment.
Both adhere to standard EU and NATO statements, calling for ceasefires and humanitarian aid while carefully avoiding high-profile bilateral disputes or bold independent diplomatic initiatives.
Further east, Romania and Bulgaria maintain a cautious tone that sometimes leans towards Israel. Grounded in historic bilateral relations and deep strategic defence partnerships with the United States, Bucharest and Sofia balance carefully worded statements at the United Nations with ongoing military and intelligence coordination.
Meanwhile, in Greece, consecutive governments in Athens have maintained a robust strategic military and energy partnership with Israel; Athens recently signed a $3.5bn missile deal with Israel. Originally forged alongside Cyprus to balance regional maritime rivalries in the Eastern Mediterranean, this alliance has held firm despite significant domestic public backlash and protests over the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.
Ultimately, the disparate responses across the Balkans demonstrate that Middle Eastern policy in the region is rarely about the Middle East itself.
Whether driven by defence profits, constitutional rivalries, or the search for political backing in Washington, regional actors continue to view Israel almost exclusively through a transactional lens.

Chiang entered politics in 2015, defeating incumbent KMT Legislator Lo Shu-lei (羅淑蕾) in the party’s primary for Taipei’s third legislative district. He won the seat in 2016 and served two terms, focusing on social welfare and domestic issues, per CNA.
In 2019, Chiang broke with the KMT’s legislative caucus to support key provisions legalizing same-sex marriage, per Ettoday. He later called for discussions on transforming Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall.
Chiang resigned from the legislature in 2022 to run for mayor. He won a three-way race with 575,590 votes, or 42.29%, returning the KMT to Taipei City Hall after eight years.
His administration introduced a city-funded weekly milk program for schoolchildren and later expanded it to junior high schools, reaching about 289,000 students. The city also announced free lunches for elementary and junior high school students at public and private schools starting in the 2026 academic year.
Chiang has proposed smaller classes, more teacher training, and improved school facilities. These measures form part of his campaign’s emphasis on support for families and children.
The long-delayed Taipei Dome opened in 2023, during Chiang’s first year in office, after years of construction disputes. It has since hosted sporting events and concerts.
Chiang has also promoted MRT expansion and urban renewal, including redevelopment of the aging South Airport housing complex in Taipei’s Zhongzheng District. Responding to criticism that his administration lacks new ideas, he has pointed to progress on projects that have faced delays.
Chiang has proposed relocating Taipei Songshan Airport and turning its 300-hectare site into an AI technology hub, per CNA. The plan has raised concerns over national defense, emergency medical flights, and transport to outlying islands, but Chiang said alternative arrangements could address these issues.
The city signed a land-rights agreement with Nvidia in February for the company’s planned Taiwan headquarters at the Beitou-Shilin Technology Park.
An April city government survey found 69.1% of respondents satisfied with Chiang’s performance. A TVBS poll in May put satisfaction at 59%.
His administration faced criticism over its handling of a sexual abuse case at a private preschool. Although the first complaint was filed before Chiang took office, parents and opposition lawmakers criticized city agencies for their response to warnings during his tenure, per Liberty Times. Chiang apologized in July 2024 and promised stronger oversight.
An Oct. 8 TVBS poll put Chiang ahead of Shen by 49% to 41%, compared with a 28-percentage-point lead in May. Chiang has said he will continue focusing on city affairs while seeking another four years in office.

The non-governmental organization that the Israeli army arrested six children overnight in the towns of Sa'ir and Al-Shuyukh in the Hebron governorate of the occupied West Bank.

Austria students resist school headscarf ban over targeting Muslims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:29:00 UTC
18:29:00 KST

A headscarf ban for girls under 14 has triggered widespread protests across Austria as the new school year begins, with dozens of students refusing to comply in classrooms and on the streets.
Austria's conservative-led government has insisted the ban, introduced Sept. 1, promotes gender equality and protects Muslim girls from "segregation and oppression."
But critics argue it disproportionately targets Muslims, infringes upon religious freedom and is forcing young girls to dress in a way that makes them feel uncomfortable.
Since the ban took effect, education authorities across Austria have held 127 meetings with parents and filed 52 reports over alleged breaches of the law, according to the Education Ministry.
Opponents of the ban have also held protests across the country, with several hundred people gathering each time.
At a demonstration in Vienna, Zehra, 37, who did not want to give her last name, said her two daughters, ages 9 and 13, were "sad and angry" about the ban.
"We raise our children by telling them, 'You can decide who you want to be' – and this law is the exact opposite," she said.
Seham, 12, said she felt "afraid" to remove her headscarf at school "because I'd worn it for two years and it felt like a part of me."
After discussions with school leaders, she said she was allowed to cover her hair with an alternative non-traditional head covering, but would still "rather wear the full headscarf."
Roughly 8% of Austria's 9 million residents are Muslim, according to 2021 government statistics.
They suffer the highest rates of racism and discrimination against Muslims in the European Union, according to a 2024 report by Europe's FRA rights agency.
In the 2024 elections, the far-right Freedom Party won for the first time even though it failed to form a government. The anti-immigration party continues to top voter opinion polls.
The new law is Austria's second attempt to restrict headscarves in schools after a coalition between the conservatives and the Freedom Party introduced a ban for primary school students in 2019.
That law was overturned by the constitutional court on the grounds that a regulation targeting only Muslims was incompatible with religious neutrality.
The Islamic Religious Community in Austria, which is supporting legal action against the new headscarf ban, said it had received about 70 reports from families about difficulties during its implementation.
"A law that was justified as protecting children's welfare is putting precisely those children under pressure at school," the group said in a statement.
The constitutional court confirmed to Agence France-Presse (AFP) that it had received a legal complaint about the law and a decision is expected in the first half of 2027.
When girls refuse to comply with the law, schools are required to hold a series of discussions with students and their parents before cases are referred to education authorities.
Ultimately, parents who continue to ignore the ban can be fined.
In a statement sent to AFP, Education Minister Christoph Wiederkehr said the fact there had only been 127 meetings so far showed "that the vast majority of pupils and parents are cooperative."
"In addition, the figures show that the discussions held with the parents concerned in the event of a violation are, for the most part, successful," he added.
Education authorities in Vienna said that "on the basis of the discussions held so far, the impression has emerged that the girls wish to wear the headscarf of their own accord."
Sandy, 12, said she began wearing a headscarf about a year ago because "I place a lot of importance on my religion and I want to be able to live it."
A teacher who has worked with two affected girls in the capital told AFP there was no sign they were being forced to wear headscarves.
The girls had spent weeks adapting to the new rules and searching for acceptable alternatives to headscarves, said the teacher, who wished to remain anonymous. "It is very uncomfortable for them."

El Niño vs climate change: Which had more influence over the powerful Hurricane Polo?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:27:18 UTC
18:27:18 KST

El Niño turbocharged the Pacific hurricane – but climate change had an even greater impact, scientists find.
A new study finds that climate change and El Niño combined to rev up last month's explosively intensifying Hurricane Polo, which was the longest-lasting Category 5 storm ever to churn in the Pacific.
Global warming caused by the burning of coal, oil and gas was the bigger of the two culprits, adding nearly 10 kph to its already monstrous strength, according to a joint study published on 14 October by scientists from World Weather Attribution and Climate Central. El Niño contributed a bit less, about 8 kph, a study co-author said.
Climate change made the conditions that fuelled the hurricane 23 times more likely, while El Niño – the natural and temporary warming of parts of the Pacific – made it 14 times more likely, the study found. It all has to do with the 31.2°C waters that were as much as 2°C warmer than normal, the study said.
This year, with a super strong El Niño, has set records for strength and longevity of Pacific storms. Polo set the record for time spent at Category 5 in the Pacific at two-and-a-half days.
'El Niño comes and goes, but climate change only gets worse'
“El Niño and climate change both made this hurricane stronger than it would have otherwise been, but the effect of climate change is even bigger than the one of El Niño,” says climate scientist and study co-author Friederike Otto, who coordinates the international science team behind World Weather Attribution.
“El Niño comes and goes, but climate change only gets worse. That means that now every hurricane that will occur in the East Pacific has at least this climate change signal making it stronger. And as long as we keep burning fossil fuels, that will only get bigger,” Otto adds.
Researchers found that without climate change and El Niño, Polo would have been a monster storm anyway. But every bit of additional wind speed can dramatically increase the damage.
Decoding Polo's rapid strengthening
While Hurricane Polo ultimately weakened considerably before it hit a sparsely populated part of Mexico, scientists remain fascinated by how it turbocharged from a tropical storm to a top-of-the-chart Category 5 hurricane in about 24 hours.
The study puts the different atmospheric dangers in perspective, says Kristina Dahl, a climate scientist and vice president of science at Climate Central, a science and journalism nonprofit out of New Jersey.
“It’s a powerful reminder that even though El Niño right now is shifting hazards around the globe and changing where it’s flooding and getting dry, the really dominant signal behind all of this remains climate change,” she says.
The study looked at the warm water that fuels storms, using a measure of how strong they can get. But the study didn't focus on the upper level wind shear where El Niño has a huge footprint. El Niño usually increases those storm-decapitating high altitude winds in the Atlantic. However, in the Pacific because of changes in wind patterns, El Niño decreases the winds that weaken storms.
The two sets of researchers measured conditions slightly differently and used different techniques but came to the same general conclusion, making them more confident in the result. However, the rapid study has not had time to be peer-reviewed, which is the gold standard of science.
To calculate the impact of climate change on Polo, both teams used the scientifically accepted method of comparing what happened in our warmer real world to a hypothetical world that hasn't warmed by 1.4°C since pre-industrial times.
How El Niño and climate change interact
Study co-author Daniel Gilford, a Climate Central scientist, says the process they looked at was similar to cars on a road. Wind shear from El Niño can be a red light, as it is in the Atlantic, or a green light, as it is in the Pacific. In the Pacific that green light says go, and then the water warmed by both climate change and El Niño acts like a driver flooring the accelerator.
University at Albany atmospheric scientist Brian Tang, who wasn't part of the study, says he was initially surprised that the research found climate change to be the bigger influence on Polo, “given how extreme this El Niño is, but from a long-term standpoint, perhaps the result isn’t as surprising as it might seem.”
But three other outside scientists – Jeff Masters of Yale Climate Connections, University of Pennsylvania's Michael Mann and North Carolina State University's Carl Schreck – say they believe the study underestimates how much climate change has added to Polo's strength. Masters points to Gilford's own 2024 study that found climate change added 30 kph to hurricanes in the Atlantic from 2019 to 2023.
Gilford acknowledges that Thursday's report could be underestimating climate change's impact a bit, but says he was factoring in other conditions and being conservative.

Zelensky said Russia launched 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones overnight Tuesday, targeting energy facilities and critical infrastructure across Ukraine. According to the Ukrainian president, approximately 500,000 people were left without electricity following the attacks.
Britain's defense secretary Sterling did not discuss Starlink outage cause with Hegseth
Britain's defense secretary said on Thursday the he and US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth welcomed the restoration of the Starlink service in Ukraine, but did not get into why the interruption happened.
During an appearance on Fox News' "The Story with Martha MacCallum," British defense chief Wes Streeting was asked if the Pentagon restricted offensive and defensive capability for Ukraine in order to prevent strikes on Russian energy installations.
He replied, "That's not my understanding. We didn't really get into why the service interruption had happened. We did reflect briefly on the fact that it had been restored and welcome that."
Starlink restrictions follow Trump-announced energy ceasefire
The Starlink restrictions also follow Trump's surprise announcement Sunday of an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. Kyiv had refrained from attacking Russian oil refineries, strikes that Trump had blamed for driving up diesel prices on global markets.
The announcement followed Trump's declaration Friday that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the United States and other global markets.
Trump announced the arrangement in a Truth Social post following what he described as a "highly successful" discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin. 
Amichai Stein contributed to this report.

Counting the Cost
Could France trigger another Eurozone debt crisis?
France is facing a growing crisis of confidence in its public finances.
Its borrowing costs have reached their highest level in more than two decades.
Investors now demand higher yields on French government bonds than on Italian or Greek ones.
With public debt nearing 120 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and a deficit above 5 percent, the government is under pressure to rein in spending.
But protesters are demanding more investment in education.
With parliament deeply divided and a presidential election approaching, agreeing on a solution is proving difficult.
The concern now is whether France’s troubles could spread across the Eurozone.

Gadi Eisenkot sought to put Netanyahu’s wartime record at the center of the election campaign, promising that a government under his leadership would end Hamas rule in Gaza within 18 months.
Speaking near the Gaza border, the former military chief and leader of Yashar! with Eisenkot accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of squandering the opportunities created by Israeli troops. “How will you topple Hamas without getting permission from your partners, Mansour and Tibi?” the party said, referring to Mansour Abbas and Ahmad Tibi.
Eisenkot’s pledge combined a deadline with two possible routes: implementing President Donald Trump’s proposed framework, which he said Netanyahu’s government had accepted, or using military force.
“Within 18 months of my taking office as prime minister, Hamas will no longer rule the Gaza Strip,” he said. “We will bring about the destruction of Hamas’s military wing.”
His central argument was that Israel’s military successes had not produced the political and security outcomes needed to prevent another war. Three years after the October 7 massacre, he said, Hamas remained in control of Gaza, was acquiring weapons and was rebuilding its fighting capacity.
“As long as Benjamin Netanyahu remains in power, Hamas will remain in power,” Eisenkot said.
The criticism extended beyond Gaza. Eisenkot argued that the government had failed to turn battlefield achievements in Iran and Lebanon into the strategic results Netanyahu himself had promised. He accused the prime minister of yielding to coalition demands and draft evaders while presenting himself to voters as an uncompromising leader.
The speech builds on a dispute that began while Eisenkot was inside Netanyahu’s government. Eisenkot, who led the IDF from 2015 to 2019, is now presenting that military experience as a qualification for national leadership. In his address, he said he had the knowledge needed to oversee the military, Mossad and Shin Bet.
He also pledged to establish a state commission of inquiry into October 7, arguing that investigating the failures and implementing its findings were essential to preventing another disaster.

Türkiye’s budget posts 532 billion lira deficit in September

18:22:18 KST

Türkiye’s central government budget posted a deficit of 532 billion Turkish Liras in September, according to data released by the Treasury and Finance Ministry on Oct. 15.
Budget revenues rose 22.7 percent year-on-year to 1.25 trillion liras in September, while expenditures increased 34.1 percent to 1.79 trillion liras.
Non-interest expenditures climbed 39.1 percent from a year earlier to 1.52 trillion liras, while interest payments increased 11.2 percent to 263 billion liras.
The primary deficit was 269.2 billion liras in September, marking a 269 percent increase from the same month last year.
In the January-September period, budget revenues increased 34.5 percent year-on-year to 12.1 trillion liras, while expenditures rose 36.4 percent to 13.9 trillion liras.
As a result, the central government budget recorded a deficit of 1.84 trillion liras in the first nine months of the year.
The primary surplus for the January-September period fell 7.7 percent from a year earlier to 410.8 billion liras.

Mental health at work starts by breaking the taboo, EU agency says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:21:16 UTC
18:21:16 KST

Nearly half of European workers face mental health risks on the job, yet the subject remains taboo.
Health and safety is the backbone of working life. However, as workplaces and working practices evolve, new challenges emerge while old ones remain unsolved.
Against a backdrop of staff shortages and ageing populations, Europe’s workforce is battling poor mental health; however, the issue is still not being recognised at workplaces, William Cockburn, EU-OSHA executive director, told Euronews.
“Whether we're asking employers or workers, they identify a reluctance to speak openly about mental health issues as the … main obstacle to actually taking action,” he said.
Many EU employees say their jobs are hurting their mental health. Nearly half of workers (45%) face risks to their mental health on the job, according to the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work (EU-OSHA).
“We see psychosocial risks at the workplace, for example, long working hours, highly intense work, emotionally demanding tasks … and we link that to increased impact on workers’ health,” Cockburn said.
Around 44% of workers report severe time pressure or overload. According to the European Trade Union Institute (ETUI), work-related depression costs the EU more than €100 billion a year, when absenteeism, reduced productivity, and healthcare and wider social costs are combined.
Despite the burden these conditions place on employers, Cockburn said a reluctance to talk and persistent stigma among workers are slowing action.
So, what can be done about it?
For Cockburn, mental health issues “need to be addressed like physical health issues at work”.
The approach, he noted, is to assess the risks first and then adapt whatever is needed to minimise harm.
“We identify hazards like long working hours, like adverse relationships at work … to an extreme you can go to bullying and harassment, violence or threats of violence,” he added.
Workers should be part of the conversation
While many see mental health as a personal issue, Esther Lynch, general secretary of the European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC), argues that prevention should focus on the workplace rather than on the individual affected.
“We don't wait until people have a finger chopped off before we put guardrails in place,” Lynch said. “We do a risk assessment and say what's the risk associated with the way this work is carried out and then we put the guardrails in place”.
To achieve this, experts agree, workers must be part of the conversation. Yet only 45% say they are consulted about the stressful aspects of their jobs, according to EU-OSHA.
“Worker participation is a legal obligation under European law, but it's also a key success factor for successful interventions in health and safety at work,” said Cockburn.
This week, the European Commission launched the Healthy Workplaces campaign, an initiative to help employers prevent, assess and manage psychosocial risks at work. One of its aims is to overcome this reluctance to speak about mental health struggles.
“When we invest in building and keeping healthy working environments, we improve not only people's well-being, we reduce sick leave and staff turnover; we improve performance, and we don't put pressure on our health systems,” said Roxana Mînzatu, executive vice-president for social rights and jobs, at the campaign’s launch on Tuesday. “It’s a win-win for everyone.”

Aurelius Systems is showing its Archimedes autonomous laser weapon mounted on an American Rheinmetall unmanned ground vehicle at the Association of the U.S. Army annual meeting in Washington this week, where the two companies are pitching mobile laser defense against small drones to U.S. Army buyers.
The San Francisco-based startup said in a post on X that Archimedes is on display in motion at the Rheinmetall booth through the end of the show, as part of the companies’ partnership to bring counter-drone lasers to uncrewed combat vehicles.
Archimedes is a lightweight turret that combines a high-power laser with machine vision and radar, and Aurelius says it can find, track and burn down a drone on its own without an operator initiating each engagement. The system is aimed at Group 1 and Group 2 drones, the small and medium-size types that include commercial quadcopters and many of the one-way attack drones used in Ukraine, and the company says it can defeat them at more than a kilometer.
The two firms announced their partnership in July. According to Tectonic, Archimedes is being integrated first on the Ox, the unmanned ground vehicle American Rheinmetall has entered in the U.S. Army’s Ground Optionally Autonomous Transport competition for a vehicle that hauls supplies and equipment over rough terrain. With a laser on board, a cargo-carrying vehicle can defend itself against drones during resupply runs, a role Rheinmetall has described as protection for autonomous logistics missions.
Aurelius first showed the laser on a Rheinmetall vehicle at the Reindustrialize 2026 conference in Detroit in June, in a display built with American Rheinmetall and electric vehicle startup Harbinger.
In August, the company raised a $40 million Series A round co-led by Draper Associates and KAS Venture Partners to scale up Archimedes production. During the Pentagon’s T-REX 26-2 experimentation event, the laser downed more than 20 quadcopters and more than five drones supplied by the U.S. Army, Tectonic reported, and at the U.S. Army’s Operation Jailbreak exercise at Fort Carson, Colorado, Aurelius linked Archimedes with Anduril’s Lattice software and the Army’s Forward Area Air Defense command and control system, which ties sensors and shooters together.
Lasers appeal to militaries because each shot costs only the electricity needed to fire it, compared with tens of thousands of dollars or more for a missile interceptor, and Aurelius says it builds Archimedes largely from commercially available parts to keep the system’s own price down.

Editor's note: The story has been updated to include comments from Ukrainian officials.
Ukraine's parliament passed a bill on taxing e-commerce and international parcels on Oct. 15, meeting a condition linked to international financial assistance after missing earlier deadlines.
The bill passed its final vote with 252 lawmakers in favour after facing criticism from some lawmakers. Parliament had previously failed to advance the bill and sent it back for revision.
Its adoption is linked to Ukraine receiving the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) tranche of around $700 million and the EU tranche of 3.7 billion euros ($4.1 billion) in macro-financial assistance.
The legislation introduces the value-added tax (VAT) on international parcels worth up to 150 euros ($168), which are currently tax-exempt. Lawmakers also backed new customs regulations for international mail and express shipments.
The changes could take effect on July 1, 2027, but only after a separate government decision.
Finance Minister Serhii Marchenko said the tranches would be disbursed to Ukraine’s state budget "in the coming weeks."
"The adopted bills will ensure a level playing field for Ukrainian businesses and allow the state budget to raise an additional Hr 10 billion ($222 million) annually to fund the Armed Forces," he added.
The parliament repeatedly failed to pass some of the conditions set by Ukraine's partners throughout 2026, amid widespread unpopularity of the changes. Most toxic was a package of new taxes, including a tax on small imported parcels, and a tax on income received from digital platforms, such as Uber.
In recent days, lawmakers have advanced several key bills tied to Western aid, with $29.5 billion in funding at stake if parliament and the government fail to meet the required conditions.
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said on Oct. 15 he hoped lawmakers would maintain the pace of passing bills.
"The results of this plenary week give us all reason to be optimistic, but there is still a lot of work ahead," Koretskyi wrote on social media.
"We count on the same constructive cooperation in the coming plenary weeks to ensure that all necessary decisions are adopted on time and Ukraine receives the full amount of international financial aid."

Australia introduces digital safety bill allowing users to switch off social media algorithms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:18:20 UTC
18:18:20 KST

Faisal Mahmud
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Australia introduced legislation Thursday requiring social media platforms to let users switch off algorithm-driven recommendations, as part of sweeping measures aimed at strengthening online safety.
The Digital Duty of Care Bill 2026 would require technology companies to proactively prevent online harms rather than respond after they occur.
According to a statement published on Communications Minister Anika Wells’ official website, Australians aged over 16 would be able to choose between algorithmically recommended content as their primary feed or accounts they follow.
The proposed law would establish minimum safety standards for social media platforms, gaming services, applications and artificial intelligence chatbots.
Platforms would also be required to protect users under 18 from harmful content, including material promoting eating disorders, dangerous stunts, criminal behavior and hostility toward women.
The legislation would empower Australia's eSafety Commissioner to remove AI-powered nudification services and reduce response deadlines for cyberbullying and online abuse complaints from 48 to 24 hours.
Companies violating the requirements could face penalties of up to $109.2 million Australian dollars ($75 million).
Professional news content and entertainment media would be exempt from the proposed provisions.
"The Digital Duty of Care is the next step in our world-leading online safety laws," Wells said.
"It will set basic safety standards for the digital services we use every day, just as we have for food, cars and kids’ toys," she added.
The bill was introduced in the House of Representatives and must pass both houses of Parliament, including the Senate, before becoming law. 
The proposal follows Australia's landmark restrictions on social media access for children under 16, part of Canberra's broader efforts to regulate digital platforms.

Why South Korea has fallen out with Ukraine but seeks reconciliation with North Korea: Korean expert explains
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:17:00 EEST
18:17:00 KST

Why South Korea has fallen out with Ukraine but seeks reconciliation with North Korea: Korean expert explains
Just two weeks ago, relations between Ukraine and South Korea seemed almost trouble-free. Russia and North Korea were deepening their military cooperation, North Korean soldiers were fighting against Ukraine, and Kyiv and Seoul appeared to have an increasing number of shared security interests.
On 23 September, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha met his South Korean counterpart Cho Hyun in New York. They discussed strengthening political dialogue, trade, investment, Ukraine's reconstruction, and the common threats posed by military cooperation between Russia and North Korea.
The meeting was a continuation of an eventful year in bilateral relations. In July, Volodymyr Zelenskyy met South Korean President Lee Jae-myung for the first time. Seoul announced an additional US$100 million in non-military assistance to Ukraine. Economic cooperation also held considerable potential: a framework agreement between the two countries provided for up to US$2.1 billion in preferential South Korean loans for Ukraine's reconstruction by 2029.
But on that very same day, 23 September, relations between the two countries began to deteriorate rapidly.
During his address to the UN General Assembly, Zelenskyy announced that Ukraine had transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea. Both soldiers had been captured by Ukrainian forces in Russia's Kursk Oblast in January 2025.
On the face of it, this should have been seen as an example of successful cooperation between Kyiv and Seoul. After all, South Korea had previously advocated the transfer of prisoners to its territory, where they could live in safety.
Instead, on 24 September, President Lee Jae-myung publicly accused Ukraine of violating a confidentiality agreement. According to Seoul, the transfer was supposed to remain undisclosed to protect the prisoners themselves and their families still living in North Korea. Ukraine denied that any such agreement existed.
South Korea demanded an official explanation and an apology. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described the situation as a diplomatic misunderstanding. His South Korean counterpart, Cho Hyun, later confirmed that he had received a letter of apology but said it fell short of Seoul's expectations.
On 2 October, Lee Jae-myung threatened Ukraine with further measures unless Kyiv acknowledged its breach of the agreement and issued a public apology. He also criticised Ukrainian statements about the threat of a military conflict between North and South Korea, accusing Kyiv of using rhetoric that could push the Korean Peninsula towards war.
On 8 October, the diplomatic crisis escalated to the recall of an ambassador: South Korea's Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced its decision to bring its ambassador to Ukraine, Park Ki-chang, back to Seoul.
Ukrainian–South Korean relations had thus entered one of their most serious political crises since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion.
All this is happening as President Lee Jae-myung seeks to ease tensions with North Korea and restore inter-Korean dialogue. Pyongyang, however, has shown little interest in reciprocating.
Quite the opposite. On 7 October, Kim Jong Un sent Vladimir Putin a birthday message in which he called the Russian president his "dearest friend", reaffirmed his commitment to developing the strategic alliance with Moscow, and once again expressed support for Russia's "sacred war".
While Seoul is looking for ways to reconcile with Pyongyang, North Korean troops are gaining combat experience in Russia's war against Ukraine, and Moscow is helping North Korea develop its military technologies.
Why did the transfer of two prisoners of war provoke such a strong reaction from South Korea? Does Seoul's policy of reconciliation with Pyongyang stand any chance of success? What is North Korea gaining from its involvement in Russia's war against Ukraine, and how could this change the balance of power on the Korean Peninsula?
Ukrainska Pravda spoke about these issues with Sangmin Shim, Senior Research Fellow at the Center for Foreign Policy and National Security at the Asan Institute for Policy Studies, who specialises in international law and security affairs. His analytical articles and commentary on security and environmental issues in East Asia have appeared in international publications, including the American magazine The National Interest, as well as leading South Korean newspapers such as Chosun Ilbo and JoongAng Ilbo.
Although Shim is critical of certain policies and approaches pursued by the current South Korean administration, he is not a political opposition figure. His perspective is primarily that of an independent policy expert, shaped by his background in international law, diplomacy and national security. He previously taught international law at the Korea National Diplomatic Academy and has advised the government on legal and foreign policy issues.
The crisis in Ukrainian-South Korean relations
Ukrainian-South Korean relations are experiencing their first political crisis since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. South Korea recently even recalled its ambassador from Ukraine. Why has the issue of the two North Korean prisoners become so sensitive for President Lee Jae-Myung's administration?
Well, this is my personal take, but I believe the South Korean government is so pro-Russian that anything potentially sensitive for bilateral relations between North Korea and the Russian Federation is largely discounted. That is what we are seeing today. Even though Ukraine has graciously sent those North Korean prisoners to South Korea, the South Korean government is not really appreciative of it. South Korea is so preoccupied with normalising relations with the Russian Federation that the many gestures the Ukrainian government approaches us with do not really count from the South Korean perspective. This is a truly sad matter, in my view.
Did the situation with those two North Korean prisoners create any domestic debate in South Korea?
In the general public's view, it is great that these prisoners have been transferred to South Korean territory to live in a free state. But the current South Korean government is extremely worried about the consequences of having these North Korean prisoners on its territory.
They fear the possible negative effects of holding them in South Korean custody, which makes them highly sensitive about their presence. This is completely irrational from my perspective. South Korea has always strongly argued for the transfer of Korean prisoners of war to its territory, as the government deems these POWs to be its own citizens.
There is a total inconsistency in logic between the South Korean government's general policy and what they are doing in this specific situation.
Inter-Korean tensions
What we see in the news now is that the South Korean president wants to ease tensions and restore inter-Korean relations and dialogue. But how realistic is this when there appears to be very little interest in dialogue from North Korea?
This might be my personal judgement, but looking at the South Korean government's attempts to ease tensions with North Korea, I don't think it is going to happen. The North Korean government is completely focused on differentiating the two regimes. Pyongyang believes that any ties it might have with South Korea will not bring any real benefit to the prosperity of the North Korean regime. Therefore, the North Korean regime has decided to totally sever ties with South Korea, and that is exactly what they are doing. Unfortunately, the South Korean government is not ready to give up its hope for reconciliation with North Korea. This is where the real tragedy begins.
We also see that North Korea has physically reinforced the separation. They are building barriers, laying mines, and fortifying the border with South Korea. From your point of view, is this just another period of rising tension, or has Kim's "two hostile states" policy changed these relations?
From what I can see, North Korea is highly focused on differentiating between the South Korean and North Korean regimes. They started by laying mines to prevent South Korean troops from crossing into North Korean territory. This is extremely unfortunate, and as you know, it has led to unnecessary casualties among South Korean soldiers. I do not know how this issue can be resolved between the governments of South Korea and North Korea, but I really hope it will be smoothed over. I hope we can find common ground to talk to each other, with the understanding that this issue should not destroy us. There are still many factors that can influence a hopeful outcome in the future.
President Lee's opponents accuse him of being overly cautious about provoking North Korea. How strong is this criticism inside South Korea, and does it explain the unusually sharp reaction to Ukraine?
There is a deep political divide between the progressive and conservative fronts. The conservative front argues that any engagement with North Korea is basically a concession. Meanwhile, the progressive front believes it is a necessary step toward reconciliation. So, there is a huge divide regarding how they want to move forward in the current situation.
President Lee also criticised Ukraine's statement regarding a possible future conflict between North and South Korea, saying such rhetoric could push the peninsula towards war. Why is this topic particularly sensitive for him?
This is anyone's guess, but as I perceive it, a high-ranking official from the Ukrainian Presidential Office stated that ignoring the ties between North Korea and the rest of the world would have a ripple effect on South Korea's security. But is South Korea ready to accept that?
They believe that through peaceful inter-Korean relations, we will have better relations with every country south of the Korean peninsula. But this is unproven. So we will continue to have contentious relations with both the Ukrainian and North Korean governments.
The role of the North Korean military in the war in Ukraine
North Korea has already sent roughly 15,000 troops to Russia, and thousands of them have reportedly been killed or wounded. Before this, North Korea lacked military experience in such a large-scale war. How different is the North Korean army today because of its experience in Ukraine?
After sending their forces to defend or take over the Kursk region, those North Korean troops have gained valuable battlefield experience in modern warfare — particularly combining drone warfare with conventional warfare. From a South Korean perspective, this is not something we can easily discount. South Korea now needs to prepare for potential provocations from North Korea. However, the current government is not taking this seriously. Because this administration leans pro-Russia, pro-China, and pro-North Korea, they do not see these signs of provocation as something to truly worry about. I am sorry to criticise my government, but this appears to be the reality.
And have you already seen evidence that the lessons learned by North Korean soldiers have been incorporated into North Korean training or doctrine at home?
What I can see from the collaboration between North Korean and Russian forces is that the Russians have been sharing technical advice to further develop North Korea's military expertise — particularly in military tactics and drone warfare. Because of this, North Korean forces are in a better position. I do not know how else to put it, but those North Korean forces are now superior to South Korean forces in terms of dealing with drone warfare and other non-conventional forces involvement.
So, could you say that soldiers returning from Russia will eventually form a new, combat-experienced elite within the North Korean military?
First of all, the initial group sent to Russian territory consisted of combat troops from their special operations forces. They sent about 10,000 of their best elite troops, and the results speak for themselves. The involvement of these forces has genuinely contributed to retaking territories crucial to the Russians from Ukrainian control. This has had a major effect. I do not know if this trend can continue, because the North Korean government will also face difficulties with the continuous mobilisation of its armed forces. We do not know how the next stage will play out.
Let us look at the evidence the North Korean government is presenting. They are doing everything they can not to reveal the presence of their personnel on the battlefield. They want to limit their manpower to factories and other workforces – helping Russian forces and industries build stronger weapon systems. So, from what I perceive, North Korean personnel are not going to be seen anywhere near the front lines. But what I really want to emphasise in this case is that North Korea is collaborating with the Russian government and military to build up Russian stockpiles, ensuring the Russian military is prepared for incoming attacks from Ukraine or other countries.
We have a fairly good picture of what is moving from North Korea to Russia: soldiers, ammunition, and missiles. But we know much less about what is moving in the opposite direction and so from your point of view, what's North Korea actually getting in return from Russia?
I mean, what North Korea really hopes to gain from the collaboration with the Russian regime is that they will get military expertise in terms of ballistic missiles development and other top-notch military development. And in turn those current regimes will provide war forces in the form of manual labour and everything to provide the help necessary for the Russian Federation to rebuild their drone systems. So, then they will be able to compete with Ukraine in terms of non-conventional forces engagement.
The Russian government is seeing that the Ukrainian government will not be able to provide all the necessary supplies for all the necessary equipment for forever. And then this is going to be a kind of a war of attrition between Russia and Ukraine in which both will be subject to having to pay the highest consequences from this military conflict. This is so sad but this is also a fact.
If North Korea is developing the capacity to mass produce Shahed-type drones with Russian assistance, how would that change the threat facing South Korea and is South Korea prepared for the kind of mass drone warfare we have seen in Ukraine?
I mean, we have heard the most recent report from the National Security Advisor of the Korean Republic that if North Korea has been engaging too much in this Russia-Ukraine conflict, this would be the best opportunity for Korea to start taking over the northern part of the Korean Peninsula and making the whole Korean Peninsula as a unified nation. But this is not going to be the case that I have been seeing because this is not going to involve the political discussions between the major powers and basically the military aspect will not resolve the matters as we see it.
So what I perceive to be the case is that whatever happens in the territories between Ukraine and Russia will not have any consequences for the inter-Korean relations.
Inter-Korean relations will have to be dealt with by their own dynamics. Meaning that Russia, the United States, Japan, Korea and both North and South Korea will have to be sitting at the same table to negotiate away the differences. This is not going to be a short-term matter but it has to include the case of negotiations.
How Ukraine іs perceived in North Korea
Maybe you know how North Korean propaganda explains Ukraine to its own population? What have North Koreans been told about why their soldiers are fighting and dying thousands of kilometres from home?
I mean the North Korean government is ready to just decorate their lost lives as their national heroes. But this is not going to be the case if the loss of the lives and casualties continues to accrue for the North Korean regime. We have a report that records those current casualties at around 3,000 soldiers who have lost their lives and then another 33,000 soldiers who have basically lost their capability to re-engage in the world.
But with the intensification of the war and tensions within Russia and Ukraine, this will lead to more casualties for North Koreans. And I don't know if the North Korean government will be able to continue to persuade their general public with this loss of life as an unavoidable matter.
I don't know, but the North Korean government is not a democratic nation but they will not be subject to national approval or to answering the questions of the people but they will still feel the pressure from the North Korean populace about the loss of life that has been the consequence of the involvement of North Korean troops in the Ukrainian military conflict.
Is Ukraine portrayed as an enemy in its own right or is it simply as part of a larger confrontation with the United States and the West?
This is a really interesting question. Between the US and Ukraine, they don't seem to have much differences. But by just looking at the recent episode between the Ukraine and Republic of Korea, they seem to have some impending conditions to be dealt with between these two nations.
But from my perspective, these would be only diplomatic matters and if these matters were to be entrusted with both countries' foreign ministers, these differences will be easily negotiated away. What matters to Korea for now is that the current president of the administration. He's so active in voicing criticism about the Ukrainian government. This is not going to be helpful for settling the battle between Ukraine and South Korea. I really hope that the South Korean president will stay silent for at least for the next two weeks for the two ministers to be able to reach a mutually satisfactory agreement.
And from your point of view, how much do the average North Koreans actually know about the scale of their country's involvement in Russia's war?
From the conservative people's point of view, this government is so pro-North Korea and they suspect that North Korea has a huge influence over the matters of the South Korean government, but I don't believe this. But whatever is the case with the North Korean and the South Korean government, I suspect that the South Korean government needs to be in a better position to fight away the incoming threats from North Korea.
Basically in terms of cybersecurity and maritime security. But without those concerns, we have to see that the South Korean government is going to live their lives as if nothing has happened. This is not going to be a very positive case for the South Korean population.
And what happened with thousands of soldiers who return home with direct experience of Russia, of modern warfare, of modern technologies which are most likely not represented in North Korea?
I mean, these North Korean soldiers who have been sent back to the North Korean territories have returned with better experience with drone warfare and better experience with modern warfare. So they may have something to say to their military leadership. But what are considered to be the barricades with these North Koreans, they have been so exhausted with the too-stressful battlefield conditions. So, they may be the key. I mean, this is my hopeful suggestion, but these people will be the driving forces for asking for more changes regarding the South Korea and North Korea territories. And then, if the current administration fails to address these questions then there will be more political decisions, moving forward.
And could these people potentially be a problem for the regime now?
This is another matter that we don't really know the answer to. Military and civilian society have been in co-existence for a long time. But what I perceive in that case is that the military, they are taking the upper hand with the civilian structures. So whatever situation may arrive, it's going to be down to the hands of the military that will take the final decisions.
How South Korea іs helping Russia and what the consequences could be
What we see in the recent investigation by Reuters is that South Korean petroleum product experts have reportedly helped Russia with fuel shortages caused partly by Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries. How is this issue perceived in South Korea or is it even discussed there?
There are two different opinions about this matter. For conservative people, this is a really serious matter because it seems to be the case that the South Korean government is basically just looking away in the case of helping the Russian economy by support with petrochemical fuels.
But at the same time, from a purely technical perspective, the South Korean government is not prohibited from providing petrochemical products to the Russian Federation because this is not going to be subject to any country's sanctions regimes. So this is kind of revealing a kind of difference between many different countries' sanctions regimes.
From my perspective, it should be right to tighten the grip upon the differences in the different countries' sanction regimes. But at the same time, we have to hold our countries to settle out the differences between many unlike-minded nations to achieve the core missions of these sanctions which is to weaken the fighting ability of the Russian Federation in terms of the battlefield between the Russian Federation and Ukraine.
From the Ukrainian perspective this trade could be the next major source of tension between Seoul and Kyiv. From your perspective, how could these South Korean-Ukrainian relations be mended?
I mean, we have current issues between Ukraine and the Republic of Korea, but I strongly believe that this case will be settled away between the diplomatic negotiations between these countries.
What I perceive to be the more worrisome outcome is if the South Korean president Lee Jae-myung continues to press hard on the relations between Ukraine and the Korean Republic. And if that would be the case, then there's not going to be a case for these two bilateral regimes to be reconciled pretty much soon. Because as long as the president's mandate is not going to be met, there's not much that the South Korean foreign minister will do proactively to settle the differences. So all it might come down to is the president changing his position between Ukraine and the Republic of Korea.
In a way, the revealing of the identity of the prisoners, those North Korean soldiers, would not be so much to disrupt the bilateral relations between these countries. It's really important that the South Korean government is so aware of this importance and also about the importance of not being too far away from these two government's positions.

Norway’s Kongsberg to Make Anti-Drone Cannon Turrets in Poland From 2028
Norwegian defense manufacturer Kongsberg is preparing to build a production facility for anti-drone hardware in Poland to support the domestic SAN air defense network.
The agreement is expected to be signed by the end of the year, with construction starting immediately afterward, Defense Express reported on October 14.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The total financial commitment stands at 200 million Polish zlotys ($51 million), equivalent to €45 million ($50.2 million), with operations expected to launch in 2028.
Integrating production facilities within Poland aims to streamline supply chains for the country's national defense architecture. The plant will produce Kongsberg PROTECTOR weapon stations equipped with 30mm cannons, which serve as core modules for the SAN counter-drone system.
Establishing localized manufacturing addresses prior concerns regarding reliance on external components, helping to ensure greater domestic control over military hardware while creating economic value within the country.
The SAN air defense network relies on a combination of defensive platforms. Alongside 30mm cannon turrets, the network incorporates 12.7mm machine gun mounts, self-propelled 35mm SA-35 anti-aircraft systems, electronic warfare units, APKWS precision rockets, and Merops interceptor drones. These capabilities are configured onto Legwan all-terrain vehicles and Jelcz heavy trucks, as reported by Defense Express.
Polish armed forces have ordered 18 batteries of the system, comprising 18 command platoons and 52 firing platoons to expand protection against unmanned aerial threats. Neighboring Slovakia has also indicated interest in the platform through regional defense cooperation frameworks.
Cannon and machine gun turrets offer a cost-effective countermeasure compared to traditional surface-to-air missiles, despite functional constraints regarding operational ceiling and maximum engagement range.
Previously, Poland signed a major defense contract valued at approximately $4.2 billion with a consortium of PGZ and Kongsberg to acquire the SAN anti-drone system.
The contract, which was scheduled for delivery between 2026 and 2028, included 18 batteries, 18 command platoons, and 52 fire platoons capable of autonomously detecting, classifying, and neutralizing drones.

Herzog flies over Turkey despite ban on Israeli state planes, joins summit alongside Iranian representative

Israeli President Isaac Herzog arrived in Azerbaijan for an international summit attended by representatives of countries that have no diplomatic relations with Israel, including Iran, after taking an unusual flight through Turkish airspace despite Ankara's ban on Israeli government aircraft.
Among those attending were the emir of Qatar, Kuwait's deputy foreign minister, the ambassadors to Azerbaijan of Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Pakistan, Malaysia and Indonesia, Bangladesh's acting foreign minister and Iran's deputy foreign minister. When Herzog addressed the summit, the representatives of Iran, Turkey, Kuwait, Pakistan and the Palestinian Authority left the hall. The emir of Qatar remained, as did representatives of Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and Central Asian countries.
Herzog landed in Baku on Wednesday aboard a commercial Azerbaijan Airlines flight, allowing him to reach the Azerbaijani capital without taking a longer route over the Black Sea, which his team considered potentially dangerous because of the war between Russia and Ukraine.
The flight also provided an unexpected workaround to Turkey's restrictions on Israeli official aircraft, which have previously disrupted visits by senior Israeli leaders to Azerbaijan.
Herzog arrived for a day-and-a-half visit to participate in the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA), an international forum dedicated to strengthening cooperation and relations among Asian countries.
Alongside the Israeli president, the summit includes representatives from several countries that do not maintain diplomatic relations with Israel, including Qatar, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Malaysia and Indonesia. An Iranian representative is also attending.
According to a report by Middle East Eye, flight-tracking data from Flightradar24 and footage from Herzog's welcoming ceremony in Baku indicate that the Israeli president traveled on Azerbaijan Airlines flight J222. The flight departed Ben-Gurion Airport at 11:35 a.m. Wednesday, crossed Turkish airspace and landed in Baku at 3:40 p.m. local time.
Images from the welcoming ceremony showed Herzog arriving on an Azerbaijan Airlines Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner, matching the aircraft type recorded for the flight.
The president's team reportedly chose the commercial flight rather than a longer alternative route through Greece, Bulgaria and the Black Sea. The alternative raised security concerns because of continuing attacks on vessels in the Black Sea amid the Russia-Ukraine war.
Turkey has barred Israeli government aircraft from using its airspace, but commercial flights operated by Israeli and foreign airlines are still permitted to pass through the country on routes to and from Israel.
According to Middle East Eye, an official familiar with the matter said Azerbaijan had not informed Ankara that Herzog was aboard the flight.
"Naturally, Turkey cannot get the passenger manifest for every airliner just passing through the airspace," the Turkish official said. The official added that Israel had stopped submitting requests to use Turkish airspace because it was already familiar with Ankara's position.
Turkey's restrictions have previously interfered with Israeli diplomatic travel. In May 2025, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu postponed a planned visit to Baku, with reports at the time citing Ankara's refusal to allow Israel's official Wing of Zion aircraft to pass through Turkish airspace. Netanyahu's office cited developments in Gaza and Syria and a demanding political and security schedule.
Herzog himself canceled a planned visit to the COP29 climate conference in Azerbaijan in November 2024, amid reports that Turkey had refused permission for the Israeli state aircraft to cross its territory. This time, Wing of Zion was unavailable because of maintenance work, and Herzog traveled aboard the Azerbaijani aircraft instead. The President's Office declined to comment on the flight details.
The unusual journey also attracted attention because of the name of the aircraft carrying Herzog. Social media users identified the Azerbaijani plane as "Shusha," a name associated with the Shusha Declaration, a 2021 agreement between Azerbaijan and Turkey strengthening their strategic and defense cooperation following the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War.
Some commentators interpreted the choice of aircraft as a further symbolic jab by Baku at Ankara, although there has been no confirmation that the aircraft was selected for that reason.
The diplomatic symbolism extended to the summit itself. Herzog met Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev ahead of the gathering, which brings together countries with sharply differing positions on Israel and the wider Middle East.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan did not attend the summit, with Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan representing Ankara instead. Some reports suggested Erdogan's absence may have been connected to Herzog's participation, although this has not been officially confirmed. The meeting comes at a sensitive moment in relations between Turkey and Azerbaijan, two close regional allies.
Azerbaijan's recent school dress-code restrictions, which have prevented some students and teachers wearing Islamic headscarves from entering classrooms, have triggered protests and a public dispute involving political figures in both countries.
The restrictions have become another source of friction between Ankara and Baku, adding a further dimension to Herzog's appearance at the international gathering. On Thursday morning, as voting opened at Israeli diplomatic missions around the world ahead of the October 27 election, Herzog visited the Israeli Embassy in Baku alongside Israel's ambassador to Azerbaijan, Ronen Krausz.
"This is a very important moment during my state visit here to Azerbaijan," Herzog said. "I have the opportunity to see how the election process begins and how voting is actually conducted at Israeli diplomatic missions abroad, here at the embassy in Baku."
The president encouraged Israelis to participate in the democratic process and emphasized the importance of the upcoming election after a difficult period for the country.
"These elections are a celebration of democracy in Israel and at its embassies abroad," he said. "I call on all Israeli citizens to exercise their right to vote and, of course, to influence Israel's future."
Herzog also appealed for restraint amid political tensions surrounding the election campaign. "These are very important elections after a difficult period for the State of Israel, and the main thing I want to say to every Israeli citizen is that elections are not a civil war," he said.
"On the contrary, they are the genuine democratic process through which we influence our lives and determine the direction our country takes."

Croatia pumps the brakes on Montenegro’s EU membership bid
