Croatia pumps the brakes on Montenegro’s EU membership bid
Zagreb is pressing Podgorica to resolve long-standing disputes over war crimes, compensation and border demarcation before wrapping up EU accession talks.
BRUSSELS — Montenegro as the EU’s 28th member by 2028? Not so fast, says Croatia, the bloc’s most recent member.
Ahead of a debate on enlargement among EU leaders at Thursday’s summit, Croatia — which joined the bloc in 2013 — is among the countries raising concerns about Montenegro’s accession bid.
Speaking to POLITICO at a pre-summit meeting of the European People’s Party, Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković said Zagreb had been “extremely constructive” but pointed to unresolved issues under negotiating Chapter 23 (Judiciary and Fundamental Rights) and Chapter 31 (Foreign, Security and Defence Policy), some of which date back decades.
Advertisement
“Some have been on the agenda for the last two years [with] no progress whatsoever,” he said, urging Montenegro to make headway. “We will ask our colleagues to help them to make progress, if there’s an objective to conclude the negotiations.”
Croatia’s concerns are laid out in an orientation paper, obtained by POLITICO, in which Zagreb insists it supports Montenegro’s EU membership ambitions while identifying several outstanding disputes that need to be resolved.
“Croatia seeks to facilitate Montenegro’s accession, not obstruct it,” the paper reads. Several of the unresolved issues stem from Montenegro’s involvement in the military aggression against Croatia in the 1990s, including attacks on Dubrovnik and the occupation of parts of Croatian territory, according to the document.
Among Zagreb’s demands is compensation for Croatian nationals detained at the Morinj camp, where more than 300 Croatians were held between October 1991 and August 1992, following the occupation of part of the Dubrovnik region by Serbian and Montenegrin forces.
Croatia is also calling for the preservation and permanent display of a memorial plaque at the former detention camp, as well as the renaming of a municipal swimming pool in Kotor dedicated to Zoran Gopčević, a former international water polo player who, according to the document, served as a guard at Morinj in 1991 and 1992.
Other outstanding demands include the prosecution of war crimes committed during Croatia’s War of Independence and further talks on the delimitation of the border between the two countries.
Despite those disputes, Croatia has so far consented to Montenegro’s progress in accession negotiations. The country has provisionally closed 21 of its 33 negotiating chapters, making it the frontrunner in the EU’s enlargement process.

Ukraine has received 50,000 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine for children

Ukraine has received 50,000 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine for children
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine has received 50,000 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. Routine vaccinations are free of charge and available at healthcare facilities.
50,000 doses of the combined measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine have arrived in Ukraine for free vaccination of children in accordance with the Immunization Schedule. This was reported by the Public Health Center of Ukraine, UNN reports.
Ukraine receives these vaccines as part of cooperation between the Ministry of Health and the Global Alliance for Vaccines and Immunization (Gavi). The partnership agreement between the Global Alliance and Ukraine was signed at the end of 2024. Under the agreement, Gavi finances part of the vaccines supporting the national immunization program, in accordance with the national Immunization Development Strategy through 2030
According to the available information, במסגרת this partnership, UNICEF procures and delivers the vaccines to the country, while the Public Health Center of the Ministry of Health of Ukraine coordinates their distribution to regional disease control and prevention centers (DCCs). The vaccines have now reached healthcare facilities, which will ensure the continuity of routine immunization for children.
Where a child can be vaccinated
To vaccinate a child, you should contact your family doctor, pediatrician or the nearest healthcare facility. The Public Health Center emphasizes that vaccination under the National Immunization Schedule is free of charge.
If a child has missed any routine vaccinations, you should contact a doctor as soon as possible; the doctor will draw up an individual catch-up schedule
Why these infections are dangerous
Measles is a contagious infectious disease that can lead to serious complications, from pneumonia to encephalitis (inflammation of the brain) and even death. In pregnant women, measles can cause premature labor or miscarriage.
Mumps is one of the most common and contagious infections in the world, and can cause a number of severe complications, such as orchitis in men (inflammation of the testicle, which can lead to infertility), acute pancreatitis, meningitis and deafness.
Rubella is an infectious viral disease that can lead to miscarriage or congenital malformations in the child in pregnant women.
Vaccination is the most effective protection against these diseases.

Artemis III Scientist Shares What to Expect From NASA’s Next Lunar Mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:15:00 UTC
18:15:00 KST

For years, NASA hoped to bring humans back to the moon’s surface, and Artemis III was going to be the mission to accomplish this feat. That will no longer be the case.
Following the successful Artemis II flyby last April, the program’s schedule was revised. According to the most recent announcements, the next mission will have to wait until 2028, and while the new plans are admittedly less spectacular than a lunar landing, they’re hardly dispensable.
In 2027, NASA plans to test in Earth orbit whether the Orion capsule can safely rendezvous and operate with commercial lunar landing systems from SpaceX and Blue Origin before attempting those same maneuvers around the moon. WIRED en Español spoke with Barbara Cohen, a scientist on the Artemis III project, to better understand this upcoming mission—the conversation ranging from the role humans still play in the face of increasingly capable robots and sensors to what we can learn about the solar system’s violent past from traces preserved on the moon.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
JORGE GARAY: What should people expect from Artemis III, and why does this mission matter even if it won’t land astronauts on the moon?
BARBARA COHEN: Artemis III is an Earth-orbiting mission. That’s the one that’s coming up next. We will send the Orion capsule to Earth’s orbit with the people in it. Blue Origin and SpaceX are the companies that are making the lunar landers, so each one of those companies will make a test article. It won’t be the full lunar lander, but those companies will send their version of the test article into Earth’s orbit to meet up with Orion. This is to make sure that Orion can meet with the lunar landers, so that when they do go to lunar orbit, they can do that safely.
Where does science fit into the Artemis program, and what have you learned so far about how astronauts can contribute scientifically?
The Artemis missions, just to be clear, are not science missions. They’re exploration for a lot of different reasons. We do that for technology development. We do that for inspiration. And we try to get the science that we can from the opportunity. And so we still work really hard to identify unique science opportunities that exist because the mission exists.
One of the things on Artemis III we’re doing is like a dress rehearsal for bringing samples back from the moon. When we land on the moon and start to bring samples back, those samples change as soon as you take them out of their natural environment. We try to make sure that they change as little as possible, but they are going to change.
You have to bring them back and put them into curation so that scientists can study them. We want to understand every step along the way: What could be changing the samples, how the samples could be reacting, especially to the environment around them. So we’ll have our crew deploy these witness materials—pieces of aluminum foil, pieces of Teflon, maybe pieces of ceramic. They’re very clean surfaces, very small pieces, maybe the size of a quarter or a nickel. And the team will be opening those up and exposing them to the crew cabin throughout their flight. That’ll give us a feel for how the humans change the environment around them.
With the capabilities of probes and other robotic tools today, what is the purpose of sending human astronauts into space?
If you just want to take pictures, you do that with robotic assets. Robots can take pictures. They do that all the time. We have lots of pictures in the area. We also have, on the International Space Station, a way for us to ask, “Please take a picture of this. Please take a picture of that.” That’s not what we did with Artemis II, and that’s not what we’re trying to do with Artemis III or Artemis IV, V, VI. With the Artemis missions, we’re trying to use the humans to their best capability, and what the humans are really good at is seeing a wide scene, zooming in on details very naturally, and then trying to interpret what they’re seeing and take the next step.
We don’t know everything about the moon. To learn more, we need to literally go on the surface and figure out what’s there and where to go next. So some of this is trying to train—not just the crew onboard—but the flight directors and the science team and the engineers. We all need to work together to enable humans to do what they do best.
We also give the crew science prompts. We say, “What do you think is happening in this scene? There’s something like a storm or an algal bloom or a fire. What do you see? How do you see the scene changing? What do you think that means? What do you think is causing that change? What do you think is going to happen next? If you could do anything, what would you do next?” That helps us understand what they’re looking at, which is not just taking pictures. It’s making observations, making understanding, making inferences with their brains. That’s what humans are really good at. That’s what we’ll be asking them to do.
From a science point of view, we learned a lot about how crew really wants to use their powers of observation, and how we should participate in the observations and train them in the science that we want them to do. We also had the ability to include science directly in flight. On Artemis II, we had our science officer talk directly to crew. That was a new thing that we’ll be carrying forward to Artemis III and beyond.
When humans return to the lunar surface, what scientific questions would you most like Artemis to help answer?
I have a personal opinion. My personal scientific interest is how old craters on the moon are. If you look at the moon—with binoculars or a small telescope, or even in pictures—you see that it is covered in craters. In fact, we call it saturated, because every crater that forms does so on another crater. The whole surface is covered in craters. The Earth is not, but I promise you that for every crater that formed on the moon, there was a crater that formed on Earth.
The moon doesn’t get hit more than the Earth, but we have a lot of water. We have erosion on our continents. Our continents move around. They get subducted. We get new land that forms. All of those processes on the Earth erase craters. And so, if we want to know what was hitting the Earth in the past—and I promise you that things were hitting the Earth—we can’t find that evidence on the Earth anymore. We’ve erased it. So we have to go to the moon to figure that out.
There was a period in time when the solar system was forming—4.5 billion years ago, 4 billion years ago. Humans weren’t around. Life hadn’t arisen on Earth yet. We think that the solar system was very dynamic, and there were a lot of impacts happening, a lot of material being exchanged. So there were a lot of craters—big, big craters, basin-size craters, craters the size of continents. They really disrupted the moon, and they would have disrupted the Earth as well. Like I said, we don’t have any evidence of that because we don’t have any rocks from that time anymore. But it’s really worth knowing. Did we disrupt the Earth several times? How did life get going? How did we get nutrients? How did material move around the solar system? That evidence is preserved on the moon.
There is a big crater called the South Pole-Aitken Basin. It’s on the lunar far side, but it intersects the South Pole of the moon, where we expect humans to be going. It would be my personal desire that humans could collect pieces of that big crater, and we could understand when it formed and what it did to the moon and what was happening in the solar system at that time.
Artemis III won’t do that just yet. Lunar touchdown is currently expected as part of Artemis IV, which is expected to take off in early 2028. Before then, the upcoming third mission will have to demonstrate something far less spectacular, but crucial for the program’s future: That the spacecraft, procedures, and the people who will one day carry out these missions can work together safely.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

Zelenskyy: 850 Shaheds came as Starlink limits hit defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:11:10 UTC
18:11:10 KST

- Zelenskyy said Russia launched over 850 Shaheds between Oct. 14 and 9 a.m. Oct. 15, during a SpaceX speed cap on Ukraine’s Starlink terminals.
- The 160 km/h Starshield limit, imposed overnight Oct. 13–14, cripples interceptor drones needed against Russian jet-powered Shaheds flying up to 600 km/h.
Russia launched more than 850 Shahed attack drones at Ukraine in roughly a day and a half, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Oct. 15, an onslaught that came as a new speed cap on SpaceX’s Starlink network curtailed the interceptor drones Ukraine uses to shoot them down.
Zelenskyy said the count covered the period from the start of Oct. 14 until 9 a.m. on Oct. 15. He said attacks came in constant waves and that Ukrainian airspace was not free of drones for a single hour. Russian strikes killed three people in Kropyvnytskyi and three more in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukrainian media reported.
“From the start of yesterday until 9 a.m. today, there have already been more than 850 Shaheds, and this is precisely at a time of an artificial speed restriction on our defensive capabilities. Some of the Shaheds were shot down. But unfortunately, there were also dozens of hits,” Zelenskyy said, in remarks translated from Ukrainian.
The restriction he referred to took effect overnight on Oct. 13–14, when SpaceX capped Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink used by Ukraine’s armed forces, at 160 km/h (about 100 mph) for terminals in motion. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said SpaceX imposed the limit unilaterally and without warning, and that any terminal moving faster than that loses its connection, disrupting interceptor and mid-range drone missions as well as frontline reconnaissance, logistics and signal relays.
Under the cap, the restriction falls most heavily on Ukraine’s air defense. Russia’s jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones can fly at up to 600 km/h (about 370 mph), so interceptors that must chase them down need far more speed than 160 km/h. Starlink has been blocked over Russian territory since February 2026 under a whitelist of approved terminals, and Ukraine’s long-range strikes on Russian targets rely on other communications. The capped terminals instead serve tactical drones and uncrewed ground vehicles operating over Ukraine and the occupied territories, which means the limit cuts into Ukraine’s defense.
Service was later restored below the 160 km/h threshold, and Mykhailo Fedorov said attack and interceptor drones should be able to fly again, while adding that Ukraine now needs the Starshield speed limit removed altogether.
Elon Musk said on X that the military version of Starlink is controlled by the U.S. military and, ultimately, the U.S. president, the Associated Press reported, while the White House told Kyiv it does not control SpaceX, according to Axios. Zelenskyy told the Financial Times on Oct. 15 that the restriction was a deliberate decision on the American side rather than a technical fault, though he said he did not know whether SpaceX or the U.S. government made the call.
Zelenskyy also accused Moscow of escalating its strikes after seeing sanctions eased and attempts to pressure Kyiv, and urged Americans to side with Ukraine’s defense instead of the aggressor.
The Defense Ministry said it is in contact with the United States, SpaceX and NATO partners and is setting up backup communication channels, but neither SpaceX nor the U.S. Department of War has said whether or when the 160 km/h cap will be lifted.

Ayhan Simsek
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Arriving for a summit in Brussels, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Thursday that European leaders remain widely divided on the European Union’s next long-term budget.
“We are facing difficult negotiations,” Merz told reporters at the summit venue, adding that leaders would hold intensive and constructive talks but that an agreement was unlikely to be reached in the coming days.
“I wish that we can reach a result on the multiannual financial framework by the end of the year, although the ideas within the European Union are very far apart today,” he said.
“We face difficult negotiations, but I enter these negotiations with the firm will to bring them to a good result. Because Europe must remain capable of acting and become sovereign,” he added.
Merz criticized Ireland’s latest compromise proposal for the EU budget, saying that the planned reductions fall far short of what is needed for a deal.
“We must significantly reduce the common budget compared with the (European) Commission’s proposals. No member state in the European Union can afford to pay contributions to the European Union on this scale,” he said.
Merz noted that the current proposal lies 50% above the funding level of the ongoing multiannual financial framework and insisted that defense and the EU’s competitiveness should be priorities in the next budget.
Asked about the EU’s aid pledges to Ukraine, the German chancellor said Europeans need to boost funding to ensure that support for Ukraine remains sustainable in the long term.
“It remains my firm conviction that we are not only defending the territorial integrity of Ukraine, but we are defending the political order of Europe, which is being challenged by Russia in every respect,” he said.
Asked about placing Russian assets frozen in the EU under US control, Merz rejected the idea.
“These are assets that are frozen in Europe. They should remain frozen in Europe. This is our matter, and we decide on it,” he said.
The Financial Times reported Wednesday, citing insiders, that the United States had proposed to European states that part of the frozen Russian assets be released and transferred to a financial vehicle controlled by Washington to revive peace talks with Moscow.
The plan was presented by US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, but was rejected by European representatives, the newspaper said.

EU pushing for action over trade deficit with China
Jennifer Rankin
The EU is set to call for further action to curb the bloc’s vast trade deficit with China, widely blamed for job losses and factory closures across the continent.
EU leaders meeting in Brussels on Thursday to discuss the trade deficit with China - which hit €360bn in 2025 - are expected to call for “new instruments to better address these imbalances” according to a draft statement.
The European Commission, which negotiates trade policy on behalf of the 27 member states, agreed a deal this month with Beijing that will see the EU limit hybrid car exports from China to 350,000 vehicles a year, potentially halving Chinese market share.
EU countries have welcomed the deal, but think it is not enough and want steps to protect other industrial sectors, such as chemicals, plastics and machinery.
The debate has sharpened since Germany - long reluctant to use trade defences against China - converted to a more hawkish position amid pressure from German industrial leaders, who are laying off workers and closing factories.
Germany and France last week called for better use of existing trade defence measures, including urgent action in the chemicals and plastics sectors.
The EU’s two biggest economies are also seeking “a diversification instrument” that would cut off access to the EU market when faced with severe imbalances. Dubbed the “kill switch”, the law is intended to be country agnostic, but is clearly aimed at China.
Member states have welcomed the deal negotiated by EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič on hybrid cars, but are sceptical as to whether Beijing will stick to it. China would adhere to the agreement because they began to realise “they are killing their customers” , Šefčovič was reported to have said, according to a senior EU diplomat.
The EU diplomat highlighted the urgency of the situation from the EU’s point of view: “We don’t have much time because every month that goes by, thousands of jobs are lost.”

SYDNEY, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have launched a new study to examine whether cervical cancer can be detected through a non-invasive blood test.
Led by the University of Queensland (UQ), the CLARITY cervical cancer study at the Royal Brisbane and Women's Hospital will investigate the potential of blood biomarkers in the screening, monitoring and management of cervical cancer, according to a UQ statement released recently.
"The project has the potential to improve early detection, treatment responses and post-treatment surveillance, as well as support more personalized treatment approaches for women with cervical cancer," said Andreas Obermair, chief investigator at UQ's Queensland Center for Gynecological Cancer Research.
Despite advances in prevention and treatment, including the Gardasil vaccine, cervical cancer continues to impose significant physical, emotional and financial burdens on women worldwide, Obermair noted.
A reliable, non-invasive test could offer "a more accessible and acceptable alternative" to current cervical screening methods, particularly for women facing cultural, systemic or personal barriers to screening, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women and culturally diverse communities, he said. ■

LANZHOU, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- China's C919 passenger jet has carried more than 8.4 million passengers and served 27 cities since entering commercial service, Shen Bo, president of the Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China (COMAC), said Thursday.
Speaking at an industry conference in Dunhuang, northwest China's Gansu Province, Shen said COMAC has also continued to expand the regional aviation network served by its C909 aircraft, a regional jet designed for short- and medium-haul routes.
The C909 has safely carried more than 41 million passengers since entering commercial service, Shen said, adding that the aircraft is providing travelers with more convenient options.
Wang Changshun, chairman of the China Air Transport Association, said China's regional aviation fleet has been rapidly transforming in recent years, with domestic aircraft accounting for a substantially larger share.
The C919 is accelerating its scale-up in commercial operations, while the C909 has become a mainstay of the regional aviation market, contributing to the high-quality development of China's regional aviation sector, he said.
The C919 is the first trunk jetliner independently developed by China in accordance with international airworthiness standards and with independent intellectual property rights.
The baseline model is designed for 158 to 192 passengers and a range of 4,075 to 5,555 kilometers. It completed its first commercial flight in May 2023. After successful operations on multiple domestic routes, the aircraft completed its first scheduled international commercial passenger flight in August this year.
The C909, formerly known as the ARJ21, entered commercial service in 2016. According to COMAC, it is suitable for regional airports or sub-hub airports to build route networks and supplement transport capacity for hub airports.
China's civil aviation market continued to expand in 2025, carrying 770 million passenger trips, up 5.5 percent year on year, according to the Civil Aviation Administration of China.
The country's latest five-year plan for civil aviation development from 2026-2030 calls for improving transport infrastructure, efficiency and services as well as fostering independent innovation and industrial integration. It sets a 2030 goal of reaching world-class standards in aviation safety, service capacity and infrastructure. ■

UK Pledges $23M for Chornobyl Repairs Amid Support Strains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:08:45 UTC
18:08:45 KST

Britain pledged £17 million ($23 million) on Thursday, Oct. 15 toward repairs to the protective shelter and ventilation system at the Chornobyl nuclear power plant, as far-right parties question continued aid to Kyiv and Ukraine’s military faces disruption to satellite communications.
The UK government said the funding will help restore the shelter’s confinement and ventilation functions. The contribution is part of an international program coordinated by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), working with Ukraine and G7 donors.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
However, it is not the full cost of the repairs. The EBRD has estimated that the work could exceed €500 million ($585 million).
Why Chornobyl’s shelter needs repairs
The New Safe Confinement is a 35-story arch built over reactor No. 4 to contain radioactive material and allow engineers to dismantle the remains of the reactor and the original sarcophagus. The €2.1 billion ($2.5 billion) structure was designed to last 100 years and was constructed with contributions from 45 countries.
A Russian drone struck the plant on Feb. 14, 2025, punching a hole through its roof and igniting a fire in the cladding. The fire smoldered inside its layers for two weeks before it was extinguished. The strike damaged the ventilation system and the structure’s seal, allowing moist air to enter and raising the risk of corrosion in the steel arch.
In May, the EBRD said that radiation was not escaping the confinement, but warned that corrosion could undermine the structure if repairs are delayed. Engineers also face difficult working conditions: the site’s radiation levels limit how long workers can remain inside.
Musk Tells Zelensky to ‘Go’ as Ukraine Questions US Support
The extent of the damage is still being assessed, and the final repair estimate could change. More detail on the damage to the confinement and the repair work shows why the British contribution is one part of a much larger funding effort.
The UK has previously donated €8 million ($9 million) to the International Chornobyl Cooperation Account, which supports nuclear safety at the site. It announced another £54 million ($72 million) in winter support last week, including £20 million ($26 million) for energy assistance. The government says Britain has provided nearly £25 billion ($33 billion) in total support to Ukraine.
During a meeting in London, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told President Volodymyr Zelensky that Britain was “behind you and that will not change,” The Guardian reported.
Far-right parties challenge continued aid
The pledge comes as European support for Ukraine faces political pressure.
Marine Le Pen, leader of France’s far-right National Rally party and a potential contender in the 2027 presidential election, said France “cannot keep financing Ukraine,” citing the country’s economic situation. Le Pen has said she would end French financial aid to Kyiv if elected, while leaving military assistance and training open.
Her comments raise questions about future French policy, but do not signal an immediate change in France’s current support. The Guardian said current polling predicts Le Pen could win next year’s vote. Her position also comes as European governments debate how to finance further support for Ukraine.
In Germany, the far-right Alternative for Germany and the leftist BSW party backed a motion in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament calling for Berlin to end military support for Ukraine. The measure is symbolic: state parliaments do not set Germany’s foreign policy, so it does not change the federal government’s aid. It does, however, show how opposition to military assistance is entering regional political debate.
Europe has no immediate Starlink alternative
The political debate coincides with a disruption to military satellite connections. On Wednesday, Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials said restrictions had affected Starshield terminals, the military-grade service associated with SpaceX’s satellite network. Some units reported losing connections while moving at speeds ranging from about 72 to 161 kilometers per hour (45 to 100 miles per hour), according to Ukrainian defense ministry sources.
The disruption affected drone missions, including interception and medium-range strike operations, as well as frontline logistics, reconnaissance, and communications relays. Ukraine’s defense ministry said it was gathering reports from units, contacting the US, SpaceX, and NATO partners, and checking backup communications channels. The cause of the restrictions had not been established. The timing added to concerns over strained US-Ukraine relations, but did not prove the restrictions were politically motivated.
Reuters reported that Europe has no ready-made satellite system Ukrainian soldiers could attach to drones as an immediate replacement. Eutelsat’s OneWeb network does provide connectivity in Ukraine through partners, but consultant Christian Freiherr von der Ropp said its terminals’ capacity, weight, size, and power requirements make them less suitable for frontline use.
Starlink and OneWeb terminals also use different technology, meaning Ukraine could not simply connect existing Starlink equipment to OneWeb – thousands of terminals would need to be replaced.
Bohdan Sas, co-founder of Ukrainian defense technology company Buntar Aerospace, told Reuters the disruption showed that users “can’t rely solely on one solution that can be switched off.” European governments and companies are working on longer-term options, but those plans do not offer a quick fix. The dependence extends beyond communications. Ukraine and European countries rely on US satellite systems for early warnings of ballistic missile attacks.

Pakistan school collapse kills almost 30 students and a teacher

Pakistan school roof collapses in Peshawar, killing almost 30 young students and a teacher
Islamabad — Almost 30 students and a teacher were killed Thursday when the roof of a private school collapsed in the Pakistani city of Peshawar, local officials said.
The bodies of 17 children were brought to Lady Reading Hospital in the city following the incident, in addition to the body of a female teacher, Mohammad Asim, a spokesperson for the hospital told CBS News, adding that some survivors were also admitted in critical condition.
At least 29 people were killed in total after the collapse at the Al-Khair Education Center in Peshawar's southwest Dir district, according to Asim and other local officials.
The cause of the disaster remained unconfirmed, but a witness told CBS News the building appeared "not suitable" for use as a school, and a local police official said there was ongoing construction on the roof that could have overweighted the structure.
"We have taken out at least 45 children," district emergency officer Iftikhar Khan said, according to the Reuters news agency.
Mahwish Zaman, a teacher who was injured in the collapse, told the Associated Press after regaining consciousness in her hospital bed that the school had about 1,200 students enrolled, and she was in her class when the roof collapsed. She described it as feeling as if the sky had fallen.
Zahir Hussain, who lives a couple of blocks from the school, told CBS News he was walking to work when he saw people running out onto the street.
"I rushed to the spot and the school with others to see what had happened," he said. "Apparently first-period classes had just started … The building was overcrowded. The lesson had barely begun" when the collapse occurred.
He said the school was in a relatively small residential building on a narrow street, and that it catered mainly to children from low-income families. Signage on the outside of the building indicated that there were classes for both boys and girls.
"The parents and families were in unbearable pain. The street was extremely narrow, which made it difficult for rescue teams to reach the site quickly," he told CBS News.
"The building was not suitable for use as a school at all. It is a very tragic incident, seeing dead innocent children's bodies left me silent, and it was extremely painful," Hussain said, calling it a "heavy tragedy for parents and the entire Dir colony."
"It was a weak building structure," Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed said, according to Reuters. "Its roof was overweight with construction on a weak structure that caused the collapse."

Breaking: Starlink service in Ukraine 'restored,' Defense Ministry source says

18:07:44 KST

Connectivity for Starlink systems used by the Ukrainian military have "been restored and remains operational," a source in the Defense Ministry told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 15.
SpaceX, the owner of Starlink, implemented speed restrictions on Oct. 14 without warning, limiting speed to 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour). The unexpected restriction disrupted active military operations, including the use of mid-range strike and interceptor drones.
"As of now, (Starlink military package) Starshield service while on the move has been restored and remains operational. We have confirmed this through reports from our units," the source said.
"The Defense Ministry is also continuing its engagement to clarify all the reasons and circumstances surrounding yesterday’s restrictions."
The source did not say if all restrictions had been lifted or if some speed restrictions still applied.
Serhii Sternenko, an activist and former advisor to Fedorov who was one of the first to report the restrictions, also said on Oct. 15 that "Starlink (Starshield) service has been restored."
But a source in Ukraine's drone industry who requested anonymity due to the nature of their work told the Kyiv Independent that "in some cases, it works perfectly, in some places it does not."
The source of the disruption has yet to be confirmed, but Ukrainian officials as well as SpaceX CEO Elon Musk have pointed towards Kyiv's deteriorating relationship with the White House.
"Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is associated with the current political situation," presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said on Oct. 14.
A post on X from Musk said only U.S. President Donald Trump had the power to determine the speed restrictions for Starshield systems.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately (the president). .... Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action," he said.
Ukraine relies on Starlink for several military applications including operating its "middle strike" campaign in Russian-occupied Ukraine, as well as interceptor drones that defend against Russia's new jet-powered attack drones. It is restricted from using it inside Russia itself.
The speed restrictions that were put in place on Oct. 14 were accompanied by signal disruptions and instability, even at lower speeds. Military personnel from multiple units reported serious issues with Starlink throughout the day.
Ukraine's Defense Ministry told journalists that the actual speeds available during the day were even lower than the 160 kph limit.
A soldier working on mid-range strike drone operations, who requested anonymity, confirmed that "certain issues are being observed" but declined to elaborate, citing operational security.
Two other commanders — both from elite drone units working on the eastern and southern front lines — reported issues with Starlink terminals on "middle strike" drones flying at higher speeds.
Both likewise requested to remain anonymous, and declined to describe the problems in more detail, so as to not assist the enemy.

Türkiye’s electric car fleet nears 500,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:05:54 UTC
18:05:54 KST

The number of electric cars registered in Türkiye rose to 486,359 as of the end of September 2026, up from just 80,043 in 2023 and 14,552 in 2022, according to motor vehicle data released by the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) on Oct. 15.
At the same time, hybrid vehicle ownership climbed to 915,892, highlighting the country’s accelerating shift toward alternative-fuel vehicles.
The data showed a sharp increase in EV and hybrid cars over recent years, while the share of diesel and LPG-powered vehicles continued to decline. EVs accounted for 2.7 percent of all registered cars in September, compared with 0.5 percent in 2023 and just 0.1 percent in 2022. Hybrid cars represented 5.1 percent of the fleet, up from 1.5 percent three years earlier.
Diesel cars, once the dominant fuel type, made up 32 percent of all registered automobiles at the end of September, down from a peak of 38.3 percent in 2020. At the same time, gasoline-powered vehicles increased their share of the fleet to 31 percent, while remaining below the levels seen in the mid-2000s, when they accounted for more than two-thirds of all passenger cars.
According to TÜİK, 18.12 million automobiles were registered in traffic as of the end of September.
The total number of registered motor vehicles in Türkiye increased 6.2 percent year-on-year in September to 35.07 million.
Automobiles accounted for 51.7 percent of all registered vehicles, followed by motorcycles at 21.9 percent, pickup trucks at 14.2 percent, tractors at 6.7 percent, trucks at 3 percent, minibuses at 1.6 percent and buses at 0.6 percent.
Among passenger cars newly registered in September, Renault held the largest share at 16.1 percent. TOGG ranked second with 9.8 percent, followed by Hyundai with 8.6 percent, Volkswagen with 7.1 percent and Toyota with 6.8 percent.
Other major brands included Mercedes-Benz with 5.3 percent, Skoda with 5 percent, Kia with 4.5 percent, Peugeot with 3.7 percent, Nissan with 3.3 percent, Opel, Fiat and Tesla with 2.7 percent each.
In the January-September period, the number of newly registered vehicles fell 14.5 percent year-on-year to 1.5 million, said TÜİK.

"We will seriously consider (the possibility) in a concrete and realistic manner," Takaichi told parliament Wednesday, according to Kyodo News Agency.

Earlier this month, Takaichi told parliament that no decision had been made on submarine propulsion.
Government officials are reportedly considering including nuclear-powered submarines among the options in Japan's revised national security and defense documents later this year.

"People need to be able to afford to adapt to climate change" says architect founder of Shaded
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:05:05 UTC
18:05:05 KST

"People need to be able to afford to adapt to climate change" says architect founder of Shaded
London-based architectural designer Aimée Daniels has invented an awning system that sold out multiple times this summer. In this interview, she argues the UK needs to get on board with the power of shading.
Self-described "clean-tech startup" Shaded sells simple and colourful external awnings that can be easily installed on or removed from sash windows and retail at £89.
"It's a detachable awning for sash windows," Daniels told Dezeen. "It's sort of an alternative to air conditioning."
Daniels, who is originally from New York and grew up with the comforts of air conditioning, founded Shaded in 2023 after struggling with UK temperatures that reached 40 degrees the previous summer.
"There is an appetite for affordable passive cooling products"
Concerned by the lack of shading across UK homes and privy to the benefits of shading techniques through her ten years in architecture, Daniels became dedicated to retrofitting buildings.
"I guess the 40-degree weather of summer 2022 put me in an inventive mood, initially in response to my own discomfort and the lack of accessible, sustainable solutions available to deal with it," she said.
"The idea for the awning came through a combination of doing passive design at work, and knowing about the principles and how shade is so effective," she said.
With the UK's summers continuing to break temperature records ever since, Shaded has become extremely popular and gained significant attention online, with the awning system selling out three times since being launched earlier this year.
"I had doubts and launched the product with the goal of breaking even," Daniels admitted.
"The product's success was a great validation that there is an appetite for affordable passive cooling products that also look good."
Daniels conceived Shaded as a more affordable and sustainable alternative for cooling Britain's homes than air conditioning, which is also becoming much more popular among those who can afford it.
"[Passive solutions] should be the first thing people do, at the very least, before bringing in mechanical cooling," she said.
"I think that making that more accessible is a big component of how to promote it and get people to buy in."
External shading systems can be highly effective, reducing room temperatures by several degrees Celsius.
But despite their widespread use across other temperate climates, awnings remain fairly uncommon in the UK, especially on residential buildings.
"UK hasn't clocked on to shading windows"
Much more common, says Daniels, are blinds and curtains, which can contribute to overheating.
"The UK seems to be the only European country that hasn't clocked on to shading windows as a first line of defence," she said.
Affordability is a major factor in this lack of adoption, Daniels suggests.
"Right now, it's actually really hard to choose passive cooling for reasons like costs being too high," Daniels said.
"Installation is a big driver of cost," she continued. "The fact that you have to fix something externally to the facade means that you probably need to put up scaffolding, et cetera. It requires specialist help."
In contrast, Shaded's awnings are clipped on from the inside – reducing installation costs to zero.
Even in the case that someone might be able to afford to install a traditional, permanent awning, Daniels says, the route to gaining planning permission can be costly.
In addition to this, the lack of a blanket policy for the installation of awnings in the UK can make the process convoluted, with existing regulations often specifying limitations for buildings that are rented, listed or located within a conservation area, Daniels explains.
"Permanent awnings are drilled into facades, becoming a material component of a building, and their cassettes have a year-round presence," she said.
In the London Borough of Islington, for example, planning permission is required for awnings on front elevations of flats, multiple-occupation houses and properties within a conservation area.
Meanwhile, London's Westminster City Council, in collaboration with property investment company Grosvenor, has recently given blanket consent for awnings and other retrofit measures on listed buildings in Belgravia's Eaton Square.
Daniels' second design marker was therefore meeting regulatory requirements.
"I went around in circles a lot around figuring out what I have to do to meet regulations," she said. "[Typically], if you wanted to install external shading you'd have to put a planning application in."
"You might have to submit drawings, and that all costs money and time – on top of the fact that the existing products are expensive," she added.
"My motivation is making sure the mass of people can actually afford to do it"
Daniels' awning offers a temporary, "zero-trace" alternative, meaning that it side-steps the bureaucracy of installing a permanent one.
"It's completely temporary and doesn't interact with the building fabric at all. It leaves zero trace," she said.
Following the success of her first product, Daniels has plans to create a new range of awnings that cater to more window types, alongside the creation of other affordable passive solutions.
"We need to adapt our built environment to temperatures," Daniels said. "My motivation is making sure the mass of people can actually afford to do it."
"Why can certain people adapt to climate change and not others? People need to be able to afford to adapt to climate change," she added.

Children are being left behind in the Ebola disease response
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:03:32 UTC
18:03:32 KST

- The Ebola disease outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo is disproportionately impacting children, with the youngest children facing the highest risk of death.
- Children are also being left behind in the research of innovative medical tools.
- Ongoing and future studies on Bundibugyo virus, the virus driving this outbreak, must include children.
Children are paying a devastating price in the Ebola disease outbreak unfolding in northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). While children face a higher risk of death from Ebola than adults, they also represent a significant proportion of the people affected by the current outbreak.
According to Epicentre, Médecins Sans Frontières’ (MSF’s) epidemiological research centre, nearly one in four confirmed Ebola cases in North Kivu province is a child. MSF is deeply concerned by the disproportionate impact of the disease on children and calls for more attention to their specific vulnerabilities, in both the medical and research response.
While Ebola remains a deadly disease for all age groups, the youngest children face the highest risk of death. In North Kivu, children have been particularly affected by the current outbreak: 24% of confirmed cases are among children under five years of age, compared with 13% in Ituri province, while infants under one year old account for 13% of cases, compared with 6% in Ituri.
At the Ebola treatment centre (ETC) in Butembo, North Kivu, MSF teams have observed that the case fatality rate among children was particularly high. Between June and September 2026, 24 out of 30 children – most of whom were under the age of five – died from the Bundibugyo virus in this ETC alone. The rapid progression of the disease in communities and limited access to specialised care at health facility level are contributing to such alarmingly high fatality rates.
“General health facilities often lack the specialised expertise, equipment, and infection prevention and control measures needed to identify and safely manage suspected cases,” explains Stéphanie Hoffmann, project coordinator for MSF in Butembo. “Most of the paediatric cases admitted in our ETC in Butembo, North Kivu, over the summer, had already been hospitalised for other illnesses in several facilities during the days or weeks before their admission. Their family members did not have Ebola themselves, and it is highly likely that these children contracted the disease inside healthcare facilities.”
Most of the paediatric cases admitted in our ETC in Butembo, North Kivu, over the summer, had already been hospitalised for other illnesses in several facilities during the days or weeks before their admission.
Stéphanie Hoffmann, project coordinator for MSF in Butembo
Strengthening infection prevention and control measures in health facilities, ensuring the availability of personal protective equipment, and reinforcing the training of healthcare workers in non-Ebola health centres across at-risk areas are critical to maintaining essential services while preventing healthcare-associated transmission.
While efforts have been made to reduce the emotional toll of isolation on children in ETCs, including the creation of visibility areas where parents can see and communicate with their hospitalised children, being admitted to an ETC remains a deeply distressing experience for young patients. Children may be too young to understand their situation or meet their own basic needs.
To help address this situation, MSF has recruited and trained caregivers who provide daily support and comfort to children inside several MSF-supported ETCs while wearing full personal protective equipment. These caregivers come from diverse backgrounds, including, but not limited to, being Ebola survivors. Today, 13 caregivers are supporting children at the Kitatumba ETC in Butembo. While far from a perfect solution, this initiative provides essential human contact and emotional support for children facing the outbreak.
“On top of enormous challenges caring for young patients, medical facilities are dealing with a lack of paediatric dosing guidance, and limited availability of child-friendly formulations of investigational medicines,” says Dr Guyguy Manangama, epidemiologist and deputy director of operations at MSF. “A child-centred approach must be at the heart of medical care, operational planning, and research efforts.”
A child-centred approach must be at the heart of medical care, operational planning, and research efforts.
Dr Guyguy Manangama, epidemiologist and deputy director of operations at MSF
Children have been disproportionately affected by the current outbreak, yet they are left behind when it comes to access to innovative medical tools. Historically, children are often excluded from clinical research or included only after significant delays, creating dangerous gaps in evidence and access to potentially lifesaving interventions.
“Treatments, vaccines, and other preventive tools should be evaluated for use in children from the outset of research efforts and made available to them without delay,” says Dr Manangama. “Yet in the current outbreak, children are still being left behind, with very limited access to vaccination trials and campaigns, as well as the latest therapeutic innovations despite bearing a significant burden of disease.” 
“Children cannot continue to wait for data generated in adults before benefiting from advances in Ebola care and prevention,” says Dr Manangama.
MSF urges national authorities, research institutions, pharmaceutical developers, and international funders to prioritise the inclusion of children in all ongoing and future Bundibugyo virus studies. Ensuring equitable access to research and new medical tools, including vaccines, is essential to reducing preventable deaths and improving outcomes for one of the most vulnerable groups.
The impact of the outbreak on children extends beyond Ebola infection itself. Disruptions to essential health services can rapidly increase risks from vaccine-preventable diseases, malnutrition, and other common childhood illnesses. Preserving routine immunisation, nutrition programmes, and access to general healthcare must therefore be considered a core component of the outbreak response, not an afterthought.
Note to editors:
Treatment: One ongoing study, EBO-PEP, is evaluating an oral antiviral drug, obeldesivir, to prevent Ebola infection after high-risk exposure. If proven effective, the treatment could provide a practical way to protect people who have recently been in contact with an Ebola patient. While the trial is expected to expand eligibility to include some children, those under 20 kilograms remain excluded because an appropriate paediatric formulation is not yet available.
For the youngest children, the current alternative involves a 10-day course of intravenous treatment, an approach that is particularly difficult to implement in outbreak settings and can be especially challenging for young patients and their caregivers. More information here: An urgent opportunity to ensure children's access to oral post-exposure prophylaxis trials for Bundibugyo virus disease - The Lancet Child & Adolescent Health.
Vaccination: While the results of ongoing trials evaluating vaccines specifically designed for the Bundibugyo virus are not expected for several months, ERVEBO® is an immediately available option. Its safety profile is well established, it is approved for use in children aged one year and older, and health authorities in DRC have extensive experience using it in outbreak settings. Emerging evidence also suggests that it may offer some protection against the Bundibugyo virus, although the degree of protection remains to be clarified. In areas at high risk of Ebola transmission, vaccinating contacts of confirmed cases, including children over one year of age, could help prevent severe illness and save lives.

- Come Back Alive delivered 80 experimental interceptor drones built to hunt jet-powered Shaheds, buying them for 13.6 million hryvnias donated by OKKO.
- The foundation says it has contracted several hundred experimental counter-drone systems since September, with the best performers set for refinement and possible serial production.
Ukrainian charity Come Back Alive has handed frontline units 80 new interceptor drones designed to bring down Russia’s jet-powered Shahed attack drones, also known as Geran-4, paying 13.6 million hryvnias, roughly $302,000 or about $3,800 per drone, with money donated by Ukrainian fuel station chain OKKO.
The foundation announced the delivery in a post on X on Oct. 15, describing the drones as test samples that troops will now evaluate in combat. It did not name the manufacturer or give the interceptors’ speed, range or warhead, and photos released with the announcement show rows of white, four-rotor drones with stubby wings packed in crates.
Come Back Alive said this is not the first batch of jet-Shahed interceptors it has sent to the front, only the first it has made public. Since September, the foundation has contracted several hundred experimental counter-drone systems from different manufacturers under its Dronopad program, with the best performers sent back for refinement and some later moving into serial production.
The charity said it followed the same approach with interceptors built to stop older piston-engine Shaheds, which have since become a standard part of Ukraine’s air defense against Russian long-range drone attacks.
“We think ahead: we analyze the prospects for rapidly scaling up production, retraining pilots and the possibility of an uninterrupted supply of the necessary components,” the Dronopad team said, in a statement translated from Ukrainian.
Russia has been shifting its drone attacks toward faster jet-powered models in the Geran family, its domestically built version of the Iranian Shahed. The newer Geran-4 and Geran-5 can fly at up to 600 km/h (about 370 mph), several times faster than the propeller-driven Shahed-136, and Russia launched nearly 800 jet-powered drones at Ukraine over four days in late August, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky. On Sept. 15, Zelensky said Ukraine had successfully tested another interceptor against jet-powered Shaheds, while acknowledging that some aspects of controlling it still needed work.
Interceptor drones that cost a few thousand dollars have become one of Ukraine’s main answers to Russia’s mass drone raids, since firing a surface-to-air missile worth hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars at each attacker is not sustainable. Catching a jet-powered drone is harder because the interceptor needs much higher speed and a shorter reaction time to close on its target.
Founded in 2014, Come Back Alive is one of Ukraine’s largest charities supplying the armed forces and is licensed to buy military equipment directly for frontline units.

The irony of OpenAI crying foul over spying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:03:02 UTC
18:03:02 KST

The irony of OpenAI crying foul over spying
A company that owes much of its existence – and enormous valuation – to stealing other people’s work is now up in arms about people trying to steal from it.
Americans can rest easy – for the moment, at least. The fine folks at the Federal Bureau of Investigation have thwarted a major national security threat.
On October 9, the FBI arrested 35-year-old engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi citizen employed at the California-based artificial intelligence company OpenAI, which makes the chatbot ChatGPT and describes its corporate mission as ensuring that “artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity”.
A press release from the United States Department of Justice said that Alfozan was accused of installing a “surreptitious audio recording device” in an executive conference room at the OpenAI offices in San Francisco.
The statement quoted Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton’s assessment that “this serious situation underscores why winning the global super intelligence race is a national security prerogative”. (For those who have not yet got the memo, US President Donald Trump recently decreed that the term “artificial intelligence” be changed to “super intelligence” or “SI.”)
FBI director Kash Patel concurred that “protecting American SI innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security”, and assured everyone that the FBI would continue doing its part “to ensure our country maintains its competitive edge”.
So much for the separation of corporation and state in the world’s self-appointed greatest democracy.
The covert device was reported to have been concealed in toilet paper and attached to the back of a television monitor. The Gizmodo website has noted with amusement that, despite being cast as a “sophisticated” spying apparatus, the device in question can in fact be easily ordered online “for the low low price of $13.99”.
If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in jail and a fine of $250,000.
Now, some of you may still be asking what the big deal is – and why the US government is acting like it’s 1950 and the Soviets are stealing our nuclear secrets.
The spectacle becomes all the more curious when we consider that the company up in arms over the alleged attempted theft of its technology owes much of its existence – and massive valuation – to stealing stuff from people.
The day before Alfozan’s arrest, USA Today and several other newspapers sued OpenAI in a Manhattan federal court for copyright infringement and the unauthorised use of hundreds of thousands of news articles and other materials to develop ChatGPT.
And back in July, various US media outlets including the New York Times and the New York Daily News requested that a federal judge impose sanctions on OpenAI for “hiding and destroying evidence showing how ChatGPT was trained on stolen journalism”, as attorney Steven Lieberman put it.
The moral of the story, perhaps, is that when OpenAI steals things it’s to “benefit all of humanity” – but when a 35-year-old Saudi engineer does it, it’s a national security crisis.
In case we were not already bored to tears hearing about national security, US Attorney General Todd Blanche took to X on Tuesday to preach that the “theft of intellectual property involving cutting-edge super intelligence technology poses a serious threat to our national security”, necessitating continued “swift action … to protect American innovation and safeguard our nation”.
Of course, many Americans might wonder why “innovation” gets such special treatment when they themselves are so often on the receiving end of government abuse. The frequency with which US police officers murder unarmed Black people, for instance, would seem to indicate that there are far more literal threats to the nation’s security than a $14 device hidden in toilet paper.
But human security is of no interest to a corporatocracy increasingly dominated by AI, an industry that thrives on putting people out of jobs and that is deeply entwined in a number of sordid developments at home and abroad. Among them is mass surveillance, which combines AI-assisted violations of civil liberties and constitutional protections with good old police state “innovation”.
To that end, a bunch of US cops have taken advantage of new AI-powered technology, such as automated licence plate readers, to stalk their exes. Then there is the matter of the FBI and other government agencies buying up data en masse from tech companies in a bid to keep tabs, Big Brother-style, on everyone’s personal information at all times.
It makes you think twice about the sudden concern for “spying” in the Alfozan case.
As for threats to other people’s national security, OpenAI and like-minded tech companies that do business with the Pentagon have been complicit in recent US aggression – from Venezuela to Iran – as the US pursues its strategy for “Accelerating America’s Military AI Dominance” (concocted before Trump mandated the renaming of AI as SI).
Israel, too, has exploited OpenAI technology, among other US-made goodies, to conduct its contemporary apocalyptic exercises in the Middle East. Last year, the Associated Press news agency (AP) revealed that US tech giants had “quietly empowered Israel to track and kill many more alleged militants more quickly in Gaza and Lebanon through a sharp spike in artificial intelligence and computing services”.
The AP report went on to note that “the number of civilians killed has also soared, fueling fears that these tools are contributing to the deaths of innocent people”.
But while it might be news to the AP, that is unfortunately how a genocide works.
And as the US goes to war for AI dominance while the tech giants bank on a post-human world, one can’t help but feel that the toilet paper was a nice touch, indeed.

The policing of Muslim women&#8217;s bodies, from West Asia to Europe and beyond
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
09:01:03 UTC
18:01:03 KST

There is something profoundly vile about discriminating against women and policing their bodies in the name of secularism. Dictating what a woman should or should not wear is fundamentally at odds with freedom of choice. When institutions use their authority to compel women to dress according to a particular vision of society, secularism begins to resemble the very authoritarianism it claims to oppose.
The question has never been whether women should wear the hijab. The question is why everyone seems to believe they have a say in the matter.
As I write this, in October 2026, Azerbaijan is witnessing protests following new school clothing restrictions that have resulted in hijabi students and teachers being denied entry to some schools. The government’s amendment, approved in September, prohibits clothing deemed inconsistent with the principle of secularism, indirectly restricting the wearing of the Muslim headscarf. Women are now being forced to choose between their religious beliefs and their access to education or employment.
But what kind of freedom requires a woman to abandon part of her religious identity before she can enter a classroom? What does secularism achieve when its application excludes the very people it claims to liberate?
The language of secularism often obscures the power relations at work. Rather than allowing religion to remain a matter of personal conviction, the state assumes the authority to determine which expressions of religion are acceptable in public. The woman’s body becomes the site on which the state performs its commitment to a particular national identity. Her clothing is no longer simply clothing. It becomes a political problem to be managed, regulated and, ultimately, removed from the public sphere.
This is not to suggest that secularism necessarily requires such restrictions. A secular state can protect the right to practice a religion while refusing to impose religious doctrine on its population. The contradiction emerges when secularism is interpreted as a mandate to make religious women less visibly religious. And Azerbaijan is hardly the only place where women’s clothing has become a battleground.
The freedom to wear the hijab, and the freedom not to
If the justification for banning the hijab is women’s liberation, what are we to make of Iran, where women have faced state enforcement of compulsory veiling? How can a politics that claims to liberate women through unveiling coexist with a politics that claims to protect them through veiling, while both deny women the authority to decide for themselves?
These systems are not identical, and their histories, institutions and methods of enforcement differ. Yet what they share is a troubling premise that women’s bodies are legitimate objects of state intervention, and that women cannot be trusted to make their own decisions about how they appear in public.
A woman who chooses to wear the hijab is not necessarily oppressed. A woman who chooses not to wear it is not necessarily liberated. Clothing alone cannot tell us whether a woman is acting under coercion, religious conviction, personal preference, cultural attachment or some combination of these.
The insistence that it can tell us more about the observer than the woman herself.
Freedom of choice cannot be conditional on making the choice that the state approves of. If a woman is compelled to veil, her autonomy is violated. If she is compelled to unveil, her autonomy is violated too. Defending one freedom while dismissing the other is not a consistent defence of women’s rights.
It is also worth asking why the language of women’s liberation so readily becomes a justification for excluding women from public life. When a student is denied access to education because she wears a headscarf, or a teacher is prevented from entering her workplace, the consequences are not abstract. The woman loses access to institutions, opportunities and their livelihoods. The supposed liberation takes the very form of exclusion.
READ: Hamas marks Al-Aqsa Intifada anniversary, urges Arab, Muslim support for Palestinians
Who gets to be modest?
The policing of Muslim women’s bodies does not always come from the state. Sometimes it comes from a restaurant door, a private beach, a dress code or the unspoken expectations of a particular social class.
In Egypt, investigations have documented cases of hijabi women being denied entry to upscale restaurants and other venues. A 2022 BBC News Arabic investigation found that 11 of 15 venues contacted during its reporting said women wearing the hijab were not permitted entry.
In Lebanon, allegations of hijab-based exclusion at private beach resorts have continued to generate public debate. In June 2026, a visitor reported being denied entry to Nowhere Beach because her friend wore a hijab, prompting renewed criticism of discriminatory admission policies.
These incidents reveal another dimension of the problem. The woman who covers her hair or wears a full-coverage swimsuit is not always being asked to conform to religious expectations. She is sometimes being asked to conform to an entirely different aesthetic: one that treats visible expressions of Muslim identity as incompatible with leisure, luxury, modernity or even social prestige.
This is where the policing of women’s clothing intersects with class and racialisation. Certain spaces cultivate an image of exclusivity by deciding which bodies belong in them and which bodies disrupt the atmosphere they are trying to sell. A headscarf can become a marker through which women are judged as insufficiently fashionable, insufficiently modern or somehow out of place, even in societies where Muslim women are part of everyday public life.
The contradiction becomes especially striking when we consider the attention given to celebrities who wear full-coverage swimwear. In June 2026, photographs of Anne Hathaway wearing a full-body swimsuit in Saint-Tropez prompted comparisons between the praise directed at her choice and the restrictions faced by Muslim women who wear similar swimming suits. There is nothing wrong with celebrating Hathaway’s clothing choice. But it is the double standard through which one woman’s covered body becomes a symbol of skincare, practicality or personal style, while another woman’s covered body is treated as evidence of backwardness.
The same garment can be fashionable on one woman and politically threatening on another. Its meaning is assigned according to who wears it, how she is perceived and what her body represents to the people looking at her.
The racialisation of Muslim identity
The policing of Muslim women’s bodies also raises questions about the relationship between religion, ethnicity and national identity.
Consider Azerbaijan. The country is predominantly Muslim, yet its official commitment to secularism has become central to the controversy over the visibility of religious clothing in schools. The current dispute raises a broader question about what forms of identity are permitted to appear in public and under what conditions.
I find myself wondering whether the discomfort with the hijab is also, in some contexts, a discomfort with the visible presence of an identity that is treated as foreign, even when it belongs to the people being asked to conceal it. In some political imaginaries, Muslimness and Arabness are conflated, despite the fact that most Muslims worldwide are not Arab and that Arab identity is not synonymous with Islam.
This conflation has consequences. It allows Muslim women to be racialised through their clothing, their bodies turned into symbols of a cultural identity that others wish to regulate, distance themselves from or erase.
It also makes the relationship between domestic exclusion and foreign policy worth examining. Azerbaijan’s restrictions on hijab in schools and its military relationship with Israel are distinct political matters; establishing a direct causal connection between them would require further evidence. But their coexistence raises questions about how national identity, Muslim visibility and solidarity with Palestinians are understood within the same political landscape.
The question is not whether these policies have a single motive. It is whether the boundaries drawn around acceptable Muslim identity at home can be examined alongside the state’s political and military relationships abroad.
The same scrutiny should extend to Europe, where secularism has frequently been invoked in debates over Muslim women’s clothing. France, in particular, has made the hijab a recurring site of political conflict. In September 2026, French National Rally MP Julien Odoul shared an AI-altered image of a Muslim woman’s photograph that removed her hijab and changed her clothes, captioning it “LIBERTÉ FRANÇAISE!”
There is something deeply revealing about invoking freedom while digitally altering a woman’s appearance, without her consent, to remove the very thing that makes her religious identity visible. It is a contradiction that deserves to be taken seriously.
When a politician uses AI technology to manufacture an unveiled version of a Muslim woman and presents that image as an expression of freedom, whose freedom is being represented? The woman’s, or the politician’s desire to see her differently?
The incident demonstrates how the demand to unveil can move beyond legislation and into the realm of public humiliation. A woman’s image becomes material for someone else’s political performance and agenda. Her consent is displaced by an assumption that her body would be better, freer or more acceptable if only it looked different.
READ: US Muslim group urges White House, Congress to demand release of American teen held by Israel
I am a hijabi, and my life is not smaller
I want to bring this discussion back to the everyday lives of the women who are so frequently discussed but so rarely allowed to define themselves.
I write this as a hijabi woman who travels. Wearing the hijab has not prevented me from hiking, swimming, travelling or pursuing the things I want to do. Across professions and walks of life, hijabi women are doctors, nurses, teachers, dancers, researchers, business owners, chief executives, politicians, employees and students. They occupy public space, develop expertise, build careers, create art and participate in the world around them.
Their lives are not adequately described by the fabric they wear.
I am not suggesting that every hijabi woman experiences the same freedoms, or that the hijab is never imposed on anyone. Some women experience family pressure, social coercion or state enforcement. Others choose to wear it freely. Some women change their minds over the course of their lives. Their experiences are not interchangeable, and none of them should have to prove that she is sufficiently independent before her rights are respected.
What I reject is the assumption that the hijab itself is proof of a woman’s oppression, or that removing it is necessarily proof of her liberation.
As a hijabi, I do not want my life reduced to a debate over whether the way I dress is acceptable to someone else other than myself. I do not want my ability to study, work, travel, swim or enter a public space to depend on whether another person approves of my appearance. I do not want to be treated as a political symbol before I am recognised as a person.
And I should not have to demonstrate how much I can accomplish while wearing the hijab to deserve that freedom in the first place.
The right to autonomy does not have to be earned through productivity. A woman who wants to become a doctor and a woman who wants a quiet life deserve the same respect. A woman who wears the hijab and a woman who removes it deserve the same freedom to participate in society without coercion or discrimination.
It is unacceptable that people are still discriminated against because of their headwear or skin color. We must reject these outdated prejudices and judge everyone by their character and actions—not their appearance.
A meaningful commitment to women’s freedom must resist that premise wherever it appears. It must oppose compulsory veiling without turning that opposition into a justification for compulsory unveiling. It must defend secularism without confusing it with the removal of religion from public life. And it must challenge discrimination against Muslim women without assuming that all Muslim women share the same beliefs, experiences or relationship with the hijab.
Secularism, if it is to mean anything in a plural society, should protect the freedom to practise any religion and any belief, and the freedom not to practise it too. It should not require women to erase visible expressions of their beliefs to gain access to education, employment or public life.
Women’s liberation cannot be measured by how closely women’s bodies conform to someone else’s preferred image of freedom.
A woman should not have to remove her hijab to enter a classroom, put it on to satisfy a religious authority, change her swimsuit to gain access to a beach or watch strangers digitally alter her appearance to make a political point.
She should be able to decide for herself.
That is what freedom of choice means. Not the freedom to choose what we approve of, but the freedom to make choices that belong to us, even when others disagree.
And if we truly believe in that freedom, we must be prepared to defend it even when a woman’s choice is not the one we would make for ourselves.
