SEOUL, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's household loan growth at banks slowed last month due to a cooldown in stock and property markets, central bank data showed Thursday.
Debt owed by households to deposit-taking banks totaled 1,198.9 trillion won (about 889.6 billion U.S. dollars) at the end of September, up 0.6 trillion won from a month earlier, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
It marked a significant slowdown from the previous month's 3.5 trillion won increase.
The slowdown was caused by a slump in retail stock investments and a reduction in newly completed housing.
Other loans, including credit loans, credit lines, and commercial real estate-backed loans, decreased by 2.3 trillion won in September from a month earlier, after a 0.6 trillion won decline in August.
Mortgage loans grew 2.9 trillion won last month, but the increase was smaller than the 4.1 trillion won expansion in the prior month.
The number of move-ins of newly built apartments across the country fell to 14,000 in September from 19,000 in the previous month.
Corporate loans extended by domestic banks totaled 1,441.5 trillion won at the end of September, up 10.7 trillion won from a month earlier, compared with a 9.7 trillion won rise the previous month.
Lending to large corporations rose by 7.5 trillion won, while loans to small and medium-sized enterprises increased by 3.2 trillion won in September. ■

2026 Major League Soccer: Toronto FC vs. Orlando City SC

Backlash in Kashmir over proposal for uniform Friday sermons across mosques
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:21:36 UTC
16:21:36 KST

Backlash in Kashmir over proposal for uniform Friday sermons across mosques
Political and religious critics accuse India’s Modi government of curbing Kashmir’s freedom of religion and expression.
A proposed move by the Waqf Board in Indian-administered Kashmir to introduce uniform Friday sermons at mosques across the region has drawn backlash from politicians and religious leaders, who have accused the government of trying to assert control over Muslim religious spaces.
The Jammu and Kashmir Waqf Board is headed by Darakshan Andrabi, a local leader associated with the Hindu majoritarian Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, whose government stripped the region of its previous semi-autonomous status in 2019. Jammu and Kashmir was also partitioned into two federally governed territories, instead of functioning as a full-fledged state as it used to.
The board, which oversees Muslim religious endowments as mandated by Islamic laws, announced the controversial move last weekend, prompting a political controversy as the region’s top Muslim scholars slammed the proposal as “irresponsible interference into the religious affairs of Kashmiri Muslims”.
While defending the imposition of the uniform sermons, Andrabi told a leading Indian newspaper that a proposed committee formed under the board’s auspices “will be solely responsible for identifying the issue regarding the uniform sermon … [This step] is necessary to deal with issues in the [region], especially social evils, including drug abuse.”
Andrabi told the media that religious scholars will approve Friday sermons with no role for any government official in the decision.
‘Brushed aside our concerns’
On Sunday, the Waqf Board had summoned about 1500 top scholars and preachers from the Kashmir region. While some leaders were present at the venue, others from remote areas attended the meeting virtually.
A scholar from the mountainous Rajouri district, some 180km (110 miles) from the region’s biggest city of Srinagar, who had attended the meeting online, told Al Jazeera that Andrabi had passed instructions stating that only a pre-approved sermon drafted by a committee of senior-most scholars would be uniformly recited at the mosque pulpits on Fridays.
He said they were not told exactly who would be part of this committee.
“When we objected, saying that we won’t adhere to the directives if the sermon was found to be violative of Islamic teachings, she brushed aside our concerns and didn’t let us speak,” the scholar said on condition of anonymity as he feared reprisals by the authorities. “She [Andrabi] said that their decision was final as it had been four years in the making.”
A disputed region claimed by India and Pakistan, Kashmir has been at the centre of political turmoil for four decades. Years of peaceful demands for a referendum, to determine which country the Kashmiris would choose, transformed into an armed uprising against Indian rule in 1989 in response to allegations of election fixing.
In 2019, India scrapped the semi-autonomous status of Kashmir, imposing direct federal rule. The elections did not happen until 2024, when the local government was re-elected, albeit with a restricted mandate. De facto authority still rests with the New Delhi-appointed administrator.
The special conditions afforded under the erstwhile status had protected land and residency-related privileges while allowing Kashmiris to make their own laws.
One consequence of the 2019 decision was that Indigenous legal arrangements that governed the management of waqf, the charitable bequests that Muslims commit for the larger communal welfare, were replaced by those prevailing across India.
‘Trying to undermine religious freedom’
The new system gave broad powers to the federally controlled bureaucracy in the management of local religious boards such as waqf.
Since then, the Waqf Board has been accused multiple times by the local Kashmiri leaders of trying to undermine their religious freedoms or interfering with how the traditional religious practices have continued for generations.
“Centralised khutba or sermons used to take place in the name of a sultan or khalifa (Islamic caliph) during the medieval times. But that had sanctity because Kashmir was [then] an Islamic state. Today, we are supposed to be living in a secular state,” Nayeem Akhtar, a senior politician who served as Kashmir’s education minister during the previous elected government, when its special status was still operational, told Al Jazeera.
“As long as he has an audience, every cleric has freedom to speak about any topic of his choice. This freedom is enshrined in the very fundamentals of law,” he added.
Akhtar said the new instructions were coming from an office bearer associated with the BJP, which is why the latest move had provoked furious responses. “The board’s job is just managerial. It is exceeding its remit by trying to preach or guide the clerics on how they must do their job. Can a Muslim political party in India ever dictate how a Hindu pujari must conduct prayers or how a Christian pastor must deliver a sermon on Sunday?”
On Tuesday, Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, the region’s top Muslim religious leader, cautioned that such a move would amount to “direct interference”.
The Mutahida Majlis-e-Ulema, a joint body of several religious organisations that he leads, said “determining sermon content was the responsibility of Islamic scholars and not of an administrative body.”
The condemnation was also shared by Omar Abdullah, the region’s elected head and member of the National Conference party that supports accession to India, albeit with the autonomous powers that New Delhi nullified seven years ago.
Following the backlash, the Waqf Board head Andrabi retracted her statement and said it had been left to the discretion of “independent scholars, preachers (and) sermonists” to talk about social issues such as rising suicides, mental trauma, substance abuse and more.
‘Exerting control on religious institutions’
This is not the first time that the BJP-led administration has been accused of trying to exert control over local religious institutions.
Earlier in January, Kashmiri Muslim scholars accused the government of discriminatory practices after the police distributed a four-page form titled “profiling of mosques” which sought intrusive details about the imams, muezzins and khatibs (preachers) of the mosques across the disputed region, including their biometric information.
For years, Muslim groups in the region have faced various restrictions on prayer, with Srinagar’s 600-year-old Jamia Masjid often being shut for important religious events such as Eid prayers or Laylat-al-Qadr, the most venerated night of the Islamic calendar, which falls in the month of Ramadan.
The administration argues these restrictions are imposed to ensure peace, but religious leaders insist that such prohibitory measures form a “systematic assault on the religious identity, dignity, and fundamental rights” of Kashmiri Muslims.
Farooq, the chief scholar, himself has been frequently subjected to such restrictions on his mobility, preventing him from giving Friday sermons on occasions when he is expected to speak on matters such as Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
Previously, the Waqf Board has also sought to prohibit the practice of distributing yellow rice inside the compound of the major shrines in the region, a centuries-old tradition tied to the Sufi missionary councils that promoted Islam in Kashmir.
Religion has been a factor of political mobilisation
In 2022, the board also banned the age-old practice of collecting voluntary nazr-o-niyaz donations offered by devotees to the spiritual peers, mujawirs (attendants of a shrine) and khadims (caregivers). It cited the newly applicable federal laws as a reason for taking direct control over all financial collections and installing new donation boxes where all offerings went to the board.
Noor Ahmad Baba, a veteran Kashmiri political scientist and historian, said religion had always been a factor for political mobilisation in Kashmir, which is why attempts to manipulate or change the traditional religious arrangements evoke political outrage.
“The kind of political dispensation that we have and the kind of politics it has had with regard to Muslims is what makes the whole exercise suspicious,” Baba told Al Jazeera, referring to the BJP. “If the standardisation had come, for instance, from clerics with public acceptability, it wouldn’t have become an issue. No one can deny the need for religious leaders to talk about topics such as drug addiction, late marriages, climate change, social harmony and more.”
A Srinagar-based political analyst who has written about the conflict in Kashmir for four decades said such decisions reflected attempts to pre-emptively contain protests in Kashmir amid the rising wave of Hindu nationalism in India.
“A spate of recent mosque demolitions in cities such as Ujjain and Saharanpur in Uttar Pradesh showed how vehemently the far-right strains within India’s ruling apparatus were resurfacing,” the analyst told Al Jazeera, speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution. “This renewed communal posturing by the Modi regime was sufficient to provoke reactions in a place like Kashmir. The attempts to assert control over mosques must be seen in light of that.”

Dutch parliament backs move to protect ICC from US sanctions

16:20:31 KST

The Dutch parliament has approved a motion calling on the government to explore ways to ensure the International Criminal Court (ICC) retains access to international payment systems despite US sanctions targeting the court.
The motion was submitted on 8th October by Hanneke van der Werf of the D66 party, alongside MPs Kati Piri of the Progressive party, Sarah Dobbe of the Socialist Party and Maes van Lanschot of the Christian Democratic party.
It calls on the government, in cooperation with the Dutch central bank and the European Central Bank, to examine ways to ensure that the ICC and other legal entities affected by sanctions can continue accessing international payment systems.
One option under consideration is routing payments through a public financial institution, allowing the affected entities to meet their financial obligations despite external sanctions pressure.
The motion argues that it is undesirable for third countries to be able to indirectly determine whether an independent international judicial body can access international payment systems.
It also stresses that the Netherlands, as the ICC’s host country, has a special responsibility to ensure the court can continue operating.
The motion further calls on the Netherlands to take a leading role within the European Union in strengthening Europe’s autonomy in dealing with other major powers.
Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen expressed a positive view of the motion. It was also supported by the parties represented by its sponsors, other parties in the governing coalition and most opposition parties.

Clock ticking for leap second: Why timekeeping could change forever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:16:50 UTC
16:16:50 KST

Clock ticking for leap second: Why timekeeping could change forever
Timekeepers add a leap second occasionally to keep our clocks and the Earth’s rotation in tune. That could now change.
The world’s timekeepers are meeting on Thursday near Paris to decide whether to scrap the “leap second”, which could disconnect the clocks we use from the Earth’s rotation and realign timescales.
The world’s clocks are designed on the idea that the Earth completes one rotation on its axis in exactly 24 hours. But it actually wobbles, making the time the Earth takes to rotate less exact. And over time, the Earth’s rotation is gradually slowing.
To compensate for that, since 1972, timekeepers have added a leap second every few years – the last one was added in 2016 – to keep clocks and Earth’s rotation in synchronisation.
But pressure has been mounting to scrap the leap second since it complicates matters for financial markets and data centres, which rely on precise timing down to milliseconds.
So what is a leap second? Could it be scrapped? And how might it change our understanding of time?
Here’s what we know:
What is a leap second?
Clocks work based on Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), the global standard that has been based on high-precision atomic clocks for more than seven decades. Atomic clocks mark time by observing the vibration of atoms.
But the Earth’s rotation works independently of atomic clocks.
A leap second is a second added periodically to UTC to make it synchronise with the Earth’s rotation. The first leap second was added to world clocks in 1972.
There have been 27 leap seconds added so far with the previous leap second being added on December 31, 2016. No further leap seconds have been added since.
According to the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), a nonregulatory federal agency of the United States Department of Commerce, leap seconds occur at the end of December or the end of June. The NIST also cites differences between the precision of the atomic second and the Earth’s rotation to explain the need for a leap second.
“The speed of the Earth’s rotation is not constant. …. This gradual decrease in the rotational rate is causing the duration of the mean solar second to gradually increase with respect to the atomic second,” the NIST added.
Why is pressure mounting to scrap leap seconds?
While leap seconds close the discrepancy between the Earth’s rotation and UTC, their addition has posed challenges for technology companies, financial markets and other businesses that depend on precise timings.
In 2012, LinkedIn and Reddit crashed after the addition of a leap second. The same year, ticket bookings for Qantas, the Australian airline, collapsed after the leap second was added.
Three years later, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission also issued a warning against it. And in July 2022, engineers at Meta said: “Every leap second is a major source of pain for people who manage hardware infrastructures.”
With pressure mounting, the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, which has the French acronym BIPM, voted in 2022 to scrap the leap second by 2035. But countries like Russia have wanted to push the implementation date back to 2040. Russia incorporates leap seconds directly into its GLONASS satellite-navigation system, so delaying the scrapping of leap seconds would buy Russia time to update its satellite systems.
Despite Moscow’s concern, the 69 member states of BIPM are now meeting on Thursday in Versailles outside Paris to debate and vote on a resolution to scrap the leap second by 2027.
What’s up for debate on Thursday?
According to the BIPM, the timekeeping authorities of countries around the world will discuss three proposals at Versailles.
First, they will consider whether atomic clocks are still the most accurate device when it comes to measuring what constitutes a second. Optical frequencies are now in fact more precise than atomic clocks. If a proposal to change how time is measured is accepted, the second might have a new definition, characterised by optical frequencies rather than the vibrations of atoms.
The second, most significant proposal pertains to dumping the leap second.
And finally, the third proposal on the table is a pitch to synchronise time measurements on Earth with a new time standard that NASA is developing for the moon.
Proposals that are accepted are expected to come into effect from May 20, 2027, World Metrology Day.
What happens if the leap second is scrapped?
If the leap second is scrapped, then it means our clocks will no longer be tied to the Earth’s rotation.
According to the NIST, if this happens, “then adjustments would have to be made to time stamps and legacy equipment and software which synchronise to UTC for astronomical observations.”
“Some proposals have been made to implement larger corrections like leap hours, which would occur much less often than leap seconds,” it added.
Scientists said human routines will not be impacted and software glitches, data server crashes and network failures for financial markets will be eliminated with the abandonment of leap seconds.
But over a period of centuries, the gap between the Earth’s cycle and our clocks will become more apparent: By 2100, clocks will be ahead of the Earth by 54 seconds. In another two millennia, that gap would have widened to several hours. The result? Sunrise and sunset times that would feel out of sync with people’s natural rhythms today.

2027 budget: French cinema fears a catastrophic scenario
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:15:12 UTC
16:15:12 KST

More than 170 figures from France's film industry warn about the impact of the 2027 budget, fearing hundreds of films could vanish if measures like doubling VAT on Canal+ pay-TV offers go through.
In an opinion piece published in the newspaper Le Monde, directors and producers denounce the threat posed by the draft 2027 finance bill to the funding of French cinema. The signatories believe that the measures currently being debated in Parliament could lead to the disappearance of 400 films over five years, around 80 productions a year.
Among the signatories are several leading figures in French and European cinema, including Jacques Audiard, Costa-Gavras, brothers Luc and Jean-Pierre Dardenne, Claire Denis, Michel Hazanavicius, Agnès Jaoui, Justine Triet, Julia Ducournau, Cédric Klapisch and Alice Winocour.
"The new finance bill risks wiping French cinema from our screens on a scale never seen before", they write. The authors of the op-ed condemn a build-up of measures likely to weaken the two pillars of funding for the sector: public money and private investment.
Budgets for public broadcasting and the CNC cut back
On the public funding side, industry professionals point out that the budget for France Télévisions (which helps finance many films, around 70 a year) is set to fall by 47 million euros by 2027.
In addition, the general rapporteur for the budget, Philippe Juvin (Les Républicains), is proposing a 35‑million‑euro levy on the resources of the National Centre for Cinema and the Moving Image (CNC) in 2027. The aim would be to return to the state part of the additional revenue expected from changes to advertising tax rules.
The CNC is the beating heart of French cinema: it redistributes money to support writing, shooting, distribution and the screening of films in cinemas. This system has a unique characteristic: it does not cost the state a cent.
The CNC is funded by small taxes collected directly on cinema tickets, television and streaming platforms. It is topped up by private copying levies, which apply to devices used to store creative works, such as smartphones, tablets, external hard drives and USB sticks.
It is therefore the sector itself that pays for its own creation.
The CNC is in fact funded by several earmarked taxes, collected notably on cinema tickets, television channels and streaming platforms. It is topped up by private copying remuneration, which applies to devices that can store works, such as smartphones, tablets, external hard drives and USB sticks.
Funding for creation therefore rests to a large extent on contributions collected directly within the sectors concerned and from consumers.
"French cinema therefore runs without costing taxpayers a single cent", the signatories recall. They also highlight the "major" economic weight of this industry, which generates 260,000 jobs (compared, for example, with 400,000 in the car industry), "brings life to the regions thanks to location shooting and sustains an exceptionally dense network of cinemas across the country".
Canal+: fears that a VAT hike could spell the final curtain for hundreds of films
The other major threat concerns the private sector, and Canal+ in particular, which is the biggest private contributor to French cinema. In France, Canal+ has a legal obligation to reinvest part of its revenue in funding national film production.
The government is considering doubling VAT on pay-TV subscriptions by 2027, raising it from 10% to 20%. To absorb this extra tax, the pay-TV channel could pass the cost directly on to its subscribers or decide to invest far less money in cinema.
It is worth remembering, however, that at this stage it is still only a draft budget under examination. There is no guarantee that this VAT hike will be retained in the final version of the 2027 budget.
If adopted, the measure could nonetheless have far‑reaching consequences. Filmmakers point out that a cross-industry agreement signed at the end of July stipulates that any increase in VAT for Canal+ would render its investment obligations in cinema null and void. They estimate that such a break would mean a reduction of 750 million euros for film creation between 2028 and 2032.
"Very concretely, over a five‑year period, this means 400 films simply will not exist", they warn. The most fragile productions could struggle even more to raise finance, with knock‑on effects on shoots, jobs and ultimately the diversity of films available to audiences.
Canal+: a love-hate relationship
The situation is not without irony.
In May, during the Cannes Film Festival, several of the signatories to this new op-ed took part in the "Zapper Bolloré" movement, launched by some 600 film professionals to protest against Vincent Bolloré’s growing influence over the sector, notably through Canal+, which belongs to the group controlled by the conservative billionaire.
The protest prompted a sharp reaction from Canal+: its CEO, Maxime Saada, then announced that he no longer wished to work with the signatories.
A few months on, some of these filmmakers are therefore sounding the alarm about the impact that a VAT hike for Canal+ could have, when its financial contribution remains vital for French production.
A paradox that illustrates how dependent French cinema has become on a player whose influence is nevertheless contested by part of the profession.
A new law on cinema
Beyond budget measures, the signatories call for a complete overhaul of the sector’s legal framework, still largely governed by the audiovisual law dating back to 1986. They are therefore arguing for a genuine cinema law that would safeguard the "chronologie des médias" – a French rule which sets out how long after a theatrical release a film can be shown on different platforms, from VOD and free-to-air television to Netflix.
They also want tighter regulation of artificial intelligence and protection of the remit of the National Centre for Cinema and the Moving Image (CNC).
The signatories are urging MPs to back the amendments proposed by professional organisations in support of public broadcasting, the CNC budget and the retention of a 10% VAT rate for Canal+, in return for firm commitments in favour of creation.
The filmmakers believe that the stakes go far beyond the sector’s economic balance. Faced with the standardisation of content, which they blame on major US platforms such as Amazon Prime, Disney+ and Netflix, they defend a model which, in their view, helps sustain France’s cultural influence.

Drone attack causes fire at Russia’s Ryazan refinery, regional governor says
Oct 15 - A big Ukrainian drone attack on Russia's Ryazan region caused a fire to break out at an oil refinery, the regional governor said on Thursday.
It was the first Ukrainian attack on a Russian energy facility since U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an energy ceasefire. The truce was not confirmed by either side.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy told the Financial Times in an interview published on Thursday that Ukraine had paused energy strikes for 3 days to comply with US wishes but would now resume them because Russia was still attacking its energy infrastructure.
"The material damage is now being assessed. Emergency services are working at the scene," Ryazan governor Pavel Malkov said in a post on Telegram.
A warehouse elsewhere was damaged in the attacks, he said, without giving further details.
The Ryazan refinery is owned by Russian oil major Rosneft and feeds Moscow with fuel. It has been attacked several times by drones in recent months. The refinery accounts for almost 5% of Russia's total oil refining throughput.
Malkov said earlier on Thursday that classes in schools and kindergartens in two districts had been cancelled because of what he called mass drone attacks. REUTERS

School headscarf ban meets resistance in Austria

School headscarf ban meets resistance in Austria
- Austria’s new ban on headscarves for girls under 14 has triggered protests and classroom resistance, with critics saying it targets Muslims and limits religious freedom.
- The government says the law, which started on 1 September, protects girls and promotes equality; officials report 127 parent meetings and 52 breach reports.
- Legal action is under way, with the constitutional court expected to rule in 2027, while affected girls and families say the rule causes fear, sadness and pressure.
AI generated
VIENNA – As the new school year gets under way in Austria, a headscarf ban for girls under 14 has sparked protests on the streets and in the classroom, with dozens of pupils refusing to comply.
Austria’s conservative-led government has insisted that the ban, introduced on Sept 1, promotes gender equality and protects Muslim girls from “segregation and oppression”.
But critics argue that it disproportionately targets Muslims, infringes upon religious freedom and is forcing young girls to dress in a way that makes them feel uncomfortable.
Since the ban took effect, education authorities across Austria have held 127 meetings with parents and filed 52 reports over alleged breaches of the law, according to the education ministry.
Opponents of the ban have also held protests across the country, with several hundred people gathering each time.
‘Part of me’
At a demonstration in Vienna, Zehra, 37, who did not want to give her last name, said her two daughters, aged nine and 13, were “sad and angry” about the ban.
“We raise our children by telling them, you can decide who you want to be – and this law is the exact opposite,” she said.
Seham, 12, said she felt “afraid” to remove her headscarf at school “because I’d worn it for two years and it felt like a part of me”.
After discussions with school leaders, she said she was allowed to cover her hair with an alternative non-traditional head covering, but would still “rather wear the full headscarf”.
Roughly 8% of Austria’s nine million residents are Muslim, according to 2021 government statistics.
They suffer the highest rates of racism and discrimination against Muslims in the EU, according to a 2024 report by Europe’s FRA rights agency.
In the 2024 elections, the far-right Freedom Party won for the first time even though it failed to form a government. The anti-immigration party continues to top voter opinion polls.
The new law is Austria’s second attempt to restrict headscarves in schools after a coalition between the conservatives and the Freedom Party introduced a ban for primary school pupils in 2019.
That law was overturned by the constitutional court on the grounds that a regulation targeting only Muslims was incompatible with religious neutrality.
‘Under pressure’
The Islamic Religious Community in Austria, which is supporting legal action against the new headscarf ban, said it had received around 70 reports from families about difficulties during its implementation.
“A law that was justified as protecting children’s welfare is putting precisely those children under pressure at school,” the group said in a statement.
The constitutional court confirmed to AFP that it had received a legal complaint about the law and a decision is expected in the first half of 2027.
When girls refuse to comply with the law, schools are required to hold a series of discussions with pupils and their parents before cases are referred to education authorities.
Ultimately, parents who continue to ignore the ban can be fined.
In a statement sent to AFP, Education Minister Christoph Wiederkehr said the fact there had only been 127 meetings so far showed “that the vast majority of pupils and parents are cooperative”.
“In addition, the figures show that the discussions held with the parents concerned in the event of a violation are, for the most part, successful,” he added.
Education authorities in Vienna said that “on the basis of the discussions held so far, the impression has emerged that the girls wish to wear the headscarf of their own accord”.
Sandy, 12, said she began wearing a headscarf about a year ago because “I place a lot of importance on my religion and I want to be able to live it”.
A teacher who has worked with two affected girls in the capital told AFP there was no sign they were being forced to wear headscarves.
The girls had spent weeks adapting to the new rules and searching for acceptable alternatives to headscarves, said the teacher, who wished to remain anonymous.
“It is very uncomfortable for them.” AFP

ACCC takes Kmart to court over nail glue burns and button battery safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:09:51 UTC
16:09:51 KST

In short:
The ACCC has accused Kmart of selling millions of bottles of a nail glue that caused burns without adequate safety warnings.
The consumer watchdog also accused the retail chain of selling watches with button batteries that had not been tested and smart tags without mandatory safety information.
A Kmart spokesperson said it was disappointed at the ACCC's decision to take action on historical matters that had been addressed.
The consumer watchdog has taken legal action against Kmart, alleging it breached Australian Consumer law by selling millions of bottles of nail glue that caused burns requiring medical treatment.
The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) has taken action against the retail giant in the Federal Court in Victoria, alleging Kmart sold cosmetic nail glue without warning consumers of a risk of serious injury from burns associated with it.
The ACCC said other safety warnings were set out on the packaging and bottle, which was sold individually and with a pack of nails.
According to court documents, between August 2017 and December 2024, at least 51 consumers complained to Kmart of skin burns caused by contact with the nail glues, of which at least 33 expressly referred to contact with fabric.
A further seven complaints not involving skin burns referred to the nail glues causing steaming, smoking, burning or melting when in contact with fabric, with consumers reporting suffering serious injuries including burns requiring medical treatment and, in some cases, hospitalisation and skin grafts.
The ACCC claims customers sent Kmart's customer service team photos of burned clothes and skin, and some described the nail glues causing an exothermic or chemical reaction, heat and smoke, some of which were escalated internally to senior Kmart management including the CEO.
"We consider that Kmart's failure to warn consumers of the risk of burns after receiving numerous consumer reports of burn injuries associated with the use of the nail glue exposed consumers to an ongoing risk of serious injury, as an incredibly serious matter," ACCC Deputy Chair Catriona Lowe said.
"It was important for Kmart to address this, once it was made aware of these serious product safety concerns."
The ACCC further alleges Kmart failed to submit mandatory serious injury reports to the Commonwealth minister as required.
A Kmart spokesperson said it took its reporting obligations seriously and submitted mandatory injury reports about the products to the ACCC.
"While the incidents with nail glues are also historical, we regret any injury associated with these products and apologise to anyone affected. Kmart remains of the view the labelling and warnings were appropriate to prevent misuse," they said.
Watchdog alleges button battery non-compliance
The ACCC also alleged Kmart failed to test several digital and analogue watches that contained button batteries prior to supply as legally required.
It alleges Kmart sold about 64,000 button-battery-powered watches between June 2022 and November 2024 which did not comply.
"These watches contained button batteries, but Kmart did not test them prior to supply to show that young children could not open the battery compartments. This is despite many of the watches being specifically designed for children," Ms Lowe said.
The ACCC has also accused Kmart of supplying GPS tracking devices known as Smart Tags that did not comply with the mandatory button battery information standard. The devices were recalled in 2024.
A Kmart spokesperson said no injuries were reported for any of the products and it had continued to strengthen the product safety and compliance processes.
"We have cooperated with the ACCC throughout its investigation and are disappointed at its decision to take action on historical matters that Kmart has addressed," it said.
"As the matter is now before the court, we will not be commenting further on the proceedings."
Ms Lowe said all businesses, especially large retailers like Kmart, are expected to have consumer safety front of mind.
"Withholding safety information can amount to false or misleading representations in breach of the Australian Consumer Law, but it also exposes consumers to risk," she said.
A court date for the matter is yet to be set.

‘They took land off people’: Obama faces backlash over Israel remarks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:05:18 UTC
16:05:18 KST

Former U.S. President Barack Obama has come under fire from conservative and pro-Israel commentators over remarks about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict in which he said Jews who sought refuge from persecution "took land off people" and "were excessive." Critics accused him of distorting the history of Israel's establishment and overlooking more than 3,000 years of Jewish ties to the Land of Israel.
Obama made the comments Tuesday during a conversation with journalist and author Susan McKay at the O2 arena in Belfast, Northern Ireland, as part of a speaking tour that also includes Glasgow and Manchester. His remarks, which largely addressed the responsibilities of both Israelis and Palestinians, drew particular criticism for what opponents described as a portrayal of Israel's founding primarily as a response to European persecution.
During the discussion, Obama emphasized that the millions of Jews and Palestinians living in the region were not going anywhere and said critics of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu should remember that not all Israelis supported his government.
He urged Israelis to reconsider how their children and grandchildren would live in the region, questioning whether they could remain behind walls indefinitely or whether they needed to find a way to defend themselves while upholding ethical and moral principles.
Obama also challenged Palestinian leaders to recognize the limits of armed confrontation. Palestinians, he argued, could not "outkill, outweaponise the Israelis" and would need to pursue change through moral arguments, ethical appeals and nonviolent strategies.
He cautioned against expecting a rapid resolution. His immediate priorities, he said, were alleviating suffering, achieving a genuine end to violence, halting what he described as the continuing encroachment into the West Bank and helping rebuild Gaza.
Even those objectives, he acknowledged, would require considerable diplomatic effort and an American administration willing to engage creatively, something he suggested might not happen in the near future.
Referring to the hardening of Israeli attitudes following the October 7 Hamas attack, Obama said the region needed a genuine cessation of violence before meaningful discussions of long-term peace could resume. He described the conflict as an example of societies becoming trapped by history, tribal divisions and entrenched grievances, a pattern he compared to periods of conflict in Northern Ireland and elsewhere.
It was Obama's discussion of Jewish history and the origins of the conflict, however, that provoked the strongest reaction. "The fact is that the Jewish people, for millennia, were oppressed, discriminated against, killed," Obama said.
He noted that Europe had been responsible for much of that persecution and argued that Jews had understandably sought refuge. "What is also undeniable is that they took land off people and they were excessive," he continued. He said those who lost land understandably regarded it as an injustice and wanted it returned.
Obama went on to argue that the stronger party in a conflict bears particular responsibility for breaking the cycle of violence because of the power it holds.
He warned that if Israel believed its military and technological superiority allowed it to guarantee security by acting as it wished, taking what it wanted and refusing concessions, such a strategy might succeed temporarily but would undermine its moral standing.
In that scenario, he said, Israel would have "ceded moral ground," adding that the current Israeli government appeared to have adopted such an approach.
He emphasized that Israel needed to recognize that approximately seven million Palestinians would remain in the region and that indefinitely imposing conditions they would not accept could not provide a sustainable solution.
At the same time, Obama said Palestinians also had to acknowledge Israel's military superiority and adopt a strategy that did not depend on defeating its armed forces. He criticized Hamas' October 7 attack, arguing that it was exceptionally unlikely to produce meaningful political change for Palestinians.
Obama's description of Jews seeking refuge and taking land prompted accusations from conservative and pro-Israel commentators, particularly in the United States, that he had presented a misleading account of the Jewish state's origins.
The conservative news website The Daily Wire, co-founded by Jewish political commentator Ben Shapiro, published an article accusing Obama of erasing more than 3,000 years of Jewish history and presenting a revisionist account of Israel's establishment.
The publication argued that Obama's remarks framed the creation of Israel primarily as a response to European antisemitism and the Holocaust while overlooking the Jewish people's historical connection to the territory. Critics contended that his account suggested Jews arrived from Europe as outsiders and dispossessed the local population, without acknowledging their ancestral ties to the Land of Israel.
Media watchdog HonestReporting also criticized the former president, arguing that his remarks omitted both the Jewish people's millennia-old connection to the land and centuries of continuous Jewish presence there. "Israel's legitimacy did not begin with European persecution," the organization wrote. "Neither did Jewish history."
Another criticism focused on the history of Jewish land acquisition before Israel's establishment. Critics pointed to decades of documented legal purchases of land from Arab property owners, including wealthy landowners, during the period before 1948.
They argued that such transactions, recorded in British Mandate-era documents, complicated Obama's broad characterization of Jewish land acquisition.
Obama did not explicitly say that Jewish migration to the region was illegitimate, nor did he deny the Jewish people's long history of persecution. His critics nevertheless argued that his account omitted a central element of Jewish history: the connection between the Jewish people and the land long before the persecution they faced in modern Europe.

China launches 10 satellites aboard Zhuque-2E rocket to advance space-based AI computing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:04:14 UTC
16:04:14 KST

Faisal Mahmud
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
China successfully launched 10 satellites aboard a Zhuque-2E Y4 carrier rocket Wednesday, including eight designed to advance artificial intelligence computing capabilities in orbit.
The rocket lifted off at 7.40 pm local time (1140GMT) from the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone in northwestern China, placing all 10 satellites into their designated orbits, according to state-run Xinhua News Agency.
Eight satellites belong to the second group of the "Star Compute" project, developed by Chinese commercial aerospace company ADAspace.
Designed to operate in dawn-dusk orbits, the satellites carry high-performance computing systems, laser communication equipment, and low-light cameras.
They will test advanced technologies, including 10,000-watt liquid-cooling systems, large deployable cooling structures, space-based laser communication networks, and the training of AI foundation models directly in orbit.
ADAspace said the mission would help accelerate technological development and commercial applications of space-based computing.
The company plans to establish an orbital AI infrastructure network comprising 2,800 computing satellites.
The first group of 12 satellites was launched in May 2025. In January, the company announced it had deployed Alibaba's Qwen3 AI model aboard its orbital computing network, enabling AI processing directly in space. 
The company aims to establish a 1,000-satellite network by 2030 and complete the larger constellation by 2035.

Flooded homes and rising costs: Why some Thai villages are paying the price to protect Bangkok
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:03:17 UTC
16:03:17 KST

As climate change causes more frequent and severe flooding, could cities in Europe face the same tough choices?
Inside their home, raised more than three metres above the ground in the central province of Ayutthaya in Thailand, Kamonchanok Sathaphonamonwut’s family of three sleeps on makeshift platforms and cannot use the waterlogged toilet.
Her village has been flooded six years in a row, pushing some to move away, while others have raised their houses higher.
"Our area simply cannot cope with this much water anymore," the 34-year-old says as she wades through her soaked home.
But while authorities prioritise protecting Bangkok and other business hubs from floods, "when it comes to our residential communities, they neglect us", she says.
Flood defences protect cities but leave villages submerged
Thailand experiences flooding every year during the monsoon season, and scientists say human-made climate change has made heavy rain and floods more frequent and severe.
After devastating floods in 2011, the government expanded embankments, water gates and other infrastructure to direct water away from Bangkok, the historic city of Ayutthaya and industrial zones along the Chao Phraya River, which flows through the capital.
The defences have largely kept commercial centres safe, but residents of other areas have been left to fend for themselves.
Around 20 kilometres from Ayutthaya's centuries-old temple ruins, a UNESCO heritage site, residents say floods that once reached their knees now rise above their heads in some areas and can take several months to recede.
Office worker Kamonchanok has been forced to commute by boat and hoist her household appliances and other belongings above the waterline.
"All we can do is deal with the consequences," she says.
"There's only so much we can do to adapt."
The 'cruel' cost of flood protection
Climate change, low-lying geography and recently built embankments that have altered the natural flow of the Chao Phraya have contributed to more severe flooding in downstream communities, says Thai irrigation department spokesman Thanet Somboon.
"Even when water is released from the Chao Phraya Dam at the same rate as before, the impact is greater than it used to be," he explains.
And after irrigation channels are completely full of diverted water, he says authorities have "no choice but to discharge the remaining water downstream".
But Thanet acknowledges that officials may need to review infrastructure to "ensure floodwater can be kept within the intended limits".
Environmental conservationist Sasin Chalermlarp adds the government has done "an excellent job" managing floods across the central plains, but its efforts were "cruel" to those bearing the brunt of the flooding.
In low-lying riverside districts that serve as flood retention zones, stretches of villages were left underwater this October, with some homes abandoned and others submerged up to their roofs.
Sasin says floodwater that once spread across much of Ayutthaya is now concentrated in just "five to 10 percent" of the province.
The rising costs of staying dry
As flooding in hard-hit districts has become more severe, many who remain have paid to lift their stilt houses higher and keep their living space dry.
Kamonchanok's family raised their home twice in the 1990s, the second time by 1.5 metres. But floodwater still reached their house in 2011, and again for the past six consecutive years.
Raising a house can cost between 100,000 and one million baht (about €2,700-€27,000), depending on its size and height, residents say.
Some families have lifted their homes twice in just a few years, exhausting their savings and borrowing to get by.
Despite spending more than one million baht (€27,000) to raise her home, Sawong Raksri, 87, has become resigned to the reality she now faces. "It floods like this every year recently. What's the point of complaining?" she says.
Could a 'flood-free tax' help?
Sasin acknowledges that the area's low-lying land makes it a natural route for floodwater. "But the villagers have no choice. They are being forced to make sacrifices," he says.
Sasin, who lives in a protected part of Ayutthaya, has proposed a "flood-free tax" on those who benefit from the defences to help impacted families raise their homes and repair damage.
Thanet, meanwhile, says the idea warranted further study to determine "how to support people who sacrifice their land to accommodate floodwater".
The government's flagship fix is a €700-million flood diversion canal, designed to carry 1,200 cubic metres of water – around half the volume of an Olympic-size swimming pool – per second around the bottleneck where the Chao Phraya narrows through Ayutthaya.
It is expected to be completed by 2030.
Until then, Kamonchanok says that her community is not even demanding an end to intentional flooding, but rather a cap on water levels and financial support for those whose homes sit below the flood line.
"All we're asking for is to be able to live comfortably in our own homes," she says. "Why can't they give us that?"

The vapes weighed 633 kilograms in total. About 80% were collected in northern and central Taiwan, while southern and eastern Taiwan accounted for 20%, per Liberty Times.
The government has encouraged the public to continue depositing vapes at 432 collection boxes nationwide. The administration said the anonymous process meant some people may have deposited devices in a city or county other than where they lived.
Since the program began on Sept. 8, collection has been the priority, with destruction of the e-cigarettes planned for a later phase, Liberty Times reported. The administration has asked local governments to add collection points based on demand.
In June, the Cabinet approved draft amendments to the Tobacco Hazards Prevention Act that would criminalize the manufacture and import of e-cigarettes and impose fines for possession. The Legislative Yuan has yet to approve the changes, according to a Taiwan News report published in June.
The proposed amendments would provide a one-month grace period after they take effect. During that period, possession would not be penalized, but devices would still be confiscated. Afterward, possession would be punishable by fines of NT$30,000 to NT$100,000 (US$925 to US$3,000).

Niu questioned whether the government and CPC could afford the investment while both faced financial pressures. He noted that CPC had required government cash injections to avert financial turmoil, adding that part of the company’s deficit stemmed from the government’s prioritization of natural gas for power generation.
DPP Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) also commented on the proposal, saying a responsible government should diversify its energy sources, per Newtalk. However, he said CPC and the Ministry of Economic Affairs needed to provide more details about the project to the public.
Experts offered mixed assessments of the proposal.
Stimson Center Senior Fellow Michael Cunningham said the deal could strengthen Taiwan’s energy resilience while helping reduce the US trade deficit with Taiwan, per CNA. He added that increasing Taiwan’s importance among US export markets could also bolster its security.
Hudson Institute Senior Fellow Riley Walters said Taiwan’s positive response was significant, particularly after South Korea raised concerns about the project’s profitability. He argued that Taiwan’s commitment to purchase one-third of the pipeline’s output would help ensure its commercial viability.
Research Center for Taiwan Economic Development researcher Liang Chi-yuan (梁啟源) said shipping natural gas from Alaska could reduce transportation costs but warned of other significant risks, per UDN. These included engineering challenges in the Arctic, opposition from environmental groups, and the possibility that a future Democratic administration in the US could oppose the pipeline project.
Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research Senior Analyst Jheng Ruei-he (鄭睿合) warned that CPC would struggle to secure US$4.4 billion for the investment amid its ongoing financial difficulties. If the plan proceeded, he proposed allowing CPC to end its gas price stabilization efforts and providing additional funds to shore up its finances.
Jheng added that, if the deal went ahead, Taiwan could import 8 million metric tons of natural gas from the US annually, accounting for nearly one-quarter of its total imports. However, he warned that concentrating energy supplies in a single source would pose another significant risk.
Jheng also noted that Taiwan’s goal of achieving carbon neutrality by 2050 could complicate the investment. A 20-year contract beginning in 2032, the pipeline’s projected start of operations, could leave Taiwan importing substantial quantities of LNG even as it seeks to reduce domestic consumption.

The technology allows actors in films to be made to look decades younger or to speak a different language, whilst their voice and facial expressions remain the same. “This means a Flemish film can also conquer the American market.”
“When AI began to gain ground, I started applying the technology in the film industry. For instance, I helped set up Disney’s AI division in 2018, when it became clear that AI could be used for digital characters,” he explains.
“Since then, these systems have become much more advanced and I now run my own company: BRAHMA AI. We specialise in AI-based visual effects for films, concerts and other businesses.”
Actors who suddenly look older or speak perfect French
That company has now won a prestigious Technology & Engineering Emmy Award for its technology relating to ‘AI-Based Face Replacement and Performance-Preserving Post-Production Transformation’. In simple terms: AI-based facial alterations that preserve the actor’s performance.
“This means we can alter an actor’s face or age whilst keeping their performance completely intact: think of their gaze, emotions and timing,” explains Plaete.
“With this technology, we can, for example, turn a 70-year-old Tom Hanks back into a man in his twenties, or bring a deceased actor back to life in a sequel,” says Plaete. He was, in fact, involved in the film ‘Here’, in which we see virtually every stage of life of the lead actors, Tom Hanks and Robin Wright.
‘We can even use the latest generation of this technology to dub films. This allows us to make an actor speak in a different language, whilst retaining their own voice, facial expressions and articulation. A film shot in English can thus appear as though it was originally made in French.’
‘We moved from silent films to sound, from black and white to colour. I believe this will be the next major step for the film industry. At present, the reach of a strong Flemish film is often limited because the market is relatively small. With this technology, a film like that can be released credibly in English and thus also conquer the American market.’
“Next month, we’re releasing a major Indian film, ‘Ramayana’, in the United States. The film has been fully translated into English, but you can still hear the voices of the original actors and see their facial expressions. I think that will be a significant milestone for this technology,” said Plaete.
“Meanwhile, we are also in talks with major film studios and distributors to apply this on a much larger scale.”

Wallace & Gromit maker Aardman falls short of return to profit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:00:25 UTC
16:00:25 KST

Don’t break out the celebratory Wensleydale just yet. Aardman, the British animation studio behind the cheese-loving inventor Wallace and his beloved dog Gromit, has fallen short of a target to get back in the black, its accounts show.
The employee-owned business was aiming to record a small profit in 2025 after two years of consecutive losses but was hit by production delays and a “challenging market” in children’s content.
So although its revenues jumped 8% to £20.4m last year, it was in the red to the tune of £1.1m, albeit an improvement on the previous year’s £4.1m loss.
Aardman, which also produces the popular Shaun the Sheep series, said the timing of some “significant” deals and weaker income in some parts of the business had hurt its bottom line.
It will be hoping for a boost from new projects, such as a recently opened exhibition at Lightroom in London that explores its 54-year history, as well as a third Shaun the Sheep film, which was released last month.
And the famously silent Gromit will soon be getting a voice, with this month’s audiobook of his autobiography read by the actor Martin Freeman.
In 2024 the studio launched a five-year business plan, which involved more investment in its intellectual property and cutting back costs.
Since then it has enjoyed the success of Wallace & Gromit: Vengeance Most Fowl, which broke viewing records over Christmas in 2024 as the most watched animated film broadcast on British television since 2002.
The film won two Baftas and received an Oscar nomination for best animated feature film.
Aardman said in its annual accounts that it had undertaken a further strategic review in early 2026 as it looked for ways to manage inflationary cost pressures, which resulted in “several redundancies”.
Its headcount for the 2025 financial year had already shrunk from 297 to 230 people, with permanent staff falling from 128 to 110.
The studio also recognised artificial intelligence as a principal risk and uncertainty to its business. It wrote that AI and generative AI were “reshaping parts of the creative industries, creating opportunities to improve workflows and support innovation while also raising important legal, ethical and authorship issues”.
It said it was vital this technology was developed and used responsibly and selectively, but only in ways that “support and celebrate human creativity and craft rather than replace it”.
Peter Lord and David Sproxton co-founded the studio in the early 1970s in Bristol. They began animating as teenagers, selling their first short – starring a superhero called Aardman – to the BBC’s Vision On in 1972.
They created Morph for the children’s programme Take Hart in 1977. The studio began appealing to adult audiences through Channel 4’s Conversation Pieces series, and its animators, including Nick Park, went on to make Wallace & Gromit.
Aardman became employee-owned in 2018, with Lord and Sproxton transferring majority ownership to staff to safeguard the company’s independence. The pair were knighted earlier this year.

UK goods trade deficit narrows to $26.2B in August, below expectations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:00:07 UTC
16:00:07 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
The UK's goods trade deficit stood at £19.8 billion ($26.2 billion) in August, below market expectations of £21.9 billion, as imports fell more than exports, official figures showed Thursday.
The deficit, excluding precious metals, narrowed by £200 million from July, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
Goods imports decreased 2.3% month-on-month to £54.2 billion, while exports fell 3.1% to £34.4 billion.
Imports from non-EU countries dropped 6.3% to £25.6 billion, driven primarily by lower purchases of machinery and transport equipment following a record increase in July. Aircraft imports from the US and ship imports from China declined.
Imports from the EU rose 1.6% to £28.6 billion, supported by higher purchases of German aircraft and pharmaceutical products, alongside refined oil from the Netherlands.
Goods exports to the EU fell 7.3% to £15.8 billion, reflecting declines in machinery and transport equipment, manufactured materials, fuels and chemicals.
Lower aircraft exports to the Netherlands and reduced crude oil shipments to Germany, Poland and Italy contributed to the fall.
Exports to non-EU countries increased 0.9% to £18.6 billion, supported by higher shipments of inorganic chemicals to the US.
After adjusting for inflation, total goods imports fell 2.5%, while exports declined 2.8%.
 
3-month trade deficit widens
The total goods and services trade deficit widened by £1.4 billion to £8 billion ($10.6 billion) in the three months to August compared with the three months to May.
The goods deficit increased by £2.5 billion to £59.1 billion, partly offset by a £1.1 billion rise in the estimated services surplus to £51.1 billion.
Early estimates for August showed services exports increased 0.4% from July, while imports rose 0.2%.

The U.S. military has developed new plans for strikes against Iran that envisage the possible use of the largest non-nuclear bomb in the U.S. arsenal — the GBU-43/B, known as the "mother of all bombs." Potential targets include Iran’s energy infrastructure and nuclear facilities. CNN reports this, citing U.S. officials familiar with the military plans, UNN reports.
Details
According to CNN sources, one of the plans involves strikes against a significant number of Iran’s energy infrastructure facilities, with the possible use of the MOAB bomb. Another option concerns nuclear facilities, including Pickaxe Mountain, where, according to U.S. and Israeli assessments, Tehran stores components of its nuclear program. President Trump has repeatedly threatened to strike Pickaxe Mountain. He says the U.S. goal is to prevent Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons.
The use of a MOAB in the conflict with Iran would mark a new stage of escalation. At the same time, according to the publication, sources familiar with discussions of the military plans have expressed doubts about whether this weapon would help achieve the strategic goals of U.S. President Donald Trump or change the balance of power in the war.
Although the U.S. military continues to provide Trump with options for potential strikes against important Iranian targets, some officials continue to privately question whether the White House has a strategy that takes these plans into account in a way that would actually bring the war to an end — something only the president has the authority to do. For months, Trump and his advisers have discussed options that could serve as the "final" end to the war, at least from a communications standpoint, recognizing how unpopular the conflict has become among Americans. Although some administration officials have characterized the war as effectively won, Trump has been more cautious in his latest statements, not declaring victory and saying that the U.S. still has unfinished business in the country
At the same time, over the past several weeks, White House advisers have held meetings to discuss various courses of action regarding Iran.
Although Trump publicly announced that he would take no new action until the midterm elections, several advisers privately said they did not know whether this statement was final or could change before Election Day. One source told CNN that Trump had ordered the military to develop additional strike packages against Iranian targets, including a "significant number of energy infrastructure facilities" and the potential use of the Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB). The same source said the wording used was that this attack would take place "before the U.S. regression in the CENTCOM area of responsibility," indicating that the administration could carry out additional strikes, try to declare victory, and quickly withdraw everyone

Romania’s nominated prime minister secures support ahead of confidence vote
BUCHAREST, Oct 15 - Romania's leftist Social Democrats said they will join the government of Prime Minister-designate Luca Niculescu while other parties pledged their votes, edging the country closer to ending a political crisis that has pressured its investment-grade rating.
The Social Democrats (PSD), parliament's largest party, will have 11 ministers in the proposed government Niculescu will unveil on Thursday before a parliamentary vote of confidence, PSD leader Sorin Grindeanu said late on Wednesday.
Technocrats will fill other ministerial posts, including finance, energy and foreign affairs.
While other pro-European parties refrained from joining the cabinet, many said they will back Niculescu, ensuring the 233 votes required to win the vote of confidence.
Niculescu, 55, a diplomat, former journalist and currently interim deputy foreign minister, will lead centrist President Nicusor Dan's fourth attempt to install a government in the five months since a pro-European broad coalition cabinet collapsed.
The four-party government led by Liberal Party head Ilie Bolojan collapsed in early May when the PSD quit and teamed up with the far-right opposition to file a no-confidence vote.
The PSD have repeatedly said they would form a similar coalition with a different prime minister, but the Liberals and two other centre-right parties have refused.
The months-long political crisis has pushed the Romanian leu currency to record lows while debt yields surged. The European Union state narrowly avoided a ratings downgrade from the last rung of investment grade.
Ratings agencies have all said that Romania's ability to approve a 2027 budget that further cuts one of the EU's largest deficits will be key for the country's rating.
While Niculescu's government was set to get parliament's approval, it was unclear how long it would last. The PSD will join on condition that a 2027 budget plan be unveiled by December 1, with no further tax hikes, and Grindeanu said it will assess the cabinet in six months.
Romania has agreed with Brussels to bring its budget deficit below 3% of economic output - from over 9% in 2024 and an expected 6.2% this year - by 2030. REUTERS

Russia miscalculated by sidelining Europe in US talks, Kallas tells Euronews
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:54:55 UTC
15:54:55 KST

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas tells Euronews that Russia miscalculated by seeking a deal with Washington alone, adding that Europe will continue to back Ukraine and "pressure aggressor" Moscow.
Russia will not succeed in forcing Ukraine to surrender through a deal with Washington because Europe will continue to back Kyiv, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told Euronews in an exclusive interview.
Kallas, the EU’s High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, said Russia had miscalculated since last year’s Anchorage summit by trying to force Ukraine to cave in through a deal with the US.
“The Russians want to discuss and negotiate with the US, so that the US would deliver what they want. But we have our own requests to Russia,” she said. “The message is that you need to talk to the Europeans.”
Asked about the diesel deal and energy ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump, under which Russia would supply 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global markets, Kallas said the arrangement was a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“The question is: what has he given in return? What we see is that he’s actually increasing the attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure. The ceasefire that was also announced is not really working on the Russian side,” she said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Financial Times that Kyiv would resume strikes on Russian refineries despite US pressure, including interruptions to intelligence sharing and a weakened Starlink signal during heavy Russian attacks.
For Kallas, the central issue is that Russia must end its war of aggression, which would also bring an end to Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries.
“If we look at the big picture, the majority of the financing for this war comes from oil. And that is why Ukraine is also targeting them [the refineries], while Russia is targeting the energy infrastructure inside Ukraine, to cause as much suffering as possible to the Ukrainian people in the upcoming winter,” she said.
Kallas insisted that international pressure should be directed at Russia to end its invasion, rather than at Ukraine to accept Moscow’s demands – a position she said Europe had consistently maintained.
“If we did this together with the US, then the message to Russia would be clear: stop this war, and all your worries when it comes to oil refineries and whatnot will also stop,” she said.
Asked whether a wave of elections in key EU countries, including the prospect of Marine Le Pen becoming French president, signalled waning support for Ukraine, Kallas acknowledged that public attitudes had shifted over four years of war.
However, she said Europe needed to present a united front for its foreign policy to be effective.
“This is what the Russians are actually playing at: that the Europeans will get tired and then they will get what they want. And what I want to stress is that their appetite will then grow,” Kallas said.

Pope Leo had a good night in hospital as he recovers from lung cancer surgery
VATICAN CITY – Pope Leo had a good night in hospital and has eaten breakfast, the Vatican said on Oct 15, as the 71-year-old recovers from surgery for lung cancer.
The Pope has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer, and doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung in a surgery on the afternoon of Oct 13.
The Vatican has said the surgery was completed successfully, without complications.
It has not yet disclosed the size of the tumour or whether the disease had spread to nearby lymph nodes, key factors in determining prognosis.
Blood tests and a chest X-ray carried out on Oct 14 showed normal post-operative results, the Vatican said.
US President Donald Trump, who has clashed with Pope Leo on a number of issues, added his voice on Oct 14 to the global chorus of goodwill for the ailing pope.
“I want to see Pope Leo get well,” Trump told reporters. “I just want to wish him well, get better fast.”
Vice-President J.D. Vance, a Catholic convert, also added his prayers.
“May God grant him strength as he works to get better. I hope he knows that millions of American Christians are thinking about him,” Vance wrote on X.
Further updates are expected on the Pope’s condition on Oct 15, but his pathology report may not be available for several days.
His public schedule has been cancelled until Oct 20.
The cancer diagnosis for a pope known to be relatively young and energetic and who was elected only in May 2025 caused shock and raised questions about the future shape of his papacy as he deals with the illness.
Pope Leo normally has a packed schedule. He is due to make a tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from Nov 6 to 17 and the Vatican press office said on Oct 14 that “nothing has changed” regarding the planned trip.
However, Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori said that the dates could change because of the amount of time that Pope Leo’s recovery would take. REUTERS

First swans return to Bruges’ canal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:48:22 UTC
15:48:22 KST

The first swans are back in Bruges. The swans at 't Stil Ende waterway had to be moved away during the summer because blue-green algae caused the water quality to deteriorate, but they have now returned. Swans from other Bruges’ canals will remain in the enclosure for the time being. The city is continuing to monitor the water quality of its waterways.
The number of blue-green algae in Bruges’ canals is gradually decreasing. The lab provides a weekly update, enabling the city to continue monitoring water quality. “It is the water quality that determines when the swans can return safely. We monitor the test results weekly and assess the situation at each location. The welfare of the animals is always our top priority,” says alderman Franky Demon.
“We are keeping the swans in their familiar location for as long as possible. If their health or welfare is at risk, we will take the necessary measures. Thanks to targeted monitoring and good care, all the swans are doing well.”
Removed earlier than last year
The city also took measures last year. In 2025, the swans at Wijngaardplein were able to remain where they were, but they were kept on dry land for around two weeks with fresh drinking water. In August 2025, the city removed a family of swans from the vicinity of the Carmers Bridge, the Potterierei and the Sint-Annarei because the water quality was inadequate.
In October 2025, these swans were allowed to return after spending around two months in the enclosure. The swans from Stil Ende spent the same amount of time in the enclosure this year, but the city had to remove them earlier. The long spell of warm weather early in the year encouraged the growth of blue-green algae and put pressure on water quality.
Number of swans on the rise
Bruges now has a total of 59 swans. In the swan enclosure, the city is still looking after 22 adult swans and eight newly purchased young swans for the Wijngaardplein. In addition, there are two swans from the children’s farm and seven swans from the Potterierei.
A few months ago, the number of swans fell below 52. According to a persistent legend, the city must maintain at least 52 swans on its waters. With the purchase of eight young swans, the total now stands at 59 once again.
According to Demon, the city did not buy the swans to uphold the legend. “The purchase is part of the routine management of the swan population in our city,” he says.
