This Spanish poet's work was banned and censored. Now it's an epic movie
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:21:58 UTC
15:21:58 KST

Penélope Cruz lights up La Bola Negra, but the boys will break your heart
A titan of Spanish culture, the proud socialist, poet, playwright and theatre director Federico García Lorca was most likely executed, aged 38, by General Francisco Franco's Nationalist forces in August of 1938 as the country was torn apart by bloody civil war.
Lorca's works were banned until 1953, then heavily censored until Franco's death in 1975. Even then, Lorca's family concealed his overtly queer work for fear of tainting his legacy. The Sonnets of Dark Love emerged in 1983 against the family's will.
La Bola Negra, four pages of which Lorca penned shortly before his murder, has been adapted into an astonishing queer epic spanning 80-plus years by directorial duo Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, known collectively as Los Javis.
Drawing on that fragment and the play La Piedra Oscura by screenplay co-writer Alberto Conejero, the Palme d'Or-nominated triumph is one of the biggest box office hits in Spanish history. It's easy to see why.
Slings and arrows
Told across three distinct storylines, La Bola Negra opens on bored-looking trumpet player Sebastián in 1937. Played by real-life musician and singer Guitarricadelafuente, replete with a mop of curly dark hair, he's part of a band tasked with musically accompanying a flyover by Benito Mussolini's Aviazione Legionaria.
But the Italians mistake the Nationalist-sympathising villagers practising the Nazi-inspiring saluto romano for Republicans, strafing the town square in a Guernica-like atrocity, leaving countless dead, including Sebastián's mother.
Sebastián goes on the run. Finding temporary sanctuary in a partially collapsed church, he scrabbles over the rubble as his lips almost touch those of a shattered sculpture of the saint that shares his name. The arrow punctures are an image that bleeds through this beautiful film.
He is soon captured by Nationalist soldiers and pressed into service as a prison guard. His ward is real-life Atlético Madrid player, actor and sometime Lorca lover Rafael Rodríguez Rapún (Miguel Bernardeau) who arrives, guts exposed, in a cart carrying the mostly dead.
As the maimed Rafael recuperates, a clearly dazzled Sebastián can't keep his eyes off the fallen soldier, illustrated by cinematographer Gris Jordana's aching camerawork fluttering erotically on the rise and fall of Rafael's Adam's apple.
Blackballed
Another storyline is set in Granada, 1932, before the war, and is centred on a wealthy young man named Carlos (novelist Milo Quifes, in his screen debut). Natty in a white pinstriped suit, he is attempting to gain membership of a prestigious private club. After each member votes via a white ball (for yes) or black (for no), he is cruelly rejected.
The whirr of the baubles dropping is another example of the film's potent imagery and a nod to the etymological origin of the film's title. He's barred because of his penchant for illicit meetings with men after dark and stolen glances at sunbathing sailors, which have become common knowledge.
Carlos's stern father (Antonio de la Torre) insists he must man up, explicitly linking gender to sexuality, and deny these "scurrilous" rumours and gain entry — but a subtler blow comes from his loving sister (Natalia de Molina) as she reflects on how she curbs her own wishes and hews to societal expectations, imploring him to do likewise.
The unique burble of a notification on hook-up app Grindr bursts the bubble of these historical strands.
This time it's queer music historian Alberto (Carlos González) who's cruising. It's now 2017, and he's stunned by an unexpected inheritance from his late grandfather, a man he does not know. Alberto's ferociously cranky mother (a magnificently bolshy Lola Dueñas), still aggrieved at his abandonment of their family, yells at Alberto to ignore the summons to Cantabria.
Similarly reluctant, Alberto is cajoled into going by his boyfriend, Juan (a surprisingly understated cameo by comedian Julio Torres), who points out the perversity of a historian uninterested in his own past.
What awaits him in Cantabria will tear off the scabs of his family history and that of the country, as these seemingly disparate strands twist tighter.
Face the music and dance
That La Bola Negra can paint on such a large canvas, holding close to its characters and their truths while honouring Lorca — portrayed by Alberto Cortés in black-and-white flashbacks — is remarkable. Particularly as Los Javis shoot for something grander than a bog-standard biopic.
Depressingly rare these days, the filmmakers understand that film can use light and sound in subtly destabilising ways. They know how to frame their players, adored by Jordana's lens, in conversation with one another beyond the verbal.
In union with their frequent editor Alberto Gutiérrez, they stitch these non-linear threads together in supple fashion, finding room for fireworks on the beach and Glenn Close speaking Spanish.
A show-stopping cameo from Penélope Cruz as Nené, a spectacular cupletista in the grand mould of Olga Ramos, is a performance for the ages that delivers loaded drama.
In one of the film's most tender moments, Nené encourages Sebastián to flee the army and find himself in Madrid, sharing her adoration of historic drag star Edmond de Bries, saying that his bravery, "Is the fantasy of the possible, and war is the opposite."
Snowdrifts
La Bola Negra is full of such tantalising possibility, of hope for a better, truer life, with Carlos's mother (María Morales) also begging him to leave for Madrid. It's the city where Lorca and Rafael fell into one another's embrace, inspiring those once-lost sonnets.
As Cortés's Lorca says, "This country has too many love stories buried in the fields. We have to scratch the earth so they can emerge. So more of them can exist."
La Bola Negra is such a releasing scratch, a great heaving sigh for the stories never told, for the lovers bold and lost, their stories resurfaced. There are moments, like a stolen embrace in a darkened cell, a pinprick of light piercing the dark like a Goya painting, that will wound you. It is a work of art as soft and scalding as the snow that drifts to Los Javis's majestically unmooring conclusion, then lingering on.
La Bola Negra is in cinemas now.

The administration of US President Donald Trump will consider easing sanctions on tankers belonging to Russia’s shadow fleet. Reuters reports this.
Washington hopes the move will increase the availability of maritime shipping and bring downfreight rates, which have reached record highs.
The proposed easing would allow tankers previously placed under sanctions to transport oil that is not subject to sanctions.
This would not mean lifting sanctions on Russian or Iranian oil. Instead, the tankers would be allowed to carry oil that is legally permitted to be traded.
The US administration aims to increase shipments of crude oil and petroleum products from the Persian Gulf. The war in the Middle East and disruptions to shipping in the region have caused maritime freight rates to surge, making it more difficult to supply global energy markets.
Companies wishing to use these tankers will have to submit applications to the US Department of the Treasury.
Discussion of the initiative comes shortly after Donald Trump temporarily eased sanctions on Russian diesel fuel.
Shadow fleet tankers are used to transport oil and petroleum products from Russia, Iran and Venezuela. They help circumvent Western sanctions through opaque ownership structures, questionable insurance arrangements or registration under the flags of third countries.
Despite these measures, the United States continues to strike vessels linked to the shadow fleet. On October 10, 2026, aUS fighter jet attacked the cargo vessel M/V Ocean Molica, also known as Arika Sun, in the Gulf of Oman.
The strike was carried out after the crew ignored repeated warnings and attempted to breach the naval blockade of Iran.
Militarnyi previously reported that US Coast Guard specialists had revealed the technical methods used by shadow fleet vessels to conceal their activities.

Details: "The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We're done," Zelenskyy said in a forthright interview with the FT in London. He also sharply criticised Washington's eagerness to strike business deals with Moscow and Trump's apparent affinity for Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
Asked to explain the relationship between the two leaders, Zelenskyy said Trump has an instinctive affinity for autocrats and extremely wealthy people.
"He [Trump] speaks about it openly and loudly that he loves such people and he respects such people. Because for him people who can be leaders 20 years, 30 years, 40 years, it means they can be very strong," Zelenskyy said.
The FT noted that Washington has increased pressure on Kyiv to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries, arguing that a moratorium on the attacks, together with an agreement to purchase hundreds of thousands of tonnes of Russian diesel fuel, is necessary to bring down fuel prices in the US.
Zelenskyy said he had suspended strikes on energy facilities for three days to accommodate the US request. However, Moscow continued to attack Ukraine's energy infrastructure and kill civilians, with more than 100 people killed in the past week.
The president also said that, despite Ukraine suspending its strikes, its forces had been left without US early-warning systems for incoming ballistic missiles. Starlink satellite communications, operated by Elon Musk's company, had also been slowed across the country, making battlefield operations and medium-range strikes against Russian military facilities more difficult.

Asked whether Ukraine would stop striking oil refineries even if Russia continued its attacks, in an effort to repair relations with the White House, Zelenskyy said he would agree to do so only if the US supplied him with more American-made Patriot interceptors.
He believes that halting strikes on oil refineries could simply encourage the US and Russia to strike further deals, potentially providing additional funding for Putin's war machine.
"The question will be when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas," Zelenskyy said.
He added that the US suspension of intelligence sharing and disruption of Starlink services has become "dangerous" for Ukraine.
"We will find a way out . . . but it's better not to give him [Putin] the new life or the new will to fight," Zelenskyy concluded.
Background:
- On 11 October, Trump published a post on his social media Truth Social announcing an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, which allegedly took effect immediately. He said that both sides had consented to cease strikes on energy infrastructure, although neither party had been informed of this.
- Barak Ravid, a journalist at American news portal Axios, stated that Zelenskyy had been unaware of the "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia announced by Trump, but added that Ukraine supports it.
- Later, Zelenskyy reported a Russian strike on CHP-5 [a combined heat and power plant] in Kharkiv and a power station in Kyiv following Trump's statement.
- On 13 October Zelenskyy stressed that Ukraine has refrained from striking Russian oil refineries and energy facilities for two days in response to a proposal by Trump. Russia, meanwhile, has attacked Ukrainian energy facilities and critical infrastructure.

G20 finance ministers, central bankers gather amid fallout from Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:16:46 UTC
15:16:46 KST

G20 finance ministers, central bankers gather amid fallout from Iran war
Officials meet in Thailand as conflict drives energy prices higher and casts uncertainty over global economy.
The G20 finance ministers and central bank governors are gathering in Bangkok, Thailand, on Thursday amid an uncertain global outlook shaped by the US-Israel war on Iran.
The meetings are being held in conjunction with the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, taking place in the Thai capital from October 12 to October 18.
Here are some of the key details about the meetings:
What are the G20, the IMF and the World Bank?
The G20 is an economic forum comprising 19 large economies, including the United States, China, the United Kingdom, Australia, Brazil, India, Japan, Indonesia and Saudi Arabia, as well as the European Union and the African Union.
The grouping has an annually rotating presidency, currently held by the US.
Together, the G20 countries account for about 85 percent of global gross domestic product (GDP) and three-quarters of global trade.
The G20 was established in 1999 as a forum for finance ministers and central bank governors to address shared economic concerns in the wake of the Asian Financial Crisis, before expanding into a broader forum for national leaders.
The IMF, based in Washington, DC, is an international financial institution that promotes international cooperation on monetary policy, trade and economic growth.
Its membership includes all but a handful of the world’s sovereign states, including North Korea, Cuba, the Vatican City and Monaco.
The World Bank, also based in Washington, DC, primarily serves as a provider of loans and grants to developing countries. It has 189 member countries.
The IMF and the World Bank were created at the 1944 Bretton Woods conference in the US, convened by the Allied Powers to establish the contours of the post-World War II international financial order.
Who will be attending the meetings?
Most finance ministers and central bank governors of the G20 will be in Bangkok, along with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva and World Bank Group President Ajay Banga.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will be a notable absence from the gatherings, as the top economic official of the world’s biggest economy and G20 chair.
US officials have cited “domestic engagements” for Bessent’s decision to skip the events, at which Washington will be represented by Deputy Secretary Francis Brooke and Undersecretary for International Affairs Erin Browne.
The G20 meeting, one of several gatherings of the group’s finance ministers each year, will help shape the agenda for the headline leaders’ summit in Miami, Florida, taking place on December 14-15.
What is on the agenda?
The economic fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran is expected to dominate discussions.
Attacks across the Middle East have upended economic activity across the region, while disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz has driven a surge in energy prices worldwide.
Crude oil prices have exceeded $100 a barrel for much of the past eight months, placing a strain on government coffers and household budgets, particularly in the Gulf region and the rest of Asia.
In advance of the meeting, Australia’s Treasurer Jim Chalmers MP said he would use the discussions to call for an end to the conflicts in the Middle East and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz “because that’s what the global economy desperately needs”.
“The war in the Middle East is having a devastating economic impact and is pushing up fuel prices, inflation and interest rates around the world,” Chalmers said in a statement.
Other issues likely to feature on the agenda include the ballooning debt levels of many countries, which exceed 100 percent of GDP in the US, Canada, Japan, Italy and France.
In a speech on Wednesday, Georgieva warned that mounting debt posed a threat to the global economy and that there was no “magic” formula that would allow governments to avoid tax hikes or spending cuts.
G20 members will also bring more specific individual concerns to the table based on their economic and geopolitical priorities.
The US, for example, has repeatedly expressed concern about “global imbalances”, a veiled reference to China’s state-driven industrial model that has allowed Chinese exporters to flood overseas markets with cheap goods.
US President Donald Trump has long claimed that China’s large trade surplus, which stood at a cumulative $938bn in September, proves that international trade is stacked against US manufacturers.
In a statement addressed to the IMF on Wednesday, Bessent called for action to address mismatched trade balances.
“This especially includes strengthening its analysis and engagement on the role non-market policies and practices and exchange rates play in driving external imbalances,” Bessent said.
“Policymakers around the world are having difficult discussions about how to sustain market-based systems amid distortionary policies from some economies that skew competition and hurt employment.”
Divisions and competing interests cloud the prospects for coordination, however.
At the last meeting of G20 finance ministers in Asheville, North Carolina, US, held on August 31 and September 1, member countries failed to issue a joint communique after China objected to language to do with trade.

What is Palestine Action? Sally Rooney Books to No Longer Be Sold in U.K. Over Ties to Group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:15:15 UTC
15:15:15 KST

Sally Rooney’s publisher said the Irish author will no longer sell her books in the U.K. after the country banned a pro-Palestinian group she promised to financially support.
Rooney had pledged to donate royalties from her bestselling novels, which include ‘Intermezzo’ and ‘Normal People,’ to Palestine Action, a group banned as a terrorist organization by the British government. Her publisher, Faber, said in a statement on Wednesday that it decided to no longer supply her work “in the U.K. in any format.”
“Current legislation in the U.K. has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on U.K. earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher,” Faber said.
The news has inflamed debate over the British government’s unprecedented decision to use terrorism powers to ban a group primarily known for property damage and disruption. The group describes its aim as halting the supply of weapons to Israel and ending what it describes as British complicity in Israel’s “genocide” of Palestinians.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed since Israel launched its military campaign in Gaza following the Hamas terror attack on Oct. 7, 2023, which killed approximately 1,200 people in Israel and resulted in 251 others taken hostage. In the absence of independent monitoring on the ground, the Gaza Health Ministry is the primary source for casualty data relied upon by humanitarian groups, journalists, and international bodies. Its figures do not differentiate between civilians and combatants and cannot be independently verified by TIME. Data from the Israel Defense Forces as of May 2025 suggested a Palestinian civilian death rate of 83%.
Israel denies allegations of genocide.
Rooney has long expressed her support for the group, and called the British proscription “a truly extreme assault on ordinary rights and freedoms.”
Here’s what to know about the group and how the British government’s ban affects Rooney.
What is Palestine Action?
Palestine Action is a pro-Palestinian group based in the U.K. that describes itself as a “direct action movement committed to ending global participation in Israel’s genocidal and apartheid regime.” The group has targeted facilities linked to Israeli weapons manufacturing or supplies.
“Every moment we can disrupt them is a victory, as halting production at one site interrupts their whole supply chain and has a knock on effect to other factories. If one action stops one weapon from killing a Palestinian, then it’s all worth it,” the group’s website reads.
Since its founding in 2020, members of Palestine Action have repeatedly damaged U.K. facilities linked to Israeli arms manufacturer Elbit Systems. Elbit Systems U.K. denied claims that its facilities supplied the Israeli military.
In June 2025, Palestine Action members broke into R.A.F. Brize Norton, the U.K.’s largest air force base, and spray painted two aircraft.
The British government banned the group in July 2025, proscribing it as a terrorist organization. It was the first British proscription primarily based on property damage, rather than threat or use of violence against people, although the government said the group’s members have demonstrated “a willingness to use violence.”
The group’s leaders have said it does not advocate or use violence against people.
“In several attacks, Palestine Action has committed acts of serious damage to property with the aim of progressing its political cause and influencing the Government,” then-Home Secretary Yvette Cooper said in announcing the proscription.
The ban has faced a series of legal challenges. In February, the High Court ruled it unlawful and disproportionate, but the Court of Appeal overturned that ruling in June. The ban remains in force, with the Supreme Court scheduled to hear a further appeal early next month.
How does the ban affect Rooney and others?
Since the ban, more than 3,000 people have been arrested for expressing support for the group at demonstrations. Among these were protesters holding signs with the words, “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.”
The ban and ensuing arrests prompted debate over free speech and the use of counterterrorism laws against political protest. The U.K. protects freedom of expression under the Human Rights Act, but permits broader restrictions than the U.S. First Amendment, including on national security and public order grounds. Inviting or expressing support for a proscribed organization, even without inciting violence, can be a criminal offence in the U.K. Critics argued that criminalizing support for Palestine Action threatened peaceful dissent. The government, however, has maintained that the ban on the group does not prevent lawful protests in support of pro-Palestinian causes.
After the ban, Rooney pledged to donate money from her book sales to the group. In an August 2025 op-ed in the Irish Times, Rooney wrote, “I want to be clear that I intend to use these proceeds of my work, as well as my public platform generally, to go on supporting Palestine Action and direct action against genocide in whatever way I can.”
“To ensure that the British public is made aware of my position, I would happily publish this statement in a U.K. newspaper—but that would now be illegal,” the author added. “The present U.K. Government has willingly stripped its own citizens of basic rights and freedoms, including the right to express and read dissenting opinions, in order to protect its relationship with Israel.”
Providing financial support to organizations designated under the U.K.’s Terrorism Act is a criminal offense. In a statement circulated by her agent, Rooney said “the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the U.K. could now constitute a serious criminal offence. After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the U.K.”
The decision to withdraw Rooney’s books from the U.K. has reignited debate over the ban. Huda Ammori, co-founder of Palestine Action, told The Guardian that “Sally Rooney being unable to publish her work in the UK marks a new low in the escalating assault on free speech caused by the proscription of Palestine Action.”
British Member of Parliament Ian Byrne called on the government to reconsider the ban, noting that he had “warned of the draconian consequences it would bring.”
“Now this injustice against one of the finest writers of her generation. An utterly disgraceful attack on freedom of expression,” he said on social media.
Rooney reaffirmed her intention to support Palestine Action, “which is not a proscribed or otherwise prohibited group here in the Republic of Ireland.”
“I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions,” the author said. “And I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences.”

Coalition and Greens unite to be a thorn in the government’s side
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:13:55 UTC
15:13:55 KST

analysis
Government takes a battering as departing senator urges Liberals not to give up
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.
As parting messages go, Jonno Duniam's was upbeat as he urged his colleagues not to wave the white flag in the battle against a rising One Nation.
It was a packed crowd for the Tasmanian Liberal senator's valedictory speech as he said farewell to the chamber he's spent the last decade serving.
Many, including Labor's Katy Gallagher, tried to convince Duniam to stay on after he came to realise the toll the job was having on him and his family following the Liberal leadership contest earlier this year.
As Angus Taylor watched on, Duniam's final speech addressed — without naming — One Nation's accession in the polls. He urged the Coalition not to stray too far from its roots as it tries to claw back support that's fallen away to Pauline Hanson's party.
"My party can give Australians what they need, not by pretending to be someone else or seeking to appease certain actors but by returning to our roots — by backing in [our values] with conviction … and explaining why it is better than the alternative," he told the chamber on Wednesday.
The question of how to tackle One Nation has plagued the opposition for the better half of the year, with some suggesting the way forward is to strike up preference deals with the party.
Others — such as the man Duniam called a "brother", Andrew Hastie — think the party should confront the issue head on.
Duniam said he could not deny the impact several election losses had, but insisted the challenge wasn't insurmountable.
"My party has been around for decades. It isn't populist. It isn't flash in the pan. It is here to stay," he said.
"Sure, we may have spent some time in the wilderness, but we have our bearings now and I know we will be able to get back over there into government."
Public shaming and Powderfinger
Small business frustration with the government has been pretty easy pickings for the Coalition.
The minister in charge, Anne Aly, was the target for much of the week, as the Coalition singled her out as a weak link. Liberal frontbencher Angie Bell went too far when she declared Aly, and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, should be "shamed and stoned" over the ATO's decision.
She later conceded it was a poor choice of words after Aly, the first Muslim woman elected to federal parliament, shared that she'd received 19 death threats that week couched in similar language. The opposition quickly dismissed criticism the remarks were "racist and misogynistic" as a distraction from Aly's performance as minister.
The backlash over changes to negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount, the ATO credit card ban and now the fight over discretionary trusts are adding up.
As David Speers wrote this morning, it's not been an easy couple of months for Treasurer Jim Chalmers.
The result is a jittery caucus. The prime minister tried to calm the farm this week by reviving an old slogan.
He reminded Labor it wanted to "kick with the wind in the fourth quarter" — a phrase he repeated a lot when caucus was equally anxious back when he was opposition leader.
The prime minister didn't help matters by giving the impression he made a captain's call on the ATO's credit card ban after a text message from a business leader.
Chalmers denied he'd been rolled. Albanese had to walk back the statement in question time when Taylor asked how much longer he was going to "humiliate" his treasurer.
"The whole premise of it is completely wrong," he said.
It wasn't just tension between Albanese and Chalmers on show: an old colleague came back to haunt the Liberal Party this week.
The reemergence of Josh Frydenberg, and the unanswered question of whether his recent memoir was just the first step in a mooted comeback, frustrated some within the party.
Overall, the Liberals gave the former treasurer a pretty lukewarm response. If he can win preselection and be successful in 2028, then he's welcome to join Taylor's frontbench, Deputy leader Jane Hume said.
Garth Hamilton, a backbencher from Queensland, was less excited about the prospect.
"The only comeback I'm interested in seeing at the moment is Powderfinger," he told Afternoon Briefing.
Loading
Sometimes it makes sense, sometimes it doesn't
It's not just tax changes giving the government headaches. When it comes to a contentious wind back of a Howard-era private health insurance rebate, it appears Labor is well and truly up against it.
It wants to scale back the rebate Australians aged 65 and over receive on private health cover from next year. The changes would bank $3 billion that would then be spent elsewhere in the aged care sector.
But the bill is pretty friendless. Partially because it'll capture more Australians than first flagged, but also because about $1.6 billion of the forecast savings would be clawed back from pensioners.
The Coalition isn't for turning on this one; it'll oppose it to the bitter end, and as my colleague Stephanie Dalzell foreshadowed last week, the Greens aren't fans either. While they're against private health of any kind, they also don't want to be taking away benefits from pensioners.
Anyone closely watching this, i.e the government, shouldn't have been surprised when the Coalition and Greens teamed up with independent Jacqui Lambie to have the bill struck off the parliamentary agenda on Wednesday.
In her typical bluster, Lambie urged Health Minister Mark Butler not to reintroduce the bill.
She warned if he carried on "like a two-year-old" and did so anyway; the Senate would just "slap" it back down. Butler re-introduced the exact same bill again.
In his valedictory address, Duniam compared the Senate to a French film: sometimes it makes sense, sometimes it doesn't.
As the fight over private health showed this week, the chamber does have a flare for drama.
With three sitting weeks left, the dramatics will be on show as the government tries to negotiate its way through before the parliament rises for the year.

Precise Listeners Learn Languages Easier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:09:13 UTC
15:09:13 KST

Study suggests developing a ‘good ear’ for sounds instead of practice alone
People who are better at noticing fine details in sound—known as auditory precision—can master the pronunciation of new languages faster and more accurately than other learners, a new study finds.
Even when hearing a human voice, some people’s brains do not immediately treat new sounds as language, instead they understand them as unfamiliar acoustic signals. This ability may be one of the keys to successfully mastering pronunciation of a new language.
Researchers from UK’s University College London and Japan’s Tohoku University measured the auditory precision of 67 Japanese learners of English by measuring their ability to detect slight acoustic differences, such as changes in pitch, length, and tone, in non-speech sounds.
They then used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) technology to measure the participants’ brain activity as they tried to distinguish between the English vowels /æ/ (like the ‘a’ in ‘cat’) and /ʌ/ (like the ‘uh’ in ‘cup’). Neither of these sounds map directly on to Japanese vowels.
In a second task, the participants distinguished similar subtle differences in non-speech sounds.
The results, published in The Journal of Experimental Psychology: General showed that learners with higher auditory precision relied less on the brain’s left sensorimotor system (involved in language processing) when processing foreign-language sounds. Their brain activity patterns were similar to those that occur when the brain processes non-speech sounds. With less interference from pre-existing patterns of their native language, it was simpler for these learners to accurately process new sounds.
In contrast, the fMRI results showed learners with lower auditory precision relied more on the brain’s left sensorimotor network when listening to foreign-language sounds. They used the pronunciation patterns of their native-language when processing unfamiliar foreign language sounds.
Lead author Dr Kazuya Saito-van Poeteren (UCL Institute of Education) said: “Learners with a ‘good ear’ for auditory differences can hear a new foreign-language sound objectively, without immediately processing it as ‘language’. Instead, their brains analyze the acoustic information itself, and this may be the key to why some people grasp new languages with more ease than others.
“Most people approach foreign language learning by memorizing vocabulary and listening to speech, but our study indicated that language learners might also benefit from training the auditory abilities that underpin language learning itself.
The research team aim to develop a new form of combined language and auditory training designed to improve the ability to detect fine differences in pitch and other acoustic properties.

"We ask the President, our Congressional representatives, and our fellow citizens to act to prevent this barbaric abuse of authority," the letter read.
According to the retired officials, executing Nidal Hasan in such a public manner could turn him into a martyr.
Other objections to the livestream of the execution by firing squad detailed in the letter included that it could constitute a violation of the US Constitution's protections against cruel and unusual punishment, and that it would turn what should be a "solemn and grave punishment" into a "carnival for the enjoyment of voyeurs and spectators."
"This type of exploitative broadcasting - that debases human dignity- will taint the honor of the military that employs it, and a nation that allows it," the retired officials wrote.
Trump reconsidering livestream plans after learning Hasan uses wheelchair
The letter followed reports that US President Donald Trump was wavering on whether to livestream the execution after learning that Hasan was paralyzed from the waist down and uses a wheelchair, CNN reported on Wednesday.
According to multiple officials, Trump was not initially aware that US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth would be announcing the livestream of the execution, and polled several advisers and allies on how he should proceed.
“There are two thoughts: Don’t show it and show it," Trump told reporters over the weekend. "Because, you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So, I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.”
Sources also told CNN that the Pentagon was reevaluating the livestream plans, and that even if it did go ahead, footage would likely be cut before shots were fired.
Hasan sentenced to execution after mass shooting in military base medical facility
A military jury sentenced Hasan to death in August 2013, after finding him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder for opening fire with a laser-sighted handgun in a medical facility at the sprawling central Texas military base.
The shooting came weeks before Hasan, now 56, was scheduled to be deployed to Afghanistan. He was left partially paralyzed and confined to a wheelchair after being shot by police during his arrest.

The UK economy unexpectedly continued to grow in August despite a fall in consumer spending before John Healey’s first budget as chancellor.
Figures from the Office for National Statistics showed gross domestic product (GDP) rose by 0.1% last month, compared with 0.4% growth in July. That confounded a forecast by City economists of a 0.1% contraction.
With less than a fortnight before Healey’s tax and spending announcement, the ONS reading represents a surprise boost given that the Middle East war is rattling the global economy and hitting British households and businesses with a surge in energy costs.
After petrol and diesel prices rose and with higher energy bills hitting household spending, the ONS said the consumer-facing services sector fell by 0.3% on the month, after a decline of 0.1% in July.
Despite the overall services sector showing no growth in August, the surprise headline improvement was driven by strength in manufacturing with 0.8% growth in the wider production sector, which includes manufacturing, mining and energy generation. Construction output fell by 0.2%.
The largest negative contribution came from sports, amusement and recreation activities, alongside a slump in food and drink services. Analysts said the fall could be a sign of a reversal from an earlier boost from the World Cup and unusually hot weather, or could reflect households trimming their spending.
The ONS said GDP over the wider three months to the end of August rose by 0.7%. On an annual basis, it said the economy had grown by 2.1%, the strongest growth rate since August 2022.
It comes after the International Monetary Fund this week upgraded its growth forecasts for the UK this year but warned it expected a modest slowdown in 2027 as higher energy prices take their toll.
Speaking from Bangkok, where he is attending the meetings of the IMF and World Bank, Healey welcomed the figures: “Despite conflicts in the Middle East and Europe hitting people across the world, today’s figures offer more proof of Britain’s resilience in the face of these global shocks.
“This week the IMF have upgraded UK growth for 2026 and said that our fiscal discipline stands out with the lowest deficit in the G7 forecast by 2029 … my budget will build on this approach to drive good growth in every postcode.”
Sanjay Raja, chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, said: “Undoubtedly, there may be some hiccups to come in the runup to year-end, especially as energy prices continue to bite household incomes, and higher rates continue to drag on spending and investment.
“The good news? The UK’s resilience story continues. It’s hard to overstate how strong the UK performance has been all year.”
Against a volatile backdrop, the chancellor is under pressure to use his tax and spending address to the Commons on 28 October for a package of support to soften the blow for households, including help with rising energy bills. However, he will face a delicate balancing act amid a sharp increase in government borrowing costs.
In recent months, Britain’s economy had shown more resilience than had been expected at the start of the Iran war after recording the strongest rate of growth in the G7 in the first half of 2026. Official figures suggested a strong expansion in AI-related business activity as one factor behind the surprise rise.
Jake Finney, senior economist at PwC, said: “The UK’s growth performance has been a bright spot amid a less impressive run of economic news following events in the Middle East. Business investment has been an important driver, particularly spending on ICT hardware, likely linked to the build-out of AI infrastructure.”
In a fillip for the chancellor, the IMF this week upgraded its UK growth forecasts for this year, but warned that it expected a modest slowdown in 2027 as higher energy prices take their toll.
However, economists said momentum was likely to falter at the end of the year as households come under pressure from rising inflation.
Financial markets now anticipate the Bank of England to raise interest rates next month from 3.75% to 4%, before four more quarter-point rate increases in 2027.
Matt Swannell, the chief economic adviser to the Item Club, said: “We’re sceptical this strength can last … Some pullback looks inevitable. The impact of the conflict in the Middle East is also starting to be felt. Higher energy bills and petrol prices are pushing up inflation and hitting consumers’ spending power.”

‘I introduce myself to anyone who looks a bit jumpy’: a security guard’s take on anti-shoplifting fixes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:00:24 UTC
15:00:24 KST

I’ve run into volatile thieves for years – from opportunistic phone snatchers to people ripping computers off desks and biofuel bandits trying to steal vats of used cooking oil – and every time I file an incident report, I try to make a recommendation for preventive measures.
It’s safer to try to avoid a situation where things get physical with a suspected criminal. I don’t want to let my employers down, but I also don’t want anyone to have to go to hospital – myself included.
Greggs seems to be following a similar train of thought: earlier this year the chain phased out self-service cabinets in areas where shoplifting is rife and has installed safe pod “robocops” with 120-decibel sirens in some stores.
But snatch thefts seem to be on the rise everywhere, from “steaming” (large groups overwhelming a store) in city centres to machinery being swiped from rural farm shops. The cost of this crime – in terms of lost merchandise and measures to tackle it – further erodes margins at a time when retailers are battling higher employment costs and increases to business rates.
Customers, ever squeezed by rising energy bills, are becoming doubly impatient: those who are not tempted by grabbable goods are rightly affronted by measures such as sliding shields that seem to imply that everyone is a criminal.
But is it possible to make a store thief proof and welcoming to law-abiding clientele?
Discreet high technology is a happy medium. PTZ cameras (pan/tilt/zoom, which can be adjusted to track and focus on a single suspect) are one of the most-effective choices. They’re more efficient than fixed-camera CCTV, less controversial than AI surveillance and a serious upgrade on the convex mirror mounted at the end of the aisle in your local corner shop.
PTZ camera manoeuvrability means high-quality facial images, a must-have when trying to build evidence. Freeze-frames can also be used to generate stills that some premises owners choose to turn into warning posters, or share on a chat group with other local businesses.
My advice here is to be wary of GDPR regulations and remember that an incorrect time signature can render recordings inadmissible.
As useful as movable cameras are, they still require a human operator. Hiring guards can feel like a tax on businesses – but one that goes unpaid at considerable risk.
Ask anyone who lives in a village whether they’d prefer a CCTV camera or a “bobby on the beat” and the answer would be probably unanimously the latter.
The sight of a uniformed officer can be a strong deterrent. However, it comes with an upper limit. For example: if a 3,000 sq metre supermarket can accommodate 40,000 goods and 4,000 daily customers, one guard will not be able to cover it all.
It is also hard to identify which customers might be preparing to swipe something, especially given the rise of “middle-class shoplifting”. As someone whose job pays just above minimum wage, this is an interesting phenomenon.
I get that inflation presses down on all of us, but people further up the pyramid than me should know it won’t be shareholders or bonus-receiving bosses taking the hit for goods being pinched: it will be prices. Higher costs will further imperil the most vulnerable people who walk on site, the ones who already cannot afford bread or baby formula.
My best approach in these cases is empathy. I try to introduce myself to anyone who hangs around but looks jumpy; explain that every tap of my bank card makes me sweat too.
I also try to build local knowledge of repeat offenders: insight that made the bobbies on the beat so valuable. I know it won’t work against content creators who film me for “lols” while I’m administering first aid, and who half of all young Brits apparently want to emulate. I honestly fear them more than I do getting punched, stabbed or spat on.
But doing your revision pays off, especially when encountering an unsettled local resident with a penchant for threatening people with kitchen utensils. As the resident in question strode towards the premises one morning, my shiftmate quickly asked me whether I knew his name and address (I did).
“Morning, Mr Beddlington,” said my colleague as the resident got level with us and before he could grab his first frying pan. “Everything OK at Thorn Court today? Anything we can help with?”
The resident did an about-face and left the site. Loss prevention done low-cost and painlessly.
Names and addresses have been changed
What the Bouncer Saw: Life on the Front Line of the Security Business by George Bass is published by Hachette. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply

No timeline for lifting Land Registry paywall as ownership remains opaque
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:00:24 UTC
15:00:24 KST

The government has refused to say when the public will be able to freely access information about who owns large plots of land across England and Wales.
Emma Reynolds, the previous secretary of state for the environment, announced in March that the paywall protecting large amounts of the Land Registry would be partly lifted.
Campaigners called for this change in order to make large landowners more accountable, particularly for key areas such as river catchments, grouse moors and peatland.
But Reynolds did not put a date on when the paywall would be lifted, and the Land Registry is an “arm’s length body”, a non-ministerial government department that falls under the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government.
In setting out the land use framework in March, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) pledged only that it would “work with HM Land Registry this year to provide access to free, spatial land ownership data for larger properties covering the vast majority of England and Wales, excluding almost all homeowners”.
This may require a further public consultation, in addition to the consultation that preceded the land use framework. In July, a spokesperson for the Land Registry said: “HM Land Registry is supportive of initiatives that promote the more effective use of land. However, our plans with regard to this are still at a very early stage, and a number of aspects will be subject to consultation before any firm decisions are made. As such, we are currently unable to comment on timelines, what may be released, the format, or any associated attributes. We anticipate being in a position to provide more of an update early next year.”
In August, a Land Registry spokesperson said it was not clear which parts of the Land Registry data would be made public, nor who might be allowed to access the data and by what means.
Guy Shrubsole, the environmental campaigner and author of Who Owns England?, said: “It’s ridiculous that in the 21st century the public are kept in the dark about who owns the land beneath our feet. This is data that will help councils build more homes, expose who’s polluting our rivers and help communities restore nature.”
Andy Burnham, who took over as prime minister from Keir Starmer this summer, has made localism a key priority of his premiership. Shrubsole said allowing people to see data on the ownership of land should be part of that agenda. “Burnham has come to power promising place-first politics, and to bring unaccountable government agencies to heel,” he said. “Who owns our land underpins any politics of place, and it’s high time the Land Registry was made to reveal this profoundly important information.”
A Defra spokesperson said: “We are improving the transparency of land ownership data, and will provide free access to land ownership data for the vast majority of England, as we committed to in our land use framework. We are taking forward this commitment and will share further details as this work continues.”

The Welsh mountain inn that helped conquer Everest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:00:24 UTC
15:00:24 KST

In the early hours of 2 June 1953, guests at the Pen-Y-Gwryd hotel in the heart of Eryri (Snowdonia) were woken from their sleep by the sound of footsteps running down the corridor outside their rooms. The commotion was followed by gleeful shouting and the sound of champagne corks popping. A late-night telephone call to the hotel’s owner had moments earlier confirmed that Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay had successfully summited Mount Everest. It had taken two days for the news to travel from the Himalayas to London. Serendipitously, news of the historic achievement coincided with the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II later that day.
In the days and weeks that followed, the two mountaineers were feted across the front pages of newspapers around the world. Posing awkwardly for the cameras, their beaming smiles shone out of frost-burnt faces. In the decades that followed, Tenzing Norgay’s role in the expedition was increasingly marginalised – he was a Sherpa, indigenous to the area, and the load-carrying guide, while Hillary firmly planted his ice axe in the history books.
A new film, set for release this week on Apple TV, aims to set that record straight. Tenzing, starring Genden Phuntsok and Tom Hiddleston, tracks Tenzing Norgay’s life from a young boy growing up in the Khumbu Valley to his rise as one of the most accomplished climbers within the Sherpa community, and his eventual recruitment to the 1953 British expedition to Mount Everest (known locally as Chomolungma) led by Colonel John Hunt.
The film opened the Zurich film festival last month, where its director, Australian film-maker Jennifer Peedom, told audiences: “It’s often reduced to a familiar shorthand: Hillary conquered Everest, assisted by a Sherpa. But Tenzing had more experience on Everest than anyone else on that 1953 expedition. He wasn’t just helping another man achieve his dream. He had his own dream.”
In the spring of 1952, a full year before the British expedition, Tenzing, alongside Swiss climber Raymond Lambert, came agonisingly close to reaching the summit – less than 250 metres stood between them and glory. After a storm-lashed night on the south-east ridge, and with little oxygen, they were forced to retreat, albeit having set a new altitude record.
Meanwhile, back in the UK, Hunt, having been assigned by the Joint Himalayan Committee to assemble a team of climbers, set up base camp at the Pen-Y-Gwryd hotel at the foot of the Llanberis Pass. It was here they would practise their technical climbing skills and test the state-of-the-art equipment that had been designed specifically for this adventure, in particular the closed-circuit oxygen tanks that would be critical in keeping them alive in the “death zone” above 8,000m. The teams spent weeks on Yr Wyddfa’s (Snowdon) notorious Crib Goch ridge and on Y Lliwedd mountain, testing the revolutionary new high-altitude boots that would replace the old leather and hobnail ones, which offered little to no protection from the freezing temperatures of Everest.
Artefacts from those pioneering days can be seen at the hotel today. A glass cabinet contains some of the summit team’s original equipment and mementoes: goggles, an ice axe, a ledger of Sherpas’ fingerprints as most could not read or write, a compass and a battered tin mug. Little has changed in the 73 years since Christopher Briggs woke his guests with those glasses of champagne. The Pen-Y-Gwryd is a time capsule; it remains in family hands, now run by Briggs’s grandsons, Nick and Rupert Pullee, who are determined to maintain the hotel’s legacy and the traditions that have made it a beloved destination for those with a penchant for adventure and late-night conversations in front of roaring fires.
“My grandfather was originally from Scarborough,” Nick says. “He was a chemist, but his shop was bombed during the war, so [in 1947] he persuaded a friend to lend him the money to buy a hotel in Wales. The building had been used to home children during the blitz and had fallen into terrible disrepair, but he somehow managed to turn it into a success.”
Briggs also started the Snowdon Club, where guests under the age of 16 who have successfully climbed the mountain take part in a small ceremony in which they are quizzed on their mountain knowledge. Those who answer correctly get to drink (lemonade) from Hillary’s pewter tankard and are awarded a sterling silver ice-axe brooch, with their name added to a book of members – a ritual that still happens today.
The Smoke Room serves as the residents’ bar, a tiny wood-panelled snug whose walls are adorned with photos of the Everest team, with Tenzing featuring prominently. In one, he’s perched in the bar drinking tea with George Band, the youngest climber on the 1953 expedition. In another, he’s on a rocky outcrop of Tryfan, another famous Snowdonia peak, with team leader Hunt.
“I was only a toddler when Tenzing last visited the hotel,” says Nick. “I remember he was incredibly kind and was constantly smiling. He used to give Rupert and myself piggybacks up the stairs. He was great friends with my grandfather, who visited him in Nepal often.”
Built in 1810 on the bedrock that makes up the Glyderau range, the Pen-Y-Gwryd hotel is also the original starting point of the Pyg track, one of the most iconic routes to the summit of Yr Wyddfa, and today guests can walk directly from the hotel’s door to the path that snakes upwards towards Pen y Pass. The timeless interior of the hotel is devoid of TV screens or piped music, and the only concession to the 21st century appears to be the wifi.
This summer’s endless heatwaves saw sun-scorched hillwalkers cool their limbs in the natural outdoor pool in the grounds of the hotel. Fed by mountain streams, it offers unparalleled views of the hills and sweeping valley towards the mountain village of Capel Curig. The addition of an outdoor sauna and the popularity of cold-water swimming mean it’s now a year-round proposition.
The 20 rooms are all named evocatively after local peaks: Pen yr Ole Wen, Elidir Fawr, Crib Goch, Y Garn. Each is as cosy as one would expect from a rain-lashed mountain hotel: softly lit and with comfy mattresses wrapped in vintage Welsh wool blankets. In the labyrinthine corridors upstairs, you’ll discover bathrooms with Victorian roll-top tubs and Heath Robinson-esque showers. The bathroom doors are adorned with illustrations in the style of Aubrey Beardsley, and photos and artworks capturing the surrounding landscape and its mountaineering history adorn virtually every wall.
Dining at the Pen-Y-Gwryd is an event in itself: mealtimes are announced by the banging of a gong, the dining room is an unapologetic whirlwind of Axminster and silverware, and the menu features roast Welsh lamb and Welsh steak and ale pies, sticky toffee puddings or rhubarb crumble – everything you’ll need to replenish after a long mountain trek.
The ceiling of the Everest Room in the public bar has been signed by pretty much every big-name mountaineer of the past 100 years, and each corner of the building appears to have a story and artefact attached. It’s this authenticity that Nick believes gives the hotel its charm.
“I think our greatest attraction may be that things remain unchanged,” says Nick. “We have a lot of regular guests from all over the world, and for many people the opportunity to step back from the world in the wilds of Snowdonia is extremely enticing. It’s something we aim to protect and cherish.”
Rooms at the Pen-Y-Gwryd hotel range from £114 to £172 B&B; three-course dinner £49. Tenzing is on Apple TV from 16 October

For Gaza's chronically ill, every missed dose carries a risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:00:23 UTC
15:00:23 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza's healthcare collapse leaves chronic patients facing life-threatening complications
Three years into Israel’s genocide in Gaza, people living with chronic illnesses are struggling to access the medicines, tests and routine treatment they need to stay alive. For patients with diabetes, heart disease, kidney failure and cancer, shortages of essential drugs, medical equipment and fuel have turned the management of everyday conditions into a daily struggle for survival.
Across Gaza, disrupted medical care means patients are increasingly unable to monitor their conditions, attend follow-up appointments or complete essential treatment.
The consequences can be life-threatening: uncontrolled blood sugar, untreated heart problems, interrupted dialysis and cancer patients left uncertain about whether their disease is progressing.
The World Health Organisation says noncommunicable diseases, which accounted for the largest burden of disease in Gaza before the war, are now being underdiagnosed and undertreated because of limited access to diagnostic tests and treatment services.
According to 2026 figures, more than 18,500 people with injuries or chronic illnesses were in need of treatment unavailable inside Gaza and were awaiting medical evacuation.
'Diabetes has become a ghost'
Khalil al-Turk, 59, displaced from northern Gaza, once understood his illness well. Before the genocide, diabetes was something he could measure and manage: a tablet in the morning, an HbA1c test every three months, and regular medical follow-up.
Today, he says, diabetes has become "a ghost I cannot see."
"There are no glucose testing strips, and the insulin that is available is either constantly running out or spoils because there is no proper refrigeration. Sometimes I feel extremely dizzy, and I don’t know whether my blood sugar is too high or too low."
In those moments, even the decision to eat becomes frightening. "I eat a date and risk pushing my sugar higher, or I avoid eating because I’m afraid I might die."
Then came a small wound on his foot. Two months ago, Khalil developed a wound that, he says, did not receive the follow-up care it needed. It eventually developed into a deep infection threatening his foot.
Diabetes is not simply a temporary rise in blood glucose. Persistently high blood sugar can damage blood vessels, nerves, kidneys, eyes and the heart, making regular monitoring an essential part of treatment rather than a medical luxury.
In stable conditions, doctors can detect deteriorating blood-sugar control or the early signs of complications before they develop into a crisis. But when laboratory tests, monitoring equipment and follow-up appointments disappear, patients may not realise that their illness is no longer under control until their bodies begin sending far more serious warning signs.
'I don’t know how many attacks my heart has endured'
In Deir al-Balah, Aisha Juha, 62, lives with high blood pressure and heart disease. She used to attend a cardiology clinic every two months and took her blood-pressure medication regularly.
Now, she says, everything has changed. "For a year and a half, I have not stood in front of a single blood-pressure monitor," Aisha shares.
Her medication is no longer consistent either. "The medicine available at medical points changes from one week to another depending on whatever aid happens to arrive. Sometimes they give me an alternative; other times they simply tell me, ‘You’ll have to manage somehow.’"
Then came a night when she felt a heavy pressure in her chest and numbness spreading through her left arm. She knew the symptoms could be serious, but she could not find an ambulance or reach a nearby hospital equipped with an ECG machine.
"I took a patience pill, so to speak, and waited until morning. I don’t know how many attacks, or small heart events, my heart has gone through without any of them ever being recorded in a medical file," she says.
High blood pressure and heart disease require long-term monitoring and treatment. In Gaza, however, care for chronic conditions remains constrained by shortages of medication and equipment, as well as difficulties in reaching healthcare facilities.
The problem is not simply the absence of medication. It is also the absence of medical information.
Four hours became two
For Yousef Hammad, 41, a dialysis patient from Khan Younis, routine healthcare isn't an occasional visit to the doctor. It means staying alive. Under normal circumstances, he says, each dialysis session lasted four hours, three times a week.
"Today, a session lasts only two hours, twice a week — or sometimes just once, if we are lucky and there is enough diesel and treated water," Yousef tells The New Arab.
He describes reaching a dialysis machine as though competing for the chance to breathe. "I arrive at the machine competing with hundreds of other patients, our bodies full of toxins and fluid that are suffocating us," he adds.
The World Health Organisation says dialysis services in Gaza remain under intense pressure, with shortages of dialysis machines and essential medicines. Gaza’s Ministry of Health has estimated that as many as 1,100 patients require regular dialysis to stay alive.
For someone with kidney failure, treatment cannot simply be postponed until "conditions improve." When the kidneys stop functioning, they can no longer remove waste products and excess fluid from the body. In end-stage kidney failure, patients depend on dialysis or a kidney transplant to survive.
"A delay of just one day means I cannot sleep lying down because my lungs fill with fluid," Yousef says. "We are not waiting to recover. We are simply waiting to leave the dialysis session able to breathe."
When epilepsy medication runs out
For the mother of eight-year-old Karim, epilepsy was not an emergency before the genocide. Her son had lived with well-controlled epilepsy for years, and regular medication helped keep his seizures under control.
But when supplies of his medication began disappearing from pharmacies, she was unable to obtain it for three consecutive days.
Then the seizures began.
She says Karim suffered repeated, prolonged convulsions, and that she watched him struggling to breathe without knowing what to do.
The family tried replacing his medication with another drug they managed to find, but she says the seizures became worse.
With chronic illnesses, an "alternative medication" is not always a simple substitution that families can safely make on their own.
Some anti-epileptic drugs require careful selection, precise dosing and medical follow-up, because uncontrolled changes can result in a loss of seizure control.
Epilepsy also reveals something fundamental about routine healthcare: patients do not need doctors only when a seizure occurs. They need medical care to prevent that seizure from happening in the first place.
The cancer Khadija cannot see
Khadija Ahmed, 52, a breast cancer patient, has been displaced twice. Before Israel's war on the besieged enclave, she underwent surgery and was expected to begin adjuvant radiotherapy and chemotherapy at the Turkish-Palestinian Friendship Hospital.
Then the treatment plan stopped. She says the closure of the hospital, the destruction of medical equipment and the interruption of patients’ ability to leave Gaza for treatment brought everything to a halt.
Today, she can no longer undergo the tests that were meant to help her and her doctors monitor her condition.
"I cannot get tumour-marker tests. I don’t know whether the cancer has returned or whether it is spreading through my body," she tells The New Arab.
Sometimes, she feels pain in her bones. "I ask myself: is this simply exhaustion from displacement, or has the cancer reached my bones without me knowing?" she adds.
This is one of the less visible faces of war: not only living with illness, but living with medical uncertainty.
The World Health Organisation has confirmed that cancer patients in Gaza continue to face serious difficulties accessing treatment because of shortages of medicines, equipment and specialised services.
From chronic illness to emergency
Modern medicine does not treat chronic illnesses as conditions that patients can simply “put up with” indefinitely.
Diabetes requires monitoring, follow-up and treatment.
High blood pressure requires regular checks and medication adjustments when necessary.
Heart disease requires assessment and continuing care.
Kidney failure requires regular dialysis.
Epilepsy requires medication and medical follow-up to prevent or reduce seizures.
Cancer requires completion of a treatment plan and continued monitoring for response to treatment or recurrence.
When this system functions, patients may appear to be "well." But that apparent stability does not mean their illness has disappeared. It means the healthcare system is doing its job: keeping the disease under control.
When that system collapses, diseases that once remained silent can return as medical emergencies.
That is what makes routine healthcare part of the humanitarian response to war — not a secondary concern that can simply be postponed until the fighting stops.
According to the World Health Organisation, only 19 of Gaza’s 36 hospitals were functioning in September 2026, even partially, and none was operating at full capacity. Severe shortages of essential medicines, diagnostic tools, medical equipment and fuel persisted.
The care that disappeared
Nearly three years into the war, the problem may be more than just patients losing access to hospitals.
They have also lost the daily rhythm that once separated chronic illness from medical crisis: the scheduled blood test, the doctor’s appointment, the blood-pressure reading, the dialysis session, the prescription refill, the scan that reassured a patient that what was happening inside their body was still being watched.
When these seemingly small details disappear, chronic diseases do not.
They accumulate quietly, until some eventually emerge as emergencies that may be far more difficult to treat.
In Gaza, many patients are no longer waiting to be cured of their illnesses. They are simply waiting for their bodies to keep holding on.
Images of war tend to show injuries, explosions and destroyed hospitals. But another war is unfolding inside bodies we cannot see: people whose blood sugar rises without their knowing it, hearts functioning without medical monitoring, kidneys waiting for the next dialysis session, children waiting for medication that will prevent another seizure, and cancer patients waiting for a test that might finally tell them what is happening inside their bodies.
These illnesses may not appear in photographs of war. But every day, their patients continue to pay its price.
Dr Haya Hijazi is a gynaecologist and obstetrician from Gaza

Burnham v Swinney: will the UK PM overshadow the SNP’s conference?

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15

15:00:23 KST

This year, even Andy Burnham is invited to the Scottish National party conference. But by the time John Swinney stands up to address members on Saturday afternoon in Aberdeen to reinvigorate the case for a second independence referendum, his party may regret giving the UK prime minister so much prominence in the conference buildup.
Burnham is expected to visit Scotland on Friday – the middle of the event – in a thinly veiled attempt to overshadow the SNP gathering. While he will be in a different venue, the former Manchester mayor’s presence in Scotland will loom large over the event. Since taking over at No 10 in July, Burnham has largely avoided direct confrontations with his political rivals, rarely attacking Nigel Farage or Kemi Badenoch. But he has taken a different approach with the Scottish first minister.
The SNP leader was the only politician from a rival party, apart from Margaret Thatcher, that Burnham mentioned in his keynote address to the Labour party conference last month. He reflected on Swinney’s prediction that he would be the last prime minister of the UK at a meeting of separatist parties Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland to mark the first time all three devolved parliaments were governed by nationalists. Swinney inadvertently did so on the day Burnham’s father died.
“I quote that not to seek sympathy,” Burnham said, holding back tears. “Nor to criticise John Swinney. I relay it because I want you to know how it made me feel. Utterly determined to prove him wrong.”
Beyond ruling out a second independence referendum, recent British prime ministers have often paid little attention to Scottish internal affairs. Burnham has already said there is “no clear consensus” for another vote. But unlike his predecessors, he has decided to take on the SNP by loudly make the case for the union on Scottish soil.
Burnham presents a new challenge for the SNP as they seek to re-energise the case for Scottish independence. Swinney has said he wants a new vote before 2031. The separatists have grown used to facing off against rightwing, pro-Brexit governments in London during two decades in power in Holyrood, making it easier to argue that Scotland’s interests have been dismissed. Burnham’s devolution agenda, openness to exploring a return to the European Union and £2 bus fares are harder to confront.
Even among SNP voters, he is popular. Polling by PF Global found that 46% of Scots have a favourable view of Burnham, far higher than the Labour party itself, and double Keir Starmer’s when he left power. Only Swinney is more popular than the prime minister among SNP voters who supported yes in 2014, reaching a level not seen for a Labour leader since Jeremy Corbyn. Despite this, SNP figures have sought to capitalise on Burnham’s stance on the EU in their quest for a second independence vote.
“We are in a situation where Andy Burnham is actively and unilaterally opening up the conversation about whether we are able to go back to results of referendums and relitigate those decisions while saying that that same democratic principle does not apply to the people of Scotland,” said Lara Bird, the MP for Arbroath and Broughty Ferry. “The idea that the union can continue to exist in its current form is absolutely farcical.”
In Aberdeen, the SNP is hoping to draw a line under a bruising few years after Nicola Sturgeon’s resignation and the subsequent fraud conviction of her estranged husband and former SNP chair Peter Murrell, who is serving a five-year prison sentence for embezzling £400,000 from the party. A proceeds of crime case against Murrell is scheduled for early December.
In May, the SNP won a fifth successive election, but only enough to form a minority government in Holyrood. Despite the victory, Sturgeon criticised a “lack of vision or big picture thinking” in the campaign in the opening to her memoir. Swinney has said they were still good friends. Some SNP figures wonder how much they owe to the unpopularity of Starmer. The party also faces challenges on multiple fronts: Reform has as many MSPs as Labour in Holyrood with 17, while the Scottish Greens won a record 15 seats. The Tories have showed that they can still win seats, defeating the SNP in Aberdeen South in June.
Despite the potential for a standoff between Swinney and Burnham, there is growing appetite in Scotland for collaboration between Westminster and Holyrood. Since the May elections, there has been a sharp rise in Scots who support a closer working relationship between the UK and Scottish governments. Polling by Ipsos has found that 42% of Scots would feel happy about the SNP-led Scottish government working with London, up 12 points since Starmer was in charge in May. Just over half of Scots believe that the country is going in the wrong direction, up six points in the same time period.
This conference, the SNP has invited speakers from other separatist and pro-independence parties. Sioned Williams, deputy first minister of Wales, will give a fraternal address on Friday. Gillian Mackay, a Scottish Green party MSP, will speak at a panel about the right pathway to independence on Saturday.
“We understand, and members of the SNP know, that this is bigger than the SNP. Obviously, I fundamentally believe that the SNP will be the party who secures independence for Scotland. But that runs so much deeper throughout the Scottish population than just those who vote for the SNP. I do think that it is important at this moment to harness and to build on that support as broadly as we can,” said Bird.

AI job losses set to rein in office demand in developed Asia-Pacific economies: report
CBRE says 3.9 per cent of office jobs in developed parts of region are vulnerable to replacement by artificial intelligence
A mild displacement of jobs across the Asia-Pacific region as companies expand their use of AI would trim five percentage points off growth in office space demand in the next few years, according to property consultancy CBRE.
In a report released on Thursday it said 3.9 per cent of office jobs were vulnerable to artificial intelligence-driven displacement in developed markets in the region, including Hong Kong, Singapore, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Australia and New Zealand.
However, only 1.7 per cent were similarly vulnerable in developing markets, including mainland China, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam.
CBRE’s head of Asia-Pacific research, Ada Choi, said in an interview that occupied office space was still projected to grow under a moderate-displacement scenario, “but at a slower pace of 13 per cent” by 2030 – 5 percentage points less than under the consultancy’s base case, which assumed firms in the region would incorporate AI-related productivity gains without job displacement.

A 68-year-old woman died on Wednesday from injuries sustained during last week's 7.7-magnitude earthquake in Panama, officials said, marking the first death recorded in the natural disaster.
Thousands have been left homeless following Friday's temblor, which injured around 30 people and caused severe damage to buildings, bridges and roads, blocking access routes in the country's central region.
The victim, identified as Elena Barria, "was seriously injured during the earthquake," according to a statement from Panama's social security officials.
Local media reported she was a resident of Macaracas in the hard-hit central province of Los Santos.
‘Major disaster’

The tremor lasted about a minute and was felt across the country. In Panama City, about 200 kilometres from the epicentre, people rushed to evacuate skyscrapers as buildings shook.
President Jose Raul Mulino called the quake a "major disaster" and travelled to Penonome to coordinate the response. Health Minister Fernando Boyd said Herrera, Cocle and Los Santos were among the hardest-hit provinces, with the town of Tonosi cut off by damaged roads.
Panama City's international airport was temporarily closed, and several flights were diverted. A tsunami warning for the eastern Pacific was later lifted, while the Panama Canal Authority said shipping through the waterway continued normally.
More than 400 aftershocks have been reported since the initial quake. Earthquakes are relatively rare in Panama and more commonly occur in the western province of Chiriqui, which borders Costa Rica.
