Manosphere experts warn if we lecture boys 'we lose them'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:54:54 UTC
14:54:54 KST

What is the manosphere? How can you help someone drawn in? Your questions answered
If you're worried about the pull of the manosphere, but don't know how to help someone in your life who has been drawn in, you're not alone.
We asked a panel of experts to answer your common questions about the manosphere, masculinity and how to approach conversations about it.
Read what developmental paediatrician Dr Billy Garvey, psychologist Dr Zac Seidler from Movember and Genevieve Sheppard from Our Watch had to say below.
If you or someone you know needs help, you can click here to find a full list of resources at the end of this article.
What is the manosphere?
There's no single definition of the manosphere, but generally, it's the term used to describe online communities that promote narrow definitions of masculinity that oppose feminism and the gains of the gender-equality movement.
As UN Women describes, "these communities promote the idea that emotional control, material wealth, physical appearance and dominance, especially over women, are markers of male worth".
The ideas in the manosphere are nothing new. Misogyny has been prevalent for a very long time. What’s different today is the reach and business model. Online platforms connect these groups, algorithms amplify their messages, and influencers can profit from attention and outrage.
A recurring tactic of those who promote messages on the manosphere is to take real difficulties — loneliness, financial insecurity or uncertainty about relationships — and blame women and feminism.
That offers a simple, yet inaccurate explanation, which also reinforces male entitlement and resentment. This is a harmful message for all young people to believe and absorb.
To counter this, we need to address the challenges boys and men face while challenging the idea that women owe them sex, attention or obedience. That means well-resourced respectful relationships education in every school across Australia, supportive communities and opportunities to build belonging and connection without dominance.
What are the signs someone is in the manosphere and how can I help?
Watching out for this stuff early and discussing it in an open and curious way is the best solution to staying connected with someone skirting around the edges of this content, as it pulls you in very quickly if you are in a certain headspace.
Some things to look out for:
New language: Terms like "alpha", "high value", "red pill", "simp" or "the matrix", or talking about women in transactional or contemptuous ways.
One-source thinking: Constantly quoting the same few influencers, and treating them as the only people telling "the truth".
Rising grievance: A growing sense that the world is rigged against men, or that women, feminism or "the system" are to blame for how they feel.
Pulling back: Withdrawing from friends or family who disagree, or becoming dismissive and defensive when challenged (this can also be a sign of broader mental health challenges or a change in character).
Rigid self-improvement: Gym, money and discipline aren't bad things. It's a flag when they come with shame, contempt for "weak" men, or the idea that your worth depends on dominance.
Some recommendations for what to do:
Stay close! Your relationship is the best antidote, but it's key to avoid shocking or shaming them.
Get curious, not combative. What does he like about this guy? What does that video tell him about what it means to be successful and what it is giving him? Usually there's a real need underneath: loneliness, rejection, feeling lost or unseen.
Don't try to win in one conversation. You won't argue your way to victory. Be consistent and caring.
Offer an alternative. Take him out, show him the world, and help him interact with other people.
How can we challenge misogynistic views without alienating boys?
This can be tough, and I fail at it too. Start with curiosity because correction often leads to conflict. "What makes you feel like that, mate?" If we lecture them, we lose them.
Separate the belief from who they are. "You've got such a big heart mate, you're better than saying those things about girls and women". We hold the line while also keeping our belief in them as good people.
Look for the underlying need. Many boys are lost and unhealthy messages hook them with the promise of confidence, power and success. Once we understand that, we can offer better pathways for them to meet these needs, and help them see those voices are chasing their own money, status and control.
We can also share our own story, the traps we've fallen into, the hurt we've experienced and caused, and most importantly how we repaired and found a better way ourselves.
How can I approach this with my younger kids?
These conversations can be scary but they are already happening for our kids without us there to guide them. Our best chance is to start with low pressure, when our kids feel safe, like during a walk around the block with just us or while playing together with no-one else around.
We know body language, tone of voice and lack of judgement are just as important as what we actually say, if not more. Getting down to their eye level, sitting side by side facing the same direction, and keeping the conversation slow and casual helps. We also want to explore their experiences. "What do you think boys are like? What about girls?" is a gentle way to understand their beliefs without pressure or shame.
We can also go first as a way for them to be safe too. "When I'm scared, sometimes I get angry. It doesn't help much so I try to work on asking others for help instead." It's also important this never feels like a single conversation we need to deliver perfectly. The most important part is that over time our children feel more safe to come to us for support in understanding their world.
Is the manosphere a 'passing wave' or something bigger?
Honestly, I don't think it's either/or yet. It's going to take time to understand how the moment we are in potentially differs from the gender reckonings that have come before, but it would be remiss of me not to say that this is in no way a 'passing wave', given the volume and ferocity of online misogyny fuelled by tech platforms. The underpinning themes have not changed, their reach has.
What I see clinically is that the content itself is a symptom. Our research at Movember has told us that young men aren't drawn in by misogyny. They're drawn in by someone finally speaking to their loneliness, their sense of purpose and their worries about the future. The misogyny comes bundled with that, and therefore can probably be purposefully decoupled.
What are young men searching for in these spaces?
Many young men are lonely, often more than they'd admit, and these spaces offer an instant sense of brotherhood. You're part of something, you share a language and someone's on your side.
Then there's direction. Plenty of boys feel lost about who they're meant to be and where their life is heading. The manosphere gives them a clear script: Here's what a man is, here are the rules, here's the plan. When everything feels uncertain, that clarity is very attractive.
Respect and status matter too. Young men want to feel they count and that people see them as capable. When that isn't happening at school, at work or in relationships, someone promising to make them "high value" is hard to ignore.
Underneath many of these is a need to make sense of pain. Rejection, failure, anxiety and feeling invisible all hurt, and most boys haven't been given the words or the space to talk about that. These spaces give them an explanation and often someone to blame. That can feel better than sitting with the hurt.
None of these needs are the problem. They're completely normal, healthy human needs. The problem is that the manosphere offers a distorted way of meeting them. If we want boys to walk away, we have to offer them real belonging, purpose and respect in their everyday lives.

Romania probes possible drone attack on tanker in its Black Sea territorial waters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:54:29 UTC
14:54:29 KST

The incidents have renewed scrutiny of Europe's ability to protect shipping and critical infrastructure in the Black Sea, more than a year after the EU launched a strategy to strengthen security in the region. Romania's president warns that "there will surely be a reaction."
Romania said seven people were missing after a fire broke out on a vessel flying the San Marino flag on Thursday morning, the latest incident in the Black Sea which has seen an increase in drone attacks both off Romania and Bulgaria's coasts, on NATO's Eastern flank.
The vessel, named the Wine Trader, reported a fire at around 7:00 am (0600 CET), inside Romania's territorial waters, approximately 13 nautical miles southeast of the city of Sulina, the Romanian Naval Authority said in a press release.
"Five of the sailors on board the Wine Trader have been rescued, a further seven people are still missing," the Naval Authority said in an update.
A search and rescue operation was underway, involving a vessel and a helicopter, it said.
Romanian authorities did not say whether a drone caused the fire, but Euronews Romania quoted sources claiming the ship was hit by two drones.
Romania's president Nicusor Dan reacted to the latest attack as he arrived for the EU summit in Brussels saying that "we want to gather all the data about what happened exactly, but there will surely be a reaction."
He said that he had a brief discussion with the Bulgarian prime minister after the latest incident and that together they will meet NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte later on Thursday "to see how we can coordinate better to respond to the increasingly frequent security provocations in the Black Sea."
Dan also said that Romania and Bulgaria may together propose additional conclusions to the European Council summit, which would include increasing security teams in the Black Sea and setting up a civil protection center.
The VesselFinder tracking website identified the ship as a chemical tanker. The Romanian authorities said it was not carrying any cargo.
The incident comes one day after after Romania said it was probing a possible fresh drone attack on a tanker off its Black Sea coast.
Rescuers on Wednesday rushed to help the Comoros Islands-flagged Yara J after a fire broke out, but the ship's crew managed to douse the fire themselves.
"Whether it was struck by a drone or not, an investigation is currently underway," Romanian Defence minister Radu Miruta said.
"This is a matter of significant gravity, given that such incidents are occurring in Romanian territorial waters," he said.
Suspected Russian drones have hit several ships off Romania and neighbouring Bulgaria in a sudden increase of attacks.
At least 163 civilian and commercial vessels were hit on the Black Sea in the first eight months of this year, according to Turkey's IMEAK chamber of shipping.
Black Sea strikes
Meanwhile on Wednesday, Bulgaria said Russia was likely behind drone attacks that struck four ships in the Black Sea in the past week, sinking two, but there was no way of proving Moscow's culpability.
Rescuers are still searching for 11 crew members missing after drone strikes on Tuesday sank two ships in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone and adjacent waters, while five other crew members were rescued.
One of the ships is registered to Guinea-Bissau but the other one, the Chelsea-3, is Ukrainian-owned, registered in Odesa and sails under the flag of Malta, a European Union member.
“There is no logic in Ukraine attacking its own ships and crews, given that the outcome of all these attacks favours Russia and indeed, the logic points in that direction. The problem is that we cannot prove it,” Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told Parliament.
On Tuesday, Radev summoned the Russian ambassador to Sofia, who said she does not have any information from the Russian defence ministry but she did not rule out the possibility that “these attacks represent a provocation by a third party.”
The Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo ship Dignity sank on Tuesday after it was hit by a military strike. Four sailors, three Syrian nationals and one Egyptian, were rescued and arrived in the port of Varna, district Gov. Mario Smarkov said.
“All four appeared to be in relatively good condition and had sustained no injuries,” he said. A fifth sailor is expected to arrive later on Wednesday.
Smarkov said the search for the 11 missing crew members continues.
Bulgaria has requested international assistance for the investigation into attacks on commercial vessels, as well as NATO support to strengthen surveillance and control systems and response capabilities against drone attacks.
Black Sea security
The incidents have renewed scrutiny of Europe's ability to protect shipping and critical infrastructure in the Black Sea, more than a year after the EU launched a strategy to strengthen security in the region.
When the Black Sea Security Strategy was unveiled in May 2025, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned that the region was bearing the spillover effects of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"The Black Sea region is the prime target for hybrid actions. The European Union aims to boost cooperation to combat cyberattacks, disinformation, and other hostile actions," the EU High Representative said, adding that “recurring airspace violations and attacks on ports and shipping lanes highlight this reality."
The policy was aimed at ensuring the security of this maritime corridor, as well as protecting critical infrastructure and assets, such as offshore installations and subsea cables.
It also promised the development of a Black Sea Maritime Security Hub aimed at coordinating support and boosting coast-guard cooperation, among other activities.
The hub would also analyse seabed sensor data and alert allies to potential dangers and incoming threats.

Türkiye, Italy seek to expand archaeological cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:49:23 UTC
14:49:23 KST

The Göbeklitepe show at Rome’s Colosseum draws 6 million visitors.
Türkiye and Italy are seeking to expand archaeological cooperation through joint excavations, conservation projects and exhibitions, Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said on Oct. 14 at the opening of the 17th Symposium of Italian Archaeological Missions in the ancient city of Hierapolis in Denizli.
Noting that Italian excavations at Hierapolis began 70 years ago, Ersoy said scientists from Pamukkale University were also contributing to the work under the Culture and Tourism Ministry’s Legacy to the Future Project.
Archaeology today extends beyond uncovering ancient structures to include conservation, restoration, visitor management, museum work and scientific research, Ersoy said, stressing the importance of preserving archaeological sites for future generations.
Türkiye has expanded archaeological research in recent years while strengthening cooperation between Turkish and foreign research teams, he said. Italian scientists are working at sites including Aslantepe, Hierapolis, Uşaklı Höyük, Karkamış Höyük and Yumuktepe, with Turkish academics participating in the excavations.
Denizli is also home to ongoing research at ancient sites including Laodicea, Hierapolis, Tripolis, Kolossai and Attouda. Conservation and visitor-management projects are being carried out alongside excavations, Ersoy said.
Ersoy highlighted cultural initiatives between the two countries, including the exhibition “Göbeklitepe: The Mystery of a Sacred Place” at Rome’s Colosseum, which attracted approximately six million visitors.
A subsequent exhibition, “Troy and Rome: Myths, Legends and Stories of the Ancient Mediterranean,” features 221 artifacts from Turkish museums and explores the historical and mythological connections between the two civilizations.
Plans are also underway to develop scientific and cultural cooperation between the ancient city of Ephesus and the Pompeii Archaeological Park. A joint project at the ancient city of Elaiussa Sebaste in Mersin, in cooperation with Italy’s Central Institute for Archaeology, is targeted for launch in 2027.
Turkish and Italian specialists are also collaborating on cultural heritage conservation in Cappadocia, particularly the preservation of wall paintings.
Ersoy said the return of cultural artifacts seized in Italy demonstrated the countries’ cooperation in combating illicit trafficking.
A concert featuring Italian violinist Riccardo Zamuner and the İzmir State Symphony Orchestra, scheduled to take place at Hierapolis’ ancient theater following the ceremony, was canceled due to rain.

US weighs using 'Mother of All Bombs' in potential strikes on Iran: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:48:45 UTC
14:48:45 KST

The US military has developed new strike plans that include the potential use of the “Mother of All Bombs” against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders a resumption of combat operations, CNN reported on Wednesday, citing multiple US officials familiar with the plans.
The proposed use of the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB) bomb, the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal, would mark a significant escalation in the conflict with Iran.
However, officials have questioned whether the weapon could achieve Washington’s military objectives.
According to CNN, Trump has directed the military to prepare additional strike options against Iranian targets, including energy infrastructure and facilities linked to the country’s nuclear programme.
The plans could be activated before or after the upcoming US midterm elections if the president decides to resume major combat operations.
One source familiar with the planning told CNN that strikes could take place before US forces withdraw from the US Central Command area of responsibility, potentially allowing the administration to launch further attacks before declaring victory and pulling out its forces.
A second source said plans targeting Iranian nuclear sites explicitly included the possible deployment of the MOAB, including against a suspected underground facility at Pickaxe Mountain.
Trump has repeatedly threatened to target Pickaxe Mountain in the Isfahan province, where Washington and Israel believe Iran has stored components of its nuclear programme.
The president has maintained that preventing Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon remains a central objective of the US campaign.
Doubts over effectiveness
A US official told CNN that military planners routinely prepare a range of options for policymakers, from lower-intensity operations to more powerful strikes against heavily fortified targets.
However, the MOAB's effectiveness against deeply buried nuclear facilities remains uncertain.
The GPS-guided bomb can devastate a surface area equivalent to about nine city blocks, but it is not designed to penetrate deep underground.
Sources cited by CNN said it would likely struggle to destroy facilities protected by thick layers of granite and other fortifications.
“The MOAB is a massive information operation type weapon that is great for huge area clearance but not much else,” a source familiar with the planning discussions told CNN, describing it as unsuitable for deep penetration.
If deployed, the bomb could cause extensive destruction at the point of impact. Its large blast radius could also raise serious concerns about civilian casualties, particularly if energy infrastructure near populated areas or other civilian facilities were targeted.
The MOAB was previously used only once in combat, in 2017, against a Daesh terror group hideout in a cave complex in Afghanistan’s Nangarhar province.
Psychological pressure
Despite its limitations, US officials have reportedly considered the weapon’s potential psychological impact as part of the administration’s broader military options.
One source told CNN that Trump could face pressure to take further action against Iran despite uncertainty over whether additional strikes would force Tehran to accept Washington’s demands.
The source suggested the MOAB could be used to exert psychological pressure, particularly given the limitations of available munitions against deeply buried targets.

New artifacts unearthed at Ordu’s ancient Kurul Castle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:48:44 UTC
14:48:44 KST

Finds include a statue of Cybele, a figure of the child Dionysus and a representation of Pan, along with animal-shaped composite vessels. (AA Photo)
Archaeological excavations at Ordu’s Kurul Castle, which began in 2010, are continuing to uncover new artifacts at the ancient site.
According to a statement from Ordu Municipality, the 2,300-year-old Kurul Castle, located in the Bayadı neighborhood of the Altınordu district, stands out as the first scientific archaeological excavation site in the Eastern Black Sea region.
The excavations are being conducted under the leadership of Professor Süleyman Yücel Şenyurt, a faculty member in the Department of Archaeology at Ankara Hacı Bayram Veli University, with support from Ordu Metropolitan Municipality.
Finds unearthed at the site to date include a statue of Cybele estimated to be 2,150 years old, a figure of the child Dionysus, a representation of Pan, who raised him, and animal-shaped composite vessels associated with the cult of Dionysus and Pan.
Ordu Metropolitan Municipality Mayor Mehmet Hilmi Güler visited the ongoing excavation site and received information about the work from Şenyurt.
Güler said the site was an archaeological and historical treasure where discoveries were shedding light on the past.
Describing Kurul Castle as a source of cultural and historical wealth, Güler said approximately 40 percent of the excavation work had been completed and that academics were working intensively at the site.
“We have made important discoveries here dating to the period associated with Dionysus. These artifacts will both shed light on the past and add significant value to this region,” Güler said.
He added that the finds indicated that Kurul Castle was not merely a fortress but also a settlement.
Important discoveries
Şenyurt said the team had uncovered significant finds in the region, particularly the statue of Cybele.
Noting that Kurul Castle had attracted attention with discoveries that surprised the scientific community, he said the latest finds would introduce two divine figures from Anatolia to the scientific and cultural worlds in connection with the cult of Dionysus.
“With this year’s finds, we will introduce two god and goddess figures from Anatolia to the scientific community and the cultural world, alongside the cult of Dionysus,” Şenyurt said.
He thanked the relevant ministry and Ordu Metropolitan Municipality for their support, adding that the discoveries at Kurul Castle could serve as a model for future archaeological research.
Şenyurt noted that the Eastern Black Sea region contained cultural heritage sites hidden beneath dense vegetation.
“Kurul Castle has had the opportunity to make these discoveries, but it has also set an example for us. There is cultural heritage hidden beneath the vegetation in the Eastern Black Sea region. Kurul Castle has ignited the spark for future work,” he said.

Istanbul union’s call to pause bonito fishing sparks public backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:48:33 UTC
14:48:33 KST

AA Photo
An Istanbul fisheries union has sparked consumer outrage after calling for a fishing pause when a surge in bonito catches drove prices down, leading to accusations of price gouging.
The Istanbul Provincial Union of Seafood Fishers and Producers (Istanbul DEMBİR) set the requested pause from midnight until 8 a.m. on Oct. 12, saying a short break would help fishers earn a fair return without amounting to a ban.
Some social media users called the appeal opportunistic and urged authorities to investigate. One wrote fishers resented earning from one bonito what they had previously made from two.
Central Union of Seafood Fishers and Producers (DEM-BİR) Deputy Board Chairman Mehmet Aksoy opposed a ban, citing rising personnel wages and fuel costs. “Conditions have become harder. When we catch too much, fish sells cheaply. We do everything we can to provide people with affordable fish. No boat should catch 3,000 to 5,000 crates a day,” he said.
Aksoy said bonito is a migratory fish and could move to Georgia and return, making it harder to catch in November. He urged fishers to limit catches, saying excess fish loses value and can be crushed and spoil aboard boats. He said the goal was to balance supply with demand, not make consumers pay more.
The Istanbul DEMBİR notice said lower prices led fishers to catch more to offset losses, adding to supply and driving prices down further. It called the cycle economically unsustainable.
Türkiye’s commercial fishing season reopened on Sept. 1 after an annual ban from April 15 to Sept. 1 to protect fish stocks during spawning. Fishermen along Türkiye’s Black Sea coast had forecast an abundant bonito harvest, expecting larger catches to lower prices for consumers.

3D models recreate 7.7-million-year-old fauna
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:48:23 UTC
14:48:23 KST

DHA Photo
Anthropologists in Türkiye’s central province of Kayseri are creating 3D miniatures of 10 animals whose fossils date back 7.5 to 7.7 million years, giving visitors a glimpse of the region’s prehistoric fauna.
The figures, made from polymer clay and based on fossils found near Yamula Dam, include four elephant models, two rhinoceroses, a giraffe, a three-toed horse, a bovid similar to a modern antelope and a saber-toothed tiger. The miniatures will be displayed at Kayseri Science Center.
“We created this display to satisfy visitors’ curiosity and show what 10 different creatures from that period looked like, both morphologically and physically,” Expert Anthropologist Ömer Dağ said.
The team sculpted the figures in clay, scanned them in 3D and reproduced them with resin printers.
Kayseri Metropolitan Municipality supplied a resin printer and the models will be painted before being placed in a miniature habitat exhibit.
Rising water levels at the dam delayed fieldwork in 2026, so the team split in two, with one group continuing excavations and the other working in the laboratory. The display will show two of the elephant models in a forest setting and two in open terrain, allowing visitors to compare their physical differences.
Shepherd Murat Adıyaman found a bone fragment near the dam in the Taşhan area of Kocasinan district in 2017. Initial tests dated the fragments to between 6 million and 7.5 million years ago. The Culture and Tourism Ministry’s General Directorate of Cultural Heritage and Museums authorized excavations in 2018.

Divers reported seeing ancient amphoras preserving their original glory on the seabed.
Documentary producer Tahsin Ceylan filmed the artifacts alongside Bodrum Coast Guard dive teams, specialist instructor Ahmet Yaşar and underwater photographer Mehtap Akbaş Çiftci. A recently sunken Lebanese cargo ship resting at a depth of 20 meters covers a Rhodes wreck dating to the second century, offering a rich marine ecosystem and a visual feast.
Underwater Archaeologist Aşkın Canbazoğlu said he worked at the site between 1981 and 1983 for the Culture Ministry.
“We have always tried to open the area to tourism because it is one of the most important places in the archaeology world,” he said.
Crews excavated a Roman wreck from 1961 to 1964, while operations resumed in 1974, leading to the recovery of an Ottoman vessel in the 1980s. Experts completed excavations on three ships in total, with the site now needing international promotion. The Yassıada shallows gained international fame in the 1960s when scientists pioneered modern underwater excavation techniques on its ancient shipwrecks.

Fund repayment bill clears parliamentary committee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:42:01 UTC
14:42:01 KST

Parliament’s Plan and Budget Committee approved a bill on Oct. 14 that would allow interim payments of up to 1 million Turkish Liras to eligible investors in funds under liquidation.
The nine-article proposal concerns unfinished liquidations among 131 funds ordered wound up by the Capital Markets Board (SPK). It still requires approval by parliament’s general assembly.
AK Party lawmaker Ersan Aksu, one of the bill’s sponsors, said around 350,000 investors were expected to recover their net investment through interim payments while retaining their rights to a final settlement.
Interim payments would be calculated from investors’ actual cash deposits and withdrawals, without inflation adjustment, and deducted from the final amount payable.
If available cash is insufficient, the SPK could prioritize investors with the smallest net investments or set a minimum interim payment for all eligible investors.
Where fund assets fall short, final entitlement calculations would include inflation adjustments through the liquidation date, based on the average change in consumer and domestic producer price indices.
Aksu said payments would come from fund assets and money recovered from those responsible for losses, with no public funds used.
Committee amendments clarified how eligible investors would be identified and revised calculations for the voluntary return of gains above an inflation-adjusted benchmark.
Some repayments have already been made. The Communications Directorate said on Oct. 13 that 43,643 investors in funds managed by A1, Bulls and Pardus received 6.4 billion liras the previous week.
Separately, Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek authorized an investigation into former SPK chairman İbrahim Ömer Gönül following a preliminary ministry review.
Istanbul prosecutors had sought permission on Sept. 30 to investigate alleged abuse of office in connection with the fund inquiry. Gönül gave a statement as a suspect that day.

New Zealand regulators unveil supervisory expectations on AI-related cyber risks
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:37:19 CST
14:37:19 KST

WELLINGTON, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's central bank and financial markets regulator on Thursday outlined supervisory expectations for financial institutions to manage cyber risks associated with frontier artificial intelligence (AI).
The Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) and the Financial Markets Authority (FMA) said their expectations focus on three key risks, namely increased cyber threats, evolving governance and oversight challenges, and growing third-party and concentration risks, according to an RBNZ statement.
The expectations build on existing prudential, conduct, cyber and operational resilience obligations, aiming to support resilience of regulated entities and the broader financial system, RBNZ Assistant Governor for Financial Stability Angus McGregor said at an industry roundtable.
Regulators expect financial institutions to maintain cybersecurity strategies and frameworks that adequately address the threats they face, as well as strong foundational cyber controls and security measures, McGregor said.
FMA Executive Director of Response and Enforcement Louise Unger said advances in AI are changing the cyber threat environment, highlighting the importance of strong governance, effective oversight, operational resilience and the management of third-party dependencies as entities adapt to emerging risks.
While AI can bring benefits to financial institutions and their customers, it also changes the risks they face, Unger said, adding that boards and senior management need to understand where AI is being used, the risks involved and who is accountable for managing them.
The regulators will continue engaging with regulated entities to ensure AI-related risks are managed appropriately, McGregor said. ■

S. Korea's money supply rises for 10th month in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:37:04 CST
14:37:04 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's money supply rose for the 10th straight month, driven by the fund influx into short-term fixed-income products, especially from semiconductor companies and households, central bank data showed Thursday.
The seasonally adjusted M2, called broad money, grew 0.9 percent from a month earlier to 4,266.8 trillion won (about 3.16 trillion U.S. dollars) in August, keeping an upward trajectory since November 2025, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
The BOK delivered its back-to-back rate hikes in July and August to 3 percent, prompting an inflow of funds into short-term fixed-income products such as time deposits, money trusts, and money market funds.
Affected by the monetary tightening, the M1, called narrow money, fell 1.1 percent in August on a monthly basis.
The M1 refers to currency in circulation, demand deposits and transferable savings deposits equivalent to cash. The M2 adds money market funds, time deposits and financial products that mature in less than two years.
The liquidity of financial institutions, called Lf, increased 0.6 percent in the cited month, while the liquidity aggregate, the broadest measure of money supply, gained 0.2 percent.
The Lf includes financial products with a maturity of over two years and liquidity at insurers and brokerages along with M2. The liquidity aggregate adds state and corporate bonds to the Lf. ■

A little bipartisan bromance as Schwarzenegger, Newsom laud California's climate-change wins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:32:33 UTC
14:32:33 KST

A little bipartisan bromance as Schwarzenegger, Newsom laud California’s climate-change wins
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger and Gov. Gavin Newsom marked 20 years of California’s landmark climate law, celebrating a rare show of bipartisan unity amid deepening political polarization.
- The 2006 law helped cut greenhouse gas emissions to 1990 levels and fueled clean-energy growth, but California is falling behind its next targets.
- Schwarzenegger said the state’s climate policies show what cooperation can accomplish; California’s cap-and-invest program, extended through 2045, is now moving toward a link with Washington state’s market.
Former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, celebrated the 20-year anniversary of landmark climate legislation he signed while in office alongside Democrats including Gov. Gavin Newsom on Wednesday.
“California is the perfect example of what can be done when people work together and when we don’t look at this as a Republican or as a Democratic issue,” Schwarzenegger said at an economic conference in Long Beach, noting that Assembly Bill 32, the Global Warming Solutions Act, had significantly reduced greenhouse gas emissions while creating more than half a million clean-energy jobs.
“This is the message that is so important for the world,” he said, because the state’s policies have become a model for other states and nations.
Newsom noted that the state had met “audacious” goals for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, touting 39,000 megawatts of clean energy that have been installed in the last seven years, 23,000 megawatts of battery storage created, and that no flex alert has been issued in the state in four years.
“So we’re not in the goal-setting business; we’re in the how business,” he said.
He added that the clean energy transition is “the most critical national security issue in the United States of America,” with economic and supply chain leadership at stake as China surpasses the U.S. in electric vehicles, clean-energy manufacturing and the deployment of renewables.
The state already met the climate change legislation’s ambitious target — returning emissions to 1990 levels by 2020 — four years ahead of schedule. However, recent analyses indicate California is not on track to meet its future targets of cutting emissions 40% by 2030 and 85% by 2045.
The legislation paved the way for the creation of California’s nation-leading carbon market, cap-and-invest, which launched in 2013. The Legislature extended cap-and-invest’s life to 2045 last year, and the state is now initiating the process of linking its market with Washington state.
The event as well as a luncheon the prior day in Santa Monica were rare displays of bipartisan unity at a time of heightened political polarization in the United States. Schwarzenegger and Newsom piled praise upon each other during the Wednesday afternoon discussion, hugging at the end.
At the luncheon, former Gov. Gray Davis, whom Schwarzenegger ousted from office in the 2003 recall election, as well as billionaire hedge-fund founder turned environmental warrior Tom Steyer, who unsuccessfully ran for governor this year, were among the Democrats in attendance, as well as former state Assembly Speaker Fabian Nunez and former state Sen. Fran Pavley, who were both pivotal in the passage of the climate-change legislation.
In addition to remarks highlighting the foundation of some of the nation’s bedrock environmental policies, such as former Republican President Nixon creating the Environmental Protection Agency and signing the Endangered Species Act, there were moments of levity.
Schwarzenegger said he told fellow Republicans “f— you” when they balked at him naming Susan Kennedy, a Democrat, as his chief of staff, he said.
During a breakout session at the Wednesday conference, he referenced his former wife, Maria Shriver, a scion of the Kennedy family, as he described his desire to hear from people on both sides of the aisle.
“So I had Democrats in my administration, and of course the Republican Party went nuts,” he said. “I didn’t care because, to me, I thought I wanted to hear what the Democrats were thinking. Plus, I was sleeping with one every night anyway.”

Istanbul floods leave two dead, force school closures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:30:52 UTC
14:30:52 KST

Flash floods triggered by torrential rainfall continued to disrupt daily life in Istanbul on Oct. 15, forcing authorities to suspend classes for a second consecutive day as the city grappled with one of its heaviest downpours on record, which has left four people dead.
The downpour that began on Oct. 14 night flooded homes and businesses, inundated roads and underpasses, stranded vehicles and brought traffic to a standstill across Türkiye’s largest city.
Earlier deaths reported by local media included a 14-year-old who was electrocuted after stepping into a puddle at a park in the Fatih district, and a 34-year-old who slipped on a sidewalk in Sarıyer and struck their head.
Search efforts throughout the day uncovered another body along a stream in Istanbul’s Kağıthane district, bringing the death toll to three.
Police have launched an investigation into the death of the man, who was reportedly in his 40s.
Construction worker Faik Şentürk later died after falling into a well while draining floodwater at a school construction site in Beykoz, bringing the toll to four. Seven people remained in hospital.
Istanbul Governor Davut Gül announced that schools would remain closed on Oct. 16, following the suspension of classes on Oct. 15. He said the decision was made in anticipation of rainfall continuing for another two to three days.
Gül said Istanbul experienced its heaviest rainfall in 84 years.
Meanwhile, the Istanbul Municipality said rainfall levels reached one of the highest readings recorded since 1985.
Precipitation reached 272 kilograms per square meter in some parts of the city.
More than 1,000 flooding incidents were reported across Istanbul, leaving numerous vehicles partially or completely submerged.
Authorities urged residents to remain at home unless travel was absolutely necessary and advised people living in basement apartments to spend the night elsewhere.
Some public employees were also expected to be placed on leave, while motorcycles were banned from traffic.
Rescue operations continued throughout the city. Workers stranded overnight at a concrete plant in Sarıyer were evacuated with the help of a front-end loader after floodwaters cut off their escape routes.
One of the rescued workers, Ömer Artık, told reporters that around 30 people were still waiting to be evacuated from the facility.
“We have been stranded here for 14 hours. The loader brought us here, and we have only just been rescued,” he said, adding that the workers had also helped employees from nearby factories by taking them into their dormitories.
“The workplace was flooded, with water 2 to 3 meters deep, higher than our heads. The stream had also overflowed, so we could no longer get outside,” Artık said.
The heavy rainfall also caused the Kağıthane stream to overflow. Municipal teams rescued stray animals trapped in the courtyard of Arnavutköy Boğazköy Primary School, while construction machinery was deployed to evacuate people stranded by floodwaters near Merter metro station.
Meanwhile, 46 aircraft were unable to land at Istanbul’s airports amid the adverse weather conditions.
The torrential downpour, which began on the night of Oct. 14, is expected to continue through Oct. 17.
The impact of the flooding was also visible along the Bosphorus on Oct. 15 morning, as runoff from swollen streams flowed into the strait, turning sections of the coastal waters brown.
In some areas, the discoloration extended roughly 200 meters from the shoreline.
Following the extreme rainfall, meteorologist Professor Dr. Mikdat Kadıoğlu warned that even lower levels of precipitation forecast for Oct. 16 could trigger further serious flooding, as the saturated ground would have little capacity to absorb additional water.

EU summit: Leaders seek fast solutions to spiralling energy prices

EU leaders are meeting in Brussels for a packed two-day summit. Energy prices, trade with China and the budget dominated Thursday's session.
Following today's inconclusive summit, António Costa, the president of the European Council, has taken charge of the EU budget negotiations.
Costa intends to reflect on the feedback provided by member states, which are still attached to their red lines and maximalist positions, and propose a new compromise text in the coming weeks.

Leaders push to protect chemicals and machinery from Chinese competition
EU leaders on Thursday pushed for import quotas to protect the chemical and industrial machinery sectors from Chinese competition, Euronews has learned.
The issue was discussed at the summit lunch with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen as they addressed the bloc’s record-high trade deficit with Beijing - and potential measures counter the wave of low-cost imports.
An EU diplomat confirmed to Euronews that the 27 member states were pushing the Commission to protect both sectors, which are among the hardest hit by Chinese competition.

The deal was presented as the first phase of negotiations launched last June, but time is running out as the trade deficit with China continues to widen month after month. Chinese exports to the EU have surged by 25% over the past year, according to the latest Chinese customs data.
Analysis: Hopes dim for a budget deal in December
For months, European Council President António Costa has repeated time and time again, that leaders need to unanimously agree on the next seven-year budget by December at the very latest. If the negotiations spill over into next year, he warns, there won't be enough time to complete the complex legislative work that's necessary to get the budget up and running by 1 January 2028.
But leaders say they prefer to put quality over time. What matters for them is a good deal. The problem is that each one has their own vision of what a "good deal" looks like in reality.
The battle is split into two main camps: the frugals, who want steep cuts, versus the Friends of Cohesion, who oppose them.
However, these camps aren't uniform. Some of the cohesion friends, like Spain and Italy, have a vested interest in agricultural funds. Others, like the Baltics, are keen to boost defence spending. Among the frugals, Germany and Sweden are seen as the most radical. Meanwhile, France, the bloc's second-largest country, hasn't picked a side because it's trapped between its European ambitions and its borrowing constraints.
The red lines are so entrenched, and the space to compromise is so scarce, that Costa's December goal now looks increasingly precarious.
Credit: European Union.
EU leaders discuss new Europe-wide taxes to finance the bloc's budget
EU leaders have moved on to discuss the bloc’s next long-term budget, including several proposals to create new own resources, fresh taxes at the European level that would directly contribute to Brussels’ coffers.
Ireland’s latest compromise maintained the own resources proposed by the European Commission, in particular:
- Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM): a tariff on carbon-intensive imports. The tax is meant to create a level playing field with other countries and has received broad support from the member states, but faces opposition from the US. Ireland proposed increasing the call rate from 75% to 90%.
- Emissions Trading System (ETS): a tax on companies based on their greenhouse gas emissions, encouraging them to cut pollution most cost-effectively. Many member states have opposed moving the ETS at the EU level because it generates significant revenues for them. To mitigate this, the Irish have proposed a phase-in mechanism under the Modernisation Fund to compensate for the lost revenues.
- Tobacco Excise Duty Own Resource (TEDOR): a system under which 15% of national tobacco excise duty revenues collected by EU countries are transferred directly to the EU budget. TEDOR faces significant opposition from some member states that fear a lowering of the quality of tobacco products and an increase in the black market.
- Corporate Resource for Europe (CORE): a direct financial contribution levied on large corporations operating in the EU market. The proposal faces very strong opposition from a large majority of European governments that consider it runs counter to the competitiveness agenda.
- Electronic waste levy (e-waste): a financial contribution to the EU budget based on the amount of uncollected electronic equipment generated within a member state. The e-waste levy enjoys broad support among member states, with most of the open questions technical in nature.
- Custom duties: an already present own resources levied on products imported from non-EU countries based on the Common Customs Tariff. The member states currently retain 25%, while the Commission proposed dropping that percentage to 10%, leaving 90% of customs duties for the EU budget.
The Irish presidency has decided not to include the European Parliament’s proposals for EU-wide taxes on digital services, online gambling and crypto-assets. Critics argue that Ireland failed to act as an honest broker in this instance, in particular for the digital levy, since the country hosts the European headquarters of most Big Tech companies.

After delays, Ukraine adopts laws needed to unlock €3.7 billion in EU funding
As EU leaders meet in Brussels, the Ukrainian parliament has adopted a raft of laws needed to unlock the next payment of EU financial aid under the €90 billion loan.
The tranche, worth €3.7 billion, was expected to be released in September but was delayed after a bill designed to remove the duty-free exemption for international parcels was voted down on two separate occasions. The text proved contentious among Ukrainian legislators due to the popularity of Chinese marketplaces Temu and AliExpress.
The legislative backlog ruffled feathers among EU officials, who complained that Kyiv was asking for fast cash but failing to do the required homework. Kyiv got the message and submitted the bill for a third try, which has now succeeded.
"These reforms are essential for fiscal sustainability, reducing the shadow economy, strengthening transparency and moving forward on our European integration path," Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko said after the votes on Thursday. "Despite the war, Ukraine continues to deliver on reforms and fulfil its commitments."
The European Commission is set to confirm the €3.7 billion payment in the coming days.
Costa calls for stepping up negotiations with China
European Council President António Costa has called for the EU to “step up” negotiations with China, without explicitly mentioning the country, as the EU’s trade deficit with Beijing widens.
“We must step up a results-oriented dialogue with our international partners, while enhancing our toolbox of trade instruments,” Costa said on X.
Brussels began talks with Beijing last June in the hope of rebalancing its trade relationship with China. The two sides struck a deal last Friday, but it covers only Chinese hybrid car imports into the EU, worth €15 billion, while the bloc’s trade deficit with Beijing stands at €360 billion.
The EU’s strategy is to continue dialogue as long as it delivers concrete results, while strengthening the bloc’s trade defence instruments. France and Germany urged the Commission last week to develop a new instrument to respond swiftly to market disruptions caused by China, which has been accused of unfair trade practices.
Costa added that “European businesses must be able to compete under fair conditions.”

Visegrad and Italian plan to delay ETS2 likely to hit the wall
A plan by the four Visegrad countries — Slovakia, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Poland — to delay the next Emissions Trading System (ETS2) until 2030 is likely to fail, according to several EU diplomats.
The ETS2 is the new carbon market set to cover fuels used in road transport and buildings as of 2029. The climate tool was already delayed once over concerns about its social impact on the most vulnerable, as ETS2 will inevitably increase energy bills further. The Visegrad countries argue "price differences between the EU regions and EU countries are enormous".
Despite the concerns raised by Visegrad — and backed by Italy — one EU diplomat told Euronews that the proposed amendments "will never get the required unanimity".
"There is little support for it and they know it. That's why they try it at the European Council instead of the Environment Council because there's no majority there for this," another EU diplomat said.
However, even if the talks on energy prices are over, the drafting of the Council conclusions is still ongoing, a third EU diplomat said.
Analysis: Ukraine isn't on the agenda today. But it's on everyone's minds
Believe it or not, Ukraine is not officially on the agenda of the EU summit today. However, the leaders will nonetheless discuss the situation in the war-weary country tomorrow, in the presence of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has just arrived in Brussels.
Today's agenda is devoted mainly to energy, China and the EU budget. But Ukraine feels inescapable. It's on everyone's minds.
As they arrived at the Europa building, leaders didn't mince words as they expressed their frustration and even anger over Donald Trump's unilateral decision to strike a diesel deal with Vladimir Putin – undermining more than five years of Western economic sanctions along the way. Trump's harsh attacks on Zelenskyy, including calls for new elections, have rattled Europeans and brought back painful memories from the notorious White House clash in February 2025.
That episode prompted Brussels to convene an emergency summit to close ranks behind Zelenskyy and display a united front to counter Trump's go-it-alone diplomacy. The same will happen tomorrow.
Leaders discuss new EU trade defence tools
EU leaders meeting in Brussels on Thursday are discussing planned new trade defence tools with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to counter China’s aggressive trade policies, which threaten entire sectors of EU industry.
A senior EU official said the Commission would present a diversification instrument and a solidarity mechanism by the end of the year.
It comes after the EU accused China of weaponising its dependencies by blocking exports of rare earths, which are essential for the EU’s green technology and defence industries, in 2025 amid a trade war with the US.
The first tool aims to encourage EU businesses to diversify suppliers of strategic products whose shortages could threaten supply chains. The second,, the solidarity mechanism, is to help EU countries hit by Chinese retaliation if Beijing adopts countermeasures in response to EU moves to protect its interests.
The EU faces a daily €1 billion trade deficit with Beijing, with Chinese imports having surged by 25% over the past year, according to the latest Chinese customs data.
France and Germany also called last week for a new trade instrument that would allow the Commission to respond systematically and swiftly to market distortions. Measures adopted under the new tool could go as far as cutting off China’s access to the EU market entirely.
Why China isn't called China at EU summits
We just told you that EU leaders have started their debate on China. But if you think you're going to find that word in the conclusions, we'll have to disappoint you: China is almost never mentioned by name.
Instead, leaders use the vague moniker of "macroeconomic imbalances". The term has become a long-running joke in Brussels circles, given that everyone knows where those imbalances come from and who is responsible for them.
The tradition is maintained as diplomatic cover to portray the discussion as strictly country-agnostic – and avoid Beijing's accusations of being singled out. In practice, though, the moniker is irrelevant. Beijing is quick to lash out at any hint of condemnation from Brussels, regardless of euphemistic manoeuvres.
What’s in the trade deal the EU clinched with China?
Brussels struck a deal last Friday to limit Chinese exports of hybrid cars to the EU as it seeks to rebalance its trade relationship with Beijing.
Under the deal, the EU will introduce country-specific quotas allowing 350,000 Chinese hybrid cars onto the European market annually over four years, with a fixed annual adjustment rate of 6%.
The EU faces a record-high €360 billion annual trade deficit with Beijing whose exports threaten entire sectors of EU industry.
Last Friday, Beijing also agreed to ease export licensing requirements for rare earths, which are essential to EU industry, and to remove tariffs on EU car parts, olive oil and footwear, representing nearly €4 billion in current export value.
The deal should generate at least €225 million in tariff savings, the Commission said.

Top MEP warns EU not to sideline Parliament in budget talks
Siegfried Mureșan (Romania/EPP), a key European Parliament representative in the EU budget negotiations, has warned member states that MEP requests need to be considered to secure a majority.
“Our mission is to make sure the main demands of the Parliament are in. If the main demands of the Parliament are not in, we will not be able to secure an absolute majority in the Parliament,” he said.
Mureșan, who is also a leading contender to become Romania’s next prime minister, said that if all the parties currently in government at the national level voted in favour of the budget, it would still only have the support of 270 MEPs, 91 short of a majority.
He warned EU leaders against forcing the Parliament to back a budget against their wishes – like they did with the Mercosur agreement – as it might be rejected.
"Each prime minister wants to pay as little as possible to Europe and benefit as much as possible," he said. "It will be our obligation to see that, in the end, besides the national envelopes of member states, the European priorities are sufficiently funded."
EU leaders discuss strategy to counter China’s trade policies
The 27 EU leaders began discussing a strategy over lunch with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to counter the surge in low-cost imports from China.
Brussels struck a trade deal with Beijing last Friday aimed at curbing Chinese car imports. However, EU diplomats say it will not be enough to reduce the bloc’s €360 billion trade deficit with Beijing.
EU countries, all of which now have a trade deficit with China – including Germany, the EU’s largest member state — want the Commission to prepare a new approach for the next phase of talks.
One question is whether the EU executive — which leads talks with Beijing on behalf of the 27 member states — should seek new sector-specific concessions from China or broader commitments across the board.
Chinese car exports to the EU amount to just €15 billion, a relatively small figure compared with the bloc’s overall trade deficit.
“We need to have the capacity to protect the sectors that are exposed at the same time, so it will require a combination of measures,” an EU diplomat said. “And it is up to the Commission to tell us, sector by sector, in what order this should be done and which instrument is best suited to each sector.”

Metsola warns EU leaders not to take Parliament for granted in budget talks
EU countries should not take the European Parliament for granted in negotiations on the bloc’s next seven-year budget, the assembly's President Roberta Metsola said after addressing EU leaders at the start of the summit.
The debate on the budget, scheduled for the afternoon, is expected to be tense, as EU countries are divided over spending priorities and the size of their contributions.
European Council President António Costa is pushing for a unanimous agreement by the end of the year, a goal with a 50% chance of being achieved, according to a diplomat.
However, the final budget must also be approved by the European Parliament by a simple majority.
Metsola said MEPs “will never rubber-stamp” the Council’s decision, arguing that EU countries should take the Parliament’s position into account when reaching a final compromise.
“First, [an agreement] on the overall number needs to be the starting point before we go into the individual files,” Metsola said.
At the moment, the gap between the Parliament’s and the Council’s positions is substantial. The Parliament is pitching a total of €1,938 billion for the next seven years, while the latest proposal from the Irish presidency of the Council puts the figure at €1,622 billion, 16% less.

What can Commission do to tackle high energy prices?
Ever since the US-led war against Iran began in February, the European Commission has proposed many measures to fight rising energy prices, most of which to encourage EU capitals to cut energy demand and allow emergency energy tax cuts.
As the energy crisis drags on, EU governments are seeking more support – but without incurring massive debts.
Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will outline some options at the European Council to extend temporary state aid support for the heavy-industry sectors struggling with skyrocketing prices.
EU leaders also expect guidance from the Commission on how to revamp the lost capacity of EU refineries, in decline since 2009.
With fears rising over supplies, particularly on diesel and jet fuel, EU countries are assessing with the Commission options to bundle energy demand on a voluntary basis to avoid panic buying and higher prices.
Von der Leyen to brief EU leaders on negotiations with China
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is set to brief EU leaders over lunch on Thursday on negotiations with China, after the EU executive struck a deal last Friday to curb Chinese car exports.
EU member states have welcomed the deal, which follows from the dialogue launched last June to address the EU's record-high €360 billion trade deficit with China.
The agreement, which EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič described as the end of a “first phase” of negotiations, will introduce country-specific quotas allowing 350,000 hybrid cars onto the European market annually over four years, with a fixed annual adjustment rate of 6%.
However, “it’s not the end of the story,” an EU diplomat told Euronews. The Commission will now have to assess the best approach for the next round of negotiations between Brussels and Beijing, scheduled for January and March.
“We cannot take a sequential approach,” another EU diplomat said. “We cannot simply say that every three months we will tackle a sector worth €13 billion, because by the time we achieve a reduction in the deficit, the other sectors will have disappeared.”

EU leaders tackle high energy prices as monthly inflation hits 3.3%
EU leaders have begun their European Council summit with a debate on high fuel prices, as they seek action to tackle an unprecedented energy crunch.
Rising energy prices have combined with inflation hitting 3% in September to prompt several EU capitals to ask the European Commission for more support.
Italy and Greece, backed by other EU countries, recently urged Brussels to allow for extra spending without incurring infringements due to the extraordinary circumstances posed by the energy shock — a tall ask for the Commission, which could find itself confronted with policing ballooning debts from several EU countries.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned on 14 October that diesel markets are expected to remain tight well into 2027 and wholesale diesel prices in Europe could rise again in the coming weeks.
Diesel prices have retreated from September’s records above $200 a barrel, but benchmarks "remain nearly double the price of crude oil and their pre-crisis levels", the IEA stated.
As for natural gas, the Dutch TTF, the EU's benchmark for pricing gas, is trading at around €85.69 to €87.32 per MWh, nearly triple since the war against Iran.

Friends of Cohesion call for ambitious budget, reject rebates
The so-called Friends of Cohesion, the 17 EU countries backing more spending, have jointly called for an EU budget with a bigger capacity to deliver, ahead of expected tense talks at the European Council summit.
“We believe the final agreement should ensure that the EU budget can address existing and emerging priorities while preserving key policies,” the statement reads, referring to plans by the Irish presidency of the EU to cut the seven-year budget by €141bn..
The coalition met at a breakfast organised by Italy and Romania ahead of the summit and pushed against rebates, a discount large net contributors usually receive toward the end of the negotiations to secure their support.
The 17 have defended traditional EU policies like the funding for farmers and the poorest regions, for which “adequate resources must be accompanied by rules that safeguard the specific objectives of these policies and allow member states and regions to make effective use of the available funds.”
They also called for a balanced compromise in terms of revenues, asking that the new EU-wide taxes fairly distribute the financial burden among all member states.

OODA Transforms a Prague City Block into a Permeable Mixed-Use Complex with a Lanscaped Central Plaza

Portuguese architecture and urbanism practice OODA has released new images of an urban design project in Prague, Czech Republic. The design transforms an existing building block into a permeable site with municipal social housing, commercial units, and a landscaped central plaza. The project, titled Kodaňská 1441, prioritizes walkability, green mobility and public space. In addition to opening new connections between the existing building and the urban fabric, it includes a landscape and water management system that increases the permeable surfaces of the courtyard by 21.5%. The project is an example of urban renewal that incorporates contemporary concerns such as communal spaces, a regulated relationship with public space, planted environments, and the sustainable use of natural resources.
A cut volume defines the site footprint. The mass is divided into residential blocks, interrupted by a central void with an organic form. The incisions introduce new urban and visual connections and improve permeability, ventilation and proportion. The volume steps down toward the central void, creating terraces. The inner facade is distinguished from the exterior in geometry and materiality, while the exterior is clad in rose, cream, green, gold and blue terrazzo. Design elements such as loggias, balconies, canopies, flowerpots and shading elements add variety to the architectural language.
The central plaza is an integral part of the block redesign. It is organized into a sequence of plazas, gardens, play areas, seating, and pedestrian walkways. At the center, residents have access to a plaza and a children's playground, reached through a gated route that is open during the day and closed at night. The geometry of the planted areas and landscape design follows a radius principle, with a planting structure composed of 80% structural planting and 20% accent planting. The landscape integrates water collection systems, infiltration gardens, permeable surfaces, and bio-filtration rooftops. A second phase is planned to add more permeable surfaces to strengthen rainwater infiltration and reduce surface runoff.
Related Article
Prague Architecture City Guide: 25 Historical and Contemporary Attractions to Explore in Czechia’s City of a Hundred Spires
In terms of program, commercial units are located along the perimeter of the block, while ground-floor residential units face the interior courtyard, conceived as a quieter green space. The block is partially permeable, with passages open during daylight hours and closed to the public at night. The municipal building is differentiated from the rest of the complex. The social housing is located at the corner of the block and follows the same grid with a different architectural expression. The volume is designed with an exposed concrete facade with smooth and ribbed surfaces and a carved corner with shared spaces and community gardens.
Other recent urban design projects include Stefano Boeri Architetti's affordable housing development in Ibiza, the winning entry in Casa 47, a competition launched by Spain's Entidad Estatal de Vivienda. In Libya, a team composed of ZHA, A&O TEC, Prior + Partners, Homa, Buro Happold, Systematica and Fichtner recently unveiled its concept proposal for the "Next Generation City Plan" for Benghazi. In the United States, Heatherwick Studio unveiled new images of the redesign of Louisville's Belvedere, a 53-year-old gathering place for concerts, festivals and community events. In France, the Grand Paris Express transportation project has engaged architectural teams for the design of its 68 new stations and adjacent public spaces.

The United States military has developed strike plans against Iran that include using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB), colloquially known as the "mother of all bombs," the largest non-nuclear weapon in the US arsenal, CNN reported on Thursday.
According to CNN, multiple US officials said that the plans called for the MOAB to be used against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites, including Pickaxe Mountain.
Another source said that the phrasing used in the plan was that the attack would come “prior to US retrograde in CENTCOM AOR (area of responsibility),” meaning that the US might strike Iran and then immediately pull its forces out of the region.
Several of US President Donald Trump's advisors have also told CNN that, despite Trump's claims that he would not take further action against Iran before the US midterms, it remains unclear whether he will change his mind before Election Day.
The potential deployment of the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal would mark a significant escalation in the conflict, although officials familiar with military planning discussions told CNN that questions remain over its effectiveness in achieving Washington's strategic objectives.
MOAB unlikely to penetrate Iranian nuclear sites
According to several sources, the MOAB likely would be unable to penetrate deep below the ground, where Iranian nuclear facilities, such as Pickaxe Mountain, are believed to be.
“The MOAB is a massive information operation type weapon that is great for huge area clearance but not much else,” one source familiar with military planning discussions around Iran told CNN. “It is definitely not designed as a deep penetration warhead.”
The source said the MOAB's main tactical advantage in this scenario would be its psychological effect on Iran.
“POTUS has unfortunately put himself in a situation where he is almost compelled to do something and, without the ammunition designed to penetrate that level… you have to look at psychological effects for which the MOAB is well-equipped,” the source said.
When asked about the plan, a White House official told CNN that “President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon,” adding that they do not comment on sensitive military plans.
A Pentagon official told CNN that it "plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary‑level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment.”

'Completely reversed': Why more Australian households are feeling miserable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:26:24 UTC
14:26:24 KST

In Brief
- Inflation, high interest rates and rising unemployment are keeping pressure on households.
- Economic misery is expected to remain above historical averages until at least 2028.
Australians are feeling increasingly miserable about the economy, with financial pressures unlikely to ease anytime soon, according to new analysis.
New research from the Committee for Economic Development of Australia (CEDA) found economic "misery" has returned to post-pandemic highs, wiping out improvements made since 2023 and leaving the country on track for several more years of elevated financial strain.
The think tank expects misery levels to remain well above recent historical averages through to at least the end of 2028, as households continue to grapple with inflation, high interest rates and a gradually weakening labour market.
Fresh data released on Thursday added to those concerns, showing Australia's unemployment rate climbed to 4.7 per cent in September — its highest level since October 2021.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
CEDA's misery index combines inflation, unemployment and interest rates to provide a broad measure of the economic pressures facing households.
"When those things go up, there's more of a financial pinch for households and there's a little bit more pressure on the pocketbook," CEDA head of economics Liam Dillon told SBS News.
Progress 'completely reversed'
CEDA says higher prices and borrowing costs have been the main contributors to the recent rise in economic misery.
"What we found is that since 2023, the misery index had been coming down as inflation was trending lower and the Reserve Bank was able to lower interest rates accordingly," Dillon said.
"Since then though, inflation's been a little bit more persistent than we had hoped. That's led the Reserve Bank to increase interest rates to 15-year highs."
"The combination of those things means that the progress on lowering that economic misery has now been completely reversed and we're back at 2023 levels."
After briefly returning to the Reserve Bank's two to three per cent target range in 2025, annual inflation rose to four per cent over the year to August.
The Reserve Bank has raised interest rates four times this year, taking the official cash rate to its highest level in 15 years, with some economists expecting another increase before the end of 2026.
The report also points to broader signs of economic pessimism, with consumer confidence remaining at levels comparable to those seen during the pandemic.
Unemployment exceeding forecasts
While inflation and interest rates have driven the latest increase in the misery index, the labour market has helped cushion the impact on many households.
But that source of support is beginning to weaken.
In the decade before the pandemic, unemployment was the largest contributor to Australia's economic misery, averaging 5.5 per cent of the population and peaking at 6.3 per cent in late 2014.
Since the pandemic, unemployment has remained comparatively low, averaging around four per cent.
But fresh figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Thursday suggest labour market conditions are continuing to soften.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics said on Thursday Australia's unemployment rate for Australia in September was 4.7 per cent — the highest it's been since October 2021.
The August rate was initially flagged as 4.6 but revised up to 4.7.
Employment fell by 39,300 people over the month, while the number of unemployed Australians increased by 8,900.
The result also exceeded the Reserve Bank's forecast for unemployment to reach 4.5 per cent by the December quarter.
Despite the deterioration, Dillon said the jobs market remained a relative source of strength for the economy.
"What we've seen is that even though unemployment has been rising, the labour market is still showing signs of resilience and that's really helping to support households," he said.
About 177,000 jobs have been added since the start of the year, according to CEDA.
Dillon said that had helped insulate households from some of the effects of higher inflation and interest rates, while household savings remain above the decade average in the years before the pandemic.
The remedy to misery
The report argues reducing economic misery remains difficult because efforts to bring down inflation can often come at the expense of employment and economic activity.
To return inflation to the Reserve Bank's target range, it has largely relied on higher interest rates, increasing pressure on households already facing elevated living costs.
Minutes from the Reserve Bank's September meeting, released this week, showed staff were increasingly concerned weak productivity growth may mean unemployment needs to be higher than previously thought to keep inflation stable.
Dillon said stronger productivity growth offered the best long-term solution because it could ease pressure across all three parts of the misery index.
"What we suggest and what we argue through this is that really the only way to get at all three drivers of misery is to boost productivity growth," he said.
"That's a challenge and a long-term one at that, but really this index shows why that's so important."
CEDA expects misery levels to remain above recent historical averages through to the end of 2028 based on current trends.
— With additional reporting by the Australian Associated Press.

Israel’s voters seem more tired than engaged by crucial election

- Campaigning is unusually quiet, with fewer rallies and posters. Many voters seem fixed in their choices, while polls suggest no clear majority and a possible repeat election.
- Opposition hopes centre on Gadi Eisenkot, who promises a more transparent government. Likely changes include an inquiry into Oct 7, prime minister term limits and action on ultra-Orthodox conscription.
AI generated
JERUSALEM – Two weeks before what is widely considered Israel’s most consequential election in decades, its streets are surprisingly empty of rallies and campaign posters, with voters seemingly more exhausted than engaged.
For a society that a few years ago saw hundreds of thousands pack central squares weekly to protest against the policies of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the listlessness is noteworthy.
“It’s the most significant election since 1949 and the most lacklustre existential moment that I can recall,” said Yossi Klein Halevi, author of several books on Israel and a senior fellow at the Shalom Hartman Institute, a Jerusalem think-tank.
“Israelis are tired after three years of war,” he said.
“They also know that the war isn’t over, that whoever wins will have to fight its next stage. It makes it hard to generate excitement for the future.”
The Oct 27 election will be the first since Hamas militants attacked Israel three years ago, killing 1,200, abducting 250 and triggering a brutal war in Gaza that the territory’s Health Ministry says has killed at least 70,000 Palestinians.
Israel has since waged further battles against Iran and groups it backs in Lebanon and Syria.
Hundreds of thousands of Israelis have been called up for military service, and many have spent months in uniform, away from family and work.
The Oct 7, 2023, attack inspired patriotic unity, but as Hamas held on to hostages in Gaza, fissures opened, with some blaming the government for not prioritising their freedom over combat.
In addition, Netanyahu’s ruling coalition includes ultra-Orthodox parties who have traded their votes for keeping their young men out of military service, an issue that has infuriated most of the rest of the country.
This combination of issues could be expected to inspire an impassioned opposition to make its case and get out the vote.
But that is happening far less than many had expected, although pollsters say opposition supporters will vote in large – perhaps record – numbers.
While a Channel 12 poll on Oct 12 had the opposition bloc winning 54 seats to Netanyahu’s 49, other surveys have seen a much closer gap and neither side is expected to secure a clear majority to form a government.
That is another possible factor in keeping enthusiasm low, since it could require complex negotiations or even another election to deliver a decisive outcome.
The opposition’s main candidate is Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who has pledged to lead a more transparent government.
He is positioning himself as a self-effacing contrast to the high-profile Netanyahu, a global figure who has been in office longer than anyone in Israeli history.
Yoel Esteron, who founded business daily Calcalist, said: “You’d expect to see Eisenkot in the centre of Tel Aviv with tens of thousands of people expressing a desperate desire for change. But he’s not a charismatic candidate and does small events.”
Esteron also noted that a lot more campaigning is done on social media than in previous eras.
Shmuel Rosner, who produces analysis and polling for Channel 13, said the low-key campaigns may be a result of most people having long ago decided which bloc they support, with little movement between them.
While cars lack bumper stickers and billboards are fewer, television and radio debates have been vigorous and intense.
Oded Ben Ami, who anchors an evening news broadcast on Channel 12, said he believes some things will change if Eisenkot wins: a commission of inquiry for Oct 7, term limits for prime ministers and an attempt to address the ultra-Orthodox conscription issue.
But Lebanon, Syria, Iran, Gaza and the West Bank, not to mention education and transportation, add up to a mountain of challenges.
Tel Aviv psychologist Amalia Rosenblum, when asked why the opposition energy seemed so low, referred to a concept known as learnt helplessness – when people stop trying to escape an unpleasant situation because experiences have taught them their actions have no impact.
“Those who packed the streets a few years ago feel increasingly that they can’t move the needle,” she said.
“Even if they win, it’s like having a disease and being prescribed medicine. You take it, but it doesn’t exactly make you excited.” BLOOMBERG
