Restoring nature is key to a more resilient future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:24:40 UTC
14:24:40 KST

Restoring nature is key to a more resilient future
At COP17 and COP31, governments must accelerate positive tipping points in energy, food and finance.
Nature is humanity’s life-support system, but it is being depleted at an alarming rate, leaving our world increasingly vulnerable. From deadly heatwaves and raging wildfires to catastrophic floods and prolonged droughts, the effects of environmental change have been impossible to ignore this year. With El Nino forecast to intensify, the risks to people, nature and economies are only increasing.
These shocks are unfolding against the backdrop of widespread nature loss, with WWF’s Living Planet Report 2026 finding that the average size of monitored wildlife populations declined by 73 percent between 1970 and 2022. Nature loss is increasingly a question of economic and national resilience – affecting food and water security, health, supply chains and geopolitical stability.
The situation is serious, but science shows there are still grounds for hope.
The economic systems driving nature’s decline can be transformed, and change can accelerate much faster than many may expect. Evidence shows that under the right conditions, positive change can cross a tipping point threshold and become self-reinforcing, making a safer, more resilient future not just possible, but inevitable.
The question is: How can we accelerate the actions needed to trigger those tipping points and accelerate the transition?
Positive tipping points and the opportunity for transformational change
In environmental terms, we often think about tipping points in terms of the threats they pose to vital ecosystems, such as coral reefs or the Amazon rainforest, where constant damage risks compounding and becoming increasingly impossible to reverse. These dangers are real and urgent. However, these tipping point dynamics can also work in our favour.
Three economic systems are driving most of nature’s decline: the energy system that fuels climate change; the global food system that leads to habitat loss and climate change; and the finance system that bankrolls it all. Triggering tipping points in those systems would see them rapidly transform for the better and reduce harm to the climate and nature. Once that threshold is passed, change can happen quickly as knowledge and technology advance, with solutions becoming cheaper and more accessible and as people learn from others. Encouragingly, progress is already under way – not everywhere, and not yet at the scale required – but enough to demonstrate that change is possible.
The world does not lack goals for 2030. What it lacks is the pace of implementation. With the Global Biodiversity Framework, the UN Sustainable Development Goals and the Paris Agreement in place, governments have already agreed on a pathway. Focusing on implementing these agreements in full will create the conditions for rapid systemic change.
The global energy system has already passed a tipping point, with the transition away from fossil fuels to renewable energy now accelerating. While far from complete, this transition demonstrates how rapid systemic change is possible, offering valuable lessons for the equally urgent transformation of our food and financial systems.
Twenty years ago, solar power was used mostly in satellites and pocket calculators. Now, it is the cheapest option for new electricity generation in most countries. Affordable solar panels are electrifying rural households and improving the resilience of food and medical supply chains. Renewable technologies are displacing fossil fuels at a pace few people predicted even a decade ago.
Changing the food and finance systems is proving slower but is no less urgent.
To progress towards a food systems tipping point, we need to hit major milestones in the uptake of nature-positive food production and see wider shifts in consumer demand for healthier, more sustainable foods to reinforce and reward this shift. Some progress is under way with efforts to tackle commodity-driven deforestation, and more than 130 countries have national strategic plans for food system transformation, but commitments have not yet translated into the policies and incentives needed to accelerate the transition.
Tipping the finance system so that more finance flows to activities that protect and restore nature than activities that harm it is a fundamental challenge. Reaching this tipping point will require a combination of regulatory change, subsidy reform, and a shift in how the sector values climate and nature as material financial risks. If even a portion of the money currently directed towards harmful activities is redirected to environmental recovery, it could shift the economics of the entire transformation.
Governments meeting at the COP17 biodiversity and COP31 climate conferences have before them a vital opportunity to work together to accelerate the actions needed to trigger positive tipping points and to build resilience into societies and the global economy.
Learning from conservation success
Hidden within the broader picture of global biodiversity decline are inspiring stories of species recovery. Populations of green sea turtles and tigers are rebounding due to dedicated conservation work bringing together governments, communities and organisations.
Creating systemic change will similarly take action from all of us, from governments to businesses, financial institutions, local communities, and individuals. We know where we need to get to and the hurdles we need to overcome together; the task now is to create the conditions in which positive change gathers momentum and starts reinforcing itself.
Building strength and resilience into our natural support system will require the courage to shift from extractive, wasteful economies focused on short-term gain to systems that are sustainable and regenerative for the long-term benefit of all. We have the goals, the solutions and pathways to get there. Yes, there might be setbacks along the way, but science shows nature and the climate can still recover and that change can happen faster than we might think.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

New four-lane bridge between China and North Korea opens after a decade of delay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:23:28 UTC
14:23:28 KST

The new bridge's opening comes about a month after North Korea and Russia opened a road bridge as part of their efforts to cement relations.
A new four-lane road bridge linking China and North Korea finally opened on Thursday, 12 years late, enabling the Asian giant and its isolated nuclear-armed neighbour to substantially step up cross-border trade.
China is North Korea's largest trading partner and a vital diplomatic and political backer, although relations have not always been smooth with the ruling Kim dynasty.
Hundreds of people gathered on Thursday in the northern Chinese border town of Dandong, taking selfies in front of the 3,026-metre New Yalu River vehicle bridge before it opened.
Trucks bearing the nations' flags began moving in both directions late in the morning, with some of the North Korean vehicles decorated with flowers.
"It's great," one woman who came to watch told the AFP news agency in the town dotted with Chinese as well as Korean shops and restaurants, where residents were relieved the bridge had finally open.
"It's already been over 10 years. It's certainly going to be good for business," she said, without wishing to be named, accompanied by her friend and her dog.
"I hope the standard of living in North Korea can rise to the level we have here," Dandong local Yu Shuyan, who before the pandemic had visited North Korea, said.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang said that the bridge symbolised Beijing's friendship with Pyongyang and that relations were "entering a new stage and opening a new chapter".
"Thanks to the joint efforts of both sides, the successful opening of the bridge will not only strongly boost economic and trade cooperation between the two countries, but will also further facilitate people-to-people exchanges and tighten the bonds of affection between the two peoples," Li said by video link at the opening ceremony, China’s Xinhua news agency reported.
The structure was completed in 2014 but its opening was delayed due to a lack of connecting roads and customs facilities on the North Korean side, South Korea's Yonhap news agency reported.
North Korea also sealed its borders during the COVID-19 pandemic and train journeys between the East Asian neighbours only restarted in March after a six-year halt.
The new bridge is not the only border crossing between the two countries.
But the new structure will supersede the "extremely narrow" rail-and-road Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge downstream on the Yalu River, said Lim Eul-chul, a North Korea expert at Kyungnam University.
"Previously, transporting heavy cargo such as industrial machinery, raw materials, construction materials and energy-related supplies required extreme caution because of safety concerns surrounding the ageing bridge," Lim told AFP.
"The new crossing will make such shipments much easier and more efficient," he said, calling it a "groundbreaking development" that will substantially increase cargo traffic.
Russia-North Korea bridge
The new bridge's launch came about a month after North Korea and Russia opened a road bridge as part of their efforts to cement relations.
Experts say Chinese officials likely felt uneasy about its opening.
China has long been North Korea’s biggest trading partner and economic pipeline. But in recent years, North Korean leader Kim Jong-un has prioritised Moscow, sending thousands of troops and conventional weapons to support Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine, apparently in exchange for military and economic assistance.
But Kim has recently drawn closer to China with the apparent intent to improve his country's economy and build a front against the United States.
China, for its part, wants to restore its unique influence over North Korea. Last year, about 98% of North Korea’s external trade was with China.
North Korea has not yet resumed issuing tourism visas to Chinese citizens, who once made up the bulk of its overseas visitors.
South Korea's unification ministry said that Seoul is "closely monitoring" the situation regarding the new bridge.

Home Affairs 'unlawfully' jailed Australian citizen for 945 days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:20:23 UTC
14:20:23 KST

Home Affairs 'unlawfully' jailed Australian citizen for 945 days, ombudsman reports
In short:
An ombudsman report has set out a litany of errors spanning four decades that led to a citizen's unlawful detention.
Another non-citizen was wrongfully detained for 304 days.
What's next?
The report has made three recommendations to the government, including better communication between the Home Affairs Department and the minister.
An Australian citizen is among 30 people unlawfully held in immigration detention in the last financial year, according to a Commonwealth Ombudsman report.
The person, named as Mx B, was wrongfully detained by Home Affairs for 945 days — two and a half years — due to incorrect reading of Australia's citizenship laws.
Mx B was born in Australia in 1989 to New Zealand parents, briefly left, then returned in 1992, and should have been granted automatic citizenship on their 10th birthday in accordance with the Citizenship Act. But this did not occur due to "poor record keeping".
The ombudsman report sets out a litany of departmental errors, incorrect assumptions and failed checks spanning four decades.
Three incorrect citizenship assessments
After growing up in Australia, Mx B was convicted of criminal offences and sentenced to prison in 2010 at the age of 21.
In 2018, while in jail, Home Affairs carried out a citizenship status assessment and incorrectly found Mx B was not an Australian citizen, due to their brief departure from the country as a baby.
"They [Mx B] were assessed as not having been ordinarily resident [in Australia] for the first 10 years of their life," the ombudsman report said.
"Officers failed to consider relevant case law about absences from Australia."
In 2019, the department, acting on the mistaken understanding that Mx B was a New Zealand citizen in Australia on a special category visa, considered whether to cancel Mx B's visa on character grounds, but found their visa had ended in the 1990s.
A second citizenship assessment again determined Mx B was not a citizen, which the ombudsman described as another "failure to consider all available information and relevant case law".
Upon Mx B's release from jail in 2022, the department placed them into immigration detention.
"Mx B claimed to be an Australian citizen on multiple occasions throughout their detention," the ombudsman report stated.
In 2024, Mx B's legal representative sent the department correspondence regarding Mx B's claimed Australian citizenship.
"The Department completed a further citizenship status assessment for Mx B based on existing information in its systems," the report states.
For the third time, the department determined Mx B was not an Australian citizen, "failing to take into account the new information indicated by Mx B's legal representative".
Eventual release after High Court NZYQ ruling
In November 2023, the High Court's NZYQ ruling found the indefinite detention of non-citizens where there was no reasonable prospect of removal was illegal.
That triggered the release of more than 300 people from immigration detention.
Mx B was not one of them, remaining in detention until April 2025, when the New Zealand government told the Home Affairs department that Mx B was not a New Zealand citizen.
"The Department subsequently found Mx B to be affected by the outcome in NZYQ because their removal from Australia was not reasonably practicable in the foreseeable future," the ombudsman report said.
"On the same day, the Department granted Mx B a Removal Pending bridging visa on strict conditions and released them from held detention."
A fourth and final citizenship assessment found that Mx B was an Australian citizen.
'Mx A' wrongfully detained for 304 days
Mx B is not alone. The ombudsman report found 30 out of the 4,247 people placed into immigration detention between July 2024 and June 2025 were unlawfully detained.
Of those, 60 per cent of cases were due to a delay in communicating a ministerial visa approval to the department, leaving 18 people in unlawful detention for one day.
One individual, known as Mx A, was wrongfully detained for 304 days due to a decision maker's "incorrect understanding of the law".
Of those affected, none have filed compensation claims against the government.
The report has made three recommendations, including that the department work with the Home Affairs minister to "formalise policies and procedures relating to the communication of Ministerial intervention decision".
It also recommended Home Affairs apologise to those impacted.
The Home Affairs department has been contacted for comment.

King Abdullah II's first visit to Australia in a decade delivered a pledge for deeper defence ties and a joint push for a two-state solution, but fresh uncertainty over Palestinian elections has cast a shadow over Canberra's recognition of a Palestinian state.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and the Jordanian monarch this week reaffirmed support for a two-state solution and condemned Israel's proposed E1 settlement project in the occupied West Bank — considered illegal under international law — in a joint statement issued during talks in Canberra.

Australia also reiterated support for Jordan's humanitarian efforts in Gaza and for the United Nations Relief and Works Agency, which helps refugees.

Jordan's growing strategic role

"There is a lot of violence occurring against Palestinians in the West Bank, but it is also close to Jordan and close to Lebanon, so it has to deal with the outflow of radical tendencies from Lebanon, particularly from Hezbollah," Parmeter said.

Abbas, now aged 90, has remained president since 2005 and has ruled by decree since his term ended in 2009.

The election postponement is particularly significant for Australia because the Albanese government's recognition of a Palestinian state was linked to expectations of governance reform and future democratic elections.

"When Australia announced the recognition of a state of Palestine a year ago, there were conditions attached and a key one was that there would be Palestinian elections held as soon as possible," he said.

Both nations participate in the Jordan-led Aqaba Process, established in 2015 to bring governments and security experts together to address terrorism, violent extremism and emerging security threats.
Australia said it may host an Aqaba Process meeting in 2027 focused on cybersecurity, online radicalisation and the misuse of new technologies.

The administration of US President Donald Trump is considering easing sanctions on shadow fleet tankers to lower shipping costs and increase oil supplies from the Persian Gulf, Reuters reported on Oct. 15, citing people familiar with the discussions.
The proposal would allow sanctioned vessels to transport “legitimate” fuel, excluding Russian and Iranian oil subject to sanctions, the sources said. Companies seeking to use the vessels would have to obtain authorization from the US Treasury Department.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The move could make a small number of additional tankers available for short-haul trips through the Strait of Hormuz, but is unlikely to lead to a widespread drop in freight rates, maritime industry sources told Reuters. Insurers would still have to comply with European Union and UK regulations.
The US Energy Department said any easing of restrictions on the shadow fleet would not help Russia transport oil or petroleum products.
Trump lifts sanctions on Russian diesel, blames Zelensky for high prices
The latest proposal comes days after Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports following an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to US and global markets.
The US Treasury Department authorized the sale and import of Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
Trump said lower fuel prices for Americans were his top priority ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Republicans hope to retain control of both chambers of Congress.
Musk Says US Government Controls Ukraine’s Starshield Limits as Zelensky Accuses Russia of Exploiting Outage
The US president has repeatedly blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries and other energy infrastructure for driving up fuel prices.
On Oct. 10, he called for Ukraine to replace President Volodymyr Zelensky, saying Kyiv needed a leader willing to reach a deal with Moscow.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals, but for some reason he never does,” Trump said.
Zelensky condemned the diesel agreement, arguing that easing sanctions would provide Moscow with additional revenue to continue its war against Ukraine.
“Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world,” Zelensky wrote on X on Oct. 9. “Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged.”
In an interview with Axios, Zelensky described Trump’s decision to lift sanctions as “not fair and not honest,” adding that it looked like a “happy birthday present” for Putin.
The Ukrainian president also argued that any halt to Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure should be reciprocal, with Moscow stopping its attacks on Ukraine’s energy facilities.
The diesel agreement drew criticism from US lawmakers, including some Republicans, who argued that allowing Russian fuel sales would undermine sanctions intended to restrict Moscow’s ability to finance its war against Ukraine.
Russia seeks relief from energy restrictions
The US also temporarily exempted some Russian oil and petroleum product shipments from sanctions in the spring amid the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
The Kremlin argued at the time that stabilizing global oil markets was impossible without significant volumes of Russian oil. Putin also warned that attempts to damage Russia’s oil fleet would create problems for everyone, particularly those seeking to harm Moscow.
The latest discussions on easing shadow fleet restrictions come as the Trump administration seeks to contain fuel prices amid disruptions to global energy supplies. However, any broader reduction in shipping costs could be limited by insurance restrictions and the continued enforcement of European and British sanctions.

Opposition to closing Taipei’s Songshan Airport grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:15:57 UTC
14:15:57 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Defense and transportation officials have raised concerns about Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an’s (蔣萬安) proposal to convert Songshan Airport into an AI park, citing military, transportation, and emergency medical needs.
Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄) told the Legislative Yuan’s Foreign Affairs and National Defense Committee on Wednesday that Songshan Airport plays an important role in Taiwan’s defense in peacetime and during war, per UDN.
When KMT Legislator Huang Jen (黃仁問) asked whether the airport could be targeted in a decapitation strike, Koo said it was possible and that Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport could face the same threat.
Koo added that closing Songshan would make Taoyuan Airport even more difficult to defend. He also agreed with KMT Legislator Huang Chien-pin (黃建賓) that the risks of abandoning an airport should not be overlooked.
Koo said legislators representing outlying islands and eastern Taiwan had opposed phasing out Songshan, which provides an important transportation link for residents seeking medical treatment in Taipei. Those areas have fewer medical resources, making access to the capital’s hospitals especially important.
Deputy Civil Aviation Administration Director Yang Kuo-feng (楊國峯) told the committee that the Taipei City Government had not submitted proposals or applied for budget subsidies related to planning or research on relocating or closing Songshan Airport in the past four years, per LTN.
DPP Legislator Wang Ting-yu (王定宇) asked whether the city had raised the issue during that period. Yang said former Taipei Mayor Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) had proposed relocating the airport, but the current Chiang administration had not. Yang added that the airport’s overall plan, approved in November 2023, designates Songshan as an international business airport and a hub for domestic air transport.
Deputy Transportation Minister Lin Kuo-hsien (林國顯) said the planned third terminal and third runway at Taoyuan Airport were intended to expand capacity, not accommodate flights currently using Songshan. After the third runway is completed, Taoyuan’s existing second runway will also need to be taken out of service temporarily for maintenance, Lin said.
Lin said Taoyuan primarily serves international routes and medium- and large-sized jet aircraft, while Songshan handles domestic and regional services, including flights by slower aircraft such as ATR turboprops.
Transferring Songshan’s flights to Taoyuan would require changes to terminal and apron arrangements and could be costly, Lin said. A Ministry of Transportation report estimated that passengers traveling on ATR-72 aircraft would add about an hour to their journeys compared with flying from Songshan.
Taoyuan Airport handled about 47.8 million passengers in 2025, exceeding its stated annual capacity of 42.8 million, according to the report. Terminal 3 is scheduled for completion by the end of 2027.
Songshan handled about 2.39 million passengers traveling to and from Kinmen, Matsu, and Penghu in 2025, the report said. It also cited 38,651 outlying-island residents who traveled to Taiwan for medical treatment and noted that nine major emergency hospitals are within a 10- to 15-minute drive of Songshan, per Liberty Times.
The two airports can also serve as alternate landing sites for each other during bad weather or other exceptional circumstances. Lin said the Songshan Airport proposal remained open for public discussion but would be considered in the next five-year plan only after its consequences and necessary supporting infrastructure had been adequately assessed.

China and Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) relations are entering a new stage and opening a new chapter, Premier Li Qiang said in a video address on Thursday at the opening ceremony of the New Yalu River bridge that links the North Asia neighbours.
Li said he hopes the two sides will use the bridge link as an opportunity to continue enhancing connectivity and tap cooperation potential in border areas, Xinhua news agency reported.
The opening of the two countries' most significant land border crossing is aimed at rejuvenating trade and commerce.
The three-kilometre New Yalu River Bridge and the end where Chinese customs operates saw increased activity over the past few days, with trucks adorned with national flags making the crossing on Thursday.
Crowds also gathered on the Chinese side along a road overlooking the bridge.
Chinese and DPRK flags also lined the cable-stayed bridge with towering pylons that had been completed in 2014 but remained unused, while approach roads and a customs compound on the North Korea end remained unfinished.
The opening signals progress in bilateral relations between Beijing and Pyongyang, marked by two summit meetings between their leaders in the past year.
China is by far Pyongyang's largest trading partner, even after a series of UN sanctions banned the flow of goods and workers to and from the DPRK.
China and Russia, two UN Security Council permanent member states that voted to approve sanctions resolutions until 2017, have since questioned  the legitimacy and efficacy of such bans.
The bridge will help move heavy equipment, raw materials and energy products needed for DPRK's development projects, said Lim Eul-chul at Kyungnam University's Institute for Far Eastern Studies.
China's exports to the DPRK rose to a six-year high of US$2.3 billion last year, a 25 percent increase, That was still well below levels before UN sanctions were tightened in 2017. (Reuters)

Russia turns to new tactics to destroy Ukraine’s energy grid this winter for good
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:06:27 UTC
14:06:27 KST

Russia turns to new tactics to destroy Ukraine’s energy grid this winter for good
Employees work at a power plant of Ukrainian energy provider DTEK, which was damaged by constant Russian air attacks, at an undisclosed location in Ukraine, on Nov. 13, 2025. (Roman Pilipey / AFP via Getty Images)
Volleys of explosions deafened Kyiv in the early hours of Oct. 14, as Russia targeted multiple energy facilities powering the embattled capital amid a new campaign to isolate and disconnect the city following a brutal summer of relentless strikes on businesses and critical infrastructure.
While Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s energy system have been ongoing throughout the year at a low level, Moscow has recently ramped up mass attacks to wipe out power plants, substations, and gas infrastructure for its fifth winter offensive during the full-scale invasion.
The latest attack on Oct. 14 alone targeted 26 power facilities, President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on social media.
There’s also been a recent uptick in Russian drones and missiles flying near nuclear plants, one energy official with knowledge of the matter told the Kyiv Independent under the condition of anonymity.
The drones are likely monitoring the plants and their infrastructure, with the official warning that Russia may be preparing to strike them — something Moscow has largely refrained from throughout its invasion.
Ukraine is in a vulnerable position. In just the week of Oct. 5-11, there were around 200 hits on power sector facilities and 17 on the oil and gas sector, the Energy Ministry’s press department told the Kyiv Independent. And Ukraine lacks critical air defense against Moscow’s expanding arsenal, energy specialists told the Kyiv Independent.
As the winter draws closer, Russia will likely expand its campaign to other major cities to sow panic.
Meanwhile, Russia’s tactics and weapons technology have changed since last winter. In addition to ballistic missiles, Moscow overwhelms Ukraine’s air defense by launching jet-powered drones and AI-powered loitering munitions en masse, attacking during the day as well as at night, and hitting infrastructure that power plants rely on, like railways for coal deliveries, energy experts said.
The recent attacks have already left hundreds of thousands of citizens in Kyiv and front-line regions suffering power and water outages. The situation has deteriorated so much in Kyiv that power to the metro was even temporarily cut off following attacks on Oct. 8 and 14.
"The overall pattern is systematic: the strikes damage the network, force emergency restrictions, and slow down repairs, especially when crews cannot work safely during air-raid alerts," Viktoria Gryb, a lawmaker and head of the parliament’s subcommittee on energy security, told the Kyiv Independent.
"The methods and targets can change, so I would not call this a simple repeat of last winter. But the goal remains the same: to destabilize the energy system."
read also
New tactics
The first few weeks of Russia’s latest campaign have primarily targeted Kyiv, continuing Russia’s months-long offensive on the capital’s economic centers that has made life in the city increasingly harder and more dangerous.
For now, Moscow is picking up where it left off last winter — focusing on disconnecting Kyiv by targeting power plants in and around the capital, as well as key substations, Olena Pavlenko, president of the Kyiv-based energy-focused think tank DiXi Group, told the Kyiv Independent.
The capital is particularly vulnerable as it is reliant on thermal and cogeneration plants that are exposed to enemy strikes, while substations that connect it to generation sources, including nuclear plants in western Ukraine, are protected against drones but not against ballistic missiles.
Meanwhile, the city hasn’t prepared enough backup generation supplies for when its power plants are inevitably taken offline. Despite experiencing a humanitarian crisis last winter when residents lacked heating and power in minus 25 degrees Celsius, political infighting and funding shortages mean the city will likely experience the same difficulties again.
Kyiv and other cities are also frequently attacked by jet-powered drones, which weren’t widespread last winter. They are faster and more precise than the older propeller-powered drones, making them harder for Ukraine’s limited air defenses to shoot down.
"Jet-powered drones changed the game to some extent. They are cheaper than missiles and can destroy more distributed generation infrastructure," Pavlenko said.
"It’s easier for jet-powered drones to attack transformers, smaller transformers, and infrastructure for cities. This has a huge impact on cities in terms of heating supply, water supply, and sewage."
In addition to striking power plants and substations, Russia has also increasingly hit power lines around big cities over the last few weeks to cut power supplies to consumers. While not a new target, Russia’s tactics have improved, including attaching a new type of warhead to a jet-powered drone designed to destroy high-voltage electricity pylons.
Ukraine’s three operational nuclear power plants, which generate around 60% of the country’s electricity, will likely be the country’s lifeline again once other power plants are taken offline.
Unlike substations, which are largely protected against jet-powered drones via massive concrete fortifications, power lines and pylons are more exposed since they can’t be easily shielded. But damaged power lines can be restored in 24 hours, in contrast to substations, which require complex repairs, the anonymous energy official said.
The problem with pylons could surface in the long run, as Ukraine’s steel industry has shut down amid debilitating strikes on factories. Stockpiles of products to reconstruct pylons will gradually deplete until steel firms can safely resume production, the press service of Metinvest, Ukraine’s largest steel company, told the Kyiv Independent.
"The situation regarding future supplies is becoming critical," Metinvest’s press service wrote in a statement to the Kyiv Independent.
What’s next?
After the last autumn and winter period, which saw Russia wipe out more than half of Ukraine’s gas production and 9 gigawatts of energy generation, the energy sector expects the same challenges again this year.
There’s little else that Russia can target, said Volodymyr Kudritsky, former head of Ukraine's state-grid operator Ukrenergo and co-founder of energy firm Nedzhen.
"We’ve already seen 95% of the menu. The Russians have left themselves with very little room to surprise us more," Kudritskyi told the Kyiv Independent.
The key issue for the energy sector is the air defense situation, as Ukraine struggles to down the jet-powered drones, said Kudritskyi. In recent months, Ukraine has developed interceptors that are showing increasingly positive results, but more time is needed to scale production.
At the same time, Ukraine continues to upgrade and reinforce protection at its energy facilities, including concrete fortifications, electronic warfare, early threat detection systems, and critical equipment reserves, the Energy Ministry said.
As the winter draws closer, Russia will likely expand its campaign to other major cities to sow panic, said Pavlenko. While attacks so far this autumn have largely impacted cities like Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia, Russian drones and ballistic missiles can reach deep into western Ukraine.
There’s also a heightened threat to nuclear infrastructure, like substations, this winter, said Pavlenko. Ukraine’s three operational nuclear power plants, which generate around 60% of the country’s electricity, will likely be the country’s lifeline again once other power plants are taken offline.
The risks to nuclear plants were majorly tested last winter, as Moscow targeted substations connected to the plants. One of the worst Russian attacks in February halved the output of nuclear plants, with Ukraine stabilizing the situation before it could worsen.
In a worst-case scenario, a big attack on substations could disconnect nuclear plants from the grid, forcing the plants to shut down, said the anonymous energy official. The consequences would be "extremely serious," they added.

‘They’re not dead yet’: Bleached corals recover in record time after touching healthy clones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:02:27 UTC
14:02:27 KST

In the lab, bleached corals recovered within just seven weeks of being put in brief contact with healthy corals.
Dying corals may have found an unexpected lifeline: their neighbours.
Scientists at Stanford University have discovered a way to bring corals back from the brink of death by placing them in contact with healthy corals for just a few days.
Published in Science Advances, the study presents a promising new approach to restoring coral reefs as rising sea temperatures cause more frequent and severe coral bleaching events.
When water becomes too hot, corals expel the microscopic algae that provide much of their energy, an event known as bleaching, which leaves them vulnerable to starvation.
After bleaching events, it can take months or years for surviving corals to recover – but the scientists contend hope is not lost for them.
“While bleached corals may be dying, they are not dead yet,” says lead author Danny Collins, a PhD student at Stanford. “The question we wanted to answer is, once a coral has bleached, what can we do?”
How scientists brought bleached corals back to full strength
The discovery happened by accident in 2025, when Steve Palumbi, a professor of oceans and marine biologist at Stanford’s Doerr School of Sustainability, noticed two pieces of coral that had fallen against each other in a laboratory tank. One was healthy while the other was bleached. But where the two touched, the bleached coral was beginning to regain its colour.
Collins then arranged 10 pairs of coral fragments, each containing a healthy and bleached piece from the same colony. Five pairs were placed in contact with one another, and the others were kept a few millimetres apart.
Within seven weeks, all five bleached fragments put in contact with their healthy clones had recovered. The ones that were kept apart had died.
Under a microscope, the scientists discovered the corals had fused together, creating tiny channels that allowed algae and nutrients to pass from one to the other. Within three days, beneficial algae had begun moving from the healthy corals into the bleached ones. After about a week, some had received enough algae to recover on their own.
Once inside the damaged corals, the beneficial algae began multiplying rapidly. “They flood in and start dividing at the fastest rates seen in corals,” says Palumbi.
During the second week, the algae doubled in number every four days – about 10 times faster than in wild corals – allowing the damaged corals to continue recovering even after they were separated from the healthy ones.
The finding marked a breakthrough in the lab. “Bleached corals are often considered a lost cause because recovery after a heatwave is very slow, if it happens at all,” says Fiorenza Micheli, a Stanford professor and one of Collins’ faculty advisors.
But the scientists say the technique isn’t ready for wide-scale application in the oceans.
The corals must be genetically identical for their tissues to fuse. In other words, every damaged coral would need a healthy copy of itself – an impractical solution for restoring whole reefs. But the researchers hope to find ways to deliver the beneficial algae without requiring direct contact or identical twins.
Coral reefs may be running out of recovery time
The revelation comes at a crucial time for coral reefs.
According to the Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network’s latest assessment, the world's reefs have lost nearly 10 per cent of their living coral over the past four decades. Between 2023 and 2024 alone, it fell almost 9 per cent during a global bleaching event – the largest single-year decline ever recorded.
Global bleaching now occurs roughly every five to six years, leaving reefs less time to recover between bouts of extreme heat. The report warns that reefs will continue declining unless man-made emissions fall and threats such as overfishing, water pollution and coastal developments are curbed.
And while combining coral to help them recover from bleaching might save some of them, Palumbi stresses that it can’t protect them from rising sea temperatures.
“This is a recovery story. It doesn’t blunt heatwaves; it just helps the aftermath. There is still a huge need to reduce heatwaves and protect all of Earth’s life from rapid climate stress,” he says.
“Eventually, it can hopefully help the huge effort being put into restoration succeed better by helping those coral gardens survive heatwaves more completely.”

Jonas Hejduk's blurry furnishings are deliberately low resolution
Designer Jonas Hejduk has released a collection of rugs and benches that have ambiguously pixellated aesthetics.
Hejduk's focus on deliberately compressed, low-resolution versions of popular furnishings were informed by his childhood fixation with video game graphics.
"Youngsters like myself were already caught in the spiral logic of infinite growth, trained never to tolerate technological stagnation," Hejduk told Dezeen.
Stools and rugs are among the French designer's output, each of which were named using computer filename formats.
In the case of the designer's rugs, the filename, initial file size and post-processing size are woven onto the surface of the piece.
Made from digitally woven wool and cotton jacquard, the designer described the Traditional-rug-1.jpeg as "poetic and gently ironic".
"Once a symbol of prestige and early global exchange, the Persian rug gradually shifted into a standardised archetype of mass culture and uniformity," Hejduk told Dezeen.
"Here, it is reduced to its own thumbnail – an enigmatic blurry image of troubled origins, copied and pasted too many times."
Hejduk's Tiger skin rug is part of a wider collection called Crash.jpeg, in which the designer explored the contemporary obsession with digital clarity and technological advancement.
"By embracing the ambiguity of the poor image, the collection presents works that are deliberately difficult to photograph and rendered anachronistic to the eyes of social media algorithms: high-definition designs are deliberately sabotaged down to lower resolutions," said Hejduk.
Similarly, Hejduk's Log-texture-1.jpeg bench recalls the nostalgia of logs as resting places in 1990s video games.
The benches were wrapped in a blurry bark skin with cut-through textures at either end, tacked together with traditional nailhead trim.
Like many of the designer's works, the logs act like an optical illusion, contrasting with their surroundings in a jarring way owing to their not-finished-loading appearance.
"Visually, it 'has no business being there', and yet, its digital nature conveys an authenticity that brings a smile, far removed from what AI offers in our daily lives," the designer continued.
In addition to rugs and benches, Hejduk produces similarly blurry ceramics, garments, bed sheets and wallpapers.
"These pieces of furniture are not just 'designer jokes about 3D', but objects of mourning and resistance," said Hejduk.
"Through the physicality of craft and raw materials, they serve as tangible reminders of the unfulfilled promises of digital modernity, all while rejecting the sanitised present that tech oligarchs attempt to impose on us."
Other products on Dezeen created in rejection of AI include a shirt that prevents the wearer from being picked up by AI video surveillance and a font that cannot be read by AI software.

Embryo gene editing is getting more precise, but how safe and ethical is the practice? | Euronews Tech Talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:00:26 UTC
14:00:26 KST

The use of a precise gene editing technique to edit human embryos has caught the attention of academics and society, yet doubts over its safety and ethics remain.
In the summer of 2026, two studies revived the debate on embryo gene editing, a technique that consists of manipulating the DNA of a human embryo for reasons ranging from better understanding human development to preventing children from developing certain diseases.
One study was led by Kathy Niakan at Cambridge University in the United Kingdom, and the other by Dieter Egli at Columbia University in the United States.
Both researchers employed base editing, a technique developed in 2016 to alter genetic material with greater precision than earlier methods. Both conducted their research on human embryos instead of mice, and both delivered results which caught the attention of many around the world.
Embryo gene editing is not yet a medical reality. Scientifically, modifying the genes of a human embryo is extremely challenging. In addition, no country allows the modification of cells that can be passed on to offspring.
With these studies, is society closer to the possibility of safely creating gene-edited babies? What are the ethical concerns surrounding this practice?
The studies
Using base editing, the Cambridge study targeted NANOG, a specific gene which was found to be essential for the formation of future bodies from an embryo.
“Base editing represents a significant advance on conventional CRISPR-Cas9 because it carries a far lower risk of causing unintended chromosome errors,” Kathy Niakan said in a press release.
On the other side of the Atlantic, Columbia’s research group tried base editing in three genes: one linked to high cholesterol and cardiovascular disease, and the other two related to haemoglobin production.
“By introducing such damage using editors, we are starting to understand how human embryos handle damage in their genomes. Long term, we hope to learn how to prevent genetic and developmental abnormalities during IVF to create more efficient, safer, and more affordable fertility treatments,” said Dieter Egli in a press release.
According to Robin Lovell-Badge, principal group leader and head of the laboratory of stem cell biology and developmental genetics at the Francis Crick Institute in London, the two studies are on the right path, but there’s room for improvement.
“The methods look much safer. But there's still work to do,” he told Euronews Next. “It looks like the levels of mosaicism are low, but not zero. So there's going to have to be more work done there,” he added.
Mosaicism is one of the main obstacles of gene editing. It happens when base-editor molecules fail to find and modify certain cells. This phenomenon could potentially cause the development of certain diseases.
The ethical debate
Although research on embryo gene editing might be advancing, several ethical questions remain unanswered.
“A question that very often pops up in regard to that is the tension between therapy versus enhancement,” Pascal Borry, professor of bioethics at the University of Leuven, in Belgium, told Euronews Next. “Where do we put the line? What is therapeutic? What is an improvement?” he added.
Borry also highlighted other ethical puzzles, ranging from the issue of consent to the problem of stigmatising a community already living with a certain disease.
In addition, he underlined that embryo gene editing might not be necessary: “There are many other alternatives to this technology, and I think it’s important to reflect upon that. And I’m thinking about the pre-implantation genetic testing,” he said.
Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis is a medical test that takes place during in vitro fertilisation treatment to detect any abnormalities in the embryos.
Björn Heindryckx, professor at Ghent University in Belgium and principal investigator coordinating research in the infertility department, agrees with Borry on the non-necessity of using embryo gene editing to prevent certain genetic conditions.
Yet, he argues that this technique could still have benefits: “If we understand, and with this tool we can really test it much better, if we can get more insight into embryo development, it will give us more insight into certain forms of infertility.”
Badge, on the other hand, is less worried about the ethical implications of this technique. “I don't have a problem with doing it if it's safe and there's a good ethical reason for doing it. I think it's unethical to allow people to have children that have a genetic disorder if you can avoid it,” he explained.
According to Badge, countries should regulate the practice; however, they should not adopt a restrictive ban. “Let's say you want to fly to Mars. You're going to be in space for a long time; you're going to have an environment with very high levels of radiation. So you may want to be modified to deal with high levels of radiation,” he told Euronews Next.
Euronews Tech Talks is a podcast produced, written, presented and published in English.

The day bad weather brought half a million birds to England
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:00:24 UTC
14:00:24 KST

My birding mentor, the late Derek Moore, was also a keen cricketer. But one autumn day in 1965 he was unable to concentrate while fielding because many hundreds of songbirds were landing around him on the pitch at Lowestoft.
The arrival of hundreds of thousands of birds along the Suffolk coast that day became known as the “Great Fall”, and it was caused by a weather system bringing cloud, winds and heavy rain.
The conditions caused migrating songbirds heading south across the North Sea from Scandinavia to become exhausted, with many falling into the waves and drowning. But an estimated half a million survived and made landfall along a 24-mile stretch of English coastline. Having rested and fed, they then continued their long journey south to sub-Saharan Africa.
When I began birding in the 1970s, older birders waxed lyrical about the autumn falls from their youth. Yet today they are few and far between. Not because the weather patterns have changed, but simply because there are now far fewer songbirds breeding in northern Europe and migrating through Britain to Africa.
One place they do still occur – though with smaller numbers of birds – is Spurn Head on the East Yorkshire coast. Last month, birders gathered there for the annual MigFest, which, since 2013, has celebrated the wonders of bird migration – with attenders ever hopeful of witnessing one of these extraordinary falls.

Rachel Roddy’s recipe for spaghetti with Marmite | A kitchen in Rome
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:00:24 UTC
14:00:24 KST

Here is a simple, practical recipe that I trust will be useful to many who don’t have the time for lengthy kitchen preparations. Boil the spaghetti as usual, drain it, and toss it with a little butter and parmesan. Then, for four, take a spoonful of meat extract and dissolve it in a small saucepan with just a few drops of boiling water. Pour the meat extract over the pasta, stir and serve. You will be pleasantly surprised by the exquisite flavour the pasta acquires – achieved with such a negligible investment of time.
This is a roughly word-for-word translation of an Italian recipe for spaghetti con l’estratto di carne (spaghetti with meat extract). It is another dish from Ada Boni’s Il Talismano della Felicità (The Talisman of Happiness), which was published in English for the first time last month and, according to the food writer and editor Angela Frenda, is “still considered one of the most precise and accurate of all cookbooks”.
I was alerted to spaghetti con l’estratto di carne by the food historian and author of A Brief History of Pasta, Luca Cesari. I recently met Luca for dinner at St John in London and, over bone marrow on toast, kidneys on toast, welsh rarebit and fried tripe, we talked about many things, including recipe outrage. Spaghetti with Marmite came up as an example, and Luca pointed out that, in terms of approach, taste and spirit, it was more or less identical to Ada’s iconic and “exquisite” recipe.
He also noted that using a spoonful of meat extract as a pasta sauce is in the spirit – and a short-cut version – of pasta al sugo d’arrosto (pasta with sauce of the roast). That is, the pan juices, and those fat and tasty, crusty bits left at the bottom of the tin when you’ve roasted a joint of meat, are lengthened with a bit of water or wine, maybe more rosemary (or whatever you fancy) added, before being used as a pasta sauce. Pasta with gravy, if you like. (When I make braised chicken with rosemary, garlic and wine, I particularly like the last of the congealed pan juices as a pasta sauce.)
It was the great Anna del Conte, who was born in Milan in 1925 and moved to London in 1949, who first wrote about spaghetti with butter, cheese and Marmite, noting in her autobiography Risotto and Nettles that this was a dish she herself made (and that was loved by her children). I wonder if Anna knew Ada’s version? She certainly mentions pasta al sugo d’arrosto in her writing. And Anna inspired Nigella Lawson to make her own version of spaghetti with Marmite, which is the recipe I followed, although it is hardly a recipe.
Marmite is, of course, a dark, sticky, salty-savoury spread made from concentrated yeast extract. What yeast extract and meat extract have in common is glutamic acid or free glutamates, an amino acid that provides a savoury, lip-smacking umami flavour. Tomatoes, mushrooms and cheese are high in free glutamates, too, so in the Ada-Anna-Nigella recipes all provide a double dose of umami by adding parmesan; butter is vital for adding fat, flavour and slippiness to the final dish. I hope you will be pleasantly surprised by the exquisite flavour this pasta acquires, and all achieved with such a negligible investment of time.
Spaghetti with Marmite, Bovril or Vegemite
Serves 4
400-500g spaghetti
  
Salt
  
1-2 tsp Marmite, or Bovril or Vegemite
  
60g 
 unsalted butter, cubed 
  
2-4 tsp 
 grated parmesan, or grana padano
Boil the spaghetti in plenty of lightly salted water, because both the Marmite and the cheese are already salty.
Meanwhile, in a very small saucepan on a low heat, warm two tablespoons of water with the Marmite until it has dissolved.
Once the pasta is cooked but al dente, lift it into a warm bowl (reserve some of the pasta cooking water), then add the cubed butter and cheese, and toss well. Pour the dissolved Marmite over the spaghetti and stir again, adding a little of the reserved cooking water, if you think it needs it, until the sauce is soft and slippery. Serve immediately.

Parents of Chloe Moffat want Treasury staff held to account over her death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:00:23 UTC
14:00:23 KST

The parents of a woman who killed herself after facing disciplinary proceedings at the Treasury will call for anyone found to have contributed to their daughter’s death to be held to account.
A coroner found in August that the Treasury had “materially contributed” to Chloe Moffat’s death after the 26-year-old personal assistant was called into a surprise disciplinary meeting about anonymous complaints alleging she had disclosed sensitive information at work, which she denied.
The Treasury’s response to the coroner’s prevention of future deaths report, seen by the Guardian, acknowledges the department’s role in her death and commits to safeguards so this does not happen again. A review of the civil service by the Cabinet Office found that the conditions Moffat was subjected to had been replicated in other disciplinary meetings.
“We have some tough questions to ask,” David Moffat, Chloe’s father, told the Guardian before a meeting with the Treasury’s permanent secretary, James Bowler. “We do want to know that staff have been held to account. The coroner didn’t ask for that, but obviously that is very important. Chloe was held to account; we need to know that the managers and HR staff are being held to account.”
Moffat’s managers declined to allow her to bring a colleague to the meeting, did not give her any advance notice of it, and refused to tell her whether she was likely to lose her job. They also removed access to her director’s email and changed her work responsibilities. This was despite the meeting being described as “informal”.
Moffat left the meeting “devastated” and convinced she would lose her job, the coroner found, and the next morning she took her own life.
She had worked at the Treasury as a personal assistant for almost three years, “loved her job” and had an “exemplary employment record”, the coroner heard.
During the inquest, Moffat’s line manager was asked if she would have done anything differently and told the court: “No, I think we did all we could at the time with the information and advice we were given.”
Moffat’s parents have spent the year since she died fighting to get answers from the Treasury, which initially did not take any responsibility.
“It has taken us a long time to get to this point, and they have not helped us in any form,” said Anne Moffat, Chloe’s mother. “Now we are also trying to think how we want lessons to be learned so no other young person suffers in the same way as Chloe suffered. So we are looking at Chloe’s legacy, to ensure that there is learning across all organisations in HR departments.”
They say they have not had the chance to grieve properly yet and are thinking about holding a second celebration of life for Chloe. David said: “The funeral was in some ways uplifting as so many people chose to join us, but we didn’t really know what we knew now. We want to revisit it and have a more joyful time and celebrate Chloe as the person she was.”
The prevention of future deaths report issued by the coroner found there was still a risk at the civil service due to its disciplinary procedures. The civil service has put in place multiple safeguards to address these issues.
Documents seen by the Guardian read: “HM Treasury has accepted the findings in the report in full. In direct response to the inquest findings, HM Treasury immediately stopped using informal fact-finding meetings for allegations of potential serious or gross misconduct, introduced strengthened procedural and wellbeing safeguards, and issued urgent interim guidance.”
This guidance includes allowing staff to have a supporter in disciplinary meetings, giving proper notice of any such meeting, and informing staff if a dismissal is not likely. The Treasury is also hiring an on-site occupational therapist to support staff wellbeing.
Of this, David Moffat said: “We feel a lot better than we did about it going through the inquest. This is a step forward, but we still have some difficult questions to ask the permanent secretary.”
The coroner heard that during the disciplinary meeting, Moffat repeatedly asked for her best friend at work to be allowed to come in for support. This was not felt by her managers to be “appropriate”, the court heard, despite the obvious distress the young woman was in.
The department has now changed its policy. An email sent to staff at the Treasury last week, seen by the Guardian, reads: “Where concerns may amount to minor misconduct, these will continue to be handled informally. You will be able to ask to bring a colleague with you for personal support if you would like.”
Anne Moffat hopes other young people will not be put in the same position as Chloe. “It is so avoidable what happened, and such a waste. I wish we had known the risks. As parents we are still taking a bit responsibility that we could have done things differently. And if we had, the result wouldn’t have been so catastrophic.”
Chloe’s friends have been keeping her memory alive by running marathons for Shooting Stars Children’s Hospice, a charity for which her mother used to work, and volunteering for Samaritans.
Her parents hope their experience can stop other families from going through the same tragic event.
“We are hoping when we see the Treasury they will give us more reassurance and work with us on how Chloe is remembered,” Anne said. “We so miss having Chloe now. Our lives will never be the same again as we have lost her through something that was so preventable.”
A HM Treasury spokesperson said: “The Treasury’s deepest sympathies continue to be with Chloe’s friends and family, and the department continues to mourn our colleague. Our response to the coroner’s prevention of future deaths report sets out the action we have taken following this tragic case. An independent review found staff acted in good faith and with a duty of care throughout.”
- In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

UK households have paid extra £13,961 on bills since 2021 amid soaring inflation, TUC says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:00:23 UTC
14:00:23 KST

UK households have paid almost £14,000 on average in additional costs for mortgages, loans, energy and water bills over the past five years, according to a report urging the chancellor to tackle soaring living costs at the budget.
With less than a fortnight before John Healey’s first budget as chancellor, the Trades Union Congress (TUC) said the cost of living crisis was weighing on the economy as hard-pressed households held back on spending.
Urging the chancellor to support households through a series of measures in the budget, it said the UK had recorded the weakest growth in consumer spending in the G7 since before the pandemic.
According to analysis of official figures by the union umbrella body, British households have forked out an additional £13,961 on bills on average since 2021 – an extra £2,792 a year – amid soaring inflation triggered by the exit from the Covid pandemic and wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.
Paul Nowak, the TUC general secretary, said: “From austerity to the pandemic to energy shocks and Trumpflation, working people have borne the brunt of crisis after crisis. When the crackpots in the White House or the Kremlin launch an illegal war, everyone pays the price in their bills.”
In his speech at Labour’s conference in Liverpool, Healey pledged to use his 28 October budget to give households “breathing space”. However, he warned that the government had limited resources to soften the global economic shock hitting Britain.
Against a volatile backdrop, the Treasury has been preparing for a “tightly focused” budget to limit the potential for a market backlash provoked by large tax and spending measures. The International Monetary Fund this week urged Healey to “stay the course” to cut the budget deficit amid rising borrowing costs in global financial markets.
The chancellor is however under growing pressure to take action to support households and businesses before the winter amid predictions that consumer energy bills could reach £2,000 a year from January for the typical household.
After retail industry bosses pressed Healey for support in Downing Street meetings on Tuesday, the Confederation of British Industry said he should listen to calls for a cut in employer national insurance contributions to encourage firms to take on younger workers.
The lobby group also called for cuts to business electricity costs, changes to business rates and measures to support private investment.
In a separate report, the centre-left IPPR thinktank urged Healey to raise £16bn, mostly through a rise in capital gains tax that would be softened by a new entrepreneur “super exemption”.
It was reported on Tuesday that Healey had rejected calls from Labour MPs and thinktanks to use the budget to equalise the rates at which capital gains and income from work are taxed.
However, the IPPR said headroom against the chancellor’s fiscal rule was likely to have shrunk by between £7bn and £15bn since the spring amid the impact on government finances from the Middle East war.
Calling for a cost of living package funded largely by higher taxes on wealth, it urged Healey to introduce a “rent stabilisation mechanism” to cap private rent increases, alongside a £2,000 cap on consumer energy bills, a freeze in fuel duty, and an increase in housing allowance benefits for households on universal credit.
The TUC said Healey should launch a social energy tariff and take action to help poorer households and young people with rising living costs. It also called for a rise in capital gains tax and higher taxes on banks.
Highlighting the costs from sticky inflation and higher interest rates, the analysis showed households with mortgages had spent on average £9,034 extra on repayments (£1,806 extra a year) since 2021. Those with loans had paid £1,911 extra in total (£382 extra a year).
Average rental costs have risen at a higher rate than mortgages, suggesting mortgage costs are being passed on to renters.
In the study of Office for National Statistics figures, it found households had spent on average £2,644 extra on electricity and gas bills since 2021 (£529 extra a year), and £372 extra on water bills (£74 extra a year).
Meanwhile, growth figures show that consumer spending remains behind pre-pandemic levels, after a period of broadly flatlining growth in household disposable incomes since the 2008 financial crisis.
Nowak said: “Eye-watering bill rises have hammered household budgets, squeezing consumer spending. That’s being felt on high streets up and down the country, holding our economy back.
“The chancellor needs a serious plan to put working people at the heart of growth, raising living standards so Britain can afford to spend. That means shielding households from punishing energy spikes and putting more money in workers’ pockets.”
The Treasury has been approached for comment.

====================================================================================================

Poland looks to economic heights in a country transformed since Soviet days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:00:22 UTC
14:00:22 KST

Above the rain-soaked streets of Warsaw, the observation deck of the Varso tower overlooks Joseph Stalin’s gift to Poland that has divided opinion for decades.
For some, the Soviet-era Palace of Culture and Science is a drunk confectioner’s nightmare; standing as a relic of oppression that should have been demolished. For others, it is an icon on the skyline and a monumental warning from history.
For the managers of the Varso – completed four years ago, as the tallest building in the EU – with its 310m-high spire rising symbolically above its Stalinist neighbour, it is a waypoint on Poland’s rapid path to economic prosperity.
“We look down on it,” says Cezary Błaszczyk, the managing director of HB Reavis in Poland, which owns the tower, gesturing at the palace opposite. A few months ago a slackline walker traversed the 500m gap between the buildings. “It was a symbolic walk from the past to the future,” says his colleague Natalia Kasperska.
“Since we are higher and taller than the Palace of Culture, we treat it as: ‘We got over communism, and now we are a country with a strong economy,’” Błaszczyk says.
Over the four decades since regaining its independence from Soviet-dominated rule, Poland has been transformed. Excluding oil-exporting states and financial hubs, incomes have converged with western levels at the fastest rate in the world; from 40% of the EU average in the mid-1990s to 81% last year.
National income surpassed $1tn (£755bn) last year, ranking Poland among the world’s 20 largest economies. International Monetary Fund projections show income per capita will soon overtake Japan and Spain.
“Four decades ago, we were in – excuse my English – deep, deep shit,” says Marcin Bosacki, the Polish deputy foreign minister.
Stirring a cup of tea and lemon in his opulent Warsaw office, he recalls queueing after school in the 1980s for up to five hours to buy butter and meat as the communist government imposed martial law.
However, the Gdańsk shipworkers’ Solidarność movement and Pope John Paul II’s 1979 pilgrimage to his home country paved the way for Poland’s transition to democracy in 1990 and an “economic miracle”. Integration with western institutions, including Nato in 1999 and EU accession in 2004, also helped.
For years, many Poles chose to emigrate to earn more abroad, in a brain drain accelerated by EU membership. Polish plumbers became shorthand in Britain for foreign labour amid the political battles over EU freedom of movement before the Brexit vote.
Now Britons are increasingly likely to have their taps fixed by Romanians and Bulgarians, after a surge in the number of Polish nationals leaving. In each year since 2021, when Brexit was enacted after a year-long transition period, twice as many Poles left the UK than arrived.
Meanwhile, Germany recorded more non-Germans moving to Poland in 2024 than heading in the opposite direction for the first time on record.
On the Varso’s 44th floor, in the Warsaw practice of Foster + Partners, Jedrzej Kolesinski and Krzysztof Gornicki are among those returnees. Both moved to London in their 20s to work in the British architecture firm’s head office – where they led the design team behind the tower they now occupy.
Gornicki says Poland has changed dramatically in the years he was away. He always wanted to return to contribute to the country, and raising a family near his parents in a safe, green city that is more affordable than London also has its plus points. Now the pair are working to design Warsaw’s new airport – the biggest greenfield infrastructure project in Europe.
“You can work globally from one location. In London we worked on projects from North America to Asia … right now, we’re doing the same thing, just from Warsaw.”
On the streets below the Varso, the sights and sounds of progress are unmistakable. Modern electric trams glide past skyscrapers, there are cranes and construction work, giant advertising boards, and dockless e-scooters.
The traditional working-class bar mleczny (milk bars) still do a roaring trade serving beetroot soup and Polish dumplings. But at the oldest, Prasowy, orders are taken on a digital touchscreen.
Once an asphalt desert designed for columns of Soviet tanks, the old Parade Square surrounding the palace has had a green makeover. Further development is planned to bolster Warsaw’s bid for the 2040 summer Olympics.
There are also growing pains. Just as the facades of Warsaw’s medieval old town – rebuilt from the rubble of the second world war – conceal 20th-century concrete, Poland’s stellar growth obscures tensions. The influx of global capital has driven up living costs, squeezing out poor Varsovians. Income inequality is among the highest in Europe, while growing political divisions set the stage for a fractious general election next year.
Convergence with the west also presents a novel challenge for a country with a reputation as a low-cost hub within the EU.
For years Poland’s cheap, skilled workforce attracted companies such as Volkswagen to build cars, Cadbury to make chocolate and banks such as JP Morgan to open global support centres. At €19.10 (£16.10) an hour, average labour costs (wages, taxes and other costs) are still half the level of Germany and France, but the gap is closing.
Since 2004, the average monthly wage has more than tripled in nominal terms to 8,904 złoty (£1,723) last year. The net monthly salary in Warsaw has risen by 120% since 2016, according to Deutsche Bank, lifting it above Rome and Lisbon. A meal for two in the capital now costs more than in Tokyo and the price of a cappuccino has doubled.
Rafał Brzoska, the billionaire founder of InPost, the pan-European parcel locker company started in Kraków, says Poles deserve their reputation as hard workers. But now the country must focus on working smarter, in higher-value-added manufacturing and knowledge-intensive services.
“The next phase will depend less on catching up, and more on productivity. We don’t have labour cost advantage at all. We need to focus on productivity, technology, cheaper energy and better regulation.”
He is, however, concerned about the tensions in Polish politics. Divisions between the nationalist president, Karol Nawrocki, and Donald Tusk’s liberal government have grown increasingly acrimonious. Meanwhile, fringe far-right parties together hold a fifth of public support. Poland is also investing heavily in defence and energy security – aiming to boost economic growth in the process – amid Europe’s response to Russian aggression and US disengagement.
“People may put trust in someone else that has a magic remedy. [But] there is no magic remedy. We need to be super careful in terms of believing there is a secret sauce that will magically change things,” Brzoska says.
“In my opinion – unfortunately for all of us – we still need to work hard.”
As part of its growth plans, Poland is pushing to become a regional tech hub, bolstered by a $1bn investment fund backed by public and private capital to support tech startups and AI companies. The number of high-growth firms is rising, including ElevenLabs, an $11bn AI audio generation and voice cloning company named after 11 November – Poland’s national independence day.
There are strong foundations for its ambition. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s annual programme for international student assessment (Pisa) scores ranks Poland equal to the UK among the top countries in Europe and globally for maths, while a greater share of adults have higher education qualifications than in Germany.
On the eastern side of the Vistula River in the gritty and creative working-class district of Praga, the campus of the games company CD Projekt Red shows the progress being made.
As the developer behind the smash hit games series The Witcher and Cyberpunk 2077, the company started life in the 1990s as an importer of CD games made by US publishers.
Michał Nowakowski, its co-chief executive, says this was about the limit of Polish ambition in the early days. Now he competes globally to attract coders, games developers and graphic designers.
“In the late 90s and early 2000s I feel there was a massive inferiority complex. Among everybody who was young, you wanted to catch up with the west.”
Growing up in the 1980s, his family were expelled from Poland in the period of martial law. He recalls visiting London aged 15 and being “blown away” by the Virgin megastore and British culture. “I could never imagine Poland being like it.”
Within a generation, though, he says this attitude would be alien to his own children. “For young people now they have no inferiority complex. They don’t stop and think: ‘Can we be as good as Brits, French, Spanish?’ It’s not holding them back.
“We have really good universities and skills teaching people. I think that can take us to unprecedented heights as a country.
“We’re a proper-sized country. Not too small, not too big; no inferiority complex any more. There’s nothing holding us back.”
