AI in healthcare: from fighting epidemics to family doctors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
04:05:49 UTC
13:05:49 KST

A situation report in an hour instead of a day: in Africa's fight against Ebola, AI shows how it can bolster healthcare, in Germany too. But experts warn of opaque systems and unresolved risks.
Since May, teams on the ground in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) have been fighting the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus. Every day, so-called health workers knock on doors and offer advice. They record recoveries and deaths and refer people with suspicious symptoms to medical facilities.
The knowledge of these health workers, whose notebooks reflect the condition of entire communities, has been digitised, according to a report by the AI company Anthropic.
Who has fallen ill? Who did the person have contact with, and where were they staying before they knew they were infected? To evaluate the answers and reports, Anthropic's Claude model was used. Among those involved in the study were CEPI, the WHO Regional Office for Africa and the national biomedical research institute INRB.
AI helps to assess the spread of epidemics more quickly
"A situation report is now produced within an hour instead of taking an entire working day," explains Marie Roseline Darnycka Belizaire, Director for Emergency Preparedness and Response at the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Africa. Artificial intelligence can help to assess the spread of epidemics more quickly and to target medical assistance more precisely, the WHO deputy director said on stage at the World Health Summit.
While analysing the data, potential outbreak hotspots were identified and preparations made, such as getting stocks of medical supplies to key hubs or high-risk areas.
That can be decisive in an emergency. The earlier health authorities respond to a potential outbreak, the better they can prepare and organise care. AI is intended to help process information from different sources more quickly and support decision-making by those in charge.
This positive example of how artificial intelligence can be used in healthcare illustrates a level at which AI can be deployed with relatively little risk. Experts, however, see far more possibilities for the future use of artificial intelligence.
The technology could improve diagnoses, relieve medical staff of administrative tasks and help to deploy scarce resources more strategically. At the same time, it raises fundamental questions: how reliable are the results? Can medical professionals understand how an AI arrives at a decision? And do patients really benefit?
AI as a support for overstretched healthcare staff
Demand for healthcare is growing worldwide. At the same time, many places lack staff, time and equipment. For Thomas Zapata, Director of the WHO Academy in Lyon, this is a key starting point for the use of artificial intelligence.
"We have to think about a paradox we are currently facing. We have more health professionals worldwide than ever before, and we have unprecedented technologies at our disposal," Zapata said in a panel discussion at the World Health Summit. Yet, he added, there is still an enormous shortage of healthcare workers. "Demand for health services keeps on rising."
He sees AI as a way to narrow that gap. It is crucial, however, not to see it as an end in itself, but as a tool to be integrated into existing health systems.
"AI is an enabler, a means to an end. At the moment we are very fascinated by technology and AI, but I think we need to place it in the right context within the health system," warns Zapata. In his view, artificial intelligence fits in two areas. On the one hand, AI could change the way care is organised; on the other, training and continuing education for health workers must adapt to the new possibilities.
Ultimately, AI can of course help to reduce workloads, streamline administrative tasks, improve clinical decision-making and enhance diagnostic processes. For him, it is particularly important that the technology frees up time for what cannot and should not easily be automated: caring for patients.
Above all, the Ebola crisis in the Democratic Republic of Congo has shown that trust in local health systems is lacking.
That gives doctors more time for their patients
Automated processes can make a particular difference where healthcare staff work under intense time pressure. Cecilia Mbaca, Senior Technical Adviser for Health and Emergencies at the aid organisation CARE, knows these challenges from more than 15 years on the front line.
For her, three questions are crucial: can AI support clinical decision-making? Can it take over repetitive tasks? And does it help to tailor care more closely to the individual needs of patients?
"If AI does this work very well, that leaves more time for the personal aspects of care, so that we can ask questions, listen, examine patients and refer them on to the next level of care," explains Cecilliah Mbaka, Senior Technical Adviser for Health and Emergencies at the aid organisation CARE as well.
She herself spent more than 15 years working on the front line, with little support, limited resources and a heavy workload.
In epidemics in particular, it is not just about medical data. Trust within the population also plays an important role. People must be able to trust that they will be protected and properly cared for in a health facility. In affected communities, this trust can be decisive in whether people seek medical help in time.
It is estimated that around 50% of deaths in villages in the DRC occur outside medical facilities, according to epidemiologist Maximilian Gertler. The local health system is under pressure and was not prepared for the Ebola outbreak. Thousands of protective suits are needed every day to shield nursing staff from contamination. Germany recently increased its aid by 21 million euros.
AI can therefore support the organisation of care. On its own, however, it cannot ensure that people trust medical facilities. As AI experts themselves criticise, the path leading to a diagnosis is still often opaque.
The transparency problem: how does AI arrive at its diagnosis?
Modern AI systems can analyse large volumes of data and detect patterns that humans might miss. Yet in many cases it remains unclear exactly how they reach their results.
Thomas Thesen, Professor of Medical Education and Informatics at the Geisel School of Medicine at Dartmouth University in the United States, describes the problem like this: "They are extremely good at recognising patterns, but they are really bad at explaining to us what those patterns actually are." Chatbots and large language models such as Claude or ChatGPT have what he calls an explanation problem. In this respect, artificial intelligence remains a black box.
This so-called black-box problem is particularly relevant in the healthcare sector. When a system provides a diagnosis or treatment recommendation, medical professionals need to be able to judge whether it makes sense in the specific case. A result on its own is not always enough; the path leading to it also has to be traceable.
"That is the problem of explainability. They cannot explain in human-understandable language how they arrive at these conditions."
This black-box issue concerns not only transparency but also responsibility: who is liable if an AI provides a wrong recommendation? That is why, for Mbaka, it is crucial that AI does not simply spit out results, but genuinely supports decision-making.
Expert: AI must not replace learning in training
Artificial intelligence can also help in training medical professionals, for instance by making information more accessible or assisting with repetitive tasks. But when it comes to learning itself, Thesen, the professor of medical education and informatics, also sees risks.
He points to a study that compared searching for information via conventional search engines with using an AI chatbot. The students who used the chatbot ended up with more superficial knowledge that was less firmly anchored.
"These so-called desirable difficulties are actually very important for the learning process. And if you outsource all the cognitive work of learning to a chatbot – which may be highly efficient – you do not actually learn anything."
Anyone who needs to retain knowledge in the long term should not, in his view, let an AI take over every mental step. Especially in medicine, it can be crucial to make the right decisions even when technological support is not available.
Thesen therefore also recommends using AI primarily where it reduces workload. Where the aim is to understand knowledge and retain it in the long term, independent learning must continue to have its place.

Brazil Senate approves Bill to shorten work week in election boost for Lula

Brazil Senate approves Bill to shorten work week in election boost for Lula
- Brazil’s Senate passed a Bill to end the “6x1” work schedule and cut weekly hours to 40 without lower pay, giving Lula a possible election boost.
- The vote passed 75-1, and Lula said it means “more time to live, rest, be with family” and is “a victory for workers.”
- Bolsonaro changed his stance and backed the Bill, while business groups warned it could raise costs and cut productivity.
AI generated
BRASILIA – Brazil’s Senate approved legislation to shorten the work week without reducing pay, handing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva a potential lifeline days ahead of an election he is trailing.
The Senate voted 75-1 in favour of the Bill on Oct 14 in two rounds of votes, granting final passage to a proposal that will end the so-called “6x1” work schedule, under which some 16 million Brazilians work six days a week with one day off.
A former trade unionist, Lula has put the proposal, which will give workers subject to the 6x1 schedule an extra day off, at the centre of his efforts to mount a comeback from a first-round upset that turned right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro into the front runner ahead of Brazil’s Oct 25 run-off.
The leftist leader earlier in 2026 made the reduction in weekly working hours – to 40 from 44 – the flagship promise of his campaign.
Since finishing behind Bolsonaro in the Oct 4 first-round vote, he has challenged the Senator to back the proposal in social media videos and staged rallies in Sao Paulo and Brasilia where many attendees called for passage of the plan.
Bolsonaro, who previously opposed the Bill and sought to delay the vote until after the election, reversed course on Oct 13, saying he would vote for the legislation because most workers support it.
Investors and prediction markets consider Bolsonaro the favourite, and no candidate who trailed in the first round has won a run-off since Brazil returned to democracy in 1989.
Polls, however, suggest Lula is still within striking distance.
Bolsonaro would take 51% of valid votes, excluding blank and null ballots, to Lula’s 49% in the run-off, according to a Quaest survey released on Oct 14.
Bolsonaro outperformed Quaest’s final poll of the first round by about two points, while Lula underperformed by one.
Lula hailed the Senate vote, saying the policy is “more than just a change in working hours”.
“It means more time to live, rest, be with family, watch one’s children grow up, take care of oneself, and enjoy life,” he said in a social media post. “This is a victory for workers.”
The question facing Lula is whether broad popular support for the measure will translate into an electoral boost.
Many of his major policies, including new tax exemptions for workers, debt renegotiation initiatives and a programme to provide basic medicines at no cost, are overwhelmingly popular.
But the 80-year-old President has struggled to turn that into votes, and segments of his working class base have moved rightward amid labour market shifts, crushing household debt levels and the rising cost of living.
Bolsonaro has continued advocating for an alternative proposal that he argues would provide greater flexibility in labour rules by letting employees negotiate hours with businesses, calling it a better solution than Lula’s.
Business groups have opposed the work week change, arguing it will increase costs while reducing productivity.
Lula’s government also unveiled a debt relief proposal for so-called micro-entrepreneurs on Oct 13, targeting voters who typically lean conservative. BLOOMBERG

Adelaide laneway named in honour of hip hop pioneers Hilltop Hoods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
04:00:39 UTC
13:00:39 KST

Hilltop Hoods honoured with laneway and mural in Adelaide CBD
Pioneering Australian hip hop group Hilltop Hoods rapped about "Goin' down a hard road" in 2006.
Now, the Adelaide trio are being honoured with a laneway in their hometown.
Clubhouse Lane, running off Hindley Street in Adelaide's CBD, was renamed Hilltop Hoods Lane at a ceremony today.
Two large-scale murals featuring the group and their associated iconography, created by Adelaide artist Vans the Omega, run down both sides of the laneway.
The Hoods, who still call Adelaide home, say it's an "incredible honour" to have their own laneway in the heart of the city they know and love.
"We have great memories of gigging in that part of town," Pressure told Double J's Dylan Lewis.
"When we were paying our dues and coming up there was heaps of old bars and clubs that we used to play. Some of them are still there, some are not."
Paying tribute to one of Australia's most successful and enduring musical acts, Hilltop Hoods Lane is the sixth addition to City of Adelaide's City of Music Laneway trail.
The growing collection includes landmarks recognising South Australian music legends Cold Chisel, Sia, Paul Kelly, No Fixed Address, and The Angels.
Hilltop Hoods even have some suggestions for the next honorary music landmark.
"I reckon Funkoars need a lane! Surely Guy Sebastian should have one," they told Lewis. "Guy Lane? Does have a ring to it."
Lord Mayor Jane Lomax-Smith said Hilltop Hoods's enduring impact on Australian music and culture made them a worthy addition to Adelaide's City of Music Laneways.
"Once considered the Australian music industry's underdogs, the Hoods have harnessed their talent and determination to not only top the charts but build a multi-generational fan base in their mosh pits," Dr Lomax-Smith said.
"Despite their global success, they have never forgotten their Adelaide roots. That's why it's fabulous to permanently recognise their achievements on the streets."
Starting as teenagers in 1994 around the hills of Blackwood, Hilltop Hoods elevated Australian hip hop from the underground and into the mainstream. And to resounding success.
The trio — Suffa (Matthew Lambert), Pressure (Dan Smith) and DJ Debris (Barry Francis) — have released a record-making seven ARIA number one albums, won 10 ARIA Awards, six APRA Awards, and sold out multiple national arena tours.
They have made triple j's annual Hottest 100 on a record 27 occasions, the most entries of any music group.
Their 2003 breakout single The Nosebleed Section came second place to INXS's poll-topping Never Tear Us Apart in last year's Hottest 100 of Australian Songs, in which they charted twice more (Cosby Sweater at #64 and 1955 at #73).
"Few music acts are as deeply woven into the cultural fabric of South Australia as Hilltop Hoods," said Vans the Omega, wanting his artwork to honour their connection to devoted fans and the wider public alike.
"This work aims to be both uplifting and historic, offering a place to reflect on our own lives and the journey we have shared alongside music that has shaped generations of fans of all ages.
"Like the Hoods, these walls stand as a lasting testament to what can be achieved through hard work and determination in our beautiful, humble city of Adelaide."
The first Australian hip hop group to have a laneway named in their honour, Hilltop Hoods join a growing list of musical landmarks around the country. That includes lanes named for AC/DC and Chrissy Amphlett in Melbourne, and The Go Between Bridge in Brisbane.

Unpolished, anti-Bibi, but evasive on peace: who is the Israeli opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
04:00:23 UTC
13:00:23 KST

He has been called the man who is everything the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, is not.
Gadi Eisenkot, a former general and the main opposition candidate in Israel’s elections this month, is unpolished where Netanyahu is slick.
To Israelis he is both menschy (decent) and schlumpy (unkempt), his crumpled appearance contrasting with Netanyahu’s hair rinse, makeup and obsessive need to control his media depiction.
In the Israeli commentator Anshel Pfeffer’s framing, he is the anti-Bibi among a roster of wanna-Bibis.
And in an era of Israeli politics that has been defined by betrayals, dirty tricks and public and private smears, Eisenkot’s brand is rectitude. He only entered politics four years ago, and the name of his party – Yashar – means “straight” or “honest”.
But on key issues, an Israel under Eisenkot may not look very different, as he has been non-committal on crucial issues – including the two-state solution and Israeli settlement of the occupied West Bank.
“He’s not sleek. He’s not corrupt. I think he’s going to be looking more inwards than outwards. Because he’s a military guy, he’s interested in calming the waters,” said Mairav Zonszein, a senior analyst for the International Crisis Group.
“[But] he’s hedging a lot.”
For many voters, Eisenkot’s appeal is less about ideology than the vibe around him.
Key to his appeal, said Dahlia Scheindlin, an Israeli pollster and political analyst, is his “very modest background”.
While Netanyahu is the son of a Polish-born academic, Eisenkot’s family were Mizrahi Jews from Morocco. He joined the army as an infantryman, and worked his way through the ranks to become the Israeli military’s chief of staff.
“The fact that he’s from a working-class background, from a peripheral area, contributes to an overall sense that voters see in him somebody who is more with the people,” Scheindlin said.
“He’s seen as empathetic. He’s seen as straightforward. That’s why I think they probably focus-tested the names of the party, and people probably thought he seemed very honest.”
But if ideology remains an important predictor of how Israelis will vote, what precisely does Eisenkot believe in?
On the domestic front, he is pushing for a full investigation of the intelligence failures that allowed Hamas’s deadly 7 October 2023 attack. More divisive is his support for the end of the military draft exemption for the ultra-Orthodox, long a source of friction in Israeli society.
On the biggest issues, not least a two-state solution that would create a Palestinian state – he is ambiguous.
“I’ve never said that the solution is two states for two peoples,” Eisenkot said on the campaign trail. “There is a very deep religious-national conflict here, and anyone who thinks an agreement can be reached now is gravely mistaken.”
On the broader issue of Jewish settlements in the West Bank, Eisenkot is also evasive. He opposes the planned E1 settlement block that is seen as a potential obstacle to any future Palestinian state, but he supports settlement in general.
Where Eisenkot separates himself from the current government, is over Netanyahu’s decision to place the far-right, pro-settler minister Bezalel Smotrich in charge of the occupied West Bank, where there has been a surge of settler violence, prompting widespread international condemnation and sanctions.
Eisenkot has said he would immediately “reverse” that situation and put the army back in charge of the West Bank.
Sceptics say Eisenkot and his allies are pushing for a return to an old, failed strategy: managing the conflict with the Palestinians – not solving it – with an aim of mitigating international pressure on Israel.
“What Eisenkot and the rest are basically saying,” said Prof Yossi Mekelberg of the Chatham House thinktank, “is we’ll be better CEOs. We’ll manage the country better, not take it in a different direction … They are not really talking about the Palestinian issue.”
Eisenkot is unequivocally not a dove in his views on the use of military force. As Israel’s northern front commander during the 2006 second Lebanon war, he was the architect of the notorious Dahiya doctrine, promising that Israel would wield “disproportionate power … and cause immense damage and destruction” – a policy that would see its fullest expression in the current Gaza war.
On Gaza, he has been more of a military realist, insisting two years ago that Israel was unlikely to win “total victory” over Hamas, and calling for a strategy that prioritised the lives of hostages still held by Hamas. His son Gal Meir Eisenkot, 25, died of his wounds in late 2023 after an operation in Gaza to recover the bodies of Israeli hostages.
Eisenkot’s philosophy governing the use of state violence is not the same as Netanyahu’s, who he criticised last year for saying that Israel needs to become a “super-Sparta” – a militarised state, feared by its neighbours.
But while observers say an Eisenkot administration would be likely to crack down on settler violence in the West Bank, they wonder if it would go much further.
“I think that is the low-hanging fruit and about half of Israeli society feels it would be good to crack down more [on violent settlers],” said Scheindlin. “It would help his foreign relations,” she added, but wondered whether there would be “a second step”.
And even if Eisenkot wins sufficient votes to take the lead in putting together a coalition, there is question of how long such a government could survive – and what room he would have for making policies.
“There will be a change if there is a different government,” said Mekelberg, “But I think it’s about managing expectations.
“He would not be a prime minister who is facing corruption allegations [like Netanyahu]. I see it potentially as a government of containment, where there is an opportunity to build relations with the world again and not just [have ministers making] statements that lead you to the international court of justice and the international criminal court.”
While Eisenkot has captured a moment for those who oppose Netanyahu, Scheindlin wondered how much is down to his character – and how much is projection.
“I think Israel can get back to a normal path as long as there’s somebody who actually cares about the people. And people have projected on to him that he really cares about the people.
“The more people see him, the more they project on to him the things that they want to see: he’s the one who will bring ‘professionalism’; he is the one who enjoys the aura of being ‘above politics’ because he comes from the army.”
Shai Bazak, an Israeli former diplomat and communications figure and former adviser to Netanyahu, argued that Eisenkot’s main selling point may well be that he will not take dramatic action.
“After a very charismatic and dominant leader, people deliberately choose someone less charismatic because they simply want peace and quiet,” he told Politico. “They do not want all the drama any more.”

‘I am still a child, it cannot be good to be married’: how drought forces Afghan families to sell girls as brides
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
04:00:21 UTC
13:00:21 KST

‘I’m not happy about this,” says 11-year-old Khatira, who was sold into marriage to repay debts, sitting in her home in Qala-e-Naw, capital of Badghis province in north-west Afghanistan. “She was healthy before her engagement, now she is worried and cries a lot,” says her 40-year-old mother, Noor Bibi.
When her 20-year-old husband-to-be comes to her home, Khatira runs away. Since her engagement, she has stopped going outside because she “is ashamed of having a husband in front of the other girls”, says her mother.
Khatira’s father grew wheat and herded cattle before the family was displaced from its rural village by drought.
In Badghis, 95% of the population relies on rain-fed agriculture and livestock to live. But droughts, made more frequent and extreme by climate breakdown, have robbed people of their incomes.
As a result, selling young daughters into marriage to repay debts, feed the family or pay for medical treatment has become a common way to cope.
“As a mother, I cried a lot, but I knew my husband had no choice,” says Gul Bobo, who does not know her own age, regarding her daughters, aged two and five, at her home in Tayz Nāwah, a village 12 hours’ drive from Qala-e-Naw. Both girls are engaged to be married.
Like many there, Gul Bobo’s husband used to buy seeds each year and rent a tractor or donkey to cultivate a wealthier man’s plot of land.
“I know they are too young to be engaged but we had no choice – otherwise we would have waited until after 18,” says Gul Bobo.
“I expect them to be beaten, but there is nothing I can do about it. And at 14, they will be pregnant.”
Underage brides are often expected to have children when they reach puberty, leading to well-documented health problems – in a country where maternal mortality is among the highest in the world.
They are also expected to know how to run a household. When they are unable to do so like adults would, domestic violence from in-laws is not unusual.
Five-year-old Nazila’s husband-to-be is 15. According to Gul Bobo, she could leave to live with her in-laws in two or three years.
‘I would have preferred for her to be dead rather than be married off to such an old man,” says Bana, the mother of Gulalai, 11, who is engaged to a shopkeeper in his late 40s. Her parents owed him money.
The story is always much the same. Gulalai’s father was a farmer and the family were displaced by crop failure from their remote village in Qadis, Badghis province.
“We have to sacrifice a family member to save the others,” says Gulalai’s father, Niaz Mohammad, who says he would have preferred to wait until his daughters turned 20 to marry them off – instead, four were married as children.
The family only eat homemade bread, tea and wild mallow leaves they gather and boil, using rubbish to make a fire.
When asked about climate change, most people in Badghis do not know what it means. In villages, most live in mud homes, with no electricity besides the occasional solar-powered battery, and little transport aside from an occasional motorcycle. The population relies on so little to live that notions of overconsumption or greenhouse gas emissions are completely alien.
In a desperate attempt to survive droughts over the past nine years, thousands have abandoned their ancestral villages to try to find work in Qala-e-Naw, often in vain.
To feed his family, Mohammad Yawaz, 55, sells ice-cream on the roadside for 100 afghanis (£1.20) a day, after spending his mornings with his six-year-old daughter Zubaida, collecting cans and bottles. They make, at best, 500 to 1,000 afghanis a month reselling them.
Yawaz eventually felt he had no choice but to marry off his first daughter, now 15, who has already left for her husband’s home, and Zubaida, who was engaged last year to a 12-year-old boy.
His neighbour, Surgul, is in the same situation. In the morning, he collects rubbish with his daughters Zartila, 10, and Bibi Aisha, seven, who are both engaged. The decision to sell Zartila into marriage was taken after the family had to endure “three days and three nights with nothing to eat”.
Recently, Surgul sold the only battery he had for lighting in his mud home to buy medications for one of his daughters. A few years ago, he and his wife lost an infant to illness.
But this was not always their life. Surgul once had cattle in his village. As droughts hit the area, he sold them.
Cattle markets in Badghis are full of men selling their precious animals because they cannot afford to buy fodder to compensate for the lack of grass. In some areas, villages have become ghost towns.
Some families go to Herat, the third-biggest city in Afghanistan, where the Shahrak-e-Sabz camp houses tens of thousands of displaced people. They come here in the hope of finding humanitarian aid – but it has dried up. Then they resort to selling their daughters into marriage to repay debts.
Darellah, 15, lives with her 30-year-old husband, Mollah. Her family was displaced from their village in 2018.
That year, Badghis suffered a historic drought, and since 2021, droughts have ruined harvests and starved livestock every year.
Now pregnant, Darellah is visiting her family. “I am still a child … it cannot be a good decision to be married at that age,” she says. Her sisters, Bibi Zat, nine, and Rahimah, 11, are both engaged but still live with their parents.
Their neighbours were all displaced by the drought as well. Bahahuddin, 40, had to sell his land.
When he found himself unable to feed his family by collecting rubbish and begging, he sold his 10-year-old son Ziauddin’s kidney for 100,000 afghanis. He wanted to sell his own but said he was not healthy enough for people to buy it.
In the camp, stories like these do not raise an eyebrow. Residents say children have often died from not being able to access health services.
Khomakha, 30, is another neighbour displaced by the droughts. Her husband made a deal to marry off their two-year-old daughter Fatemah only three months after the girl was born.
The urgency came as they could not afford the small fee for shared transport to take their eight-year-old son, Ehsanullah, who has blood cancer, to the hospital for a transfusion each week.
Khomakha may not see Fatemah ever again after she marries and moves to a village 15 hours’ drive away. “I will not be able to afford transport to visit my daughter once she leaves,” Khomakha says.
But life is not much easier for families who stay in their villages. In Khoshkian, Abdul Aziz’s wheat harvest failed seven times in eight years. Over the years of drought, he sold five of his daughters into marriage, for between 90,000 and 150,000 afghanis (£1,000-£1,750), to repay debts.
Mazari, one of Abdul Aziz’s daughters, left home at about 12 or 13. Now 16 or 17, she lives with her husband in his 40s, their two-year-old son, and a baby born just one day ago.
“Getting married at 12 was really hard; when I came to his home, I wasn’t able to cook, but my husband and in-laws have been really kind,” she says.
Her younger sisters, aged between three and 13, will live at home until their bride prices are paid. While they weed a field, they remember the years of war when soldiers from the previous government used to shoot from the mountains behind them.
“There was no difference – the previous government’s army shot whether we were Taliban or civilians,” says Shamael, Mazari’s 13-year-old sister. “We feel better now because we are not woken up by fighting.”
Sitting in the field, Shamael’s sisters nod as they continue weeding.
“People cultivate their land for several years. People invested a lot to do so, and there is no harvest, so they are in debt,” Shamael says. “Then some people sell their lands, some sell their daughters – to survive.”
There is no law regarding the age at which girls can leave home for marriage. Bride prices range from hundreds to a few thousand pounds and are paid in instalments. Once the dowry is paid in full, the in-laws are free to claim the bride. In many cases, it happens at the beginning of puberty.
“Everything that is happening to us is because of poverty,” Shamael says.
On her wedding day, in the village of Nookhil, Bibi Samia, 14, at first appears calm. She had cried a lot the night before, says her mother. She has remained stoical for hours but, just before she has to leave her home, bursts into tears. “I am not happy because I am very small,” she says.
As foreign aid dries up, programmes that should provide support for these girls are disappearing.
Mark Calder, advocacy director for Afghanistan at the aid organisation World Vision International, says: “Early marriage exposes girls to potentially deadly health risks, but the clinics treating them are disappearing as aid is cut.”
The psychological toll for child brides is immense. Despite her crushing poverty, Sara brings her daughter, Aisha, 12, to primary school every morning, walking from the same slum Khatira lives in, bordering Qala-e-Naw, since they fled droughts in 2021.
Still, Sara’s husband sold Aisha into marriage to a 20-year-old to repay debts; when it is paid, she will have to go.
The bride price has done little to alleviate the family’s poverty: their rent of 1,000 afghanis has not been paid for two months and the landlord has told the family to leave. When her last baby was born, Sara had to walk to the hospital, unable to pay for a lift.
Despite this, Sara says: “I try not to contact the in-laws to ask them for the rest of the bride price, so that Aisha will not have to leave.”
Sara cannot speak about her daughter’s impending marriage in front of her, as it makes Aisha cry. She prefers to let her continue quietly doing her homework while she still can.

How Gaza changed Europe, exposing cracks that grow bigger by the week | Shada Islam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
04:00:21 UTC
13:00:21 KST

For three painful years, Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza, in retaliation for the Hamas terror attacks on 7 October 2023, has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, wounded thousands more and reduced most of the territory to rubble. It has changed views of Israel across the world, increased support for Palestine and raised questions about US power.
Europe’s failure to hold Israel’s government to account has cost it global credibility and influence. But I fear something even more consequential than that: Gaza is changing Europe itself.
European governments did nothing to try to stop the genocide; there have been no collective sanctions, no trade restrictions or ending of arms sales to Israel. The EU sanctions Russia over its war in Ukraine but retains almost-business-as-usual ties with Israel, a blatant double standard.
Gaza has exposed how Europe’s supposedly universal commitment to human rights is now conditional on whose suffering is recognised, whose resistance is considered legitimate and whose demands for justice are considered worthy of attention. EU policymakers are selective even in the groups of women they choose to celebrate as heroic in struggles against occupation and the children whose right to life they defend.
After these three years I am convinced that the question of Palestine has become a stress test for European democracy itself. Democratic societies can only thrive when there is space for dissent, including dissent that is uncomfortable, disruptive and politically inconvenient. Yet today, across Europe, governments – which speak up against undemocratic conduct abroad – are now unapologetic in imposing restrictions on free expression and peaceful protest at home. Police violence at pro-Palestinian demonstrations has become the norm, and those whose only crime is to speak up publicly for Palestinian rights are increasingly criminalised or made the target of suspicion.
When this happens repeatedly it undermines public trust in the legitimacy of democratic governments and institutions. As Rabin Baldewsingh, the Netherlands’ national coordinator against discrimination and racism tells me: “Governments and public institutions have a responsibility not to reinforce polarisation when society is deeply divided.” Sadly, the opposite appears to be happening.
Many societal fractures existed before Gaza, but they have received new oxygen and traction over the past three years. The EU’s Fundamental Rights Agency has long warned of both anti-Muslim racism and antisemitism. What has become increasingly troubling over the past three years is the political framing under which antisemitism in connection with Gaza is rightly treated as a threat to democracy, while Islamophobia is viewed through a security and anti-terrorism lens.
This can’t all be blamed on the far right, either. True, some extremist groups hide their age-old prejudices behind accusations that it is Muslims and refugees who have “imported” antisemitism into Europe. But the European People’s party (EPP) – the EU’s largest political “family” for pro-European centre-right and conservative politicians, including Ursula von der Leyen and Magnus Brunner, the EU’s most senior official for migration – is also giving old and debunked Islamophobic tropes a new and dangerous lease of life.
The party backed a resolution in June condemning the “interference of political Islam” in European democratic processes. If “political Islam” was interfering in European democracy, the resolution may have some validity. But there is no evidence for the claim, and certainly none advanced in this document, which merely echoes French conspiracy theories about “Islamist entryism” and calls for a crackdown on alleged members of Muslim Brotherhood networks. It claims to make a distinction between “political Islam” and the Islamic faith itself but it reads more like the start of a witch-hunt of European Muslims.
An even tougher EPP resolution, backed by a majority in the European parliament on 8 October, goes a step further by casting suspicion on Muslim civil society groups’ loyalty, activity and participation in European democracy.
Hiba Latreche, president of Femyso, a pan-European network of young Muslim organisations that is explicitly mentioned in the EPP’s attack, points out the double bind of such unfounded allegations. “When we are not active we are accused of communitarianism, separatism and lack of integration. When we engage and exercise active citizenship we are accused of having a hidden agenda.”
Such an environment demands even stronger anti-discrimination action. Yet Europe’s most powerful pro-equality body, the European Network Against Racism (ENAR), has just lost European Commission funding. Worried that this could mean it has to cease operations by the end of the year, ENAR has launched a legal challenge against the decision at the EU’s general court.
Beyond the visible, there are many unwritten post-Gaza codes being applied inside the EU’s corridors of power that are harder to measure and challenge. Islamophobia has become “quite blatant”, EU officials tell me, with micro‑aggressions and remarks about Muslims’ supposedly “irrational and emotional” behaviour. Like von der Leyen in her recent “state of the union” speech, many now talk about Gaza as a humanitarian emergency, but not as a human-made genocide. There is agreement on the need for action against settler violence and illegal settlement in the West Bank, which is framed as the work of “extremists”, but confronting the Israeli government remains difficult.
For many, it has also been a time of uncomfortable conversations, ruptured personal relationships and disillusionment. But there are also moments of intense solidarity, as across Europe pro‑Palestinian movements have extended to include trade unions, faith groups – including Jewish activists – students, celebrities and senior politicians. Every Thursday, members of the EU Staff for Peace gather for a vigil outside the commission and the EU Council. Former EU commissioners, ambassadors and senior staff continue to write to their bosses urging stronger action against Israel.
So all hope is not lost. But Gaza has stripped away a great deal of self-soothing assumptions that many of us harboured about Europe. As the far right becomes more influential, too many have forgotten that democratic freedoms rarely disappear all at once. They begin to erode when some voices are silenced, some suffering is ignored and the rights of some citizens are treated as less deserving than others.
- Shada Islam is a Brussels-based commentator on EU affairs. She runs New Horizons project, a strategy, analysis and advisory company

====================================================================================================

A perfect storm: how the super El Niño is devastating the fishing industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
04:00:20 UTC
13:00:20 KST

On 10 June 2026, the government of Peru made a decision that it knew would hurt one of the world’s major fishing industries. It stopped all anchoveta fishing boats from going out to sea, suspending the fishing season. At first the order was temporary, but in mid-August, the suspension turned into a total closure. This was no easy call. For one thing, it was a brutal blow to the Peruvian economy.
Peruvian anchovies – the scientific name is Engraulis ringens – are not the salty, punch-packing little fillets in a puttanesca sauce or caesar salad dressing. That is a different species – Engraulis encrasicolus – which is smaller, tastier and found mostly in the eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Only a small part of Peru’s anchoveta catch is eaten in fish form. The rest – more than 90% – is immediately processed as fishmeal and fish oil, packed in sacks and barrels, and shipped to fish, shellfish and seaweed farms, factory farms and nutritional supplement producers around the world.
The vast majority of the anchoveta industry is concentrated off the coast of north-central Peru, and it is hard to overstate how economically significant this fish is. By weight, Peruvian anchoveta have made up about a 10th of the entire global commercial fishing catch since 1970, more than any other fish. Some years, the anchoveta catch is worth close to $3bn and directly employs almost 50,000 people, close to a quarter of a million if you include indirect jobs. The Peruvian central bank is forecasting a 30.7% contraction for the fishing sector and about 78,000 job losses in 2026, and another 44,000 in 2027.
The ripples will be felt far beyond Peru’s borders. The country is by a long way the world’s most important exporter of fishmeal – a crucial input to aquaculture and livestock agriculture virtually everywhere – and prices are skyrocketing as a result. This anchoveta closure will have a direct impact on jobs, food supplies and supermarket prices the world over. Peru’s then minister of production, César Quispe Luján, defended the decision as the only one possible: “The government has the responsibility to manage marine resources based on scientific criteria, timeliness and a long-term vision. When there is a need to strengthen conservation measures, it is necessary to act with prudence and responsibility to ensure the sustainability of the fishery.”
When the June suspension was announced, the fishing boats had already been back in port for weeks. At the start of the season, in early April, Peru’s ministry of production had set a total allowable catch of 1.9m tonnes. But in May, it closed the fishery for 15 days, with only 24% of the quota harvested. When the closure was extended to a full shutdown, there were even hints there would be no second fishing season this autumn. The main concern of the Instituto del Mar del Perú, which recommended the closure, was the risks already posed by this year’s El Niño, and a fear of what is to come.
We are heading into what global climate models forecast as the most severe El Niño since the 1880s, the earliest for which we have accurate records. The super El Niño that is developing “may end up the strongest by a truly mind-blowing margin,” said climatologist Zeke Hausfather in July. Peru’s anchoveta population was already down before the suspension of fishing. We cannot know how the anchoveta would have fared in the absence of El Niño, but we know that its presence makes things considerably more volatile. The warmer waters produced by El Niño threaten the plankton on which anchoveta feed, which in turn threatens the anchoveta population.
The oceans, which cover 71% of the Earth’s surface, are among the most gloriously alive parts of the Earth. While there are vast oceanic deserts, there are also marine versions of the Amazon basin and the Okavango Delta. These rich zones are the result of a host of wonderful contingencies: the shape of the continents, the force of gravity, the chemistry of the ocean and the crazy network of ocean currents.
Most years, the Humboldt current, which flows north along the west coast of Chile and Peru, produces the most fertile fishing grounds on Earth. The current generates massive upwellings of deep colder waters that bring nutrients up from the depths, creating some of the most biologically productive zones in the ocean. This extraordinary biological abundance astounded the first Europeans who witnessed it. Islands piled tens of metres deep with the guano of innumerable birds feeding on sea life; the ocean boiling with million-tonne anchovy and sardine shoals; tuna, bonito and mackerel virtually leaping from the water. By comparison, today’s Humboldt current system is much impoverished – industrialised extraction has taken its toll – but even so, it remains exceptionally productive. Intensive commercial fishing continues, and the most intensive of all is for Peruvian anchoveta, 6in (15cm) flashes of big-eyed, blue-backed silver.
In an average year, Peru produces 20% of the world’s fishmeal. But that word “average” obscures the extraordinary volatility of the anchoveta catch in the decades since the fishery was fully commercialised after the second world war. In 1970, Peru landed more than 12m tonnes of anchoveta. In 1973, the catch fell by 88%. The shock of this stock collapse was so existential for Peru that the military dictatorship introduced the first regulatory regime for the anchoveta fishery. In 1984, the catch plummeted again, to less than 100,000 tonnes, a fraction of what it had been 15 years earlier. The catch recovered in 2000 to about 9.6m tonnes, but has declined since then. Recent annual catches have been in the 2m-4m tonne range.
Overfishing has played a crucial role in this ecological and economic rollercoaster ride. But the crazy seesaw of the anchoveta fishery is not merely a tale of rapacious industrial extraction, but of how overfishing combines with the bouts of accelerated oceanic warming driven by El Niño, which always hit Peruvian coastal waters especially hard.
El Niño (“the little boy”) is the name that fishermen four centuries ago gave periods of unusually warm water off the coast of western South America. It is so named because the episodes usually reach their peak towards Christmas.
Like most oceanic and atmospheric dynamics, both El Niño and the anchoveta fishery are partly born of the fact that the Earth is a spinning ball, turning upon an axis that runs through the middle of the planet from pole to pole. Since the ball is rotating at a fixed rate, different latitudes on its surface spin at different speeds: in the span of one Earth day, places near the equator have a lot more distance to cover to get all the way around than places near the poles, so they rotate faster. Vancouver, the city where I live, is moving around Earth’s axis at 1,100km an hour. If you are reading this in London, you are a little bit closer to the north pole, so spinning a little slower (1,042km/h), but if you are in Jakarta, near the equator, you are whirling about at 1,665km/h. Had someone granted Patsy Cline her wish to Stop the World and Let Me Off, she would have shot out of Nashville at 1,350km/h.
If everything on the Earth’s surface just stayed where it was relative to everything else, things might be fairly straightforward, but that is not how it works. While the terrestrial parts of the Earth spin at a constant rate and in the same direction, the parts of it that are fluid – its molten core, the atmosphere and the oceans – can move at different speeds and in different directions. Often, from our perspective on the surface, it seems as though the fluid parts are somehow moving against the direction of spin. The easterly trade winds of the tropics, for example, which have carried ships across the oceans for as long as we have sailed the seas, are the result of atmospheric patterns shaped by the planet’s eastward rotation, and the higher rotational speeds around the equator. From one perspective, you might even say these “winds” are something of an illusion: it’s not the air that’s blowing past us, but we who are racing through the slower moving air.
Among the most fundamental fluid dynamics resulting from the Earth’s spin are the patterns of circulation of the oceans. These include the planet’s five massive oceanic gyres: two each (north and south of the equator) in the Atlantic and Pacific, and one in the Indian Ocean. These gyres are great circular systems of currents that span each ocean from coast to coast and from the poles almost all the way to the equator, and they too are partly created by the Earth’s roundness and rotation.
The gyres in both hemispheres are like vast oceanic gears spinning in opposite directions: the northern gyres rotate clockwise, while the southern gyres turn anticlockwise. In the Atlantic and Pacific, they meet at the equator, driving wind and water westwards. Along the eastern side of all these gigantic rotating marine gears, cold waters are moving from the poles toward the equator: the Humboldt current is the South Pacific’s version of this process. As these currents push up against the oceans’ eastern coastlines they are driven towards the surface, bringing nutrient-rich cold water to the pelagic zone. In non-El Niño or “neutral” years, the Humboldt current runs all the way up to the seas off northern Peru, where the anchoveta and everything else feast.
During El Niño events, the trade winds weaken and atmospheric pressure builds up over the coasts of Asia. As a result, the higher-temperature water spreads eastwards. With milder El Niño events, it reaches into the central Pacific, south of Hawaii, but in stronger phases it piles up off equatorial South America. Warmer water, much less hospitable to anchoveta, is driven south along the coast into the Humboldt current system, sometimes as far as Lima, Peru, 12 degrees south of the equator. There it sits at the surface, pushing the colder water into the depths and severely limiting the upwelling flows that bring nutrients to the upper layers of the ocean.
For the anchoveta and everything above it in the food web, the result is a disaster. The warm surface waters have the devastating double effect of shrinking the area of the ocean in which the anchoveta find suitable habitat, and robbing them of their main food source, the plankton that depend on the nutrients carried by upwelling. Anchoveta populations shrink, sometimes dramatically; birds starve, predators higher up the food chain that rely on anchoveta scatter or die; and there are a lot fewer fish for the fishing fleet to catch.
Every massive crash in the anchoveta fishery is the consequence of a severe El Niño event hitting already intensely exploited stocks. The climate crisis increases ocean temperatures and acidification, all of which is bad for most marine life, anchoveta included, and further exacerbates the situation by intensifying El Niño.
In its latest report on the state of the world’s marine fisheries in 2025, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization deemed more than a third to be overfished, meaning harvests exceed the rate of reproduction. Though the report classifies most of the anchoveta stocks in Peru as “maximally sustainably fished”, it is worth remembering that calling a fishery sustainable does not take account of the fact that populations are at historically low levels – and, since the onset of industrial fishing, are more vulnerable than ever before.
As with many other shrinking natural resources, what brought us to this point is a combination of increasingly efficient technology and too little regulation for too long. In the case of anchoveta, as regulation has increased, so too has fishing technology adapted itself to the behaviour of the fish. The anchoveta disperse at night to feed, but during the day, when predators like tuna can easily see them, they form large shoals or “schools”. Schooling, when vast numbers of fish mass together in a huge ball, evolved as a strategy to minimise predation. Schooling protects the bulk of the shoal by sacrificing those unlucky enough to end up on the outside edges.
The problem, at least from an anchoveta’s perspective, is that this behaviour evolved before they ran into humans and our modern fishing gear. From the deck of a fishing boat, a school is an enormous swarm of fish conveniently clustered in a tight space near the sea’s surface. Huge fishing vessels can pull anchoveta from the water in enormous volumes. When a boat finds a shoal, it circles the fish while dropping a long float line from its stern. From the float line, which can be as much as 600 metres long, hangs a 50-metre net. Once the net is set in a ring around the shoal, a cable at the bottom edge is pulled tight, and the lower reaches of the net close like the mouth of a drawstring purse, capturing the shoal in what is now a massive mesh bag full of fish. The boats have enormous holds, some as large as 800 cubic metres (equivalent to about 12 40ft-long shipping containers), and can bring millions of anchoveta to port for processing.
Schooling behaviour presents a challenge to scientists monitoring fish populations, because it means anchoveta are not evenly dispersed across their habitat, but massed together in great fish balls. We might catch a lot of them, but we can’t assume there are a lot more fish out there.
A further cause for alarm, and not just for commercial fisheries, is that in the web of predatory relationships, anchoveta are a crucial link between plankton and larger animals: the anchoveta feed on plankton, their population flourishes, which provides food for scores of predator species higher up the food chain, including humans. When anchoveta numbers plummet, it is a potential catastrophe for the whole ecosystem and those who depend on it. When this happened to the Black Sea anchovy late in the 20th century, phytoplankton populations exploded, depleting oxygen levels in the water and threatening an already fragile marine ecosystem, and the other commercial fisheries that depended on it.
The anchoveta matter in all these economic and ecological ways, but they also epitomise a widespread problem in our extractive age: in ecosystems around the world, we are pushing species into conditions of such fragility that we are no longer in control of the situation. Even if we slow or even stop destroying habitat or harvesting, things are now so precarious that “natural” environmental variability could tip them over the edge.
Anchoveta have proven resilient in the face of remarkable levels of environmental variation, from extreme El Niño events to the frenzied overfishing of decades past, but the prognosis isn’t good: research suggests that ocean warming and its effects will lead to a decrease in the amount of anchoveta in the ocean of between 8% and 14% per decade across the 21st century. As sea surface temperatures rise, and salinity and oxygen levels change, the anchoveta’s territorial range shifts, as does the stock’s fertility, spawning seasons and the distribution of the population across different life stages (a crucial consideration in fisheries, because it is imperative to avoid catching fish that are too young to reproduce). All of this is unfolding against the background of ongoing climate heating at a planetary scale, to which El Niño introduces additional and increasing stresses.
This year’s closure of the anchoveta fishery before the quota was reached came as a surprise to some in the industry, but it is not the first time it has happened. Just last year, Peru set the first season quota at 3m tonnes, but when scientists noted the juvenile population – the younger fish yet to reach reproductive age – was especially at risk, the government called the fleet off the water with just 2.5m tonnes landed. “The sustainable extraction of anchovy is a strategic priority for the country,” Jesús Barrientos, the vice minister of fisheries and aquaculture, said at the time.
The anchoveta harvest limit is usually binding: the fleet generally catches its allowance, or very near to it, by the time the season closes. Getting so close to the limit may seem like a bad thing, but it is taken as an indicator of success. A lot of what we know about fish populations is based on industry data about where, when and how many fish are captured, and how old those fish are. However, illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing are estimated to be as large as a fifth of the legal commercial harvest worldwide. For that very reason, the Peruvian government polices all commercial fisheries very tightly: in 2024 alone it undertook 163,000 inspections, and confiscated 1,000 tonnes of illegally harvested anchoveta.
If all these efforts work out as planned, then when a fishery hits the quota in a fishing season, it means (at least in theory) that the industry is accurately reporting their operations, the stock assessment was more or less correct, and the regulators and inspectors are doing their jobs. The alternative – a quota that is never reached – might at first glance seem better, but would be very bad news if the whole fleet was out there and couldn’t find enough fish to meet the allowance. This has happened before, most famously during what fisheries expert Dean Bavington calls the “managed annihilation” of Atlantic cod. For centuries, cod had made Newfoundland’s Grand Banks one of the planet’s most productive fisheries. By the time the fishery collapsed completely in the early 1990s, the absurdly high quota didn’t matter because the boats couldn’t find anywhere near enough fish to meet it. The oceans had been emptied; the cod were gone.
In contrast to Newfoundland, Peru’s fisheries managers decided to protect the anchoveta population, despite pressure from an industry that has a lot of sway with the government and is increasingly concentrated in the hands of massive corporations, foreign and domestic. (In November 2024, the Canadian conglomerate Cooke Incorporated paid $1bn for Copeinca, the largest anchoveta firm in Peru. Cooke now controls a sixth of Peru’s anchoveta fishery, and a fifth of its meal and oil processing.) Corporate power like that doesn’t take massive revenue losses lying down. When the government delayed the start of the fishing season in 2023, the CEO of an anchoveta conglomerate moaned that regulators were “lost in a sea of ignorance”, creating an existential crisis for an industry that was “fighting to survive”. At that point, the ministry budged a little, and temporarily reopened the fishery. This year, it held firm: “Sustainability takes precedence over any short-term decision,” Juan Carlos Requejo, the minister of production, said in mid-August.
The stakes are enormous. Peru’s fisheries sector contracted by almost 75% in June and July, and fishmeal production is plummeting just as prices have skyrocketed to almost $3,500 a tonne, more than twice what they were at the same time last year. The same is true of all the fisheries for high-value species that prey on anchoveta: the bonito, jack mackerel and the rest of the bigger torpedo-shaped beauties that bring in premium prices.
The privatisation of the Peruvian anchoveta fishery began in 1992 and culminated in the introduction of a vessel quota system under the guidance of the World Bank in 2009. The creation of private property rights in the fishery has had complex repercussions, not least the increasing marginalisation and impoverishment of tens of thousands of smaller-scale fishers and their communities. Almost all the anchoveta catch is controlled by a collection of wealthy boat owners and big firms with close ties to the state.
Monitoring is continuous, sophisticated and data-driven. The idea is to operate a sensitive, real-time regulatory regime based on the assumption that there is no longer any such thing as “normal” – and there isn’t. Every day of the anchoveta season, Peru’s ministry of production pays close attention to scientists’ advice and is ready to step in, not just to end the season altogether but to make tweaks on the fly, for example ordering temporary closures of local fishing zones.
In August, the ministry declared a national fisheries and aquaculture emergency, which included launching a marine survey, Operation Eureka LXXVIII, to undertake an intensive stock assessment coordinated with the largest vessel owners. The outcome has not yet been officially announced, but in early October, Diario de Chimbote, the newspaper of Peru’s main fishing port (one of the largest in the world), reported that 2026’s second season will be cancelled entirely: the water is too warm, forcing the anchoveta in deeper and closer to shore, and the risks to juveniles are too great. Though this decision has not been confirmed, if it goes ahead, the closure is expected to cost Peru’s economy about $1.4bn. As Jessica Luna, president of Peru’s National Fisheries Society, an industry organisation, put it, the sector is “in the ICU”.
Prior to these most recent calamities, many industry observers have noted that by some measures, Peru’s management of fish populations is a remarkable success story, all the more impressive in light of the way that multinational capital often gets what it wants in similar situations. In the past 20 years, the see-sawing catch numbers that plagued the industry for so long have declined considerably. But so too have average harvests, and the trend is decidedly downward. In the midst of what has been called a “Godzilla” El Niño, it is worth reconsidering what counts as success in a world in which crisis has become normal. Is the goal just a slightly slower road to the same destination?
So far, despite everything, the anchoveta keep coming back, albeit in drastically diminished numbers compared with a few decades ago. It does sometimes seem as though they can survive whatever we throw at them, and their persistence can easily be mistaken for indestructibility. But there are limits to the robustness of any species or natural system. The fact that we don’t know where those limits are doesn’t mean they aren’t there, and as we push the anchoveta, and so much of the planet, we inevitably press upon fragilities we never knew were there, sometimes because until very recently they probably weren’t. Many of our leaders would have us believe that we can continue as before, but we have never been here before, and we need to proceed with modesty and care. Often, you only recognise a threshold once you have crossed it.

Architecture Between Land and Water: Design Lessons from the Bayou
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

A bayou is a slow-moving body of water, typically a creek or river that winds through low, flat terrain in a broader wetland landscape. Found throughout the Gulf Coast, bayous are distinct from swamps, which contain forested wetlands characterized by standing water, and from marshes, where tall grasses and herbaceous plants grow in saturated soils. The currents of a bayou landscape support biodiverse ecosystems of plants, trees, insects, birds, and fish, while the shifting water levels, saturated ground, humid air, heavy rainfall, and long, hot summers create a blurry environment between land and water, wet and dry, interior and exterior.
Communities have inhabited bayou environments for thousands of years, and the architectural language within them reflects generations of adaptation to unique environmental and hydrological conditions. Buildings are elevated above wet, flood-prone grounds with steep roofs and deep overhangs to shed rain and provide shade, while porches, courtyards, breezeways, and tall interior spaces move air through occupied spaces. Certain aesthetic characteristics, like earth-toned materials or broad front porches, will recur throughout the region, but beneath these elements lies a more consequential architectural logic. Bayou architecture patterns historically accommodate this variability, negotiating water, heat, humidity, and airflow through the way buildings meet the ground, shape their envelopes, and organize the spaces between inside and outside.
From Houston, often referred to as the Bayou City, to New Orleans and the landscapes of southern Louisiana, the following lessons demonstrate how accumulated local knowledge continues to inform contemporary design in the twenty-first century. As architects design for places where established climatic conditions are becoming less predictable, these projects offer a perspective on architecture with a careful observation of place and respond through adaptation. Foundations, roofs, envelopes, landscapes, and social spaces become part of an environmental strategy, revealing how vernacular knowledge translates into contemporary architecture and how buildings respond to the landscapes they inhabit.
How to Touch the Ground
In bayou environments, the ground is not a reliable foundation. High water tables, poorly drained soils, periodic inundation, and the movement of water through the landscape leave the ground saturated for extended periods, while storms and seasonal flooding raise the water beyond its ordinary limits. The first architectural question is how to touch the ground.
Across the region, buildings respond by rising above it. Slender piers and stilts allow water and air to pass beneath a structure, while more substantial columns, raised foundations, and elevated plinths keep occupied spaces above anticipated flood levels. The appropriate approach depends on soil conditions, flood exposure, building scale, and program, but the underlying principle remains the same. The foundation is treated as a negotiated edge between architecture and a landscape whose conditions are expected to change seasonally.
How to Move Air
In a hot, humid climate, an essential component of interior comfort will depend on creating sustained air movement. Courtyards, deep porches, breezeways, and other shaded thresholds extend the building outward while drawing air deeper inside. When oriented and proportioned for the scale of the building, courtyards encourage cross-ventilation through adjacent rooms and allow warm air to rise through the open space above, while vegetation and shade reduce solar exposure within the interior courtyard surfaces. Openings in the building envelope positioned across from one another strengthen air movement, allowing prevailing breezes to pass through the building through skylights, open doors or windows, and courtyards.
Deep porches perform a complementary role in drawing air movement. By shading walls and windows from direct sun, they reduce the amount of heat absorbed by the building envelope, while their depth protects doors and operable windows from rainfall, allowing them to stay open through rainy weather conditions. Porches, whether they wrap the entire building or frame the primary entrances, create a thicker, more adaptable boundary threshold between inside and outside, one that tempers sun, rain, and moving air. In the bayou, the edge of a building is an inhabitable space that helps the architecture adjust to changing conditions throughout the day and across the seasons.
How to Shed Water
In a landscape defined by frequent, intense rainfall, the roof is one of a building's most consequential environmental systems. Vernacular builders across the bayou region respond with pitched roofs and deep overhangs that move water quickly away from interior spaces while shading the walls below and protecting openings from sun and rain. The dogtrot house offers a clear example of a single pitched roof that extends across two enclosed volumes and the open breezeway between them, sheltering the passage from rainfall while creating a shaded corridor through the center of the home where air can circulate.
Contemporary architects continue this logic, using shed roofs, folded planes, butterfly forms, and clustered gables to direct rainfall, collect water, frame views of the surrounding landscape, and extend protective canopies over the porches below. Not every building in a wet climate requires the same roof form, but the movement of water is essential to shape the form and orientation throughout the design process. Roof geometry, overhangs, gutters, drainage, and collection systems work together to determine where water falls and how it returns to the ground. In this way, the roof gives architectural expression to environmental forces, turning practical decisions of managing rainfall into the building's identity.
How to Design with Moisture
In the persistent humidity of the bayou, materials and wall assemblies must release moisture, allowing walls, roofs, and other exposed surfaces to dry before prolonged dampness leads to mold or corrosion. Traditional builders relied on durable and decay-resistant materials, such as cypress, brick, and stucco, while contemporary projects expand this palette with metal cladding, fiber cement, and other materials selected for their ability to withstand repeated exposure to moisture. Ventilated rainscreens extend this logic into the construction of the wall, creating a drained and ventilated cavity behind the exterior cladding where water escapes and air circulates.
Shutters, louvers, jalousie windows, transoms, and screens are tools of operable assemblies that create adjustable layers between occupied spaces and the exterior, allowing buildings to admit breezes when conditions are favorable, reduce solar exposure during the hottest times of the day, and provide protection when storms arrive. Contemporary construction balances operability with the demands of moisture control, airtightness, and mechanical conditioning. The designers in this environment create a building envelope that is capable of responding to humid conditions.
How to Design for Heat
In the bayou climate, heat and humidity reinforce one another, making the control of solar heat gain essential to maintaining comfortable interior spaces. Light-colored exterior walls and reflective roofing materials reduce the amount of solar energy absorbed by the building envelope, while shade from deep eaves, porches, vegetation, and adjacent structures limit direct exposure in the interior spaces. These strategies are relatively simple, but they effectively reduce the thermal burden placed on occupants and mechanical cooling systems during the long, hot summers that characterize the region. Inside, tall ceilings increase the volume of space above occupants and allow warmer air to collect above, while clerestories, transoms, and high operable vents pull warm air outside. Even in compact floor plans, additional height creates a sense of openness while contributing to a more responsive interior.
How to Work with the Landscape
Site orientation reduces solar exposure, captures prevailing breezes, and determines interior daylight, but in cities and towns, existing street grids, neighboring structures, and zoning setbacks may limit the freedom to position a building. Even within restrictions, openings should be aligned with local wind patterns, western exposures should be shaded by trees, galleries, and deep eaves, and courtyards should be used to bring light and air into urban footprints. In a bayou environment, the site is part of a larger hydrological system. Permeable surfaces, bioswales, rain gardens, planted buffers, and areas designed to temporarily hold water will slow runoff and reduce the volume of water entering drainage systems. At a larger scale, preserving existing vegetation and maintaining connections to natural drainage patterns ensures a project participates in the hydrology of its surroundings.
How to Center Social Life
Perhaps the most compelling lesson of bayou architecture is that some of its most comfortable spaces are rarely found in the entirely enclosed, interior spaces. Deep porches, shaded courtyards, covered galleries, and dogtrot passages occupy the threshold between a controlled interior and the exposed landscape, offering long hours of shade and access to moving air. Their social value is inseparable from their environmental performance. Shade, airflow, and protection from rain make longer periods of occupation possible, while their position at the edge of the building creates opportunities for interaction that more clearly divided interior and exterior spaces may not provide. Climate-responsive design shapes how and how long people gather together, turning environmental infrastructure into social infrastructure.
Lessons from Architecture in the Bayou
The lessons of the bayou carry new weight in the contemporary practice because the landscape that shaped them is changing. Sea level rise, subsidence, coastal land loss, and increasing flood exposure alter the conditions under which communities across the Gulf Coast build and rebuild. Buildings rise above uncertain ground, envelopes open and close, landscapes hold or slow water, and air movement makes extreme climates more comfortable.
A changing climate exposes the limits of adaptation at the scale of an individual building. Architecture alone cannot indefinitely compensate for changing coastlines, subsiding land, disappearing wetlands, or increasing flood risk. Designing for the bayou asks architects to design beyond the building's boundary toward the larger systems that make inhabitation possible. The local knowledge embedded in bayou architecture is not a collection of historical solutions to reproduce, but a way of design-thinking to expand upon. Its larger lessons are of responsiveness and observation. In the bayou and far beyond it, place-based design considers the comfort, health, safety, and identity of future landscapes.
This article is part of the ArchDaily Topic: The Architecture of Water: Territories, Tensions & Transformations. Every month we explore a topic in-depth through articles, interviews, news, and architecture projects. We invite you to learn more about our ArchDaily Topics. And, as always, at ArchDaily we welcome the contributions of our readers; if you want to submit an article or project, contact us.
