Europe’s debt map flips: Belgium borrows like Greece as France pays more than Italy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
03:57:13 UTC
12:57:13 KST

Eurozone treasuries are preparing record bond sales for 2027 just as the IMF warns that borrowing costs have hit a two-decade high.
Imagine an investor who fell asleep in the summer of 2012, at the height of the euro crisis, and woke up this morning. He would remember a simple map. In the north, a core of countries that borrowed cheaply, with Germany at the centre. In the south, a periphery of debtors – Greece, Portugal, Spain, Italy, Ireland – that paid dearly for the privilege of staying in the single currency. Fourteen years later, that map no longer describes the eurozone.
Belgium, home to the European Union institutions, now borrows for ten years at 4.29%. Greece, bailed out three times, pays 4.35%, almost the same rate. Portugal, rescued in 2011, pays less than Spain. Ireland, rescued in 2010, pays almost the same as the Netherlands. And France, which he remembered as part of the core, pays more than Italy.
The old periphery has moved north. That is the backdrop against which eurozone governments are about to ask investors for more money than ever before.
What moved the border
Bond yields are the interest rates a government pays to borrow. They rise when investors think a country will need more money than it can comfortably repay, and they fall when it proves the opposite. Greece has spent a decade proving the opposite.
In 2025, Athens ran a budget surplus of 1.7% of gross domestic product (GDP), and its debt, though still the highest in Europe, fell by more than nine percentage points of GDP in a single year.
“For years, when markets talked about sovereign risk in Europe, the focus was usually on the periphery,” Ken Egan, head of European sovereign credit at the rating agency KBRA, told Euronews.
Over the past decade, he said, those countries have followed more prudent fiscal policy, improved their primary balances, extended debt maturities, collected taxes better through digitalisation and rebuilt their banks.
“That has helped smooth refinancing risks and put debt on a much firmer path than 10 or 15 years ago.”
Belgium went the other way. Its deficit widened to 5.2% of GDP last year, larger than France’s 5.1% in the same year, and its debt rose above 109% of GDP in the first quarter of 2026, and investors noticed.
“The traditional core has changed as well, but in a different direction,” Egan said.
“In some cases there is less clarity around the policy path, more political uncertainty, rising structural spending pressures and much higher refinancing costs than governments had become used to during the low-rate period.”
France’s position on the map is defined by one figure above all: the state spends 57.2% of everything the economy produces, the highest share in the G20. Debt has reached €3.6 trillion, or 119% of GDP, up from 98.2% before the pandemic.
The bill due in 2027
On 29 September, the French Treasury set out how much it will need to borrow next year: €340 billion in medium- and long-term bonds, a record, equal to about 11% of GDP and up from €310 billion this year.
Much of it is not new spending but old debt coming back for refinancing, as bonds issued during the pandemic and the energy crisis mature.
Every euro of that debt is being renewed at a higher price.
France has paid an average interest rate of 3.55% on medium- and long-term bonds issued so far this year, up from 3.14% last year. Its annual interest bill is forecast to rise from €62.6 billion in 2026 to €72.9 billion in 2027, roughly a fifth of what the state collected in revenue last year.
That last number is the one investors now read first.
“Markets are looking much more closely at the fiscal story, and not just at how much governments are borrowing, but what they are borrowing for,” Egan said.
“Borrowing that supports investment and future growth is one thing; borrowing mainly to cover a rising interest bill is viewed quite differently.”
Germany is issuing a record €512 billion of securities this year, but to pay for defence and infrastructure, which is the kind of borrowing markets forgive.
Italy and Spain will each refinance several hundred billion.
And the IMF, in its latest World Economic Outlook, pointed to a detail that makes every government more exposed: in the G7 and Spain, nearly 30% of public debt now matures within a year, so a change in interest rates reaches the budget within months rather than decades.
Why sovereign yields keep rising
Between February and September, the average 10-year yield across the G7 rose by more than a full percentage point to its highest level in nearly two decades, the IMF’s fiscal chief Rodrigo Valdés and his deputy Era Dabla-Norris wrote this week.
The oil shock, persistent inflation and the money pouring into artificial intelligence all played a part. But at the centre, they wrote, are fiscal fundamentals: investors demand more to lend for ten years to governments that keep spending more than they collect.
The European Central Bank (ECB) has added to the cost, raising its deposit rate twice this year to 2.50% to contain inflation.
The German 10-year yield, the floor for the whole eurozone, has climbed from 2.64% in February to 3.45%. France’s has risen twice as fast and briefly touched 5% in early October, the widest gap with Germany since 2012.
The danger, Egan said, is that the market itself becomes part of the problem.
“A political headline or weak budget can push the curve higher, refinancing becomes more expensive, fiscal space narrows, and the market then has another reason to demand a higher premium.”
That loop turns faster than it used to, because the buyers have changed.
For a decade the ECB bought government bonds with newly created money; now it lets them run off.
“There is less natural long-duration demand in the market, with central banks stepping back, pension demand changing and more of the marginal buying coming from price-sensitive investors,” Egan said. Higher energy prices, he added, make it worse by “weakening growth while keeping inflation and rates higher”.
The IMF describes the result in one sentence: in a growing number of countries, the interest rate on new debt is now higher than the growth rate of the economy.
When that happens, debt rises on its own unless the government runs a surplus before interest.
Most of Europe does not. “The more countries wait, the more painful the adjustment becomes,” the Fund wrote.
Is this 2012 again?
Not yet, says Lombard Odier. The Swiss bank’s investment office argues that markets are “pricing uncertainty rather than the conditions for a new sovereign debt crisis”. France’s interest payments remain affordable, at slightly above 2% of GDP, half Italy’s.
Its current account deficit is small, and it does not depend on foreign money the way Portugal, Spain and Greece did in 2012, when they imported capital worth 7% to 12% of their economies every year.
The bank’s forecast is dull rather than dramatic: French spreads stay wide until a credible budget passes parliament, probably not before the May 2027 presidential election, and the euro drifts lower, to $1.09.
Clara Raposo, vice-governor of the Banco de Portugal, offered a different warning this month.
Sovereign bond markets, she said, have become more sensitive to inflation, fiscal doubts and geopolitics, and shocks now spread faster from one country to another, amplified by funds that sell first and ask questions later.
“Trust may be intangible, but its economic consequences are real,” Raposo said.
Your debt, my inflation
The transmission is not only financial.
A randomised experiment with German firms in the Bundesbank’s panel, which surveys roughly 7,000 firms, published by the Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR) earlier this year, found that half of them think the ECB will hold back on rate rises to protect weaker treasuries.
When researchers showed them a pessimistic forecast for the average debt-to-GDP ratio of France, Italy and Spain, the firms raised their expectations for German inflation three years ahead by 1.4 percentage points among those who distrust the ECB.
Fiscal stress in one member state, in other words, can raise inflation expectations in another, and the channel is trust.
In 2012, the question was whether the periphery could pay. In 2027, the question is who, exactly, the periphery is.

U.S. inflation accelerates in September amid high prices
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:54:54 CST
12:54:54 KST

WASHINGTON, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- U.S. inflation accelerated in September, according to data released Wednesday by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) jumped a hefty 3.7 percent year on year, exceeding Wall Street estimates of 3.6 percent and rising from the previous month's 3.4 percent.
Headline inflation increased by 0.6 percent month on month, driven primarily by a 9.1 percent surge in gasoline prices, according to the data.
Core CPI, which strips out volatile food and energy costs, also ticked up, climbing 2.6 percent over the last 12 months.
Price increases for shelter, car repairs and medical services rose at a time when Americans have been reeling from price hikes since inflation took hold in 2021.
Some experts noted that inflation is ramping up rather than tamping down.
Dean Baker, a macroeconomist and co-founder of the Center for Economic and Policy Research, told Xinhua, "Inflation is getting higher, not lower and it's in the core, not just energy ... If you're the Fed looking to hit a 2 percent target, you're going the wrong way."
The news caused markets to drop on Wednesday, on fears that a rate cut is even further off than investors had expected. Some experts said the Fed would have to raise rates to get inflation down.
Gary Hufbauer, a nonresident senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, said "the outlook is for continued high PCE inflation, near 4 percent. To push the rate down, the Fed needs to increase the policy rate to near 5 percent."
Meanwhile, the midterm elections are just around the corner and Republicans are expected to take the brunt of voters' blame for high prices.
Some experts noted that inflation remains a risk to the GOP, the party in power.
Brookings Institution Senior Fellow Darrell West said "inflation remains painfully high and that poses serious risks for Republicans in November."
However, even if Democrats grab control of Congress, prices are unlikely to come down this year.
While halting the Iran war could bring down energy prices, addressing underlying inflation would require significant interest rate hikes, an unlikely move by the Fed given concerns that aggressive tightening could trigger an economic downturn. ■

8 U.S. states sue OpenAI over alleged ChatGPT safety risks
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:54:42 CST
12:54:42 KST

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Attorneys general from eight U.S. states filed separate lawsuits against OpenAI on Wednesday, accusing the artificial intelligence company of endangering children through its ChatGPT chatbot and misleading consumers about the product's safety.
The lawsuits were filed independently in state courts by Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana, as part of a coordinated bipartisan legal effort.
According to statements released by the state attorneys general and court filings, OpenAI allegedly designed ChatGPT to be overly agreeable and to simulate human compassion, encouraging users to develop trust in the chatbot and spend more time interacting with it.
The lawsuits allege that ChatGPT can reinforce delusional thinking, provide dangerous medical advice and, in some instances, encourage users to harm themselves or others.
The states accuse OpenAI of misleading consumers about ChatGPT's safety while failing to adequately disclose known risks, in alleged violation of state consumer protection laws.
The lawsuits seek court orders requiring OpenAI to modify ChatGPT's operations and strengthen user protections, as well as civil penalties and damages.
Some of the legal demands also seek to restrict the development of self-improving AI models unless their alignment with human values can be demonstrated.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company had implemented age-specific safety measures, including parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections.
The company would continue working with experts to strengthen safeguards and cooperate with states on developing AI policies applicable to the broader industry, Pusateri said.
The coordinated legal action follows a lawsuit filed by Florida's attorney general in June over alleged safety risks associated with ChatGPT. ■

Feature: Winter Universiade flame reaches Changchun, passed from hand to hand
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:54:38 CST
12:54:38 KST

CHANGCHUN, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The flame lantern was carried into the Changchun History and Culture Museum on Wednesday morning, past a crowd gathered in the cold. It had come from Turin, Italy, where the flame was kindled on October 8 at the birthplace of the Universiade.
Its destination was Changchun, capital of northeast China's Jilin Province and co-host with neighboring Jilin City of the 2027 Winter Universiade.
Inside, 12 people waited to pass the lantern from hand to hand. They were chosen not for fame but for their work in the city, including a firefighter, a delivery courier, a student, a pilot, a police officer, a bank clerk, an insurance claims worker and a WorldSkills award winner. Organizers said the selection was intended to show that the flame belongs to everyone who helps build the city.
The last of the 12 to receive the lantern was Zhou Yang, a three-time Olympic short track speed skating champion. She then passed it to Changchun Mayor Gu Gang.
"The flame is very warm," Zhou said. "It represents athletes' burning dreams. The weather is cold today, so it feels warm. But it traveled thousands of miles from Turin to Changchun. This lantern is a heavy honor."
Zhou competed at the 2007 Asian Winter Games in Changchun and the 2009 Harbin Winter Universiade, where she won the 1,500m title. She said the Universiade gave her confidence ahead of the 2010 Vancouver Winter Olympics, where she won two gold medals.
"For me, it's a kind of inheritance," she said of going from competitor to flame bearer. "When I was a competitor, I received the baton from my predecessors. Now I've become a passer."
Among the 12 was Nilava Darya, a Belarusian sophomore majoring in Chinese language education at Jilin International Studies University, who will volunteer at the Games.
"I feel very excited and proud to witness and participate in this flame event," she said. "I welcome young people from all over the world to Changchun."
Darya said Changchun is quieter than other Chinese cities she has visited, and warmer. "I can say it's my second hometown," she said.
In the audience was 90-year-old Gao Xiangchen, who learned to skate as a child and took up figure skating at 65. He continued until he was 83, when his family persuaded him to stop.
"I'm so excited that a world-class winter sports event like the Universiade will be held in Changchun," he said. "I will definitely go watch in person. My favorite sport is figure skating."
His daughter, Gao Yan, was a volunteer at the 11th National Winter Games in 2008 and a torchbearer for the 2008 Beijing Olympics. She said the arrival of the flame symbolized both sportsmanship and Changchun's ice and snow culture.
The flame was collected in Turin, where the first Summer Universiade was held in 1959. Since 2018, Turin has been home to FISU's "Flame of Knowledge," and the flame for each Universiade is kindled there before being taken to the host city.
"The lighting of the 'Flame of Knowledge' in Turin always represents a strong link between the birthplace of the Universiade and the future host," said FISU President Leonz Eder, who attended the collection ceremony.
The 33rd Winter Universiade will run from January 15 to 25, 2027. It will be the first Winter Universiade held in China since Harbin in 2009, following the Beijing 2022 Winter Olympics and the 2025 Harbin Asian Winter Games.
Changchun 2027 will feature 97 events across 12 sports. Freestyle skiing will be the only snow sport staged in both host cities. All competition venues are existing facilities being upgraded, while 8,100 volunteer candidates have been recruited.
Nan Chunhua, an executive with the Games' large-scale activities department, was a member of the team that traveled to Turin for the collection ceremony. She said the flame's journey served as a bridge between the two cities.
"When the flame was successfully introduced into the lantern, I was very excited and moved," she said. "This flame carries the hard work of the entire preparation team and the good wishes of the world for the Changchun Universiade."
After the lantern was passed among the 12 representatives, it was used to light the Games' torch, named "Jixiang," or "Auspicious Soaring." Jilin provincial governor Hu Yuting then lit the cauldron, "Zhuxue Yangyan," which translates roughly as "Chasing Snow, Raising Flame."
For Zhou, the message was simple.
"I hope China's sports, especially winter sports, will get better and better," she said. "I hope athletes coming to Changchun will feel the warmth of the people here." ■

by sportswriter Liu Yang
FUZHOU, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The Fujian Sturgeons have retained their core roster, re-signed head coach Aleksandar Kesar and added three imports as the young squad prepares for the 2026-27 Chinese Basketball Association (CBA) season, which marks the return of relegation after a 22-year absence.
Fujian has kept nearly its entire domestic rotation from last season. Veteran Su Ruoyu, a key offseason addition, is recovering from a preseason injury and is expected to return to team training soon. Meng Yi, the leading scorer on the club's youth team, has been promoted to the first team, underscoring the club's commitment to developing homegrown talent.
The young squad drew widespread attention last season with a series of upset victories. Fujian earned its first-ever away win over powerhouse Guangdong Southern Tigers and went on to sweep the season series. The Sturgeons also snapped the Zhejiang Golden Bulls' seven-game winning streak and came from behind to beat the Beijing Ducks.
Fujian opens its new campaign on October 17 with an away game against the Jiangsu Dragons.
"Being captain is not about glory; it is about responsibility," captain Zou Yang said. "We cannot guarantee a playoff spot, but we will fight until the final buzzer every game. I hope the fans can see the resilience and tenacity in our play."
The 26-year-old forward spent the offseason training overseas to improve his ability to cope with physical pressure, sharpening his finishing through contact and his shooting consistency.
"As captain, I need to serve as a bridge between the coaches, local players and imports," Zou added. "I will try to help our younger teammates, making sure every player understands their role during games."
Three new imports headline Fujian's offseason additions. U.S. combo guard Javion Hamlet joins after three seasons with the Tianjin Pioneers, where he averaged 21.8 points and 5.8 assists per game last season. American guard Daryl Macon, who has NBA experience, adds perimeter firepower and defensive versatility, while big man Bennie Boatwright provides frontcourt depth.
The Sturgeons finished 14th in 2025-26 in Kesar's first full season in charge, narrowly missing the playoffs. The domestic players have an average age of 23.5 this season, making Fujian one of the youngest squads in the league.
"We had one of the youngest rosters in the league and came close to the playoffs last season, beating several top teams along the way," Kesar said. "We aim to build a winning culture here. Our young players have improved through summer training and will receive meaningful minutes."
The 2026-27 relegation framework introduces a new competitive dynamic for all 20 CBA clubs. Under the new system, the bottom two teams in the regular season will face the top two National Basketball League (NBL) sides in April 2027.
Club executive director Wu Bolan expressed confidence in Kesar while acknowledging the increased pressure brought by the league's structural reform.
"We give full trust to Kesar and his coaching group," Wu said. "Our focus is on internal development, team chemistry and competitive spirit, so that we can meet the new challenges."
"We aim to compete for higher standings, and we must hold onto the fighting spirit. This team will withstand whatever pressure the new season brings," she added. ■

Australia's unemployment rate rises to 4.7 pct
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
11:54:29 CST
12:54:29 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Australia's unemployment rate rose to 4.7 percent in September, as employment fell and more people became unemployed, official statistics showed on Thursday.
The number of employed people fell by 39,000, while the number of unemployed people increased by 9,000, Sean Crick, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) head of labor statistics, said in a statement.
The employment-to-population ratio fell 0.3 percentage points to 63.6 percent, while the participation rate fell 0.2 percentage points to 66.8 percent, Crick said.
The underemployment rate, which measures people who want and are available to work more hours, rose 0.1 percentage points to 6.3 percent, according to the latest data.
Part-time hours worked fell 1.5 percent in September, while full-time hours increased 0.4 percent, Crick said.
On a trend basis, which the ABS recommends for assessing underlying labor market conditions, the trend unemployment rate remained at 4.6 percent. Trend employment grew by 0.1 percent, while hours worked remained steady in trend terms in September, statistics showed.
Annual growth in employment and hours worked stood at 1.2 percent and 1.3 percent, respectively, the ABS said. ■

It originally planned to establish 14 security platoons under its Air Defense and Missile Command in 2027, per Liberty Times. One-year conscripts will serve in the platoons. The Air Force will now establish them in phases, with the rollout scheduled for completion in 2029.
To improve personnel safety, the Air Force also planned to acquire new vehicles in 2026 and deliver them to radar stations before the platoons are formed. This would allow service members to train in maintenance and repair, Liberty Times reported.
The procurement was delayed because manufacturers’ vehicle supply chains could not completely exclude Chinese components. As a result, companies declined to participate in the bidding process. A new round of tendering has begun.
The Defense Ministry said the Air Force follows the national security policy requiring non-Chinese supply chains, according to Liberty Times. Tender documents explicitly prohibit components and products manufactured in China, as well as Chinese brands, to ensure procurement quality and reduce information security and supply chain risks.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan could begin exporting pineapples to the US as early as February 2027, with administrative preparations complete and final import rules still pending from US authorities, Agriculture Minister Chen Junne-jih (陳駿季) said Wednesday.
The US Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) published a proposal outlining import requirements for Taiwanese pineapples in the Federal Register on March 3, per SET News. The public comment period has ended, but the US has yet to publish final rules.
Chen told reporters before a Legislative Yuan Economics Committee meeting that he hoped the US would finalize the requirements before Taiwan’s peak pineapple season, which runs from February through May. Initial shipments would primarily consist of the golden diamond variety, which accounts for more than 90% of Taiwan’s pineapple production.
Under the proposed rules, Taiwanese pineapples would be eligible for export after passing phytosanitary inspections, being confirmed free of pests of concern to the US, and receiving a phytosanitary certificate, SET News reported. The requirements would not mandate irradiation, vapor heat treatment, or removal of the fruit’s crown.
The proposal would allow pineapple varieties in the Cayenne group, including golden diamond and mango pineapples. The Agriculture Ministry plans to continue encouraging farmers to grow mango pineapples because they are better suited to storage and transportation.
According to the Agriculture Ministry’s latest statistics, Taiwan exported 15,700 metric tons of pineapples to Japan this year, per UDN. Shipments to Canada, South Korea, and Australia rose by nearly 409%, 171%, and 29%, respectively, while Taiwan also expanded into markets including New Zealand, Singapore, and Malaysia.

Bay watch with first approval for 5 mainland yachts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
03:38:53 UTC
12:38:53 KST

Five yachts from the Greater Bay Area have received approval to enter Hong Kong waters as a new scheme facilitating such cross-border visits takes effect on Friday, according to Director of Marine Wong Sai-fat.
The scheme allows yacht masters across the border to sit for accreditation exams up north without needing to travel to Hong Kong and authorises mainland organisations to conduct the assessments.
Visiting yacht owners and masters can submit pre-arrival vetting information online, doing away with the need to do so with a visit to a district marine office.
Visiting yachts can berth freely at five designated anchorage areas: Stanley, Tai Tam and Repulse bays as well as Three Fathoms Cove in Sai Kung and Tai O.
Speaking on an RTHK radio programme on Thursday, Wong stressed that there was currently no need to cap daily yacht visits from the mainland.
“Across the five anchorage areas, we can accommodate up to 115 yachts measuring 40 metres in length," he said.
"So we believe we have sufficient berthing space for yachts to dock smoothly where they want. That’s why we really don't see any need for a quota for now.”
Wong noted that around 300 mainland yacht masters had completed the training and passed accreditation to operate in Hong Kong waters so far.
To ensure safety, he said, the department has set up a monitoring system to track the yachts.
The system will alert vessels if their automatic identification system malfunctions or if they accidentally enter restricted waters.
Wong added that patrols and enforcement action would also be strengthened in the designated anchorages for visiting yachts.

Healthy corals help bleached neighbours regain colour: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
03:32:00 UTC
12:32:00 KST

Healthy corals help bleached neighbours regain colour: Study
- Stanford scientists found healthy corals can help bleached corals recover when they touch for three to five days. The study was published in Science Advances on Oct 14.
- The effect comes from healthy symbionts moving between corals through fused tissue, creating a “nutrient highway”. Bleached corals were not a lost cause.
- The method only worked with the same genet, and mixed pairings caused stinging cells. Researchers now want to scale the idea by reintroducing symbionts to reefs.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The world’s coral reefs face an existential threat from rising seawater temperatures that trigger widespread bleaching, a problem driven by climate change and compounded by 2026’s intense El Nino phenomenon.
But a new lab study by scientists at Stanford University finds that simply placing healthy, colourful coral in contact with their bleached counterparts is enough to bring the dying ones back from the brink – a finding that could eventually pave the way for real-world interventions if it can be scaled.
“It’s stunning,” lead author Daniel Collins told AFP about the outcome of the experiments, recalling the “eureka moment” when he first saw positive results and rushed to his PhD supervisor’s office to share the news.
The paper was published on Oct 14 in the journal Science Advances.
Coral reef recovery is a highly active area of research, with efforts ranging from using artificial nurseries to rescue reefs to finding and cultivating more heat-tolerant species.
Bleached corals had been largely written off because of their high mortality rate, said Collins – though the new work instead demonstrates they “really shouldn’t be thought of as a lost cause”.
The Stanford team ran a series of tests with pairs of cauliflower corals, finding five days of contact between healthy and bleached fragments was all it took for the latter to mount a spectacular recovery, at which point they could be safely pried apart.
The key to the success of the method – which the team informally dubbed “helping hands” – is the transfer of healthy photosynthetic algae, also known as symbionts, from which corals derive their colour.
Corals are marine invertebrates made up of hundreds to thousands of tiny, soft-bodied organisms called polyps.
They have a mutualistic relationship with symbionts, which produce the vast majority of food the corals require, in return for shelter, as well as water and the carbon dioxide they need to photosynthesise.
But in times of heat stress, algae can produce toxins, forcing their hosts to expel them.
Collins said the idea for the experiment came from two sources.
The first was a study that showed plastic waste in the ocean can promote disease in corals by transferring harmful pathogens, which made him wonder whether it would be possible to flip that mechanism on its head with a health-promoting transfer.
The second was a happy accident observed by Stephen Palumbi, the study’s senior author, also at Stanford, who noticed in his lab that a healthy coral and bleached coral had tipped over and were touching each other, and the bleached coral had started to recover.
The scaling challenge
The experiments revealed important constraints.
Three days of contact was the minimum required for a bleached coral to begin to recover, and five ensured full recovery.
They also had to be in direct contact – a few millimetres apart, and nothing significant happened.
A major limitation was that the process worked only when the two corals shared the same genetic background, or “genet”.
Mixed-genet pairings resulted in the corals deploying stinging cells, a hostile response that can be likened to organ rejection in humans.
Powerful laser microscopy revealed the mechanism: After a day or two of contact, the corals’ tissues began fusing, creating a “nutrient highway” between the pair.
The biggest challenge will be translating an exciting lab finding into a real-world solution.
“We likely will not be touching corals to one another on reefs,” said Collins, noting the sheer size of reefs tends to preclude this option.
However, it is possible to extract healthy symbionts and culture them – and the team is now thinking about ways to re-introduce them en masse to bleached coral.
This also has the benefit of side-stepping the genetic mismatch problem, which applies to the corals, not the symbionts. AFP

OpenAI bugging suspect allegedly booked one-way trip to Saudi Arabia
Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan was due to fly to Saudi Arabia on October 12, US prosecutors say in a court filing.
The Saudi national accused of bugging OpenAI’s headquarters booked a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia before his arrest, US prosecutors have alleged.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, a former OpenAI engineer, had been scheduled to fly to Saudi Arabia with his wife and another family member on October 12, prosecutors said in a court filing unsealed on Wednesday.
The FBI arrested Alfozan, who worked at OpenAI for about 15 months until his termination last week, on October 9, after OpenAI personnel reported the discovery of a hidden listening device in a conference room at the company’s San Francisco headquarters.
Alfozan, 35, has been charged with “using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications”.
The offence carries a maximum punishment of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.
Prosecutors disclosed the alleged flight booking to a judge on October 8 in a motion seeking to seal the criminal complaint against Alfozan, arguing he had the “means – and will have an incentive – to flee” the United States.
William Pernik, Alfozan’s lawyer, said he and his client planned to contest the criminal allegations and his client’s ongoing detention in court.
“We trust that the American justice system will treat our client fairly, despite the narrative painted in the media at this time,” Pernik told Al Jazeera.
“Our client is a well regarded professional with long standing ties to the community,” Pernik added.
“He is presumed innocent and is entitled to fair treatment and due process of law. The emphasis on his national origin and therefore suggestions of lack of trustworthiness or flight risk harken back to dark chapters of our nation’s history that we intend to fight fully.”
Alfozan’s arrest has shone a spotlight on concerns that frontier tech firms are a target for spying and industrial espionage amid the global race to gain an upper hand in AI.
Before joining OpenAI in July last year, Alfozan worked as a systems engineer at Meta and interned at Microsoft, according to a LinkedIn profile in his name.
Alfozan is also listed as a venture partner at Raed Ventures, a Riyadh-based venture capital firm whose other partners include Prince Khalid bin Bader al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family.
In a statement announcing Alfozan’s appointment in February 2025, Raed Ventures described the engineer as “a seasoned professional with extensive experience in tech startups” and said his role would involve “identifying promising investment opportunities and supporting startups on their journey toward growth and success”.

Vietnam Set to Sign Free Trade Pact With European Bloc This Week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
03:25:00 UTC
12:25:00 KST

Vietnam is set to sign a European Free Trade Association (EFTA) this week, as Hanoi closes in on a final trade agreement with the United States.
Reuters reported yesterday that the agreement with the EFTA bloc, which consists of Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, and Liechtenstein, will be signed in Hanoi on Sunday in the presence of Swiss Economy Minister Guy Parmelin, who is currently on a trip to Asia.
The talks between Vietnam and the ETFA began in 2012 and have proceeded at a steady pace since. The two sides officially concluded the negotiations in July, following a ministerial meeting in Reykjavik that involved “intensive technical talks.”
At the time, the ETFA stated that the agreement covered “trade in goods, trade in services, rules of origin, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, technical barriers to trade, investment, intellectual property rights, trade remedies, government procurement, trade and sustainable development, small and medium-sized enterprises, and cooperation and capacity building.” Bilateral trade between EFTA and Vietnam amounted to $5.4 billion in 2025, up from around $561 million a decade earlier, according to the bloc.
Hovering over the planned signing ceremony is Vietnam’s recent arrest of a Norwegian national of Vietnamese descent on terrorism-related charges. Nguyen Duc Thuan, 52, was among three activists from the pro-democracy group Viet Tan whom the Vietnamese authorities said were arrested for entering the country illegally. Rights groups, as well as Viet Tan itself, say that the three men were abducted in Cambodia, although Phnom Penh said that it had no record of the men leaving the country.
According to Reuters, Norway’s Foreign Ministry said that State Secretary Astrid Bergmal, who will attend the signing ceremony, “will raise the case of the detained Norwegian citizen with the Vietnamese authorities during her visit.” The Ministry added that it was treating Thuan’s case “as a high priority” and expressed hope that it “may be resolved without unnecessary delay.”
The imminent signing of the EFTA deal comes as Vietnam and the U.S. move toward the signing of their Agreement on Reciprocal, Fair, and Balanced Trade.
Vietnam has sent its “final wording” for a trade agreement to the U.S. with hopes the deal can be quickly signed, Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc told a business summit yesterday, according to Nikkei Asia.
Hanoi and Washington began negotiations on the trade deal in April 2025, shortly after President Donald Trump’s “liberation day” tariff announcement, when Vietnam was hit with an eye-popping 46 percent tariff. The two nations signed a framework for a trade agreement in October that lowered the tariff rate by 20 percent, but despite months of negotiations, they have yet to reach a final agreement.
The negotiations have been held up by the turbidity in U.S. trade policy. Vietnam is currently the subject of a number of Section 301 investigations that the Trump administration has been using to get around the Supreme Court ruling in February that struck down the sweeping “liberation day” tariffs.
Vietnam was among 60 nations that the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative threatened in June with tariffs of 10-12.5 percent due to their alleged failures to take action on forced labor. It is also the subject of separate Section 301 probes into alleged excess manufacturing capacity and intellectual property rights.
After meeting with Vietnamese President To Lam in New York last month, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that the two sides had made “substantial progress” and were “very close to reaching the final outcome.”
Vietnam signed a free trade agreement with the European Union in 2020.

India questions UN rights body's response to PoK, accuses it of 'extreme selectivity'
NEW DELHI: India has asked the UN human rights body when it would issue a report seeking answers from Pakistan on steps taken to address concerns over the situation in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), including investigations into killings and restrictions on internet access.First Secretary at the Permanent Mission of India, Anuj Swarup, delivered the statement during an interactive dialogue with the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights at the 81st session of the UN General Assembly’s Third Committee on Wednesday.
“When can we expect OHCHR to issue a report on the steps taken by the Government of Pakistan on this? Pakistan would do well to look inwards and reflect on how such rights are not being enjoyed in its large part, including Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and for that matter, in Rawalakot, which is under its illegal occupation,” Swarup said.Swarup referred to detailed statements by the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) and the High Commissioner on the situation in PoK. The statements called for prompt, thorough and impartial investigations into killings allegedly carried out by armed and security forces.They also urged authorities to ensure that detained leaders of the Joint Awami Action Committee had access to legal representation and their families, and were afforded due process and a fair trial.
The statements further called for lifting internet restrictions across Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir and holding meaningful political dialogue to address the grievances of the local population.The High Commissioner had also noted that dozens of people, mostly protesters but also law enforcement personnel, had reportedly been killed since June, ahead of the July 27 Legislative Assembly elections. Swarup said the OHCHR had adopted an approach of “extreme selectivity” in addressing such incidents.“Violent responses to protests in our neighbourhood as well as in the west have gone uncommented. Needless to say, such double standards contribute to loss of trust in multilateralism and the work of OHCHR,” he said.Swarup said India’s freedom movement, led by Mahatma Gandhi, championed non-violence and equality, values that also shaped the Constitution, which guarantees fundamental rights to every citizen.“Indian citizens exercise rights subject to maintenance of public order and safety. Our law enforcement authorities act strictly in accordance with the law, and our courts remain available for redressal of any grievance,” he said.Swarup said India, as a member of the UN Human Rights Council, had contributed constructively to discussions on contemporary issues and would continue to engage with the High Commissioner and OHCHR in a “spirit of trust and partnership without selectivity and double standards”.He also stressed that the Indian Constitution guarantees people in Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh the same fundamental rights as citizens in other parts of the country, adding that both regions are integral and inalienable parts of India.India’s remarks came days after New Delhi described comments by the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights on protests in the national capital as “unwarranted” and “unacceptable interference” in the country’s internal affairs.Last week, the UN Human Rights Office expressed concern over “reports of mass detentions of demonstrators, protest leaders, members of civil society organisations, lawyers and journalists, before and during today’s large-scale demonstrations in Delhi.”
In a statement, the ministry of external affairs (MEA) said, "India is the world’s largest democracy, where the right to peaceful assembly is guaranteed by our Constitution and safeguarded by robust institutions, an independent judiciary and a free media."“As in every democracy, Indian citizens exercise this right subject to the maintenance of public order and safety. Our law enforcement authorities act strictly in accordance with the law, and our courts remain available to all for the redressal of any grievances,” the ministry said.The MEA also accused the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) of selectivity in its public statements, alleging that it had remained silent on violent responses to protests in neighbouring countries and law enforcement actions closer to its own headquarters.

North Korea tests two submarine-launched missiles, state media reports

2026-10-15

North Korea tests two submarine-launched missiles, state media reports
The tests showcase North Korea’s war deterrent capabilities in the region, KCNA says.
North Korea has test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles in the sea off its east coast, state media KCNA reports.
The test-fire on Wednesday aimed to examine the reliability of war deterrents and improve the navy’s skill in performing strategic missions, the outlet said.
One of the missiles fired was a Pulhwasal-3-31, the same type of strategic cruise missile North Korea said it test-fired from land last week, according to KCNA.
Senior military officers observed the tests conducted at sea off the country’s east coast. KCNA added that the tests had no adverse impact on the security of neighbouring countries.
North Korea is not yet believed to have launched a modern missile submarine in full operation. This is a top military priority of the country’s leader Kim Jong Un, who has overseen the development of a range of strategic ballistic and cruise missiles.
Last year, Kim Jong Un criticised a nuclear submarine deal between the US and South Korea while he toured his country’s submarine production facility, where state media images showed an 8,700-tonne nuclear-powered missile submarine under construction. On his tour, he described the deal as a threat to the stability of the Korean Peninsula, KCNA reported.
Recent developments
Pyongyang has fired off a flurry of missiles in recent weeks.
Earlier this week, North Korea fired multiple ballistic missiles towards the sea off its east coast, adding to a series of tests as tensions between Seoul and Pyongyang are on the rise.
On October 3, North Korea also tested a hypersonic intermediate-range missile designed to evade missile defences in South Korea and Japan.
After the ballistic missile launch, Seoul’s Joint Chiefs of Staff spokesperson Jang Do-young said the move appeared to be a show of force as it came days after South Korea tested its own hypersonic weapon.
Last week, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung oversaw the country’s first test firing of a hypersonic missile, a rare public showcase of a missile test by a South Korean president.
Lee’s office said the hypersonic weapon, once fully developed, would enhance South Korea’s ability to strike key targets by surprise in the “Korean Peninsula theatre of operations”.
Inter-Korean relations have further soured as a landmine blast, which Seoul blamed on North Korea, wounded three soldiers in September in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) between the two countries.
A joint South Korean-United Nations investigation concluded that two landmines that exploded last month in the DMZ were planted by North Korean forces about a year ago, prompting Seoul to demand an official apology.
Pyongyang has sharply accelerated military fortification along the DMZ as part of leader Kim Jong Un’s “hostile-states” policy, launched in 2023, to permanently sever ties with South Korea.
Diplomatic efforts on the Korean Peninsula have stalled since the collapse of denuclearisation talks between Washington and Pyongyang in 2019 during the first Trump administration. While Trump has floated the possibility of meeting Kim Jong Un in his second term, no such meeting has materialised.

12:21:36 KST

Israel has fallen from outperforming the world’s leading advanced economies on a key productivity measure to trailing them, according to a Shoresh Institution report warning that the next government must address educational and budgetary priorities that threaten the country’s long-term economic viability.
The report, published last Thursday by the Shoresh Institution for Socioeconomic Research, places Israel’s total factor productivity at 15% below the G7 average in 2023, compared with 9% above it in 1975. The measure assesses how efficiently an economy combines labor and capital to produce goods and services.
Written by Shoresh President Prof. Dan Ben-David, the report said weak education, rapid demographic change, and the departure of skilled Israelis reinforce one another, leaving the country increasingly dependent on a narrow group of workers to sustain its economy, healthcare, and defense capabilities.
“The upcoming election will determine who governs Israel, but the deeper question is what kind of country the government will govern a generation from now,” Ben-David said in a statement accompanying the report.
The historical comparison showed how sharply Israel’s relative position changed. In 1954, its total factor productivity was 27% below the G7 average. It overtook that benchmark within roughly two decades, then fell behind again.
Israel exceeded every G7 country in 1972, slides massively by 2024
A separate measure, output per hour worked, tells a similar story. According to Shoresh’s calculations, Israel exceeded every G7 country in 1972 but trailed six of the seven by 2024. Its output per hour was 34% below Germany’s and 30% below the United States'. Japan was the exception.
These are relative comparisons: falling behind other countries does not necessarily mean Israel produces less than it did in the past. It means, rather, that its performance has failed to keep pace.
Ben-David attributes the change to a shift beginning in the 1970s away from investment in infrastructure, education and public services toward sectoral interests. He said that defense spending alone cannot explain the shortfalls, pointing to decades when civilian government expenditure, measured against the size of the economy, matched or exceeded the OECD average.
Israel’s hi-tech success masks a much weaker performance across the rest of the economy. According to the report’s 2022 figures, each hour worked in hi-tech generated 22% more economic value than the average hour worked across OECD economies. But outside hi-tech, where roughly nine in 10 Israeli workers were employed, each hour generated 24% less than that average.
Highly-skilled workers incentivized to leave by taxes
The report also said the highest-earning fifth accounted for 93% of income-tax revenue in 2024, up from 83% in 2000. That concentration, Ben-David said, makes the country vulnerable when highly skilled workers leave.
Expanding that skilled workforce will depend on the education children receive today. According to the report, haredi (ultra-Orthodox) children account for 25% of first graders in 2026 and Arabic-speaking children for another 23%. Haredim make up approximately 6% of Israelis aged 50-54, but 26% of children aged four and under.
The question, Ben-David asked, is whether today’s pupils receive the education needed to become tomorrow’s engineers, physicians and other skilled workers.
Shoresh’s analysis of the 2025 PISA assessments places pupils in state-religious schools below 76% of OECD countries and those in secular Jewish schools below 81%, based on average performance across mathematics, science and reading. Arabic-speaking pupils scored below every OECD country and six of the seven participating Arab countries.
Most haredi boys, who do not study the full core curriculum, do not participate in the tests, the report noted.
When the PISA results were released, the Education Ministry stressed the wartime conditions under which students took the assessments, including displacement and interrupted schooling.
The report also points to a growing number of Israeli physicians abroad. In 2000, the number working in other OECD countries, excluding the United States, was equivalent to 0.7% of the number of physicians in Israel. By 2023, that ratio had risen to 1.9%, according to Shoresh’s analysis.
Ben-David warns that departures could increase the burden on those who remain, encouraging further emigration.
His proposed “Israel 2.0” program calls for an upgraded compulsory core curriculum for all pupils, public funding only for compliant schools, and a shift in national spending priorities. It also proposes electoral and governance reform, stronger checks and balances.
“The window for change is still open – but it is closing,” he said.

Israeli election campaigns must move past political gimmicks to tackle critical issues - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
03:21:05 UTC
12:21:05 KST

As the campaigns before the fateful October 27 elections head into their final two weeks, the “shtickim” and “trickim” – as Israelis refer to the shtick and tricks that typify every election and the debate in this one until now – need to stop.
The coalition has plastered billboards and issued online clips warning of “Yamin or Falestine” – a campaign without any attempt to hide its racist overtones that shows Yashar leader and primary contender Gad Eisenkot with the likes of Mansour Abbas and Ahmad Tibi peering out from behind his broad shoulders in a crass attempt to say that if Eisenkot becomes prime minister, he will form a coalition with Abbas’s Ra’am Party.
The Shinui (Change) bloc has nonstop focused on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s role in the lead-up and aftermath of the October 7 massacre at the expense of outlining and detailing their platforms and plans once they’re in power (save for the B’Yachad party, which has published comprehensive programs for each ministry).
The lack of real content is a major problem for such a crucial election, but more than that, Israeli election campaigns often rely on manufactured crises and last-minute disclosures.
Foremost is the one that could potentially postpone the election – a return to war with Iran. According to an Axios report on Wednesday, Netanyahu spoke to US President Donald Trump last week to discuss the possibility of a renewed military campaign that could target Iran’s nuclear and military sites, with Netanyahu citing alleged Iranian efforts to rebuild nuclear capacity as the reason for launching new strikes.
Renewed fighting could lead to postponement of elections
IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir has warned that renewed fighting before the Israeli elections could delay them. For his part, Trump has said he would not make that decision until after the US November midterms.
We, the voters, without the information, of course, have no way of knowing whether Iran’s reported moves pose an immediate threat that would require action within the next two weeks.
But the prime minister has built his campaign and garnered loyalty among his supporters by portraying himself as the strong man who saved Israel post-October 7 against Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran. An attack and an election delay would certainly bolster that image.
Of course, on the other side, the pre-October 7 timeline and its immediate aftermath are what is driving the opposition. And they’re getting ammunition from timely disclosures almost daily.
Netanyahu’s former military secretary Avi Gil last week alleged that the premier presented an incomplete account of the events surrounding Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack.
In a splash on Israel Hayom and Channel 12, Gil alleged that Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Tzahi Braverman, sought to alter an official record from that morning by changing the time Netanyahu first received an update on the October 7 Hamas invasion via phone call from Gil from 6:40 a.m. to 6:29 a.m.
Major defamation lawsuit against Netanyahu by Shin Bet's Ronen Bar
Adding to the flame is Wednesday’s bombshell: a NIS 3 million defamation lawsuit filed by former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar against Netanyahu, alleging that the premier falsely accused him of knowing in advance about the October 7 attack and deliberately withholding that information.
Despite the seriousness of the accusations by Gil and Bar, the timing of the disclosure, less than three weeks before the elections, is suspect. Both Gil and Bar said they remained silent until now, hoping to testify before a state commission of inquiry that Netanyahu has refused to authorize.
But either Gil’s or Bar’s disclosure could have come two weeks ago, after voters went to the polls. These, along with the slew of other accusations that Netanyahu was warned of October 7 by the United Arab Emirates and Egypt, coming so close to the elections, can only be seen as creating an artificial crisis.
Instead, with two weeks to go, let’s hear how the parties are going to deal with education, transportation, the environment, the unequal IDF draft, the worrying wave of emigration, the future of the West Bank, and the scourge of settler violence, among others.
These elections are too critical to the country’s future for the final two weeks to focus on sensational headlines instead of the issues the country faces.

‘Putin Is Laughing’ – Zelensky Calls Trump’s Russian Diesel Deal a Victory for Moscow

President Volodymyr Zelensky described US President Donald Trump’s Russian diesel deal as a victory for Vladimir Putin, warning that Moscow was exploiting Washington’s decisions to pressure Ukraine into concessions.
In a wide-ranging interview with British broadcaster Piers Morgan on Wednesday, Oct. 14, Zelensky criticized Starlink restrictions that he said had cost Ukrainian lives.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Morgan ended the interview with a direct appeal to Trump, comparing Putin to Adolf Hitler and warning against appeasement.
The interview took place during Zelensky’s visit to Britain for meetings with Prime Minister Andy Burnham and King Charles III, amid renewed Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and growing tensions between Kyiv and Washington.
‘Putin is laughing’ – Trump’s diesel deal hands Moscow a victory
Morgan questioned Trump’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel amid rising energy prices linked to the war involving Iran, arguing that the deal would have little impact on US fuel prices.
Zelensky agreed, describing the arrangement as a tactical victory for Putin.
“Now Putin is laughing,” he said, suggesting that the Kremlin was gaining concessions from Washington even as Russia struggled on the battlefield.
Zelensky said the diesel agreement and restrictions affecting Starlink had handed Putin victories without requiring Russian forces to achieve military breakthroughs.
Morgan suggested Trump might be seeking to deflect public anger over rising gasoline prices ahead of the US midterm elections.
King Charles Welcomes Zelensky as Britain Steps Up Military Support for Ukraine
Zelensky acknowledged that domestic political pressures could be influencing Washington, but said Russia was also trying to exploit the situation to force Ukraine into concessions.
He warned that Moscow was looking for ways to force Ukrainian troops out of Donbas without defeating them militarily.
Zelensky also suggested that Russia was offering Washington potential business ventures and economic projects to influence its decisions.
He insisted that the real cause of rising fuel prices was the conflict in the Middle East and disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, not Ukraine’s strikes against Russian energy infrastructure.
‘We’re losing America – but not because of us’
Asked how he reacted to Trump’s diesel agreement, Zelensky expressed deep disappointment.
“It’s a pity that we are losing. We are losing a strong partner,” he said.
“You think you’re losing America?” Morgan asked.
“Yeah. But not because of us,” Zelensky replied.
The Ukrainian president stressed that Kyiv could not sacrifice its sovereignty to maintain Washington’s support.
“We can’t be weak. Otherwise we can’t survive… We are not selling our country. Look, guys. It’s not about business for us. It’s just our life, and this is our country.”
He described Ukraine as the home of its people and children, rather than something that could be traded in negotiations.
“That’s why it’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side,” Zelensky said.
He argued that Trump could remain a neutral mediator, but should not move toward Moscow.
“We are okay that he’s in the middle. But if you’re in the middle, you have to stay in the middle, not on the wrong side.”
Zelensky questioned the advice Trump was receiving.
“I think his advisors are wrong. I don’t know who is pushing him not to the right side… This is not the right side of history.”
Morgan also quoted Trump supporter Laura Loomer, who questioned why Moscow was not being held accountable for violating the energy ceasefire.
Loomer had described Putin as the “Hitler of our time.”
Asked whether he agreed, Zelensky replied: “Absolutely.”
But he challenged the perception that Putin was overwhelmingly powerful.
“He’s not so strong as [he is] evil, I think. But people are afraid of him,” Zelensky said.
He argued that the United States was stronger than Russia and had the power to stop Moscow’s aggression.
“The United States is stronger... and they have to be on our side.”
Zelensky said Putin’s strength depended on how far other countries allowed him to go.
“He’s strong till the world will stop him.”
‘Russia wants Trump to be weak’
Asked what message he would send directly to the US president, Zelensky began by thanking Trump and the American people for their support.
But he warned that Russia was deliberately undermining Trump’s authority.
“He has to understand that Russia wants him to be weak,” Zelensky said.
He characterized Moscow’s continued bombardment of Ukrainian energy infrastructure after Trump’s ceasefire announcement as an act directed against the American president himself.
Morgan suggested Russia was openly mocking Trump.
“They’re mocking him, aren’t they?”
“Absolutely,” Zelensky replied.
Morgan argued that Russia was demonstrating its disregard for Trump’s demands by continuing to launch missiles and drones against Ukraine.
Zelensky said the Kremlin cared far more about destroying Ukraine than about American political considerations.
“They hate Americans. It’s absolutely clear,” he said.
Zelensky said Ukraine supported Trump’s proposed energy ceasefire even though Kyiv had not been informed before the US president announced it.
“We need our people to live, to go through this winter and to stop the war,” he explained.
According to Zelensky, Ukraine refrained from striking Russian energy infrastructure for three days and did not immediately retaliate when Moscow resumed attacks.
“We didn’t attack during three days any kind of energy objects,” he said. “We didn’t respond.”
He recalled warning American officials that Russia would take advantage of the arrangement.
“They will attack energy. They will do it.”
Russia subsequently launched another massive barrage, including approximately 40 ballistic missiles aimed at Ukrainian energy infrastructure, Zelensky said.
Morgan noted that Ukrainian defenses intercepted only four of the ballistic missiles, leaving dozens to penetrate the country’s defenses.
Zelensky argued that Moscow was exploiting the ceasefire rather than honoring it.
Starlink restrictions – ‘We are professionals, we know what’s going on’
Zelensky also criticized restrictions affecting Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite communications system during Russian attacks.
He said Ukrainian forces lost connectivity around 1 a.m., affecting interceptor drones used to destroy incoming Russian Shaheds.
Morgan asked whether the restrictions had been imposed deliberately.
“I’m sure that they knew what they did. Absolutely. Because it was 1 a.m.,” Zelensky replied.
He said Ukrainian soldiers attempted to contact SpaceX, American generals and other US partners after discovering the disruption.
“We are professionals. We understand what’s going on. If you are losing the speed of Starlink, we understand what’s going on. So they switched off. That’s their decision,” Zelensky said.
The Ukrainian president stressed that Starlink was not used solely for offensive missions.
“It’s not just about attack. As I said, we didn’t attack their energy. It’s also about defending the lives.”
Asked whether he was angry with Musk, Zelensky described the restrictions as a serious mistake.
“I don’t know, him or somebody pushed him to... I don’t know really,” he said.
But he warned that disruptions to air defenses were already having deadly consequences.
“People are dying because of his decision.”
Zelensky urged the restoration of full connectivity, while acknowledging that a major technical problem remained a possibility.
“I hope that it’s a mistake, maybe huge technical problem, I don’t know,” he said.
He also emphasized that European countries, including Poland, had paid for the Starlink services used by Ukraine.
The operational restrictions have been confirmed by Ukrainian officials, although responsibility for ordering them remains disputed.
US missile warnings also disrupted
Zelensky said Ukraine was facing another serious problem: interruptions in intelligence warnings from the US about incoming Russian ballistic missiles.
“It’s two big problems,” he said, distinguishing between Starlink connectivity and advance missile intelligence.
American officials had attributed the intelligence disruptions to technical difficulties, Zelensky said, but the problems continued during Russian attacks.
Without timely warnings, Ukrainian civilians have less opportunity to reach shelters before ballistic missiles strike.
Trump has denied suspending American intelligence-sharing with Ukraine.
Despite Russia’s continued strikes against Ukrainian cities, Zelensky said Putin was suffering enormous military losses.
“Putin, he’s losing at the battlefield.”
He estimated that Russia was suffering approximately 43,000 casualties each month. Of those, Zelensky said approximately 20,000 to 25,000 were being killed monthly.
Asked how Ukrainian losses compared, he described a casualty ratio of approximately one Ukrainian for every seven to ten Russians.
Zelensky also said Ukraine had approximately five or six wounded soldiers for every soldier killed, while Russia’s casualty ratio was closer to 50–50 between killed and wounded.
“For them it’s nothing, for us it’s important,” he said.
Zelensky maintained that Ukrainian forces had stabilized the front despite continued Russian offensives and argued that Moscow was seeking political victories because it was struggling to achieve decisive battlefield gains.
Trump wants Zelensky replaced – ‘No Trump, no Musk can choose our president’
Morgan played a recording of Trump calling for Ukraine to replace Zelensky with someone willing to negotiate a deal with Russia.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal,” Trump said. “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
Morgan asked whether Trump was attempting to force Zelensky from office.
Zelensky recalled that Russia had already occupied Crimea and parts of Donbas before he became president in 2019.
He argued that replacing Ukraine’s leader would not resolve Russia’s aggression.
“No Trump, no Musk, nobody in the world can choose the president… in other countries,” he said.
Zelensky stressed that only Ukrainians could choose their president and expressed confidence that whoever succeeded him would continue defending the country.
“I’m sure the new man or woman will defend our country. This is our home.”
‘I will never accept Ukrainian land as Russian land’
Morgan pressed Zelensky on whether a peace agreement could involve Ukraine formally surrendering territory to Russia.
Zelensky suggested that his refusal to recognize Russian sovereignty over occupied Ukrainian territory was one reason powerful figures might want him replaced.
“Some big guys want to change me, because I will never accept Ukrainian land as Russian land,” he said.
He nevertheless acknowledged that avoiding further loss of life was essential.
“I’m a realist, and I understand that people are more important than one kilometer or two kilometers.”
“It’s not about kilometers. I mean, this is about land and homes.”
He distinguished between acknowledging Russian occupation and legally recognizing the territory as Russian.
“Yes, it’s occupied, but this territory is occupied. It’s temporary.”
“These territories are Ukraine.”
Zelensky expressed confidence that Ukraine would eventually recover its occupied regions, potentially through diplomacy rather than further military offensives.
“In any way it will come back, but without weapon,” he said.
‘I’m not resigning’ – elections impossible during Russian attacks
Asked whether he intended to resign, Zelensky rejected the suggestion.
“No, of course. It’s my responsibility.”
He also said Ukraine could not hold a secure presidential election while Russian missiles and drones continued attacking the country.
“From the point of security, you can’t do elections.”
Zelensky stressed that Ukrainian service members on the front lines must be able to participate in any national vote.
“We can’t choose the president without soldiers, because they give and gave their lives.”
“They are first who have to vote, and I think it’s fair.”
Asked whether Ukrainian citizens supported him, Zelensky emphasized national unity.
“We are all Ukrainian people, and we are all on one side.”
“We have only one enemy: it’s Russia.” ‘We will not lose our independent country’ – even without America
Morgan asked whether Ukraine could prevail without US support.
Zelensky distinguished between preserving Ukraine’s independence and forcing Putin into negotiations.
“We will not in any way lose our independent country,” he said.
But he acknowledged that a diplomatic settlement would become much more difficult without Washington.
“We will have huge problems with how to push Putin to diplomatic way of ending this war – to negotiations.”
He praised European leaders, including Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and French President Emmanuel Macron, for their continued support.
Zelensky said Ukraine needed clear commitments from its partners on weapons, sanctions and funding.
“Putin will not win, will not prevail, 100%,” he declared.
‘Putin’s goal is total occupation of Ukraine’
Toward the end of the interview, Morgan asked whether Zelensky genuinely believed Ukraine could achieve victory.
Zelensky returned to what he described as Putin’s original objective.
“Putin’s goal is total occupation of Ukraine,” he said.
Asked what Ukraine wanted, Zelensky replied: “To stop this war, make peace, stay where we stay.”
He maintained that occupied Ukrainian territories remained Ukrainian and would eventually return.
“Everything will come back because we are a real country.”
He said that Russian political circumstances would eventually change and could create opportunities for the peaceful return of occupied land.
Morgan’s final warning to Trump: ‘Don’t appease Hitler’
Morgan concluded the interview by addressing Trump directly, telling him that siding with Putin against Ukraine would place Washington on the wrong side of history.
“It’s what we called in World War II appeasement to Hitler. Don’t be that guy,” Morgan warned. “Give this guy the support he needs to defeat the modern-day Hitler.”
Zelensky thanked Morgan and the British public, praising the United Kingdom for supporting Ukraine since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
He described Britain as a friend that had stood on the right side of history.

The senator has taken leave from the party room and referred the matter to the WA Greens.
The Greens say WA senator Jordon Steele-John has taken leave from the party room following reports he made inappropriate comments towards women.
The Sydney Morning Herald has reported that a letter from seven party members was sent to Greens leader David Shoebridge on Tuesday night.
The letter states the group has been made aware of "multiple allegations" against the senator that span from 2017 to 2025.
"These allegations all concern his behaviour in the presence of women," the authors wrote, according to The Sydney Morning Herald.

"These claims are made without specifics, any allegation of this nature is extremely serious and must be treated accordingly.
"If someone has made an allegation, I am prepared to address it."
In relation to one of the alleged complaints, the senator said he was the victim of abuse and had been working with WA Police to address it.
Senator Shoebridge said the party was taking the concerns "extremely seriously" and that the matter had been referred to the WA Greens, who will commission an independent inquiry.
In a press conference on Thursday afternoon, Senator Shoebridge said he was unaware of any allegations against Senator Steele-John before he received the letter on Tuesday.
"I've dealt with it with the urgency which I think is appropriate," Senator Shoebridge said.
"I will not be engaging in a running commentary on the matter, because it is going to a fair and independent and timely process."

crafted from dual-tone solid oak, TUPI lamp by estudio gris resembles bird at rest

crafted from dual-tone solid oak, TUPI lamp by estudio gris resembles bird at rest
designed by medellín-based estudio gris, tupi table lamp features a hand-turned solid oak body resembling a bird, complete with a dark wooden beak that conceals the light source to project a warm downward glow.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
ESTUDIO GRIS SHAPES SOLID OAK INTO A LAMP RECALLING A BIRD AT REST
TUPI is a table lamp by Estudio Gris, the Medellín-based studio led by Gustavo Rodríguez and Estefanía Agudelo. The piece starts from a single observation: the stillness of a bird at rest, that moment when it stops moving and simply watches. The body is turned from solid oak in a local workshop in Medellín, Colombia, and assembled by hand. Its tapered silhouette rises to a rounded head, where a darker wooden beak extends forward, and a small turned eye completes the figure. The beak works as the lamp’s shade: the light source sits beneath it, so the glow falls softly down the oak body instead of reaching the eye directly.
DUAL-TONE WOODS AND FLUSH DETAILS ILLUMINATE OAK GRAIN texture
When switched on, the grain of the wood becomes part of the light. The studio’s approach, which it calls introverted design, guides every decision. TUPI does not try to dominate a room. It sits on a desk, a bedside table or a shelf as a quiet presence, and reveals its character slowly, through the contrast of the two woods, the proportions of the head and the warmth of the light it casts. A switch is set flush into the base, and a beige fabric-covered cable completes a palette of natural materials. Each lamp is made to order, so small variations in grain and tone make every piece unique.

Teenager dies as heavy rain floods Istanbul
Roads collapse and hospitals take in water as floods swamp Turkiye’s largest city, shutting schools and halting traffic.
A teenage boy has died after torrential rain battered Istanbul, flooding hundreds of homes, causing roads to cave in and bringing traffic to a near standstill in Turkiye’s largest city.
Footage verified by Al Jazeera showed a surveillance camera capturing the moment the 14-year-old boy was electrocuted in the Balat area of Istanbul’s Fatih district, after stepping into a puddle during heavy rain.
The footage showed the boy walking through puddles at the entrance of a car park before suddenly collapsing to the ground.
The Istanbul governor’s office said the boy was taken to hospital unconscious, but he died despite rescue attempts, noting that an investigation into the incident had been opened.
Istanbul Governor Davut Gul urged residents to stay at home on Thursday unless travel was necessary. He called on people living in basement flats to spend the night on higher floors and to avoid creek beds, underpasses and other flood-prone areas.
The governor’s office suspended classes across the city for Thursday and banned motorcycles from the roads, the Associated Press reported. State employees with disabilities and mothers with young children were placed on leave.
The motorcycle ban took effect at 9pm on Wednesday and would stay in place until further notice.
Turkiye’s Interior Ministry warned of sudden flooding in several provinces on Wednesday and Thursday.
About 8,000 personnel, along with 2,000 vehicles and construction machines, were deployed across the city, home to about 16 million people, Turkish outlet Daily Sabah reported.
Road closures
The rain began on Tuesday evening after warnings from Turkiye’s weather service.
Water filled roads and underpasses, leaving vehicles stranded in several districts, including Esenyurt and Sultangazi.
Water also poured into homes, shops and basements.
Emergency services received more than 2,500 reports of weather-related incidents, Daily Sabah reported.
Authorities recorded 1,277 floods and 15 landslides, and 47 people were stranded. More than 800 homes, 280 businesses and 76 vehicles were affected.
Sections of road collapsed in the Eyupsultan and Gaziosmanpasa districts, the Turkiye Today news website reported.
Local media reported that passersby rescued a woman after floodwaters swept her along in Istanbul’s Esenyurt district.
Several neighbourhoods were affected, with roads submerged, vehicles stranded and homes and businesses inundated. Floodwater also reached two hospitals and poured through the ceiling of the Haciosman metro station. In Sultangazi, a primary school’s retaining wall collapsed while students were inside their classrooms.
No injuries were reported among students.
The heaviest rain fell in the Omerli area of Beykoz, on Istanbul’s Asian side, where nearly 194mm (7.6 inches) was recorded, according to Daily Sabah. Acting Istanbul Mayor Nuri Aslan said parts of the city received nearly 100mm (3.9 inches) in 12 hours.
Traffic density reached about 90 percent during the evening rush hour, and flights were operating normally, the newspaper said.

One of the accused is a Korean man identified by US media as Winston Lee.
The problem is that the world is full of people named Winston Lee.
The rage misdirected at people who share that name, some of whom live outside the United States and look nothing like the accused, lays bare the perils of a chaotic internet, where people distrustful of public institutions become digital detectives.
One of those wrongly identified was a Chinese American whose LinkedIn profile identifies him as a New York-based finance professional who graduated from Cornell University in 2020 – four years before the alleged rape.
“You can’t hide. Your future is over,” said one message he received via LinkedIn.
“You’ll get exactly what you deserve...which is prison!! You’ll be gang raped there.”
Another said that a “black magic” spell had been cast upon him.
In a video on TikTok – where his bio reads “Not part of Cornell7” – he said he had hired a lawyer to press charges against a woman who posted his phone number and his parents’ address online.
‘Mob’
After a deluge of hateful messages, another man misidentified as Winston Lee posted a personal appeal to TikTok detectives.
“I am Indonesian and not the Winston Lee named in the recent Cornell University case,” he said.
“Please verify the identity of the person you are looking for before contacting, tagging, or making accusations against someone.”
After a similar flood of messages, a Chinese-American student named Winston Lee at the University of Pennsylvania added a disclaimer to his LinkedIn profile: “I do not go to Cornell.”
Those appeals did not appear to slow what Reddit discussion boards described as an “online hunt” for the seven accused, drawing many users down internet rabbit holes.
With few verified details about the man actually accused, internet users continued searching aggressively for his whereabouts.
One Reddit post claimed Winston Lee was now serving in the South Korean army. Another user on X said she had received tips suggesting Lee had been spotted on Cornell University’s campus.
People with names like the other six accused also complained about rage spamming and threats.
“These social justice warriors are literally messaging and harassing the wrong” people, said podcast host Brad Polumbo.
“These things should be litigated through the criminal process or through some sort of fair process, not through a social media mob or witch hunt.”
‘Hounded’
A group of former Cornell students, who belonged to the same Chi Phi fraternity as the seven accused but graduated before the alleged incident, also complained of online smear campaigns.
“They are being wrongfully accused on social media of having involvement, are consequently receiving death threats and related hate mail,” their attorney Adam Ford wrote in a letter to the university that was obtained by AFP.
“Most of them have had their employers and higher education institutions take adverse actions against them, including being placed on leave.”
Digital sleuths have for years misidentified accused perpetrators of high-profile shootings and other crimes, exposing them to abuse.
Such misidentification can further roil an already chaotic information ecosystem and hinder the actual investigation by generating false leads, warned Mike Rothschild, a researcher who studies conspiracy theories.
“The wrongfully accused are often hounded,” Rothschild told AFP.
“They sometimes have to go into hiding, or get death threats, or are even violently attacked themselves. And there is no penalty for being wrong on the part of those accusing them.” AFP
