Frontex suspends reintegration program after blowing through its budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Frontex suspends reintegration program after blowing through its budget
The pause comes ahead of a proposed expansion of the EU border agency’s role in returns, sharpening questions over how Brussels will fund its tougher deportation policy.
BRUSSELS — The EU border agency Frontex is suspending a support program for deported migrants after its budget for the year ran out earlier than anticipated, emails seen by POLITICO show.
The border agency paused new applications for reintegration support under its program on Oct. 2 after estimating that costs had “reached a level that does no longer ensure full financial coverage,” according to an email sent by Executive Director Hans Leijtens to staff on that date.
The program, which has operated since 2022, offers financial assistance, healthcare, vocational training and counseling to people who are returned to their home countries after being refused the right to stay in the EU. Reintegration support forms part of the EU’s plan to boost returns of unsuccessful asylum-seekers.
Advertisement
The suspension comes as the EU seeks to step up deportations from the bloc — a leading pillar of EU migration policy, and the object of new legislation adopted earlier this month — and weeks before the European Commission is expected to propose expanding the mandate of the border agency, including its role in returns and reintegration.
Frontex cannot resume the program without additional cash. The agency asked the Commission for more funds, but is waiting for clarity on the EU budget for 2027, and the next seven-year budget starting in 2028, the emails said.
“There is no point in talking about a more ambitious European return policy without also talking about the resources needed to deliver it,” Frontex spokesperson Chris Borowski told POLITICO. “Ambition and funding have to go hand in hand.”
Borowski confirmed that the agency had suspended new cases, but stressed that individuals already been accepted into the program wouldn’t be affected and that Frontex would also continue to offer EU countries “other forms of assistance” on returns, such as operational and technical support.
“Returns do not end when a plane lands. Helping people rebuild their lives after returning to their home countries is an important part of making migration management work. It takes planning, people and money,” he said.
With 2,368 new cases per month on average, the agency took on significantly more migrants seeking reintegration support than it expected. Cases in September were 63% higher than Frontex’s target, according to Leijtens’ email to staff. In the first half of this year, the agency took on around 75% more cases than it did in the same period last year.
Advertisement
In previous years, Frontex was able to assign additional funds from other parts of its budget, the email says — signaling the agency has had to search to find the cash to keep the program running in the past.
“Frontex does not have the necessary appropriations to cover the needs further as MFF allocations did not consider that Frontex would be expected to take over EURP funding at the scale we have seen today,” Leijtens wrote, referring to Multiannual Financial Framework, the EU’s seven-year budget.
The agency has raised the issue with the Commission but “no further commitments could be made onwards,” according to the email.
The program’s suspension raises questions about the future of the bloc’s migration approach. Reintegration is “the key ingredient” to making the EU’s returns strategy work, Lukas Gehrke, the director of the U.N.’s migration organization’s global office in Brussels, told POLITICO.
Forced returns are expensive and come with a higher risk of human rights infringements, whereas reintegration support boosts voluntary returns, reduces people’s propensity to attempt to reach the EU again, and tends to ease cooperation with the country to which they return, he argued.
“That means every euro spent on return with reintegration is a euro spent in a more sustainable way,” Gehrke said.
Advertisement
‘Do not argue or defend the EU policy’
In emailed guidance on how to communicate the suspension to migrants who applied for support, seen by POLITICO, staff were told to “acknowledge the institutional problem” with reintegration program funding “so the returnee does not feel personally targeted or punished.”
Counselors should be transparent, validate migrants’ disappointment, wait for their emotions to pass and shift the conversation to what they could still do upon their return, the guidance read, advising: “Do not argue or defend the EU policy.”
Migrants wait to return to a temporary camp in Ceuta, Spain on Oct. 10, 2026. | Thomas Coex/AFP via Getty Images
Potential returnees “may feel deceived, leading to anger, despondency, or complete withdrawal from the return process,” it also warned.
Expanding the agency’s Frontex mandate featured in the Commission’s five-point plan to address sudden mass movements of people, in the aftermath of migration crisis in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. Besides stepping up the agency’s role in returns and reintegration, the plan also noted an intention to charge Frontex with monitoring the bloc’s external borders and add capacity to quickly deploy forces in the event of an emergency.
“The Commission will propose that Frontex becomes a genuinely European capability with the scale, tools and agility to support Member States wherever and whenever needed,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote in a letter to EU leaders ahead of a summit on Thursday and Friday, where migration is likely to be a flashpoint.
The plans have already raised concerns that the border agency’s mandate is being expanded more quickly than its resources.
Strengthening the border agency’s emergency response capacities, for example, comes with a tradeoff as staff that can be deployed on a moment’s notice cannot be deployed elsewhere, Leijtens, Frontex’s executive director, said at an event earlier this month. “If they’re in Narva in Estonia, you can’t use them in Italy right now.”

How Russia plans to revive its ties with Slovakia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

BRUSSELS — Slovakia is reviving a dormant cooperation forum with Moscow, putting Russia’s gas and oil supplies, nuclear fuel and the treatment of Russian athletes high on the agenda of their first such meeting in five years, according to a Russian government note obtained by POLITICO.
The note, written by Russian Science and Higher Education Minister Valery Falkov, says Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár agreed during an Aug. 20 video call to hold a meeting of the Russian-Slovak Intergovernmental Commission in Moscow.
Slovakia’s foreign ministry said Thursday the meeting is scheduled for Oct. 25. The Russian note — which is dated Sept. 10 — initially set the date of the meeting as Oct. 26-27.
Advertisement
The IGC, which covers economic, scientific and technical cooperation, has been dormant since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The last meeting was the commission’s 21st session, held in Bratislava on Nov. 12, 2021.
The meeting comes as Moscow finds openings in other international arenas. The U.S. has invited Vladimir Putin to December’s G20 summit in Miami, while the International Olympic Committee has provisionally lifted its suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee and urged sports bodies to ease restrictions on Russian athletes.
Asked about the purported agenda for the IGC, the Slovak foreign ministry directed POLITICO to Blanár’s public statements after the Aug. 20 call. “We pursue a policy in all directions and maintain dialogue with all countries that are interested in pragmatic cooperation with us for the benefit of the Slovak Republic’s national interests,” Blanár said at the time.
The Russian foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
The renewed push for warmer Slovak-Russian relations follows Fico’s May 9 visit to Moscow, where he met Russia's President Vladimir Putin during Victory Day commemorations. It comes after Viktor Orbán’s defeat in Hungary’s April election, which cost Putin one of his closest partners in Europe and forced him to look elsewhere for EU allies.
Months before losing the election to Péter Magyar, Orbán rebooted the Russian-Hungarian Intergovernmental Commission on Economic Cooperation, which had been suspended for several years after the 2022 invasion. Magyar's government did not confirm to POLITICO whether the commission would go ahead next year.
Advertisement
EU leaders, including Fico, will gather in Brussels on Thursday for a two-day summit focused on issues including energy prices and support for Ukraine, with the country's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expected to join them for a conversation on Friday.
Oil imports and cultural integration
In the August video call, Blanár raised Slovakia’s opposition to the EU’s phaseout of Russian gas imports and asked to discuss supplies at the Moscow meeting, according to the document, which POLITICO could not independently verify but bears the hallmarks of a legitimate Russian ministerial note. Slovak representatives also stressed the importance of continued Russian oil deliveries through the Druzhba pipeline and welcomed regular shipments of nuclear fuel for Slovak power plants, according to the note.
Slovakia remains heavily reliant on Russian oil and gas, and Fico has argued that ending imports would raise costs. When the two leaders met in Moscow on May 9, Putin said Russia would do everything to meet Slovakia’s energy needs.
The agenda for the meeting next month reaches beyond energy, according to the document. The sides plan to explore working groups on culture, tourism, agriculture and environmental protection, and to discuss the status of the Russian Center for Science and Culture in Bratislava.
Falkov also records Blanár’s opposition to what the note calls the “discrimination against Russian athletes” at international competitions, noting the issue is to be discussed at the IGC meeting.
The International Olympic Committee lifted the suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee in July and said its previous recommendations restricting Russian athletes’ participation no longer applied. World Archery lifted restrictions on Russian athletes and officials in August. FIFA President Gianni Infantino has also called for Russia to be allowed back into international football.
Advertisement
The approach echoes Moscow’s recent effort to lock in closer ties with Orbán’s Hungary. Budapest and Moscow in December agreed on a 12-point plan to expand cooperation in areas including energy, trade and culture. The plan was signed by then Hungarian Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó and Russian Health Minister Mikhail Murashko after talks in Moscow in December. The Slovak note points to a similar breadth of ambition.
The Kremlin’s outreach to Fico shows how Moscow can use energy ties to pull individual EU countries away from a united stance on Ukraine. Putin made a similar pitch in Washington last weekend: After a call with the Russian leader, President Donald Trump said Russia would supply diesel to U.S. and global markets to bring down fuel prices. The deal would provide revenue to Moscow while weakening efforts to maintain a united front against the Kremlin.
But there are questions over whether Putin can follow through on his pledge to Trump. Ukraine has been stepping up drone strikes on Russian refineries, aiming to disrupt fuel supplies and cut revenue for Moscow’s war effort. Kyiv said this month that strikes had disabled 51 percent of Russia’s oil-refining capacity.
CORRECTION: The next Russian-Slovak Intergovernmental Commission will be held on Oct. 25, the Slovak foreign ministry confirmed Thursday, correcting an earlier statement. The story has been updated to reflect his.

Why Ukrainian strikes on data centers are a real problem for Russia — and beyond
Unknown

02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Russia's President Vladimir Putin chairs a meeting with members of the government via videoconference in Moscow on June 23, 2026. | Pool photo by Gavriil Grigorov via AFP/Getty Images
Ukraine’s strikes on data centers inside Russia aimed to disrupt military planning and communication services. There were also reports of another kind of disruption: to customers waiting for their dinner from food-delivery apps.
Kyiv’s drone strikes on three Yandex data centers in Sasovo, Kaluga and Vladimir saw delays and interruptions for thousands of businesses and households that rely on Yandex's cloud infrastructure, including e-commerce, digital payment platforms and apps of food delivery and car services. Ukrainian drones on Wednesday targeted a major Sberbank data center in Russia’s Saratov region, though a senior company executive said it hadn’t affected operations.
After the strikes on Russian data centers, Kyiv noted that Moscow has already repeatedly targeted its digital infrastructure. “Ukrainians wanted to show Russians that two can play this game,” a senior official familiar with the operation told POLITICO, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.
Advertisement
The attacks and counter-attacks point to a new frontline in war: the infrastructure powering the digital economy.
The attacks on the buildings that supply compute power are akin to striking a power plant supplying the electricity, heating and fuel that both militaries and civilians depend on. It may weaken an enemy's war effort but can also bring everyday life to a standstill.
Experts say the cost of rebuilding in Russia will be particularly high as the centers require scarce materials that must be imported. “Obtaining a large amount of equipment to replace what was destroyed is not going to be easy,” said Oleg Shakirov, a cyber policy and international security researcher, noting that most hardware needs to be imported and that is complicated by high global demand and sanctions on Russia.
“To be honest, no one really knows what’s the actual damage. Since two data centers are still offline, we can assume that it’s significant,” said Shakirov.
Joseph Jarnecki, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, warned that normalizing strikes to data centers could have a new set of dangerous consequences.
“These strikes likely breach International Humanitarian Law and it’s a big risk when global populations increasingly rely on digital services,” he told POLITICO.
Advertisement
When servers become targets
Data centers have entered the crosshairs of other recent armed conflicts. During the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran earlier this year, drone strikes hit three Amazon Web Services (AWS) facilities in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain.
Since data centers can serve civilian and military purposes simultaneously, the legal status of targeting them is far from straightforward.
Kubo Mačák, an expert on international humanitarian law, said a data center must meet two conditions to qualify as a military objective under the Geneva Conventions: it must make an effective contribution to military operations and destroying it must offer a “definite military advantage.”
A Yandex delivery robot moves through Moscow on Aug. 11, 2022. | Alexander Nemenov/AFP via Getty Images
“If you know that they are storing military intelligence or that they're using the data center to power military artificial intelligence tools,” Mačák said, there could be grounds to consider it a military objective.
Following the most recent strikes of the Yandex data centers, users on social media platform X reported a sudden drop in automated bot activity, including from accounts associated with pro-Russian, pro-Trump and Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) narratives.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy seized on the reports to boast that the strikes had made social media less toxic, even as independent researchers and national research institutes found no evidence they specifically disrupted any Russian disinformation campaigns.
Advertisement
Mačák said that even if a data center is being used to “let's say, run some trolls or these bot farms to interfere with elections abroad … that would not be sufficient.” In other words, hosting propaganda bots does not, by itself, make a data center a lawful military target.
The dual-use quandary has often focused on the targeting of energy infrastructure, which has been frequent in the Russia-Ukraine war. On Saturday, U.S. President Donald Trump urged Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries, blaming the attacks for rising fuel prices. He has since called for both sides to halt attacks on energy infrastructure, although the existence of any ceasefire agreement remains disputed.
As data centers become increasingly central to national economies, they will become more consequential targets. A senior NATO official granted anonymity to discuss the matter told POLITICO that data centers are already considered potential targets and that the alliance is factoring their vulnerability into its planning.
NATO allies recognize that their data centers could come under attack in a conflict, the official said: “We would get it in a fight.”
Veronika Melkozerova in Kyiv contributed to this report.

Frontex suspends reintegration program after blowing through its budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Frontex suspends reintegration program after blowing through its budget
The pause comes ahead of a proposed expansion of the EU border agency’s role in returns, sharpening questions over how Brussels will fund its tougher deportation policy.
BRUSSELS — The EU border agency Frontex is suspending a support program for deported migrants after its budget for the year ran out earlier than anticipated, emails seen by POLITICO show.
The border agency paused new applications for reintegration support under its program on Oct. 2 after estimating that costs had “reached a level that does no longer ensure full financial coverage,” according to an email sent by Executive Director Hans Leijtens to staff on that date.
The program, which has operated since 2022, offers financial assistance, healthcare, vocational training and counseling to people who are returned to their home countries after being refused the right to stay in the EU. Reintegration support forms part of the EU’s plan to boost returns of unsuccessful asylum-seekers.
Advertisement
The suspension comes as the EU seeks to step up deportations from the bloc — a leading pillar of EU migration policy, and the object of new legislation adopted earlier this month — and weeks before the European Commission is expected to propose expanding the mandate of the border agency, including its role in returns and reintegration.
Frontex cannot resume the program without additional cash. The agency asked the Commission for more funds, but is waiting for clarity on the EU budget for 2027, and the next seven-year budget starting in 2028, the emails said.
“There is no point in talking about a more ambitious European return policy without also talking about the resources needed to deliver it,” Frontex spokesperson Chris Borowski told POLITICO. “Ambition and funding have to go hand in hand.”
Borowski confirmed that the agency had suspended new cases, but stressed that individuals already been accepted into the program wouldn’t be affected and that Frontex would also continue to offer EU countries “other forms of assistance” on returns, such as operational and technical support.
“Returns do not end when a plane lands. Helping people rebuild their lives after returning to their home countries is an important part of making migration management work. It takes planning, people and money,” he said.
With 2,368 new cases per month on average, the agency took on significantly more migrants seeking reintegration support than it expected. Cases in September were 63% higher than Frontex’s target, according to Leijtens’ email to staff. In the first half of this year, the agency took on around 75% more cases than it did in the same period last year.
Advertisement
In previous years, Frontex was able to assign additional funds from other parts of its budget, the email says — signaling the agency has had to search to find the cash to keep the program running in the past.
“Frontex does not have the necessary appropriations to cover the needs further as MFF allocations did not consider that Frontex would be expected to take over EURP funding at the scale we have seen today,” Leijtens wrote, referring to Multiannual Financial Framework, the EU’s seven-year budget.
The agency has raised the issue with the Commission but “no further commitments could be made onwards,” according to the email.
The program’s suspension raises questions about the future of the bloc’s migration approach. Reintegration is “the key ingredient” to making the EU’s returns strategy work, Lukas Gehrke, the director of the U.N.’s migration organization’s global office in Brussels, told POLITICO.
Forced returns are expensive and come with a higher risk of human rights infringements, whereas reintegration support boosts voluntary returns, reduces people’s propensity to attempt to reach the EU again, and tends to ease cooperation with the country to which they return, he argued.
“That means every euro spent on return with reintegration is a euro spent in a more sustainable way,” Gehrke said.
Advertisement
‘Do not argue or defend the EU policy’
In emailed guidance on how to communicate the suspension to migrants who applied for support, seen by POLITICO, staff were told to “acknowledge the institutional problem” with reintegration program funding “so the returnee does not feel personally targeted or punished.”
Counselors should be transparent, validate migrants’ disappointment, wait for their emotions to pass and shift the conversation to what they could still do upon their return, the guidance read, advising: “Do not argue or defend the EU policy.”
Migrants wait to return to a temporary camp in Ceuta, Spain on Oct. 10, 2026. | Thomas Coex/AFP via Getty Images
Potential returnees “may feel deceived, leading to anger, despondency, or complete withdrawal from the return process,” it also warned.
Expanding the agency’s Frontex mandate featured in the Commission’s five-point plan to address sudden mass movements of people, in the aftermath of migration crisis in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. Besides stepping up the agency’s role in returns and reintegration, the plan also noted an intention to charge Frontex with monitoring the bloc’s external borders and add capacity to quickly deploy forces in the event of an emergency.
“The Commission will propose that Frontex becomes a genuinely European capability with the scale, tools and agility to support Member States wherever and whenever needed,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote in a letter to EU leaders ahead of a summit on Thursday and Friday, where migration is likely to be a flashpoint.
The plans have already raised concerns that the border agency’s mandate is being expanded more quickly than its resources.
Strengthening the border agency’s emergency response capacities, for example, comes with a tradeoff as staff that can be deployed on a moment’s notice cannot be deployed elsewhere, Leijtens, Frontex’s executive director, said at an event earlier this month. “If they’re in Narva in Estonia, you can’t use them in Italy right now.”

EU leaders head for showdown over bloc budget

EU leaders head into high-stakes budget battle as elections loom
EU leaders on Thursday are holding talks seeking a deal on the bloc’s nearly €2 trillion budget for 2028-2034 by Christmas amid deep divisions over spending and fears that upcoming elections, particularly in France, could strengthen eurosceptic forces. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned that EU leaders were still "very far apart" as he arrived at the summit.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
EU leaders on Thursday head for their biggest clash yet over the bloc's next long-term budget, as they race to lock in a deal before next year's French presidential election.
The 27-nation European Union wants an agreement by Christmas, worried that any future dealmaking will be derailed by potential eurosceptic wins in polls taking place across the bloc – most crucially in key power France.
The fears are not unfounded. The frontrunner in the French vote, far-right candidate Marine Le Pen, wants to slash the country's contribution to the EU budget to help cost savings in the bloc's second-biggest economy.
Putting the screws on the EU, Le Pen said on the eve of the summit that it would be a "democratic scandal" for leaders to adopt a budget before next year's votes.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned that EU leaders were still "very far apart" as they kicked off the crunch talks.
"We are facing very, very difficult negotiations," Merz told journalists arriving at the EU talks in Brussels, voicing hope a deal could yet be sealed this year, but adding that leaders should prepare to "pack a few extra shirts" at a final summit set for December.
At stake is the nearly two-trillion-euro budget, which will determine the EU's main priorities for the period between 2028 and 2034, from agriculture to defence, competitiveness to migration.
The leaders must agree on how much to give to farmers, what to spend on defence and how to make the economy more competitive against the United States and China, and whether to pour European money into migrant "return hubs" in Africa.
EU leaders appear to be losing faith in an agreement by December as the latest draft conclusions dated Wednesday referred only to a "timely agreement" rather than "by the end of the year" featured in an earlier version.
A deal by year-end would be challenging in any case as the leaders remain as divided as ever, with three opposing camps unhappy with the latest proposal.
Spectre of Le Pen
The sense of urgency is real, with elections looming in Italy, Poland, Greece, Finland and France – and the awareness that eurosceptic new governments could make it much harder to reach a 2027 deal.
Even if Le Pen is just a candidate at this stage, a European diplomat said "she'll be in the room tomorrow" with the leaders, as her potential victory hangs over their talks.
Read moreLe Pen vows to save €140 billion by 2032 if elected to prevent French 'default'
No agreement before France heads to the polls in April and May would mean the fraught negotiations restart in the summer, which a second EU diplomat said would be "an awful exercise".
Ireland, which holds the rotating EU presidency, presented the latest proposal that will form the basis of the talks with cuts of some 140 billion euros to the budget total.
None of the camps was happy.
On one side is Germany, leading a group known as the "frugals" that includes the Netherlands and Sweden, who demand cuts of several hundred billion euros.
In another corner is France, which opposes massive cuts to the budget and believes the continent needs a larger pot to match the rising challenges it faces.
And in the third camp are the so-called "Friends of Cohesion", demanding more funding specifically to support agriculture and regional development.
France has made clear it is unhappy with the focus on cuts, with a French official warning there can be no agreement without "substantial" new bloc-wide taxes including on large companies, environmental taxation and levies on tobacco.
Paris wants EU-wide taxes on digital services, crypto-assets and online gambling, which the European Parliament also demands.
Some are still optimistic for December. Ireland's Europe minister Thomas Byrne said on Tuesday it was possible "if compromise can be found".
Now, European Council President Antonio Costa will lead negotiations, with an extraordinary meeting added in late November to help get the budget over the line.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Thousands of Colombians march against new right-wing president's policies
Thousands of Colombians protested peacefully across the country on Wednesday against right-wing President Abelardo de la Espriella, in the opposition’s first major demonstrations since he took office in August. Former leftist president Gustavo Petro led a rally in Bogota joined by trade unionists, Indigenous groups, students and feminist activists.
Thousands of Colombians took to the streets of cities across the country on Wednesday to protest the policies of new right-wing President Abelardo de la Espriella.
The demonstrations, which proceeded peacefully, mark the first show of force by the opposition since De la Espriella took office in August vowing to combat crime and eradicate "narco-terrorists".

Trade unionists, Indigenous Colombians, students and feminists gathered at a rally in Bogota led by former left-wing president Gustavo Petro.
"It's going to fall!" some of the demonstrators chanted, referring to Colombia's most right-wing government in decades.
Read moreColombia court orders President de la Espriella to hide social media videos of him with dead bodies
Petro headed Colombia's first-ever leftist administration, which expanded free access to public universities, oversaw record increases to the minimum wage and improved labour conditions for employees.
Leftists fear that these advances are under threat from his successor, a US-backed millionaire who is part of a US-backed right-wing wave sweeping Latin America.
"I feel like we have no guarantees and that the little we did obtain...we're about to lose," teacher Ester Guerra, 32, told AFP in Bogota.
De la Espriella is one of the most divisive Colombian leaders of modern times.
He has been cheered by conservatives for taking the fight to guerrilla groups that refused to lay down arms a decade ago when the powerful FARC rebel army disbanded.
His critics accuse him of endangering the country's fragile peace process, threatening minority rights and of showing an authoritarian streak.
"Everything we have fought for for so long is at risk today," said Unzo Vargas, a 44-year-old civil servant, who protested in Bogota with a rainbow flag for the LGBTQ community.
On the eve of the marches, De la Espriella issued a decree giving the authorities greater powers to crack down on demonstrations in the event of damage to property or blocking of streets.
Read moreRubio hails Colombia's new pro-Trump leader De la Espriella on first stop of Latin American tour
"Violence, vandalism, and blockades that trample on the rights of millions of citizens will not be tolerated," he wrote on X.
His threat to unleash force on the demonstrators was slammed by his opponents as an attempt to silence his critics.
"They're trying to frighten the population so people don't go out to protest, but it's in the Constitution as a right," said Oscar Perez, a 40-year-old teacher.
Protesters also voiced strong disapproval of De la Espriella's foreign policy.
A trained lawyer, he has restored diplomatic relations with Israel, which Petro broke off over the country's offensive in Gaza, and announced controversial plans to recognize Jerusalem as Israel's capital.
De la Espriella is also an enthusiastic US ally, and protesters burned an American flag in the streets of the capital while others waved Palestinian flags.
"Yankees go home," read a placard held aloft by a demonstrator in the second city of Medellin.
Left-wing Senator Ivan Cepeda, who lost a June election runoff to De la Espriella by less than a percentage point, also attended the march in Bogota.

US considers lifting sanctions on Russian shadow fleet vessels – Reuters
US President Donald Trump's administration is exploring the possibility of lifting sanctions on vessels belonging to the so-called shadow fleet that have been transporting oil from Russia and Iran, in the hope of bringing down record-high global shipping rates, which have reached record highs.
Source: Reuters
Quote: "The new talks centre on the United States potentially allowing 'legal oil' to flow on previously sanctioned vessels, the US official said. That means crude or petroleum products not sanctioned by Washington rather than Russian and Iranian oil, which are under punitive measures."
Details: According to a source cited by Reuters, the main aim of such measures is to increase exports of oil and petroleum products from the Persian Gulf.
If the proposal is approved, companies wishing to use these tankers would have to obtain individual licences from the US Department of the Treasury.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright confirmed in a video address to the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh that the administration is considering easing restrictions on the shadow fleet. He stressed that the surge in freight rates had significantly reduced demand for US crude oil.
The US Department of Energy said that any move to ease sanctions on the shadow fleet would not help Russia transport oil or petroleum products.
Analysts at Energy Aspects are sceptical about the potential impact of such a move. They note that shadow fleet tankers are old and technically worn out, and would add little new capacity, as most have already been transporting oil continuously over the past three months.
Experts suggest that easing the restrictions "could make a small number of additional tankers available for certain [Strait of] Hormuz shuttle runs".
In addition, maritime industry representatives stress that US measures are unlikely to lead to a significant reduction in freight rates, as ship insurers would still have to comply with EU and UK rules.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s benchmark stock index ended higher Wednesday, breaking a four-session losing streak.
The Taiwan Stock Exchange Capitalization Weighted Index (TAIEX) gained as much as 717.81 points to reach 49,059.12 during the session. Selling in heavyweight stocks toward the close narrowed the gains, with the index ending up 284.52 points, or 0.59%, at 48,625.83, according to Taiwan Index Plus and CTEE.
Turnover totaled NT$982.6 billion (US$30.6 billion), down from NT$1.13 trillion in the previous session. The total market capitalization of listed companies stood at NT$159.11 trillion, according to the Taiwan Stock Exchange.
Among the most heavily weighted stocks, TSMC closed unchanged at NT$2,490. MediaTek fell 1.1% to NT$4,475, according to Anue.
Foxconn gained 1.25% to NT$243. Delta Electronics rose 0.56% to NT$1,785, and ASE added 0.95% to NT$747.
Technology stocks posted mixed results as funds rotated among individual shares. Higher-priced and AI-related stocks generally recovered.
The printed circuit board (PCB) sector performed particularly well as investors shifted funds toward stronger performers across the electronics supply chain. Abonmax, Microcosm Technology, Asia Electronic Material, APCB, Career Technology, Ventec International, Flexium Interconnect, and Taiflex Scientific all hit their daily limit-ups.
PCBs serve as the base for mounting electronic components in devices. AI servers require more advanced PCBs to accommodate their growing number of components, while faster data transmission requires higher-performance circuit boards, according to Sinotrade.
Passive component stocks also attracted buying interest. Sector leader Yageo gained 4.67%, while Kaimei Electronic, Ta-I Technology, Nichidenbo, Taiwan Chinsan Electronic Industrial, and Honey Hope Honesty all hit their daily limits.
Passive components can consume, store, or release electrical energy. The sector has drawn market attention as rising AI demand and tightened supply create potential order opportunities for Taiwanese suppliers, according to UDN Money.
Optical communications stocks also recovered after underperforming in the previous session. LuxNet and Pcl Technologies both hit their daily limits.
Optical communications use light-based rather than electrical signals to transmit data, offering lower signal loss over long distances and greater bandwidth. The sector has gained ground as AI server transmission speeds increase and conventional electrical signals face physical limitations, including signal loss and rising power consumption, according to Pocket Securities.
Petrochemical stocks were another market highlight, with major companies reporting strong third-quarter earnings. Formosa Chemicals & Fiber and Formosa Plastics both hit their daily limits, while Nan Ya Plastics gained 9.4%.
Glass stocks also saw buying interest, with sector leader Taiwan Glass gaining 8.41%. China Glaze rose 3.66%, and Hocheng added 2.16%.
Despite Wednesday’s rebound, lower turnover and TSMC’s unchanged closing price weighed on sentiment ahead of its earnings conference. Huang Wen-ching (黃文清), general manager of Taishin Investment Advisory, said investors were looking for signs that the market’s recovery could continue, according to CTEE.
He expected TSMC to offer a positive outlook that could support further gains in the TAIEX. The company’s earnings call is scheduled for Thursday after market close.
With the month more than halfway over, Huang said investors had become more cautious about buying at elevated prices after the index recently reached record highs. The benchmark could resume its upward trend following a period of consolidation, while further shifts in buying interest among sectors would also be worth monitoring.
He identified TSMC-related supply chain stocks as potential areas of strength. Financial stocks could also offer opportunities as they benefit from the interest rate hike cycle.

North Korea has test-fired two distinct types of cruise missiles from a submarine, its state media reported, following weeks of friction with South Korea triggered by a landmine explosion along their heavily fortified border.
The projectiles were launched on Wednesday into the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan, without "any adverse impact on the security of neighbouring countries", the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) confirmed.

Submarine-launched capabilities remain a critical objective for Pyongyang, offering lower-altitude flight profiles that complicate detection and radar interception compared to traditional ballistic weapons.
Tactical significance
State-media photographs showed one projectile emerging vertically from the sea, trailed by thick smoke, while a second missile breached the water's surface at a 45-degree angle.
Accompanying imagery depicted a projectile skimming horizontally over open water alongside a surfaced submarine.
The test forms part of a wider tit-for-tat escalation across October, with both nations testing hypersonic technology.
South Korea launched its first domestic hypersonic glide vehicle last week, days after Pyongyang announced tests of an AI-assisted intermediate-range hypersonic weapon.
The two Koreas remain technically in a state of war after the 1950–1953 conflict concluded with an armistice rather than a peace treaty.

White House spokesperson Katie Zacharia’s law career faces scrutiny
Katie Zacharia has repeatedly claimed to be a lawyer, but critics question if she passed the bar exam to be licensed.
Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary under United States President Donald Trump, has drawn increasing criticism over claims about her professional background.
On Wednesday, a public accountability nonprofit filed a complaint with the State Bar of California over Zacharia’s repeated claims that she was a lawyer.
If made falsely, such a claim is a crime in the state. According to Zacharia’s LinkedIn profile, she received a degree from the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law in 2011, but critics have questioned whether she received a licence to practise law, as she has suggested.
“Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson,” Michelle Kuppersmith, the head of the Washington, DC-based Campaign for Accountability, said in a statement. “Yet it seems it was all a lie.”
Her organisation filed the complaint with California’s bar office, a regulatory agency that oversees the licensing of lawyers.
“In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn’t puffery; it’s a crime,” Kuppersmith said.
“The State Bar should investigate whether Ms. Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials and hold her accountable if she has.”
Zacharia, a commentator who has appeared frequently on Fox News and Newsmax, began her term as White House press secretary on Tuesday.
In a news briefing that day, she seemed to falter and speak haltingly, sometimes having to repeat herself.
Her appearance was brief, lasting under 15 minutes. She spent much of her time at the podium thanking Trump for the opportunity and reading from a prepared statement.
“I have wanted to work for him for a very long time,” Zacharia said.
Later, she joined Trump outside the White House to speak further with reporters. When asked where she had passed the bar exam, Zacharia replied, “When I moved to China.”
The response was an apparent reference to a three-year stint in which she claims she worked at a law firm in Beijing.
A biography on the website for the pro-Trump women’s organisation Trumpettes USA Inc says she “served as outside counsel” for the World Bank and International Finance Corporation while in Beijing.
Her LinkedIn profile, meanwhile, indicates Zacharia served as an associate at the Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011 to 2013. More recently, from 2024 to 2025, it lists her as general counsel for Fix California, a voter rights group started by a Trump administration official.
On her Instagram profile, Zacharia describes herself as a “Wife, Mom, & Lawyer”.
But Zacharia’s assertion that she passed the bar in China has fuelled media scrutiny. China’s equivalent of the bar exam, the notoriously difficult National Unified Legal Professional Qualification Examination, can only be taken by Chinese citizens.
China has, on rare occasion, allowed foreigners to practise law in the country if they have several years of experience in their home countries first.
But that does not appear to be the case for Zacharia. According to media reports, Zacharia has not been found to be licensed as a lawyer in any state in the US.
In a statement to The Associated Press, Zacharia responded to the scrutiny by saying, “I practice international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials.”
Since Trump’s return to office for a second term, Zacharia has spent several months as a communications adviser at the Department of Homeland Security.
Since June, she has also worked as the senior communications adviser at the Trump Media and Technology Group, which owns the Truth Social platform.

Trump suggests those who leak government information should ‘be shot’
The US president has long been unhappy with inside information about his administration being leaked to the media.
United States President Donald Trump has suggested that those who leak information to the news media should be shot as punishment.
Trump made the remarks at a campaign rally in Bullhead City, Arizona, as he urged supporters to vote in the November 3 midterm elections.
“In my opinion, leakers should be shot,” Trump told the crowd. “In the old days, we used to shoot leakers, you know, when they leak what time you’re going to attack a country.”
Trump made the statement in an apparent reference to Operation Midnight Hammer, which saw the US launch a surprise attack on Iran in June 2025 during the 12-day war between Israel and Iran.
In the aftermath of the attack, several media outlets published findings from a preliminary report by the US Defense Intelligence Agency.
That report – which had not yet been released to the public – indicated that Iran was able to move some of its enriched uranium away from the sites the US had bombed.
It also suggested that the extent of the damage to Iran’s nuclear facilities was more modest than what Trump had asserted.
Trump, however, appeared to signal that the timing of the US attacks was among the leaked information. He accused the news media of putting military members in danger, calling out The New York Times and CNN in particular.
“They leaked the time we were leaving, the time we were arriving,” Trump said, claiming he had to reschedule the bombing campaign two days later as a result.
“Somebody leaked. Some sleaze-bag, they ought to go to jail or be shot. For the rest of their life, they should be in jail.”
Trump has long had an adversarial relationship with the news media, and he has previously called for harsh punishment against any official who passes on confidential information to news outlets.
After parts of the Defense Intelligence Agency report became public, he blamed lawmakers in the Democratic Party for its release.
“The Democrats are the ones who leaked the information on the PERFECT FLIGHT to the Nuclear Sites in Iran,” Trump wrote on social media at the time. “They should be prosecuted!”
Under Trump, the White House has taken aggressive action to track down the source of leaks.
Staff in his administration, as well as officers in the military, have also been asked to take polygraph tests.
Journalists at several news outlets, including The New York Times, The Washington Post and The Wall Street Journal, have also received subpoenas aimed at determining the sources of internal information made public.
The newspapers had reported on stories such as a botched Navy SEALs raid in North Korea and how Trump ignored internal Pentagon warnings against launching the Iran war.
Last year, the Department of Defense demanded that journalists who wished to access the Pentagon sign an agreement not to publish unauthorised material.
Much of the Pentagon press corps refused to agree, and a federal court struck down many of the new demands made on journalists at the department.
Trump has long raged against leakers, going back to his first term as president from 2017 to 2021.
Former White House official Alyssa Farah Griffin told a podcast in 2024 that Trump had called for leakers to be executed, after media outlets reported that he had taken shelter in a White House bunker during racial justice protests in 2020.
Trump appeared to reprise that sentiment in his speech to Arizona voters on Wednesday, less than three weeks before the November 3 midterms.
“Leakers should be dealt with very, very strongly,” Trump said. “To me, they are the scum of the earth.”

Police also submitted videos of CJP representatives jumping a gate and unfurling the flag at Jantar Mantar Tuesday. Seven missing after two tankers catch fire off Romania’s Black Sea coast
Romanian president says NATO to hold a summit to discuss increasing drone attacks on shipping in the Black Sea.
Seven people are missing after after two drone attacks on ships in and just outside Romania’s territorial waters in the Black Sea.
Romania’s naval authority said rescuers were searching for the seven missing sailors from the San Marino-flagged Wine Trader, one of two chemical tankers that caught fire overnight and early on Thursday. It added that five other people were rescued.
The cause of the fire aboard the Wine Trader, which was travelling from Tunisia to Romania, wasn’t immediately clear, but a recent spate of drone strikes on ships in the Black Sea has raised fears that Russia’s war in Ukraine is spreading.
On Wednesday evening, Romania said it was probing a possible drone attack on the Comoros-flagged tanker Yara J. It said a fire had broken out on board, but the ship’s crew managed to douse the flames themselves.
Then, at around 7am (04:00 GMT) on Thursday, Romanian authorities reported that a fire had broken out on the Wine Trader, approximately 24km (13 nautical miles) southeast of the Romanian city of Sulina.
At a summit of European Union leaders on Thursday, Romanian President Nicusor Dan said, “Two drones hit them.”
“There will be a reaction from the Romanian state” once more information is gathered, he added.
The two ships were hit while anchored near the mouth of the Sulina Canal leading into the Danube River, a major shipping route used by Ukraine.
The Interior Ministry said it had sent two Black Hawk helicopters to the search-and-rescue mission, as well as two ships with medical staff on board.
“At the moment, the rescue cannot be done safely because of very big waves,” it said in a statement.
Earlier shipping attacks
The incident comes amid growing concerns over hybrid attacks in the Black Sea involving Russia.
On Tuesday, two ships were hit in drone attacks off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, with one of them sinking, Bulgaria’s Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.
Neither Romania nor Bulgaria have directly blamed Russia for the attacks, although Bulgaria’s Radev did summon Russia’s ambassador.
“We don’t believe that Ukraine will attack its own ships and crews,” Radev said. ‘There is no logic here. So the results of this attack favour Russia. However, we don’t have any solid evidence that the drones are Russian.”
Earlier this month, a grain ship caught fire and sank outside Romania’s territorial waters. Ukraine blamed Russian drones for the incident, in which two people were killed and 11 others rescued.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte met with Bulgaria’s PM Radev and Romania’s President Dan on Thursday to address the escalating number of drone attacks in the Black Sea.
“NATO has strengthened our posture along the eastern flank including with increasing counter-drone capabilities,” Rutte said in a post on X. “NATO will continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed.”
Romania’s President Dan said NATO is due to hold a summit to address the incursions by drones into eastern European airspace that are testing the Western military alliance and the EU’s defences and response capabilities.
Romania, a NATO member, shares a land border with Ukraine.
Since the Russia-Ukraine war started, drones have breached its airspace while mines floating in the Black Sea threaten key trade and energy routes.
“All EU leaders see this as part of the spillover of the war between Russia and Ukraine, because since Russia launched its full-scale invasion, the Black Sea has become a key battleground,” said Al Jazeera correspondent Rosie Birchard.

Conroy targets 'rot' in Defence after $15.6m bungle unmasked
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
01:19:37 UTC
10:19:37 KST

Defence hit by $15.6m in missile contract blunders as Conroy targets 'rot'
In short:
Defence files have unmasked more than $15.6 million in unauthorised contractor payments within Australia's flagship missile program.
The government has conceded the errors and is using the compliance failures to justify greater oversight of spending.
What's next?
The program, known as Guided Weapons and Explosive Ordnance (GWEO) Group, will be folded into the new Defence Delivery Agency starting in July 2027.
Defence officials behind Australia's flagship missile program racked up at least $15.6 million in financial and procurement blunders, a freedom of information document shows, including paying out $13.3 million before securing basic legal sign-off.
The defence file exposes a pattern of basic accounting and administrative failures within the Guided Weapons and Explosive Ordnance Group (GWEO), the $36 billion initiative designed to manufacture and stockpile advanced weapons and ammunition on Australian soil.
The federal government acknowledged the errors exposed in the document, with Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy telling the ABC: "We agree the rot has to stop."
The defence document shows the administrative errors included two payments of $8.1 million and $5.2 million, which were made in June 2023.
Officials paid out the money to cover contract price hikes before getting the mandatory legal approval required to increase the contract's value.
A further four transactions broke basic rules when staff went out to market to get quotes before getting required sign-off from their managers.
In another instance, officials broke spending rules on a $631,365 order by approving a bill that was higher than the allowed spending limit, then mistakenly filing the paperwork in Australian dollars instead of the foreign currency, distorting the exchange rate used.
The money represents a tiny fraction of the multi-billion-dollar defence procurement budget but it raises concerns about how the funds are handled.
There is no suggestion any of the money was lost, but Defence records make it clear the funds were spent "contrary to Defence procurement policy".
More breaches redacted from document
An unknown number of additional breaches and their costs were redacted from the document.
However, "yes" boxes confirm corrective action was required on at least eight additional occasions.
The paperwork also highlights broader procedural lapses across the program, including an August 2025 breach where staff relied on outdated spending rules, missing a policy change that dropped the manager sign-off threshold from $200,000 to $80,000.
The errors were only identified when a new contract management team conducted a review of previous transactions.
"The personnel involved in processing the escalation payment are no longer within the Contract Management Team," the Defence document said, explaining the current team reviewed the arrangement, identified the non-compliance, and formally reported it.
Officials ultimately granted retrospective approval to the $13.3 million in payments on July 10, 2025, about two years after the cash went out the door.
Mr Conroy used the ABC's revelations to justify the Albanese government's creation of the newly minted Defence Delivery Group to improve oversight, enforce tighter controls on contracts and get "more bang for the buck for taxpayers".
He also laid blame at the feet of the former Liberal government.
"The management of this contract, a legacy of the former government that outsourced important work to a legion of consultants and contractors, was just not good enough," he said.
"We agree the rot has to stop. That's why since coming to office, we have acted to ensure that the management of this contract is now done by Defence public servants.
"That's why we have ramped up investment in GWEO and made it a priority, which includes greater oversight of management of this contract."
The FOI document shows the unauthorised price-hike payments occurred in June 2023, more than a year after the Albanese government first took office.
Greens want accountability
Greens leader David Shoebridge, who is also the party's spokesperson on defence, said the issue highlighted deep issues with defence procurement.
"GWEO is one of the government's big-ticket items on defence spending. Questions need to be asked about who was held to account here," he said.
"The documents only say the 'personnel involved' have been moved on.
"In most cases in Defence, 'moved on' is code for promoted away from a problem.
"What is 100 per cent clear is that no-one in a leadership position has even been held to account."
A Defence spokesperson told the ABC the department took issues of non-compliance and transparency seriously.
"[It has] demonstrated this through proactive referrals, stronger controls, and increased oversight," they said.
Audit office looks into domestic munitions
The internal disclosures come amid an extensive, two-part investigation by the Australian National Audit Office (ANAO) into Defence's domestic munitions contracts.
The national audit body first exposed severe probity gaps and sole-sourcing failures in June 2024, before handing down a damning second report in July 2026 that criticised the GWEO enterprise for delivering "limited assurance" on value-for-money.
The government has committed between $26 billion and $36 billion over the next decade under the Integrated Investment Program to accelerate the GWEO enterprise.
GWEO is among the divisions set to be consolidated into the new Defence Delivery Agency, which will manage Australia's $56 billion annual defence spending from July 2027.
The initiative aims to curb costly project blowouts on major military assets.

One Ukrainian source said the operating speed would need to reach at least 450 kilometers per hour (280 miles per hour) to effectively counter the faster Russian drones.

Washington continues to lobby regional governments to authorise combined operations and escalate offensives against cartels, though only a few countries—including Colombia and Honduras—have formally agreed.
To date, the US military has executed 71 boat strikes across the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, killing at least 239 individuals it claimed, without making evidence public, were narcotics traffickers.

Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski addressed Musk on X (Twitter) on 14 October, saying: "Hey, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, we are watching you."

"Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company," he added.

What I Learned From a Year of Interviewing a Thai Sex Worker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:53:00 UTC
09:53:00 KST

When I started interviewing a Thai sex worker named Ying for my recent book, I was initially looking for something far different from what I eventually wrote. I wanted sleaze: something raw and stimulating. I had wanted to write about a harlot, someone immoral, for whom money took precedence over all. I had expected to write about their greed, their lack of morals and the hypocrisy that arose from an industry surrounding a deeply religious society.
My assumptions were both critical and ignorant. In every way, I had already decided on the book I was going to write without attempting to understand the mechanics or psychology behind them. What I have since learned is about choices, and how few meaningful ones there were for someone caught between family obligation, economic status, and religion. What I learned was about the life of a tortured soul, fighting to make the best of what she had.
Ying had spent most of her adult life selling sex for a living, starting when she was 19 years of age. Like many girls around her, she had dreamed of a better life – one that seemed impossible for someone born into poverty with little education. Ying grew up in Thailand’s mostly agrarian northeast. She arrived in Bangkok at the age of 17, and began work in a restaurant, where she faced long hours and poor earnings with no hope of advancement. Alongside this, she became involved in sex work, present in every nook and cranny of Bangkok. As Ying told me, “There was no choice. It was the only way to earn enough for myself and my family.”
Of course, Ying knew what she was doing. She wasn’t coerced or forced. But still the question remains: what else was available to her? The economics of her situation were inescapable. Ying was earning 6,000 baht per month at a restaurant in the early 2000s. At her peak in the sex industry, she was making close to 80,000 baht each month. Her mother back home in Isan sold food by the road, making less than 200 baht per day. Her father was an odd-job laborer earning even less. For a family like hers, the difference was colossal.
Decades of research into Thailand’s illegal sex industry have long identified economic privation as a leading cause of entry into the trade, which offers substantially superior earnings than the agricultural, domestic, or other poorly paid forms of work available to women who come from rural provinces. Those findings do not apply to every woman in the sex industry, but they help us understand how seemingly voluntary decisions may be constrained in practice.
Another thing became clearer through the interviews. Customers were not buying sex; they were buying a performance. Ying had to convince customers she was interested in them. To make each man feel desirable. To fulfill their every desire, no matter how detestable. Each customer was its own enterprise, and she had to remember their every eccentricity in order to encourage their return. As the industry moved online through the years, women had to improve their skill sets, to understand how to digitally market themselves. To master the psychology of attraction, and the manner in which to exercise it. Ying explained, “You have to make every man like you, or he won’t come back.”
What further surprised me was the power the customer held, even after he had paid and left. The digital world brought private encounters into the public sphere: a displeased customer could affect a woman’s future earnings by becoming an online critic, capable of influencing the market value of her services. The strength of a single review could make or break the personal enterprise she had set up for herself.
Beyond performance, Ying’s experience of sex work also revealed many personal boundaries were up for sale. Many men refused to use condoms; others demanded violent or depraved acts. Blowjob bars in particular distinguish themselves by the absence of condoms. This is an easy boundary to maintain when a sex worker is first starting out, fresh and attractive. But that balance shifts rapidly when they remain in the industry for too long, presenting them with a hard economic decision: refuse the money, or accept a greater health risk. For Ying, ageing and increasing competition intensified those decisions; she described how quickly such considerations become typical when rooted in the industry. The same market that had rewarded her youth gradually made it more costly for her to protect herself.
Her account also revealed the darker experiences of rape and abuse. In one disturbing revelation, she recounted how she was heavily intoxicated, unable to defend herself, while men around her used her sexually. Yet, when pressed on her emotions during that encounter, she seemed more bothered by her boyfriend’s inability or refusal to protect her, rather than the assault itself, a reaction I found difficult to grasp. What affected me was how nonchalant she was in recalling these experiences. It made me question if her career in sex work had created an unavoidable overlap, where consent and violation had become intertwined with her professional need to please every man she came across.
The money Ying earned was not always spent on herself. One of the recurring themes in our interviews was the importance of family responsibility and karma – and how both of these contributed to her decision to enter the sex industry. According to her strict religious upbringing, filial piety is a source of merit that can help to expunge past transgressions and ensure a positive reincarnation. Parents give their children a life, food, and protection. Children repay this debt by sending money home – something that is a moral and religious responsibility.
The same Buddhist moral universe that rejects any immoral behavior now expects a diametrically opposed sacrifice in the name of filial piety, a devastating contradiction I had struggled to understand.
Years later, that contradiction became painfully obvious when even cervical cancer could not keep Ying from returning to sex work. Her family had already structured their lives around her regular financial sacrifices and were reliant on her. She said, “There was no other job at my age that could pay so much.” Nobody forced her back after her hysterectomy. There was no trafficker waiting at her door, no one imposing their will upon her. She did it because she had no other option.
I started out with a plan to write a book about the colorful life of a sex worker. In the end, I was writing about a human being – one of us – trying her best, imperfectly and relentlessly, to survive. I now understand how morality can appear from a distance and how simple any choice can be when proper alternatives exist. And really, given those circumstances, would we have done anything so very different?

SC: Cops can’t seek digital footprints for roving probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:51:16 UTC
09:51:16 KST

NEW DELHI: SC has said police cannot direct social media platforms under IT Act to share an accused’s digital footprints for periods well before the crime he is being probed for, in an order that is likely to become a precedent for protection of privacy, reports Dhananjay Mahapatra.“Information and Technology Act provisions cannot be misused by police to launch a roving and fishing inquiry by obtaining personal data of an accused in breach of right to privacy,” said SC quashing a Ghaziabad Police order asking ‘X’ to furnish digital footprints of journalist Abhishek Upadhyay since June 1 when he was accused of a road rage incident in Aug 18.Cops must apply principles of proportionality, says SCA bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi said: “Police must apply the prin-ciples of proportionality while taking steps to investigate a crime and can resort to seeking digital footprints only after recording that alternative methods to obtain information about a crime has proved inadequate”. The court also kept in operation its interim order pro-tecting the journalist from arrest as long as he cooperated with the investigators.
Upadhyay, through senior advocate Pradeep Rai, said he had carried out a journalistic investigation into theft of donations at Ayodhya Ram Temple and was first to publish a news article on his digital platform on June 7. The real intent behind the cooked-up FIR of Aug 18 was to seek information from June 1 to identify the sources who informed him about pilferage of donations by devotees, Rai argued.
Ghaziabad Police commissioner had informed the court that police searched for the petitioner for three days in connection with the road rage case, in which he is accused of hurling caste slurs at the complainant bike rider, and when he was untraceable, police sought details of digital footprint from ‘X’.
SC said the commissioner’s explanation and the order seeking digital footprint details appear to be at variance for the purpose of investigation of the road rage case.“Police can surely look for digital footprints if the crime was committed with long planning and conspiracy, but not in such cases where questions of privacy and right to act as a journalist are involved,” said the bench.Rai with advocate Anoop P Awasthi complained to the court that the journalist’s vehicle, which was seized after the FIR against him, has not been returned. The bench directed Ghaziabad Police to return the vehicle to the petitioner within two days.The bench cautioned Ghaziabad Police against using any of the private and personal information related to the petitioner it has obtained from ‘X’.

Unemployment rate remains at 4.7pc in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:50:22 UTC
09:50:22 KST

Unemployment remains at 4.7pc in September with interest rate hike possible
In short:
The unemployment rate held at 4.7 per cent in September after the August result was revised up from 4.6 per cent.
The participation rate slipped to 66.8 per cent, down 0.2 percentage points.
What's next?
Some economists still expect another interest rate hike this year.
Australia's unemployment rate remained at 4.7 per cent in September, after August's jobless rate was revised upwards.
It means the national unemployment rate remains at its highest level in the post-COVID era, in seasonally adjusted terms.
An estimated 39,300 fewer Australians were in work last month, and the number of officially unemployed people increased by 8,900.
The participation rate, which is the proportion of people in work or actively looking for work, also fell, to 66.8 per cent from 67 per cent.
It means the average unemployment rate in the September quarter was 4.63 per cent, well above (and ahead of) the Reserve Bank's forecast of 4.5 per cent for the December quarter this year.
The Bureau of Statistics data show that, in trend terms, things remained steady last month.
The trend unemployment rate remained at 4.6 per cent (with no upward revision), the participation rate held at 66.9 per cent, hours worked remained steady, and the employment-to-population ratio held at 63.8 per cent.
Unemployment will keep rising
Tom Kennedy from JP Morgan said the unemployment rate had now increased by 0.6 percentage points since the RBA started lifting interest rates in February.
He said outside of the COVID-19-related volatility, it was the largest nine-month increase in more than a decade.
"The deterioration is also more pronounced than the RBA had forecast back in August, with the Statement on Monetary Policy projecting an unemployment rate of 4.5 per cent by year-end," he said.
"Importantly, it's too early to see any effect from the RBA's September rate hike, which we think will weigh on both GDP growth and labour demand in coming quarters."
Oxford Economics Australia economist Oscar Guth said unemployment would keep rising over the next 12 months.
He expects the unemployment rate to exceed 4.8 per cent late in 2027 as the lagged effects of oil price shocks and tighter monetary policy continue to affect the labour market.
BDO chief economist Anders Magnusson said the RBA's restrictive monetary policy and slow economic growth were beginning to flow more clearly into the labour market.
"The result suggests that the labour market is moving further in the direction the Reserve Bank has been seeking," he said.
RBA November meeting is still 'live'
Despite the clear signs that labour market conditions are still loosening, some economists think the RBA may soon lift rates again.
EY senior economist Paula Gadsby said today's data had not changed the monetary policy outlook.
"Given persistent price pressures across the economy, we continue to expect at least one rate hike before the end of the year, potentially as soon as Melbourne Cup Day," she said.
CBA economist Ashwin Clarke said next month's RBA Monetary Policy Board meeting would be closely watched.
"The data suggests the labour market continues to gradually loosen," he said.
"On the margin, this supports our expectation that the RBA will hold interest rates steady at its November meeting, though risks remain firmly tilted to the upside and the meeting is live."
Westpac's economics team still expect a rate hike in November.
David Bassanese, BetaShares chief economist, said he also thought the RBA would lift rates in November, but that decision would hinge on an "all-important inflation reading" later this month.
But Tom Kennedy said he thought rates would probably be on hold for a while.
"While price pressures are still elevated and the RBA remains focused on inflation, the steady increase in the jobless rate, in our view, argues for a period of policy stability and we expect rates on hold from here," he said.

Air Force May Buy Land for 120 New Sentinel ICBM Silos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:46:59 UTC
09:46:59 KST

The Air Force may wind up buying land to build 120 new intercontinental ballistic missile silos as part of its revamped infrastructure approach for the new Sentinel ICBM.
The service revealed that and other new details about its Sentinel plans as it announced the start of an environmental impact analysis meant to supplement the program’s original review, which was completed in 2023.
The environmental impact statement released in March 2023 cleared a key procedural hurdle in the Air Force’s effort to replace the aging Minuteman III with the Sentinel across three bases in the western U.S.: F.E. Warren Air Force Base, Wyo.; Malmstrom Air Force Base, Mont.; and Minot Air Force Base, N.D. But much has changed since that EIS—in early 2024, critical cost and schedule overruns for Sentinel triggered a notice to Congress and a Pentagon review under the Nunn-McCurdy Act.
The program’s issues are not caused by the missile, but rather by the massive infrastructure and civil engineering work needed to build the systems it requires, officials say. The Air Force had hoped to reuse much of the infrastructure that supported Minuteman, but analysis showed much of it was too old or too expensive to upgrade.
Eventually, Pentagon leaders certified the Sentinel program to continue. But in an effort to control costs, Air Force officials decided in spring 2025 it would be more effective to build entirely new silos instead of reusing the old ones. There are 450 active Minuteman silos, which the Air Force plans to replace on a one-for-one basis.
At the time, a spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the new silos would be “predominantly Air Force-owned real estate, which means reusing the existing missile sites but not the 55-year-old silos.”
A new website associated with the supplemental environmental impact analysis, launched Oct. 9, states that just over a quarter of the sites could be on land not currently owned by the Air Force, with the service considering:
- Acquisition of land and construction of up to 30 new launch silo sites around F.E. Warren
- Acquisition of land and construction of up to 30 new launch silo sites around Malmstrom
- Acquisition of land and construction of up to 60 new launch silo sites around Minot
Additionally, the service said it is evaluating old sites at Malmstrom formerly operated by the 564th Missile Squadron, now inactive, to reuse for up to 60 new launch silo sites.
The Air Force is planning to buy up to 12 acres per silo, according to the supplemental EIS website.
Launch Centers
Silos aren’t the only ICBM infrastructure getting a refresh in the Air Force’s latest plan for Sentinel.
Currently there are 45 missile alert facilities across the three bases where Airmen stay on watch 24/7. The original plan for Sentinel called for building new “launch centers” to command and control the ICBMs at 24 of those facilities and razing the rest.
The new EIS website states that the Air Force will reutilize Missile Alert Facility sites for Launch Centers “where feasible,” but at Minot specifically, officials are considering “construction of new launch center sites in previously undeveloped areas,” the website states. Each Launch Center would have a footprint of up to 16 acres.
Another new consideration is the construction of a “purpose-built Operations Group Facility” at Malmstrom.
Timeline
Now that the Air Force has announced its plans to craft a supplemental EIS, there is a 30-day public “scoping” period where federal, state, and local agencies, interested organizations, and members of the public can all provide comments on the proposed actions.
After that, the service will release a draft of its supplemental EIS, and there will be another window for public comments. The Air Force plans to release its draft by fall 2027.
A final supplemental EIS is scheduled for release in spring 2028, after which the Secretary of the Air Force can sign a Record of Decision, clearing the way for the acquisition of land and construction.
After that, it will be several more years before Sentinel is in the ground—the current Air Force estimate is for the new missile to reach initial operational capability by the early 2030s.
For now, though, the Air Force and contractor Northrop Grumman are already building a prototype silo for Sentinel at Northrop’s Promontory, Utah, facilities.

US Space Force electromagnetic weapons played key role in Venezuela, Iran operations - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:37:39 UTC
09:37:39 KST

US Space Force electromagnetic weapons played a crucial role in US military operations in Venezuela and Iran, The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday.
The WSJ was granted access to a US Space Force base in Colorado, where it was shown some of the Pentagon's space warfare capabilities, including systems designed to disrupt enemy satellites and detect threats to the US military.
Among the weapons demonstrated was Meadowlands, an offensive system that can jam enemy satellites and disrupt their communications.
According to the WSJ, these satellites are used for surveillance, communications, and navigation.
Meadowlands often operates alongside a defensive system known as Bounty Hunter, which scans the electromagnetic spectrum to detect and locate potential threats to US forces, the report explained. Commanders can then pinpoint the location of a specific threat and order a defensive strike.
Transportable jamming system used by US Space Force
The US Space Force has also accelerated the deployment of a newer jamming system known as the Remote Modular Terminal. The equipment can be packed into a container and transported to locations around the world, allowing US personnel to deploy electronic warfare capabilities quickly.
Over the past year, US Space Force soldiers, known as Guardians, have transported and deployed these systems to support US military operations in both Venezuela and Iran.
According to the WSJ, “In a sign of how important space systems are, Iran repeatedly targeted US space capabilities, including satellite communications terminals, to try to degrade those advantages.
“Satellites help the US detect missile launches, guide weapons, and get a clear picture of the battlefield,” taking high-resolution imagery from above.
Tech.-Sgt. Joshua Lomax, who helped counter threats during operations in Venezuela before being deployed to defend against threats from Iran, described the pressure of preparing for the missions.
“The threat is real,” Lomax told the WSJ.
He recalled having just 72 hours to pack the equipment in Venezuela, load it onto an aircraft, and depart for Iran.
“It was incredibly intense,” he told the WSJ. “Everybody was head on a swivel.”
Importance of electromagnetic waves in modern warfare
The US Space Force also highlighted the importance of electromagnetic waves, which travel at different wavelengths and frequencies and underpin many of the technologies used in modern warfare. These systems connect military assets ranging from submarines and drones to radar installations.
According to US Space Forces’ Combat Forces Command, led by Lt.-Gen. Greggory Gagnon, a key mission for the US is to dominate the electromagnetic spectrum.
“That thing you never see is incredibly important in warfare,” he said. “If we can dominate the spectrum, we can keep our systems, our satellites, our ships, our planes, all connected and working more effectively, but we can also disrupt the adversary’s ability to do it.”
