US considers easing sanctions on shadow fleet vessels to cut freight rates, official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:36:54 UTC
09:36:54 KST

The Trump administration is considering easing sanctions on so-called shadow fleet vessels that have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela, in an effort to reduce record-high global freight rates, a US official said on Wednesday.
The discussions are happening days after President Donald Trump temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel fuel, a move met with a torrent of criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, European countries and some of Trump's fellow Republicans in the US Senate.
Both Zelenskiy and the US senators called that move a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin that would provide Russia with revenue to keep funding its war in Ukraine.
The new talks center on the United States potentially allowing "legal oil" to flow on previously sanctioned vessels, the US official said. That means crude or petroleum products not sanctioned by Washington, rather than Russian and Iranian oil, which are under punitive measures.
The goal is to get more refined products and crude out of the Gulf, the official said.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a video to the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh this week that the administration was talking about easing the sanctions on shadow fleet vessels in an effort to cut record freight rates that have cut into demand for US crude, according to Energy Aspects, a research group.
Bits of the talk were broadcast on social media, but Reuters was not able to obtain the full video or a transcript. The Department of Energy said it was not available.
Companies seeking to use the sanctioned vessels would have to apply to the US Treasury Department to use the vessels, the official said.
The Department of Energy said any move to relieve sanctions on the shadow fleet would not help Russia to move oil or oil products. The Treasury Department referred questions to the Department of Energy.
But Trump's push to move Russian diesel to global markets quickly could put pressure on the departments to allow shipment via the vessels.
The White House did not respond immediately to a request for comment.
High oil and fuel prices are a risk for Trump in the November 3 midterm elections in which Republicans are hoping to maintain control of both chambers of Congress. He lifted the sanctions on Russian diesel through April 7.
Tanker freight rates soar to record highs
Tanker freight rates have soared to record highs as the wars in Iran and Ukraine have stoked inflation and put US crude oil out of reach for Asian refiners, pushing them to seek alternatives from the Middle East and Latin America.
Energy Aspects said in a note to clients that easing the sanctions on the shadow fleet would not greatly impact freight rates but could allow more movement of oil in the Middle East.
Lifting the sanctions on the tankers that are mostly old and not well maintained is "unlikely to add meaningful mainstream fleet capacity overnight, especially as most tankers sanctioned over Russian or Venezuelan links have been actively trading over the past three months," it said in the note.
Easing the restrictions "could make a small number of additional tankers available for certain (Strait of) Hormuz shuttle runs," in the waterway between Iran and Oman.
Lifting the measures is unlikely to result in a broad easing of freight rates as ship insurers will still be bound by EU and UK regulations, maritime industry sources said.

Israel blocks Gaza base for Trump's Board of Peace as election nears, Guardian reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:30:48 UTC
09:30:48 KST

Israel is blocking construction of a military outpost in the Gaza Strip intended to serve as a base for an international stabilization force operating under U.S. President Donald Trump's Board of Peace, The Guardian reported Wednesday, citing a person with direct knowledge of the project.
According to the British newspaper, the Board of Peace awarded its first Gaza construction contract in early August to Arkel International, a Louisiana-based company tasked with building a fortified compound for approximately 150 international troops.
More than two months later, construction has yet to begin because Israel has not authorized contractors or construction vehicles to enter the territory, the source said.
"Israel won't open the border," the source told The Guardian.
The newspaper said a Board of Peace spokesperson declined to comment, while the Israeli government and IDF did not respond to requests for comment.
A military base holding up Gaza reconstruction
The proposed compound would measure approximately 100 by 100 meters and be built on a site formerly used by the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF), the now-defunct aid distribution operation that delivered humanitarian supplies through private contractors.
The facility is intended to accommodate rotating deployments of 150 armed international troops, drawn from a larger contingent of approximately 500 personnel dispatched from Morocco and Kosovo, according to the report.
The troops would form part of the International Stabilization Force (ISF), a multinational security mission planned to operate in Gaza under the Board of Peace.
But the source warned that the absence of the military base is preventing the broader reconstruction program from moving forward.
Without the stabilization force on the ground, there would be no security arrangements to enable construction crews to enter, deliver equipment, install utilities or establish basic infrastructure, the source explained.
The delay therefore threatens far more than the construction of a single military facility. It could prevent the launch of the initial reconstruction projects planned for southern Gaza.
Is Israel's election behind the delay?
The source told The Guardian that officials involved in the Board of Peace believe Israel will allow construction to proceed after the country's October 27 election.
That assessment raises questions about whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government is reluctant to permit the start of Gaza reconstruction during the election campaign.
However, the report did not establish that electoral considerations were the reason Israeli authorities had withheld the necessary approvals.
The delay comes despite Israel having already approved the Board of Peace's entry into Gaza and the launch of a limited reconstruction initiative.
In July, Israel's security cabinet approved a pilot program to restore basic services in the territory, with the first stage expected to take place in Rafah, in southern Gaza.
The initiative is intended to lay the groundwork for a broader international effort to stabilize the territory and begin rebuilding infrastructure damaged during the war.
Countries expected to contribute troops to the stabilization force include Uganda, Morocco, Kosovo and Kazakhstan. Discussions have also been held with Albania, Vietnam and Georgia about possible participation.
Temporary housing and a Palestinian administration
Beyond the military outpost, the reconstruction initiative calls for temporary housing facilities in Rafah to accommodate Palestinian residents.
Under the reported plans, Palestinians seeking to move into the designated areas would undergo extensive security screening intended to prevent individuals affiliated with Hamas or connected to the terrorist organization from entering.
The pilot area would be the first in Gaza administered by the Palestinian technocratic body known as the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG).
The committee would operate with the backing of the international stabilization force, which is intended to provide security for the reconstruction effort and support the establishment of civilian administration.
The arrangements form part of Trump's broader postwar framework for Gaza, which places the Board of Peace at the center of efforts to stabilize and reconstruct the territory.
For now, however, the plan remains dependent on Israeli authorization to move the first contractors and equipment into Gaza.
According to the source cited by The Guardian, officials involved in the initiative expect that approval may come only after Israelis go to the polls on October 27, leaving the first phase of the reconstruction effort on hold.

In line with the budget, the Bangladeshi government aims to reduce inflation to 7.5 percent and raise GDP growth to 6.5 percent in the fiscal year. ■

Ecuador to shore up electric system ahead of peak El Nino months: president
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:25:04 CST
09:25:04 KST

QUITO, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Ecuador is set to shore up its electric system to ensure service during the critical months of the El Nino weather phenomenon, forecast to run from late November through February, President Daniel Noboa said Wednesday.
"We are facing a very harsh weather situation, especially along the coast, though highland areas are also being affected," Noboa said in an interview with Radio Centro in the central city of Ambato.
According to Noboa, adverse weather conditions have led to an increase in disruptions in electricity, with incidents climbing from an average of "20-odd" times per day in a normal year to between 60 and 70 currently.
The government has added more than 400 megawatts of electricity generation capacity by granting permits and providing support to the private sector, with the goal of strengthening the system's capacity, he said.
The announcement comes amid Ecuador's dry season, marked by a lack of rainfall in the southern part of the country, home to the reservoirs that supply the Paute Hydroelectric Complex of the National Interconnected System.
The complex is the country's largest hydroelectric system and supplies about 35 percent of national electricity demand.
Currently, large industries in Ecuador are facing up to 72 hours of power cuts a week due to the dry season, a measure intended to reduce consumption and ease pressure on the national electrical system.
In 2024, the country went through an unprecedented energy crisis, with power outages lasting up to 14 hours a day that affected households, businesses and industries.
Ecuador was hit with extreme weather from El Nino in 1982-1983 and 1997-1998, including torrential rains and flooding, particularly in the coastal region. ■

====================================================================================================

Costa Rica opens mega-prison as Bukele model embraced across Latin America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:24:03 UTC
09:24:03 KST

Costa Rica opens mega-prison as Bukele model embraced across Latin America
President Laura Fernandez says mega-prison is part of ‘tough-on-crime model’ embraced by her government.
Costa Rica has announced the opening of a new mega-prison amid near-record homicide levels and growing organised crime, as countries across the region embrace police crackdowns that have proven popular but often weaken key civil liberties.
President Laura Fernandez opened the High-Containment Centre Against Organised Crime, or CACCO, on Wednesday. The prison will have capacity for 5,100 people, equivalent to about 20 percent of the country’s current prison population.
“The CACCO will force criminals to face a new model – a tough-on-crime model. Costa Rica will become a global benchmark for prison security,” Fernandez said during an inauguration ceremony.
Candidates across Latin America have embraced mega-prisons, seeking to replicate the policies of Nayib Bukele, the president of El Salvador, who has won widespread popularity through a campaign of mass arrests and the suspension of basic rights in the name of combating crime.
Costa Rica, long spared from high levels of violent crime compared with its neighbours, saw a record-setting 905 homicides in 2023, followed by 876 in 2024 and 873 in 2025.
Analysts say that is partly due to increased fighting between criminal groups over lucrative drug routes.
The first transfers to Costa Rica’s new mega-prison will take place at the end of October, with Justice Minister Gabriel Aguilar saying the facility will help the government reassert control over the prison system and diminish infiltration by organised crime.
Right-wing leaders in other Latin American countries have also sought to replicate the mega-prison model.
Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, inaugurated in July, has announced plans to tour El Salvador’s Terrorism Confinement Centre (CECOT), in anticipation of creating a similar facility in her country. CECOT can hold about 40,000 people.
In Colombia, meanwhile, newly elected leader Abelardo de la Espriella campaigned for the presidency, in part, on a pledge to build 10 mega-prisons. He took office in August.
Brazil, the largest country in Latin America, is currently in the midst of its own presidential election, and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has advanced to the final round of the vote. His platform also includes building five mega-prisons, citing the Salvadoran model.
El Salvador first imposed a “state of exception” under Bukele in 2022, expanding police and military powers.
That emergency declaration has been credited with a sharp drop in that country’s homicides, but rights groups say it has led to severe rights abuses and has been weaponised against critics of the government.
The “state of exception” has also resulted in mass arrests and mass trials, with rulings delivered against hundreds of defendants at a time. Some defendants have been detained without charge.
While the Bukele administration frequently touts its success in dismantling the gangs, the government has continuously extended the state of exception since it was first imposed.
Critics have warned that conditions inside mega-prisons are often poor, with imprisoned people facing overcrowding, due process violations and alleged torture in facilities like CECOT.

The protests coincided with the official opening of Colombia's embassy in West Jerusalem on Wednesday, reversing the previous administration's decision to sever diplomatic relations with Israel.
De la Espriella, who took office in August, restored ties that former President Gustavo Petro had cut in 2024 over Israel's genocidal war in Gaza.
His administration also reinstated a free trade agreement with Israel that had been suspended under Petro.
Colombian Foreign Minister Omar Bula attended the embassy's inauguration ceremony in West Jerusalem, describing the move as a step towards strengthening bilateral relations.
Bula said diplomatic relations between the two countries "should never have been broken."
"Israel is a strategic partner. It always has been, and from now on, it will be an even stronger one," he said.
The embassy opening represented "a concrete step towards fully restoring bilateral relations," he added.
Palestinian officials condemned the inauguration, warning that the decision undermined international law and damaged Colombia's longstanding diplomatic position on the Palestinian cause.

Israel may be left out of global climate summit in Turkey amid security fears

00:22:43 UTC

A total of 197 countries are expected to participate in the global climate summit in Turkey next month. Unfortunately, Israel will likely not be among them, due to a combination of security concerns and diplomatic isolation.
The Ministry of Environmental Protection said it had submitted a request to security officials on behalf of both the ministry and the Foreign Ministry, but noted: "At this stage, approval for the joint delegation's departure has not yet been granted. However, the matter is currently being reconsidered, and no final decision has been made."
'It's more of a political conference'
The summit is an annual gathering of countries that are parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. This year's agenda will include a review of national emissions reduction targets and mark a decade since the Paris Agreement, aimed at limiting global warming, entered into force.
Asked how important Israeli participation is, Prof. Colin Price, head of Tel Aviv University's Climate Initiative, said: "It's more of a political conference, which is why it's important for us to be there, just as we participate in the United Nations even though we don't have much influence. But being there matters. This year, the situation is apparently different. The fact that the conference is being held in Turkey is preventing many people from attending.
The Ministry of Environmental Protection barely functions these days, so there's less interest. It's a combination of security concerns and a lack of interest on the government's part. So we won't be there, although there may be private-sector representatives.
"Scientists working and conducting research in the climate field don't feel that there's any boycott or that the current situation is affecting international cooperation, including conferences," he added. "I think there's much less politics at the scientific level. I served as a reviewer for one of the chapters of an Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) report."
At the same time, Price warned that the private sector could suffer from Israel's absence.
"There's no exposure, no networking and no investment. Four years ago, there were far more foreign investors in companies. I'm involved in a startup, and over the past year or two, investors have stopped responding. They simply don't answer our emails. There's much less foreign investment in climate tech [innovative technologies designed to address climate change]. If we don't attend the summit, we miss out on those connections and meetings."
Udi Avni, co-country director of Greenpeace Israel, also expressed concern over Israel's likely absence from the event.
"Against the backdrop of extreme climate events around the world, Israel's participation in the summit is essential," he said. "The absence of official representation harms the national interest and the Israeli public. If this were Eurovision, things would look and sound very different. The government should be doing everything in its power to demand that the host country guarantee the Israeli delegation's safety or ask the United Nations to relocate the summit. Turkey was chosen as the host nearly a year ago.
"Unlike Eurovision, the climate summit produces technical but important decisions on issues such as renewable energy transition targets, environmental regulations and funding for green technologies. These decisions directly affect the quality of life of all Israelis, the cost of living and the economy, national security and our ability to cope with the consequences of the climate crisis, including wildfires and drought."
Avni added that "the summit is also an opportunity to promote Israeli technologies and international cooperation that could help improve Israel's diplomatic standing by supporting key demands on the agenda, including a rapid, just and adequately funded transition away from fossil fuels, the development of an ambitious national roadmap for phasing out fossil fuels and support for the 'polluter pays' principle by taxing the windfall profits of energy corporations to finance climate compensation funds."
'Another blow to the environment'
Dr. Avner Gross, Head of the Climate Change Research Laboratory at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, said: "The climate crisis is one of the greatest challenges facing humanity, and it will be with us from now on. To address it, we need the entire global community, including Israel. One way to have an impact and be part of the effort is to participate in the international climate summit, which nearly every country in the world attends. Israel's absence would signal a further withdrawal from the global dialogue, potentially harming the country academically and economically."
Mor Gilboa, CEO of Zalul, an Israeli environmental organization focused on protecting marine and freshwater ecosystems, said Israel's failure to attend the summit would be another blow to environmental and climate efforts in a region that urgently needs cooperation to better protect and manage the resources shared by Mediterranean countries.
"It is deeply regrettable that political tensions and security threats will likely prevent Israel from participating in the summit," Gilboa said. "The climate crisis will not wait for political circumstances to change. In reality, it continues to worsen and even adds further tensions to an already strained political situation."

US rejects recommendation for ICE body cams to be automatically activated

US rejects recommendation for ICE body cams to be automatically activated
WASHINGTON – The Trump administration has rejected a government watchdog’s recommendation that US immigration officials should use technology that would automatically activate body-worn cameras when an officer pulls their weapon or sets off a car siren.
Automatic activation of body-worn cameras was one of a number of recommendations outlined in a report released on Oct 14 by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), an independent nonpartisan watchdog agency for Congress.
The recommendation comes as US agencies face mounting scrutiny over enforcement tactics used in an immigration crackdown that has included fatal shootings of two US citizens in Minneapolis, raising questions about officers’ accountability.
The GAO report said US Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection “should improve body-worn camera programme management”, adding that CBP and ICE have not updated their programme plans since 2022 and 2024, respectively.
Covering the period from February 2025 until September 2026, the report recommended that ICE implement additional controls to make sure that cameras are activated.
“We maintain that additional controls, such as automated camera activation, would provide greater assurance that body-worn cameras meet ICE’s desired results for transparency, accountability, and public trust,” the GAO said in the report.
The Department of Homeland Security, of which ICE is a part, said in comments cited in the report that it did not agree with the recommendation, citing what it said were privacy and operational risks.
For ICE, automatic activation risked the possibility of inadvertent or false activations during routine movement, the DHS said in the report.
DHS also said in the report that inadvertent or false activations could result in the unauthorised recording of sensitive interactions with informants or victims, or the recording of bystanders engaged in free speech activities in areas where camera use is restricted.
ICE has been the face of President Donald Trump’s deportation drive, which he says aims to improve domestic security.
Rights advocates say the crackdown has violated due process and free speech rights and created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.
Responding to the GAO report’s publication, a DHS spokesperson said on Oct 14 ICE had acquired devices to equip all officers and agents with body cameras.
“Training required to equip individual officers remains ongoing and we expect to complete this training soon,” the spokesperson said. REUTERS

As Indonesian Fires Continue, Singapore Records Highest Air Pollution Reading Since 2015
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:19:00 UTC
09:19:00 KST

Air pollution readings in some parts of Singapore yesterday spiked to their highest levels in more than a decade, as Indonesia came under increased pressure for its failure to contain the wildfires that have caused a dramatic decline in air quality across the region.
Hourly PM2.5 readings rose across all regions of Singapore yesterday afternoon, with the reading in the west of the island climbing to 288 micrograms per cubic meter. The reading, which is in the National Environmental Agency (NEA)’s “very high” range, was the highest recorded since 2015, Channel News Asia reported.
PM2.5 readings were in the “high” range in the south, east, and central regions of the country, while the reading in the north was in the “elevated” range.
With readings entering the “very high” range, the government also began the phased distribution of N95 masks to vulnerable segments of the population, and temporarily closed all outdoor and non-air-conditioned sports facilities in western Singapore.
Indonesia is currently battling the most intense wildfire season in 11 years, which has been exacerbated by an unusually severe dry season linked to a global El Niño weather pattern. The fires, which are concentrated mostly on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, have created a haze that has affected much of maritime Southeast Asia, forcing school closures and impacting the health of tens of millions of people.
The government of Timor-Leste, which borders Indonesia, said in a statement yesterday that it was suspending face-to-face learning activities for three days starting from October 15 “due to contamination by pollutant particles from wildfires in neighboring regions or countries.” This comes after the Malaysian government last week ordered the closure of schools across peninsular Malaysia, including in the capital Kuala Lumpur, due to the worsening haze.
In Indonesia, authorities said more than 280,000 respiratory problems have been recorded in affected regions since August 18. In the province of Central Kalimantan, the country’s ISPU air pollution index yesterday exceeded 1,200, four times higher than the “hazardous” level of 300.
While some fires naturally occur during the annual dry season, many are caused by agricultural burn-off on monoculture plantations, such as palm oil, maize, paper pulp, and sugar, that are controlled by powerful Indonesian conglomerates. The country’s Forestry Minister Raja Juli Antoni said last month that most of the fires in Kalimantan and Sumatra had been deliberately set by individuals or companies, and pledged to investigate and punish those responsible.
As I noted earlier this week, the crisis has highlighted the inadequacy of regional mechanisms for combating transboundary haze. Malaysia this week announced that it would raise the issue with Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) foreign ministers ahead of the bloc’s summit in the Philippines next month.
For now, however, the region is reliant on the actions of the Indonesian government, which has been subject to increasing criticism for its failure to contain – or prevent – the fires. In addition to a wave of complaints from Singaporean and Malaysian social media users, the frustration is now breaking into the political realm. Andrew Chen Kah Eng, the head of the Johor state branch of Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Pakatan Harapan coalition, said on Monday that Indonesia “must be held accountable” for its failure to contain the wildfires.
“Indonesian spokespeople need to stop being indifferent and unapologetic to all ASEAN countries affected, including its own people, by human-induced haze pollution,” he said. “Allowing toxic haze containing PM2.5 fine particles to pollute the air of neighboring countries is unacceptable.”
The following day, Malaysian lawmaker Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman called on Southeast Asian governments to lodge formal diplomatic protests with their Indonesian counterparts, suggesting that Malaysian and Singaporean banks cut off financing to Indonesian companies linked to land burning. “You need to treat them like an outcast in the region,” he said.
On Tuesday, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto ordered the mobilization of additional resources to combat the wildfires, which are particularly difficult to control due to the fact that many are in geographically remote areas and are burning on areas of dried peatland, where fires can smolder for weeks underground.
“This is a top priority for us. We must resolve it immediately,” Prabowo told a meeting with the relevant Indonesian authorities, according to a government statement.
Even if it is successful, without continuing action to control the activities of powerful agri-business interests, the region will continue to be subject to the choking externalities of Indonesia’s dysfunctional political economy.

Israel's largest Hasidic sect threatens to withhold 30,000 votes in election feud
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:18:54 UTC
09:18:54 KST

Less than two weeks before Israel's October 27 election, the country's largest Hasidic movement is threatening to withhold its support from United Torah Judaism (UTJ), potentially costing the ultra-Orthodox alliance some 30,000 votes as an internal power struggle threatens to spill over into the ballot box.
The Gur Hasidic movement, which traditionally holds the most senior position within the Hasidic Agudat Yisrael faction and its representation in the broader UTJ alliance, has yet to begin encouraging its followers to vote. The silence has drawn criticism from within the party, particularly as other ultra-Orthodox communities intensify their election campaigns.
In Hamodia, the newspaper affiliated with Gur, there has been no reference to the election and no public instruction from the movement's spiritual leader, Rabbi Yaakov Aryeh Alter, urging followers to support the party.
The absence is especially unusual so close to election day. In previous campaigns, calls to vote for UTJ were prominently featured in the newspaper weeks before Israelis went to the polls.
Initially, Gur officials dismissed the need for an early campaign, arguing that "the rebbe will tell people on election day whom to vote for, and they will listen."
But the continued silence now appears to reflect a deeper dispute over the balance of power within the ultra-Orthodox political alliance.
The split threatening 30,000 votes
The crisis began just hours before the deadline for submitting candidate lists, when lawmaker Meir Porush, representing the Shlomei Emunim faction, and Elyakim Stark, the representative of the Belz Hasidic movement, broke away from Agudat Yisrael.
The two established a separate party, Homat Torat Yisrael, while remaining within the broader United Torah Judaism electoral alliance.
The move effectively freed them from the authority of Agudat Yisrael's institutions, particularly its Council of Torah Sages, the senior rabbinical body that guides the party's decisions.
Porush and Stark occupy the fourth and sixth positions, respectively, on the joint UTJ candidate list.
In Gur, leaders are now considering withholding an official call for their followers to vote, a move that could reduce the number of seats won by the alliance and prevent Stark from entering the Knesset.
"Goldknopf will get in anyway. Our representative is number two on the list, so his seat is secure," a Gur source said, referring to Yitzhak Goldknopf, the movement's senior political representative.
Gur has approximately 30,000 eligible voters, whose support could translate into roughly one to one-and-a-half Knesset seats.
"If Gur gives its mandate or mandate and a half to the party, it will bring Elyakim Stark into the Knesset, even though he is not loyal to the council and has left Agudat Yisrael," the source added.
The calculation is straightforward: Gur's own representative is placed high enough on the list that his election is considered secure, while Stark, in sixth place, could lose his seat if the alliance wins fewer mandates.
Negotiations before election day
Gur representatives are currently engaged in negotiations aimed at securing an agreement on the distribution of positions within the alliance before the election.
If those negotiations fail, the movement could maintain its current position and refrain from encouraging its followers to vote, potentially depriving UTJ of tens of thousands of ballots.
Agudat Yisrael is seeking understandings with Degel HaTorah, the Lithuanian ultra-Orthodox faction that forms the other major component of UTJ, regarding the standing of Porush and Stark.
It is also demanding that Degel HaTorah refrain from negotiating separately with Homat Torat Yisrael in future elections until the breakaway faction returns to Agudat Yisrael and again accepts its organizational framework.
Agudat Yisrael did not respond to a request for comment.
Another concern within Gur is that a last-minute voting instruction from the rebbe could carry less weight among some followers than the traditional campaign appeals issued well in advance of election day.
Nevertheless, the prevailing expectation within the movement is that its leadership will ultimately instruct followers to vote for UTJ, whose ballot designation is the Hebrew letter gimel, as it has in previous elections.
Before that happens, however, Gur officials want an agreement on the allocation of political positions to prevent the dispute from continuing after the election.
The internal struggle has also been fueled by the leadership change within the Belz Hasidic movement.
The Belz rebbe appointed Stark, a powerful figure within the community, as its new representative on the UTJ list, replacing veteran lawmaker Yisrael Eichler.
Eichler has served in the Knesset almost continuously since 2003 and currently holds the position of deputy communications minister. He previously chaired the Knesset's Labor and Welfare Committee and served as a deputy Knesset speaker.
With election day approaching, the dispute has left one of Israel's most influential ultra-Orthodox voting blocs without its customary campaign instructions, while negotiations continue over whether its 30,000 voters will be mobilized to support the joint list.

Mexican court closes case against official over 2023 detention centre fire
Victims’ groups, however, have denounced the ruling as ‘selective’ justice that exonerates a former government head.
A Mexican judge has closed the case against Francisco Garduno, former head of the country’s immigration agency, for crimes related to the 2023 fire at a Ciudad Juarez detention centre that killed 40 migrants and injured 30 others.
The incident was the deadliest event ever to occur at a Mexican immigration centre, and critics said it exposed the shortcomings and irregularities in the country’s detention system.
Garduno faced trial for the crimes of abuse of public office and dereliction of duty after footage from the fire showed guards had failed to respond to cries for help.
On Tuesday, Judge Victor Manlio Hernandez Calderon ruled that Garduno had fulfilled the court-mandated measures required to address the damage. But victims rejected that decision and announced they would appeal.
“Yesterday, corruption and the impunity of politicians protected by power won again,” the Foundation for Justice, one of the NGOs representing some of the victims, wrote on social media on Wednesday.
The victims have also compared the judge’s decision to close the criminal case to a de facto exoneration for Garduno.
In their view, the ruling “confirms that justice in Mexico is selective” and denies the victims “full reparations” and concrete guarantees that such an event will not be repeated.
Miguel Zenteno, one of the foundation’s lawyers, noted that the ruling is not yet final because it will be appealed and because another injunction is pending against the court-mandated reparations, which critics say failed to meet the standards for serious events.
On March 27, 2023, some 70 men were crammed into a locked dormitory with no ventilation and barely any water at the Ciudad Juarez immigration detention centre, on the border with El Paso, Texas.
As night fell, a small group set fire to some mattresses in protest, and within seconds, smoke engulfed the entire area.
Security cameras recorded the guards leaving the area despite cries for help. They made no attempt to open the gates of the dormitory. Only the women, held in another cell, were released. Most of the victims were Central Americans and Venezuelans.
Garduno, a former prison guard and current official at the Ministry of Education, led the National Migration Institute (INM) starting in 2019 and continued in the role until 2025 despite the fire.
The judge had previously ordered Garduno to compensate the families, provide them with free specialised medical care, issue a public apology, provide human rights training to migration personnel and guarantee that the events would not be repeated.
Zenteno acknowledged that the measures were implemented only partially because Garduno did not pay the damages as stipulated by the legal process.
Instead, Zenteno pointed out that the funds came from the INM, and the payments did not fully compensate the families. Furthermore, he added, the victims were not even informed how to access free medical services, and the apology “was a mere formality, not substantive”.
In addition to Garduno, prosecutors accused another former director of the institute of the same crimes.
Six immigration agents – including a military officer and a private security guard – and the two migrants accused of starting the fire are charged with homicide and assault. Most of the officials remain free pending trial.

Israeli prison guards have shot Palestinian detainees with rubber bullets in confined spaces, leaving one prisoner requiring surgery and another undergoing an operation for a fractured shin, Israeli daily Haaretz reported, citing medical records and inmate testimonies.
According to Physicians for Human Rights Israel and the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel, at least 21 shooting incidents have been documented across five Israeli prisons since October 2023.
Rights investigators noted that most cases occurred in late 2025 and the first half of 2026, often at point-blank range and without any preceding unrest or security disturbance.
The most severe incident occurred in June at Ketziot Prison in southern Israel.
Hospital records from Soroka Medical Centre confirmed that an inmate's organ was completely destroyed by rubber-coated ammunition, necessitating immediate surgical excision.
In formal legal testimony, the prisoner stated that guards initially kicked him during a strip search a week earlier before members of the prison service's specialised Masada unit discharged rubber rounds directly into his cell, striking his previously injured groin and knee before dragging him roughly 50 metres while bleeding heavily.
Systemic abuse
Further records from Ketziot revealed that another prisoner underwent emergency surgery in July after sustaining a fractured left shin from a rubber bullet.
A former detainee told Haaretz he was shot at close range in April and denied medical care for 15 days, receiving surgery only upon release.
Rights organisations confirmed that shootings occurred inside sleeping cells, exercise yards, and legal consultation waiting areas.
Although rights monitors formally petitioned authorities in August to prohibit the use of rubber and plastic ammunition in confined settings, the Israeli Prison Service rejected a blanket ban.
Meirav Ben Zeev, a lawyer with the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel, emphasised that detainees remain fearful of reporting abuse due to potential retaliation, noting that previous complaints failed to produce prosecutions.
Around 9,350 Palestinians, including 350 children and 90 women, remain incarcerated in Israeli facilities amid widespread reports of torture, starvation, and severe medical neglect.

Florida can enforce state law barring young kids from social media, appeals court rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:00:00 UTC
09:00:00 KST

Florida can enforce state law barring young kids from social media, appeals court rules
- Florida can enforce H.B. 3, a law barring under-14s from social media with addictive features, after the 11th Circuit said it does not breach free speech rights.
- Tech groups NetChoice and the CCIA, backed by Meta, TikTok and Snap, sued to block the law. NetChoice said it is “currently evaluating all of our options”.
- The court also sent Florida’s case against Snap back to state court. Florida says the law protects children’s mental health, while critics say it limits teens’ online speech.
AI generated
ATLANTA – A federal appeals court on Oct 14 allowed Florida to enforce a state law barring children under 14 from accessing social media platforms like Instagram, TikTok or Snapchat, rejecting tech industry groups’ claims that the law violates the US Constitution’s free speech protections.
In a unanimous ruling, a three-judge panel on the Atlanta-based 11th US Circuit Court of Appeals vacated a lower court’s preliminary injunction blocking the law, known as HB3.
The court said the law does not regulate the content hosted by social media sites and therefore does not run afoul of the First Amendment. “HB3 applies to platforms wholly without regard to the topics discussed or the ideas or messages conveyed on them,” wrote Circuit Judge Kevin Newsom, an appointee of President Donald Trump. “Truth Social is just as likely as Instagram to be affected by HB3.”
Representatives for Florida Attorney-General James Uthmeier, who defended the law, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The law bars social media platforms that have so-called addictive features, which include things like video autoplay and infinite scroll, from allowing children under the age of 14 to create accounts.
Tech industry groups NetChoice and the Computer & Communications Industry Association, which count Meta Platforms, TikTok and Snap as members, had sued in 2024 to block the law.
In a statement after the ruling on Oct 14, Paul Taske, director of the NetChoice Litigation Center, said the group is “currently evaluating all of our options as we continue the fight to ensure Floridians’ rights to free expression online are protected, and parents remain in the driver’s seat when it comes to making decisions for their families”.
Snap sued
Florida was among the first of several states to pass a law regulating social media use for children amid a broader reckoning over the apps’ role in young people’s mental health.
After HB3 took effect, Uthmeier sued Snapchat owner Snap in April 2025, accusing it of illegally employing features that addict children and opening accounts for children aged 13 and younger. Snap said HB3 and the lawsuit sought to restrict teens’ speech online, in violation of the US Constitution.
A few months later, the judge overseeing the industry groups’ lawsuit granted their request for a preliminary injunction blocking the law’s enforcement, saying HB3 was likely unconstitutional. Uthmeier appealed that ruling to the 11th Circuit, and the court stayed the injunction while it weighed the case.
Separately, a lower court overseeing Florida’s case against Snap had rejected the state’s request in August 2025 to order Snap to comply with HB3, also finding the law likely violated constitutional rights. But in a second ruling on Oct 14, the 11th Circuit vacated that decision and said the case should move forward in state court, not federal. A representative for Snap declined to comment. REUTERS

Text description provided by the architects. Located in the heart of the Taoyangli Historic District in Jingdezhen, Zhuozhuo Community is an urban regeneration project that transforms a collection of existing buildings, residential structures, and traditional alleyways into an open, multifunctional cultural community. Situated between Zhongshan North Road, a historic commercial street dating back approximately 600 years, and the Imperial Kiln archaeological site, Taoyangli preserves the layered urban fabric of Jingdezhen's ceramic heritage. Former workshops, residences, guild halls, and narrow alleyways form a dense urban environment shaped by centuries of porcelain production, commerce, and everyday life. Rather than preserving individual buildings as isolated objects, the project explores how historic urban spaces can accommodate contemporary functions while retaining their architectural identity and cultural continuity.

Text description provided by the architects. Located in the heart of the Taoyangli Historic District in Jingdezhen, Zhuozhuo Community is an urban regeneration project that transforms a collection of existing buildings, residential structures, and traditional alleyways into an open, multifunctional cultural community. Situated between Zhongshan North Road, a historic commercial street dating back approximately 600 years, and the Imperial Kiln archaeological site, Taoyangli preserves the layered urban fabric of Jingdezhen's ceramic heritage. Former workshops, residences, guild halls, and narrow alleyways form a dense urban environment shaped by centuries of porcelain production, commerce, and everyday life. Rather than preserving individual buildings as isolated objects, the project explores how historic urban spaces can accommodate contemporary functions while retaining their architectural identity and cultural continuity.

Eight U.S. states have sued OpenAI over ChatGPT, accusing the company of having a dangerous impact on users
Kyiv • UNN
Prosecutors from eight states accuse OpenAI of ChatGPT’s dangerous impact on users, particularly teenagers. They are demanding changes, compensation, and fines.
As many as eight U.S. states have filed lawsuits against OpenAI, accusing its ChatGPT chatbot of having a dangerous impact on users, particularly teenagers. Prosecutors believe that artificial intelligence may encourage people to harm themselves and others. Reuters reports, according to UNN.
Details
The lawsuits were filed by the attorneys general of Iowa, Kansas, Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Montana, Nebraska, and West Virginia. They claim that ChatGPT was specifically designed to build users' trust through friendly interaction.
At the same time, according to the plaintiffs, the chatbot may reinforce dangerous beliefs, encourage risky behavior, and even help plan violent acts, including mass attacks.
Prosecutors demand that OpenAI change how ChatGPT operates
The prosecutors accuse the company of violating consumer protection laws and misleading people about the chatbot's safety.
The states are asking courts to order OpenAI to change the principles governing ChatGPT's operation, pay compensation, and pay civil penalties. The demands also include restrictions on developing artificial intelligence models capable of improving themselves independently unless the company guarantees that they align with human values.
As Reuters notes, this is the largest coordinated legal campaign by U.S. states against OpenAI. Florida filed the first similar lawsuit in June.
The company is also involved in dozens of private lawsuits related to ChatGPT's potentially dangerous impact. As of publication, OpenAI had not provided comment on the new allegations.

What is celebrated on October 15 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
02:43:25 EEST
08:43:25 KST

What is celebrated on October 15 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On October 15, several international commemorative dates are observed around the world, while believers commemorate saints according to the new and old calendars.
On October 15, the world observes International Rural Women's Day, Global Handwashing Day, and International White Cane Safety Day. According to the new-style church calendar, Saint Euthymius the New is commemorated, while according to the old style, Hieromartyr Cyprian, Holy Martyr Justina, and Venerable Andrew are remembered, UNN writes.
International Day of Rural Women
An official UN international observance proclaimed by the General Assembly in 2007. The event highlights the important role of rural women in ensuring food security, developing the agricultural sector, preserving traditional communities, and overcoming poverty. The day calls on governments to eliminate gender barriers to access to land resources, credit, modern education, and medical services in rural areas.
Global Handwashing Day
Launched in 2008 by the Global Handwashing Partnership with the support of UNICEF and WHO. This educational observance highlights a simple but vitally important hygiene practice — washing hands with soap, which is the cheapest and most effective way to prevent the spread of intestinal and respiratory infections, especially among children in developing countries.
International White Cane Safety Day
Established in the United States in 1964 at the initiative of the National Federation of the Blind and subsequently supported by the World Blind Union. The white cane is an international symbol of blind and visually impaired people. The event aims to draw public attention to the needs of people with visual impairments, ensuring an accessible urban environment, road safety, and equal opportunities in employment and everyday life.
Pregnancy and Infant Loss Remembrance Day
A commemorative observance established in 2002 in the United States and Canada that has since gained international scope. This day gives parents and families who have experienced the loss of a child through miscarriage, pregnancy loss, stillbirth, or sudden infant death syndrome an opportunity to share their grief.
The Day of Remembrance of Venerable Euthymius the New
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate Venerable Euthymius the New of Thessalonica — an outstanding Byzantine ascetic who embraced monasticism on Mount Olympus, pursued asceticism on Mount Athos, and founded a monastery near Thessalonica. On this day, they also remember Saint Venerable Martyr Lucian, presbyter of Antioch — an outstanding theologian and founder of the Antiochian School of Theology, who carried out a detailed translation and editing of the books of Holy Scripture and suffered a martyr's death for his faith during the reign of Emperor Maximian Galerius.
According to the old calendar, believers commemorate Hieromartyr Cyprian and Holy Martyr Justina. According to tradition, Cyprian was a pagan sage and sorcerer in Nicomedia, but after witnessing the steadfastness of the virgin Justina's faith in the face of his magic, he sincerely repented, was baptized, became a bishop, and together with Justina suffered a martyr's death during the reign of Emperor Diocletian.

Scientists reveal 93% of Australia's Indigenous population was lost in just 73 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
23:34:00 UTC
08:34:00 KST

Scientists reveal 93% of Australia's Indigenous population was lost in just 73 years
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- Flinders University
- Summary:
- A groundbreaking study suggests that 2.22 million Indigenous Australians lived on the continent before European colonization, far more than previously believed. Researchers estimate that 93% of this population was lost within 73 years, revealing a demographic catastrophe on a scale that dramatically changes our understanding of Australian history.
- Share:
New research suggests that Australia's Indigenous population before European colonization was far larger than historical estimates have indicated. Scientists now estimate that approximately 2.22 million Indigenous people lived across the continent before the arrival of the First Fleet in 1788, potentially up to seven times the number suggested by some earlier calculations.
The findings also reveal the devastating scale of the population decline that followed colonization. According to the researchers, an estimated 93% of Australia's Indigenous population was lost within less than 80 years of European arrival, a much greater decline than previously recognized.
Professor Corey Bradshaw, a Global Ecology Professor at Flinders University and Chief Investigator at the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for Indigenous and Environmental Histories and Futures (CIEHF), contributed to the national research effort. Working alongside Indigenous partners, the team is investigating how Indigenous population numbers have changed throughout Australia's history.
By combining advanced computer models with several sources of historical and scientific evidence, the researchers developed new estimates that substantially challenge previous assumptions.
"Understanding the size of Indigenous populations in Australia before European invasion in 1788 is essential to truth-telling and reconciliation," says Professor Bradshaw.
New Evidence Reveals Millions of Indigenous Australians Before Colonization
To reconstruct Australia's Indigenous population before European settlement, the researchers brought together ethnographic observations, archaeological findings, genetic reconstructions, and computer models. They also examined how many people different environments across the continent could have supported.
Earlier population estimates often relied heavily on calculations made during the 1930s by anthropologist Alfred Radcliffe-Brown. His influential assessment placed Australia's Indigenous population before colonization at approximately 250,000 people.
However, Radcliffe-Brown recognized that his estimate did not fully account for the devastating effects of deadly diseases, violence along colonial frontiers, and broader structural violence. Subsequent research has shown that these forces had a much greater impact than was historically acknowledged, suggesting that many early population figures were already substantial underestimates.
Using modeled and genetics-based estimates (supported by, but not relying on, historical or ethnographic accounts), the team calculated a median Indigenous population of 2.22 million before colonization. This corresponds to approximately 0.29 people per square kilometer across Australia.
The figure is substantially higher than earlier historical estimates, which generally ranged from 250,000 to 1 million people.
Researchers believe those lower estimates were influenced by the widespread population losses caused by disease, frontier violence, and systemic oppression before the earliest Australian censuses were conducted.
A Devastating 93% Population Collapse After 1788
The revised population estimate also allowed scientists to calculate the scale of the demographic catastrophe that followed European colonization.
Using their model alongside early census records, the researchers estimated that approximately 2.06 million excess deaths occurred between 1788 and 1861. That represents an average of roughly 28,200 excess deaths annually over the 73-year period.
By 1861, the Indigenous population had declined to an estimated 7% of its size before colonization, representing a staggering 93% reduction.
"These devastating findings highlight the major impacts of invasion experienced by Indigenous Australians, and demonstrate their remarkable survival, resilience and recovery over the past century," says lead author Associate Professor Alan Williams, a Partner Investigator in CIEHF representing EMM Consulting and who is also an Adjunct Research Fellow at James Cook University.
Although Australia's Indigenous population has increased since the 1950s, it has not yet returned to its estimated size before European arrival.
According to the 2021 Australian census, the Indigenous population was approximately 37% of the study's estimated median population in 1788.
If population growth continues along current trends, the researchers project that Indigenous population numbers may not return to their estimated pre-colonial level until around 2047.
What the Findings Mean for Australia's History
Beyond revising historical population figures, the study highlights the long-lasting consequences of colonization for Indigenous Australians.
The researchers say the scale of the demographic collapse has important implications for understanding intergenerational trauma, persistent disadvantage, and the development of policies that better support Indigenous communities.
"The findings highlight the scale of demographic catastrophe experienced by Indigenous Australians due to colonization, with the implications being a heightened understanding of intergenerational trauma and to inform future policy that assists Indigenous people. In addition to recognizing this intergenerational trauma and disadvantage, it is also time to recognize intergenerational privilege," says co-author Distinguished Professor Lynette Russell of the Monash University Indigenous Studies Centre and CIEHF.
The findings also demonstrate why scientists must draw on several independent methods when reconstructing population histories, particularly when written records are incomplete, unreliable, or shaped by historical biases.
By combining genetic research, archaeological evidence, environmental modeling, and historical information, the team was able to develop a more comprehensive picture of Australia's Indigenous population before and after European colonization.
Distinguished Professor Larissa Behrendt AO, Chair of the CIEHF Centre Advisory Committee, says the findings demand a fundamental reassessment of the country's history while also recognizing the extraordinary endurance of Indigenous Australians.
"These research findings challenge us to rethink the scale of what happened after 1788. We are not talking about a marginal consequence of colonization but a demographic catastrophe at the heart of the Australian story. But the research also tells us something extraordinary. Our survival is one of Australian history's most remarkable stories," said Distinguished Professor Larissa Behrendt AO Chair, CIEHF Centre Advisory Committee.
The study, "Large size of the Australian Indigenous population prior to its massive decline following colonial invasion," was published in Nature Human Behaviour. Its authors are Alan Williams, Raymond Tobler, Billy Griffiths, Sean Ulm, Matthew Nitschke, Michael Bird, Shane Ingrey, Frédérik Saltré, Kirsty Beller, Ian McNiven, Nicholas Pitt, Lynette Russell, Alistair Paterson, Christopher Wilson, and Corey Bradshaw.
The research received joint funding from the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for Indigenous and Environmental Histories and Futures (CE230100009) and the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for Australian Biodiversity and Heritage (CE17010001).
Story Source:
Materials provided by Flinders University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Alan N. Williams, Raymond Tobler, Billy Griffiths, Sean Ulm, Matthew C. Nitschke, Michael I. Bird, Shane Ingrey, Frédérik Saltré, Kirsty Beller, Ian J. McNiven, Nicholas Pitt, Lynette Russell, Alistair Paterson, Christopher Wilson, Corey J. A. Bradshaw. Large estimated size of the Australian Indigenous population before its extensive decline following colonial invasion. Nature Human Behaviour, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41562-026-02571-9

Hosted by Azerbaijan as the current CICA chair, the summit convenes representatives from member states, observer nations, and international organisations to bolster regional connectivity, digitalisation, and sustainable development.
The gathering is expected to adopt the Baku Declaration alongside a formal framework on occupational safety and health, whilst announcing Laos' accession as a new member.
Addressing the forum on Thursday, Fidan will stress the need for collective solutions based on consultation, consensus, mutual trust, and regional ownership to tackle global crises and geopolitical challenges, while calling for the preservation of UN-centred multilateral diplomacy.
Fidan is also scheduled to raise Israel's continuing genocide in Gaza, condemning illegal settlement expansions and severe restrictions on humanitarian aid to Palestinians.
Institutional transition
Fidan will also champion deeper economic integration across Asia, highlighting Türkiye-backed infrastructure initiatives such as the Middle Corridor and the Development Road.
He will advocate aligning the Middle Corridor with China’s Belt and Road Initiative to consolidate transcontinental trade routes.
On emerging technologies, Fidan will urge a human-centred approach to artificial intelligence that safeguards digital sovereignty, whilst reaffirming Ankara's climate commitments as future host and president of COP31.
Established as a dialogue platform, CICA brings together 28 member states encompassing roughly 90 percent of Asia's landmass and more than half the global population.
Under its 2024–2026 chairmanship, Azerbaijan is spearheading efforts to accelerate CICA's transformation into a fully fledged international organisation.
Türkiye, a founding member that chaired CICA from 2010 to 2014, coordinates key institutional portfolios spanning military-political cooperation, counterterrorism, and trade.

Roundup: Houthis, Saudi-led coalition trade fresh strikes as Houthis vow further attacks on airports, oil facilities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15

A civil defense worker inspects damaged facilities inside a house damaged by missile debris in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, Oct. 14, 2026. (The Saudi Civil Defense/Handout via Xinhua)
RIYADH/SANAA, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Fighting between the Saudi-led coalition and Yemen's Houthi group continued on Wednesday, with both sides carrying out fresh attacks and the Houthis vowing to continue targeting airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia in the coming days.
In a statement posted on social media platform X, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said the group's forces targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile, claiming it was a "precise and direct" hit.
The announcement came hours after the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis toward Riyadh. Loud explosions were heard in the Saudi capital earlier in the day, while residents received aerial-threat alerts on mobile apps.
The Saudi Civil Defense said later in the day that one Arab resident was injured and a residential building and a vehicle sustained minor damage after debris from an intercepted ballistic missile launched by the Houthis fell in Riyadh.
Earlier in the day, Sarea claimed a large-scale missile and drone attack targeting Saudi energy giant Aramco in Dhahran in the Eastern Province, as well as King Khalid International Airport and an Aramco refinery in Riyadh. He said the operation was carried out in retaliation for Saudi strikes.
Sarea vowed that the group's attacks "deep inside Saudi Arabia" would continue in the coming days, targeting airports and oil facilities. He also renewed a warning to international airlines, civilians and employees to stay away from airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia that the group had designated as targets.
Houthi-run al-Masirah TV reported Wednesday that an unnamed Houthi military source advised Aramco shareholders to "dispose of their shares" to avoid potential losses in the coming days, without providing further details on the basis for the warning or whether it was linked to possible further Houthi attacks on Aramco.
Meanwhile, fighting and airstrikes continued across Yemen. Sarea said Wednesday evening on X that Saudi-led coalition forces had carried out 42 strikes using warplanes and missiles on what he described as civilian facilities in the capital Sanaa and the provinces of Taiz, Lahj, Marib and Amran, as well as Mayyun Island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Majid Al-Nuzaili, spokesperson for Yemen's government forces, said in a statement that the forces had carried out 2,309 "precise and direct" attacks against Houthi positions using warplanes, drones, field artillery, rocket launchers and sniper units.
The spokesperson claimed the operations had neutralized about 1,250 Houthi fighters and destroyed or damaged more than 460 military vehicles and other equipment.
The Houthis, meanwhile, said they had fired three ballistic missiles at gatherings of government forces backed by the Saudi-led coalition in the Ras al-Arah and Al-Mudarabah areas of southern Lahj province, causing a large number of casualties and damage to several military vehicles.
The continued fighting drew fresh regional reactions. During a meeting with Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud in Riyadh on Wednesday, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi condemned the attack targeting King Khalid International Airport and attacks on civilian and vital facilities in Saudi Arabia, describing them as a threat to regional security and stability.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Wednesday reaffirmed Pakistan's commitment to protecting Saudi Arabia's sovereignty, security and territorial integrity as well as its support for the kingdom's legitimate right to self-defense.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. ■

China calls for end to political deadlock in Libya

08:28:24 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese envoy to the UN on Wednesday called for efforts to break the political deadlock in Libya as soon as possible.
The agreement reached through the UN-facilitated "4+4" smaller convening marked important progress in implementing the political roadmap in Libya. China hopes that the agreement will help unify Libya's state institutions and lay the foundation for national elections and the completion of the political transition, said Sun Lei, China's deputy permanent representative to the United Nations.
At the same time, he said, whether the agreement can be truly implemented depends on whether it can gain broad support from all Libyan parties. In supporting Libya's political process, the international community must uphold the Libyan-led and Libyan-owned principle and avoid imposing external solutions.
The political deadlock must be broken as soon as possible, he told the Security Council.
"Libya's security situation is closely linked to its political process. Any new armed conflict could undermine hard-won mutual trust and render political efforts futile," he said.
Recently, attacks on energy facilities have continued in western Libya, and the resulting tensions are a cause for concern. The parties concerned should stop the attacks and refrain from taking any action that could lead to a deterioration of the situation, Sun said.
The unification of military and security institutions is crucial to maintaining a lasting ceasefire and is also an important condition for ensuring the smooth conduct of elections and the transfer of power. China supports the eastern and western sides in strengthening dialogue, building mutual trust, and accelerating the process, he said.
The international community, on the basis of respecting Libya's sovereignty and ownership, should provide greater support to the country in strengthening border management, combating transnational criminal networks, and curbing the illicit flow of weapons, he added.
Sun also called for efforts to improve economic governance and people's livelihoods in Libya.
The international community should call on all Libyan parties to fully implement the unified budget framework, strengthen fiscal transparency and independent oversight, and make greater efforts to support Libya in combating oil smuggling, to ensure that its oil revenues are used for national development and the well-being of its people. International partners should support Libyan authorities in improving public services and advancing development and reconstruction, to strengthen public confidence in national unity, stability and development, he said.
As a good friend of Libya, China stands ready to continue working with all parties and make greater efforts to help Libya achieve lasting peace and stability and enable its people to live and work in peace and contentment at an early date, Sun said. ■

NEW YORK, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- U.S. stocks closed lower on Wednesday after a hotter-than-expected September inflation reading revived bets on further Federal Reserve rate hikes.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 48.62 points, or 0.09 percent, to 51,621.48. The S&P 500 fell 86.51 points, or 1.11 percent, to 7,718.94, its first decline of at least 1 percent in more than 50 trading days. The Nasdaq Composite decreased 511.51 points, or 1.88 percent, to 26,692.87.
Three of the 11 primary S&P 500 sectors finished higher as investors rotated into defensive names. Health Care rose 2.44 percent and Consumer Staples added 2.38 percent, while Energy edged up 0.8 percent. Technology led declines with a 2.62 percent drop, followed by Communication Services down 1.73 percent.
The U.S. consumer price index (CPI) grew 0.6 percent month on month and 3.7 percent year on year in September, up from 0.4 percent and 3.4 percent in August, respectively, according to data released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics on Wednesday.
"Inflation remains public enemy number one for the market and for the Fed," said Adam Sarhan, CEO of 50 Park Investments.
U.S. Treasury yields were whipsawed by the inflation data. The benchmark 10-year yield spiked above 5.32 percent after the CPI report but later eased to 5.186 percent, ending lower on the day as investors fled to safer assets.
Oil prices gained ground amid Middle East supply concerns. West Texas Intermediate settled at 95 U.S. dollars a barrel, up 1.01 percent, while Brent crude settled at 106.06 dollars, up 0.35 percent.
On the corporate front, Bank of America tumbled 4.76 percent after its profit disappointed, even excluding a 1.2-billion-dollar regulatory fine. Morgan Stanley also declined despite beating estimates, while BlackRock gained after reporting record assets.
AI-linked names were hit hard as fears of higher rates mounted, with Oracle, CoreWeave, Nebius, Marvell and Advanced Micro Devices all tumbling. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 4.3 percent for a sixth straight session.
According to CME FedWatch, traders are pricing in a 37 percent chance of a Fed hike at the Oct. 28 meeting, up from 22 percent on Tuesday, with about a 91 percent chance of at least one hike by December. ■

The sanctions regime itself cannot automatically improve the security situation in Haiti and UN member states must take concrete actions to ensure that the sanctions measures are effectively implemented, he said.

SC: Tough PMLA bail conditions can't override accused's right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
23:27:22 UTC
08:27:22 KST

NEW DELHI: SC has said that stringent bail conditions set under special laws such as PMLA cannot override rights granted by the Constitution, holding prolonged incarceration of an undertrial violates the fundamental right to speedy trial.A bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi said an accused could not be kept in custody till completion of trial and held that the accused was entitled to bail in case of delay in trial despite the stringent bail conditions under the anti-money laundering law.Section 45 of PMLA prescribes twin conditions for grant of bail.PMLA accused can't be in jail till trial ends, says SCThe PMLA section says no accused shall be released on bail unless the public prosecutor has been given an opportunity to oppose the application for such release, and the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that he is not guilty of such offence and that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail. The second condition puts the onus on an accused to convince the court that he is not guilty.The bench, however, said, "The twin conditions under Section 45 of PMLA cannot override the constitutional safeguards under Article 21 of the Constitution, as has been held in the case of Manish Sisodia vs Directorate of Enforcement. Prolonged incarceration, if allowed to continue, will set at naught the constitutional safeguards extended to accused persons."
The court granted bail to an accused who was allegedly involved in money laundering of over Rs 6,210 crore. ED said the accused had created 62 shell companies, 34 people were made dummy directors and 20 companies were manned by his relatives who contributed to the offence. He was arrested in Dec 2024.Granting him relief, the bench said, "We are of the opinion that the culmination of the trial is a time-consuming process, since the trial court will have to go through documents running into thousands of pages and examine around 98 witnesses. The appellant must not be subjected to the rigours of custody as long as the trial is pending. Hence, the appellant must be released on bail, subject to furnishing of bail bonds to the satisfaction of the trial court and subject to such other terms and conditions as may be imposed by it."The bench admitted that economic offences were very serious as they impacted the financial fabric of the country but said the rights of accused too have to be protected."In a bail matter, especially in serious offences, the job of a court is to balance the rights of the state with those of the arrestee. In special laws such as PMLA, the conditions for granting bail are stringent, and the circumstances in which bail can be granted are rare, for the simple reason that economic offences of a large magnitude punch a hole through the financial fabric of the country, causing a top-down ripple effect into the entire ecosystem, resulting in large consequences for most of the population.
That is the justification for making the provisions of PMLA stringent. In the same breath, sight must not be lost of the fact that the institutions have a duty to expeditiously investigate the cases. Process must not be turned into a punishment unto itself," the court said.The bench referred to its earlier verdict in the Manish Sisodia case in which it was held that prolonged incarceration before being pronounced guilty of an offence should not be permitted to become punishment without trial, and keeping the appellant behind bars for an unlimited period of time in the hope of speedy completion of trial would deprive him of his fundamental right to liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution.

37 venomous snakes and 55 lizards packed into a suitcase: German airport customs left stunned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
23:09:02 UTC
08:09:02 KST

German customs officers were stunned to discover 92 reptiles, including 37 venomous snakes and 55 lizards, crammed into a passenger's suitcase at Cologne Bonn Airport, authorities announced Thursday. The animals had been concealed inside shampoo bottles, cream containers and socks, and about 30 died during or after the journey from Mexico.
The unusual discovery occurred approximately three weeks ago, when a 45-year-old Mexican man, whose identity has not been released, arrived at the airport on a connecting flight from Istanbul. The passenger, a firefighter by profession, had originally departed from Mexico City and attempted to pass through the green customs channel, reserved for travelers with nothing to declare.
According to customs officials, the man attracted suspicion because of his nervous behavior. Officers initially suspected he might be carrying drugs and subjected him to a drug test, which returned a positive result for cocaine.
But when customs officers searched his suitcase, they found no narcotics. Instead, they uncovered dozens of snakes and lizards packed into plastic containers, shampoo and cream bottles, and rolled-up socks.
"My colleagues at the airport are used to all sorts of travel souvenirs in suitcases, but we've never had 37 venomous snakes and 55 lizards from Mexico before," said Jens Ahland, a spokesperson for the Cologne customs office.
The reptiles included vipers, rattlesnakes and several species of lizards, including iguanas. Authorities said the animals had been transported in conditions that violated animal welfare regulations, with no access to food or water during the long journey.
About 30 of the reptiles died during or after the trip, according to customs officials. The surviving animals were given veterinary care in Cologne before being transferred to a specialized reptile facility near Braunschweig in central Germany.
The passenger told authorities he had traveled to Germany on vacation and was bringing the reptiles as a favor for a Brazilian acquaintance.
German authorities classified him as a public safety risk and denied him entry to the country. He was sent back to Istanbul, the city through which he had transited on his way from Mexico.
Ahland condemned the treatment of the animals, describing the ordeal as a disturbing example of the cruelty associated with wildlife trafficking.
"It's distressing to see what some people do to animals out of sheer greed for profit," he said.
